texts.cleaned_text: Official Aruba tourism board page marketing the island as an established LGBT destination: positions feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering, and quotes a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. Self-description by the destination's own marketer, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

Aruba's own news site (Sep 9, 2016): parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5 on Sep 8, 2016, making Aruba the first island in the Caribbean; the campaign ran 2.5 years, with openly-gay MP Desiree de Sousa-Croes as sponsor and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

GlobalGayz cultural report (edited Jan 2017): Aruba described as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curacao; notes the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands, and that same-sex adoption is legal; Catholic influence noted as the main brake.

Associated Press (Sep 9, 2016): parliament voted 11-5 with four abstentions to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights; marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognized kingdom-wide, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route; religious and cultural opposition was strong, and neither Sint Maarten nor Curacao allowed unions at the time.

texts.cleaned_text:
Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Aruba for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. The Aruba Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including 'heterosexual or homosexual orientation'. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed. On 12 July 2024 the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba.

Aruba is frequently called one of the Caribbean's most LGBT-friendly islands. Several specific gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. The last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.' Openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes publicly introduced the registered partnership bill in August 2016.

Harassment has nonetheless occurred. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004–2007), which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognize same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Aruba with an equal age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. Same-sex marriage has been legal since the 12 July 2024 ruling of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognize same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. On 8 September 2016 the Aruban Parliament voted 11-5 to legalize registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024. The Aruba Criminal Code enacted in 2012 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including "heterosexual or homosexual orientation" as defined in Article 1:221. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year imprisonment, and the article states these protections in terms of sexual orientation with no transgender-specific or gender-identity provision cited.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten, and Aruba's representation acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth in Aruba who were stigmatized as disordered.

The destination's official tourism page markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years; self-description by the destination's marketer, not independent evidence.

A local news site (September 2016): parliament passed the civil-law amendment granting civil partnerships to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5 on 8 September 2016; the campaign ran two and a half years, with an openly-gay legislator as sponsor and a local equality organisation's petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

A travel-culture report (edited January 2017): the island described as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than a neighbouring island; the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the governing state; same-sex adoption is legal; the dominant religious influence noted as the main brake.

A wire report (September 2016): parliament voted 11-5 with four abstentions to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered same-sex unions, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights; religious and cultural opposition was strong.

A legal compilation: same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms with an equal age of consent of 16; the criminal code enacted in 2012 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, with penalties from fines to one year of imprisonment.

An encyclopedic account: same-sex marriage has been legal since the governing state's supreme court ruling of 12 July 2024, and marriages registered in the governing state and on neighbouring islands have had to be recognised since a 2007 ruling of that court; parliament voted on 8 September 2016 to open registered partnerships.

A dated record of an April 2015 intergovernmental meeting: representatives of all governments in the wider kingdom endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on the region's island territories in the framework, and the territory's representation acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth, who were stigmatised as disordered.

EUAA Country Guidance: Afghanistan, section 3.17 'LGBTIQ persons' (profile last updated Jan 2023, in guidance May 2024): treats LGBTIQ Afghans as persons perceived to transgress religious/social norms, alongside minors without support networks and persons facing the death penalty — the asylum-framework basis for assessing Afghan LGBTIQ protection claims in the EU.

EUAA COI Report — Afghanistan Country Focus, section 4.5 (Feb 2026): no legal protections for sexual orientation or gender identity before or after the 2021 takeover; the 'Morality Law' of 31 Jul 2024 specifically prohibits lesbianism, anal intercourse and enabling same-sex relationships; per Amnesty International, same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Human Rights Watch / OutRight report (Jan 26, 2022), 43 pages based on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans: Taliban members and their supporters attack, threaten and expel LGBT people from their homes; family, neighbour and partner abuse surged after the takeover; many went into hiding or fled.

OutRight International report (Feb 14, 2023), 22 interviews Sep-Oct 2022 with LGBTIQ Afghans still in-country: Taliban security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in early rule, with physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations — punishments the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed on social media.

DW feature (Oct 2, 2021): profiles a trans man and a gay friend in their mid-20s hiding in Kabul after the Taliban takeover, stating that under Taliban rule LGBTQ people face the death penalty and their only option is to leave; documents street attacks on men coded as gay (clothing changed, confinement indoors).

JURIST feature (Nov 8, 2024) summarising the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan (formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees in Bremen): reports systematic persecution after Aug 2021, noting that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework and that visibly transgender individuals face the gravest risks including exploitation and violence.

Translation of Article 22 of the Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice (PVPV) Law, dated 31 Jul 2024: the overseer must prevent listed 'evils' including lesbianism and homosexuality 'even if with one's own spouse', codifying moral surveillance over same-sex conduct alongside adultery, gambling and other offences.

OHCHR press release (Mar 2026): UN human-rights experts condemn the Taliban's surging use of public corporal punishment — at least 1,110 people flogged in 2025 alone, nearly double 2024 — warning women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for 'moral crimes' such as adultery, 'illicit relationships' and 'sodomy'.

Human Dignity Trust country profile (updated Jan 19, 2026): Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; Penal Code 2017 provisions on 'sodomy' and 'inciting sodomy' carry up to two years, while the Penal Code's Sharia-reference clause allows the death penalty for same-sex activity.
CNN (Nov 2024): 'LGBTQ Afghans say they face abuse in detention as Taliban crackdown intensifies' — first-person accounts of arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody.

Under the Islamic Republic, the 1971 Law of Marriages required a legal marriage to be between two Muslim adults of the opposite sex, with Article 41 directing that gaps in the law be resolved by Islamic law principles, so no same-sex marriage, civil union or domestic partnership was recognized; the 1949 Law on Marriages, Weddings and Circumcision likewise framed marriage as between a Muslim man and woman. Under Taliban rule post-2021, same-sex relationships and marriages are not recognized at all. Article 430 of the criminal code made it an 'Instigation of Delinquency' for an adult to promote or assist a minor in adultery, homosexuality or prostitution, a provision that can criminalize any adult including a caregiver or partner involved with a same-sex partner or family, and Article 427 increased punishment where the victim was under 18. Article 398 offered lesser punishment for vigilante honor killings that can target minors found engaging in homosexuality, and Article 373 imposes fines or murder-equivalent penalties for spreading a 'dangerous disease'. Persons convicted of homosexuality were generally sentenced to prison in the cities under the Islamic Republic.

No law addressed discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and political parties were prohibited from advocating anything opposing Islamic morality. The 2017 U.S. State Department report found that LGBTI community members 'did not have access to certain health services' and could be fired from jobs because of sexual orientation, and that organizations protecting LGBTI freedom 'remained underground because they could not legally register with the government', a status the 2020 report confirmed.

Care access is constrained by law, stigma and limited infrastructure. Before 2003 little or no HIV-AIDS education or treatment existed; the 2008 official count was 504 people living with HIV-AIDS, though the true figure was suspected to be in the thousands. The first HIV-AIDS treatment center opened in Kabul in 2009 with more clinics promised, access to anti-retroviral drugs is 'at best limited', and the 2020 report states that the government only permits condom distribution to married couples, excluding same-sex couples, while noting stigma against people living with HIV. Low literacy, weak infrastructure and social taboos impede comprehensive public health education.

Youth are a documented target. Bacha bazi involves teenage boys kidnapped, dressed in women's clothing, made to dance in competitions and forced into sexual acts; militia members without access to women kidnap boys to be humiliated and raped, other boys become prostitutes regardless of sexual orientation, and the practice was prevalent in big cities and reported in 2007 as still common in northern Afghanistan. US-backed Northern Alliance warlords kidnapped, trafficked and raped young boys after 2001, yet neither the U.S. Department of Defense nor the Afghan government acted despite awareness. President Hamid Karzai signed an agreement to ban the practice and a law prohibited Afghan soldiers from having their 'ashna' ('friend') live with them, but it was rarely enforced and police were reportedly complicit. When the Taliban came to power in 1996 they banned bacha bazi alongside homosexuality, both carrying the death penalty, and under the Islamic Republic young victims were often charged rather than the adult perpetrators. Article 430 can deter adults from seeking care for minors by treating any adult who promotes or assists minors in adultery, homosexuality or prostitution as committing 'Instigation of Delinquency'.

Education access is hampered by low literacy, weak infrastructure, taboos, abstinence-only sex education programs, censorship provisions including Article 32 of the 2002 Press Law prohibiting 'incitement to depravity' and Article 27(D) of the 1973 Postal Law barring material 'repugnant to public decency', and a 2009 memoir about growing up gay in Afghanistan, Hamid Zaher's It Is Your Enemy Who Is Dock-Tailed, which cannot be distributed within the country. A 2011 survey found young men displaying rainbow symbols unaware of their meaning and quickly removing them, and the 2017 and 2020 State Department reports noted that awareness of sexual orientation or gender identity remained limited and homosexuality was widely seen as taboo.

On 23 January 2025, ICC Prosecutor Karim Ahmad Khan requested arrest warrants against Taliban leaders Hibatullah Akhundzada and Abdul Hakim Haqqani for persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ community, the first time the court has recognized crimes against the LGBTQ community.

The 2024 morality law obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism", including "even if with one's own spouse"; penal-code 'sodomy' provisions carry up to two years, while a religious-law reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity.
International experts: flogging documented in the country nearly doubled in 2025 to at least 1,110 people, and corporal punishment is escalating into 2026.

A human-rights organisation's report (26 January 2022, 43 pages, 60 interviews with residents in-country and abroad) documents wrongful-detention risk, threats, assault and blackmail of LGBTI people since the 15 August 2021 takeover, and records the ruling movement's members using leaked personal data to pursue individuals considered gay or gender-nonconforming; it describes no trans-prisoner placement practice.

Interview-based reports from residents in-country and abroad (2022-23) record physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations; family, neighbour and partner abuse surged after the 2021 takeover; security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in earlier rule.
International guidance treats LGBTIQ people in the country as those perceived to transgress religious and social norms, and refugee-led organisations abroad document systematic persecution.

Southern Africa Litigation Centre chapter 'Transgender Rights in Angola': maps constitutional protection gaps — Article 23 does not list gender or sexual orientation as prohibited discrimination grounds — and locates identity, privacy, liberty, torture-protection and expression rights across Title II articles of the Angolan Constitution.

VICE continental overview (Oct 28, 2019): rates Angola as having gone furthest among African reforms, both removing the colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision and criminalising discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment and services; compares legislative drafting strategies across the continent.

BBC profile (Apr 12, 2012): kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, becomes a mainstream star at 25 in what the article describes as a Catholic country where homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour — evidence of visible trans presence alongside formal criminalisation at that time.

texts.cleaned_text:
Two LGBT groups operate in Angola, and only one, Iris Angola Association, has received official and legal recognition, granted by the Angolan Justice Ministry in June 2018. At that time it had about 200 members, based in Luanda with offices in Benguela and Lubango. The three major political parties have not formally addressed LGBT issues in their platforms. The government does allow non-governmental organisations to exist, and some charities have begun working with LGBT community members on HIV/AIDS education. In 2010 the Angolan Government refused to receive openly gay Isi Yanouka as the new Israeli ambassador, allegedly due to his sexual orientation, a diplomatic reception decision rather than a visa rule.

No specific law allows transgender people in Angola to change their gender marker on official documents and passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 states that, in general, there should be no alteration of details entered into registration records, but section 87 gives the Civil Registrar general authority to make changes, including changes of name and where a change of facts alters a person's legal identity and status, meaning transgender people could possibly use this section to change their legal gender. A 2017 ILGA poll found 49% of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

Legally, people living with HIV/AIDS in Angola are entitled to health care services and protection from employment discrimination. On relationship recognition, there is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Angola, and social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant; in 2005 an unofficial same-sex commitment ceremony was reported as 'shameless' and 'abominable' in national news magazines.

Education-focused work for LGBTQ Angolans is nascent and underfunded: the first association, Acção Humana (Human Action), launched in 2006 but has been unable to receive funding, and efforts to develop educational programs specifically for LGBT people have struggled to get NGO funding. An HIV/AIDS educational program for LGBT people is only just beginning to develop through NGOs such as Population Services International, and a 2007 study estimated roughly five percent of HIV infections were among men who have sex with men.

The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct and prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of the region's stronger statutory packages on paper; the same code criminalises discrimination based on sexual orientation with up to two years' imprisonment.

A 2024 shadow report by local LGBT organisations documents the gap between the statutory protections and implementation: persistent discrimination across health, education and employment, no legal gender recognition, and under-investigated violence; it contains no data on where trans prisoners are housed — nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice.

The same report's closest custody finding is the June 2024 case of a transgender woman attacked by police because of her gender identity, physically injured, arbitrarily detained and subjected to degrading treatment, under investigation by the judicial military police — police custody with no prison-placement information produced.

texts.cleaned_text: GlobalGayz country report on Anguilla (2012): profile of a 35-square-mile island about 100 miles east of the British Virgin Islands, framing gay life against dependent-territory law — Britain holds ultimate legal authority and decriminalisation came by British order rather than local repeal, with local religious protest against the change; Anguilla never had the exact prohibition law itself in the same form.

texts.cleaned_text: Commercial destination-wedding page for Anguilla: states plainly that 'Same-sex marriage is not currently recognized under the law in Anguilla', while marketing the island's venues for ceremonies.

Associated Press via SodomyLaws (Jan 5, 2001): Britain's Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories — Anguilla, Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and Turks and Caicos — acting unilaterally after local legislatures refused to repeal, drawing protests from religious leaders.

AFAR first-person travel piece (Jun 2023): a queer family's visit finds gay sex legal in Anguilla through the British decriminalisation order (article says 2000) but a muted, not 'out and proud' scene rooted in that imposed colonial legacy rather than local choice; notes roughly 15,000 residents as one reason the gay scene stays small.

Wikipedia country coverage: LGBT expression in Anguilla is constrained by a 'subdued and subtle climate of homophobia' that has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia. There are no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs, which the source attributes to the island's small population, and no community infrastructure, though non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place. Anguillian law provides no legislative protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity: the Constitution outlaws discrimination only on grounds of 'race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex or place of origin'. The age of consent is higher for homosexuals (18) than for heterosexuals (16). The Marriage Act defines marriage as 'the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife'; same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla is one of the British overseas territories that has not legislated for civil partnerships. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 2001, following an order of the United Kingdom Privy Council that also affected four other UK overseas territories. Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as 'gay-friendly' and reported that 'nobody was discriminatory in any way', though the source cautions that the situation for locals may differ.

A cultural country report (2012): a small island with roughly 15,000 residents, where gay life is framed against dependent-territory law; the governing state holds ultimate legal authority and decriminalisation came by its order rather than local repeal, with local religious protest against the change.

texts.cleaned_text: The UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity visited Albania from 1 to 12 July 2024. The end-of-mission statement assesses good practices and challenges and offers recommendations to the State.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) Albania chapter: discrimination complaints filed over the film 'Strange World' screenings were mediated, with the Commissioner ruling in favour in one case; Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people; groups ran support schemes including food packages for trans sex workers and people living with HIV.

UN report A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 (17 June 2025) by Independent Expert Graeme Reid covers the Albania visit of 1-12 July 2024. It evaluates Albania's adherence to national and international human-rights standards on sexual orientation and gender identity, drawing on information gathered before, during and after the visit.

PinkNews (Feb 5, 2010): Albania passed an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation but without same-sex marriage; homosexuality had carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995; Prime Minister Sali Berisha had voiced support for gay marriage in July 2009, framing the law as EU-integration driven.

Koha Jonё (Jul 30, 2021, Albanian): Democratic Party MP Luçiano Boçi attacked LGBT campaigning in high schools as extra-curricular groups with a 'suspicious, revolting agenda' — a record of parliamentary hostility toward LGBT education work under the Berisha-led opposition.

Koha Jonё (Jul 30, 2021, Albanian): MP Nard Ndoka's Facebook post branding the government 'LGBT' and accusing it of pushing LGBT values in schools, illustrating political anti-LGBT messaging in the same week as the schools campaign row.

Balkan Insight (Oct 27, 2011): Albania's Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded ruling Democratic Party MP Tritian Shehu for telling parliament that 'homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones', warning him to avoid remarks that create an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community.

Wikipedia country coverage: On 4 May 2013 the Albanian Parliament amended the criminal code to put hate crimes against sexual orientation and gender identity on par with race, ethnicity, religion and disability offences, and simultaneously passed a law punishing dissemination of homophobic information through any means, including the internet, by a fine and up to two years imprisonment. Public expression of LGBT identity is discouraged by social attitudes: 56.1% of Albanians told Gallup's Balkan Monitor (2010) that homosexuals should not show their preferences in public, and 56.2% said they should not hold public posts such as teacher. Visibility efforts exist nonetheless, e.g. the first Miss Trans Albania pageant in Tirana in 2014 and the news portal historiaime.al launched by Pro LGBT in 2012. Wikipedia country coverage: The source confirms that same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised in Albania in any form, and that households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. In April 2018 People's Advocate Erinda Ballanca pledged to support the right to legally change one's gender, but the text does not state whether a legal gender recognition procedure exists or how documents are handled. In 2016, under pressure from faith-based leaders, members of parliament removed sexual orientation and gender identity from Article 18 of the Constitution at the last moment, contrary to promises; PINK Embassy condemned this on 20 July 2016. Wikipedia country coverage: The 2010 comprehensive anti-discrimination law (in force from 4 February 2010) applies to health care as well as employment, goods and services, education and housing, and in October 2020 it was expanded to prohibit discrimination on the grounds of sex characteristics and HIV status. In practice access is weak: in December 2010 Deputy Commissioner for Labour, Social Affairs and Health Tritan Shehu said homosexuality should be treated by medical staff as a hormonal and psychological disorder; the Commissioner for Protection from Discrimination reprimanded him only on 30 September 2011 after a lengthy delay, and LGBT groups had already lost trust in the body over slow, bureaucratically impeded investigations (only 1 of 9 LGBT-linked cases concluded by December 2012). A 2022 nationwide questionnaire found only 9.3% of Albanians would accept an LGBT person as a family doctor, and youth-specific data show 55% of Albanians aged 16–27 (2015) would not want homosexual neighbours, with a 2016 study finding homophobia among Albanian university students associated with being male, politically conservative and religious. In June 2016 the government passed a National Action Plan for LGBTI addressing bullying and discrimination in primary and secondary education, which drew strong political opposition.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), Andorra chapter: a transphobic opinion piece in El Periòdic d'Andorra (27 Sep) was removed online with a public apology after DiversAnd's request though it had already run in print; in August DiversAnd met the Ministry of Health to press for gender-affirming protocols — puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16-year-olds, in some cases 14 — following the 2022 regulatory changes.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025), Andorra chapter: Andorran police recorded an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents each month; DiversAnd flagged incidents during June Pride celebrations and called for a formal system to register and classify bias-motivated violence so it can be recognised as hate crime; the Ministry of Equality implemented equality measures during the year.

PinkNews (Sep 12, 2023): Andorra's head of government Xavier Espot Zamora, in office since 2019, came out as gay publicly saying 'I never hid it' — a societal-climate signal for a country where he remains the serving prime minister.

GayLawNet's Andorra laws page sets the age of consent at 16 under Penal Code Article 206 and indexes civil unions, discrimination, hate crimes, marriage, sodomy and trans legal status. The page carries a 'limited information' marking.

Andorra protects public LGBT expression and has a visible history: the first LGBT demonstration was held on 6 September 2002, and the first gay pride parade followed on 23 June 2003 at Plaça del Poble in Andorra la Vella, organised by the association Som Com Som. The LGBT group DiversAnd was formed in 2019, after Som Com Som ended its work in 2018, and organised a pride parade in June 2019; on 17 May 2019 the Department of Equality launched the short film "#lovingdiversity" to raise online awareness. Expression-related bias is penalised: hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation carry additional legal penalties, and Law 13/2019 of 15 February 2019 bars discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity or expression across employment, education, health care, social services, housing and public establishments. Law 14/2019 of 15 February 2019 on the rights of children and adolescents establishes that transgender children must be respected in their gender identity, and Law 13/2019 extends non-discrimination protection, including gender identity and expression, to education settings. The age of consent is 16 for both same-sex and heterosexual relationships under Penal Code Articles 162 and 163, and same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the prohibiting law was abolished in 1791. Preventing and addressing bullying and discrimination in schools is a stated focus of DiversAnd. Risks to LGBT youth are documented: in 2000 a 17-year-old gay man, Nuno Ribeiro, was murdered in the country because of his sexual orientation, prompting public outcry, and cases of parents expelling their children from home over their sexual orientation are also reported. Since the 2014 civil union law, adoption has been open to same-sex couples, and the Family Law passed 21 July 2022 lets trans people update name and gender on legal documents via a simple process without medical intervention. In September 2023 Prime Minister Xavier Espot Zamora publicly came out as homosexual.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2024 (covering 2023), chapter on this country: the 2022 personal/family-law reform entered into force in February 2023, introducing legal gender recognition. A newspaper opinion piece linking trans identities to mental illness was removed after protest, with a public apology. A local trans-rights organisation met the health ministry on gender-affirming-care protocols following the 2022 regulatory changes; microaggressions were reported but rarely to authorities, attributed to fear.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2026 (covering 2025), chapter on this country: police record an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents per month; the local trans-rights organisation calls for a formal hate-crime registration system. In October a decree on trans-specific healthcare entered into force: HRT via the social security system from age 16, surgery from 18, plus consultation coverage for under-16s. New workplace harassment protocols were criticised for not explicitly addressing gender diversity or trans-specific harassment.

Independent travel-safety index (2023): ranks 203 countries for LGBTQ+ travel safety based on laws plus international sources; also publishes a global transgender-rights index - a comparative travel-safety framework covering this country among all countries.

LGBTQ+ news outlet (Sept 2023): this country's head of government came out as gay, saying he had never hidden it & hoping it shows young people that anyone can reach the highest office; during his premiership the country legalised same-sex marriage, introduced gender identity/expression anti-discrimination laws, as well as advancing trans rights.

Legal-directory site's country laws page: age of consent 16 (under a penal-code provision); a registered-partnership law since March 2005 gave same-sex partners some marriage rights; discrimination prohibited since 2005 - dated but specific legal reference.

texts.cleaned_text: TMZ (Aug 9, 2016): trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was denied entry and detained at Dubai airport, headlined as 'Dubai won't let me in because I'm transgender'.

Wikipedia country coverage: No LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organizations operate openly anywhere in the UAE; in Dubai no formal LGBTQ organizations or nightclubs exist, and a nightclub that sponsored a special night for the LGBTQ community was shut down by the government. Social attitudes toward homosexuality and varied gender expression, together with the likelihood of state repression, prevent the establishment of such organizations or community education. Sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited, highly state-regulated circumstances, and detainees have been held in cells designated for 'effeminate' people. Involuntary medical and psychological treatments, including hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatments, have occurred in connection with suspected or established same-sex sexual conduct. Gay conversion practices are not prohibited or discouraged by any law or regulation. No protections exist under any UAE law or policy against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law (2021), carrying a minimum of six months' imprisonment with no maximum prescribed. Under Article 409(5), no action may be brought except upon a complaint by the spouse or guardian of the complainant, who may withdraw it at any time; because civil guardianship ends at age 18, no eligible complainant exists for consensual male-male conduct between adults, so federal prosecution is not possible, whereas for female-female relations an unmarried Muslim woman's father or male relative may qualify as guardian under the Islamic wali concept and a married woman's husband as spouse, so prosecution remains possible where such a complainant exists. Under Article 412(2), men who disguise themselves as women to enter a women-only space may be imprisoned for up to one year and fined up to AED 10,000, replacing a broader previous ban on clothing 'inappropriate for one's sex'. The UAE does not recognise same-sex marriage. Censorship targets youth-facing material and LGBTQ content: the country's sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word 'gay' or 'sex'; the Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 for depicting a same-sex relationship and banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a 'Protect Trans Lives' transgender flag; the Arabic children's comic Majid came under investigation in 2022, with an edition withdrawn over dialogue using the Arabic word مثلي (mithli); Amazon blocked 150 search terms including 'lgbtq', 'pride' and 'closeted gay' on its UAE site in June 2023 under threat of penalties, removing listings including Roxane Gay's Bad Feminist. Officials have publicly declared there is 'no room for homosexual and queer acts in the UAE', and the band Steps refused a Dubai show in June 2023 over a contract clause barring disclosure of their sexuality. Reports of mistreatment in detention, including beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture, have been consequences of suspected or established same-sex conduct. Police raids and arrests for same-sex conduct and cross-dressing include the 2005 Abu Dhabi desert resort raid on 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a 'gay wedding', of whom 12 were found guilty, 11 receiving five-year sentences and one receiving a year, with initial reports that some were ordered to accept hormone treatments in exchange for lighter sentences; a 2012 raid breaking up a gay party of 30 men in Dubai; and two Indian men arrested that year for consensual sex in a public toilet who received six months each plus deportation. In December 2013, two Brazilian transgender women who called police about prejudice they witnessed in a nightclub were themselves arrested for 'imitating women', held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported. Gigi Gorgeous was detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport in August 2016 because authorities did not recognise her gender as legitimate, and her passport was confiscated. In July 2007 in Dubai, a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy was kidnapped and raped, was initially treated by police as a suspect, and fear of being charged under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country, though he was later awarded AED 15 million (US$4 million) in civil compensation; a 17-year-old acquaintance was implicated in luring him, and the family accused UAE authorities of failing to notify them that one of the rapists was HIV-positive, delaying medical attention. Youth are directly criminalised and vulnerable, and the UAE ranked 85th with a score of 37 on PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index.

Sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited circumstances which are highly regulated by the state. Under Article 412(2) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law (2021), only men who disguise themselves as women to enter a women-only space may be prosecuted for cross-dressing, replacing the previous broader prohibition on wearing clothing inappropriate for one's sex in any circumstances, with a penalty of up to one year's imprisonment and a fine not exceeding AED 10,000. Documented enforcement includes the December 2013 arrest in Dubai of two Brazilian transgender women for imitating women who were held until March 2014 then fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported, the August 2016 detention for five hours at Dubai International Airport of transgender woman Gigi Gorgeous with passport confiscation after authorities did not recognize her gender as legitimate, and the 9 August 2017 conviction in Abu Dhabi of two Singaporean nationals sentenced to one year in prison for attempting to resemble women who were deported on 28 August after nearly three weeks in custody including time in a cell they said was designated for effeminate people. In 2005 Abu Dhabi Police raided a hotel gathering and arrested 26 young men alleged to have engaged in cross-dressing and preparing a gay wedding, resulting in twelve convictions with eleven five-year sentences and one one-year sentence after reported confessions to homosexual practices, with initial reports that some men were ordered to accept hormone treatments in exchange for lighter sentences. Involuntary medical and psychological treatments including administration of hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatments have occurred. In June 2023 the UAE banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse for failing censorship due to a glimpse of a transgender flag displaying the words Protect Trans Lives, and the article states there are no protections under any UAE law or policy against discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression or sex characteristics and no LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organizations operate openly in the country. Consensual same-sex sexual conduct is explicitly criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law, Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, which came into force on 2 January 2022 replacing the 1987 Federal Penal Code, with a minimum penalty of six months' imprisonment and no maximum prescribed, alongside criminalisation of extra-marital heterosexual intercourse. Under Article 409(5) no criminal action may be brought except upon a complaint by the spouse or guardian, who may withdraw the complaint at any time to terminate ongoing action or suspend imposed penalty, and the article states that since same-sex marriage is not recognised and civil guardianship ends at age 18 no eligible complainant exists for consensual male-male conduct between adults making federal prosecution not possible, while prosecution of female-female conduct remains possible where a husband as spouse or a father or male relative as guardian under the Islamic wali concept exists. The 2020 amendment removed stoning and flogging as prescribed punishments and the 2021 law does not prescribe the death penalty for consensual same-sex conduct, with the death penalty for sexual offences applying exclusively to non-consensual acts such as rape of a minor or rape resulting in death, and the article states there has never been a documented case of the death penalty applied for homosexual activity and all documented stoning sentences involved heterosexual adultery and were commuted or overturned. There have been no known arrests or prosecutions for same-sex sexual activity since at least 2015 as of 2026, consistent with United States Department of State annual human rights reports after 2015 stating no records and its 2022 report stating no known reports of arrests or prosecutions for consensual same-sex conduct. Individuals have still been prosecuted for offences related to sexual identity under public decency laws for acts such as kissing in public, with documented cases including 2012 jailing for six months plus deportation of two Indian men for consensual sex in a public bus-station toilet, three-year sentences plus deportation for a British man and another man for drunken public sex in 2012, a 21 March 2012 police raid breaking up a gay party of 30 men, and a one-year sentence plus deportation for a Belgian man in June 2012 after admitting a homosexual relationship with a Filipino. In July 2007 a sixteen-year-old French-Swiss boy kidnapped and raped by a group of men was initially treated by police as a suspect prompting fear of charge under Article 177 and departure from the country, with no formal charges brought against the teenager who testified and AED 15 million in civil compensation awarded, and in October 2017 a Scottish tourist arrested for public indecency after touching a man's hip had charges dropped following intervention of Dubai ruler Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum. Reports state mistreatment in detention such as beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture have been consequences of suspected or established same-sex conduct, gay conversion practices are not prohibited or discouraged by any law or regulation, there are no protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, and no formal LGBTQ organizations or nightclubs exist with a nightclub's special LGBTQ night shut down by the government.

UAE federal law criminalises trans gender expression under Article 412 of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law issued September 2021 and effective January 2022, punishing a man disguising as a woman to enter a women-only space with up to one year imprisonment and a fine up to 10,000 dirhams, replacing the broader 1987 Federal Penal Code Article 359 male-in-female-apparel offence; transgender and gender non-conforming people are regularly arrested on dress and behaviour grounds with airport questioning and detention of trans visitors, including detention and questioning of trans blogger Gigi Gorgeous in 2016, detention in August 2017 of two Singaporeans including a trans woman convicted and sentenced to one year for attempting to resemble women then deported 28 August 2017 after nearly three weeks in custody including in a cell for effeminate people with alleged forced anal examinations, 2020 arrests and deportations of foreign residents for clothing deemed inappropriate for one's sex, March/July/December 2012 arrests for disguising as a woman, a June 2011 Dubai police campaign targeting transsexuals and boyat, and May 2025 detention in Dubai of Armenian trans defender Lilit Martirosyan while transiting who was told she could not enter as a transgender person before being allowed to leave.

On August 8, 2017 Singaporean transgender woman Nur Qistina Fitriah Ibrahim and companion Muhammed Fadli Abdul Rahman arrived in Abu Dhabi as visitors and on August 9, 2017 were arrested in Yas Mall, a mixed-gender shopping mall, while wearing jeans, sneakers and long-sleeved shirts for 'looking feminine' / 'attempting to resemble women'; they were charged under UAE federal penal code article 359 (male disguised in female apparel entering a women-reserved place, punishable by up to one year imprisonment and 10,000 dirhams fine) and Abu Dhabi local penal code article 58 (violation of public morals, punishable by up to two years imprisonment and 15,000 dirhams fine), sentenced on August 20, 2017 to one year imprisonment without legal representation for being disguised in women's dress and violating public morals by appearing as women in public, held for nearly three weeks including in a cell designated for 'effeminate' detainees where guards shaved their heads and discarded Ibrahim's hormone pills, then on August 27, 2017 had sentences converted to deportation plus fine and were deported on August 28, 2017; other transgender women and feminine-appearing people were held in the same facility for solely 'looking feminine' in mixed-gender public places including malls while wearing men's clothing or work uniforms.

Outright International Argentina overview (updated Mar 12, 2026): Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality (2010) and passed one of the world's most progressive gender-identity laws in 2012 allowing legal gender change without medical procedures or judicial approval; anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. The overview's current assessment records negatives on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration.
Buenos Aires safety guide (updated May 28, 2026) gives a first-person account of walking Buenos Aires at every hour, offering practical safety impressions for gay visitors to the Argentine capital.

Wikipedia, Gender Identity Law (Argentina), Law 26,743: approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated 24 May 2012; lauded by the United Nations as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region; allows legal gender change without surgery or court approval.

Infobae (Apr 5, 2025): Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence for Gabriel Marino, convicted of the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that a cassation court had removed in 2020 — meaning the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is currently not applied.

The 2012 Gender Identity Law allows adults to change legal gender, image or birth name on civil registries without hormone therapy, surgery, psychiatric diagnosis labelling abnormality, or approval of a doctor or judge. The same law grants adults sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy as part of public or private health care plans, with equal healthcare access for non-binary, transgender or gender non-conforming individuals. Precedents and early applications include a 2007 Supreme Court ruling that a 17-year-old had the legal right to undergo the sex-change process and change documents, Marcela Romero winning legal identity change in 2009, and six-year-old Luana designated male at birth becoming in 2013 the first transgender child to have her new name officially changed. Mendoza Province and Santa Fe Province first allowed leaving sex entry blank, and on 20 July 2021 Decree 476/2021 mandated RENAPER to allow a third gender X on all national identity cards and passports, including for non-citizen permanent residents with Argentine identity cards. In February 2025 the government banned gender-affirming care under age 18, but in April 2025 a Federal Court ruled the ban unconstitutional, restoring access nationwide. Penal Code Article 80(4) as amended in 2012 imposes life imprisonment for killing motivated by hatred based on gender identity or expression, while as of 2019 no national law expressly dealt with discrimination or harassment on the basis of gender identity. Historical enforcement violence includes the 1978 World Cup cleansing arrests, beatings and violent suppression, the January 1982-January 1983 Comando Condor murder of 18 gay men including an FLH activist, and 2023 court testimony by trans women survivors of dictatorship blacksite imprisonment about being hunted by the state and, once imprisoned, forced to perform sexual acts in exchange for food. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1887 under Law No. 1,920, which made no reference to consensual adult acts, though provincial, municipal and local regulations targeting homosexualism persisted and LGBT people were heavily persecuted. Same-sex marriage was legalized on 15 July 2010 after positive votes in the Chamber of Deputies and Senate, making Argentina the first in Latin America, second in the Americas and tenth worldwide, with same benefits and protections as opposite-sex couples including adoption legal since July 2010. Earlier relationship recognition included civil unions in Buenos Aires city and Rio Negro Province endorsed in 2002-2003, Villa Carlos Paz in 2007 and Rio Cuarto in 2009 without adoption, followed by nationwide union convivencial effective 1 August 2015 under the Civil and Commercial Code. Parenting provisions gave lesbian couples equal IVF access under a 2013 law approved 204 to 1 with 10 abstentions and Article 562 procreative-will filiation, but in 2024 the Supreme Court rejected a gay couple surrogacy claim seeking a new birth certificate omitting the surrogate woman. Military reform passed 27 February 2009, effective six months later, allows gay, lesbian and bisexual service and bans sexual-orientation discrimination in the armed forces, the ban on gay and bisexual men donating blood was abolished in September 2015, and since 2010 no mental-health diagnosis may be made exclusively on sexual choice or identity. Discrimination against National Public Administration employees on the basis of sexual orientation has been illegal since 2006, but as of 2019 no national law expressly covered sexual-orientation discrimination or harassment, with only Buenos Aires city and Rosario providing local coverage and a Chamber-approved 2010 amendment never voted by the Senate. The Penal Code amended in 2012 provides up to life imprisonment for hate crimes based on sexual orientation under Article 80(4), the anti-discrimination agency was abolished and shut down in February 2024 to reduce public spending, and in 2005 a judge ordered Cordoba prison authorities to allow conjugal visits between gay prisoners and partners. The article provides no transgender-specific public-attitude polling, preserving the distinction that all attitudinal percentages cited concern homosexuality rather than transgender people. For homosexuality, a 2020 Pew poll found about 76% saying it should be accepted, ranking Argentina highest in South America, a 2013 poll found 74% acceptance rising to 81% among younger respondents, a 2009 survey found two-thirds favoured same-sex marriage, and an early 2007 Buenos Aires poll found 75% supported marriage. The only trans-specific societal characterization quoted is BBC Mundo's 2014 assessment that "Argentina leads the trans revolution in the world," tied to the law, alternative schools and the first transgender community centre, not to tolerance polling. The World Health Organization in 2015 cited Argentina as an exemplary country for providing transgender rights. The article describes a post-1983 shift from dictatorship-era persecution in which LGBT people were murdered, beaten, raped or disappeared as viewed as disordered, decadent and sub-human to big strides, acceptance and tolerance with increased visibility and coming out. Despite advances, reports of bullying against LGBT people especially youth remain common, sex education under the 2006 law is criticised for insufficient prevention of LGBT bullying, and a 2015 case in which a judge reduced the sentence for raping a six-year-old boy on the basis of the child's homosexual orientation was condemned as a disgrace.
In 2023 trans women survivors testified in court that during Argentina's dictatorship they were held in secret prisons where they suffered severe abuse.

Argentina enacted the Gender Identity Law in 2012 as the world's first law permitting change of name on all official documents without judicial process or psychological certification and guaranteeing free hormonal treatments and surgical interventions through public and private healthcare, and by May 2014 over half of the trans population had updated their DNI including a 6-year-old in October 2013 as the first minor recognized without judicial process, with increased access to health, education, work and civil-political rights, physical mistreatment and sexual abuse of detained trans women falling from 48.3% and 43% before the law to under 10% after, avoidance of health centers for fear of discrimination falling from nearly half to 5.3% with hospital placement by affirmed gender and name, a publicly funded Casa Trans scheduled to open in December 2014 in Caballito, Buenos Aires and the Mocha Celis school in Chacarita serving as trans educational refuge alongside a proposed tax exemption for firms hiring trans workers, while formal employment exclusion persisted with most trans women limited to sex work, 5 in 10 trans men reporting suicidal ideation and 4 in 10 reporting attempts, life expectancy at 35 years, and continued family expulsion and hostile treatment in more machista provinces.
Interviews (April 2025) with trans activists saying the president's policies have made the community more vulnerable to violence; the situation described as 'chaotic, desperate'.

A national hate-crime observatory recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025 — a record year, averaging one every 38 hours, marking an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people.

The government issued a decree modifying the gender-identity law as it pertains to minors, plus another decree on housing of transgender people in prisons; legal experts call the decree illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights.

Documents discrimination, torture and inhuman/degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion targeting LGBT people, violations of private and family life, education and work rights, and hate speech - including a chapter on pressure around a transgender individual participating in a beauty pageant.

Equaldex comparison of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia: Armenia decriminalised in 2003; legal gender change is legal but requires surgery (since 2006); gender-affirming care is restricted; no nonbinary recognition; hate-crime protections 'ambiguous' since 2022; no SOGI discrimination protections; same-sex marriage banned. ILGA-Europe/COC fact-finding report 'Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia' (Feb 2009): comprehensive mission report covering visibility, coming out, societal and institutional homophobia, media coverage, HIV/AIDS, discrimination, harassment and violence, community organising, and legislation affecting LGBT people in Armenia.

Unzipped: Gay Armenia blog (May 2012): neo-Nazi arson attack on the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan - Molotov cocktail thrown, fire set; police took 12 hours to respond; two suspects detained via CCTV - documents anti-LGBT hate violence in Armenia.

The Guardian (April 2019): Armenia's first registered trans woman, Lilit Martirosyan, received death threats (including MPs calling for her to be burned alive) after a historic speech in the national assembly on LGBTI discrimination - documents extreme political hostility toward trans people.

Armenian authorities and private actors have repeatedly restricted LGBT expression and media. In 2013, police proposed a bill criminalizing 'non-traditional sexual relationships' and LGBT 'propaganda' to youth modeled on Russian law; it failed to pass after Pink Armenia argued it was a distraction tactic. In 2017, organizers of the Yerevan International Film Festival canceled the screening of two LGBT-themed films following negative public reaction. In November 2018, a Christian LGBT group was forced to cancel planned forums and events due to 'constant threats' and 'organized intimidation' from political and religious leaders and what it described as insufficient police readiness to protect them. Public expression carries social cost: a 2012 study found 55% of Armenians would end a relationship with a friend or relative who came out, and 70% find LGBT people 'strange'; in 2014 the Iravunk newspaper published a list of dozens of Armenian LGBT Facebook accounts calling them 'zombies', and the Court of Appeals ruled the newspaper had not offended anyone, ordering plaintiffs to pay 50,000 dram (~US$120) to the newspaper. Transgender activist Lilit Martirosyan, who in April 2019 became the first transgender person to speak at Armenia's National Assembly, received numerous death threats via Facebook and email, and in February 2020 a nationalist party member attempted to 'clean up' the same lectern by burning incense over it, denouncing her speech as a desecration.

Local rights organisation’s annual report on the human-rights situation of LGBT+ people in this nation during 2024: documents discrimination, torture and inhuman/degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion targeting LGBT people, violations of private and family life, education and work rights, and hate speech — including a chapter on pressure around a trans individual participating in a beauty pageant.

Comparison service covering this nation and two neighbours: this nation decriminalised in 2003; legal gender change is legal but requires surgery (since 2006); gender-affirming care is restricted; no nonbinary recognition; hate-crime protections ‘ambiguous’ since 2022; no protection statute; same-sex marriage banned. Public-opinion acceptance scores are very low.

Regional monitors’ fact-finding mission report (Feb 2009): comprehensive mission report covering visibility, coming out, societal and institutional hostility, media coverage, discrimination, harassment and violence, community organising, and legislation affecting LGBT people in this nation.

Community blog (May 2012): arson attack on the gay-friendly community bar in the capital — Molotov cocktail thrown, fire set; police took 12 hours to respond; two suspects detained via security cameras — documents anti-LGBT hate violence in this nation.

News report (April 2019): this nation’s first registered trans woman received death threats (including legislators calling for her to be burned alive) after a historic speech in the national assembly on LGBTI discrimination — documents extreme political hostility toward trans people.

The UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities, last updated 2026-07-23, states that the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride: 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.

2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. The article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative in American Samoa, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality.

Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). As of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

USA TODAY (7 Mar 2025): Trump executive order requires all US identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; ACLU sued the State Department for seven plaintiffs; trans/nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad.

Lambda Legal's FAQ sets out passport and identity-document rules for TGNCNBI people under the current federal policy change: which documents to consider, how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the current status of document updates.

HRC (updated 2025): since Jan 2025 executive order, new/renewed US passports show sex assigned at birth regardless of gender identity or name change; the 'X' marker (available since 2022) eliminated; policy challenged in federal courts -- current passport posture for trans US travelers.

Condé Nast Traveler (Feb 2025) reports that the State Department stopped processing X-marker passports and markers not matching sex assigned at birth; existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration; new applications are processed only as M or F per supporting documents.

ILGA monitor items: (Sep 2023) the US Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee; (Jun 2023) a federal civil action cited a 'hostile work environment' in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity; (Feb 2023) a 51-year-old man charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Federal measures reaching US territories through federal agencies in 2025: EO 14168 (binary sex, documents, federal facilities, care funding), EO 14187 (care funding), EO 14201 (sports; State Dept visa ban with SWS25 marking).

The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates should only be altered to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption. The Office of Vital Statistics has interpreted this ruling to cover applications from transgender individuals. The Office will change the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order. The Office may change the gender marker on a birth certificate with medical documentation of the sex change. The first criminal law against sodomy was enacted in 1963 and made male homosexual and heterosexual sodomy illegal, but did not address lesbian sex. In 1979 the Fono revised criminal law so that consensual sodomy was no longer illegal unless it involved public acts, prostitution, minors or people unable to give consent due to mental illness, with the law taking effect in 1980. The age of consent is set at 16 years, regardless of gender and/or sexual orientation. The American Samoa Code does not specify the sex of the parties to a marriage but refers to the age of "the male" and "the female" and prescribes a form in which parties identify as "son" and as "daughter," and a 2003 bill to ban same-sex marriage was voted against by the House Judiciary Committee and then the full Senate. Same-sex marriages are currently not licensed in American Samoa, with the Attorney General in July 2015 reviewing applicability of Obergefell v. Hodges and the Governor stating the ruling does not apply due to preamble, constitution, Christian values and unorganized and unincorporated political status. Under the Respect for Marriage Act passed by the 117th United States Congress and signed by President Joe Biden in 2022, all territories including American Samoa are required to recognize, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples. The article states American Samoa remains the only part of the United States along with select Native American tribal jurisdictions to enforce a ban on same-sex couples marrying, while same-sex couples married legally in other jurisdictions are recognized and must be treated equally under US federal law since 13 December 2022. The article states "American Samoa, like the neighboring country of Samoa, tends to be tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities." It notes a long-standing tradition of raising some boys as girls to play an important domestic role in Samoan communal life, with such individuals known as the fa'afafine. It states nevertheless American Samoan society is highly religious and conservative attitudes regarding gender and sexuality tend to dominate. It states open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. The main LGBTQ organization is the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (S.O.F.I.A.S.) which annually organizes events and festivals and campaigns for the betterment of the fa'afafine community. The first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei with pageant, song, dance and poetry choral competitions, beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community are quite popular, and families generally turn up en masse to support candidates.

On 20 March 2003 the American Samoa Senate rejected Representative Sua Carl Schuster's bill to outlaw same-sex marriage after the House judiciary committee recommended it be killed, with fa'afine witness Tiffany Poutasi testifying that fa'afine are men who express femininity through dress and speech and oppose marriage with other men as against Christian upbringing.

As of July 10, 2015, American Samoa had not authorized same-sex marriage and no same-sex marriage license applications had been filed while Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale reviewed the U.S. Supreme Court marriage-equality ruling for applicability to the territory, which maintained a tradition of embracing faafafine — males raised as females taking on feminine traits — alongside dominant conservative Christian churches.

An academic research guide (updated 2026): a fa'afafine community organisation was formed in 2010 by merging two earlier community groups, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride; fa'afafine defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, integral to traditional culture.

A travel-advice column (2009): the island culture tends toward traditionalism, with reserved behaviour by people of all orientations expected, while local culture broadly accepts gender-diverse people; roughly 57,000 residents across several islands and atolls; the column is a publication's own framing.

A news report (July 2015): the territory was then unsure whether the governing state's 2015 marriage ruling applied; its chief legal officer said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while sibling territories moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

A legislative record: the upper chamber voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after a committee recommended it be killed; the bill's sponsor wanted to preempt marriage lawsuits then unfolding elsewhere; a fa'afafine witness testified against the ban on religious grounds.

A confirmation record (January 2016): the legislature unanimously confirmed a former chief legal officer as district court judge; at his hearing he said he had not read the 2015 marriage ruling, that the district court does not deal with it, and that he would not perform same-sex weddings unless local laws change.

A 2026 law-review article by two local attorneys concludes the governing state's 2015 marriage ruling does apply despite officials' statements and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; it records that no couple has applied and sets out a litigation path.

A local news report (July 2024): an on-island survey by a constitutional law professor tested whether the territory's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the governing state's constitutional equality provisions.

A rights-monitoring bulletin (2023): the governing state's federal law-enforcement department secured a settlement with the territorial government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee; a federal civil action that June cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's suit against the territorial government.
Human Rights Watch (Jul 2022): 'Antigua and Barbuda: High Court Decriminalizes Gay Sex' — the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court strikes down the 'sodomy' and 'gross indecency' provisions.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): in 2022 the High Court found Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 unconstitutional, decriminalising same-sex conduct, and interpreted 'sex' discrimination to include sexual orientation and gender identity. However, no explicit antidiscrimination protections exist, same-sex unions are not recognised, and trans people are particularly vulnerable because there is no mechanism to change legal gender markers - only name changes.

El País/AP (June 2023): profile of Orden David, the Antiguan LGBTQ activist who challenged the country's anti-sodomy law and won in 2022 - he had been bullied and physically attacked (struck in the head, knocked out in daylight); the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court ruled the law unconstitutional; six Caribbean countries still criminalise.

St Lucia Star (Dec 2019): ECADE announced court challenges to buggery and indecency laws in Barbados, St Kitts-Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and Saint Lucia, arguing the laws stigmatise and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence.

The Advocates for Human Rights (January 2025): submission to the UN Human Rights Committee for Antigua and Barbuda listing LGBTQ+ rights issues ahead of its review — documents the open SOGI-protection questions the state still faces post-2022 decriminalisation.

Wikipedia country coverage: Official positions rather than media reporting document state hostility toward LGBTQ people in Antigua and Barbuda. At the May 2016 Universal Periodic Review of the UN Human Rights Council, Argentina, Australia, France, Germany, the Netherlands and Nicaragua all urged the government to repeal its sodomy ban and guarantee full human rights to LGBTQ people. Minister of Social Transformation Samantha Marshall called the ban antiquated and said it should be repealed, while Parliamentary Secretary Maureen Payne-Hyman assured the Council that LGBTQ people are not persecuted in the country. On 24 August 2016 the government announced it had no intention of repealing the ban, while acknowledging that a lawsuit would most certainly strike it down given the identical jurisprudence in Belize. On 1 November 2019 the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality announced it would file a legal challenge by the end of 2019, which culminated in the 5 July 2022 ruling in Orden David et al v The Attorney General of Antigua and Barbuda, in which the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court declared Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 unconstitutional and void. Before that ruling the sections criminalized consensual same-sex intimacy with imprisonment of up to fifteen years for adult-on-adult buggery, five years where a minor committed the act, and life where an adult committed it on a minor; 'serious indecency' carried up to ten years where the target was a child under sixteen, and people convicted as repeat offenders of buggery were placed on the Sex Offenders Register for the remainder of their life. Antiguan law does not address discrimination or harassment on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not recognize same-sex unions in any form, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights given to opposite-sex married couples.

A July 2022 High Court ruling struck down the sodomy and gross-indecency laws, reading the constitutional bar on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity; the ruling covers Sections 12 and 15 of the 1995 sexual offences act, and same-sex unions remain unrecognised with no explicit anti-discrimination protections having followed.

An international human-rights organisation's profile (page states 'Last Update: March 12, 2026') records transgender people as particularly vulnerable because no legal gender recognition mechanism exists — only name changes are available — and it contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement: no birth-sex vs identity rule, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation practice.
