ANROWS research briefing maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia: organised exclusionary campaigns, facilities and records-access disputes, and rights-rollback pressures.

Queensland Parliamentary Library research brief (2003) 'Protecting Transgender Rights under Queensland's Discrimination Law Amendment Act 2002': introduced 'gender identity' as a protected attribute; documents trans people's difficulties with sex designations on passports, licences and birth certificates, high job-loss rates around transition, and greater exposure to assault and harassment in public places.

Organisation Intersex International Australia briefing: argues intersex is not a gender identity and warns against folding intersex into SOGI legal frameworks (recommends SOGIESC terminology) — relevant to how Australian gender-diversity protections are scoped.

Australian Lesbian & Gay Archives, 'Towards Homosexual Equality in Australian Criminal Law - A Brief History' (Carbery, 2nd ed. 2014): state-by-state history of decriminalisation, from British-inherited buggery laws (death penalty in Victoria until 1949) through reform - historical legal context for Australia's current framework.

Queensland placement policy: the 2009 Corrective Services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective (Jenny Samiec, Queensland Law Student Review 2009). Replacement oversight came via the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022 (fully in force 2023), whose August 2023 inspection standards for Queensland prisons and youth detention centres direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally to be admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender. Staff still hold discretion at admission, and only transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that process - so Queensland placement is identity-based with a discretionary admission caveat and a surgery exception.

Federal hate crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) explicitly covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status with up to 7 years' imprisonment, and Victoria's Anti-vilification Act 2025 (effective 30 June 2026) covers the same grounds. Vilification laws in NSW, ACT and VIC cover only sexual orientation, those in SA, TAS and QLD also cover gender identity, and NT and WA cover neither. Public expression is protected and visible: Sydney hosts an annual Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras and has been named one of the most gay-friendly cities in the world.

Medicare covers many major sex reassignment surgeries, but the gap between the benefit and the surgeon's fee can run to thousands of dollars, and private hospital policies or insurers typically impose a waiting period of about 12 months before claims for SRS. Since November 2017 a transgender child can access puberty blockers and hormone treatment without court approval where child, parents and doctors agree; puberty blockers are Stage 1 (from around age 10, reversible) and hormone therapy Stage 2 (usually from 16, irreversible), with sex reassignment surgery generally unavailable until 18. In January 2025 the Queensland government paused new prescriptions of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for under-18s in public health services, existing patients exempted; the Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025, and a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, with a legal challenge filed in December 2025. A NSW independent review released September 2024 found puberty blockers 'safe, effective and reversible' but called for more long-term research. From 1 August 2013 religious aged care providers receiving Commonwealth funding can no longer exclude people based on LGBTI status or same-sex relationships. From April 2025 Medicare IVF rebates were extended to single individuals and same-sex couples, not surrogacy.

Same-sex marriage was legalized on 9 December 2017 under the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017, following a 61.6% 'Yes' postal survey result, making Australia the last of the Five Eyes countries to do so; overseas same-sex marriages are automatically recognized and couples could no longer be barred from divorcing. Federal law has recognized same-sex couples as de facto relationships since 2009, through reforms amending 85 federal laws across taxation, superannuation, health, social security, aged care, child support, immigration, citizenship and veterans' affairs, with Centrelink recognizing same-sex de facto partners from 1 July 2009. States and territories have offered domestic partnership or relationship recognition from 2003 onwards: civil partnerships in the ACT and Queensland, registered partnerships in NSW, Tasmania, Victoria and South Australia, while Western Australia and the Northern Territory lack such schemes, so couples often need judicial approval to prove a de facto relationship. De facto partners face higher eligibility periods and a burden of proof that married couples do not, differing under Centrelink, migration and family law, which can impede arranging a partner's funeral and is poorly understood by some government departments.

Since 2016 every jurisdiction has an equal age of consent of 16 for all sexual acts, except Tasmania and South Australia where it is 17; Queensland was the last to equalise in 2016, dropping anal intercourse from 18 to 16. Religious educational institutions may still discriminate against LGBT students and teachers under sections 37 and 38 of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984, though discrimination against LGBT students is barred in Queensland, the Northern Territory and Tasmania, and Tasmania has the fewest exemptions overall. The Safe Schools Coalition Australia, begun in Victoria in 2010 and national from 2014, was curtailed under the Turnbull government (restricted to high schools, role plays removed, parental consent required) and lost federal funding after mid-2017, though Victoria, the ACT and South Australia fund it themselves; GaLTaS lobbied for LGBT students from 1991 to 1998. Tasmania's 2019 law lets a person change legal gender at 16 without parental permission and recognises non-binary genders. The 2021 Census counted 13,554 (17.3%) children in same-sex couple families, up from 6,915 (14.8%) in 2016.

National sex-discrimination legislation has protected gender identity since 2013; an August 2024 national court ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women, with compensation awarded — a case that arose from organised exclusionary activism.

In April 2024 one state/province strengthened discrimination and vilification protections and another state/province passed an equality legislation amendment act in 2024; national research documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people, and a court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against an activist who had targeted her.

A 2022 detention-services oversight act (fully in force 2023) with August 2023 inspection standards: transgender and intersex prisoners are generally to be admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, with staff discretion at admission and a surgery exception; the 2009 corrective-services procedure it replaced was assessed as largely ineffective in a 2009 law-student review.

A 2003 research brief documented trans people's difficulties with sex designations on identity documents, high job-loss rates around transition, and greater exposure to assault and harassment in public places.

Documents a neo-Nazi network uncovered in March that used fake dating profiles to lure gay and bisexual men to ambushes by masked assailants (attacks filmed and shared); a rejected Vienna petition for queer sauna time slots; new Ministry of Education rules restricting outside sex-education providers; and Ombud guidance for gender-inclusive forms for intersex and non-binary people.

Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report (2025), part of an EU-funded project, sets out the legal framework governing LGBTIQ people in Austrian prisons and their situation and rights in detention, including gender self-determination and anti-discrimination protection.

Austrian Justice Ministry answer to parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 (May-June 2025): official rules on housing transgender people in Austrian penal institutions — the authority to cite if a trans visitor is detained; German-language.

DW report (March 2025): Austrian police arrested 15 people (aged 14-26) over a wave of hate attacks in which at least 17 LGBTQ people were lured via fake dating-platform accounts to remote locations, ambushed by masked groups, filmed, and falsely accused of being paedophiles. Investigators believe the real victim count is much higher.

The Local Austria (July 2026): Austria recorded 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 7,327 prejudice motives in 2025, with 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence; police data broken down by who faces violent hate crime, while acknowledging under-recording.

GGG (July 2026): official Austrian hate-crime statistics for the reporting year show homophobic offences rising while transphobic incidents declined — against 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence in 2025 (The Local, same data).

PinkNews (Sept 2024): Austria's far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) won the most votes in a national election for the first time since WWII (29.2%), raising concerns about what an FPÖ-led government could mean for LGBTQ+ people.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity legal since 1971, marriage equality since 2017, full adoption rights since 2016. Legal gender recognition is possible without mandatory medical procedures, and individuals may obtain an 'X', indeterminate, or no gender marker; intersex people can choose 'diverse', 'inter', or no designation. Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation, with recent amendments broadening 'gender' to include gender identity, expression and sex characteristics.

PinkNews (May 2019): Austria recognised a third gender option in official documents - intersex activist Alex Jürgen received the country's first non-binary passport ('X' marker) and birth certificate ('divers'), following the June 2018 Constitutional Court ruling that gender identity must be accurately reflected in official documents; the Interior Ministry restricted 'divers' to people with a medical panel certificate of intersexuality.

Wikipedia country coverage: Austria permits LGBT people to serve openly in the Austrian Armed Forces, and since 2014 transgender people have been allowed to serve openly. The Equal Treatment Act has covered employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2004; gender identity and intersex status are not explicitly listed but are treated as covered under "gender." As of January 2017 every federal state had anti-discrimination laws covering sexual orientation in goods and services, Lower Austria being the last, and from 1 January 2016 hate speech based on sexual orientation is banned, with crimes committed on that ground treated as an aggravating factor. The 1993 Security Police Act obliges police to avoid actions perceived as biased on sexual orientation grounds. LGBT advocacy operates openly, including HOSI Wien (founded 1979), HOSI Salzburg, ALGF and Afro Rainbow Austria, and the National Council passed a non-binding resolution on 2 July 2019 calling for a government bill banning conversion therapy on minors, with all parties voting in favour at the final vote. Transgender people can change legal gender and name without prior sex-reassignment surgery, but the change is conditional on submitting a psychiatric opinion, and public health insurance payment for sex-change treatment is likewise bound on submission of psychiatric opinions. Puberty blockers for youth experiencing gender dysphoria have been endorsed by the Austrian Society of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (ÖGKJP) and the Austrian Society of Gynecology and Obstetrics (OEGGG). Lesbian couples can access artificial insemination and IVF treatments. Youth-specific: in 2018 the ultra-conservative association TeenSTAR was found offering minors conversion therapy classes teaching that sexual orientation was "changeable"; the Education Directorate Salzburg banned TeenSTAR workshops pending review, the association was banned in April 2019, and Parliament passed a resolution in July 2019 calling for a legal ban on conversion therapy on minors. The source notes that many LGBT minorities still think that being different is a problem, a sentiment shaped by Catholic influence. Political visibility is high: seven National Council politicians were openly gay after the 2019 election, Iris Eliisa Rauskala became the first openly LGBT government minister in June 2019, Georg Djundja became Austria's first openly gay mayor in April 2019, and President Alexander Van der Bellen took part in the 2019 EuroPride parade in Vienna. Community infrastructure exists in Vienna, Linz, Innsbruck, Salzburg and Graz, with an annual Vienna Gay Pride/Regenbogenparade; the ÖVP and FPÖ have historically opposed LGBT rights, and historical prosecutions were harsh, with lesbianism criminalised after the Anschluss and 1940 court alignment to Paragraph 175. Public opinion as of 2023 showed 65% support for same-sex marriage and 66% agreeing nothing is wrong with a same-sex relationship; as of July 2020 no expungement or compensation scheme for historical convictions had been implemented.

National report (2025) on LGBTIQ detainees in this country: covers the legal framework for LGBTIQ people in detention, gender self-determination, anti-discrimination protection, and the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in the national prisons.

National justice ministry answer to a parliamentary question (May-June 2025): official rules on housing transgender people in the national penal institutions — the authority to cite if a trans visitor is detained.

Investigators believe the real victim count is much higher.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Azerbaijan. Documents the March murder of a trans woman in Baku met with an inadequate police investigation; state-affiliated Real TV airing discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march demanding trans healthcare access; a family forcibly transporting an 18-year-old woman to Baku after she came out; and an April ECtHR ruling on the September 2017 police arrests and mistreatment of LGBTI people, which Azerbaijan acknowledged in 2019.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Azerbaijan. Documents a July police raid on a private birthday party where queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of outing; QueeRadar monitoring found 77% of 428 analysed media pieces hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people; and an activist being told to remove a rainbow flag in a Baku cafe.

OC Media feature by Ali Malikov on trans people in Azerbaijan: discrimination has direct economic impacts - trans people are rejected from jobs and housing, pushed into black-market work and precarious housing. Profiles 'Durdana', 29, arrested, denied housing and employment, and dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer shut down.

HRW (Oct 2017): Azerbaijan's anti-gay crackdown — police raids in Baku (Sept 2017) detained dozens of LGBT people on dubious charges with beatings documented; HRW called for investigation and release.

Gender & Development Social Union shadow report to CEDAW (44th session) on discrimination and violence against lesbian, bisexual and transgender people in Azerbaijan: documents state-approved ignorance, employment discrimination, militant homophobia/transphobia in official and private media, forced marriages, and the impossibility of changing identity documents for trans women; the organisation serves 200+ LBT people.

The Guardian (Sept 2017): outcry as Azerbaijan police launch crackdown on the LGBT community - at least 60 people imprisoned or fined after raids in the capital; part of a wave of arrests ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games.

Azerbaijan's constitution guarantees freedom of expression, and the Azerbaijan Press Council, founded in 2003, handles complaints under a Press Code of Conduct; it is not known whether it has assessed complaints that state-controlled media used homosexuality to discredit government critics. Media have been criticised for spreading fear and hate toward queer people through discriminatory language, with politicians and officials using it to shape public perception; Vahid Aliyev of the Minority Azerbaijan webpage criticised this unprofessionalism. The 2017 US State Department report recorded interference with expression, assembly and association through intimidation, incarceration on questionable charges and blocking of websites. LGBTQIA+ media nonetheless exists: gay.az, the first news website for LGBTQIA+ people, launched 25 May 2011 by Ruslan Balukhin, and Minority Magazine, the first LGBTQIA+ online magazine, founded by Samad Ismayilov in December 2015 and an NGO from August 2017; Ismayilov's documentary about a trans man premiered in Baku on 25 November 2017 with Dutch embassy support, drawing about 80 people. Same-sex couples are not legally recognised: marriage and civil unions are neither recognised nor performed, and same-sex couples may not adopt children. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned. ILGA-Europe has ranked Azerbaijan last, 49 of 49, in Europe every year since 2015, citing a near total absence of legal protection. The age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual sex. Transgender people cannot change their gender on official documents, though they may change their name to match their gender identity. Azerbaijan mandates conscription for able-bodied men aged 18 to 35, under which LGBTQIA+ enlistees can be declared unfit for service under Articles 18/b (personality disorders) and 17/b (reactive psychoses and neurotic disorders) of the Regulation on Military Medical Examinations, and queer conscripts often conceal their orientation to avoid dedovshchina hazing. In September 2017 at least 100 members of Baku's LGBTQIA+ community were arrested in a crackdown ostensibly on prostitution; detainees were subjected to beatings, interrogation, forced medical examinations and blackmail, and the 2017 US State Department report added that police threatened rape and used electric shocks. By law no groups are excluded from blood donation apart from people infected with HIV/AIDS, though it is unknown whether men who have sex with men are de facto permitted to donate. The Gender Resource Center (Gender Resurs Mərkəzi), established in 2020, is a queer-feminist platform created in response to the lack of safe space and resources for people of different genders and sexual orientations. Gender and Development, created in 2007, runs local projects in collaboration with the Ministry of Health. AZAD LGBT ran in-person programming in Baku, including LGBTQ movie nights attended by a local psychologist who joined post-film Q&As, and launched a website in 2015 providing free online LGBTQ education tools; Minority Magazine covers education topics. Nafas LGBTI Azerbaijan Alliance regularly holds talks with the EU Delegation to Azerbaijan and other European embassies about the difficulties LGBTQ people face. Critics have argued Azerbaijan should not be allowed to host international events because of its discrimination against LGBTQIA+ people, a controversy that flared around Eurovision 2012. In April 2019 14-year-old Elina Hajiyeva of Baku attempted suicide after homophobic bullying at her school; the principal took no action, tried to attribute the attempt to family difficulties and did not call an ambulance, and she died in hospital two days later. The school director, deputy director and psychologist were dismissed, and on 24 October 2019 the Sabail District Court of Baku sentenced the principal to 2 years and 2.5 months of restricted liberty plus 18,500 AZN ($10,882) compensation. The case sparked a nationwide social media campaign, a video by 2011 Eurovision winner Nigar Jamal to President Ilham Aliyev, and a Ministry of Education anti-bullying action plan launched 13 May 2019 with a new hotline to ensure a healthy environment in general education institutions, improve school-family relations and protect students from abuse.

Regional monitor annual review 2025 (covering 2024): documents the March murder of a trans woman in the capital met with an inadequate police investigation; government-affiliated media airing discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a march demanding trans healthcare access; a family forcibly transporting an 18-year-old woman to the capital after she came out; and an April ruling of the regional human-rights court on the September 2017 police arrests and mistreatment of LGBTI people, which this nation acknowledged in 2019.

News feature on trans people in this nation: discrimination has direct economic impacts — trans people are rejected from jobs and housing, pushed into black-market work and precarious housing. Profiles one woman arrested, denied housing and employment, and dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer shut down.

Human-rights monitor (Oct 2017): this nation’s anti-gay crackdown — police raids in the capital (Sept 2017) detained dozens of LGBT people on dubious charges with beatings documented; the monitor called for investigation and release.

News report (Sept 2017): outcry as police launch a crackdown on the LGBT community — at least 60 people imprisoned or fined after raids in the capital; part of a wave of arrests ahead of an international sporting event.

texts.cleaned_text: Erasing 76 Crimes (9 Apr 2024): the Hirondelles Club at Rehoboth Friendship Centre has housed LGBT+ youth in Benin since about 2020 — a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed; the report's framing is that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are not criminalised anywhere in Benin, but SOGIESC discrimination is not prohibited, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

US State Department 2023 Country Report (Benin): the law does not explicitly prohibit SOGIESC discrimination; LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised; the community — especially outside major urban areas — faces hostility, with LGBTQI+ persons routinely refused medical care (including hormone treatment) and social services.

Washington Blade (31 Aug 2015), commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups: LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describe discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments.

Erasing 76 Crimes (8 May 2012): interview with anthropologist Patrick Awondo (political sociology/medical anthropology, EHESS Paris) citing evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits' record of women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom (modern Benin); frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a colonial import.

There is no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. Healthcare providers regularly refuse to give treatments related to LGBTQ status such as gender-affirming hormone therapy and also regularly deny general healthcare like malaria treatment to LGBTQ people. Employers often will not hire people known to be LGBTQ, especially transgender and intersex people. Catholic churches bury LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries and priests are documented as "calling transgender people demons". Those reporting violence or discrimination to police conceal sexual orientation or gender identity out of fear of mistreatment, with lesbian, bisexual and queer women rarely reporting to police. Same-sex sexual acts between consenting adults are legal, with equal age of consent regardless of sex under Article 545 of the new Penal Code in force since 2018, which establishes greater penalties for an indecent or unnatural act with a minor of the same sex. Previously, Article 331 of the old Penal Code and a 1947 amendment punished an indecent act or act against nature with a minor of the same sex under 21 with six months to three years imprisonment and a fine of 200 to 50,000 francs. Article 88 of the 1996 draft Penal Code would have punished an indecent act or act against nature with an individual of the same sex with one to three years imprisonment and a 100,000 to 500,000 francs fine but was never voted into law, while the October 2008 draft includes no punishment for same-sex relations between consenting adults in private and has not been voted on, though the general indecency provision has been used to prosecute same-sex conduct. There is no recognition of legal rights for same-sex couples, except the government grants diplomatic visas and immunity to same-sex partners of foreign diplomats, and Article 104(d) of the Children's Code Law 2015-08 bars foreign homosexual couples from international adoption. Limited protections based on sexual orientation and sexual life exist: Article 394 of Law No. 2017-20 on the Digital Code (2017) prohibits processing personal data revealing sex life or sexual orientation, Article 6 of the 2009 Personal Data Protection Law similarly prohibits collection or processing without express consent, and Article 23 of Law No. 2011-26 (2012) requires business leaders to prevent, end and punish sexual or sexist acts or behavior based on sex or real or perceived sexuality infringing rights and dignity of women or girls. Article 552 on incitement to hatred and violence of Law No. 2017-20 (2017) punishes provoking discrimination, hatred or violence based on sexual orientation by electronic communications network or computer system with one year imprisonment and a five million CFA francs fine or one penalty only, in place since 2018. Decree No. 1999-639 imposes no specific blood-donation restrictions for LGBT people. For enforcement, Benin's representative stated for the 2008 review that no criminal ruling had ever been rendered although provided for by law because families would never allow children to be taken to court, and Benin rejected states' recommendations to improve the situation for LGBTQ persons in the 2012 review, with a 4 March 2013 meeting noting "certain things would be rectified." The LGBTQI+ community, especially outside major urban areas, faced hostility with discrimination common, alongside arbitrary detention, physical and sexual violence and degrading treatment, with violence and anti-gay lynchings common and mostly committed by civilians rather than state authorities while police rarely pursue perpetrators. Between 2020 and 2024 Hirondelles Club ran 20 shelters housing 380 LGBTQ people, and the government accepted two of fifteen 2023 Universal Periodic Review recommendations, one to investigate and prosecute violence against LGBTQ people and one to combat stigma against HIV. LGBTQ people are frequently rejected by families and have difficulty getting jobs, and while the government provides sexual and reproductive healthcare for people who experienced sexual violence, LGBTQ people are typically denied medical care and social services. Religion is a significant source of homophobia, with Catholic churches burying LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries, Evangelical temples and Muslim mosques participating in homophobic preaching, and imams, priests and traditional healers performing conversion therapy often coerced by families. Homosexuality is perceived as unnatural and stemming from Western culture, with homosexuals considered deviants and homosexuality often called a disease brought by white people, and on 17 May 2013 LGBTQ associations in Cotonou organized a public International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia event at the Institut Francais drawing 200 people while organizations can hold public events. For transgender-specific societal tolerance, the article provides only that priests are documented as "calling transgender people demons" and that hiring discrimination singles out "especially transgender and intersex people," with no separate finding of tolerance toward transgender people distinct from general LGBTQ stigmatization.

texts.cleaned_text: BBC (11 July 2024): Burkina Faso's military junta announced a ban on homosexual acts. Homosexivity had never before been outlawed in the socially conservative West African state. The ban formed part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage and family law and entered into force as criminal-code law on 1 September 2025.

Africanews (11 July 2024, updated 13 August 2024): the junta's council approved a decree for a new Personal and Family Code (CPF) that enshrines the ban on homosexuality, per a presidency statement, joining the roughly 22 of 54 African states that disallow same-sex relations. The code entered into force on 1 September 2025 and is the instrument that carries the criminalisation.

Human Rights Watch (3 September 2025): the Transitional Legislative Assembly passed the law on 1 September 2025 making consensual same-sex relations a criminal offence, carrying two to five years' imprisonment plus fines. It was enacted amid a junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil space.

LGBTQ Nation (September 2025): the junta unanimously passed the law. Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala states prison terms 'between two and five years as well as fines' for perpetrators of 'homosexual or similar practices', and that foreigners will be deported under the law. Junta rule dates from September 2022.

Since 1 September 2025 the criminal code in force bans homosexual acts and the promotion of homosexuality or similar behaviour, punishable by 2 to 5 years in prison and a fine. The law passed unanimously in the unelected 71-member transitional parliament and took effect immediately. Foreign nationals who violate it will be deported. France 24–AFP coverage of 22 September 2025 described fears of a witch hunt and increased self-censorship in the LGBTQ community, and as of 28 September 2025 no arrests under the law had been reported.

Same-sex activity was legal before 2025, with an equal age of consent implemented in 1996 and overturned by the 2025 code. The Constitution's Article 23 defines marriage as the free consent of a man and a woman, describes the family as the basic unit of society owed state protection, and does not authorise same-sex marriage. That article bars discrimination in marriage based on race, colour, religion, ethnicity, caste, social origin or wealth, a list that omits sexual orientation and gender identity. Pre-existing prohibitions on same-sex marriage and same-sex adoption remain in force, and the July 2024 amended family code draft under the Traoré junta targeted consensual same-sex relations.

Under the U.S. Department of State, only married, cohabiting heterosexual couples married at least five years may adopt, and single applicants are almost never permitted to adopt.

The 2011 Human Rights Report found the law did not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation in employment and occupation, housing, statelessness, access to education or health care, while societal discrimination on those grounds persisted. LGBT persons were reported as occasional victims of verbal and physical abuse, religious and traditional beliefs did not accept homosexuality, and there were no reports that the government responded to societal violence and discrimination against them. LGBTQ organisations had no legal presence in the country but existed unofficially, with no reported violence against them.

National adult HIV prevalence stands at 0.80% of those aged 15 to 49. Of an estimated 94,000 adults living with HIV, 65% have antiretroviral drugs, and 28% of children aged 0 to 14 do, against all-ages coverage of 32% in 2010.

Foreign public broadcaster (July 2024): this country's military government approved legislation to ban homosexual acts - previously not outlawed though socially frowned upon. The justice minister announced the cabinet approval as part of a marriage-law overhaul that recognises only religious and customary marriages; the law still needed passage by a military-controlled legislature and the signature of the government's military head.

Continental news outlet (July 2024): the military government approved revised marriage-family legislation criminalising homosexuality with 'severe penalties', as part of the same overhaul recognising only religious and customary marriages.

A foreign government's 2011 human-rights report on this country: pre-criminalisation baseline - no law criminalising same-sex conduct; documents security-force abuses, prison conditions and societal discrimination (no LGBT-specific section content in the retrieved text).

International human-rights organisation (Sept 2025): this country criminalises same-sex conduct - the military government's law took effect, with prison sentences; the organisation's reporting on the new penal provisions.
A cable-news report (Sep 2025): this country's parliament passes a law outlawing LGBTQ practices with prison terms attached.

LGBTQ news outlet (Sept 2025): this country's military government unanimously passed a law banning homosexuality - 2-5 years' imprisonment plus fines, per the justice minister; foreigners will be deported under the law; the country had never previously banned homosexuality.

Erasing 76 Crimes (12 Feb 2025): prominent trans advocate Shila, originally from Chattogram district, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 Feb 2025; five unidentified individuals accused; she was widely known for humanitarian work.

Erasing 76 Crimes (7 Apr 2026) citing JMBF's annual report: 260 documented human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals nationwide in 2025 — 'a sharp increase' continuing an upward trend since 2022 — including murder/attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion.

Global Press Journal: after the 2024 Monsoon Revolution, hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground; Bangladesh has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013 (a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021), but trans lives have been upended — the featured subject now lives in hiding.

Washington Blade (5 Aug 2025): a year after protests forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's ouster (August 2024), Bangladesh's LGBTQ community is increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats.

UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, Bangladesh (September 2023, updated April 2026): Section 377 ambiguity persists — it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within s.377 (ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere calling the provision relevant to 'all genders').

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Penal Code 1860 criminalises 'intercourse against the order of nature' with up to life imprisonment — rarely enforced but used by police to harass people presumed LGBTIQ; hijra are legally recognised as a third gender since 2014 with gender-marker change allowed; LGBTIQ and hijra pride events have been held.

Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Oct 2025): after hijras refused police extortion money on 10 Sep 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack in Gomdondi Phultala; on 17 Sep police arrested twelve hijras collecting money from expatriate-carrying vehicles in Narayanganj — a traditional livelihood.
Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Apr 2024): five transgender/hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, per JMBF.

UK Upper Tribunal decision PA/07096/2017 (Feb 2019): a Bangladeshi gay man's asylum appeal — Home Office country material records Islamist groups calling to prosecute LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues (citing fact-finding missions and IRB Canada).

On 11 November 2013 the Bangladeshi Government in a cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina recognized hijras as a separate gender alongside males and females for identification on official documents, with a Ministry of Social Welfare survey counting 10,000 registered hijras as of 2013. Voter lists offer third-gender options and hijra candidates have run for government positions, and in April 2019 officials introduced 'hijra' as a third-gender option on voting forms for the first time to allow voting under proper gender identity. Bangladesh has no policies outlining measures individuals must undergo to legally change gender on official documents, no clarity about who may qualify as a hijra, and no protections from discrimination for hijra, while other transgender communities beyond hijras remain unrecognised and unprotected from discrimination. In December 2014 the Ministry of Social Welfare invited hijras to apply for government employment, but in January 2015 the Ministry of Health issued a memorandum requesting necessary steps to identify hijras by conducting thorough medical check-ups that required hijras to strip and have genitals confirmed, with photographs later released to confirm hijras are 'really men'. In July 2015 after a hijra witnessed the murder of a secular blogger and helped arrest the perpetrators the government announced plans to recruit and enlist hijras as traffic police. A government housing scheme for homeless or landless individuals includes transgender people for the first time, with at least 140 transgender community members provided government-built houses across the country. Bangladesh opened its first religious school for transgender people in Dhaka with classes starting 7 November 2020 for more than 150 expected students in Islamic and vocational subjects for free with no age limit, while hijras continue to face severe discrimination and unequal access to housing and health care. Formal laws against homosexuality imposed by the British in 1860 through the Indian Penal Code effective in 1862 were carried into the Pakistan Penal Code after the 1947 partition and retained in Bangladesh's legal code since 1971 independence, and Parliament refused to overturn Section 377 in 2009 and 2013. Section 377 ("Unnatural offences") provides: "Whoever voluntarily has carnal intercourse against the order of nature with any man, woman or animal, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine," with explanation that penetration is sufficient and ambit extends to any sexual union involving penile insertion, including consensual heterosexual fellatio and anal penetration. The law is used to arrest, harass and extort individuals based on sexual orientation, with LGBTI groups reporting police used it as pretext to bully LGBTI individuals and those considered effeminate and to limit registration of LGBTI organizations, plus harassment under a suspicious behavior provision of the police code. In May as cited in the 2017 report, RAB forces raided the Chayaneer Community Center in Keraniganj Upazila during an LGBTI dinner, separating 120 present into small groups, beating them, and arresting 28 on suspicion of homosexual activity while allowing media to photograph some, later claiming arrest for narcotics possession (yaba and cannabis) with 4 remanded, 12 detained for questioning and 12 sent directly to jail. Bangladeshi law does not recognise same-sex relationship, civil unions, domestic partnership, or any adoption route for same-sex couples, and same-sex couples have been detained and can be imprisoned and/or fined. Labor law prohibits wage discrimination on the basis of sex or disability but does not prohibit other discrimination based on sex, disability, social status, caste, sexual orientation or similar factors, and there are no legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation. The article states: "While hijras are generally more accepted and have historically held culturally important roles, they also face severe discrimination and unequal access to various social services like housing and health care." The 2017 U.S. Department of State report as cited states: "The transgender population has long been a marginalized, but recognised part of society, but it faced continued high levels of fear, harassment, and law enforcement contact in the wake of violent extremist attacks against vulnerable communities." That report adds LGBTI members received threatening messages via telephone, text and social media with some harassed by police, and that following the raid and continued harassment many members including leadership reduced activities and sought refuge inside and outside the country, severely weakening advocacy and support networks, with organizations specifically assisting lesbians rare. It also notes social stigma against HIV and AIDS and higher-risk populations could be a barrier for accessing health services, especially for the transgender community and men who have sex with men. In November 2023 transgender woman Hochemin Islam faced exclusion from the North South University women's carnival on security grounds amid student threats of unrest and exam boycott and rally banners explicitly expressing "no transgender" sentiments. In August 2025 transgender woman Sahara Chowdhury, final-year English student at Metropolitan University in Sylhet, was expelled for life on stated grounds of online threats and carrying a weapon causing fear, which she denied as following her sharing a satirical caricature involving Asif Mahtab Utsha and Dr. Mohammad Sorowar Hossain. On 19 January 2024 part-time BRAC University lecturer Asif Mahtab Utsha publicly tore the seventh-grade History and Social Science textbook story 'Sharifar Golpo' in which Sharif born male later identifies as woman Sharifa living as Hijra claiming it promotes homosexual and transgender concepts, prompting student protests stating 'Say No To LGBTQ' and class boycott calls, his removal from lectures, and a five-member Education Ministry review that four months later found nineteen words 'incompatible' with Bangladeshi society and recommended omission.

On 11 November 2013 the Bangladesh cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina recognized Hijras as a separate gender alongside male and female, to be referred to as Hijra in both English and Bangla, with priority for education and other rights, noting approximately 10,000 Hijras identified in a Ministry of Social Welfare survey who were already enlisted as voters.

Released April 13, 2022, the U.S. Bangladesh 2021 Human Rights Report covers LGBT rights, and in response on April 17, 2022 Bangladesh's Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared that treating LGBT rights and same-sex marriage as human rights is a regrettable and uncalled-for imposition of values from a select few countries.
A monitoring group (12 Feb 2025): a prominent trans advocate was murdered in her home on 3 Feb 2025; five unidentified individuals accused; she was widely known for humanitarian work

A monitoring group (7 Apr 2026) citing a national rights federation's annual report: 260 documented human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals nationwide in 2025 — a sharp increase continuing an upward trend since 2022 — including murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion

A news outlet: after the 2024 political upheaval, hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground; the country has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013 (a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021), but trans lives have been upended — the featured subject now lives in hiding

A news outlet (5 Aug 2025): a year after protests forced the prime minister's ouster (August 2024), the country's LGBTQ community is increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats

A foreign government's country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity (September 2023, updated April 2026): the historic-era penal provision's ambiguity persists — it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within it (a 2019 global report on laws read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere calling the provision relevant to all genders)

A rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): the 1860 penal code criminalises same-sex conduct with up to life imprisonment — rarely enforced but used by police to harass people presumed LGBTIQ; third-gender people have been legally recognised since 2014 with gender-marker change allowed; LGBTIQ and third-gender pride events have been held

A monitoring group (22 Oct 2025): after third-gender people refused police extortion money on 10 Sep 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack; on 17 Sep police arrested twelve third-gender people collecting money from vehicles carrying returning expatriates — a traditional livelihood
A monitoring group (22 Apr 2024): five transgender women were arrested while begging near the main international airport and sentenced to about a month in custody, per a national rights federation

A foreign tribunal decision (Feb 2019): a gay man's asylum appeal — official country material records Islamist groups calling for LGBT people to be prosecuted under the historic-era penal provision and religious law, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations decriminalised in 1968; anti-discrimination laws since 2004 covering direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and medication, expanded in 2015 to cover 'sex' including 'sex change'.

DW (Sep 2025): ECJ Advocate General Richard de la Tour issued an opinion that EU law as interpreted precludes national legislation like Bulgaria's refusing a trans person ID documents matching presented gender, and the court concurred with the AG's proposed reasoning.

Strasbourg Observers (17 Dec 2024) on Y.T. v Bulgaria: the original 2020 ECtHR judgment found an Article 8 violation over refusal of legal gender recognition, and the Court made clear those obligations were unaffected by the 2024 registry revision (consistent with P.H. v Bulgaria); Judge Šimáčková dissented that the revision decision was over-formalistic.

Amnesty International (Feb 2015, 'Missing the point'): authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes — legislation exists but bias attacks (spiking in 2013 per the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee) go unpursued; Sofia Prosecution opened some cases.

Human Rights Watch (5 Jun 2017): urges authorities to protect the 10 June Sofia Pride march, noting that a group called the National Resistance rallied counter-demonstrators to 'cleanse Sofia from garbage'.

Novinite (June 2011): the 4th annual Sofia Pride parade passed without incidents under heavy police guard, drawing only a 'Family NGO' protest — after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 editions.

On 7 August 2024 Bulgaria's parliament passed an amendment to the education law banning 'propaganda, promotion, or incitement... directly or indirectly' of ideas about 'non-traditional sexual orientation and/or gender identity other than the biological one', signed by President Rumen Radev and in force from 16 August 2024, introduced by the Revival party and backed by GERB. In November 2009 the District Council of Pazardzhik voted to forbid the 'public demonstration of sexual or any other orientation'; the Administrative Court struck it down in October 2010 for procedural errors, and upheld it on appeal in July 2011. Hate speech based on sexual orientation has been banned since the Protection Against Discrimination Act took effect 1 January 2004, but gender expression and gender identity are not explicitly named in the 2015 revision. Billboards promoting tolerance toward same-sex couples in Varna and Burgas were vandalised in December 2018, and the Bulgarian Orthodox Church calls pride events a 'sinful demonstration'. Citing Coman and Others v General Inspectorate of Immigration, a Sofia court on 29 June 2018 granted an Australian woman and her French wife, married in France in 2016, the right to live in Bulgaria, after they had been denied residency a year earlier when they tried to move there. In September 2023 the European Court of Human Rights held that Bulgaria's refusal to recognise same-sex couples is an 'infringement of human rights'; that case is subject to appeals and awaiting a government response. Health services are covered by the anti-discrimination ban on sexual-orientation discrimination in force since 1 January 2004, and same-sex couples are denied the right to make medical decisions for each other. Gay and bisexual men are not explicitly barred from donating blood: the donor form, per a Ministry of Healthcare ordinance of 19 July 2004, does not ask orientation but requires confirmation of no HIV/STI-risk practices. Intersex newborns routinely have male genitalia removed as the 'easier operation', with parents 'rarely informed' of later harm to the child's gender identity, and there are no laws concerning intersex people. Single Step Foundation launched Bulgaria's first licensed online support chat in October 2017 for LGBTI youth, families and allies. State hostility is documented in law and courts: the 2024 education 'propaganda' amendment, the 2009 Pazardzhik council ban on public demonstration of orientation, the Constitutional Court's Istanbul Convention verdict condemning legislation for legal gender recognition, and the Supreme Court of Cassation's 20 February 2023 interpretative decision that 'the only meaning of the term sex should be its biological one' and that the legal system rests on 'the binary existence of humankind', effectively barring legal gender change. Hate crimes against LGBT people 'are often ignored and go uninvestigated by authorities', including the 2008 killing of a 25-year-old student in a Sofia park by a group intending to 'cleanse' the park of gays, and the 27 September 2020 assault in Plovdiv on children as young as 14 or 15 by ultra-fans of Botev. A January 2014 government commitment to outlaw such hate crimes was dropped by the government formed after the October 2014 elections, though heavier penalties for sexual-orientation-based crimes were adopted on 28 July 2023. Media and political hostility includes the 1964 show trial of 26 men, including actor Georgi Partsalev and singer Emil Dimitrov, described by experts as 'a masquerade for the public' about 'decadent Western culture', the 2020–2021 rise in anti-LGBT rhetoric where 'gender became a slur', far-right National Resistance advocating brooms and shovels against pride attendees, and the Ataka party's protests. ILGA-Europe ranked Bulgaria 37 of 49 European countries for LGBT rights protection in 2020. Article 46 of the Constitution has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 1991, explicitly banning same-sex marriage, and the Constitution does not ban civil unions, but none exist, so same-sex couples are denied inheritance, medical decision-making and joint property rights. A Bulgarian court recognised a same-sex marriage performed in France in 2019, and a Sofia court granted residency rights in June 2018 under the Coman ruling. A couple who married in the UK had their recognition claim rejected by the Sofia Administrative Court in January 2018, an appeal pursued by the LGBT organisation Deystvie. In September 2023 the ECtHR found Bulgaria's non-recognition an 'infringement of human rights', pending appeal. Same-sex couples are banned from adopting, and a 2021 ECJ ruling forced Bulgaria to issue an ID to a child of a lesbian couple after it refused a birth certificate. On 7 August 2024 parliament amended the education law to prohibit 'propaganda, promotion, or incitement... in the education system' of ideas about non-traditional sexual orientation or non-biological gender identity, defined as attraction 'contrary to Bulgaria's legal concept of... opposite sexes', in force 16 August 2024. The age of consent has been 14 regardless of sex since 2002, and since 2026 it is 16. A 2008 survey of 15 schools in Sofia, Varna and Plovdiv found 10.5% of students identified as bisexual and 1.8% as gay, with 29% saying they would refuse to sit next to a gay classmate, 5% saying they would bully gay classmates and 39% saying they would protect them. Children as young as 14 or 15 were assaulted in Plovdiv on 27 September 2020 in an anti-LGBT 'cleansing action', and the first Sofia Pride in 2008, about 150 participants, was attacked with petrol bombs, rocks and glass bottles with over 60 hooligans arrested. Single Step Foundation, founded 2016, works specifically with LGBTI youth on coming out and affirmation.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2025 (covering 2024), chapter on this country: in August 2024 a law banning representation of LGBTI identities in schools was introduced (spearheaded by a nationalist party leader); the country continues rejecting asylum requests by LGBTI people from two other states and unlawfully detains LGBTI asylum-seekers from a conflict region in closed detention; a performer at the capital's Pride event received death threats; an LGBTI youth organisation faced institutional checks.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations decriminalised in 1968; anti-discrimination laws since 2004, expanded in 2015 to cover 'sex change' under 'sex'. But a constitutional marriage-definition provision bans same-sex marriage, and there is no legal gender recognition. A 2023 regional human-rights court judgment (brought by two same-sex couples) found this country in violation of its obligations on non-recognition of same-sex relationships.

A regional union rights agency's LGBTIQ survey country sheet for this country (2024): 75% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (union-wide: 53%); 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (union-wide: 29%); only 27% are open about being LGBTIQ (union-wide: 51%); 28% felt discriminated against at work or looking for work. Indicates a strongly hostile day-to-day climate.

Foreign public broadcaster (Sept 2025): an advocate general of the regional union's court of justice issued a non-binding opinion that this country must not refuse a trans woman ID documents matching her presented sex ('lived gender identity') - the case concerns a trans woman on hormone therapy refused documents; such opinions are followed by the court in roughly two-thirds of cases.

Regional human-rights court analysis blog (Dec 2024) of a line of cases against this country: the original 2020 judgment found a violation of the convention's private-life article over refusal of legal gender recognition; on revision (July 2024) the application was declared inadmissible for abuse of process, but the court confirmed the country remains obliged (under a later judgment) to provide a framework for legal gender recognition - which it still lacks.

International human-rights organisation report (Feb 2015): the country's failure to adequately investigate and prosecute hate crimes fuels fear, discrimination and violence against asylum seekers, migrants, religious minorities and LGBT people; authorities consistently fail to identify bias motivation.
An international rights group (Jun 2017): urges this country's authorities to protect the capital's pride event and showcase a tolerant side of the country.

News outlet (June 2011): the 4th capital Pride march passed without incidents under heavy police guard - after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 parades; only a 'traditional family' NGO protested.

texts.cleaned_text: Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Bahrain' (continuously updated): legal status 'decriminalised since 1976' per ILGA-sourced infobox, with recognition limits and no SOGIESC discrimination protections. Wikipedia country coverage: The Interior Minister stated that 'suspected' (effeminate) homosexuals are banned from entering Bahrain through airport checks, and pending bills proposed to expressly ban LGBTQ foreigners from entering the kingdom or receiving residency permits. In September 2013, all Gulf Cooperation Countries agreed to discuss a proposal to establish testing to ban gay foreigners from entering, though officials later backtracked. Penalties under indecency provisions include deportation for non-Bahrainis. Wikipedia country coverage: In response to parliamentary questions about lesbianism in schools, the Assistant Under-Secretary for Educational Services stated the Education Ministry is not responsible for addressing sexuality and that 'The public shouldn't make a big deal out of this problem because it does not exist,' adding that students whose appearance is contrary to school values should be disciplined. Pending bills proposed to instruct children's teachers in warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing so that children can be punished. In February 2024, the Ministry of Education referred a private school's administration and board to investigation and dismissed its general manager after a video showed students performing a scene with two male students pretending to propose to each other. Wikipedia country coverage: No LGBTQ-specific facilities, shelters, or community organizations exist: the US Department of State reports there are no approved LGBTQ-related organizations, and ILGA concludes it is 'improbable' that any sexual- or gender-diversity group would be registered, since the body controlling association registration may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order. Gender-affirming medical care is heavily restricted: courts require medical documentation of a 'sex change operation' or medical necessity to change legal gender markers, and a 2023 court ruling held that sex-reassignment procedures are against Islamic law where cases are considered solely related to gender dysphoria, limiting eligibility to people with intersex traits. Article 330 of the penal code also mandates that anyone charged with prostitution or 'fujoor' be taken to a hospital for sexually transmitted disease testing and potentially relocated to a medical facility. Wikipedia country coverage: Bahrain has no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and hate speech against the LGBTQ+ community remains widespread with no legal consequences — partly because Article 309 protects religious groups but does not extend equivalent protection to LGBTQ+ people. Enforcement hits individuals through morality and indecency provisions (Articles 324, 329, 350), which carry 3 months to 2 years' imprisonment, fines up to 200 BHD, and deportation for non-Bahrainis; the government used these against people suspected of being LGBTQI+ or of 'cross-dressing', including a 2009 one-month jail sentence for a man wearing an abaya and purse in public and a 2011 police raid on a party described as a same-sex wedding. False accusations of homosexuality are also used as a tool to discredit and bully government critics and protesters, including human rights advocate Nabeel Rajab and 2011 Pearl Square demonstrators. Media hostility compounds this: a widely-viewed August 3, 2024 Albilad caricature depicted a pride-flag roll of toilet paper captioned 'the correct place'. Wikipedia country coverage: Youth are a direct policy target: a bill proposed in October 2021 would have criminalized promoting or inviting others to homosexual gatherings with up to 5 years' imprisonment, and other pending bills proposed instructing children's teachers to spot warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing so that children could be punished. The Education Ministry disclaims responsibility for sexuality issues — Assistant Under-Secretary Khalid Al Alawi said it is parents' job and that 'the public shouldn't make a big deal out of this problem because it does not exist', while adding that students whose appearance is contrary to school values should be disciplined. On February 14, 2024, the Ministry referred a private school's administration and entire board to investigation and dismissed its general manager after a video showed two male students pretending to propose to each other in class; a 2022 incident in which a private school distributed material perceived as promoting homosexuality also triggered calls for stricter laws. Note also that the age of adulthood under the 1976 penal code is 21 for consensual same-sex acts, and the Gulf Daily News has published articles on female homosexuality in girls' high schools.

Cairo 52 (7 Feb 2024): in a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia — including refusal of a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination he requested.

Cairo 52 country review: Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade, including UN human-rights bodies and Amnesty International, so local media often serve as the only source for this jurisdiction.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Bahrain decriminalised same-sex relations in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era law, and is the only Gulf state not explicitly penalising same-sex intimacy, but authorities still use 'indecency' and 'debauchery' provisions to arrest queer and trans people; the Feb 2024 Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation. Decriminalisation coexists with arrests under morality provisions.

exact_spans: NOTE: this is a 2001 local political newsletter with general political content; its LGBT relevance (the 2001 referendum debate on banning same-sex marriage discrimination) is not visible in the retrieved text.

texts.cleaned_text: The Tribune (27 Apr 2016): Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign; BTIU stressed there are no laws protecting transgender and intersex Bahamians, and member Torri Culmer advocates against job termination for trans/intersex workers.

GayLawNet Bahamas law page: on 16 May 1991 consensual same-sex sex was decriminalised (Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act), and in May 1998 the National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced the military, prison service and police do not discriminate.

The Tribune (8 May 2017): Adrian Brown, 24, Jamaica-born and US-resident, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being 'targeted and beat up' because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival early Saturday, and wants charges laid. Violent targeting of a gay visitor during a major tourist event, dated 2017.

Wikipedia: Government officials have opposed LGBT rights. Former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 he did not believe in same-sex marriage and in 2016 said a referendum would not legalize it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the 'Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas,' urging financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island and pledging $1,000 toward it. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal: the Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, same-sex households are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples, and in 2011 former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated a marriage is void if between persons of the same sex, calling this a community standard. The Constitution's prohibition against discrimination does not cover sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection, and efforts to include it in a proposed Constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition. Statutory protection is narrow: the Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act 2003 lists "sexual life" as sensitive personal data, and a 2001 Employment Bill clause banning sexual-orientation workplace discrimination was removed shortly after passage. The criminal code sets age of consent at 16 for heterosexual acts and 18 for same-sex acts. There are no national hate-crime laws, and discrimination in healthcare or education on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal. Surveys record 85.5% strongly disapproving of same-sex marriage in 2015 with 10.6% approving, and over 84% strongly disapproving of a gay or lesbian politician in 2013 with 12% positive. In 2016 the Canadian government issued travel advice warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia in the Bahamas. Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations treating homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence, and politicians have been leery of publicly supporting LGBT-rights legislation. No exclusively gay bars or clubs exist; the Nassau scene is underground, and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. Police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 with no arrests, and the Ministry of Tourism later apologized. Groups of LGBT tourists have been protested, including church group opposition to Rosie O'Donnell's 2004 cruise and a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise; in September 2007 the Bahamas Christian Council formed an anti-gay committee over a request to a local cable company to carry the LGBTQ channel Logo. The Plays and Films Control Board banned Brokeback Mountain in March 2006 and attempted to block a public-square screening of Children of God on 24 June 2011, though the government overruled it. The Communications Act 2009 empowers URCA to issue codes of practice against content likely to incite hatred or vilify persons on the basis of sexual preference. LGBT citizens face no prohibition on serving in the police, military or prison service, and in May 1998 National Security Minister Frank Watson declared those forces do not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation. In 2005 an 18-year-old beauty queen had her crown stripped after confirming she was a lesbian. A 2009 murder victim, a homosexual HIV-positive man, was killed by a defendant acquitted using a "gay panic" defence, and nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved. No HIV-specific or trans-specific care provisions are recorded. The 2016 referendum bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people.

Gender identity is not included in any broad anti-discrimination or anti-harassment law. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal. The Constitution's prohibition on discrimination does not include gender identity. There are no national hate-crime laws to prevent or punish violence directed toward people in the LGBT community. The 2016 equality referendum bills were not inclusive to the transgender or intersex community, while marriage eligibility was framed as between a man and a woman with male and female determined at birth. A government member, Leslie Miller, publicly called for the "Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas," urging financial contributions to relocate transgender people to their own private island to ensure "they stay out of the way" and pledging $1,000 toward relocation. Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults has been legal since 1991. The age of consent is 16 for opposite-sex couples and 18 for same-sex couples. Same-sex marriages and civil unions are not legal, and the Marriage Act defines Bahamian marriage as composed of a man and a woman, with maritime marriage law stating a marriage is void if between male-male or female-female. Sexual orientation is not included in broad anti-discrimination or anti-harassment law, and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal. The Constitution's non-discrimination provision does not include sexual orientation, and a 2006 reform proposal to treat citizens equally regardless of religion, political affiliation, race, sex and gender did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection. A 2001 Employment Bill clause banning workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation was removed after passage. There are no prohibitions on LGB citizens serving in police or military forces, with a 1998 ministerial declaration that the military, prison service and police did not discriminate based on sexual orientation. Socially conservative Christian denominations generally promote the belief that homosexuality and cross dressing are signs of decadence and immorality. Due to lack of confidence in the judicial system, legal inequalities and homophobia, many LGBT people keep sexual orientation or gender identity private, and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. Documented transgender-specific intolerance includes government member Leslie Miller forcefully denouncing "the growing transgender community" and calling for the "Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas" to ensure "they stay out of the way." Police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 but could not arrest anyone as no crime was committed, with guests demanding an apology and the Ministry of Tourism issuing an apology to the cruise company. Juries have acquitted or leniently sentenced killers invoking gay-panic defences, including a 2009 acquittal for murder of a homosexual HIV-positive man and a 10 June 2010 case where the Court of Appeal president stated "One is entitled to use whatever force is necessary to prevent one's self-being the victim of a homosexual act." Numerous murders of homosexual men from 2001 to 2015 are listed as unsolved, including an accused in the 2007 Harl Taylor slaying found not guilty.

A country page on an international LGBTI legal-rights database: documents this country's legal status for same-sex conduct (decriminalised in 1991 under a new sexual-offences law, though with a higher same-sex age of consent) and gender recognition.

texts.cleaned_text: A national newspaper (April 2016): covering trans people's plea for rights - a national transgender and intersex organisation launched a 'trans lives matter' campaign calling for equal access to healthcare, education and employment without discrimination, during the gender-equality referendum debate; a spokesperson described the constraints of socially accepted behaviour in the country.

A legal-information site's page on this country's laws: consensual same-sex sex lawful at 18 (a 1991 sexual-offences and domestic-violence statute, with life imprisonment for sex with a same-sex minor); in 1998 the minister for national security stated the military, prison service and police do not discriminate based on sexual orientation.

A national newspaper (May 2017): a visitor from a neighbouring country was beaten at the country's main annual carnival festival, alleging he was 'targeted and beat up' because he is gay; he sought hate-crime charges and planned to sue - documents violence against an LGBT visitor.

Sarajevo Open Centre, Pink Report 2024 (13 Jun 2024): annual report on LGBTI human rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina — the past year saw a number of negative events with significant impact, and the long-visible worsening trend is 'becoming increasingly evident'.

Balkan Diskurs (25 Oct 2024): legal gender recognition is formally accessible but vague and ineffective in practice — the Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions document changes on 'completed' medical transition, constraints described as discriminatory and degrading.

Human Rights Watch (4 Feb 2014): violent attack on Sarajevo Pride organisers — Sarajevo Open Centre staff said they had arranged security with police about three weeks earlier; HRW's Lydia Gall demanded prosecution of attackers.

GlobalGayz (2012): same-sex conduct decriminalised in the Federation of BiH (1996) and Republika Srpska (1998) via the two entities' own criminal codes; the 2009 Law Against Discrimination prohibits discrimination on sexual orientation but omitted gender identity as originally intended.

Sarajevo Open Centre (Jul 2016): BiH's amended Anti-Discrimination Law explicitly covers sexual orientation and gender identity with correct local terminology — SOC co-presented the amendments with the Agency for Gender Equality after fall-2015 public consultations.

Sarajevo Open Centre (Jul 2016): the Federation of BiH adopted hate-crime regulation explicitly naming sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances — SOC coordinator Vladana Vasić confirming the long-sought coalition win.

Anti-discrimination law adopted in 2016 explicitly bans discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics, and the 2009 Law Against Discrimination covers 'gender expression'. In April 2016 the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina amended its Criminal Code to outlaw hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity (published 15 June 2016), with similar bans already in Republika Srpska and Brčko District. Public expression has been met with violence: the Queer Sarajevo Festival 2008 was stormed by football fans and religious extremists shouting death threats, eight people including a policeman were injured, and in 2014 the Constitutional Court ruled authorities had failed to protect festival participants' freedom of assembly. The first BIH Pride March was held in Sarajevo on 9 September 2019 with an estimated 2,000 marchers, but in March 2023 police cancelled LGBTQ film screenings in Banja Luka for 'security concerns' and activists were chased and attacked afterwards. A 2017 PLOS ONE qualitative study documents the stigma and discrimination men who have sex with men experience from healthcare professionals and the general community. Legal gender change is available only after sex reassignment surgery and other medical treatments. A 2015 survey found 48% of Bosnians would try to 'cure' their child if the child came out as gay and 16% would stop communicating with that child. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples at national or subnational level: the Constitution is silent on gender eligibility for marriage, both entities' family codes limit marriage to opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couple households are not eligible for the same legal protections as opposite-sex couples.
