texts.cleaned_text:
Persecution on the basis of sexual orientation is not explicitly recognised in Belarusian law as a ground for refugee status, and same-sex partners are not recognised for immigration purposes. After the fall of the communist regime many Belarusians sought and received political asylum abroad, most often citing formal or informal police harassment; Amnesty International and AILGBT-Belarus documented individuals granted asylum in the Czech Republic, France, the Netherlands and Sweden. Belarus is not a member of the Council of Europe, so activists cannot appeal to the European Court of Human Rights. In 2004, when an international gay and lesbian festival was targeted, authorities made threatening phone calls stating that foreigners attending workshops and discussions would be immediately expelled from the country under the article on intervention in domestic affairs.

Qualified psychological help is generally unavailable in Belarus, and no trans-specific facilities are documented; the three Minsk universities offering full psychology courses (Belarus State University, Belarus Pedagogical University, European Humanities University) do not address the problems of sexual minorities. Suicide rates are high among gays, lesbians, bisexuals and transgender people. LGBTQ venues have been shut or raided: the gay club Oskar was closed by authorities in February 2000 and its owner Ivan Suchinski was later killed, riot police raided a 1999 pride party, and police have conducted unprovoked actions in bars frequented by homosexuals in Gomel and Minsk. In prisons, homosexuality is subject to speculation, blackmail and extortion, gays and lesbians are largely unprotected, and turnkeys often encourage prisoners to abuse homosexuals. Police do not register brutality cases against sexual minorities or investigate homophobic motives; officers instead collect personal data, passport details and mugshots of gay people at known cruising areas, as reported by Vstrecha in Brest and Gomel. In September 2008 two transgender men raped in Minsk did not report to police because they were unsure police would help. Blood donation carries no particular limitations for gay and bisexual men; all procedures and requirements are the same for all donors.

In May 2003 the administration of the European Humanities University in Minsk banned a screening of the documentary Outlawed about discrimination of gays and lesbians, with staff saying the ban came under pressure of the Russian Orthodox Church. The April 2026 law bans propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and paedophilia; in July 2001 the Organising Committee of the 1st Belarusian Youth Congress voted against admitting Lambda Belarus delegates; in March 2002 the youth organization Young Front published homophobic statements, with leader Paval Sieviaryniec calling homosexuality a death-worthy sin and perversion. Opinion among the young is comparatively less hostile but still largely negative: Pew's May 2017 poll found 22% of younger Belarusians favour legal gay marriage against 14% of elders, while a 2007 vote of Gomel region youth found 47.6% had negative feelings toward sexual and gender minorities and 10% wanted to criminalize homosexual relations.

Homosexuality remains highly stigmatized. A May 2017 Pew Research Center survey found 84% of Belarusians believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society and 81% opposed same-sex marriage with only 16% in favour; a 2002 Lambda Belarus survey found 47% of Belarusians think gays should be imprisoned, and many believe homosexuality is a psychiatric illness. Gay life is largely underground, most LGBTQ people hide their orientation in public, and those who are out face harassment, violence and physical abuse. State hostility is codified: the April 2026 law prohibits propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and paedophilia, compared by critics to Russia's 2013 law, and a 2024 Ministry of Culture decree categorized homosexualism alongside paedophilia and necrophilia as pornography, enabling prosecution under Article 343 of the Criminal Code with up to four years in prison. Pride events from 1999 to 2010 were repeatedly banned, raided or forcibly prevented, no official organization represents gays and lesbians in Belarus with other initiatives working outside the legal framework, and there is no anti-discrimination protection and no prohibition of hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

Human-rights organisation news release (12 Apr 2024): the nation's law redefines 'pornography' to include depictions of same-sex relationships and transgender people, classed together with necrophilia and paedophilia as 'non-traditional relationships'; production punishable by up to four years — framed as an attack on LGBT dignity, a persecution vector for visitors and residents alike.

On 30 December 2019 the Appeals Court upheld the unconstitutionality of Section 53 and confirmed that the Constitution's protections against discrimination extend to sexual orientation and that freedom of expression includes sexual expression. Belize held its first Pride Week in August 2017 with awareness and acceptance activities hosted throughout the country, and since the August 2016 Supreme Court ruling LGBT organisations have become more visible and active. In its 2018 Universal Periodic Review Belize accepted recommendations calling for educational campaigns to reduce societal stigma, accepted 15 LGBT-related recommendations including calls to take concrete steps to ensure universal access to HIV treatment for LGBT people, and accepted recommendations addressing discrimination, violence and hate crimes against LGBT people and training police officials to properly respond to violence; the recommendations came mostly from Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Chile, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Mexico, Spain, Ukraine, the United States and Uruguay.

Section 5(1)(e) of Belize's Immigration Act lists "any prostitute or homosexual" among prohibited immigrants. Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson filed a challenge in 2013, was granted leave by the Caribbean Court of Justice in May 2014, and was joined by CARICOM as an interested party in October 2014; on 10 June 2016 the CCJ dismissed his case, finding no violation of his freedom of movement. In the Tomlinson litigation Belize contended that Section 5(1) of the Immigration Act applies only to those offering sexual services for financial gain, and that it does not interpret or enforce the act as a blanket prohibition against homosexual immigrants. The CCJ's 10 June 2016 judgment clarified that neither Trinidad and Tobago nor Belize can ban homosexuals from CARICOM countries from entering due to their treaty obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas, notwithstanding their laws that ban the entry of gays.

The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 expressly provides prevention and protection from sexual harassment regardless of sexual preference and gender identity. Section 8(1)(c)(i) of the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024 makes evidence that an offence was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance, effective 27 April 2024.

The Supreme Court case was heard in May 2013 amid violence and death threats received by LGBT activists. After the 2016 ruling the Government first said on 17 August 2016 it would not appeal, then reversed after meeting religious leaders on 9 September and filed a partial appeal against the declaration that the Constitution bars discrimination based on sexual orientation; the Catholic Church withdrew from the appeal in March 2018, leaving the Government as sole appellant. Solicitor General Nigel Hawke argued the ruling was judicial overreach in re-defining "sex" to include sexual orientation. Religious bodies were openly hostile: the Council of Churches held a "Take a Stand" rally on 3 December 2011 and a "Belize Action/Family Forum" rally on 23 November 2011 describing decriminalisation as "an orchestrated plan of demonic darkness"; in December 2011 Prime Minister Dean Barrow publicly rejected US pressure from President Obama, saying Belize would not change its laws. A 2013 UNAIDS survey of 773 Belizeans aged 18 to 64 found 34% accepting and 34% tolerant of homosexuals, among the highest acceptance rates in the Caribbean polled.
A 2016 Court of Appeal ruling struck down the sodomy law — the region's first decriminalisation ruling.

At the country's 2018 UN human-rights review it accepted 15 of 17 SOGI recommendations — the first regional-bloc member to accept that many — pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection, with two rights-equality recommendations noted rather than accepted.

The article states there is no legal recognition of transgender people in Bermuda. The article states that, by omission, there is thus no protection from discrimination for transgender people. The article states that the ability of persons to express their gender identity is often difficult. As its example, the article states that in 2006 the Government attempted to ban Mark Anderson, also known as the drag queen "Queen of Bermuda" Sybil, from participating in a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities. The article provides no transgender-specific provisions on documents, screening, facilities, custody, care, enforcement, penalties, or protection machinery beyond that omission and example. Homosexuality is legal in Bermuda; lesbian activity has never been illegal, while consensual private sexual conduct was legalised by the Stubbs Bill in 1994 after prior liability of up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex. As of 2022 the age of consent remains unequal at 18 years for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019 versus 16 for other sexual activity, after a prior higher age of 18 for gay male conduct found in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights, and the Criminal Code provision on gross indecency between men was repealed in 2019. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2013, following failed and dropped proposals in 2004-2006 and 2009. Same-sex marriage is not legally available since 2022, having been legalised by the Supreme Court in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche marriage-license case under the Marriage Act 1944 and Human Rights Act, replaced by domestic partnerships by law given royal assent 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, restored by the Supreme Court on 6 June 2018 and Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, then banned again by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on 14 March 2022 with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. Same-sex couples are allowed to adopt equally under the Adoption of Children Act following the February 2015 Supreme Court ruling on marital-status and sexual-orientation discrimination, and binational same-sex partners were granted equal employment and benefits by the Supreme Court in November 2015. The Bermuda Regiment, formed by random lottery-style conscription, does not discriminate on grounds of sexual orientation and officially prohibits discrimination or harassment of LGBT soldiers, though such activities have been reported as tolerated by officers to the extent one conscript described the Regiment as "the most homophobic environment that exists". Gay and bisexual men may donate blood with the Bermuda Hospitals Board if they have not had sex with another man in the past 12 months, with a 12-month deferral likewise for women who have sexual relations with men who have sex with men. In November 2020 reporting, the government spent approximately £150,000 to legally appeal an unconstitutional case of a man charged and threatened with jail under the archaic "obscene behaviour law" for importing DVDs of gay porn into Bermuda.

The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report on Bolivia documents the constitutional guarantee against discrimination and societal discrimination against LGBT people. Its general assessment addresses arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions, and corruption.

Bolivia's Constitution prohibits discrimination and protects bodily integrity, citing Art 15(II) on violence and Art 45(V) on maternity, while Penal Code Title VIII governs abortion. The 2016 gender-identity law provides self-identification, followed in Jan 2018 by an Inter-American Court opinion and in Dec 2020 by civil-registry recognition of free union for same-sex couples.

eju.tv/La Razón (25 Aug 2014, Spanish): homosexuality is taboo in Bolivia's armed forces — gay soldiers report discrimination and sanctions, testimony given anonymously; the TLGB collective and human-rights activists demand openness.

Article 14(II) of the Constitution, implemented in February 2009, prohibits and punishes discrimination based on gender identity. The Law Against Racism and All Forms of Discrimination defines discrimination to include gender identity, provides definitions for transphobia, amends Penal Code article 281 to criminalize gender-identity-based discrimination, and punishes dissemination and incitement to discrimination with one to five years imprisonment. Since 2010, Penal Code article 40bis aggravates penalties for crimes motivated by grounds including gender identity. The Gender Identity Law was passed by the Chamber of Deputies on 19 May 2016, by the Chamber of Senators on 20 May 2016, signed on 21 May 2016, and took effect on 1 August 2016. It allows individuals over 18 to legally change name, sex and photograph on legal documents before the Civil Registry Service confidentially within 15 days based on a psychological test of voluntary assumption without requiring sex reassignment surgery, reversible once only. The first legal gender change under the law occurred on 1 August 2016 by activist Pamela Valenzuela. The newly assigned sex is not recognized for marriage after the Supreme Court in November 2017 invalidated a June 2017 Supreme Electoral Tribunal instruction to recognize it as unconstitutional, with an appeal filed to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights in May 2018. Bolivia allows transgender people to serve openly in the military under a 2013 Armed Forces announcement effective in 2015. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1832, with the age of consent set at 14 under Criminal Code article 308bis and a three-year close-in-age exemption. Article 63 of the Constitution limits marriage to heterosexual couples. Same-sex civil unions in the form of free unions have been recognized since 20 March 2023 when a Plurinational Constitutional Court ruling of 22 June 2022 obliging the Civil Registry Service to register them took effect, with regulations modified by 21 July 2023 to provide the same requirements and timings as heterosexual couples, and fifteen couples had registered by January 2023 under Inter-American Court Advisory Opinion OC-24/17. Single people regardless of sexual orientation may adopt and same-sex couples in a free union are permitted to adopt under Article 84 of the Child and Adolescent Code. Discrimination based on sexual orientation is constitutionally prohibited and criminalized under Penal Code article 281 as amended, with one to five years imprisonment for dissemination and incitement, and article 40bis since 2010 aggravates penalties for orientation-motivated crimes. Men who have sex with men have been permitted to donate blood since 10 July 2019 under amended Supreme Decree 24547, after a prior ban labelling homosexual and bisexual men as a high-risk group. The Armed Forces announced in 2013 that LGBT citizens could serve from 2015, though homosexuality in the military remains viewed as taboo with discretion advised. Enforcement remains weak, with the Ombudsman reporting 64 LGBT people murdered in 2017 with only 14 cases investigated and none resulting in a sentence. Reports of societal discrimination against LGBT people are not uncommon. In 2017 the Ombudsman reported that 64 LGBT people had been murdered that year, with only 14 cases investigated and none resulting in a sentence. A 2017 ILGA poll on transgender-specific tolerance found: "As for transgender people, 64% agreed that they should have the same rights, 63% believed they should be protected from employment discrimination and 53% believed they should be allowed to change their legal gender." This indicates majority support for equal rights for transgender people at 64%. It also indicates majority support for workplace protection at 63% and for legal gender change at 53%.
Bolivia's 2009 Constitution Article 14(II) prohibits and punishes discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, protecting equal recognition, enjoyment and exercise of rights.

Bolivia's Law No. 045 Against Racism and All Forms of Discrimination, enacted 8 October 2010, defines discrimination to include distinctions based on sex, sexual orientation and gender identity, prohibits such discrimination in employment, services, education, health and other public and private spheres, and criminalizes discriminatory acts with prison terms and fines, thereby establishing legal protection and sanction-based redress applicable to trans persons.

On 25 November 2015 Bolivia's government presented a Gender Identity Law proposal to allow transsexual and transgender people to change their names and genders on ID cards and birth certificates via civil registry offices, forwarded to the legislative assembly for approval, while explicitly excluding same-sex marriage.

Overview: same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013; legal gender change without surgery has been allowed since 2018 under a Supreme Federal Court ruling; the age of consent is equal regardless of orientation; and a federal anti-discrimination framework applies.

Brazil was the first country in Latin America to recognize same-sex unions for immigration benefits. On 25 November 2003 Judge Ana Carolina Morozowski of the 5th Civil Court of Curitiba granted permanent residency to the British partner of gay activist Toni Reis, and a week later the National Immigration Council issued Administrative Resolution No. 3 granting temporary or permanent visas to partners without distinction of sex. The government was slow to cable consulates, leaving binational same-sex couples confused about how to apply; Immigration Equality and the Brazilian Rainbow Group met officials at the New York consulate in February 2004 to press for clarity. A Florianópolis judge also barred immigration authorities from deporting an Italian woman partnered with a Brazilian lesbian.

Identity documents reflect gender. Passports and ID cards allow an unspecified or X marker under ICAO standards, mandatory for state-issued ID cards since 11 January 2024, and a 2025 Superior Court of Justice decision permitting a neutral gender on the civil registry affects only the plaintiff but sets a precedent.

The public health system (SUS) provides sex reassignment surgery free of charge as a basic constitutional right, per a 2007 ruling by the 4th Regional Federal Court, and roughly 250 such surgeries were performed between 2000 and 2007 at three university hospitals. Access is constrained in practice: the Health Ministry left qualification decisions to local officials, and long lines and poorly equipped public facilities push those who can afford it toward private hospitals and clinics. Partners in registered stable unions are recognized as dependents on health plans and insurers. In July 2026 the 3rd Panel of the Superior Court of Justice ruled that health insurance plans must cover facial feminization surgeries, and in March 2024 the Supreme Court extended five-day paid paternity leave to the non-pregnant mothers of lesbian couples.

Gender-affirming care for minors was banned by the Federal Council of Medicine (CFM) in April 2025, alongside a reduction of the minimum age for gender-affirming surgery from 25 to 21; LGBTQ+ advocates filed a Direct Action of Unconstitutionality at the Supreme Court. The Federal Court of Acre blocked the resolution on 25 July 2025, restoring care for minors nationwide, but on 2 October 2025 Federal Judge Flávio Dino overturned that block and reinstated the ban, leaving youth medication continuity and cross-state travel a live issue. Adult access to surgery within the public system requires patients to be at least 21, diagnosed with no personality disorder, and to undergo at least two years of psychological evaluation.

Conversion therapy has been forbidden by the Federal Psychology Council since 1999, though a Brasília federal judge approved it in September 2017 before reversing course in December 2017; the Supreme Court ultimately banned it, and in 2019 Justice Cármen Lúcia issued an injunction overturning the judge's decisions. Blood donation restrictions on gay and bisexual men, requiring 12 months without same-sex activity, were struck down as unconstitutional by the Federal Supreme Court in May 2020.

Hostility is documented both in violence and in legislative opposition. Senator Marcelo Crivella attacked the pending federal anti-discrimination bill, arguing homosexuals would receive a protection that 'should have been given to women, the elderly and children,' while conservative senators framed the law as an aggression on religious freedom. In January 2019 openly gay representative Jean Wyllys left Brazil after death threats, replaced in February by David Miranda. Grupo Gay da Bahia reported 343 LGBTQ murders in 2016, 387 in 2017 and 420 in 2018, and the figures are disputed: Veja columnist Reinaldo de Azevedo called the GGB methodology 'unscientific' because it counts all media-reported murders of LGBTQ people regardless of motive, and scholars note that international comparisons are flawed because figures reflect documentation capacity rather than crime totals. The Catholic Church and radical evangelical groups have been identified as sources of rising intolerance, and a 2007 incident saw a judge brought before São Paulo's Justice Council for calling soccer a 'virile, masculine sport and not a homosexual one.'

Education is a direct battleground. In June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that public and private schools must fight discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, sexist bullying against cisgender and transgender girls, and homotransphobic bullying. Since 2020 the Court has been overturning state and municipal laws banning gender and sexuality courses in schools, and since 2023 it has been overturning laws banning gender-neutral language in schools. Youth-specific risks include the April 2025 CFM ban on gender-affirming care for minors and labour exploitation: in the central, north and northeastern regions, transgender people from extremely poor families sometimes begin sex work as early as age 12 after expulsion from home, and travestis commonly work the streets as young as 16 or 17 in southern and southeastern regions and major capitals. On the more favorable side, the 2004 government initiative Brasil Sem Homophobia was designed to protect LGBTQ students, and a 2010 Rio de Janeiro State University and University of Campinas survey found that 95% of homosexual youth had revealed their orientation by age 18, many by 16, compared with after 21 for the 1980s generation.

Country overview (updated Mar 2026): constitutional and federal criminal provisions — after the 2019 Supreme Court ruling — prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, yet LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination in practice.

Brazil's National Council of Justice (CNJ) Resolution 348 of 13 Oct 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 20 Jan 2021, is the national framework for where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed: a person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing (Art. 4º); on arrest, the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person is consulted about their preference (Art. 7º), and the judge must inform them of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it general population or specific wings/cells (Art. 8º); the declared preference is recorded and a later change of placement is possible, with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat (Art. 9º). LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited (Art. 11, VI–VII). The resolution entered into force after publication (120 days, extended to 180 days by Res. 366/2021).

Peer-reviewed census study (Alves-da-Silva & Bonan, Dilemas 17(2), 2024; lead author also of the LGBTI health division of the Rio de Janeiro state penitentiary administration, SEAP-RJ) of travestis and transgender women in prison in Rio de Janeiro state: 138 self-declared travesti/trans-woman inmates were interviewed inside eleven units deemed 'masculine' in the metropolitan region (April–June 2021, via the SEAP's SIPEN database). It documents that in the Rio state system travestis and trans women are housed in units treated as masculine, with some held in so-called 'neutral' or 'security' units, and frames male-unit placement as a double punishment combined with recurring basic-rights violations; it also cites the 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units (hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics) and national norms (2014; 2020) that let them be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

Courts allow name and gender-marker changes without surgery, the supreme court has criminalised transphobia, courts fine businesses that discriminate, and official guidance affirms trans people's right to use bathrooms matching their identity.

A national council of justice resolution (348, 13 Oct 2020, amended 2021) governs custody placement: self-declaration before a judge, a reasoned placement decision after consulting the person's preference, information on male, female and LGBTI-specific units, recorded declared preference with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat, and no use of LGBTI-specific spaces as disciplinary isolation.

A state/province census (138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates interviewed inside eleven units treated as masculine, April–June 2021) found them housed in masculine units, some in 'neutral' or 'security' units, with male-unit placement documented as a double punishment amid recurring basic-rights violations; state/province law has since 2015 granted parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units.

The world's largest Pride parade takes place in the country; a majority of physical violence against LGBTQIA+ people in the largest city happens at night, and robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal.

The law mostly applies to Muslims (~two-thirds of the 420,000 population); Brunei has carried out no execution since 1957. AP (Apr 2019): 'Brunei death penalty moratorium applied to new Shariah laws' — the sultan says the capital-punishment moratorium covers the new Shariah penal code allowing stoning for gay sex and adultery; under the prior law homosexuality was already punishable by up to 10 years.
The France24 piece (April 2019) covers the fear gripping Brunei's gay community after the Sharia penal code came into force.

TIME (Apr 2019): first-person reporting as the stoning penalties took effect — lesbian sex newly exposes women to 40 lashes; theUN and foreign governments condemned the code; sources describe an economy-pain-fuelled rush of the law through a population of ~450,000 and speak anonymously of a climate of fear, with no assurance of enforcement against foreigners.

UK House of Commons Library debate pack (April 2019) on LGBT rights in Brunei: the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 (in force in stages, final stage 3 April 2019) requires death by stoning for extramarital sex, anal sex and abortion; 40 lashes for lesbian sex; amputation for theft. HRW called it 'barbaric'; the UN High Commissioner urged Brunei to halt it.
The SSRN paper relates to Brunei's Sharia penal code; it could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403).

HRW '#OUTLAWED' global map: at least 67 countries criminalise same-sex relations and at least nine criminalise gender expression; Brunei is one of at least two, with Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise 'posing as' or 'imitating' a person of a different sex, the trans-specific offence for this jurisdiction, with a state-sharia analogue in Malaysia.

US State Dept 2017 report: the Syariah Penal Code bans men dressing as women or women dressing as men 'without reasonable excuse', with no known convictions in 2017; 'liwat' between men carries death by stoning if implemented, and the report records LGBTI-reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services. Morality provisions (cross-dressing, alcohol, Ramadan eating, religious propagation) were enforced; sharia implementing regulations were still unissued.

Brunei does not allow a person to change their name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not allowed. On 11 March 2015, a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing. The SPC also prohibits men from dressing as women or women from dressing as men 'without reasonable excuse' or 'for immoral purposes', with no known convictions reported in 2017. LGBTI individuals reported intimidation by police, including threats to make their sexuality public, to hamper their ability to obtain a government job, or to bar graduation from government academic institutions. State-imposed corporal punishment is prescribed: under the SPCO, if evidentiary standards are not met, the maximum penalty for sex between men is seven years imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping; for unmarried men, one year in prison or 100 lashes; and sex between women is punishable by any two of forty lashes of caning, up to 10 years' imprisonment, and a fine of up to B$40,000. Bruneian society tends to associate homosexuality with 'effeminate men'. Members of the LGBTI community reported that the government monitored their activities and communications, and events on LGBTI topics were subject to restrictions on assembly and expression, with the government reportedly refusing to issue permits for such events. Media outlets described the Sharia provisions as 'medieval' and 'uncivilized', and the UN urged Brunei to review its laws when the move to Sharia law was announced. OutRight Action International has described Brunei as 'the country that has the most worrisome state of rights for LGBT people in Southeast Asia', and anyone convicted of 'tarnishing the image of Islam' may be heavily punished.

Brunei does not allow changing one's name or gender on official documents. Sex reassignment surgery is not allowed. The Syariah Penal Code prohibits men from dressing as women or women dressing as men "without reasonable excuse" or "for immoral purposes". On 11 March 2015, a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing. In 2017, there were no known convictions during that year. Members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex community reported unofficial and societal discrimination in public and private employment, housing, recreation, and in obtaining services including education from state entities, intimidation by police including threats to make public their sexuality to hamper obtaining a government job or bar graduation from government academic institutions, monitoring by the government of their activities and communications, and restrictions on assembly and expression with denial of permits for events on LGBTI topics. Same-sex sexual activity became illegal in Brunei in 1906 under Straits Settlements law applied by the 1906 Courts Enactment as updated by the Courts Enactment 1908, and remained illegal after independence in 1984. Before 2019 implementation of the Syariah Penal Code Order, homosexual acts were punishable by up to 10 years imprisonment even if private and consensual. From 2014 Brunei began staged implementation of Sharia law, with Syariah Penal Code Order adultery and sodomy provisions prescribing death by stoning and corporal punishments scheduled to come into force on 3 April 2019. In May 2019 the government extended its moratorium on the death penalty to encompass the Syariah Penal Code Order, so death-by-stoning provisions are not enacted while the moratorium continues, with the moratorium still in effect as of May 2023 but revocable at any time by the absolute monarch with minimal process and without warning. Under the Syariah Penal Code Order the de jure penalty for same-sex relations between men is death by stoning if married provided they admit to the acts or four male adult Muslim eyewitnesses testify to the acts. If those evidentiary standards are not met the maximum penalty is seven years imprisonment and whipping of thirty strokes, which is also the de facto penalty while the moratorium continues, while for unmarried men the penalty is one year in prison or 100 lashes. Sexual relations between women is punishable by a combination of any two of three stipulated penalties: a caning of forty lashes, a maximum prison term of 10 years, and a fine of up to B$40,000. Secular law criminalizes "carnal intercourse against the order of nature," with a July amendment to Chapter 22 of the Penal Code Order increasing the minimum sentence to between 20 and 50 years incarceration primarily applied in cases of rape or child abuse where both attacker and victim are male, while the Syariah Penal Code bans liwat (anal intercourse) between men or between a man and a woman who is not his wife with death by stoning if implemented.

The Brunei Project has monitored human rights in Brunei since May 2015 with LGBTI rights including transgender and intersex rights among its concerns, in May 2016 it held Brunei's first International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia event in collaboration with local LGBTI activists and regional LGBTI organisations, and no independent human rights organisations are active in Brunei.

On 17 October 2014 at 10.35pm religious law enforcers caught 38-year-old unmarried Muslim civil servant Roslani Hj Metasan posing as a woman at Bangunan Bumiputera in Bandar Seri Begawan with women's personal items in his bag, and he pleaded guilty to cross-dressing in a public place under Section 198(1) of the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 and was sentenced to a $1,000 fine with 60 days' imprisonment in default.

texts.cleaned_text: An international human-rights organisation's global 'outlawed' map feature: at least 67 countries criminalise same-sex relations and at least nine criminalise forms of gender expression; this country is one of at least two whose national laws expressly criminalise 'posing as' or 'imitating' a person of a different sex — alongside another country's analogue.

A foreign government's 2017 human-rights report on the country: the religious penal code bans men dressing as women or women dressing as men 'without reasonable excuse', with no known convictions in 2017; same-sex intimacy between men carries death by stoning if implemented, and the report records LGBTI-reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services. Morality provisions (cross-dressing, alcohol, fasting and religious propagation) were enforced; implementing regulations were still unissued.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): consensual same-sex intimacy decriminalised in 2021, but there is no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit SOGISC protections. LGBTIQ organisations may register, though activists call the process lengthy and burdensome. Legal gender recognition is unavailable; administrative gender-marker changes are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines. Discrimination and stigma persist, especially in health-care access.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service (Nov 2024): trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault; a 49-year-old trans woman describes having nowhere to report violence — police dismiss her cases because her identity card reads male ('both parties are men'), families pressure victims to accept it as fate, and help routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. Practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

UNFPA Bhutan report 'Fostering Awareness' (31 Mar 2025, 37pp): the 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, Attorney General's Office and Cabinet Secretariat, and secured the first-ever direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians; two consultation workshops convened community members with UN and National Commission for Women and Children representatives.

Erasing 76 Crimes (10 Jun 2019): Bhutan's lower house voted 43-1 to repeal Penal Code Sections 213-214 'unnatural sex' provisions, which carried 1 month to 1 year and had gone unenforced for at least 15 years; upper-house ratification was still pending at that point. Rainbow Bhutan director Tashi Tsheten: 'This is our first journey towards equality.'

Erasing 76 Crimes (11 Mar 2021): the Penal Code Amendment Act came into force 17 Feb 2021. After the upper house reinserted the ban, a December 2020 joint sitting clarified that 'homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex', completing decriminalisation and lowering the global criminalising-state tally from 72 to 71. No post-2021 reversal has occurred.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service feature 'Black and White and the Colours of the Rainbow': the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page (from c.2014) produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population. The feature profiles Dechen, one of only two trans women living publicly, who at 16 fought to wear the female school uniform kira, a first in Bhutanese society. Public trans visibility exists but remains exceptional.

The Daily Beast (28 Oct 2015): Bhutan's LGBT people report very little persecution or violence but near-total social invisibility. 'Growing up gay in Bhutan was a very alienating experience'; there is no shared language for gay or trans identities, and lesbianism is under-recognised. Karma Dupchen, one of the most public LGBT figures, founded the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page in 2013.

The Bhutan Medical and Health Council's Code of Professional Fidelity, issued in 2021, protects sexual orientation. The 2020 Standard Operating Procedure for Gender Based Violence Prevention and Response requires healthcare providers to ensure age-appropriate, culturally, and sexual orientation and gender identity sensitive care, and requires case managers to provide tailored care for people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities. Transgender people may change the gender marker on legal identification documents only after submitting a medical note plus a supporting letter from a civil society organisation. The National Strategic Framework on Comprehensive Sexuality Education (2021) covers LGBTI issues, yet Rainbow Bhutan's director states most LGBTQ youths drop out of school, and of the 316 people registered as LGBTQ in 2019, 10 were below age 19. Bhutan provides no legal recognition of same-sex relationships: 'Bhutan does not provide any form of legal recognition for same-sex couples.' A marriage bill using gender-neutral pronouns was discussed during the 2018 summer parliamentary session but was deferred due to the 2018 parliamentary election; the director of Rainbow Bhutan said the community believed the conversation would be revived under the newly elected progressive government. Partners of trans and other LGBTQ people cannot be recognised in any legal proceeding.

An international LGBTI-rights organisation's overview of this nation (updated 12 March 2026): consensual same-sex intimacy decriminalised in 2021, but there is no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on sexual orientation or gender identity; LGBTIQ organisations may register, though activists call the process lengthy and burdensome. Legal gender recognition is unavailable — earlier administrative gender-marker changes are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines. Discrimination and stigma persist, especially in health-care access.

A national broadcaster (November 2024): trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault; a 49-year-old trans woman describes having nowhere to report violence — police dismiss her cases because her identity card reads male ('both parties are men'), families pressure victims to accept it as fate, and help routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. Practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

A United Nations agency's report (31 March 2025, 37 pages): the 2024 equality campaign trained the highest court, the office of the top government lawyer and the cabinet secretariat, and secured the first-ever direct dialogue between this nation's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians; two consultation workshops convened community members with United Nations and national children-and-women commission representatives.

A news site (10 June 2019): this nation's lower house voted 43-1 to repeal Penal Code Sections 213-214 'unnatural sex' provisions (1 month to 1 year, unenforced for at least 15 years); upper-house ratification still pending at that point.

A news site (11 March 2021): the Penal Code Amendment Act came into force 17 February 2021 — after the upper house reinserted the ban, a December 2020 joint sitting clarified that 'homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex', completing decriminalisation (the global count of criminalising nations fell from 72 to 71). A later freshness review confirms this stands with no post-2021 reversal.

A national broadcaster's feature: an online community page (from around 2014) produced this nation's first public affirmation of a gay population; profiles the page's admins and one of only two trans women living publicly, who at 16 fought to wear the female school uniform — a first in this nation's society. Public trans visibility exists but remains exceptional.

A news outlet (28 October 2015): this nation's LGBT people report very little persecution or violence but near-total social invisibility — growing up gay was described as a very alienating experience, with no shared language for gay or trans identities and lesbianism under-recognised. A prominent public LGBT figure founded the online community page in 2013.

SALC, Digashu & Mmolai-Chalmers (20 May 2024): Botswana's precedent wins — 2016 Court of Appeal ordered registration of LEGABIBO (freedom of association, expression, assembly), a 2017 High Court ordered the state to change a trans man's identity documents from female to male (dignity and humanity), and the 2021 Court of Appeal decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct — yet implementation across Botswana and Namibia 'has not been satisfactory so far'.

Alta Advisory (18 Jun 2024): Botswana's draft constitutional amendment would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities; in June 2024 deliberations the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep 'intersex' and 'same-sex' distinct. Civic groups criticise the wider review process, but the intersex provision signals momentum toward broader LGBTQI+ protection.

UN UPR outcome, 43rd session (May 2023): Botswana did not accept Canada's recommendations to repeal Penal Code Section 167 (same-sex conduct between women) and to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition — 'a clear administrative process... was yet to be introduced' (para 570); abortion-decriminalisation recommendation also declined.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Botswana: the LGBT section documents that same-sex conduct was then criminalised and records societal discrimination against LGBT people. The report's wider assessment covers violence against women, prison conditions and San discrimination.

LEGABIBO official site: Botswana's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation running advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health/HIV work (e.g., World AIDS Day 2017 commemoration in Bobonong), with Coming Out, Law & Constitution and Help & Support resources — a functioning, legally registered community infrastructure (registration won in the 2016 Court of Appeal order).

The Independent (19 Dec 2017): Botswana's High Court ordered the government to legally recognise a trans woman's gender for the first time — Tshepo Ricki Kgositau won a female identity card after a four-year legal battle (gender confirmation surgery December 2016), dedicating the victory to 'every single trans diverse person in Botswana'. A landmark for legal gender recognition in the country.

Human Rights Watch (24 Jan 2018): previewed the Botswana constitutional challenge to the colonial-era 'carnal knowledge' law, with the hearing set for March 2018. The law was struck down on 11 Jun 2019 and the judgment upheld on appeal on 29 Nov 2021; the trans legal-gender right was confirmed 2017-22.

Botswana: the High Court's September 2017 ruling held that the Registrar of National Registration's refusal to change a transgender man's gender marker violated his constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment. A parallel December 2017 case brought by transgender woman and activist Ricki Kgositau produced a ruling that the government must recognise her gender identity; she dedicated her victory to "every single trans diverse person in Botswana." In June 2019 the High Court ruled that "sex" in Section 3 of the Constitution must be "generously and purposively interpreted" to include sexual orientation; per legal commentator Carmel Rickard, this gives LGBTQ Batswana "an even stronger, constitutionally-based argument" against discrimination. Custody exposure historically rested on Penal Code Section 164(a) and (c), which criminalised sodomy (heterosexual and homosexual) with up to seven years' imprisonment; same-sex acts remained illegal until June 2019, prosecution was rare, and the U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report found police "did not target same-sex activity." Former President Festus Mogae told the BBC he had instructed police not to arrest or harass gay people during his 10 years in office, while declining to change the law he said would lose him an election. On 29 November 2021 the Court of Appeal wrote that such laws "incentivise law enforcement agents to become key-hole peepers and intruders into the private space of citizens." The repealed sections were formally struck from the statute book in March 2026 by the "Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026," deleting paragraphs (a) and (c) of Section 164. In February 2011 the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly said he would have those who practise homosexuality killed if he had the power. President Ian Khama deported American anti-gay pastor Steven Anderson in September 2016, stating "we don't want hate speech in this country." In November 2018 President Mokgweetsi Masisi acknowledged that people in same-sex relationships "have been violated and have also suffered in silence for fear of being discriminated" and deserved protection. The 2011 U.S. State Department report found no reported violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity that year; LEGABIBO and activists called the Government's 2019 appeal an "affirmation of persistent homophobia and transphobia." Afrobarometer tolerance rose from 43% (2016) to 50% (2021) welcoming or not being bothered by a homosexual neighbour.

In September 2017 the High Court ruled that refusal by the Registrar of National Registration to change a transgender man's gender marker was unreasonable and violated constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection of the law, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment. The Government initially announced it would appeal but decided against it in December and supplied the trans man with a new identity document reflecting his gender identity. In a similar case heard in December 2017, activist and transgender woman Ricki Kgositau sought to change her gender marker to female and the High Court ruled the Government must recognise her gender identity. She dedicated her victory to "every single trans diverse person in Botswana". The 2017 rulings established that transgender people have a constitutional right to change their legal gender. The U.S. Department of State's 2011 Human Rights Report recorded no reports of violence against persons based on gender identity during the year. Both female and male same-sex sexual acts have been legal since 11 June 2019 after a unanimous High Court ruling declaring section 164 of the Penal Code unconstitutional. Previously sodomy, whether heterosexual or homosexual, was criminalised punishable by up to seven years' imprisonment under a law applying to both men and women, though prosecution was rare. The Government appealed in July 2019 and the appeal was unanimously rejected on 29 November 2021. In March 2026 paragraphs (a) and (c) of section 164 were formally deleted by the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026 under the Revision of the Laws Act after years of legislative inaction. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in the form of marriage or civil unions. The Employment Act 1982 has prohibited employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2010. In June 2019 the High Court ruled that "sex" as defined in Section 3 of the Constitution should be generously and purposively interpreted to include sexual orientation.

On 26 March 2026 Botswana formally deleted paragraphs (a) and (c) of Penal Code Section 164 on Unnatural Offences which criminalized having carnal knowledge of any person against the order of nature or permitting such carnal knowledge with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment, leaving only carnal knowledge of an animal as an unnatural offence, thereby implementing the 2019 High Court ruling upheld by the Court of Appeal in 2021 that criminalizing consensual same-sex sexual activity violates constitutional rights to dignity, liberty, privacy and equality.

International litigation centre article (May 2024) by two human-rights lawyers: courts in this country and a neighbouring country have issued landmark LGBTQI+ rulings (here: registration of a national LGBT organisation ordered in 2016; a 2019 high-court decriminalisation upheld on appeal in 2021), but implementation of the orders has been unsatisfactory - governments slow to comply.
Risk-advisory firm (June 2024): this country's proposed constitutional change would protect intersex rights - analysis of the reform process.

UN UPR outcome report for this country (43rd session, May 2023): recommendations to repeal a penal-code provision criminalising same-sex conduct for women and to introduce a clear administrative process for legal gender recognition did not enjoy this country's support; same-sex relations between women remain criminalised and no administrative process for legal gender recognition exists.

A foreign government's 2011 human-rights report on this country: general human-rights assessment (violence against women, prison conditions, discrimination against marginalised indigenous communities) - the LGBT section documents the then-criminalised status and societal discrimination.

National LGBT organisation's official blog: the organisation's activities - World AIDS Day commemorations, HIV stigma work, participation in a regional LGBTI network's conference - documenting the community organisation's operations after winning its registration battle.

Foreign daily (Dec 2017): this country's High Court ordered the government to legally recognise a trans woman's gender for the first time - the director of a trans-rights organisation will receive a female ID card after a four-year legal battle; a landmark for trans rights here.
An international human-rights organisation (Jan 2018): predicts 2018 as 'the year of the courts' for LGBT rights, citing this country's decriminalisation litigation among the key cases.

texts.cleaned_text: ILGA World's 'Our Identities Under Arrest' (2023) surveys laws criminalising LGBT people and covers the Central African Republic.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report, Central African Republic: no legal anti-discrimination provisions for LGBTQI+ persons; marriage constitutionally defined as a 'union between one man and one woman' with same-sex marriage banned; legal gender recognition not permitted; LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the military; criminalisation of same-sex activity in public pushed the community underground, and there were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for the Central African Republic documents extrajudicial killings, torture and rape by security forces and Seleka rebels, and harsh prison conditions; it contains little LGBT-specific material.

Erasing 76 Crimes / ILGA overview (20 May 2019): in the Central African Republic same-sex relations between consenting adults are not explicitly criminalised, but Article 85 of the criminal code criminalises 'attacks on public morals' — public same-sex acts carry harsher penalties than other moral offences. SOGI issues remain taboo and seen as 'imported from Europe'/'contrary to African values'; CAR received two UPR recommendations (SOGI non-discrimination, improving the situation of sexual minorities).
UN OHCHR summary of stakeholders' submissions for the Central African Republic's UPR (45th session, January 2024): includes SOGI-related stakeholder recommendations.

exact_spans: No transgender-specific criminal, documentary, screening, facilities, custody or care rule is provided beyond that absence; all other rules affecting transgender visitors are stated only on an LGBTQ-collective basis.
No transgender-specific societal-tolerance statement is documented; all tolerance and stigma statements are framed on an LGBTQ-collective or homosexuality-specific basis.
texts.cleaned_text: No legal gender recognition exists. There are no laws protecting LGBTQ people from discrimination in health, employment, education, and access to goods and services. Openly LGBTQ people cannot serve in the military. There are no laws against psychology or medical practices being used as conversion therapy on LGBTQ people. There is no ban on surgeries intended to normalize the bodies of intersex infants, with no reports of them occurring in 2023. Law 24-001 on the Protection of Personal Data protects sexual orientation as sensitive data and Article 17 provides "Any processing of sensitive data is prohibited due to risks of discrimination or infringement of personal freedoms." Central African Republic signed the United Nations joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity condemning violence and discrimination against LGBTQ people, while Alternatives Centrafrique founded in 2009 and registered in 2020 documented mistreatment and torture of LGBTQ people by law enforcement. Both male and female types of same-sex sexual activity are legal. The penal code criminalizes "public expression of love" between persons of the same sex with imprisonment for six months to two years or a fine of between 150,000 and 600,000 CFA francs ($300 and $1,200). When one of the participants is a child, the adult may be sentenced to two to five years' imprisonment or a fine of 100,000 to 800,000 CFA francs ($200 and $1,600). In 2012 there were no reports that police arrested or detained persons under these provisions. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples and same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned under Article 7 defining marriage as "the union between one man and one woman ... Family and marriage are under the protection of the State." Law 24-001 on the Protection of Personal Data protects sexual orientation as sensitive data with Article 17 prohibiting any processing of sensitive data due to risks of discrimination or infringement of personal freedoms. Openly LGBTQ people cannot serve in the military and Alternatives Centrafrique documented cases of arrests due to false accusations of same-sex intercourse plus mistreatment and torture by law enforcement. The collective statement including transgender persons is: "societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons was entrenched, and many citizens attributed the existence of homosexuality to undue Western influence." Cultural stigma continues to persist and religious preaching of conversion is rarely enacted since people keep their LGBTQ identities hidden. LGBTQ people face discrimination in education, healthcare, and employment and due to criminalization of public same-sex affection plus cultural stigma the LGBTQ community has to conceal itself, with maintaining queer relationships described as dangerous. While there were no reports of violence against LGBTQ people, it is unclear if this is due to a lack of incidents or victims not reporting it. Alternatives Centrafrique, founded in 2009 and registered in 2020, submitted reports for the Universal Periodic Review third and fourth cycles, while being diagnosed with HIV is used as a source of workplace stigmatization leading to harassment, blackmail, and firings.

texts.cleaned_text: A global report on laws criminalising LGBT people (2023)

An official human-rights report (2023): no legal anti-discrimination provisions for LGBTQI+ persons; marriage constitutionally defined as a union between one man and one woman with same-sex marriage banned; legal gender recognition not permitted; LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the military; criminalisation of public same-sex activity pushed the community underground, and no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ rights exist.

An official human-rights report (2012): documents extrajudicial killings, torture, rape by security forces and armed factions, and harsh prison conditions — general human-rights context with limited LGBT-specific content.

An overview (20 May 2019): same-sex relations between consenting adults are not explicitly criminalised, but a public-morals article criminalises 'attacks on public morals' and public same-sex acts carry harsher penalties; SOGI issues remain taboo and are seen as 'imported' and 'contrary to local values'; two review-cycle recommendations addressed SOGI non-discrimination.

A 2024 summary of stakeholder submissions for the national review: covers international obligations, the national human-rights framework, and institutional infrastructure, including SOGI-related stakeholder recommendations.

Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026): police-reported hate crime totalled 4,882 incidents in 2024 (+1% after a 34% jump in 2022-23); incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, down from a 2023 peak of 889 — three consecutive years of increases ended.
Egale Canada published a report on 2024 police-reported hate-crime data affecting 2SLGBTQI people in Canada.
The federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan survey findings were presented as quick stats.

Egale Canada UPR submission (2012): overview of LGBT human rights in Canada - sexual orientation in the Charter since 1995, marriage equality 2005; but trans protections limited and varying by jurisdiction, with no federal gender-identity discrimination law at the time; identifies gaps against the Yogyakarta Principles.

CBC News (Apr 2016): Prince Edward Island amended its Vital Statistics Act so a trans person changes the gender on official documents by declaring their identified gender plus a doctor's letter — the prior surgery requirement removed. A practical document-update pathway in one province.

The Globe and Mail (Jun 2017): the Senate passed Bill C-16 by 67-11, prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression and adding gender identity/expression to the Criminal Code hate-motivation provisions — framed as Canadian leadership amid a global anti-LGBT backlash.

Ontario Human Rights Commission policy (Part I): lays out the legal context, case law and legislation for sexual-orientation discrimination complaints under the Ontario Human Rights Code, which expressly covers gender identity and gender expression — official Ontario guidance a visitor/resident can invoke for discrimination recourse.

Placement policy: after Bill C-16 (2017) banned discrimination based on gender identity, transgender prisoners were to be placed in correctional facilities based on their gender identity, and Prime Minister Trudeau promised to review transgender prison assignment to ensure facilities match gender identity; transgender prisoners imprisoned for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. A 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security but with some concerns about risk to other prisoners; a 2022 CTV report alleged gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault. No special-unit or solitary/segregation policy detail beyond the federal identity-based placement rule.

Canadian lawyer Barbara findlay represented Synthia Kavanagh, a transgender prisoner, in litigation over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's correctional institution, showing that trans-prisoner placement and gender-affirming care have been contested in Canadian courts.

In 2023 Saskatchewan passed the Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act invoking the notwithstanding clause, requiring schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity; human rights groups called for repeal and legal action followed. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, Education Amendment Act, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, then shielded them from legal challenge via Bill 9 (Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025) using the notwithstanding clause. Ontario's 2012 Accepting Schools Act addresses bullying including LGBTQ students, and similar anti-bullying laws exist in Quebec, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories and Yukon.

Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the national human-rights act and the criminal code's hate-crime provisions (2017); most states/provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition, national documents offer an X marker, and a 2016 national reform created a document-update pathway (self-declaration plus a doctor's letter, the surgery requirement removed).

Police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018); a 2022 national survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical; an advocacy organisation documents a rising organised anti-trans movement, and two states/provinces enacted school-pronoun and healthcare rollbacks.

The national identity-based placement rule: transgender prisoners are to be placed in correctional facilities based on their gender identity, with those imprisoned for more than 12 continuous months considered for sex-reassignment surgery; an encyclopedia article records a lawyer representing a transgender prisoner in litigation over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's correctional institution, with no dates or final outcome given.

A 2022 news report alleged gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in the country's jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault; a 2022 study of correctional officers in one state/province found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security but with some concerns about risk to other prisoners.
A 2024 national hate-crime analysis page and a 2022 national survey page were not retrievable at research time (redirect loop; timeout).

texts.cleaned_text: Swiss Federal Office for Gender Equality rights overview: since 1 July 2020 public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is punishable under Art. 261bis Criminal Code; 'Marriage for All' has been in force since 1 July 2022 (same-sex marriage, adoption, IVF).

EPFL guidance on the Swiss civil status register: since 1 January 2022 any person registered in a Swiss municipality can change their sex marker and/or first name by personal declaration before a civil registrar — a self-declaration route without surgery or court proceedings.

SWI swissinfo (7 Aug 2022): about 350 people had used the simplified self-declaration gender-change process introduced on 1 January 2022 within its first months — early uptake of the new marker-change route.
SWI swissinfo, citing LGBTIQ Helpline monitoring: roughly six anti-LGBTIQ+ hate crimes are reported per week in Switzerland, 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020.

Federal Office for Gender Equality: on 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons 2026-2030. Its three pillars are support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence. The Federal Office for Gender Equality coordinates implementation.

exact_spans: — dated press corroboration of the federal plan and of the rising-report context that prompted it.
texts.cleaned_text: SWI swissinfo on the same first national action plan (2026): coverage of the government's new measures to protect LGBTQI+ people from hate crimes

LegalClarity (3 Jun 2026): marriage equality since 1 July 2022 after 64.1% referendum approval; criminal-law protection against sexual-orientation discrimination since July 2020; streamlined legal gender change since January 2022; the assessment runs 'from marriage equality to gender recognition, but some gaps remain'.

trans welcome (Switzerland) workplace legal framework: employers must protect employees' personal dignity under Art. 328ff. Code of Obligations, concretised for trans people by the Equality Act (GLG); trans staff may use their preferred name and gender at work without any official document change.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map country page for Switzerland reports the country's overall index score and its per-category compliance ratings, assessed after the 2021 self-determination and discrimination votes.

OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report for Switzerland: Switzerland regularly reports hate-crime data. The Criminal Code has no general hate-crime provision, so hate crimes are addressed under anti-discrimination provisions (Art. 261bis). ODIHR notes that recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes and that police do not record bias motivation.
UNHCR Switzerland records that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and that same-sex couples have been able to marry since 1 July 2022.

Primary legal text of the canton of Basel-Stadt's detention law (JVG, adopted 13 Nov 2019 by the Grand Council). §2 Trennungsvorschriften requires separation of female and male detainees and stipulates that 'the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible' (Die Geschlechtsidentität der eingewiesenen Person wird soweit möglich beachtet); the prison directorate may deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority. This is the explicit 2019 inclusion of gender identity in a Swiss detention law aimed at protecting transgender people's placement in correctional facilities.

Wikipedia's Switzerland overview records that in November 2019 the Grand Council of Basel-Stadt added 'gender identity' to its cantonal detention law (JVG) in order to protect transgender people's placement in correctional facilities. It records no federal provision on trans placement in detention, no Swiss case law on the subject, and no special trans units or federal solitary-confinement practice for trans prisoners; placement practice is cantonal. Conversion therapy remains unregulated at federal level: the National Council adopted a national ban on 12 December 2022 (143 for, 37 against, 11 abstentions) that is still pending in the Council of States, while Neuchâtel banned it in 2023 and Valais and Vaud in 2024. The Federal Council states such therapies are 'ineffective and cause significant suffering to young people subjected to them' and would breach professional duties, and a 2026 report confirms it condemns the practice while leaving further federal regulation open. Blood donation rules moved on 1 November 2023 to a 4-month deferral after last new sexual contact for gay men, down from 1 year since 2017. Support services include a helpline launched by Swiss LGBT groups in November 2016, Dialogai (founded 1982) offering helplines and advice, and Transgender Network Switzerland advising on legal sex and name changes, the armed forces and asylum. A 2018 survey of 1,700 Neuchâtel schoolchildren aged 14-15 found 10% of girls and 5% of boys identified as LGBT; 38% reported receiving slaps, kicks or punches, 25% reported frequent harassment, 16% reported being a victim of physical violence, and 7% reported discrimination by a teacher. Since the mid-1990s an annual Coming Out Day has been observed in schools, high schools and universities, often via seminars, films and group discussions, and LGBT youth groups operate at EPFL, ETH Zurich, Lausanne and St. Gallen. In June 2023 the Federal Supreme Court upheld a cantonal school's firing of a teacher who refused to call a transgender student by his chosen male first name, ruling that the school's duty to protect the student's privacy and self-determination outweighed the teacher's religious objections. On legal sex change, minors aged 12-18 originally required guardian consent; the National Council suppressed that requirement and the Council of States set 16 as the age below which guardian consent is needed.

Legal gender recognition by self-declaration since January 2022 (binary male/female only; no non-binary marker); same-sex marriage legal since 2022 (approved by referendum); gender-neutral rape law from 2024; employer duty of care toward trans employees.

An international rights organisation's map and the government's own review flag that the criminal hate-crime and hate-speech provision (Article 261bis) covers sexual orientation but not gender identity; reported hate crimes against LGBTIQ people have risen about fivefold since 2020 (around six per week, from a low base of ~309 cases in 2024); the national government adopted the country's first national action plan against LGBTIQ hate crime in January 2026 (running to 2030).

One state/province's detention law (adopted 13 November 2019): female and male detainees must be separated, the detained person's gender identity is respected as far as possible, and the prison directorate may deviate in consultation with the referring authority; a national encyclopedia overview documents no national placement rule, case law, special trans unit or solitary/segregation practice.

texts.cleaned_text: Outright International overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; hate-crime law has included sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances since 2012; civil unions since 2015; comprehensive self-determination-based legal gender recognition passed 2019; third sex option on birth certificates available for intersex children.

Washington Blade (19 Mar 2025): a Chilean advocacy group's annual report judged 2024 a 'year of regression' for LGBTQ rights — stalled equality and trans-rights legislation, blamed on the rise of the ultra-right and government inaction.
Movilh, the Chilean LGBT integration movement, published its 24th Annual Human Rights Report on sexual and gender diversity in 2025.

texts.cleaned_text: BioBioChile investigation (2 Jan 2024): profile of Ever, a young trans man murdered in 2023 and hidden for 24 hours — described as Chile's 'biggest hate crime'; the killer, an acquaintance, confessed.
