texts.cleaned_text: Chilevisión (23 Sep 2021): a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for nearly an hour in a transphobic attack at a Santiago hotel; the victim recounts 'he told me he wanted to kill me'.

La Tercera: Gendarmería's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees — placement by assumed gender, segmented housing, and entry examinations; a standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives oversees implementation and trans visitors' access rules.
F&M Global Barometers country profile for Chile: composite scores measuring LGBT rights perception, including a specific Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index.

El Universal Chile (1 Apr 2025): Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros for discrimination — relegated to administrative tasks, her private life exposed without consent, and support denied. Institutional discrimination case against the national police force.

Movilh achievements page: index of the Chilean LGBT movement's milestone wins — the anti-discrimination law, inclusive 2012 census questions, the 'El amor es amor' marriage campaign, 'Comuna Diversa' local-level work and regional branches — the campaign record behind the current legal framework.

Wikipedia country coverage: The 2012 anti-discrimination law (Zamudio Law) protects against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. A bill criminalizing incitement to hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression passed the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020. Article 373 of the Penal Code, covering offenses to morals and good customs, was historically used by police to harass homosexuals even for holding hands in public; a 2015 Movilh report noted that for the first time in seven years no police abuses against LGBT people were reported, credited to the Carabineros Human Rights Department. The Migration and Immigration Law, enacted 11 April 2021, bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that unrecognized asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk because of, among other grounds, sexual orientation or gender identity. A Ministry of Education circular of April 2017, Rights of girls, boys and trans students in the field of education, requires schools nationwide to provide bathroom and shower facilities that respect the gender identity of trans students, alongside guarantees of social name use and gender-conforming uniforms, and non-compliance is sanctionable. A 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centers in Chile to call and register transgender people by their social name. Since 2009 the National Organization of Gendarmeries has ended disciplinary sanctions against inmates that prevented them from dressing according to their gender identity. Since 2013, sex reassignment surgeries and hormone therapy have been funded by Chile's public health system (Fondo Nacional de Salud). In June 2024 the Ministry of Health's Circular 7 suggested deferring initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, though the Medical College noted physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court (7-3) annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law that had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) via the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run program continues providing support in medical centers. The Gender Identity Support Program Crece con Orgullo has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17. The Gender Identity Law 21.120 (effective 27 December 2019) lets those over 18 change name and sex by request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, while 14-to-18-year-olds must go before family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and under-14s cannot use the law but are recognized as transgender. In April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the over 14 years old wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, though the ruling applies only to that case. Education protections include the 2009 General Law of Education, the 2011 School Violence Law requiring Good School Coexistence Committees, the 2013 Superintendence of Education handbook ordering non-discriminatory treatment, the 2015-2018 National School Coexistence Policy incorporating the International Day Against Homosexuality and Transphobia into the 2016 School Calendar, the School Inclusion law effective March 2016, and the April 2017 ministerial circular on trans students' rights. Law 21,430 (published 15 March 2022) is the first regulation explicitly protecting LGBTIQA+ children and adolescents, including non-discrimination on sex characteristics and the right to develop gender identity, and obliges state bodies to create programs on sexual rights and diversity. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report (56-30-6), a non-binding recommendation proposing to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors, and repeal Circular 812 protecting gender identity in schools.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; hate-crime law includes SOGI as aggravating circumstances since 2012; civil unions since 2015; comprehensive self-determination-based legal gender recognition law passed 2019; third-sex option for intersex children on birth certificates since 2006; non-binding intersex-affirming health guidance (2023) recommends against unnecessary surgeries; in 2025 a court issued the country's first lesbophobic femicide conviction.
An LGBTQ+ news outlet (Mar 2025): an annual rights report finds this country's 2024 was a 'year of regression' for LGBTQ rights, with stalled equality and trans-rights legislation.
Investigative outlet (Jan 2024): profile of a young trans man murdered and dismembered in 2023 - described as the country's 'biggest hate crime'; the killer, an acquaintance, confessed.

National TV network (Sept 2021): a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for nearly an hour at a hotel in the capital in a transphobic attack; the victim recounts fearing for his life.

National daily: the country's prison service signed a new protocol for trans inmates - placement according to gender identity, segmented housing, medical examination on entry to determine hormonal/surgical treatment needs, and respect for assumed-gender expression.
International survey group's country profile for this country: composite scores measuring LGBT rights perception, including a dedicated transgender-rights barometer index.

Foreign newspaper (April 2025): the country's first trans police officer sued the national police for discrimination - relegated to administrative tasks, private life exposed without consent, denied support against online hate, and transition-related surgery refused.

texts.cleaned_text: A New York Times article dated October 2024 addresses the situation of LGBTQ people in Côte d'Ivoire.

UNDP report (Dec 2024) 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' - includes a Côte d'Ivoire country overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation/prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space, and inclusion of LGBT+ people.

US State Department 2023 report, Côte d'Ivoire: same-sex conduct not criminalised, but LGBTQI+ persons faced violence — three community deaths reported in the year; police responses to non-state violence were sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim; a transgender man was beaten in Abobo, Abidjan, while walking with another man. Authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Côte d'Ivoire contains limited LGBT-specific content. It covers the post-electoral crisis context, including 3,000 deaths, sexual violence and displacement.

Critical African Studies (2015), Thomann & Corey-Boulet, 'Violence, Exclusion and Resilience among Ivoirian Travestis': travestis (born anatomically male, living as women) face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention, and have been underserved by Ivoirian rights groups that distanced themselves from them; examines isolation after the 2010-11 post-election violence.
Thomann and Corey-Boulet (2015) document violence and social exclusion experienced by travestis in Côte d'Ivoire, together with their resilience. The article is archived in PubMed Central.

texts.cleaned_text: Human Rights Watch publishes no document, case or report on the housing of transgender prisoners in Côte d'Ivoire. On the HRW country page for Côte d'Ivoire, 'LGBT Rights' appears only as a topic-facet link.

There is no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. In March 2010 the Ivorian representative stated the country would begin to take measures to ensure non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, but would not start awareness-raising programs because it was not a current priority. In September 2024 the National Human Rights Council called on the public to refrain from online hatred and violence toward woubis (gay men and trans women) and lelés (lesbians and trans men), stating "despite their different sexual orientation and contrary to our customs and traditions, the members of this ‘woubi’ community remain above all human beings and benefit from the human rights enshrined in the Ivorian Constitution and international human rights treaties." Transgender women and other feminine-presenting people assigned male at birth are at especially high risk of violence because their gender expression breaks social norms and draws more hostile attention. Many transgender people lack secure housing, and reported conversion therapy in 2023 included a transgender man attempting suicide after being forced to attend prayer camp. During the 2010-2011 post-electoral crisis, the Force Républicaines de Côte d’Ivoire beat and abused gay men and transgender persons, most of them sex workers, with complaints not filed for fear of reprisals, and fighters were more aggressive toward transvestis, defined as transgender and otherwise gender non-conforming people assigned male at birth. In 2012 FRCI members repeatedly raided Le Club, a bar frequented by gender and sexual minorities, mainly targeting effeminate men and transvestis, forcing them into a cargo truck, sometimes forcing them to remove clothes, and demanding a significant fine under threat of being taken to bases. Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private are legal and have never been criminalized, due in part to Ivory Coast being a former French colony not inheriting sodomy laws. Article 360 of the Penal Code punishes public breach of decency with three months to two years imprisonment and a 50,000 to 500,000 francs fine, and where the breach consists of an indecent or contrary-to-nature act with an individual of the same sex, six months to two years imprisonment and a 50,000 to 300,000 francs fine, doubled if committed against a minor or in presence of a minor of eighteen years. Under Articles 358 and 359 the age of consent is 18 for homosexual couples and 15 for heterosexual ones. The government does not recognize same-sex couples. Gay and lesbian individuals and couples are not legally recognized as eligible to adopt. There is no legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation. In 2024 President Ouattara promised to introduce a bill to Parliament to "counter the expansion" of homosexuality. Sexual minorities, transgender and gender non-conforming people are seen as abnormal and their identities are perceived as stemming from the Global North. LGBTQ people are subject to violence, with 45 assault incidents recorded in Abidjan between early September and late October 2024, social media influencers calling for violence, misinformation including a hoax that the French President asked the Ivorian President to legalize same-sex marriage, and a homophobia-motivated attack at a market employing gay hair stylists, after which people avoided going out during the day and meeting publicly and remained hypervigilant, while wealthier people are treated with less hostility. As of 2023 state authorities are slow and sometimes ineffective at managing civilian violence but may be improving in understanding and handling complaints, yet many do not report to police believing they will not be taken seriously, with reports of police not taking violence seriously and often blaming victims. Discrimination continues in healthcare, housing and employment, with evictions and family expulsions causing school dropout, refusal to hire or promote or firing if discovered, a doctor refusing service a few years before September 2011 because of sexual orientation until protest led to care being provided, and a vocal minority of Muslim and Christian leaders preaching against the community. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance toward transgender people specifically; the only tolerance assessment quoted concerns gay people: "There is still discrimination against gay people, but generally we are moving toward relative tolerance."

texts.cleaned_text: BBC (12 May 2021): Douala court jailed trans woman Shakiro (YouTuber) and friend Patricia for five years under 'attempted homosexuality' plus 200,000 CFA francs ($370) each — the maximum statutory term — with appeal filed; detained since February 2021. exact_spans: Her case and exile form part of Cameroon's record of criminalisation prosecutions.
texts.cleaned_text: Wikipedia biography of Shakiro (b. 29 July 1997, Douala): Cameroonian trans activist who gained a Facebook and YouTube following discussing trans life; arrested and charged with 'attempted homosexuality' in 2021, sentenced to five years, and subsequently fled Cameroon to claim asylum abroad.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Cameroon: documents discrimination against gays and lesbians among societal abuses, alongside security-force killings, torture, harsh prisons, and arbitrary arrests - the criminalisation context (Article 347).

Human Rights Watch (11 May 2022): documented a 2022 uptick of violence against LGBTI people — since 9 March, security forces arbitrarily arrested at least 6 and detained 11 people, all victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity; gendarmes beat two in detention. Frames the pattern: the criminalisation law lets both civilians and security forces abuse LGBTI people without consequence, per HRW senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi.

CNN (9 Jan 2013): A Cameroon appeals court acquitted Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome, jailed for five years in November 2011 solely because they wore women's clothes and ordered Baileys; the original judge had cited their dress, speech and the drink as proof they were gay. Lawyer Alice Nkom said the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts, and Amnesty welcomed the acquittal. Arrests on effeminacy or appearance grounds under the colonial-era sodomy law carry sentences of six months to five years.

Criminalisation and sentences: In February 2021 two Cameroonian transgender women, Shakiro and Patricia, were arrested in Douala for wearing women's clothing in a restaurant and convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification. Identification failure was therefore charged alongside the anti-homosexuality counts, and both women received five years. Jean-Claude Roger Mbede was arrested in 2011 for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance. No information on legal gender recognition, name change, or ID and marker procedures appears.

Entry and visa: No visa policy, entry-refusal, or border-admission procedure for Cameroon is described. The nearest material concerns outbound asylum. In July 2010 the UK granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum, prompting Minister of Communication Issa Tchiroma Bakary to argue that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities and that 'he is not the only gay person in Cameroon.' A link to UK government travel advice on Cameroonian laws and customs is listed; no Cameroonian entry rule for LGBTQ travelers is given.

Border and carriage screening: A gay Cameroonian man was granted temporary immigration bail from the UK Border Agency in August 2011 after Air France refused to carry him to Yaoundé. In May 2012 the UK Border Agency sought to return asylum-seeker Ediage Valerie Ekwedde, finding 'no credible evidence' that he was gay, but held him in custody after he threatened to 'make a fuss' on the return flight. In May 2005 the government threatened medical examinations to 'prove' the homosexual activity of 11 men arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy. No Cameroonian border screening procedure is set out.

Facilities: Mbede served a three-year sentence at Kondengui Central Prison. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe Douala's main prison as 'hell', and Shakiro and Patricia spent five months in prison before release pending appeal in 2021. Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organization, shut down after a police raid, removing a service base. Three young men were sentenced to five years in November 2011 for oral sex in a parked car, and two men received five years on the basis of appearance, women's clothing and ordering a cream-based liquor.

Care access: Healthcare, HIV, and medication access for transgender visitors is not described. The service findings are institutional: Alternatives-Cameroon was forced to shut down after a police raid, and few lawyers are willing to defend the accused in homosexuality cases. The 2005 threat of medical examinations to 'prove' homosexual activity among detained men represents coercive contact with health services rather than care.

State and media hostility: In 2006 tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people claimed to be homosexual, boosting circulation and drawing criticism from the state communication council for privacy invasion, while President Paul Biya publicly urged respect for privacy and continued prosecuting people accused of homosexual activity. The Law on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime (Law No. 2010/012, Article 83(1)) criminalizes online same-sex sexual propositions with 1 to 2 years' imprisonment and fines of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, doubled where intercourse followed. A 2020 assessment described Cameroon as prosecuting consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any country in the world, and the US Department of State's 2010 report noted harassment and extortion of gays and lesbians by law enforcement and false allegations used to harass or extort. On 30 June 2024 President Biya's daughter Brenda Biya came out as a lesbian on Instagram, sparking national backlash and hope among LGBTQ Cameroonians.

Youth and education: No contemporary youth, school, or minor-specific legal policy is covered. The only youth-adjacent material is historical ethnography. In 1921 Günther Teonmann documented a same-sex custom among the Bafia people, where the 'kiembe' stage begins around age 15 and involves close male sexual friendships with a 'lexan', with consent symbolized by sharing earthnuts from a basketry plate, and where a father might later name his newborn after the lexan regardless of gender. Two young men were sentenced to five years in 2011 for oral sex in a parked car, and Bakary dismissed asylum claims by asserting that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private acts. Nothing on trans-youth travel, medication, or education targets is documented.

In February 2021, two Cameroonian transgender women, Shakiro and Patricia, were arrested on February 8 in Douala for "wearing women's clothing in a restaurant." They spent five months in prison following the arrest. They were later convicted of "attempted homosexuality, public indecency, and failing to carry identification." They received five-year sentences for these convictions. A judge ordered the pair to be released "until a court could hear their appeals." Douala's main prison is described as "hell" by prisoners accused of homosexuality. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is illegal in Cameroon. Cameroon's first Penal Code enacted in 1965 did not criminalise consensual same-sex sexual acts, but an ordinance issued in September 1972 by President Ahmadou Ahidjo introduced Article 347bis (now 347-1). Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime criminalises online same-sex sexual propositions, with Article 83(1) punishing sexual propositions to a person of the same sex through electronic communications with one to two years imprisonment and a fine of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs or only one of these penalties, doubled under Article 83(2) when followed by sexual intercourse. As of 2020, Cameroon prosecutes consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any country in the world. In May 2005, 11 men were arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy with threatened medical examinations to prove activity, detained into February 2006 with trials scheduled March 2006 and released in April 2006. In 2011 at least a dozen men were detained under Section 347, including Jean-Claude Roger Mbede sentenced to three years imprisonment at Kondengui Central Prison for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance, and on 24 November 2011 three young men were sentenced to five years imprisonment for oral sex in a parked car. In November 2011 two young men arrested outside a nightclub were convicted to five years imprisonment based solely on appearance and behavior, with the judge holding speech manner, wearing women's clothing and ordering cream-based liquor sufficient evidence for homosexuality, a verdict later overturned on appeal.

A news outlet (12 May 2021): a court jailed a trans woman and her friend for five years under 'attempted homosexuality' plus fines each — the maximum statutory term — with appeal filed; detained since February 2021. Lawyers called it a political decision with no proof of acts. Notes the national 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations, one of 31 countries criminalising, with beatings of gay/trans people common in public.

texts.cleaned_text: A news outlet (9 Jan 2013): an appeals court acquitted two men jailed five years in November 2011 solely because they wore women's clothes — the original judge had cited dress and speech as proof they were gay. Conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts. Arrests on appearance grounds under a historic-era sodomy law with six-month-to-five-year sentences.

Stakeholder submission to the DRC's 5th-cycle UPR (March 2024) by Savie asbl NGO and others: the DRC does not criminalise same-sex relations but neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights; public displays of same-sex affection can be prosecuted under indecent-exposure provisions (Article 176 of the Penal Code: 'anyone who publicly outrages morals by actions...').

Human Rights Watch, 4 Dec 2017: 120+ interviews, including nine Congolese security-force officers, UN officials and 21 M23 fighters, documented security forces recruiting ex-M23 fighters from Uganda and Rwanda in Oct–Dec 2016 and deploying them with orders to use lethal force against protesters in Kinshasa, Goma and Lubumbashi. State violence and impunity bear on visitor safety.

GayOut travel guide for DR Congo: rates the country 'High Risk for LGBTQ+' - no explicit national criminalisation but Article 176 ('indecent acts') and local ordinances applied to LGBTQ people; armed militia groups in eastern DRC have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity; state authority collapse means legal protections are theoretical.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror) on LGBTQ rights in the DRC: same-sex activity legal for both sexes (never outlawed, even under Belgian rule), equal age of consent; but no gender-identity recognition, no relationship recognition (same-sex marriage banned constitutionally since 2006), limited protections; church groups promote the view that homosexuality is immoral; public same-sex affection can trigger prosecution under indecency provisions.

Queer In The World (updated 3 Dec 2023; covers both Congos): DRC-specific parts — homosexuality legal but LGBT expression censored with imprisonment exposure; violence, harassment and torture against LGBT people reported involving police, security forces and army; no legal gender change for trans people; advises visitors discretion and low profile.

A stakeholder submission for the national periodic review (March 2024) by local LGBT organisations: the nation does not criminalise same-sex relations but neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights; public displays of same-sex affection can be prosecuted under indecent-exposure provisions (Article 176 of the Penal Code).

A rights investigation (4 Dec 2017): interviews with former security-force officers and others document security forces recruiting ex-rebel fighters from a neighbouring country and deploying them to use lethal force against protesters in major cities — background on official violence and impunity; no LGBT-specific content.

A travel guide rates the nation 'High Risk for LGBTQ+': no explicit national criminalisation but Article 176 ('indecent acts') and local ordinances applied to LGBTQ people; armed militia groups commit extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity, with collapsing official authority making legal protections theoretical.

An encyclopaedia mirror on LGBT rights in the nation: same-sex activity legal for both sexes with equal age of consent; but no gender-identity recognition, no relationship recognition (same-sex marriage banned constitutionally since 2006), limited protections; church groups promote the view that homosexuality is immoral; public same-sex affection can trigger prosecution under indecency provisions.

A travel guide (updated 3 Dec 2023): homosexuality legal but LGBT expression censored with imprisonment exposure; violence, harassment and torture against LGBT people reported involving police, security forces and army; no legal gender change for trans people; advises visitors to keep a low profile.

EUAA COI Query Response Q29 (May 2024) on the Republic of the Congo: systematic review of legislation, implementation, treatment by state and society, and availability of state protection for LGBTQI+ people. Key findings: no law criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between adults; Penal Code Article 331 (per ILGA) sets age of consent at 21 for same-sex vs 18 for different-sex acts; the under-21 'shameless act / against nature' provision's scope as applied to same-sex conduct is 'ambiguous', and sources say it is used to justify discrimination.

US State Department 2022 human rights report (Republic of the Congo), SOGI section: no law specifically prohibits consensual same-sex conduct between adults; a provision punishes 'shameless acts or acts against nature' with a person of the same sex under age 21 (6 months–3 years plus fine), scope ambiguous and not invoked for prosecutions. Police at times cite the provision to extract bribes from gay men; local NGOs reported violence, psychological/physical harassment, and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by government and nonstate actors.

US State Department 2023 human rights report (Republic of the Congo): no known arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the ambiguous under-21 provision during 2023; police continued using the 'act against nature' law as a pretext to solicit bribes from men; NGOs reported continuing psychological/physical harassment and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by both government actors and nonstate actors, with no anti-discrimination protections in law.

There is no legally recognized way to change one's gender identity. There is no broad legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. There are no laws addressing hate crimes. There are no laws addressing discrimination in education, healthcare, housing, or employment. There are no laws addressing conversion therapy or surgeries on intersex children intended to make their bodies fit expected norms. The personal-data protections cited in the article cover sexual orientation and sexual life, not gender identity. Same-sex relationships have been legal since 1940. The 1940 Penal Code as amended in 2006 only prohibits same-sex sexual behaviour with a person younger than 21 years, compared to 18 years for opposite-sex sexual activity. Same-sex marriage is explicitly banned under Section 2, Article 127 of the Family Code, which defines marriage as a public act establishing a lasting union between a man and a woman. The unequal age of consent is not used for arrests, but police have used the Penal Code to solicit bribes from young men perceived as gay and have falsely claimed same-sex activity is generally illegal to solicit bribes; such abuses are rarely reported due to fear of police interaction but are investigated when reported. There is no broad legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and no laws on hate crimes or on discrimination in education, healthcare, housing, or employment. Article 19 of Law No. 27-2020 on the Fight against Cybercrime prohibits placing or storing personal data revealing sexual orientation without a legal exception or expressed consent. Violation is punishable by one to five years in prison, a fine of one million to ten million CFA francs, or both. Articles 8, 10 and 15 of Decree No. 2025-66 relating to the Personal data of Air Passengers protect sexual orientation, and Articles 4, 14 and 40 of Law No. 29-2019 on the Protection of Personal Data protect sexual life as sensitive and personal data. The article contains no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; all tolerance and violence findings are framed around LGBTQ people generally or homosexual neighbors. Social stigma was linked to no significant gay or lesbian community presence in 2010, with no cases of violence or discrimination reported to non-governmental organizations or news media at that time, though instances may have been unreported. Violence toward LGBTQ+ people rose in 2022 due to forced confinement during the COVID-19 pandemic, with increasing economic hardship further contributing, and most violence was committed by family members. State authorities and regular citizens committed violence against LGBTQ+ people in 2022 and 2023, while reported violence against LGBTQ people is punished by law enforcement. In a survey conducted from 2021 to 2023, 73 percent of Congolese people in Brazzaville said they would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbor. LGBTQ civil societies were present in 2023 but had been unable to gain legal recognition. In 2020 a non-governmental organization was denied legal registration until references to the organization's focus on the LGBTQ+ community were removed.

An official country-of-origin assessment (May 2024): systematic review of legislation, implementation, treatment by official institutions and society, and availability of official protection for LGBTQI+ people; no law criminalises consensual same-sex conduct, a penal article sets a higher age of consent for same-sex acts, and that provision's scope is described as 'ambiguous' and used to justify discrimination.

An official human-rights report (2022): no law specifically prohibits consensual same-sex conduct; a provision punishes 'shameless acts or acts against nature' with a person of the same sex under 21, scope ambiguous and not invoked for prosecutions; police at times cite it to extract bribes; local NGOs reported violence, psychological and physical harassment, and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons.

An official human-rights report (2023): no known arrests or prosecutions under the ambiguous under-21 provision during 2023; police continued using the 'act against nature' law as a pretext to solicit bribes; NGOs reported continuing psychological and physical harassment and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons; no anti-discrimination protections in law.

PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.

A news outlet (April 2023): parliament voted to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law - exposure of up to ten years under the 1969 crimes act - through a crimes amendment bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people.

A news outlet (October 2020): decriminalisation stalled again - members deferred the crimes bill report by three months. Traces the full path: the 1969 sections criminalised sex between men and indecent acts between males; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and the offences were struck from the draft, then restored by members.

A news outlet (August 2017): a draft crimes bill, written with legal help from the governing state, would remove the 1969 sections - up to seven years for sex between men and five years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population roughly 21,000; the islands' only LGBTI community organisation had a submission before the committee.

A public broadcaster (August 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the crimes bill intended to replace the outdated 1969 crimes act; the clerk of parliament confirmed a submission from the islands' LGBTI community organisation.

El País (14 Apr 2025): the transphobic murder of Sara Millerey, 32, in Bello (Antioquia, near Medellín) — a 28-second video, viral since 5 April, shows her flailing in a creek unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands before drowning; her mother Sandra Borja: 'They killed her for being who she was.' President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities; the report notes 13 trans people killed in Q1 2025.

CNN (6 Aug 2025): killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case — in Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals ('All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans'); describes Millerey's limbs broken before she was pushed into churning water outside Medellín, and frames the repeated killings of LGBTQ people as calculated brutality even amid the country's decades-long civil war.

The Guardian (30 Jul 2024): more than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023, and armed groups threaten a further wave of 'social cleansing' in Caquetá — flyer campaigns announce cleansing of 'drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots'. Trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men; trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work; a friend of interviewee Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

Outright International country overview (updated Mar 2026): strong formal protections (marriage since 2016, adoption since 2015, ID change without medical exams) versus documented killing — the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025. July 2023: the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution (a crime against humanity); UN Human Rights Committee noted concern.

JURIST (May 2025): UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination Graeme Reid concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities — praised the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality, but warned of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience: widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT individuals must be urgently addressed as killings rise.
Ambito Jurídico (in Spanish): a Colombian court protected the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty in a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

International Business Times (June 2015): Colombia approved a rule change letting trans people change the sex marker on government-issued ID by signing a document before a notary. The new route replaced the previous one in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric exams, which official Reyes called 'profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice'.

Wikipedia country coverage on Colombia states that consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized in 1981, that law reforms in the 1990s equalized the age of consent at 14 for homosexual and heterosexual sex, and that Judgment C-507 of 1999 declared unconstitutional the military prohibition on 'homosexual acts'. Congress passed a law in 2011 penalizing discrimination based on sexual orientation with one to three years' imprisonment plus fines. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed: the 'Inconvertibles' bill of Congressperson Mauricio Toro, introduced 10 May 2022, had failed by 2024, and Congressperson Carolina Giraldo proposed the similar bill 'Quiérele siempre' in 2025.

The coverage records the Constitutional Court's repeated protection of public expression of same-sex affection. In 1994 the Court disapproved the National Council of Television's refusal to air a commercial featuring a same-sex couple. Judgment T-268 of 2000 permitted a gay pride parade the Mayor of Neiva had blocked. Judgment T-301 of 2004 ordered Santa Marta police to stop harassing homosexuals at the city boardwalk. Judgment T-314 of 2011 held the Tequendama Hotel's refusal of access to homosexuals at two events as discriminatory. Judgment T-909 of 2011 ordered Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali to take a course so as not to repress homosexuals expressing affection in public. As of 2020 military culture still discouraged discussion of same-sex attraction under a 'se puede ser, pero no demostrar' (you can exist, but not show off) norm.

In March 2016 the first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

The coverage states that access to public and commercial facilities has been protected by court order, citing judgment T-314 of 2011 on the Tequendama Hotel, judgment T-909 of 2011 on Cosmocentro mall's guardianship officials and security firm, and judgment T-301 of 2004 on Santa Marta police at the boardwalk. The 2016 Ministry of Interior presidential decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup. A May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. Bogotá and Medellín have thriving gay neighbourhoods, bars and counselling and legal advice centres.

The Constitutional Court extended social security (health insurance) benefits to same-sex couples on 5 October 2007 and pension rights on 17 April 2008, so same-sex couples now enjoy the main benefits heterosexual couples have under the same terms. In 2012 the Court found that sexual orientation cannot be a criterion for preventing blood donation and ordered the Ministry of Health and Social Protection to rewrite donation regulations so they assess risk by sexual behaviour rather than orientation. The 2016 government decree specifically addresses LGBTI rights in health care. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS at Universidad de los Andes, recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilization as a prerequisite for other physical changes. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed as of 2025.

Colombian society remains generally conservative despite supportive media coverage, including gay characters in programmes such as the prime-time soap opera Dr Mata and a lesbian scene in A corazón abierto. A bloc of conservative senators defeated the civil union bill in Congress on 19 June 2007. The country's Inspector General asked the Constitutional Court in 2015 to invalidate all same-sex marriages approved in Colombia. By 31 March 2016 a campaign to force a referendum repealing the November 2015 same-sex adoption ruling had gathered 1.8 million signatures including 45 members of Congress, and a Congress committee shelved it 20 to 12 in May 2017. An Invamer poll of October 2019 put same-sex marriage support at 50% against 47% opposed, and adoption at 36% in favour against 62% opposed, while 2016 polls showed 37% to 40% support for marriage and only 22% for adoption. That referendum drive targeted exactly these rights for children of same-sex couples.

The coverage states that in 1998 the Constitutional Court ruled that public school teachers cannot be fired for revealing their sexual orientation and that private religious schools cannot ban gay students from enrolling. After student Sergio Urrego committed suicide in August 2014 following discrimination by his teachers, the Constitutional Court ruled for his family and ordered the Ministry of Education to review, within a year, the manuals of coexistence of all schools nationwide so that they contain no articles discriminating against children by sexual orientation or gender identity, meaning schools across the country cannot discriminate against students on those grounds. Youth-relevant family policy has also shifted: since 2014 LGBTQ individuals can adopt their partner's biological child, the 4 November 2015 ruling granted full same-sex adoption rights barring agency discrimination, and a 12 November 2015 ruling required birth registration listing two mothers or two fathers.

Major foreign daily (April 2025): the transphobic murder of a 32-year-old trans woman in a small town - thrown into a creek with fractured limbs and left to drown, filmed - shocked the country and terrified the trans community; her family demands justice.
A cable-news investigation (Aug 2025): after the brutal murder of a transgender woman, attacks and killings of trans and LGBT people in this country continue with little accountability.

Foreign broadsheet (July 2024): more than 40 trans women were killed in this country the previous year; armed groups in one region are threatening a wave of 'social cleansing' - trans women report being killed 'for what we are' and repeatedly forced to flee.
NOTE: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying LGBTIQ rights organisation's page addresses access to rights for LGBTIQ people in this country.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): strong legal protections - 1999 constitutional-court rulings restricting nonconsensual intersex surgeries; same-sex marriage since 2011 (refusals illegal since 2016); adoption since 2015; simplified legal gender recognition since 2015; a third legal gender classification for nonbinary people recognised March 2022; 2025 court order against a volleyball-league regulator for discrimination.

Legal news outlet (May 2025): a UN independent expert, concluding a fact-finding visit across this country, praised legal reforms but warned of a stark gap between institutional progress and lived reality - discrimination and violence persist, particularly against trans women and those facing intersecting marginalisation (migrants, indigenous people, youth, persons with disabilities).
Regional legal-news outlet: a court in this country protected the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty - ruling on treatment of trans detainees.

Foreign news agency (Nov 2025): the national civil-registry authority announced that citizens will be able to record 'trans' and 'non-binary' in the sex field of identity documents - 'a key step' for recognising gender-diverse identification.

Foreign business daily (June 2015): this country allowed trans people to change name and sex on ID cards without physical or psychiatric examinations - a notarised declaration replaces the previous 'cumbersome' process that involved judges ordering bodily inspections; the justice minister approved the decree.

A Reuters report (Dec 2024) covers a couple in Comoros released after a same-sex sentencing verdict.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report (Comoros): same-sex conduct is criminalised under the penal code, but authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions during 2023 and did not actively enforce the law. No non-discrimination law exists. Police reported not to incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons, and none was reported that year. Widespread impunity is listed among major human-rights problems.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Comoros records limited content on LGBT issues. The report otherwise documents poor prison conditions, restrictions on movement, press and religion, and discrimination against women.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Art. 300 of the 2020 penal code punishes same-sex acts with 6 months–2 years plus a 100,000–300,000 franc (US$240–720) fine; no discrimination protections, no legal gender-marker change, no known LGBTIQ organisations (Art. 5 of Law 86-006/AF chills registration); enforcement documented — first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy after a leaked video (2022), first same-sex arrests of two women June 2024, conviction Dec 2024 with time served; government repeatedly refused UN decriminalisation recommendations.

Washington Blade (23 Dec 2024): Comoros court on 12 Dec 2024 sentenced two lesbian women to five and six months for homosexuality and released them with time served — the couple had been arrested in June 2024 after asking an imam to marry them; first conviction of this kind, called a human-rights violation by Human Dignity Trust; article cites Art. 318 (up to five years) as the provision.

Transgender people are not allowed to change their gender markers. There is no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. The Labor Code (2012) does not provide protections for LGBTQ people. There are no LGBTQ+ organizations in the country. Such organizations could potentially be prosecuted under Article 5 of Law No. 86-006/AF (1986) which prohibits organizations founded on an "unlawful cause or for an unlawful purpose, contrary to the law or public morals." Both male and female same-sex sexual acts are illegal in the Comoros. Article 300 of the 2020 Penal Code provides that "Any act of a sexual nature contrary to morality or unnatural shall be punished with a sentence of six months to two years and a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs." Previously, the 1982 Penal Code punished such acts with up to five years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs. The government has repeatedly refused to decriminalize homosexuality when advised to by bodies of the United Nations. The first prosecution of consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults under the 2020 Penal Code was in 2022, involving a man prosecuted after a sexual video of him with another man was leaked online. In 2024, two women were detained from June until December after allegedly asking an imam to marry them, which was not proven in court, but the women said they had previously engaged in sexual activity together. They were convicted for homosexuality and sentenced to five and six months in prison respectively, and were released after the December ruling because the sentence was shorter than the detention period. There is no recognition of legal rights for same-sex couples, and the Family Code establishes marriage as the union of a man and a woman. LGBTQ persons face stigmatization among the broader population. Most LGBTQ+ people do not disclose their sexual orientation or gender identity as of 2023. LGBTQ+ people face cultural discrimination as well as discrimination while seeking education and employment opportunities. Some LGBTQ+ people are ostracized from their homes, neighborhoods, and villages. According to Gallup, 26 percent responded in 2023 that the area they lived would be a good place for LGBTQ+ people, a 10 percent increase from the previous year. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.
Comoros's 2020 Penal Code Article 300 criminalizes an indecent or unnatural act with a person of the same sex, imposing two to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs.

texts.cleaned_text: A government annual human-rights report (2023): same-sex conduct criminalised under the penal code, but authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions during 2023 and did not actively enforce the law; no non-discrimination law; police reported not to incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons and none was reported that year; widespread impunity listed among major human-rights problems.
A government 2010 human-rights report: general human-rights baseline (poor prisons, restrictions on movement/press/religion, discrimination against women) with limited LGBT-specific content.

A human-rights organisation (updated 12 Mar 2026): a penal-code article punishes same-sex acts with 6 months–2 years plus a fine (a few hundred dollars); no discrimination protections, no legal gender-marker change, no known LGBTIQ organisations (registration chilled by an association-restricting law); enforcement documented — first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy after a leaked video (2022), first same-sex arrests of two women June 2024, conviction Dec 2024 with time served; the government repeatedly refused international decriminalisation recommendations.

A news outlet (23 Dec 2024): a court on 12 Dec 2024 sentenced two women to five and six months for homosexuality and released them with time served — the couple had been arrested in June 2024 after asking a religious official to marry them; first conviction of this kind, called a human-rights violation by a human-rights organisation; the report cites a penal-code article (up to five years) as the provision.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations not criminalised; employment discrimination protection covers sexual orientation (not gender identity); no same-sex union recognition; LGBTIQ orgs register freely; first public Pride 2013 (second African country); 2019–21 polls: 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour; Cabo Verde one of two African UN LGBTI Core Group members, made 2024 UPR anti-discrimination commitments.

Equal Eyes (20 Jul 2018): 2018 Pride Week in Praia — parade plus NGO campaigns (Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, Associação LGBTI de Praia, Associação Arco Iris) petitioning the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women engaged.

Observador/Lusa (11 Jul 2017): PM Ulisses Correia e Silva said same-sex marriage is not on the government's agenda, distancing himself from MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro's opposition, after LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 (May 2020): 'All in this together' - Africans are tolerant on ethnic, religious and national differences but not sexual differences; Cabo Verde, Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe stand out as particularly tolerant countries; tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak even among younger respondents.

Rede Angola interview (22 Jun 2016) with Tchinda Andrade, first publicly self-outed trans woman in Cabo Verde (came out 1997, age 19): describes Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed, but reports verbal violence and two physical attacks; civil law blocked her legal change to a female name — no legal gender recognition as of 2016.

The article provides no statute, provision, penalty, or procedure on legal gender recognition, change of gender markers on documents, screening, segregated facilities, custody, or medical care for transgender people. The sole transgender-specific account is that activist Tchinda Andrade came out as transgender in a local newspaper in 1998. The article states transgender people in Cape Verde are often referred to as "tchindas" by locals. The cited 2010 U.S. Department of State Human Rights Report found that societal discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity continued to be a problem. The same cited report found there were no lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender persons' organizations active in the country at that time. Cape Verde signed United Nations documents in 2008 stating human rights are not limited based on sexual orientations or gender identities and in 2011 condemning violence and discrimination against LGBT people. Under the 1886 Penal Code Article 71 unnatural acts were illegal. In 2004 Cape Verde amended its Penal Code to remove all provisions relating to consensual homosexual sex, becoming the second African country to decriminalize homosexuality after South Africa. At decriminalization the legal age of consent was 16, the same as for consensual heterosexual acts, and as of 2015 the age of consent is 14. Cape Verde does not recognize same-sex unions, and on 11 July 2017 Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva stated legalization of same-sex marriage was not on the agenda. Since 2008 articles 45(2) and 406(3) of the Labour Code have banned workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation, with penalty of a fine varying case-by-case, making Cape Verde one of few African countries with such protections. Article 406(3) provides the penalty shall also apply to unlawful dismissal based on racial grounds, belonging to a particular ethnic group, religious motives, sexual orientation or any other discriminatory reason. Internationally, Cape Verde signed a 2008 UN General Assembly document stating human rights are not limited based on sexual orientations or gender identities, a 2011 document condemning violence and discrimination against LGBT people, and in 2025 during International LGBTQIA+ Pride Day signed a Spain-proposed joint declaration in favor of LGBTQ rights as the only African country to do so. The article contains no documented statement about societal tolerance specifically toward transgender people; all tolerance findings are framed around gays, lesbians, homosexual neighbours, or LGBT people generally. It reports Cape Verde is one of the most tolerant countries in Africa towards gays and lesbians and has occasionally been described as the most tolerant nation in Africa with regard to LGBT people, though there are still reports of societal discrimination. It states Sao Vicente is known for being very welcoming to the LGBT community. It records growth from no LGBT organizations active in 2010 to establishment of Associacao Gay de Cabo Verde by 2013, the first pride parade in Mindelo in June 2013, the first Praia pride three years later, and the 2018 Praia Pride organized with ICIEG and the Praia Government calling for legalisation of same-sex marriage and anti-discrimination legislation. A 2020 Afrobarometer poll found 80% of Cape Verdeans would welcome or would not be bothered by having a homosexual neighbour, with Cape Verde one of only four African countries polled with a majority in favour. The cited 2010 U.S. Department of State report found societal discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity continued to be a problem despite legal provisions protecting homosexual conduct.

On 18 December 2008 Cabo Verde joined 65 other states in supporting a UN General Assembly statement reaffirming that human rights apply equally regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity, expressing concern over violence, harassment, discrimination, exclusion, stigmatization and prejudice, condemning killings, torture, arbitrary arrest and deprivation of economic, social and cultural rights including the right to health, and urging all states to promote and protect the human rights of all persons regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity and to end criminal penalties on that basis.

On 28 June 2025 Cabo Verde joined a 15-state foreign-ministers joint commitment rejecting violence, criminalization, stigmatization and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, supporting eradication of transphobic harassment, promoting diversity and anti-discrimination policies and socio-labour inclusion especially for trans persons, calling for repeal of and refusal to introduce laws punishing sexual orientation and gender identity, demanding an end to criminal prosecution including imprisonment and death penalty and to conversion practices targeting sexual orientation and gender identity, and committing public authorities to implement effective LGBTIQ+ equality under international human rights standards.

International LGBT-rights organisation overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations are not criminalised; employment discrimination protection covers sexual orientation (not gender identity); no same-sex-union recognition; LGBTIQ organisations register freely; the first public pride was held in 2013, only the second in its region; polls from 2019 to 2021 found most residents would accept a homosexual neighbour; this country is one of two UN LGBTI core-group members in its region and made 2024 universal-periodic-review anti-discrimination commitments.

Human-rights database (20 July 2018): the 2018 pride week, held in the capital, featured a parade plus NGO campaigns — local organisations petitioning the national legislature for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; a national gender-equality institute and a UN women's body were engaged.

News agency report (11 July 2017): the head of government said same-sex marriage is not on the government's agenda, distancing himself from a governing-party secretary-general's opposition, after LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Regional survey organisation dispatch (May 2020): respondents in the region are tolerant on ethnic, religious and national differences but not sexual differences; this country stood out with two regional peers as particularly tolerant; tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak even among younger respondents.

Media interview (22 June 2016) with a trans woman who came out in the late 1990s: she described this country as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other countries in its region, but reported verbal violence and two physical attacks; civil law blocked her legal change to a female name — no legal gender recognition as of 2016.

texts.cleaned_text: LegalClarity overview (30 May 2026): documents Cuba's arc from the UMAP forced-labour camps for gay men (1965-68, ~60 hrs/week cutting cane in Camagüey, electric-shock and injection 'curing' experiments) to today's progressive framework — 1979 Penal Code removal of consensual same-sex acts, Castro's public acceptance of blame (La Jornada, 2010), Resolution 126 (2008) trans healthcare in the public system, the 2019 Constitution (Art 42, first to name sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories), and the 2022 Family Code (same-sex marriage/adoption, legal gender change without surgery). Notes the gap between law and daily life: Labor Code Law 116 bars SOGI discrimination but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground, and the Labor Code's article 2(b) covers orientation, not identity.

Americas Quarterly (15 Sept 2022): previews Cuba's 25 Sept 2022 Family Code referendum, only the 4th national vote since 1959, which would guarantee marriage equality, surrogacy, codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights. Opponents cite religious objections and fear child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No purely to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown (1,400+ arrestees) and record emigration. The equality settlement is contested rather than state-enforced.

exact_spans: Historical baseline (pre-2019 constitution) showing official institutions campaigning for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s.
texts.cleaned_text: Links International Journal of Socialist Renewal (23 Dec 2011): sympathetic first-person account 'Rainbow Cuba' disputing claims of systematic state homophobia — documents the UMAP camps (conscripts paid seven pesos a day), the 1975 declaration-era turning point, and CENESEX's state-backed programme: a trans-rights campaign, work with the police and the supreme court, and sexual-diversity education.

Washington Blade (21 Dec 2013): Cuban lawmakers approved a labor-law amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation after intense parliamentary debate. Mariela Castro of CENESEX proposed extending the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status; the trans-specific amendment drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators, while passage of the sexual-orientation ban was the confirmed outcome. The measure predates the 2019 Constitution and the 2022 Family Code.

texts.cleaned_text: Washington Blade (26 May 2018): documents Cuba's use of 'treason'/'treason against the homeland' charges against LGBTI citizens who flee to seek asylum — Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to 8 years in prison if they returned after filing Dutch asylum claims (Jan 2018); a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained (19 May 2018), and LGBTI activists (incl. Nelson Gandulla, Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation) remained monitored.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is illegal in Cuba. Since 1993, transgender persons may serve openly in the Cuban Revolutionary Armed Forces. In 2012, Adela Hernández became the first known transgender person to hold public office in Cuba, winning election as delegate to the City Council of Caibarien in Villa Clara province. In 2001, police carried out a campaign against gay and trans people, preventing them from meeting in the street, fining them and closing meeting places. In 2004, police carried out a campaign specifically directed at travestis (transvestites), arresting those dressed in women's clothing. Pride parades in Havana are held every May to coincide with the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia, with attendance growing every year. In 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025, Cuba voted in favor of renewing the mandate of the United Nations independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity. Private, non-commercial sexual relations between same-sex consenting adults aged 16 and over have been legal in Cuba since 1979. The Social Defence Code, which characterized homosexual practices as a social threat, was repealed in 1979, the crime of public display of homosexual condition was repealed in 1987, and the crime of bothering or soliciting with homosexual requests was amended in 1997 to refer only to sexual requests. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is illegal in Cuba. The Constitution does not ban same-sex marriage, with the man-woman definition in Article 36 repealed in the February 2019 referendum and marriage now defined as based on free will and equality of rights. Following the September 2022 Family Code referendum, there is legal recognition of same-sex marriage, unions, same-sex adoption and non-commercial surrogacy. Since 1993, lesbian, gay and bisexual persons may serve openly in the Cuban Revolutionary Armed Forces. In 1988, the Public Ostentation Law of 1938 was repealed and police received orders not to harass LGBT people.

In July 2004 Cuban police in Havana targeted travestis wearing women's clothing for detention, issued municipal warnings to stop dressing as women, sanctioned three individuals under dangerousness law carrying up to four years imprisonment, closed private clubs hosting their shows, prohibited gay parties and denied entry to regular discos, forcing most to wear men's clothing in public and leading CENESEX to advise against appearing in women's clothing until the crackdown passed.

Legal overview (30 May 2026): documents the country's arc from historic forced-labour camps for gay men (1965-68, cutting cane, electric-shock and injection 'curing' experiments) to today's progressive framework — a 1979 penal-code removal of consensual same-sex acts, the former leader's public acceptance of blame (2010), a 2008 resolution providing trans healthcare in the public system, the 2019 constitution (first to name sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories), and the 2022 family code (same-sex marriage/adoption, legal gender change without surgery). Notes the gap between law and daily life: a labor-code provision bars discrimination on sexual orientation but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground, covering orientation, not identity.

GlobalGayz (updated Jan 2017): profiles the ABC islands (Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao) as 'quiet nests of gay-friendliness' inside the Kingdom of the Netherlands; Curaçao-specific findings: it opened an LGBT 'Pink House' centre in 2010, has full autonomy except defense/foreign affairs/Supreme Court alongside Aruba, and (with Sint Maarten and Aruba) acts as driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships 8 Sept 2016 — comparator context, not Curaçao law.

Caribisch Netwerk (22 Apr 2015, Dutch): representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should quickly receive equal rights; Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels (Pueblo Soberano) publicly backed 'equal rights for everyone' despite party colleague Winifred Raveneau's fierce opposition — Raveneau had forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel via a last-minute exceptionally strict permit. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites Curaçao's IGLTA award as 'most gay welcoming in the region'; a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is legal in Curaçao with an equal age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. Same-sex marriage has been legal since the 12 July 2024 ruling of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upholding the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Prior to that ruling, Curaçao was required as part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to recognize as valid same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, with no in-island marriage, civil union or other recognition available. The Criminal Code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including "heterosexual or homosexual orientation," with Article 1:221 defining discrimination as any distinction affecting recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights in political, economic, social, cultural or other social life fields. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year imprisonment. Relevant history includes the April 2015 agreement of all four constituent countries for equal rights throughout the Kingdom, the August 2015 Oliari and Others v. Italy ECHR ruling applicable to Curaçao requiring legal recognition, a 2017 limited-rights proposal to the Estates, and a marriage bill submitted 4 June 2019 and withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support.

A cultural report (updated January 2017): profiles the region's island territories in the kingdom as quietly gay-friendly; island-specific findings: an LGBT community centre opened in 2010, full autonomy except defence, foreign affairs and supreme-court matters.

A regional news outlet (April 2015, in the governing state's language): representatives of all kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on the region's island territories should quickly receive equal rights; a government commissioner publicly backed 'equal rights for everyone' despite a party colleague's fierce opposition to the rights push.

A legal compilation: both male and female same-sex sexual activity is legal with an equal age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse; same-sex marriage has been legal since the kingdom's supreme court ruling of 12 July 2024 upholding the appellate decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation.
