texts.cleaned_text: PinkNews (11 Aug 2009): UK MPs on the Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the Cayman Islands' draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave Cayman courts affording citizens less protection than the European Convention on Human Rights Art 14 requires; the FCO countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended.

exact_spans: Evidence of high official tolerance in the tourist-facing environment.
texts.cleaned_text: Cayman News Service (29 Jul 2021): around 600 people — including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs — joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade (Sat 7 Aug 2021 debut), an historic turnout with broad official participation; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection (organisers' condition amid public-space sensitivities).

Washington Blade (30 Dec 2020): immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who wed in Ireland. The Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie had struck down the same-sex marriage ban in March 2019; that ruling was overturned on appeal in Aug 2019, while the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived.

A news outlet (August 2009): members of the governing state's parliament on a foreign-affairs committee criticised the territory's draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave local courts affording citizens less protection than an international human-rights convention requires; the governing state's foreign office answered that the grounds list was open-ended.

A local news service (July 2021): around 600 people - including the premier, the governor, ministers and legislators - joined a local LGBT foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, a historic turnout with broad official participation; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection.

A rights news outlet (December 2020): immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of a couple who wed in a European country. The court of appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds; the grand court's chief justice had struck down the statutory same-sex marriage ban in March 2019 before the court of appeal restored it.

UPR-info Cyprus advocacy sheet (2024): Law 87(I)/2015 criminalises public incitement to violence/hatred on SOGI grounds; Law 31(I)/2017 makes prejudice motivation an aggravating sentencing factor; Law 39(I)/2023 bans and criminalises conversion practices; the legal gender recognition bill was approved by the Council of Ministers Sept 2022 with first parliamentary reading Nov 2022 (still pending at 2024); gender identity remains absent from equal-treatment grounds and no anti-homophobia action plan exists; prison guards received 2-day LGBTI+ training (Apr 2023) after anti-LGBTI harassment complaints to the Ombudswoman.

The European Commission Network of Legal Experts country report on gender equality in Cyprus (2024, reporting period 2023) sets out how EU equality rules are transposed into Cypriot national law, including gender-identity-related aspects of the legal framework.

Queer Cyprus Association UPR presentation (Erman Dolmacı, 4th-cycle): confirms the same three Criminal Code amendments (87(I)/2015 incitement, 31(I)/2017 aggravating factor, 39(I)/2023 conversion-practices ban), frames 'ISSUE 1' as trans and gender-diverse rights with the Sept 2022 LGR bill as the outstanding implementation step, and lists the state response to prior UPR recommendations — i.e. hate-speech law delivered, gender-identity discrimination ground and trans legislation not yet delivered.

Queer Cyprus 'Diversity of Colours' LGR booklet documents gender-recognition practice on the divided island: the framework is self-determination without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping, and the northern part of Cyprus runs its own recognition process, explicitly including recognition of non-binary identities. Queer Cyprus also operates a 7-days/week confidential psychosocial and legal support line covering identity, work, family, shelter, health and military-service issues.

ILGA 32nd UPR session report (29 Jan 2019): Cyprus received 8 SOGIESC recommendations and accepted all 8; national report stated new legislation for correcting registered sex (adults and minors) was in preparation requiring only a Registrar decision, no prior medical intervention or psychiatric reports; ECRI had urged gender identity as a prohibited discrimination ground; Cyprus joined the Equal Rights Coalition as 40th member (Aug 2018). Marks the reform promise the 2022 bill was meant to fulfil.

The European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Cyprus (2020, reporting period 2019) covers transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including SOGI grounds in Cypriot law.

PinkNews (10 Oct 2013): Cyprus amended its penal code to criminalise incitement to violence or hatred based on sexual orientation or gender identity, punishable by up to 3 years' imprisonment and/or a €5,000 fine; workplace SOGI protections were added in 2004. It is the hate-speech offence the 2015 law extended.

Cypriot law provides no general prohibition of discrimination based on gender identity, with the 2004 Equal Treatment in Employment and Occupation Law prohibiting only sexual-orientation discrimination in employment. Article 99 of the Penal Code, titled "Incitement to violence or hatred due to sexual orientation or gender identity," punishes intentional public threatening, insulting or offensive urging or incitement, orally or in writing, of violence or hatred on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity with imprisonment not exceeding three years or a fine not exceeding 5,000 euros. In October 2024 Parliament raised the hate-speech fine based on sexual orientation or gender identity from €5,000 to €10,000. No gender-recognition law is in force; a bill drafted with support of the President and Justice Minister and discussed after President Nicos Anastasiades met Accept-LGBT Cyprus in November 2017 would allow persons over 18 to change legal gender on the basis of self-determination without diagnosis, hormonal treatment or sex reassignment surgery, and on 10 June 2019 four parents of transgender children urged its speedy adoption after months of stalling and delay. In 2017 the Ministry of Education established the programme "HOMBAT-Combating Homophobic and Transphobic Bullying at Schools" to train and sensitise teachers and professors on bullying and harassment directed at LGBT students. As part of its 2019 Universal Periodic Review Cyprus accepted all seven LGBT-related recommendations, which included combating discrimination and violence, criminalising harassment, adopting an action plan against homophobia and transphobia, and adopting a gender recognition law. For 2017, antidiscrimination coverage formally extended to employment, social protection, social insurance, social benefits, health care, education, union and professional-organization participation and access to goods and services on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds, but an LGBTI NGO assessed the legislation as fragmented and inadequate, with housing benefits favouring "traditional" families and many LGBTI persons remaining not open about sexual orientation or gender identity and not reporting homophobic violence or discrimination. Male and female same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1998, after the European Court of Human Rights in Modinos v. Cyprus ruled that Criminal Code section 171 violated the right to private life, with formal Criminal Code revision in 1998 setting unequal ages of consent at 18 for homosexual and 16 for heterosexual conduct plus a crime of "promoting" homosexuality. The "promoting" ban was lifted in 2000 and ages of consent were equalised in 2002, with the universal age of consent now 17, while the military's former exclusion of homosexuals on the ground that homosexuality is a "mental illness" has been removed. In Northern Cyprus, deputies passed an amendment on 27 January 2014 repealing the colonial-era law punishing homosexual acts with up to five years' imprisonment. Marriage remains legally recognised only as a union between one man and one woman with no same-sex marriage recognition, but a civil-union law granting several marriage rights and benefits passed on 26 November 2015 by 39 in favour, 12 against and 3 abstentions and took effect on 9 December 2015, while adoption remains reserved to heterosexual couples only. The 2004 Equal Treatment in Employment and Occupation Law explicitly forbids sexual-orientation discrimination in employment to comply with the European Union Employment Framework Directive of 2000, with no prohibition of sexual-orientation discrimination outside employment. Article 99 punishes incitement to violence or hatred based on sexual orientation with imprisonment not exceeding three years and a fine raised in October 2024 from €5,000 to €10,000, while 2017 legal provisions also criminalized incitement based on sexual orientation with up to five years' imprisonment and up to €10,000, with 11 complaints examined in 2015 and five criminal prosecutions pending trial. Enforcement is inconsistent, with reports of incitement against LGBT people occasionally resulting in no police or legal action most notably when committed by clergy of the Greek Orthodox Church, including a February 2019 attack on a gay man in Nicosia where police failed to establish hate-crime motive and a second Nicosia incident four months later with no police action, and conversion therapy was criminalized by Parliament vote on 25 May 2023.

On 26 November 2015 Cyprus's House passed civil-unions legislation by 39 votes in favour, 12 against and 3 abstentions, granting legal recognition outside marriage and religion to both same-sex and opposite-sex life partners under statutory legislation termed 'civil unions' rather than contractual 'civil partnership', without extending to child adoption or gay marriage.
On 25 May 2023 Cyprus's House Plenum voted to criminalise conversion therapies.

An advocacy sheet (2024) records the protections in place — incitement to violence or hatred on identity grounds made a criminal offence, prejudice as an aggravating factor, and a conversion-practices ban — and that a self-determination legal recognition bill was approved in September 2022 and remains pending; gender identity is absent from equal-treatment grounds, no anti-homophobia action plan exists, and prison guards received two-day training after complaints.
A national network country report on gender equality (2024) records how the national equal-treatment rules are transposed into this country's law, including identity-related aspects of the framework.

Czechia: same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1962, following research by Kurt Freund concluding that homosexual orientation cannot be altered; homosexual prostitution was decriminalised in 1990, and the age of consent was equalised in 1990 at 15, having previously been 18 for homosexuals. In May 2024 the Constitutional Court ruled that forced surgery and sterilisation of transgender individuals is unconstitutional and gave the government until June 2025 to change the laws; in July 2025 the Health Ministry announced that trans people would no longer be required to undergo surgery or hormone treatment to change their legal gender. State rhetoric also framed trans bodies as criminal: on 27 June 2021 President Miloš Zeman said sex-reassignment surgery means 'you are committing a crime for inflicting self-harm' and that 'these transgenders truly disgust me.' Public expression is legal and visible but carries social risk. The first Prague Pride parade was held in August 2011 with mayoral support and drew negative responses from religious conservative groups and the far-right; it has run annually since 2012, and since 2014 organisers have barred pedophile promotional activity at Pride venues. Brno has hosted the Mezipatra gay and lesbian film festival every November since 2000, and a Prague City Council-produced gay guide and map appeared in late 2010. In the 2012 EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey of 93,000 LGBTQ people, only one in five Czech respondents was open about their orientation to all colleagues or classmates, 71% were selectively open at work or school, and 52% of gay men and 30% of lesbian women avoided holding hands in public outside gay neighbourhoods for fear of assault, threat or harassment; only one in five was open to all classmates, indicating school-level concealment. Facilities are concentrated in the capital: Prague has a large, well-developed gay nightlife scene centred on the Vinohrady district with at least 20 bars and clubs and 4 saunas, while gay venues are much more sparsely spread in other Czech towns, and the city acts as a magnet for the country's gay youth. Since 2001 the Czech Republic has granted 'persons living in a common household' hospital and prison visitation rights similar to married heterosexual couples, alongside inheritance and succession rights in housing. Blood donation opened to all citizens regardless of partner gender on 1 July 2024, replacing the previous ban on people with a same-gender partner, though people reporting anal sex with a new partner in the past four months are still excluded. Anti-discrimination protection under the 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in education as well as employment, housing and access to goods and services. Acceptance is markedly higher among younger Czechs: a 2013 Pew Research Center survey found 84% of 18–29-year-olds thought homosexuality should be accepted, versus 72% of those over 50, and a January 2020 Median poll showed younger respondents overwhelmingly supporting same-sex marriage while those aged 55 and above were mostly opposed.

Czech law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing and access to goods and services under the 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act. Hormonal treatment is prescribed through Sexology after living in the preferred social role for at least one year with positive Psychology and Endocrinology evaluation, with sexologists able to require additional evaluations or withhold treatment for any period. Transgender-related surgeries require approval by a Ministry of Health committee after one year of hormonal treatment, change of first name to a neutral one, and divorce if married because the process changes the gender marker. In May 2024 the Constitutional Court ruled forced surgery and sterilization of transgender individuals unconstitutional and gave the government until June 2025 to change the laws. In July 2025 the Health Ministry announced transgender people would no longer be required to undergo surgery or hormone treatment to officially change legal gender, a change welcomed by Trans*Parent which warned full legislative reform was still needed to prevent reversal by a new government or minister. Regarding military service, a trans woman was refused entry in 2004 and another trans recruit was rejected in 2014 for alleged reduction in morale of combat units, but by 2015 trans identity of candidates was no longer considered relevant to service. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized in 1962 and the age of consent was equalized at 15 in 1990, with homosexual prostitution also decriminalized in 1990. Since 2001 persons living in a common household have had inheritance, housing succession, and hospital and prison visitation rights, and registered partnerships for same-sex couples with many marriage rights took effect on 1 July 2006 after a presidential veto was overturned. A 2024 compromise law enshrined same-sex partnerships in the civil code equating them to marriage in all aspects except joint adoption while permitting step-child adoption, taking effect on 1 January 2025. LGBT people can individually adopt and the ban on adoption by those in registered partnership was struck down in 2016, but joint adoption by same-sex couples remains unavailable although concurrent individual adoption can give both partners parental rights. Czech law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, education, housing, access to goods and services under the 2009 law and in the military since 1999, with the Army allowing homosexuals to serve openly without questioning orientation. Since 1 July 2024 all citizens regardless of partner gender may donate blood, with exclusion only for those reporting anal sex with a new sexual partner in the past 4 months. The article provides no general-population tolerance figure for transgender people specifically; all acceptance polling cited concerns homosexuality, same-sex marriage, registered partnerships, and gay or lesbian neighbours or acquaintances. Living-conditions description refers to the country as relatively liberal and gay-friendly with a large gay community and nightlife in Prague, without a transgender-specific societal tolerance finding. The only transgender-specific attitudinal statement documented is by President Milos Zeman on 27 June 2021, who said he did "not understand 'transgender people' at all." In the same remarks he claimed: "If you undergo a sex-reassignment surgery, you are committing a crime for inflicting self-harm. It's a very dangerous procedure. These transgenders truly disgust me." No transgender-specific public-opinion outcome is provided to contrast or support that remark.

Paragraph 175 of the German Empire's Penal Code recriminalized same-sex sexual activity between men in 1871. Nazi Germany extended these laws during World War II, resulting in convictions multiplying to about 8,000 per year and 5,000–15,000 suspected offenders interned in concentration camps. East Germany decriminalized in 1968 and West Germany in 1969. In 2002 the government overturned Nazi-era convictions, and in 2017 the Bundestag unanimously passed a bill to pardon around 50,000 men convicted after the war, with compensation of €3,000 per conviction plus €1,500 per year of jail time; a compensation scheme was implemented in September 2021.

Transgender people have been allowed to change their legal gender since 1980 under the Transsexuals Act, which originally required genital surgery and sterilization. In January 2011 the Federal Constitutional Court ruled those requirements unconstitutional. Effective 1 November 2024, the Self-Determination Act, passed April 2024 by 374–251, allows adults to change gender by self-determination with three months' notice and applies to transgender, intersex and nonbinary adults. Since 1 January 2019 an intersex 'divers' option has been available on birth certificates, passports and driver's licenses under the Third Gender Act, though a doctor's statement confirming intersex status is required, which LGBT groups criticized; in April 2019 the option was clarified as applying to intersex people only, not transgender people.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is illegal in health services throughout Germany under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force 18 August 2006, and in education under the same act. Since May 2020 Germany has had a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors, making it the fifth country to do so, with penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to conversion therapy. Regarding blood donation, men who have sex with men were previously banned; a one-year deferral took effect in summer 2017, was reduced to four months in September 2021, and an individual risk-based assessment replaced the deferral from 1 April 2023. The German Medical Association is against explicit legalisation of assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and directs members not to perform such procedures, though this directive is not legally binding.

Same-sex couples have been legally recognized since 2001 through registered life partnerships, providing rights in inheritance, alimony, health insurance, immigration, hospital and jail visitations, and name change. Same-sex marriage became legal on 1 October 2017 after the Bundestag passed the bill on 30 June 2017 by 393–226, granting full marital and adoption rights. Same-sex stepchild adoption became legal in 2005 and expanded to 'successive adoption' in 2013. A Federal Court of Justice ruling in October 2018 held that the non-biological mother in a married lesbian couple is not automatically recognized on a child's birth certificate and must adopt, unlike heterosexual couples where the non-biological father is automatically recognized; a bill to rectify this inequality, initiated by the Greens in June 2018, was pending in the Bundestag.

In May 2019 the Federal Minister of Family Affairs recommended that teachers use gender-neutral forms, such as 'parent 1 and parent 2' instead of 'mother and father'. The age of consent was equalized at 14 years in East Germany in 1989 and in unified Germany in 1994. According to the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2013 survey, two-thirds of 20,000 German LGBT respondents concealed their sexual orientation at school and in public life.

texts.cleaned_text: Erasing 76 Crimes (24 May 2013): Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire of Dominica publicly called for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and 'all forms of violence' against LGBT people, citing the Holy See's position.

On 22 April 2024 the Dominica High Court ruled laws criminalising sodomy between consenting adults unconstitutional, making homosexuality legal; prior law criminalised both male and female same-sex sexual activity as well as anal intercourse between persons of the opposite sex. Under the Sexual Offenses Act 1998 as amended in 2016, section 14 punished gross indecency with 12 years imprisonment if the complainant was 16 or older and 14 years for a first offence and 20 years for a subsequent offence if under 16, exempting only private consensual adult male-female acts, while section 16 punished buggery with 25 years if by an adult on a minor, 10 years if by an adult on another adult, 5 years if by a minor, and 4 years for attempt or assault with intent, with discretion for the court to order admission to a psychiatric hospital for treatment. The court ordered section 14(2) to be read as exempting private consensual acts between adult persons who consent and section 16(1)(b) to be read as exempting private consensual adult acts from the 10-year penalty. Enforcement included 35 arrests for buggery between 1995 and 2000 resulting in fines and prison sentences up to ten years with some persons sent to psychiatric hospitals for treatment, and in 2001 15 women sentenced to five years for gross indecency and ten men sentenced to five years for engaging in gross indecency with persons of the same sex. In 2014 the Prime Minister said Dominica does not enforce its law against homosexual activity at least in private homes and has no plans to do so, while a gay man who filed suit in July 2019 challenging the 10-year and 12-year provisions reported police refused to investigate his vicious home attack because under Dominican law gay people were considered criminals. In April 2024 the High Court ruled sections 14 and 16 unconstitutional as criminalising consensual same-sex activity between adults. Dominica provides no recognition to same-sex unions as marriage or civil unions and no law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. In 2009 Evangelical Association president Bill Daniel stated "We want the government to ensure that gay tourists do not come to the island and conduct themselves in any immoral way," with the association protesting gay cruises visiting the island and promotion of Dominica as a "gay tourist destination." The article reports suspected hate crimes against individuals believed to be homosexuals and use in disputes of derogatory words like "buggerman" or "battyman" to refer to "effeminate" men. In 2010 Clement James of Portsmouth was stabbed to death after being accused of "watching" his male assailant in a public place, with accused Davis St Jean reported to preach in the street about killing gay people and to have said "all battie boi must dead" before the stabbing. A 2011 academic submission to the United Nations stated LGBTQ groups are forced to operate underground for fear members will be victimised and openly gay members complain of vandalism against their property. Reports to police by victims are reportedly not taken seriously with victims sometimes ridiculed, exemplified by the 2019 gay claimant whose report of physical and sexual assaults and home attack was refused investigation because of his sexuality. Wikipedia country coverage: Denmark's 1996 Act on Prohibition of Unequal Treatment in the Labor Market lists discrimination grounds including sexual orientation but does not explicitly name gender identity or expression; a 2015 court ruling, brought by a transgender woman suing her former employer, held that gender identity or expression is covered by the law. Danish law also prohibits discrimination based on gender identity or expression in other categories, and hate crime legislation since 2004 Penal Code amendments adds penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation. In practice, expression is policed in healthcare access: patients seeking hormone therapy report being required to present in ways reflecting stereotypical gender roles (e.g. trans men giving 'male' answers), and since 1 September 2014 legal sex change requires only a stated request plus a six-month reflection period, with Danish passports available with an 'X' sex descriptor. In the workplace, a 2019 report found 69% of LGBT respondents were open about their sexual orientation to colleagues and only 9% felt they could not be.

Danish law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity or expression through the Act on Prohibition of Unequal Treatment in the Labor Market adopted in 1996, where gender identity or expression is not explicitly listed but a 2015 court ruling in a suit by a transgender woman against her former employer held it is included. Openly transgender soldiers serve without hindrance in all branches of the Danish Defence, with discrimination in recruitment, placement and promotion prohibited. Legal sex change since 1 September 2014 requires being over 18, stating a wish to change documentation, and completing a six-month reflection period, after Parliament voted 59-52 in June 2014 to remove the requirement of a mental disorder diagnosis and surgery with irreversible sterilization, building on the Act on Sterilisation and Castration adopted in June 1929 as one of the first gender change laws in the world. Parliament decided to remove gender identity disorder from the National Board of Health's list of mental illnesses in 2016 effective 1 January 2017, making Denmark the second country after France in 2010 to do so, before the WHO in June 2018 replaced the diagnosis with gender incongruence reclassified as a sexual health condition; besides male and female, Danish passports are available with an X sex descriptor. Access to transgender health care has become more restricted since 2023, with 2023 guidelines recommending puberty blockers at Tanner stage two or three to buy time for further exploration; children under ten showing adequate signs of gender dysphoria trigger advisory information for parents, while children over ten require at least five investigative interviews, psychiatric evaluation, informational sessions on hormone therapy, and review of school and municipal records, with hormone consent from age 15 without parental involvement and no surgical options until 18, and with possible barriers including psychosis and autism if dysphoria is deemed an aspect of mental illness, plus history of abuse, self-harm and suicidal ideations. Adult wait times are generally around 11-16 months for hormone therapy and 4-6 years for bottom surgery, leading many trans adults to seek healthcare abroad, with access requiring several psychological sessions where patients report being required to present stereotypical gender roles. In February 2013 a Guatemalan woman became the first transgender person granted asylum in Denmark for persecution in her native country, but she was put in a facility for men where she was sexually assaulted several times and was initially refused, with authorities reopening the case when she proved her life would be in danger if returned to Guatemala. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized by the Penal Code of 1930 which came into effect in 1933 for persons over 18, replacing King Christian V's 1683 Danish Code punishing crimes against nature with burning at the stake and the 1866 Penal Code retaining imprisonment, with the age of consent equally set to 15 regardless of sexual orientation or gender since 1977. Registered partnerships were created by law enacted 7 June 1989 effective 1 October 1989 as the world's first such law, with almost all legal and fiscal rights and obligations of opposite-sex marriage except regulations by international treaties unless all signatories agree, with entry no longer possible since 15 June 2012. Same-sex marriage became legal on 15 June 2012 after a government bill proposed 14 March 2012, passage 85 votes to 24 on 7 June for a gender-neutral marriage law including marriages in the Church of Denmark, and royal assent by Queen Margrethe II five days later. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation was prohibited by the 1996 Act on Prohibition of Unequal Treatment in the Labor Market and complaints are considered by the Board of Equal Treatment established under the 2008 Act on the Board of Equal Treatment, while amendments to the Penal Code in 2004 provide additional penalties for crimes committed against people because of their sexual orientation. Openly gay, lesbian and bisexual soldiers serve without hindrance in all branches with prohibited discrimination in recruitment, placement and promotion, with prominent openly gay military leaders, no reported cases of threats to gays, morale or national security, and a 2010 study indicating gay men show strength and are respected. Joint adoption has been allowed since 1 July 2010 following stepchild adoption since 1999, lesbian couples gained access to artificial insemination after Parliament voted 2 June 2006 to repeal the ban with the non-biological parent written onto the birth certificate as the other natural parent since 2013 for in vitro fertilization, and gay and bisexual men have been allowed to donate blood since March 2020 provided they have not had sex in four months with waiver for stable monogamy, amended in July 2024 to no longer discriminate between heterosexual and homosexual anal sex.

In spring 2012 a trans woman was removed after a two-day warehouse work trial in Aarhus after being told to tone down femininity and then rejected as not wanted because of her feminine clothing and appearance, and after the Equal Treatment Board in September 2013 declined to decide for lack of witness-examination powers, the Aarhus court in early June 2015 held the termination was solely because of clothing and appearance and was covered by both the Equal Treatment Act and the Anti-Discrimination Act with entitlement to the same compensation whether she was characterised as transsexual or transvestite, thereby protecting both gender identity and gender expression despite no explicit statutory mention, convicting staffing agency Jysk Mandskabsservice to pay DKK 30,000 compensation while acquitting its customer for insufficient proof, with the ruling becoming final as Denmark's first trans-discrimination judgment.

In May 2016 Denmark announced it would stop classifying transgender identity as a mental illness/behavioural disorder under WHO ICD standards and would act unilaterally by October 2016 if WHO did not remove the gender identity disorder classification, establishing trans identity as not mentally disordered and requiring a neutral non-stigmatizing diagnosis.

In 2006 several gay clubs and bars in Santo Domingo were shut down as part of a police harassment programme. In 2012 police crashed the Santo Domingo LGBT Pride Parade and arrested marchers on the ground they were improperly using the national flag. Reports indicate that visible, politically active LGBTQ community signs are often targets of government crackdowns, sometimes with support of religious leaders.

Transgender people in the Dominican Republic are not allowed to change their legal gender and name to reflect their gender identity. In June 2018 President Danilo Medina issued an executive decree granting 35 transgender Dominicans the possibility to change their legal name to match their gender identity; television journalist Mía Cepeda was one of the 35 and subsequently changed her name. A 2017 ILGA poll found only a plurality of 5% of Dominicans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender. Family law statutes recognise no legal status between same-sex persons, neither marriage nor marriage-like relationships.

Citizens of the Dominican Republic have a constitutional right to access health care services, but health care programs for the LGBTQ community have generally focused on HIV/AIDS education, often run by non-governmental organizations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos. Discrimination on account of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal in areas including health care, employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services and public accommodations, so many LGBTQ people feel the need to remain in the closet. Since 2011, Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.

The socially conservative mores of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant denominations hold significant sway in both public policy and prevailing attitudes surrounding LGBTQ rights. Because most residents hold conservative views, the major political parties have not expressed much public support for LGBTQ rights legislation. Former openly gay U.S. Ambassador Wally Brewster (2013-2017) was regularly insulted by religious leaders and some politicians, and evangelical groups started an unsuccessful petition asking the government to expel him, telling him to "go home and cook since he's married to a man." A 2017 ILGA poll found 69% of Dominicans said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals.

The family law statutes recognise no legal status between persons of the same sex: neither marriage nor civil or domestic partnerships. The 2010 constitutional amendment added Article 55 stating the State shall promote and protect family organization based on marriage between a man and a woman; same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the rights given to opposite-sex married couples. Article 41 of Law 544-14 (Private International Law) could justify recognition, since marriage is valid if considered such by the law of the place of celebration, national law or domicile of at least one spouse. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion that parties to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples accession to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage, and several Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement it.

The Penal Code 1966 cited here is the same code that the 2026 CPIN confirms is still in force.

Human Rights Watch (15 Oct 2020): after a 24 Jul 2020 raid on a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province, police arrested 44 people (9 women, 35 men, mostly university students) over an alleged 'gay wedding'; on 3 Sep 2020 a court sentenced 2 to prison and 42 to suspended terms, using decorations and 'gay appearance' as evidence.

Polling data on the conservative social environment in Algeria.

The article states no transgender-specific offence, provision, penalty, document rule, screening procedure, facility rule, custody rule, care rule, or protection mechanism. The only transgender-relevant reference is that the criminal laws originate from prevailing mores viewing homosexuality and cross-dressing as against the Islamic faith. No imprisonment term, fine, age threshold, enforcement action, arrest, or case outcome is stated for cross-dressing or transgender identity itself. General statements that LGBTQ people face legal challenges and discrimination not experienced by non-LGBTQ residents and are commonly subjected to discrimination and potential arrest include transgender people only within the broader LGBTQ grouping. The stated lack of recognition or respect for civil rights of LGBTQ persons is framed generally without transgender-specific detail. No separate transgender-specific legal outcome is documented. Both female and male same-sex sexual acts are illegal in Algeria. Article 338 punishes anyone guilty of a homosexual act with imprisonment of 2 months to 2 years and a fine of 500 to 2000 Algerian Dinars, raised to up to 3 years imprisonment and a 10,000 dinars fine for the older participant if one participant is below 18 years old. Article 333 punishes outrage to public decency consisting of an act against nature with an individual of the same sex with imprisonment of 6 months to 3 years and a fine of 1,000 to 10,000 Algerian Dinars. Most attempts at unofficial same-sex marriage are blocked by police, including a 2005 attempt. The law does not recognize or respect the civil rights of LGBTQ persons. Officially there are no gay-friendly establishments and no political organization is allowed to campaign for LGBTQ rights. Homosexuality is prohibited by law. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically, so no such quote can be provided. All tolerance and attitude statements given concern homosexuality and homophobia: homophobic attitudes are normalised, the prevailing social attitude is openly negative, even violent, and LGBTQ people are commonly subjected to discrimination and potential arrest. A 2018-19 Arab Barometer survey for BBC News Arabic found about 26% of Algerians think homosexuality should be accepted, which concerns homosexuality, not transgender people. Vigilante executions, beatings and torture have occurred, with police frequently joining the attacks, being complicit, or turning a blind eye. Documented violence includes the stoning of two men in the street in 2001 and the killing of two men in 1994 and 1996 described as hate crimes against homosexuals. Assil Belatla, a student suspected of being gay, was murdered in his university-district dormitory in 2019 with the words "he is gay" painted on the wall with his blood, with the killer thinking he would avoid prosecution. Following the 2019 death of Houari Manar, a popular rai singer widely thought to be gay, several homophobic comments were made on social media.

Silueta X (leading Ecuadorian trans-rights organisation), PrisioTrans program, documents 2011-2026: trans women in Ecuador's almost universally male prisons are held in male spaces and face gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and health-care barriers. Key cases: trans woman Helen Maldonado died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; 2022 complaint over cruel/inhuman/degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast/body implants; 2026 death in State custody of a 23-year-old trans woman drew calls for an independent investigation at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison. The program explicitly does NOT push a one-size placement rule, instead advocating individualised housing decisions per Inter-American standards considering gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and cites the July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

Pulitzer Center investigation: Ecuador's prisons are 'almost always male' - the last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons (organisation Fundacion Vivir Libre says there are many more), and trans women are placed in male pavilions. Case: Venezuelan trans woman Alexa (27) detained Aug 2023 at Penitenciaria del Litoral was initially sent to male pavilion 9 with three other trans women rather than the 'prioritaria' pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations (where many sexo-gender-diverse inmates are held); she received no medical exams or HIV treatment there. The story documents rapes and torture reported to be directed at prisoners' gender identity, showing placement practice operates by birth sex/legal sex with protective 'prioritaria' placement used unevenly.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997, when Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC struck Article 516 of the Penal Code, and the 1998 Constitution made Ecuador the first country in the Americas to bar discrimination based on sexual orientation. The 2016 Gender Identity Law lets people change legal gender and birth name on ID cards solely by self-determination, without surgery. Conversion therapy was criminalised in 2014 under Article 151 of the Penal Code as equivalent to torture, punishable by 7-10 years' imprisonment, yet as of 2023 hundreds of clinics still promote it. The first gay pride march was held in Quito in 1998. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Adoption is constitutionally limited to different-sex couples (Article 68), and on 14 August 2026 new adoption legislation passed 118-0 explicitly prohibiting single and same-sex couples from adopting, although the 2018 Constitutional Court had ordered the Civil Registry to register a girl as the daughter of a lesbian couple, 5-3 with one abstention. The U.S. State Department's 2011 report found LGBT community members' right to equal access to formal education frequently violated, and clinics have confined young people against their will, including the daughter of parents who unsuccessfully sought her release. Despite a conservative, macho culture in which homosexuality tends to be viewed negatively, pride marches have been authorised in all major cities with police protection and official participation. The 2011 Guayaquil march included a vice prefect, a city councillor and a National Assembly member. Attendance reached about 20,000 in Guayaquil in 2017, with the Bolívar and San Martín monument lit in rainbow colours, and over 18,000 in Quito in 2018; the Presidential House was lit in rainbow colours in June 2017. Presidential candidate Nelson Zavala was fined over $3,000 and barred from office for a year in 2013 for calling gay people 'sinners' and 'immoral'. Diane Marie Rodríguez Zambrano became the first openly transgender candidate in 2013 and the first transgender lawmaker in 2017. The same 2011 report said gay, lesbian and transgender people still suffered discrimination from public and private bodies, and LGBT groups claimed police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals.

The last prison census counted 73 trans women across the country's prisons; placement operates by birth sex/legal sex; the protective priority pavilion is used unevenly — one trans detainee was initially sent to a male pavilion with three other trans women and received no medical exams or HIV treatment there.

Documented custody harms: gender-identity discrimination, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and health-care barriers; the death of a trans woman during the November 2021 massacre at a prison facility; a 2022 complaint over cruel and degrading treatment; 2024 allegations of forced head-shaving and beatings; a 2026 death in official custody of a 23-year-old trans woman that drew calls for an independent investigation.

The leading trans-rights organisation advocates individualised housing decisions per international standards (gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent), citing a July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

The 2024 reform's operative procedure came via the 2024 regulation of the identity law; the adolescent rulings arose from a specific teenager's case; same-sex couples remain barred from adoption by a constitutional ban.

Second, Ministry of Interior deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even without charges upheld. Violations continue inside police stations.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): homosexuality not explicitly criminalised, yet vague public-morality and debauchery laws are routinely used for arrests carrying prison sentences; NO legal protection against discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity, expression or sex characteristics.

TIMEP (6 Jan 2025): for Egypt's fourth UPR cycle, transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices violating the right to health. Barriers to equitable health services persist since the last UPR, with pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare.

Human Rights Watch, 'In a Time of Torture: The Assault on Justice in Egypt's Crackdown on Homosexual Conduct' (29 Feb 2004): documents the Queen Boat-era crackdown, including arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings over sexual orientation, with testimony from defendants.

Wikipedia country coverage: Egypt's morality and public order provisions criminalize 'any behavior, or the expression of any idea' deemed immoral or offensive to religious teachings, giving police broad leeway to prosecute LGBTQ expression. In 2017 the Supreme Media Regulatory Council issued an order preventing 'the appearance of the homosexuals' or 'promoting their slogans' in media. In August 2018 the government introduced legislation placing any social network user with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws. In 2013 comedian Bassem Youssef was charged by the Morsi government with 'propagating and promoting homosexuality and obscenity.' State officials and police routinely harass, abuse and torture LGBTQ people, particularly trans people, leading to unfair arrests and abuse in custody. After the September 2017 rainbow flag incident, TV hosts Ahmed Moussa and Mohamed Al Gheity repeatedly incited violence against the community; Moussa shared personal information of flag-raisers, leading to at least 84 arrests between 25 September and the end of November 2017, many subjected to forced anal tests. In December 2014 TV presenter Mona Iraqi collaborated with police to raid a public bathhouse, arresting around 26 men, later acquitted. In January 2019 host Mohamed El Gheity was jailed for one year for hosting a gay man on his TV show. In 2009 newspaper Al Balagh Al Gadid was shut down and two reporters jailed for printing a story about actors' involvement in homosexual prostitution. Personal and family law is governed by the religious law of the person's recognized religion (Islam, Coptic Orthodox Christianity), none of which recognize homosexual relationships, so Egyptian law only recognizes marriage between a man and a woman. If a same-sex relationship becomes public, police may use it as evidence in a criminal indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality. In 2004 a seventeen-year-old private university student received a 17-year prison sentence, including two years' hard labor, for posting a personal profile on a gay dating site. The September 2017 crackdown caused a state of trauma and despair among young Egyptian LGBTQ individuals, with many attempted suicides. Sarah Hegazi, detained for three months after the incident, fled to Canada, was granted asylum and died by suicide in 2020. Many Egyptian LGBTQ youths and individuals left the country due to social and political threats. Pew Research Center found 95% of Egyptians believe homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and polling suggests only a minority support LGBTQ rights, so Egyptian political parties and human rights NGOs do not express public support. The term 'khawalat', historically male cross-dressing dancers, has been stigmatized and used as a derogatory term for passive and gay men. Egyptian cinema has portrayed queer characters almost exclusively in a mode of stereotyping and defamation. After the 2011 revolution LGBTQ activists became more visible and online campaigns against homophobia and transphobia went viral on Twitter and Facebook by 2013, though this did not translate into legal reform. In August 2021 the Central Bank of Egypt confirmed that rainbow holograms on new banknotes were an anti-counterfeiting feature after online critics suggested they were covert LGBTQ support.

exact_spans: Directly visitor-facing risk.
texts.cleaned_text: A legal-research organisation (27 Nov 2023): analysis of the country's immigration law and case law plus 12 documented incidents (2018-2022) — the interior ministry holds broad powers to deny entry or deport anyone 'disturbing public order and morality', applied to travellers perceived as queer.

A legal-research organisation (24 Jan 2024): the country's economic courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation by reading penal-code provisions together with an article of the 1961 sex-work law; top-court interpretations from the 1970s had already removed the financial-exchange requirement (habitual or multiple partners sufficed).

A legal-research organisation (12 Dec 2024): a new interior-ministry directive to civil-registry heads nationwide closes the 1994 civil-status law loophole that let transgender residents correct gender markers via regional committees — legal gender recognition now actively being shut.

A major media investigation: no explicit law against homosexuality, but the morality (sex-work) law is used to criminalise the community; police run entrapment via dating apps with victims describing blackmail and arrests (names changed).

A local rights group's briefing (Feb 2023): documents rising arrests of gay and trans people alongside coerced anal examinations, authorities turning a blind eye, and no anti-discrimination policy or law; covers detention conditions and the situation of trans people as a reference for SOGIESC work.

A rights organisation's security documentation: police arrest patterns — first, entrapment of individuals, especially transgender women, through fake accounts on LGBTQ dating apps and websites; second, interior-ministry deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even without charges upheld; violations continue inside police stations.

A rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): homosexuality not explicitly criminalised, yet vague public-morality and sex-work laws are routinely used for arrests carrying prison sentences; no legal protection against discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity, expression or sex characteristics.

A policy research group (6 Jan 2025): in the country's fourth periodic human-rights review cycle — transgender and intersex residents face discriminatory laws, policies and practices violating the right to health; barriers to equitable health services persist since the last review, with pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare.

A human-rights organisation (29 Feb 2004): documents an early-2000s crackdown — arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings over sexual orientation, with testimony from defendants — a landmark record of official violence against gay men in the country.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): Article 310(1) of the penal code criminalises 'homosexual conduct' with up to 7 years' imprisonment — inherited from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code and retained with an enhanced sentence in the first post-independence penal code (adopted 2015).

US State Dept 2023 Country Reports (Eritrea): Section 7 records that openly LGBTQI+ persons risked imprisonment and therefore did not participate in the political process; societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons continues alongside a law making no gender distinction for assault.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Eritrea (archived): records criminalisation of same-sex conduct and societal stigma, alongside torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service.

Asmarino relay of the US State Department 2011 human rights report on Eritrea: societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians occurred; the government labelled disloyal individuals 'gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles'; the law criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity.

UK Foreign Office 'Eritrea: Country of Concern' human rights report (© 2015): same-sex activity is a crime in Eritrea and there is no anti-discrimination legislation protecting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people; the UK raised these concerns bilaterally and via the EU.

Eritrea restricts freedom of expression and sponsors censorship of LGBTQ issues. A 2023 US State Department report found no public LGBTQ organizations and tight restrictions on expression of sexual orientation and gender identity, so LGBTQI+ people cannot freely assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State censorship is compounded by heavy social stigma, and in the early 2000s state-run radio and television aired programs detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality. Foreign LGBTQ nationals have been removed from Eritrea on the basis of local law. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, a gay Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government called him a 'dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country' and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local laws including Article 600 of the Penal Code. In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one described as openly homosexual. The Eritrean ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the provisions of law prohibiting homosexual relations, and Italian diplomats condemned the action. Detention facilities are used against people suspected of same-sex conduct. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, known for housing political prisoners and journalists. Abuse, torture and beating of prisoners is commonplace and some prisoners have been illegally executed, though the UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office reported the death penalty was not used in 2013. Gays and lesbians serving in the Eritrean military are reported to have been subjected to severe abuse, including physical and verbal abuse and threats from superiors and fellow soldiers, on a 2002 UK refugee claimant account that is unconfirmed. Criminalization under Article 600 undermines health and care access: ILGA and some HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law, arguing it makes prevention programs directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an 'area of concern'. There are no laws banning conversion therapy, and OutRight Action International found conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity are widespread due to social stigma; LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time. No youth-specific care findings are recorded. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Eritrea and cannot adopt. There is no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and the government has rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review appeal to legalize same-sex sexual activity as 'in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people', with no major efforts to change or rescind existing laws. In 2010 Eritrea, with other African states, rejected the Yogyakarta Principles.

International LGBTI-rights organisation country overview (updated 12 March 2026): Article 310(1) of the penal code criminalises 'homosexual conduct' with up to 7 years' imprisonment — inherited from the 1957 penal code of the parent nation and retained with an enhanced sentence in the first post-independence penal code (adopted 2015).

A foreign government's 2023 human-rights report on this country: section 7 records that openly LGBTQI+ persons risked imprisonment and therefore did not participate in the political process; societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons continues alongside a law making no gender distinction for assault.

A foreign government's 2010 human-rights report on this country (archived): documents the authoritarian regime's abuses — torture, arbitrary detention, indefinite national service — with the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal stigma.

News relay of a foreign government's 2011 human-rights report on this country: societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians occurred; the government labelled disloyal individuals with anti-gay and other abusive epithets; the law criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity.

A foreign government's 'country of concern' human-rights report (2015): same-sex activity is a crime in this country and there is no anti-discrimination legislation protecting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people; the reporting government raised these concerns bilaterally and via a regional bloc.

Human Rights Watch dispatch (9 Dec 2005): trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests; HRW called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. Documents Moroccan state authority exercised over the territory (security services, courts) and detention of Sahrawi activists - the legal framework a visitor to the territory stands under.

PinkNews global legality roundup (Jul 2017): lists the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, and states that it has been illegal there for decades. The partially-recognised state, an African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. The status recorded for July 2017 is criminalised.

A 2009 USCRI report found that Sahrawi government officials running refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges even while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence. Multiple sources (Council for Global Equality, Equaldex, ILGA) describe same-sex sexual activity as illegal in the SADR for both males and females, punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it', and CEAR concludes this leaves no legal protection for LGBTQ people against discrimination or violence. Same-sex activity is also illegal in Morocco, which occupies most of the territory the SADR claims. Most residents of the country are Muslim and same-sex relationships are seen as a foreign phenomenon. The region was under Spanish colonial rule until 1976, and homosexuality was not decriminalized in Spain until 1979, shaping the legal and social inheritance of the territory.

An international human-rights organisation's dispatch (December 2005): trial of seven human-rights defenders from the administered part of the disputed territory on charges of fomenting illegal protests; the organisation called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial, documenting the administering state's authority exercised over the territory (security services, courts, detention).

A global legality roundup (July 2017): lists the movement's self-proclaimed state as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, and states that it has been illegal there for decades.

A 2009 refugee-policy report found that officials running refugee camps said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges even while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape; a refugee-aid organisation states there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence.
