exact_spans: For a trans visitor this documents how a policy-level restriction translates into a life-threatening delay in emergency care.

texts.cleaned_text: BBC Scotland (19 Jun 2026): Judge Lady Ross ruled the Scottish Prison Service's guidance unlawful. The guidance allowed some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching their gender identity rather than sex at birth, and the court held that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis.

BBC (5 Feb 2026): Court of Session told that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk; For Women Scotland is challenging the Scottish prison guidance (only biological females in the women's estate), government lawyers defending individual risk assessments as flexible.

The Guardian (17 Apr 2025): British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court gender ruling — trans women to be strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; prior policy had let trans women staff intimately search women holding a GRC; Sex Matters welcomed the change.

Police Scotland (25 Jun 2025): interim guidance on searching transgender persons — searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex (custody and stop-and-search); where lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request.

UK Constitutional Law Association (16 Jul 2026): in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59 (Outer House, Court of Session, 19 Jun 2026) the court struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance. The association's critique examines Equality Act 2010 Sch.22(1), the Prison Rules, GRA 2004 and the court's Article 8 approach.

BBC (Aug 2026): new EHRC guidance on single-sex spaces has come into force — the code gives organisations practical examples for compliance (Sex Matters' Maya Forstater: 'the law is clear and the code is practical'); Northern Ireland, on different equality legislation, is still assessing the Supreme Court ruling's impact.

TransActual UK 'Gendered Spaces Report 2025': survey of trans, intersex and gender-nonconforming respondents corroborating their fears of harassment from those opposed to their inclusion in public gendered spaces; full report published as PDF.
JURIST (18 Aug 2026): UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.

OHCHR (17 August 2026): UN human rights experts warn that the UK's revised Code of Practice on single-sex spaces, in force as of 5 August 2026, risks institutionalising discrimination against transgender and gender-diverse persons.

Good Law Project: announces that it is supporting a legal challenge to the revised Code of Practice on single-sex spaces and reports having backed a pre-action letter; whether proceedings have been filed, and any outcome, is not established by this source.
Surrey Police's searching and biological-sex policy, released under the Freedom of Information Act, was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403).

ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, legal gender recognition (2026 findings): for the United Kingdom, 'there is no functioning legal or administrative process for legal gender recognition', and it counts the UK among countries with explicit bans or other legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically impossible; although gender recognition certificates are still issued in the UK, the 2025 Supreme Court decision ruled that 'sex'-based protection refers to 'biological sex', so that, for Equality Act 2010 purposes, trans men with a GRC are legally treated as 'biological women' and trans women as 'biological men'.

Supreme Court press summary, For Women Scotland Ltd v The Scottish Ministers, [2025] UKSC 16 (16 April 2025): holds unanimously that the terms 'man', 'woman' and 'sex' in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological sex; explains that section 9(1) of the Gender Recognition Act 2004 treats a GRC holder's acquired gender as applying for all purposes while section 9(3) allows that rule to be displaced by other enactments; identifies separate spaces and single sex services (including changing rooms, hostels and medical services), communal accommodation and single sex higher education institutions among the provisions requiring a biological interpretation; and states that the interpretation does not remove protection from trans people, with or without a GRC, who remain protected from discrimination on the ground of gender reassignment. The press summary states that the full judgment is the only authoritative document.

Gender Recognition Act 2004, section 9 (official legislation.gov.uk text): where a full gender recognition certificate is issued, the person's gender becomes for all purposes the acquired gender, so that the person's sex becomes that of a man or a woman; subsection (1) does not affect things done before the certificate is issued but does operate for the interpretation of earlier enactments and documents; subsection (3) provides that subsection (1) 'is subject to provision made by this Act or any other enactment or any subordinate legislation', so the 'for all purposes' rule is expressly subject to statutory exceptions.

In December 2023 the UK government said it would no longer accept gender recognition certificates issued by 50 countries and U.S. states, including Sweden, New York State and Belgium, because those jurisdictions allowed people to transition 'too easily'; people from those locations would have to apply for a new GRC under British law to change their gender in the UK. Women and Equalities Minister Kemi Badenoch called the changes 'long overdue', while Shadow Equalities Minister Anneliese Dodds warned of diplomatic consequences because the list excluded Canada, the US, Australia and New Zealand.

In November 2021 a lesbian couple began a judicial review against Frimley NHS Clinical Commissioning Group over a 'discriminatory' fertility policy: heterosexual couples needed only to 'try to conceive' for two years before NHS-funded treatment, while same-sex female couples had to complete 12 rounds of private IVF first.

NHS England said in March 2024 that gender identity clinics would stop prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people, renewed indefinitely in December 2024 and to be reconsidered in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the NHS had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since the Cass Review, with some families turning to black-market or overseas hormones instead.

Same-sex marriage was legalised in England and Wales in 2014 under the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013, in force 13 March 2014, in Scotland in 2014, and in Northern Ireland on 13 January 2020 after UK Parliament intervention. Transgender people seeking a GRC have historically been required to divorce or annul their marriage first, and under current law a GRC will not be issued unless the spouse consents; if the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated. Civil partnerships, available since 2005, give most but not all rights of marriage and have recognition issues in other countries.

Section 28, which prohibited the 'promotion of homosexuality' by schools and local authorities, was repealed in 2003. Transgender youth are covered by the Equality Act 2010, but Bell v Tavistock (December 2020) found children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers, overturned on appeal in September 2021. The Cass Review (April 2024) led NHS England to stop prescribing puberty blockers to minors and to close the Tavistock GIDS in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services. The Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a GRC in January 2022, and in July 2022 the RFU and RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams.

Anti-trans rhetoric in UK media has been described as 'increasing and becoming more vitriolic' since 2016 and 'super-charged' since 2018. A 2019 study by Paul Baker found numerous UK press articles from 2018 and 2019 written to be critical of trans people and to cast them as 'unreasonable and aggressive'. ILGA-Europe rankings show the UK falling from 1st in Europe with an 86% score in 2015 to 9th in 2020 with 66% and concern about a 'hostile climate on trans rights', then 22nd in 2025 with 45%, the third steepest drop in Europe. Despite this, 86% of UK respondents agreed homosexuality should be accepted in a 2019 Pew poll and 77% supported same-sex marriage in a 2017 poll. Large LGBT communities exist in Brighton, Blackpool, Manchester and London, with gay villages and annual pride festivals.

Following Corbett v Corbett (1970) transgender people could not change the sex marker on birth certificates, and in Goodwin v United Kingdom (2002) the UK was found in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights, leading to the Gender Recognition Act 2004 effective 4 April 2005. Since that date transgender people may apply to a Gender Recognition Panel for a Gender Recognition Certificate after two years transitioned, without mandatory sex reassignment surgery, to obtain a new birth certificate and full legal recognition of acquired sex for all purposes — the original section 9(1) rule, which section 9(3) makes subject to provision made by this Act or any other enactment or any subordinate legislation. Medical gender reassignment is formally approved and available through the National Health Service or privately, and a December 2002 Government policy document categorically states that transsexualism "is not a mental illness." European anti-gender discrimination law was held to apply to trans people in P v S and Cornwall County Council (1996). Under the Gender Recognition Act 2004 as originally enacted a married transgender applicant was required to divorce or annul the marriage before issuance of a certificate, and a married couple including a transgender partner could not directly re-register but had to dissolve, obtain recognition, then register a civil partnership with associated paperwork and costs. ILGA-Europe's executive expressed concern about a "hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups" as the UK fell from highest-ranked in 2015 to 9th in 2020 and 22nd in 2025. Male same-sex acts were decriminalised in England and Wales by the Sexual Offences Act 1967 under conditions of consent, privacy and age 21, extended to Scotland by the Criminal Justice (Scotland) Act 1980 effective 1 February 1981 and to Northern Ireland by the Homosexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 1982 effective 8 December 1982, while lesbian acts were never criminalised as civilian offences. An equal age of consent at 16 for all was achieved via the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2000 effective 8 January 2001, later consolidated by the gender-neutral Sexual Offences Act 2003 effective 1 May 2004 and the Sexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 2008 lowering Northern Ireland from 17 to 16 in 2009. Discrimination protections for LGBT people existed since 1999 and were extended to all areas under the Equality Act 2010, Section 28 prohibiting "promotion of homosexuality" was repealed in 2003, and the ban on open service in the armed forces was subject to non-enforcement since 2000 and formally lifted in 2016. Civil partnerships under the Civil Partnership Act 2004 effective 5 December 2005 gave most rights of marriage, and same-sex marriage was legalised in England and Wales by the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 effective 13 March 2014 with first marriages 29 March 2014, in Scotland by the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Scotland) Act 2014 effective 16 December 2014, and in Northern Ireland effective 13 January 2020 under the Northern Ireland (Executive Formation etc) Act 2019 with first ceremony 11 February 2020. Adoption by same-sex couples was enabled in England and Wales by the Adoption and Children Act 2002 effective 30 December 2005, in Scotland effective 28 September 2009, and in Northern Ireland in December 2013, with 12% of England adoptions in 2018 involving same-sex couples. Historic convictions were addressed by "disregards" under the Protection of Freedoms Act from 2012, the so-called Alan Turing law in the Policing and Crime Act 2017 effective 31 January 2017 for England and Wales, automatic pardons in Scotland in June 2018, and Northern Ireland law effective 28 June 2018, plus the Merchant Shipping (Homosexual Conduct) Act 2017 repealing sections 146(4) and 147(3) of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994. Female homosexuality was never a civilian offence but the government announced in June 2023 pardons for women penalised for homosexuality under the Army Act 1955, Air Force Act 1955 and Naval Discipline Act 1957. The article documents no poll measuring societal acceptance of transgender people specifically, reporting only sexuality-specific tolerance figures of 86% agreeing homosexuality should be accepted in 2019 and 77% supporting same-sex marriage in 2017. For the transgender-specific climate, it quotes ILGA-Europe's executive concern about a "hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups" by 2020. It further describes anti-trans rhetoric in UK media as "increasing and becoming more vitriolic" since 2016 and becoming "super-charged" since 2018. It links this climate to backsliding in ILGA-Europe rankings from highest in Europe in 2015 with 86% progress to 9th in 2020 with 66% and 22nd in 2025 with 45%, the third steepest drop from 2024. It notes large LGBT communities and annual pride festivals across cities including Brighton, London, Manchester and others, but does not attribute transgender-specific tolerance levels to those communities.

As of the 2026 assessment, the United Kingdom maintains explicit bans or other legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically impossible and provides hate-crime and hate-speech protection on sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics only in some regions.

exact_spans: For a trans visitor this documents how a policy-level restriction translates into a life-threatening delay in emergency care.
texts.cleaned_text: The Trans Legal Clinic documents the death of Joelle, a 27-year-old trans woman with an aggressive lymphoma that is 'almost always curable when treated as a medical emergency'. A bed was available on the cancer ward when she arrived at Wolverhampton NHS Trust; after staff saw she was a trans woman she was removed from the ward and placed on a side room on the other side of the hospital. She spent 16 days there 'deteriorating in agony, without cancer pain management', and was told emergency chemotherapy could not start until she was on the right ward, though she pleaded for a bed on either the male or the female ward. By the time treatment started it was too late; her abdominal tumour measured 98cm and the delay was unsurvivable for this lymphoma. Her mother Jane states that Joelle was refused the available bed on the cancer ward because it was in a multi-bed women's ward, and that the day before, health minister Steve Barclay had announced plans to block trans women from women's wards. The Clinic is pursuing an Article 2 inquest into systemic failures and a clinical negligence claim, and notes that the April 2025 Supreme Court ruling's effect on trans people's access to hospital beds has received far less attention than its effect on toilets: if trans people are blocked from appropriate hospital wards, Joelle's case 'could become a matter of policy across the country'.

The Guardian reported that trans hospital patients in England would be banned from female- and male-only wards under plans announced by health secretary Steve Barclay at the Conservative party conference, alongside a commitment that a patient's request for intimate care by someone of the same biological sex would be respected, and an update to the NHS constitution to give effect to the proposals after consultation. The article records the backlash: the first openly transgender MP, Jamie Wallis, called it a non-issue and cited freedom-of-information requests to hospital trusts across the UK asking whether any biologically female inpatient had complained about a trans patient's presence — none were recorded; another Conservative MP questioned what tangible change was needed 'given that the future of hospitals is in individual rooms anyway'. Barclay told delegates 'we know what a woman is'. NHS Providers' chief executive said any changes to the NHS constitution should have inclusivity at the heart and be subject to wide consultation, and Unison's head of health called the speech 'deflection politics at its worst'.

The Department of Health and Social Care announced it would consult on proposed updates to the NHS Constitution for England to 'ensure the privacy, dignity and safety of all patients is respected', with changes brought forward ahead of the next routine update. Speaking at the 2023 Conservative conference, Health and Social Care Secretary Steve Barclay said the changes would 'recognise the importance of different biological needs and protect the rights of women', criticised NHS diversity spending, and confirmed he had ordered a reversal of NHS website changes and stopped the NHS 'ordering staff to declare pronouns to each new patient'. The release states the government would consider Equality and Human Rights Commission advice on 'balancing the rights of different protected characteristics of patients in certain settings'.

Broadcast reporting (19 Jun 2026): a judge ruled the regional prison service's guidance — allowing some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching their gender identity rather than sex at birth — unlawful; sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis.

Broadcast reporting (5 Feb 2026): a national court was told that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk; a campaign group is challenging the regional prison guidance (only biological females in the women's estate), with government lawyers defending individual risk assessments as flexible.

Reporting (17 Apr 2025): the transport police amended its strip-searching policy after the national-court gender ruling — trans women to be strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; prior policy had let trans women staff intimately search women holding a gender-recognition certificate; one campaign group welcomed the change.

Regional police guidance (25 Jun 2025): interim guidance on searching transgender persons — searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex (custody and stop-and-search); where lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request.

A constitutional-law analysis (16 Jul 2026) of a ruling striking down a regional prison service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance: critiques the judgment, examining the equality statute, prison rules, a 2004 gender-recognition act and the court's human-rights approach.

Broadcast reporting (Aug 2026): new equality-watchdog guidance on single-sex spaces has come into force — the code gives organisations practical compliance examples; one devolved region, on different equality legislation, is still assessing the national-court ruling's impact.

An organisation's report (2025): a survey of trans, intersex and gender-nonconforming respondents corroborating their fears of harassment from those opposed to their inclusion in public gendered spaces; full report published as a PDF.
Legal reporting (18 Aug 2026): international human-rights experts warned that revisions to the equality statute risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.

An international human-rights press release (17 Aug 2026): UN human rights experts warn that the country's revised code of practice on single-sex spaces, in force as of 5 August 2026, risks institutionalising discrimination against transgender and gender-diverse persons.

A civil-society organisation's announcement: it is supporting a legal challenge to the revised code of practice on single-sex spaces and reports having backed a pre-action letter; whether proceedings have been filed, and any outcome, is not established by this source.

A county police force's searching policy could not be retrieved at research time (access error); the underlying document is the force's searching/biological-sex policy (released under freedom-of-information rules).

The regional rainbow-index assessment's 2026 legal gender recognition findings record for the country 'there is no functioning legal or administrative process for legal gender recognition', count it among those with explicit bans or other legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically impossible, and note that although gender recognition certificates are still issued, the 2025 top-court decision ruled that 'sex'-based protection refers to 'biological sex', so that, for the national equality act's purposes, trans men with a GRC are legally treated as 'biological women' and trans women as 'biological men'.

The country's top court's press summary (16 April 2025) holds unanimously that the terms 'man', 'woman' and 'sex' in the national equality act refer to biological sex; explains that section 9(1) of the 2004 gender-recognition act treats a GRC holder's acquired gender as applying for all purposes while section 9(3) allows that rule to be displaced by other enactments; identifies separate spaces and single sex services, including changing rooms, hostels and medical services, communal accommodation and single sex higher education institutions, among the provisions requiring a biological interpretation; and states that the interpretation does not remove protection from trans people, with or without a GRC, who remain protected from discrimination on the ground of gender reassignment. The summary states that the full judgment is the only authoritative document.

The country's 2004 gender-recognition act, section 9 (official text): where a full gender recognition certificate is issued, the person's gender becomes for all purposes the acquired gender, so that the person's sex becomes that of a man or a woman; subsection (1) does not affect things done before the certificate is issued but operates for the interpretation of earlier enactments and documents; subsection (3) provides that subsection (1) is subject to provision made by that act or any other enactment or any subordinate legislation, so the 'for all purposes' rule is expressly subject to statutory exceptions.

BBC (Sep 2024): trans model and influencer Kesaria Abramidze was killed just one day after the Georgian parliament passed the anti-LGBTI law; German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path.

AP (Oct 2024): 'Georgia's anti-LGBTQ+ measures raise fears of hate crimes in the conservative South Caucasus nation' — after the stabbing death of trans actress-model Kesaria Abramidze, Russia-style 'gay propaganda' laws stoke fear.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Georgia: the foreign agents law endangers LGBTI service provision (organisations refusing to register as 'foreign agents' face fines/bankruptcy); the anti-LGBTI law eroded trust, decreasing service applications; large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing the country and seeking asylum documentation; misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

WISG et al. report to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers (5 Aug 2024) on implementation of LGBTI-rights decisions in Georgia: recommends urgent action — effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression.

IWPR Global Voices (May 2012): 'Georgian Laws Discriminate on Transgender Rights' - legal activists say the law should be changed to allow gender recognition; job applications become difficult when a person's gender identity doesn't match official paperwork - trans-specific legal barriers in Georgia.

OC Media (Jun 2019): Georgia's Interior Ministry declared Tbilisi Pride 'impossible' in the planned city-centre locations 'due to safety risks' (programme 18–23 June); organisers reported a week of pressure from an 'unidentified government official' to cancel the march, and far-right groups had vowed to thwart it — the country's first-ever pride.

In 2024 a bill was proposed to make being transgender illegal. The bill also sought removing all transgender recognition on identity documents. The Georgian Parliament passed the bill on September 4. The European Union and various human rights organizations condemned the ruling. These transgender-specific status and document provisions were separate from the bill's provisions on alternative marriage unions, general LGBT protections, and LGBT public displays. In Pride Month of 2021 a scheduled Pride March was called off after anti-LGBT protestors stormed the Tbilisi Pride headquarters and attacked approximately 50 journalists. A bill proposed in 2024 sought to remove all protections on LGBT people. The bill sought to outlaw "alternative marriage unions" and to ban all LGBT public displays. The Georgian Parliament passed the bill on September 4, which the European Union and various human rights organizations condemned. In relation to the 2021 anti-LGBT riots the authorities arrested 102 people, with 68 subsequently released on bail and the rest left in custody pending trial. On 9 July 2021 Tbilisi City Court denied bail and ordered pre-trial detention of 4 additional members of the violent group. During a preliminary hearing the judge determined that the actions "in addition to being criminal, undermine the stability of the state. They are dark and shameful...". These union and public-display provisions were framed as applying to LGBT people generally, distinct from the bill's transgender-specific provisions on illegality of being transgender and removal of transgender recognition on identity documents.

Since 2008 transgender people in Georgia can change documents and personal names to reflect their preferred gender after having undergone sex reassignment surgery, and discrimination on the basis of gender identity is outlawed. Since 2012 committing crimes against individuals based on gender identity is an aggravating factor under amended Criminal Code article 53, and Article 1 of the Law of Georgia on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination effective 7 May 2014 expressly covers gender identity and expression. On 31 March 2021 the Tbilisi Civil Registry Service registered a transgender woman as female, marking the first precedent of legal gender recognition for a transgender person. On 17 September 2024 Parliament passed by 84-0 the package "On Family Values and Protection of Minors" signed into law 3 October 2024, prohibiting all surgical operations or medical interventions for gender reassignment for people of all ages and prohibiting putting any gender "different from his own" on any state or identity documents. The same package bars adoption of a minor to people who do not identify "as their gender", voids any public or private labor obligations "aimed at neglecting biological sex", bans radio or television broadcasting, advertising and public gatherings promoting belonging to a gender different from his or her gender, and bans pride events and public displays of the rainbow pride flag. The day after final passage transgender model Kesaria Abramidze was stabbed to death in what the interior ministry called a premeditated murder, and despite the hate-crime provision there are still no official statistics about crimes on gender identity grounds with registered cases and studies indicating the law prohibiting hate crime is not efficient. Same-sex sexual activity was not officially enshrined as legal until 2000 when the Government put in place an amended criminal code to meet Council of Europe standards, with equal age of consent at 16 under Penal Code articles 140 and 141. Georgia does not recognize same-sex unions, the Civil Code since 1997 defines marriage as a heterosexual union, and the Constitution as passed 26 September 2017 and effective after the 16 December 2018 inauguration defines marriage solely as "a union between a woman and a man for the purpose of creating a family". Since 2006 Article 2(3) of the Labor Code prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, since 2012 crimes based on sexual orientation are an aggravating factor, and on 2 May 2014 Parliament approved an anti-discrimination law effective 7 May 2014 banning all forms of discrimination including sexual orientation as a prerequisite for EU visa liberalization. In July 2017 the Constitutional Court lifted the ban on gay and bisexual men donating blood as unconstitutional after an earlier 4 February 2014 ruling, noting modern technologies allow detection of HIV/AIDS in donations. On 17 September 2024 Parliament passed "On Family Values and Protection of Minors" banning "LGBTQ propaganda", outlawing "alternative marriage unions", adoption to people who are "not heterosexual", radio or television broadcasting, advertising and public endorsement promoting same-sex relationship or sexual acts with "members of the same sex", public gatherings promoting "non-heterosexual relationships", and designating May 17 as a holiday for sanctity of the family. LGBTQ events were violently cancelled in 2012, 2013, 2021 and 2023, including the 17 May 2012 Identoba march assaulted by religious counter-demonstrators with police intervening only after fighting and arresting victims, the 2013 rally stormed by thousands led by priests injuring at least 28 with participants trapped in buses and shops, and 5 July 2021 Tbilisi Pride disrupted leaving 53 media workers injured with NGO offices raided. Despite the aggravating-circumstance provision, a 2012 study found 32% of LGBTQ respondents had experienced physical violence and 89.93% psychological violence, 73% of physical-violence victims never reported to police citing ineffectiveness, fear of homophobic treatment and failure to treat seriously, with 46.15% of those reporting dissatisfied due to homophobic police reaction.

Adopted 13 October 2017 and in effect from 2018 as amended 23 March 2018, Georgia's Constitution provides that all persons are equal before the law and prohibits discrimination on grounds of sex or any other grounds while requiring equal rights and opportunities for men and women, guarantees inviolability of human dignity with prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, and guarantees to everyone free development of personality together with protection of life, physical integrity and liberty, with universally recognised human rights applying directly and international treaties prevailing over domestic acts unless conflicting with the Constitution.

Georgia's Public Defender 2017 report issued 2 April 2018 established that prosecutors examined 86 alleged hate crimes in 2017 including 37 based on gender identity, that violence in family and public spaces remained a serious unaddressed problem with transgender women in particular appealing about violence faced, that numerous complaints concerned homophobic attitudes by law enforcement with complainants withdrawing for lack of belief in timely investigation, and that law enforcement had no efficient strategy against hate-motivated violence and reacted only to individual cases.

News report (Sep 2024): a trans model and influencer was killed just one day after the elected national assembly passed the anti-LGBTI law; a foreign parliamentary committee chair and the regional bloc’s foreign-policy chief condemned the law as further derailing this nation’s membership path.

News report (Oct 2024): this nation’s anti-LGBTQ+ measures raise fears of hate crimes in a conservative regional context — after the stabbing death of a trans actress-model, neighbouring-style ‘gay propaganda’ laws stoke fear.

Regional monitor annual review 2025 (covering 2024): the foreign agents law endangers LGBTI service provision (organisations refusing to register as ‘foreign agents’ face fines/bankruptcy); the anti-LGBTI law eroded trust, decreasing service applications; large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing the country and seeking asylum documentation; misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

Rights groups’ report to the regional human-rights body (5 Aug 2024) on implementation of LGBTI-rights decisions in this nation: recommends urgent action — effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression.

News/advocacy report (May 2012): ‘laws discriminate on transgender rights’ — legal activists say the law should be changed to allow gender recognition; job applications become difficult when a person’s gender identity doesn’t match official paperwork — trans-specific legal barriers in this nation.

News report (Jun 2019): the interior ministry said holding the capital’s Pride was ‘impossible’ in the planned city-centre locations ‘due to safety risks’; organisers reported a week of pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel the march, and far-right groups had vowed to thwart it — the nation’s first-ever Pride.
States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 records the review of Adoption Law at p.1170, which led to adoption rights for same-sex couples.

BBC (10 Dec 2015): States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting both civil-partnership-only and single 'Union Civile' alternatives; implementing legislation separate and not expected before 2017. Charity Liberate: 'historic day'; debate described as 'extremely positive'.

BBC (24 Jun 2015): Guernsey repealed its 50-year Adoption Law's ban on unmarried couples adopting — States agreed same-sex couples may adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners (Jersey had approved the same change two days earlier).

BBC (23 Sep 2011): Guernsey adopted the UK's relaxed blood-donor rules — gay/bisexual men eligible after 12-month deferral, targeted ~7 Nov 2011 to match the UK change, ending the local 1980s HIV-era ban; other donation restrictions unchanged.

Guernsey's only prison, Les Nicolles, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages; it has 11 wings, capacity 139, is operated by the States of Guernsey, and held about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Guernsey for both men and women. It was criminalised until decriminalisation prior to 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the UK; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences in its criminal law, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for private-life conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Transgender people have been able to legally change their gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law only allows a new birth certificate to be issued and does not amend or remove records from existing birth certificates, so prior gender markers remain on the original record. Guernsey is also the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil partnership legislation, though UK civil partnerships were recognised for succession purposes from 2 April 2012.

A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 banned discrimination based on gender identity. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had specifically outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States of Guernsey passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously (33-0) explicitly including sexual orientation, rejecting all amendments proposing exemptions for small businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations; it takes effect from 1 October 2023.
The island parliament's formal policy paper of 24 June 2015 records the review of adoption law that led to adoption rights for same-sex couples.

Broadcast reporting (December 2015): the island parliament approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting both a civil-partnership-only option and a single 'Union Civile' alternative; implementing legislation separate and not expected before 2017. A rights charity called it a 'historic day' and the debate 'extremely positive'.

Broadcast reporting (June 2015): the parliament repealed its 50-year-old adoption law's ban on unmarried couples adopting - same-sex couples may adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners (a neighbouring dependency approved the same change two days earlier).

Broadcast reporting (September 2011): the island adopted the governing state's relaxed blood-donor rules - gay and bisexual men eligible after a 12-month deferral, ending the local 1980s HIV-era ban; other donation restrictions unchanged.

A prison profile: the island's only prison, opened in 1989, holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages, with 11 wings and capacity 139, operated by the island's government, holding about 99 prisoners in November 2024; no rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity and no trans-specific unit or segregation practice recorded.

A legal compilation: same-sex sexual activity is lawful for men and women, decriminalised before 1983 when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the governing state; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011, effective 5 November 2012; specific male homosexual offences not conducted in private remain on the statute book.

texts.cleaned_text: Reuters (Feb 2024): Ghana's parliament passed the anti-LGBT bill, which sharply increased penalties and criminalised advocacy.
Human Rights Watch (5 Mar 2024): called on Ghana's president to veto the anti-LGBT bill, which sharply increased penalties and criminalised advocacy. The bill lapsed without assent.

BBC: Ghana's Supreme Court unanimously dismissed two challenges to the anti-LGBT bill — Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson: 'Until there's presidential assent, there is no act', review deferred until the president signs; petitioners' lawyers said they would explore options. Ghana's 2024 anti-LGBTQ 'Human Sexuality' bill lapsed unsigned when Parliament dissolved pre-2024 election; colonial 'unnatural carnal knowledge' criminalisation persists; Pres. Mahama signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill

JURIST (Feb 2024): Parliament passed the Promotion of Proper Human Sexual Rights and Ghanaian Family Values Bill 2021 unanimously after its third reading — up to 3 years for identifying as LGBTQ+, up to 5 years for forming or funding LGBTQ+ groups. Ghana's 2024 anti-LGBTQ 'Human Sexuality' bill lapsed unsigned when Parliament dissolved pre-2024 election; colonial 'unnatural carnal knowledge' criminalisation persists; Pres. Mahama signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill

HRW report (Jan 2018) 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am': full PDF - violence and discrimination against LGBT people in Ghana; section 104(1)(b) criminalises 'unnatural carnal knowledge' but is rarely enforced; documents mob violence, police abuse, and extortion.

Human Rights Watch report of 8 January 2018, 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am: Violence and Discrimination against LGBT People in Ghana', provides the full report and annex downloads. Its endnotes document 2017 victim interviews in Kumasi and Tamale and cases of police and vigilante violence.

Bachelor thesis (Diaconia University of Applied Sciences, Helsinki, 2017) by Seree Yeboa-Mensa: survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland on LGBT rights in Ghana - most opposed decriminalisation/legalisation, citing religio-cultural reasons and effects on children; most supported families loving and accepting LGBT members but not blessing their marriages.

BBC (30 May 2026): Ghana's parliament approved a new bill criminalising homosexuality and the promotion of LGBTQ+ activities. Identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer carries up to three years' imprisonment, and the bill adds a duty to report prohibited acts to police. It was passed under pressure from religious leaders on President Mahama, whose ratification is still required. The bill establishes the state pathway by which trans people in Ghana can be imprisoned for identity alone and contains no provision on how such prisoners would be housed.

The Guardian (1 Jun 2026): the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill, passed by Ghana's parliament on 29 May 2026 and expected to be signed by President Mahama, mandates prison terms of three to 10 years, with up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and longer terms for promotion or advocacy. Community groups such as One Love Sisters Ghana report panic, eviction risk and self-censorship. No publicly documented policy exists in Ghana on housing trans prisoners.

texts.cleaned_text:
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of speech, expression and assembly, but these rights are actively denied to LGBTQ people, and pro-LGBTQ activism is repeatedly thwarted by the government. In 2006 the government banned an LGBTQ rights conference at the Accra International Conference Centre, and in March 2020 President Akufo-Addo banned the Pan Africa ILGA conference planned for Accra as illegal. The Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill passed by Parliament in February 2024 (reintroduced in March 2025 and passed again in May 2026) criminalises identifying as LGBTQ (up to three years), funding or forming an LGBTQ-related group (up to five years), advocacy or intentional support of LGBTQ activities (three to five years, with some proposals at 5–10 years), public displays of same-sex affection, crossdressing, and disseminating information perceived as supporting LGBTQ people. Those identifying as an 'ally' of LGBTQ people may also face prison.

the 1992 Constitution defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman (Article 39 emphasises traditional values), that a 2017 ILGA poll found 55% of Ghanaians believe transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender, and that the pending anti-LGBTQ bill would criminalise crossdressing and identifying as transgender.

Facilities for LGBTQ people in Ghana have been shut down rather than provided: in February 2021 religious and political leaders forced an LGBTQ Centre in Accra to close, and LGBT+ Rights Ghana's Accra office, opened in January 2021, was raided and closed by National Security in late February 2021 after opposition from locals, religious institutions and politicians. Most LGBTQ groups operate secretly or online, with FOTHA-Ghana members using the dark web for safety. No supported housing or shelter provision exists; instead young LGBTQ people are disowned and evicted from family homes, and the Solomon-supported Solace Initiative provides human-rights-trained paralegals to defend LGBTQ people in court.

Mental health and healthcare access are severely constrained: mental health professionals in Ghana are often not trained to work with LGBTQ populations and may hold prejudiced views, and the Ghana Mental Health Authority has not fully implemented inclusive policies under its 2012 Mental Health Act. Due to fear of persecution many LGBTQ people avoid seeking healthcare altogether, creating barriers to mental and sexual health support, and rates of anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation and some deaths by suicide are linked to forced evictions, blackmail and violence. Conversion therapy, which families often seek from religious groups when a young person discloses same-sex orientation or non-conforming gender identity, is commonly administered in abusive and inhumane settings; an August 2018 report documented conversion therapy programmes run by religious leaders, and a 2018 conference claimed about 400 people had registered for such programmes. A study found LGBTQ+ adolescents in Ghana are at significantly higher risk of suicidal ideation and self-harm than their heterosexual peers, and government HIV/AIDS campaigns present the disease as an issue for straight people, leaving gay men unaware that HIV can be transmitted through anal sex even though the country receives HIV funding.

No broad legal protections exist for LGBT people against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. Enforcement of the 'unnatural carnal knowledge' law (Section 104, Criminal Code 1960, a misdemeanour carrying up to three years under Article 296(4)) overwhelmingly targets LGBTQ people while heterosexual couples doing the same acts are rarely or never prosecuted, a disparity CDD-Ghana describes as moral policing rather than criminal justice. In a 2017 ILGA poll 59% of Ghanaians agreed LGBTQ people should be protected from workplace discrimination (62% for transgender people), while 89% reported disliking LGBTQ individuals and nearly 90% said they would report a relative or co-worker to police. The UN Human Rights Committee's October 2012 recommendation to eliminate 'unnatural sexual relations' and eradicate discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity was rejected by Ghana along with all other recommendations.

Ghana does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions: the 1992 Constitution defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and no provision of Ghanaian law allows legal recognition of same-sex relationships, leaving LGBTQ people in vulnerable legal positions around long-term relationships and shared property. Same-sex couples are explicitly excluded from the adoption process, since the system does not support joint applications from non-heterosexual partnerships. The pending Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill would additionally ban same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples outright.

Young LGBTQ Ghanaians are disowned by families and communities and evicted from their homes, and families often seek conversion therapy from religious groups when a same-sex orientation or non-conforming gender identity is disclosed, reported to be commonly administered in abusive and inhumane settings, with medical bodies warning conversion therapy is ineffective and potentially harmful. A study found LGBTQ+ adolescents in Ghana face significantly higher risk of suicidal ideation and self-harm than heterosexual peers. In January 2025 President John Mahama said he prefers teaching traditional family values through Ghana's school curriculum rather than passing anti-LGBTQ laws, and the National Coalition for Proper Human Sexual Rights and Family Values has actively opposed comprehensive sex education. The pending bill targets youth directly by criminalising identification as LGBTQ (three years), with Pan Africa ILGA's banned March 2020 Accra conference intended partly to protect queer youth in Africa.

In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed a bill on human sexual rights and family values (up to 3 years for simply identifying as LGBT, 5 years for 'promotion'); the president refused to assent pending legal challenges, the top court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when parliament dissolved.

In late May 2026 parliament passed a new bill on human sexual rights and family values: up to three years' imprisonment for identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer, longer terms for promotion/advocacy, and a 'duty to report' prohibited acts to police; the current president's ratification was still required and widely expected as of the reporting.

Under existing law, 'unnatural carnal knowledge' carries up to 3 years; mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection; the capital has a resilient underground community whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks.

The UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's Seventh Report (2007-08) on Overseas Territories sets accountability and good-governance expectations that apply to Gibraltar as an overseas territory; it also records corruption concerns raised in Turks and Caicos.

El País in English (15 Aug 2016): Gibraltar put a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act for same-sex marriage before Parliament after a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarized; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, with popular consultation and main parties suggesting support for the change.

Gibraltar Chronicle (22 Jul 2021): the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Gibraltar - legal since 1993, equal age of consent since 2012, adoption right by Supreme Court ruling 2013, civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since Dec 2016 (passed unanimously), discrimination protections for sexual orientation and 'gender reassignment' since 2007; transgender persons not allowed to change legal gender.

Wikipedia country coverage: Gibraltar's Parliament passed a bill on 19 September 2013, given royal assent on 25 September and in force on 10 October, amending the Crimes Act 2011 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime. In July 2021 the Justice Ministry began investigating a further proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, prompted by what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for 'transgender identity'. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption, after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption for lack of legal recognition of their relationship challenged the law; the government amended the law through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt children without discrimination. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy. The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender was equalised at 16. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set an equal age of consent of 16 that took effect on 23 November 2012. Before that, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009. The Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 enquiry into overseas territories recommended making discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status illegal in all overseas territories.

The Equal Opportunities Act 2006, in force on 1 March 2007, prohibits discrimination in employment and the provision of goods and services on the ground of "gender reassignment". The Act defines "gender reassignment" as "a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex". The 2008 Foreign Affairs Committee enquiry into the overseas territories concluded that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status should be made illegal in all overseas territories. In July 2026, Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for "transgender identity". In July 2026, Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy, stated generally without specifying sexual orientation versus transgender scope in the excerpt. Male same-sex sexual activity defined legally as male sodomy was decriminalized in Gibraltar in 1993 following pressure from the European Court of Human Rights and Government of the United Kingdom, with no equivalent provision for women because Victorian-drafted law only addressed men. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that an age of consent of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, mandating 16 and decriminalising heterosexual anal sex at 16, implemented in statute by the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011 approved in August 2011 and effective 23 November 2012 setting 16 regardless of sexual orientation. Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014 granting most rights of marriage including adoption as mandated by the 2013 ruling, and same-sex marriage was legalised by the Civil Marriage Amendment Act 2016 passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, receiving royal assent on 1 November and taking effect on 15 December 2016 with the first marriage the next day, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar where a deputy registrar opts out. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Constitution, in effect de jure legalising LGBT adoption, followed by civil partnership law amendments and effective 18 April 2024 the Adoption Act 2023 explicitly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority amended IVF policy to allow lesbian couples access to assisted reproductive technology, and in February 2021 surrogacy law allowed non-commercial altruistic surrogacy for individuals and married or civil-partnered couples unable to conceive with automatic recognition for children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. The 2006 Constitution does not mention sexual orientation after 2002 proposals omitted it, but the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 effective 1 March 2007 prohibits discrimination in employment and goods and services on grounds including sexual orientation defined as orientation towards persons of the same sex, opposite sex, or both. Amendments to the Crimes Act 2011 approved 19 September 2013, assented 25 September and effective 10 October 2013 criminalised hatred and harassment on the ground of sexual orientation, while in July 2021 the Justice Ministry was investigating proposals against lurking homophobia including a possible specific offence of denigrating a person as a result of sexual orientation.

A foreign-affairs committee of the governing state's parliament, in its report of 2007-08 on dependent territories, sets accountability and good-governance expectations that apply to the territory and records corruption concerns raised in another territory.

An international newspaper in English (August 2016): the territory put a draft bill amending the civil marriage act for same-sex marriage before parliament after a December 2015 consultation that left the public polarized; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints.
A local newspaper (July 2021): the justice ministry said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse.

An encyclopedic mirror: LGBT rights in the territory - same-sex conduct legal since 1993, equal age of consent since 2012, adoption right by supreme court ruling 2013, civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since December 2016 (passed unanimously), discrimination protections for sexual orientation and gender reassignment under the 2006 equal opportunities act in force since 1 March 2007.

Encyclopedic coverage: parliament passed a bill on 19 September 2013, given assent on 25 September and in force on 10 October, amending the 2011 crimes act to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime; in July 2026 parliament passed bills extending hate-crime and hate-speech protection to transgender identity and creating a conversion-therapy offence.

The 2006 equal opportunities act, in force on 1 March 2007, prohibits discrimination in employment and the provision of goods and services on the ground of 'gender reassignment', defined as a process for reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex.

The Advocates for Human Rights UPR stakeholder report on Guinea (Oct 2024): Guinea criminalises consensual same-sex relations while police commit arbitrary arrests, harassment and extortion that deepen stigma and fear; LGBTQ+ people live in a hostile, sometimes lethal environment with threats of physical violence and discrimination on orientation, gender-identity and expression grounds.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Guinea: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised (Article 325, 'indecency' provisions); documents violence and discrimination against LGBT persons and police harassment.

The Advocates for Human Rights + Khaleem Ali joint UPR stakeholder report (Oct 2024) on LGBT+ rights in Guinea: criminalisation of consensual same-sex activity; police arbitrary arrests, harassment and extortion; a hostile and 'sometimes deadly' environment; widespread stigmatisation hinders reporting of violence.

The U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report for Guinea records criminalisation of same-sex conduct and societal discrimination against LGBT people in its LGBT section; the same report documents security-force torture, prison abuse and FGM.

Guinea's 2016 Penal Code, Article 274, punishes same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment and a fine of GNF 500,000 to 1,000,000, or both. The 1998 Penal Code, Article 325, also criminalizes same-sex sexual conduct, and the 2016 text carries a higher minimum fine than before. Violence or attempted violence raises sentences to five to ten years, and acts with a minor under 21 trigger the maximum. Police arrest people on the basis of clothing and appearance, releases are commonly bought by payment to police, and the law serves as a basis for extortion. In 2016 and 2017 the organization Afrique Arc-en-Ciel Conakry reported gay men jailed and fined for release, and in 2023 the Office for the Protection of Women, Children, and Morals added a unit to investigate same-sex conduct. Security forces have arrested, harassed and used violence against LGBTQ people accused of disrupting social order. In 2010 Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate stated that consensual same-sex activity was wrong and should be illegal and that sexual orientation should not be a human right. There is no legal gender recognition and no recognition of same-sex unions. Adoption is open to a couple married at least five years or an unmarried person aged at least 30 with a 15-year age gap, and Guinean law does not specifically bar LGBTQ persons from adopting. LGBTQ people in custody are frequently abused. Transgender women are arrested and imprisoned on the stated pretext of protecting them from community violence, then held in male prisons where they often experience sexual violence. A 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submission reports LGBTQ people held for up to five days despite the 48-hour legal limit, with most released only after paying bribes or fines. LGBTQ people face discrimination when seeking healthcare, housing, education and employment, and families arrange forced heterosexual marriages, with religious, cultural and familial pressure used to attempt to convert LGBTQ people, a pressure that falls heavily on younger people. Law L/2024/001/CNT/SGG of January 12, 2024 on HIV Prevention, Care, and Protection defines members of sexual minorities to include gays, lesbians, bisexuals, intersex and transgender people whether or not they self-identify, and Ordinance No. 056/2009/PRG/SGG on HIV/AIDS lists sexual minorities as a vulnerable and marginalized group; no laws protect LGBTQ people from discrimination in health services. Section 9.9.30(b) of the Guinea Aeronautical Regulations (2022), issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, bars competent government agencies from using Passenger Name Record data that reveals an individual's sex life or sexual orientation, alongside racial, ethnic, political, religious, trade-union or health data; the text gives no further detail on entry screening, visa rules, or border checks for trans or LGBTQ travelers. A survey spanning 2021 to 2023 found 87 percent of Guineans would dislike or strongly dislike having a gay neighbor. The U.S. State Department's 2011 report described homosexuality as socially, religiously and culturally taboo with no LGBTQ organizations in the country. The 2023 report found that LGBTQ groups do exist but could not obtain legal recognition despite no law barring it, that most LGBTQ Guineans do not disclose publicly, that there is no substantial political presence of openly LGBTQ people, and that LGBTQ people are cast as part of a Western imperialist agenda attributed to the United States and France. Some LGBTQ Guineans have been internally displaced to escape areas whose religious and cultural norms endanger them.

A human-rights organisation's review stakeholder report on the country (Oct 2024): the country criminalises consensual same-sex relations while police commit arbitrary arrests, harassment and extortion that deepen stigma and fear; LGBTQ+ people live in a hostile, sometimes lethal environment with threats of physical violence and discrimination on orientation, gender-identity and expression grounds.

A government 2023 human-rights report: official assessment — same-sex conduct criminalised under indecency provisions; documents violence and discrimination against LGBT persons and police harassment.

A human-rights organisation's joint review stakeholder report (Oct 2024) on LGBT+ rights: criminalisation of consensual same-sex activity; police arbitrary arrests, harassment and extortion; a hostile and 'sometimes deadly' environment; widespread stigmatisation hinders reporting of violence.
A government 2011 human-rights report: documents security-force torture, prison abuse, harmful traditional practice, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal discrimination.

A reference encyclopaedia entry on LGBT rights in the country (current): a provision of the 2016 penal code punishes same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment, a fine, or both; enforcement operates through arrests based on clothing and appearance, releases commonly bought by payment to police, and the law used as a basis for extortion; no legal gender recognition.

BuzzFeed News (Jan 2018): in French prisons (system applicable in Guadeloupe) trans women's placement follows the legal gender on their incarceration papers, which may not match gender presentation; in practice assignment weighs the person's best interests — individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings.

CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (French context, applicable in Guadeloupe): serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, based on ~40 referrals since 2010.

Erasing 76 Crimes (6 Sep 2023): interview with Leïla of Guadeloupe's Secret's Out — community members increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, with activism described as advancing after sister island Martinique; also featuring Prisca Melyon-Reinette of Amalgame Humani's.

BI-FWI (14 May 2025): Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ Centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened 24 April 2024 — a historic first for the island, offering reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities; driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations.

France-Antilles Guadeloupe: minister Aurore Bergé's visit for the LGBT-centre opening; announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with adapted structures for overseas territories — the centre's opening cast as a concrete step toward inclusion and safety.

Erasing 76 Crimes (21 Mar 2025): Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova are partnering on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025 — described locally as a potential 'annus mirabilis' for the island's community.

French law applicable in Guadeloupe decriminalised same-sex relations in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained this in the 1810 Code, while public morality laws continued to be used against LGBTQ people; in Alsace and Lorraine, annexed in 1940, men were interned in Nazi camps and persecuted under Vichy despite the absence of a sodomy law. Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942 (later 331) set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. The Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity (art. 330, 2nd alinea), repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or €30,000. The law of December 2004, passed 31 December 2004, made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders called it a serious infringement of free speech. It created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, an MP from the ruling UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Pride has been held in Paris since 4 April 1981 (Place Maubert, about 10,000 people), reaching 500,000 participants in 2019, with events in dozens of other cities. Transgender people have changed legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis since 1 January 2017 (law signed 18 November 2016), but must still appear before a court to change the gender marker; a first name change can be done at the registry office. Self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were both dropped from the final bill. Until 2015 France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens, leaving many in legal limbo; the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change, while a 2017 legal bid for 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation. In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness, removing gender identity disorder by decree, though French trans rights organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent, self-determination model. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned the Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender care, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'; a bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access, though this did not change actual practice. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks, and a report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away. In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline for students and staff, and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms; in February 2019 the use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage. Legislation to ban medical transition for under-18s passed the Senate in May 2024, prompting large-scale protests, making trans minors a direct legislative target.

A feature (January 2018): in the governing state's prisons (system applicable on the island) trans women's placement follows the legal gender on their incarceration papers, which may not match gender presentation; in practice assignment weighs the person's best interests - individual cells or placement with men.

The governing state's detention watchdog's opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (national context, applicable on the island): serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, based on about 40 referrals since 2010.

A rights news site (September 2023): interview with an organiser of one of the island's community groups - community members increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, with activism described as advancing after the neighbouring sister island; also featuring an organiser from a second local association.

A regional news site (May 2025): the island's first LGBT+ centre opened 24 April 2024 - a historic first for the island, offering reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities; driven by a federation of local associations.

A regional newspaper: a national minister's visit for the LGBT-centre opening; announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination on the island, with adapted structures for overseas territories - the centre's opening cast as a concrete step toward inclusion and safety.

A rights news site (March 2025): three community organisations are partnering on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across the island in 2025 - described locally as a potential 'annus mirabilis' for the island's community.
