texts.cleaned_text: Outright International country profile (updated Mar 2026): same-sex conduct criminalised since the colonial era; the 2014 'aggravated homosexuality' life clause was removed by the March 2025 Criminal Code, which instead sets a five-year minimum for 'unnatural offences' (defined as any homosexual act) with no stated maximum, plus three years for 'gross indecency'; the Barrow government has not typically enforced the provisions.
West Africa Democracy Radio: The Gambia's new criminal-law package raises the minimum sentence for homosexual acts to five years.

Freedom House, Freedom in the World 2024: The Gambia rated 'Partly Free' (50/100); political freedoms improved under Barrow after 22 years of Jammeh's rule, with severe discrimination against LGBT+ people listed among ongoing concerns.

The UK Home Office CPIN on sexual orientation and gender identity in Gambia (v3.0, Feb 2023) assesses risk, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims and records country information on law and treatment.

HRW report 'State of Fear' (Sept 2015): documents arbitrary arrests, torture and killings in Gambia under Jammeh, including his anti-gay rhetoric and explicit threats against LGBT people. The findings concern the Jammeh regime's enforcement climate.
US State Dept 2020 human-rights report on Gambia: same-sex conduct criminalised (up to life under the 2013 amendment); documents arrests and societal discrimination.
US State Dept 2021 report: continued criminalisation with no prosecutions reported; significant societal stigma and police harassment of LGBT persons.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in the Gambia, and the country prohibits LGBTQ people from adopting children. No law or regulation protects residents against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and citizens cannot change their legal gender. Since 2013, section 167 of the Criminal Code forbids men to dress "as women," punishable by up to 5 years in jail or a fine of 50,000 Gambian dalasi, effectively restricting gender expression.

The 2014 Criminal Code (Amendment) Act defines "aggravated homosexuality" to include sexual acts with persons of the same gender under 18 years of age, carrying a mandatory life sentence, and imposes a mandatory life sentence specifically on gay or lesbian people living with HIV, a direct barrier to testing and treatment. In November 2014 state forces launched an investigation under that law producing at least eight arrests, including at least four adult men, a 17-year-old boy and nine women. Detainees were held at the National Intelligence Agency headquarters in Banjul and allegedly tortured to compel confessions.

Enforcement under President Jammeh was broad. On 15 May 2008 he gave homosexuals 24 hours to leave the country and ordered the Inspector General of Police and the director of the Gambia Immigration Department to conduct mass patrols to "weed bad elements in society," warning that "any hotel, lodge or motel that lodges this kind of individuals will be closed down." In June 2008 two Spanish men in their 50s, alleged to be gay, were arrested and detained at Kotu police station after taxi drivers reported them, and were released reportedly after the Spanish government intervened. On 10 April 2012 a court remanded 18 men, 16 Senegalese, one Gambian and one Nigerian, arrested at a bar in the Tourism Development Area for "indecent practice" after police said they were wearing women's clothes; all charges were dropped on 1 August 2012. Arrests of gay people are believed to have been common during Jammeh's presidency, though data is lacking. On 23 December 2008 Frank Boers, a 79-year-old Dutch national, was arrested at Banjul International Airport when officials found him in possession of pornography including nude photos of himself and Gambian men; he was convicted of indecency and fined 100,000 dalasis in lieu of a two-year sentence.

No LGBTQ+ organizations exist in the country after 2016 because it is considered too dangerous. In 2023 there were reports of healthcare workers refusing to honor LGBTQ+ people's privacy, which has negatively impacted HIV care for LGBTQ+ Gambians. No incidents of conversion therapy or of surgeries on intersex children or non-consenting adults were reported. A 2021-2023 survey found 93% of Gambians would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour. Children are raised within strict male and female gender norms, with non-conformity to the heterosexual norm treated as deviant and taboo, and the country's media promotes misinformation and harmful stereotypes toward LGBTQ+ people. The Barrow government promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts, though it has stated there are no plans for liberalisation of homosexuality laws.

Since 2013, section 167 of the Criminal Code forbids men to dress "as women", effectively discriminating against transgender women. Cross-dressing is punishable by up to 5 years in jail or a fine of 50,000 Gambian dalasi. The Gambia makes no provision for any official change of gender and does not allow citizens to change their legal gender. There is no law or regulation protecting residents against discrimination based on gender identity. Human Rights Watch reports regular organised actions by law enforcement against persons suspected of gender non-conformity. On 9 April 2012, 18 men were arrested at a bar in the Tourism Development Area on charges of "indecent practice among themselves at a public place" after police testified the men were "wearing women's clothes", carrying handbags, and "walking like ladies", with the prosecutor dropping all charges on 1 August 2012. Consensual same-sex sexual activity is illegal for both men and women, with criminalisation commencing under British colonial rule and retained from the 1933 Criminal Code implemented in 1934 as "carnal knowledge against the order of nature". Section 158 punishes homosexual acts by up to 14 years imprisonment for both men and women, extended to women in 2005 as "gross indecency" by the Criminal Code (Amendment) Act, 2005. The Criminal Code (Amendment) Act 2014 signed in October 2014 created "aggravated homosexuality" carrying a mandatory life sentence, applying to "serial offenders" and gay or lesbian people living with HIV, and to acts with persons under 18, disabled or drugged persons, or where the accused is a parent, guardian or authority figure. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition, LGBTQ people are prohibited from adopting children, and there is no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation. Enforcement is described as rarely applied but with arrests occurring, including June 2008 detention of two Spanish men at Kotu police station after taxi drivers contacted police, released after Spanish government intervention, and December 2008 conviction of 79-year-old Dutch national Frank Boers for indecency with men resulting in a 100,000 dalasi fine in lieu of a two-year prison sentence. In November-December 2014 following the aggravated law, at least eight persons including four adult men, a 17-year-old boy and nine women were apprehended for aggravated homosexual conduct, confined at the National Intelligence Agency headquarters in Banjul and allegedly subjected to torture and ill-treatment to compel confessions, with three more men interrogated in December 2014. In March 2026, Muhammad Jawo and Muhammad Krubally were each sentenced to five years imprisonment by the Brusubi Magistrates' Court for violating Section 147(1) for indecent conduct between men in an unfinished building. The current government has promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts despite stating no plans for liberalisation of homosexuality laws. Gambian society is described as conservative with strict religious and traditional beliefs where children are raised within male and female gender norms and not conforming to the expected heterosexual norm is seen as deviant and taboo. The media is described as promoting misinformation, harmful stereotypes, and violence towards LGBTQ+ people, with a 2021-2023 survey finding 93% would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbor and strong societal discrimination with some individuals shunned. There are no LGBTQ+ organizations as it is considered too dangerous, many LGBTQ+ Gambians fear arrest or killing and flee to other countries, religious leaders are widely opposed with some calling for LGBTQ+ people to be killed, and safety concerns likely prevent LGBT+ testimony to the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission. In care and livelihood, 2023 reports describe healthcare workers refusing to honor LGBTQ+ people's privacy negatively impacting HIV care alongside reported employment discrimination, with no reported conversion therapy or surgeries on intersex children or nonconsenting adults. Official hostility contributed to abuses, including former President Yahya Jammeh vowing to "cut off the head" of any homosexual, issuing a 24-hour expulsion order and threatening closure of hotels lodging them and dismissal of gay soldiers, while President Adama Barrow stated "homosexuality is not an issue in Gambia" with officials downplaying any liberalisation. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically, only general LGBTQ and homosexual-neighbor statements, which must not be conflated with transgender-specific law above.

Gambia Criminal Code Section 147(1) (Cap 10:01, 2009) makes gross indecency between males, defined in Section 147(3) to include any homosexual act whether in public or private, a felony punishable by a mandatory five years' imprisonment, and in March 2026 the Brusubi Magistrates' Court applied that provision to convict two men for same-sex conduct on 18 May 2025 in Old Yundum and imposed five-year prison terms with no reduction under Section 34 of the Criminal Offences Act, expressly holding that claimed rights to gender identification and LGBT rights do not legalize homosexuality in Gambia and that such acts in public or private remain punishable to protect societal norms and morality.

In 2017 Gambia's government promised not to prosecute consensual same-sex acts, contrasting with prior anti-LGBT rhetoric, but retained laws criminalizing same-sex conduct including the October 2014 law imposing up to life imprisonment for "aggravated homosexuality" offenses.

International LGBT-rights organisation country profile (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct criminalised since the historic era; the 2014 'aggravated homosexuality' life clause was removed by the March 2025 criminal code, which instead sets a five-year minimum for 'unnatural offences' (defined as any homosexual act) with no stated maximum, plus three years for 'gross indecency'; the current government has not typically enforced the provisions.

texts.cleaned_text: US State Dept 2012 report on Guinea-Bissau: documents the 2012 coup, arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and impunity; notes no criminalisation of same-sex conduct — general security context for visitors.

Overview of LGBT rights in Guinea-Bissau: same-sex conduct legal since 1993 (penal code decree 4/93 omits same-sex offences); signed the 2008 UN SOGI statement; only married heterosexual couples entitled to larger government housing; domestic-violence law (6/2014) Article 5 protects victims regardless of sexual orientation.

Same-sex conduct is legal in Guinea-Bissau, but the state recognises no same-sex partnerships, adoption rules do not address LGBTQ applicants, and only married heterosexual couples qualify for family-size government housing.

Mapa.gay country guide for Guinea-Bissau: legal since 1993; no partnership recognition; no trans framework; travel-safety score 34/100 ('Caution'); 9% consider homosexual behaviour morally acceptable — unusually moderate for West Africa; no visible LGBT scene; some violence cases (2018).

Social taboos against homosexuality sometimes restricted freedom to express sexual orientation, according to the U.S. Department of State's 2012 human rights report, which also found society relatively tolerant of consensual same-sex conduct. A 2010 Pew Research Center study of 19 African countries placed Guinea-Bissau among the most tolerant: nine percent said homosexual behaviour was morally acceptable and fifteen percent said it was not an issue. Government guidelines for civil servants' housing allowances restricted facilities access to heterosexual married couples, who alone were entitled to family-size government housing; same-sex couples received the single-person allotment. The U.S. Department of State's 2011 Human Rights Report recorded the same rule, finding that only heterosexual married couples were entitled to larger government housing. Article 5 (Principle of equality) of the Law against Domestic Violence (Law No. 6/2014) states that all victims, regardless of sexual orientation, enjoy the fundamental rights inherent to human dignity and are guaranteed equal opportunities to a life free from violence as well as physical and mental health. The U.S. Department of State's 2012 report found no official discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in access to health care, and no reported violent incidents or human rights abuses targeting people on that basis; antidiscrimination laws do not apply to LGBT individuals. The same report found no official discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in employment or access to education. In 2018 a local NGO director countered that there were some cases of violence targeting people based on sexual orientation or gender identity and that Guinea-Bissau lacks legal protections for LGBTI people. A French government website states single and married people are eligible to adopt children but does not say whether LGBTQ people are disqualified, leaving youth placement status unclear. No youth-specific or minor-specific health access findings, and no findings specific to trans or LGBTQ minors, school students or youth travellers, appear in the sources.

The criminal code in force is a revision of the Spanish Criminal Code dating to the Francoist era, said to carry anti-homophobic undertones. Same-sex sexual activity is legal and the age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Since 15 November 2022, Article 364(2) of the new Penal Code bars employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, the first provision explicitly protecting lesbian, gay and bisexual people, and Law 1/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data (Articles 10 and 41) protects personal data on "sexual life" where it entails discrimination. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition and are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. The Wikipedia country coverage contains no information on legal gender recognition documents, medication, hormone access or health services.

LGBTQ+ people face discrimination in education and employment: teachers have reportedly discriminated against and excluded LGBTQ+ girls, school officials have reportedly denied transgender students access to some facilities, academics and government employees can be ousted if perceived as not heterosexual, and LGBTQ+ children are often forced out of their homes, which frequently causes them to drop out of school. Transgender women have reported harassment and sexual violence while in police custody, and security forces have subjected LGBTQ+ people to sexual violence and discrimination in the military, jails and prison. In 2014 four men were detained over a video found on a phone and made to explain their actions on national television. A lesbian couple in Añisok were tied up at the police station, paraded through town with banners calling them witchcraft-practicing lesbians, photographed and shamed. In August 2023 police illegally detained Trifonia Melibea Obono, founder of Somos Parte del Mundo, after her group submitted a report on torture and ill-treatment of LGBTQI+ people to the EU headquarters in Madrid; arrests and restrictions rose significantly afterward. ILGA reports evidence that state intimidation of sexually diverse individuals persists, and although no law explicitly criminalizes homosexuality, LGBTQ+ people are still detained and punished through public shaming.

Rape is sometimes used as a form of conversion therapy, and queer women are forcibly impregnated in an attempt to make them heterosexual. LGBTQ+ women and transgender men are described as vulnerable to sexual violence in the military and from family, while laws against rape are not effectively enforced because the crime is rarely reported, and police and judicial officials may decline to act where the perpetrator has political connections or is in the police or military. Transgender children are especially vulnerable to commercial sexual exploitation according to a local NGO, and minors generally are sexually exploited for commercial sex.

The four (three Greek, one Bulgarian) had been held at Trikala and Corfu prisons, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender. First documented transfer of trans prisoners to a women's facility in Greece; it illustrates that default placement had followed the male facilities and that an on-request transfer route to women's facilities existed.

Wikipedia country coverage: LGBTQ people in Grenada face social and legal challenges not experienced by non-LGBTQ residents. The criminal code punishes male same-sex acts with up to 10 years in prison (Grenada Criminal Code Section 431, 'unnatural crime'). Section 7's gender-neutral 'grossly indecent act' provision reaches same-sex conduct committed willfully in public. The 1973 Constitution contains no clause on equality or protection of privacy, and Grenadian law does not address discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity. In May 2013 the President of the Senate publicly called for reconsideration of the ban, saying 'the day is fast approaching' for repeal. Grenada does not recognize same-sex unions in any form, whether marriage or partnerships, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the rights given to opposite-sex married couples.

GlobalGayz 'Gay Greenland - Past and Present' (May 2015) reports gay life as 'almost a non-event': low-key, integrated and non-violent, with a modest Pride march since 2010. The 1996 same-sex partnership law passed with virtually no debate.

PinkNews (Apr 2016) reports that Greenland's same-sex marriage law came into effect. It adopted Danish legislation passed unanimously twice, after the first bill lapsed due to Danish elections, and replaced the 1996 partnership law. The established church's bishop supported it.

KNR Greenlandic Broadcasting (Aug 2014): new national association LGBT Qaamaneq founded for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, working for political, cultural and social equality and open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters.

Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2010 Greenland has outlawed hate speech, with Article 100 of the Criminal Code prohibiting speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other categories, alongside penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation. Public expression is visible in the first pride parade held in Nuuk on 15 May 2010, attended by about 1,000 people. There is virtually no gay scene due to the small, scattered population, though some nightclubs and bars in Nuuk draw a mixed gay and straight crowd. Transgender Greenlanders may change the sex designation on official identity documents: a law passed in 2016 by decree allows legal sex changes based on self-determination, with no requirement for sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilization or a medical diagnosis. Applicants must be over 18 and state that they want to change their documentation, then observe a six-month reflection period to confirm the request. Greenlandic passports are available with an "X" sex descriptor in addition to male and female. Registered partnerships (nalunaarsukkamik inooqatigiinneq) ran from 1 July 1996 until the day the same-sex marriage law took effect on 1 April 2016, when the partnership law's application was repealed. Greenland's parliament passed a Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination in May 2024, taking effect on 1 July 2024, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of "sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, [and] gender characteristics" among other characteristics. The law creates an Equal Treatment Board to manage discrimination complaints and an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination. The state-funded Human Rights Council of Greenland works closely with the Danish Institute for Human Rights to promote and protect human rights.

texts.cleaned_text: Washington Blade (Jan 2018): Guatemala was among the Latin American countries urged to abide by the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, which requires marriage equality and legal gender recognition.

HRW (7 Oct 2020), Guatemala chapter: placing trans women in men's prisons facilitates anti-trans violence and exposes them to sexual assault. Bárbara Herrarte, trans activist with Redmmutrans (Red Multicultural de Mujeres Trans), described her time in a men's prison: 'Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him.' The report documents birth-sex placement in the men's prison system as of 2020 with sexual-assault risk, and records no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice, and no court ruling on trans custody. LGBTQ organisation Lambda flags forced internal displacement from violence generally.

Since 2016 transgender people in Guatemala can change their legal name to match gender identity following judicial permission, but they cannot change their legal gender, and individuals cannot self-report gender for official government documents, which must show gender and name assigned at birth, causing problems accessing government services such as education and basic resources that require official ID. Guatemala is legally bound to the 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion holding that recognition of one's gender identity on official documents is a human right protected by the American Convention on Human Rights. A December 2017 bill to recognize the right to gender identity and allow transgender people to change name and gender on birth certificates was rejected in August 2018 by both the Legislative and Constitutional Points Commission and the Women's Commission, while a later legislative proposal for a gender identity law to allow change of official documents to reflect gender status has been advocated without enactment. Bill 5490 advanced in December 2021 to remove education regarding transgender individuals in schools on grounds of protecting children and adolescents from “gender identity disorders” and to require censorship of media with transgender individuals, unanimously approved by the Congress’ Education, Science, and Technology committee and moved for full congress review. Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or other public accommodations such as cafes, restaurants, nightclubs and cinemas, with a May 2017 bill proposing to add gender identity to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 as a protected category remaining unadopted. Bias-motivated crimes on the basis of gender identity are reportedly tolerated by the Government, especially when harassment or violence is directed at transgender people, with lack of hate-crime protection attributed to prevailing attitudes about sexual identity and gender roles. United Nations and NGO reports from the late 1990s documented systematic targeting of LGBT people for death as part of a social cleansing campaign, including the 1997 gunning down in Guatemala City of transgender AIDS activist Luis Palencia, and active Evangelical-funded conversion therapy centers mainly in rural areas subject persons to electroshock therapy, “corrective” rape prosecuted only as rape not hate crime, forced marriage and coerced sex. Both male and female consensual, non-commercial, private same-sex sexual activity have been legal in Guatemala since 1871, following earlier Spanish colonial punishment of sodomy with burning at the stake. There is no legal recognition for same-sex couples as marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and a civil unions bill introduced in December 2016 by Deputy Sandra Morán has not been debated since. The 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion holds that parties to the American Convention on Human Rights should grant same-sex couples accession to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage with all rights deriving from marriage, to which Guatemala is bound. In response lawmakers introduced the life and protection bill / Initiative 5272 Protection of Life and Family Act to increase penalties for abortion, explicitly ban same-sex marriage, define family as “being a father, a mother and children,” provide that “freedom of conscience and expression” protects people from being “obliged to accept non-heterosexual conduct or practices as normal,” and describe homosexuality as “being contrary to biology and genetics.” That initiative passed first and second readings but its third reading was blocked in September 2018 with no debate since, and a renewed 9 March 2022 congressional approval of Law 5272 to ban same-sex marriage and penalize abortion with 5 years in prison was archived and discarded on 15 March after President Alejandro Giammattei announced a veto as violating the Constitution and international agreements. Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations, except for the 1997 Code on Childhood and Youth safeguarding children and youth from discrimination based on sexual orientation and that of parents, repealed in 2003, with a May 2017 bill to add sexual orientation to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 unadopted. Former President Álvaro Colom supported civil unions, President Jimmy Morales supported the ban proposal stating Guatemala believes in family based in marriage of man and woman, and openly LGBT political representation began with lesbian Deputy Sandra Morán elected January 2016 and gay Deputy Aldo Dávila elected June 2019 on a platform to criminalize hate crimes and hate speech against the LGBT community. A majority of Guatemalans affiliate with the Catholic Church or Pentecostal churches, with most residents members of Catholic, Fundamentalist Pentecostal, or Eastern Orthodox faiths, and attitudes towards LGBT people tend to reflect prevailing religious mores. Those faiths have traditionally upheld socially conservative attitudes and in particular “tend to believe that homosexuality and cross-dressing are signs of immorality,” attitudes also reflected in the dominant political parties while most other parties generally ignore LGBT rights. Despite legality since 1871, negative social attitudes have prevailed with known harassment and even targeted killings of LGBT people, with only one gay bar allowed from 1976 until the late 1990s amid a strong and growing contrast from the rise of the fundamentalist Pentecostal population. Bias-motivated crimes on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity are reportedly tolerated by the Government, especially when directed at transgender people, attributed to prevailing attitudes about sexual identity and gender roles. Late-1990s United Nations and NGO reports documented systematic targeting of LGBT people for death as part of a “social cleansing campaign,” including the 1997 killing of transgender AIDS activist Luis Palencia in Guatemala City. Since the 1990s the LGBT community has become more visible following refocus on democratization, peace and human rights, with OASIS allowed in 1993 to provide HIV/AIDS education, expanded to LGBT rights after the 1996 end of civil war, and the first gay pride parade held in Guatemala City in 2000. The article documents pre-Spanish Mayan tolerance only for homosexuality involving ritual homosexual acts by shamans and priests, not for transgender people specifically.

Guatemala's Congress approved the Law for the Protection of Life and Family on 8 March 2022 to expressly prohibit same-sex marriage in the Civil Code and to prohibit schools from teaching sexual diversity by requiring teaching that heterosexuality is the norm, and after President Alejandro Giammattei requested archiving on 11 March 2022 on grounds it violated the Constitution and international conventions, Congress archived the law with 119 votes, leaving those prohibitions without effect.

In Guatemala legal gender recognition is not possible and the penal code prohibition of discrimination on grounds including gender does not explicitly cover gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics with no convictions for discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds recorded through 2021, while attempts to ban educational materials on transgender identities persist alongside normalized conversion practices including by mental health professionals, and despite election of a more progressive government in 2024 Congress remained predominantly conservative with no significant pro-LGBTIQ initiatives and in August 2025 hosted the Meeting for Religious Freedom, Life and Family in Congress to advance an anti-LGBTIQ agenda.

On 12 July 2021 Initiative No. 5940 proposing a Law to guarantee the Integral Protection of Children and Adolescents against Gender Identity Disorders was received by the Legislative Directorate and on 13 September 2021 was presented to the plenary of the Congress of Guatemala and assigned to the Human Rights, Education, Science and Technology, and Governance commissions.

An encyclopedic article on killings of trans women records that governments in the region have long excluded trans women from femicide protections, with officials justifying the exclusion on the grounds that transgender women are not 'biological women'.

France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, becoming the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as mental illness, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale. Since 1 January 2017 under the law signed 18 November 2016 after the Constitutional Council ruling of 17 November, transgender people may change legal gender marker by court order without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatrist certificate or medical diagnosis, with first-name change available at the registry office. This followed a decades-long legislative ban on legal gender change despite the 1959 change for Coccinelle and 1979 legalisation of gender-affirming surgery inside France, overturned only after the 1992 B. v France case at the European Court of Human Rights. Discrimination on the ground of "sexual identity" was prohibited from July 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" on 18 November 2016 amending Penal Code article 225-1 and Labour Code protections covering recruitment, internships, training, sanction and dismissal. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Gender-affirming healthcare was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to lack self-determination with extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access recommending informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine advises extreme caution and actual practice is unchanged. For youth, the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the first national guidelines in late 2024 recommending puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements, while a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under age 18 following the March 2024 Little Mermaid Observatory report has had no update since 23 July 2024 and is opposed by the Macron government. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the Penal Code of 1810 applied to nations and French colonies, ending ancien régime capital punishments including castration, dismemberment and burning with the last burning on 6 July 1750. A discriminatory age of consent of 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual relations introduced 6 August 1942 as article 334, moved to article 331 in 1945 and lowered to 18 in 1974, was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under President Mitterrand, while the discriminatory 1960 Mirguet amendment to Penal Code article 330 alinea 2 doubling penalty for homosexual indecent exposure was repealed in 1980 with a March 2024 National Assembly unanimous compensation bill for pre-1980 Article 330 victims pending Senate vote. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1985 in employment, housing and public and private provision of goods and services, codified in the Labour Code. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments with a maximum penalty of 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment and amended the Law on Freedom of the Press of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation or disability, while physical assault or murder motivated by victim sexual orientation carries increased penalties, and created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité. Same-sex marriage following civil solidarity pacts in 1999 was legalised in 2013 with the law signed 18 May 2013 after the 17 May Constitutional Council ruling and first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, and is legal in all overseas departments and territories, with French Guiana's two deputies recording one vote in favour and one abstention. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people may serve openly in the Armed Forces, men who have sex with men blood-donation abstinence requirements of one year from 10 July 2016 and four months from 2 April 2020 were fully removed 16 March 2022 to an orientation-neutral policy, and the conversion therapy ban passed the Senate 7 December 2020, the National Assembly 25 January 2022 and was published 1 February 2022.

A feature (January 2018): in the governing state, trans women incarcerated on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal gray area - practice that applies in this department as an overseas region applying the governing state's law.

The governing state's detention watchdog's opinion (25 May 2021) on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations persist across that state's places of detention, applicable in this department.

An online entry on transgender rights in the department: the governing state's national framework applies - simplified legal gender recognition since 2017 (administrative declaration, no surgery/sterilisation/diagnosis), anti-discrimination protections since 2012, hate-crime provisions 2017; specialist care not provided locally.

A travel guide for the department: same-sex relations legal, same-sex marriage legal under the governing state's law, Pride events held; rated 'Very Safe for LGBTQ+'; no listed venues - a small scene anchored in the main town.

A second LGBTQIA+ travel guide covers equality index, gender-identity recognition, and same-sex union and marriage data; no specific figures or findings were available from it; one further source returned no usable finding on the safety of trans visitors.

NPR (28 Jan 2025): a Trump executive order bans transgender troops from serving openly and directs SecDef Hegseth to submit an implementation plan within 30 days; the order frames trans identity as 'radical gender ideology'. The order applies in Guam, which hosts a large permanent US military presence.

Guardian/AP (5 Jun 2015): chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's same-sex marriage prohibition after an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero denied a licence; ruling effective 8am Tuesday 9 June — Guam became the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage.

In August 2015 the Guam Legislature unanimously passed Bill 102-33 which bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity or expression in employment. Discrimination against government employees based on sexuality or identity is also forbidden. Federal law has covered hate crimes based on gender identity since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Hate Crimes Prevention Act. To change legal gender on a birth certificate transgender people must provide the Office of Vital Statistics a sworn statement from a physician that they have undergone sex reassignment surgery after which the Office amends the certificate. The Motor Vehicle Division Supervisor issues an amended drivers license upon receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicants sex has been surgically changed. In May 2018 Senator Fernando Esteves introduced a bill to permit legal gender change with judicial permission and a letter confirming gender identity supported by documentation from a certified psychologist social worker therapist or other licensed professional with no surgery required. On December 13 2018 the Legislature postponed a vote on the bill until medical and law enforcement process issues were addressed and the bill failed on December 17 2018 by a 6 to 7 vote. Private adult consensual and noncommercial homosexual acts have been legal in Guam since reform of the Criminal Code in 1978. The 1933 penal code ordained by the Naval Governor and identical to Californias prohibited sodomy fellatio and cunnilingus whether heterosexual or homosexual with between one and ten years imprisonment. The only reported sodomy case in Guam occurred in the early 1950s in Pennington v Government which resulted in victory for the defendant solely on procedural grounds when the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held the trial court had been without authority to try Pennington without a jury. Bill 102-33 passed unanimously in August 2015 bans employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and discrimination against government employees based on sexuality is also forbidden. Federal law has covered hate crimes based on sexual orientation since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The article states "The Chamorro people have traditionally accepted homosexuality and transgender people." It further describes Chamorro society as very sexually tolerant but specifies for sexuality that homosexuality was never viewed as taboo but "was taken for granted as part of life". For contemporary conditions the article states Guam is regarded as tolerant and accepting of LGBTQ people with very few reports of societal discrimination or harassment which is a general LGBTQ finding not a transgender specific finding. It reports a visible LGBTQ social scene since the 1990s with a handful of nightclubs and social functions and annual Guam Pride held since 2017 attracting a few hundred people. It notes Guam is a member of the International Gay and Lesbian Travel Association and has begun commercializing itself as a tourist destination for LGBTQ people and these contemporary observations are framed as LGBTQ general findings rather than transgender specific findings.

A national broadcast report (January 2025): a 2025 executive order of the governing state bans transgender troops from serving openly and directs the defence department to submit an implementation plan; the order applies on the island, which hosts a large permanent military presence.
Wire reporting (June 2015): the chief judge struck down the island's same-sex marriage prohibition after an April 2015 lawsuit by a couple denied a licence; ruling effective 8am Tuesday 9 June.

A legal record: in August 2015 the legislature unanimously passed an employment bill banning discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity or expression in employment; discrimination against government employees based on sexuality or identity is also forbidden.

A rights compilation: the island's own law governs legal gender recognition and requires surgery - birth certificates amended on a physician's sworn statement of sex reassignment surgery; the civil records office and licensing authority act on that documentation; a 2018 bill to drop the surgery requirement failed by 6 to 7 in December 2018.

texts.cleaned_text: Stabroek News (16 Nov 2024): at the IACHR's 191st session (OAS HQ, Washington), a hearing requested by the Guyana Equality Forum — 'Impact of Gender-Based Violence on Migrant Women, Sex Workers, and Transgender Women in Guyana' — heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition; Commission chair Roberta Clarke called on Guyana to take urgent action (69 documented cases of violence against trans women 2018-2022).

BBC (26 Mar 2017): trans woman Petronella Trotman stabbed in Georgetown Jan 2017, then told by magistrate Dylon Bess to 'dress like a man' and refused courtroom entry on 2 Mar — case dismissed. Turns on the 1893 Summary Jurisdiction Act cross-dressing offence (124 years old, 'improper purpose' open to magistrate interpretation). Documents both street violence and justice-system failure for trans Guyanese.

Stabroek News (13 Nov 2018): Caribbean Court of Justice allowed the appeal of Quincy McEwan, Angel Clarke, Peaches Fraser et al. and struck s.153(1)(XLVII) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act as unconstitutionally vague and contrary to freedom of expression. Backdrop: 2009 arrests of trans women under the 1893 act with three nights' detention; challenge filed 2010 with SASOD — removed the direct anti-cross-dressing offence.

PinkNews (26 Mar 2017) corroborates the Trotman attack: stabbed with scissors, neck wound, glass bottles, and the courtroom exclusion. SASOD's Joel Simpson called magistrate Bess's conduct a 'dereliction of duty' while arguing Parliament, not courts, must repeal the 1893 law. Named LGBT-organisation response demanding legislative repeal.

News Room Guyana (16 May 2019): SASOD's Joel Simpson documents police using residual Summary Jurisdiction clauses to extort LGBT people — men in 'compromising positions' threatened with arrest to extract bribes; same-sex couples harassed at seawalls/parks; formal complainants face secondary discrimination at stations and give 'watered down' accounts. Post-CCJ, loitering/vagrancy clauses remain usable against LGBT (mostly sex-worker) populations.

Guyana retains colonial-era criminal provisions: Section 351 (gross indecency, up to 2 years' imprisonment) and Section 353 (buggery, life imprisonment) of the Criminal Law (Offences) Act 1893, kept in force after independence, with a constitutional savings clause blocking judicial review of inherited laws. Cross-dressing was decriminalized on 13 November 2018, when the Caribbean Court of Justice struck Section 153(1)(XLVII) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act as unconstitutional, archaic and vague. No legal gender recognition procedure exists. On 2 March 2017 a trans woman was denied entry to the Georgetown Magistrates Court because she was not 'dressed like a man'; her case against her attacker was dismissed. SASOD managing director Joel Simpson stated in May 2019 that discriminatory laws have enabled law enforcement to extort LGBTQ people, with recorded cases of victims blackmailed by police who threatened arrest under the sodomy laws; hate crimes often go unreported. SASOD works with health professionals on their knowledge of LGBTQ people, and with the University of Guyana and nursing schools across the country. Discrimination and violence at the hands of law enforcement, religious leaders and others are widespread, leading most LGBTQ people to hide their orientation. No youth-specific or minor-specific care findings are recorded. Same-sex marriage and civil unions do not exist in Guyana. The U.S. Department of State reports that LGBTQ people are not disqualified from adopting, and that both married and single people may adopt; in December 2015 the Director of Guyana's Childcare and Protection Agency stated the CPA does not discriminate, as no laws bar LGBTQ individuals or same-sex couples from adopting, fostering or serving as guardians, and encouraged LGBTQ people to become adoptive parents. Public support is low but shifting: 14% backed legalizing same-sex marriage in the 2013 CADRES survey, while LAPOP's AmericasBarometer score rose from 7.2 (2010) to 20.6 (2017) on a 0–100 scale, against an Americas average of 26.8.

Under Section 153(1)(XLVII) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act, cross-dressing was criminalized until 13 November 2018, when the Caribbean Court of Justice in Quincy McEwan, Seon Clarke, Joseph Fraser, Seyon Persaud and SASOD v The Attorney General of Guyana ruled the provision unconstitutional and ordered it struck from the code as archaic, vague, violative of protection of the law and contrary to the rule of law. Enforcement included 2009 arrests of several transgender activists for wearing clothes of the opposite sex, followed by a 2010 Supreme Court challenge by Guyana Trans United, a 2013 Chief Justice ruling permitting cross-dressing unless for an "improper purpose," affirmance by the Court of Appeal, and CCJ oral arguments beginning 28 June 2018 addressing vagueness and the constitutional savings clause barring challenge to colonial-era laws. The article states: "Guyanese society tends to view homosexuality and transgender people negatively, though attitudes are slowly changing and becoming more accepting." In 2017 a trans woman assaulted in Georgetown reported to police and filed in Georgetown Magistrates Court but on verdict day 2 March 2017 was denied courtroom entry because she was not "dressed like a man," after which the court dismissed her case. In July 2019 Minister of Social Protection Amna Ally stated the government was working to remove legal gaps to prevent discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, stating "The government believes that every individual regardless of sexual orientation, gender identity has an inherent human right to live their life free from violence, abuse and discrimination." No article-stated provisions address transgender-specific documents, screening, facilities, custody, or gender-affirming care. Guyana is the only country in South America and the only mainland country in the Americas where homosexual acts remain illegal under the inherited Criminal Law (Offences) Act (1893). Section 351 punishes any male act of gross indecency with another male in public or private as a misdemeanour liable to two years' imprisonment, and Section 353 punishes buggery as a felony liable to life imprisonment. The Constitution's savings clause bars judicial review of British colonial-era laws even if they undermine human rights, blocking court-led repeal despite 2016 Belize and 2018 Trinidad and Tobago rulings striking down analogous bans. Legislative reform remains pending after a 2012 government national-debate announcement, a 2013 parliamentary commission receiving 2014 submissions, a 2017 referendum proposal later described as a misunderstanding and opposed by SASOD, a May 2019 SASOD call for the Law Reform Commission to remove archaic clauses, July 2025 support for decriminalization by 5 of 6 main parties, and a September 2025 presidential promise by Irfaan Ali to decriminalize with SASOD. Same-sex marriage and civil unions do not exist, while adoption, foster care and guardianship remain legally available as the Childcare and Protection Agency stated in December 2015 it does not discriminate and no law bars LGBTQ individuals or same-sex couples. Constitutional protection based on sexual orientation was unanimously approved in December 2000 but denied presidential assent before the March 2001 elections after religious opposition and a 2003 reintroduction was withdrawn without progress. Enforcement risk includes SASOD-documented extortion and blackmail by police threatening arrest under the buggery law with hate crimes often unreported, and a July 2019 reduction by the Court of Appeal of Clive Knights' 2015 57-year murder sentence for the 2012 killing of Bert Whyte to 30 years for manslaughter after a claim of "unwanted homosexual advances." The article states: "Guyanese society tends to view homosexuality and transgender people negatively, though attitudes are slowly changing and becoming more accepting." Pride mobilization proceeded with state tolerance: the first parade on 2 June 2018 in Georgetown by hundreds demanding decriminalization occurred without violent incident despite a Georgetown Ministers' Fellowship demand for a ban as immoral, with support from political and religious leaders including the Anglican Bishop affirming marching rights with police permission, followed by a second festival 28 May to 3 June 2019 with a 1 June parade of 200 under police protection though participants faced shouted insults, postponements in 2020-2021 for COVID-19, and the largest Georgetown event in June 2022. Widespread discrimination and violence persist with LGBTQ persons facing violence and verbal harassment from law enforcement, religious leaders and others, causing most to conceal orientation, and gay men commonly labeled "anti-men." Managing Director of SASOD Joel Simpson stated discriminatory laws contributed to extortion by authorities, and on 16 June 2019 Simpson himself was beaten by six men after harassment at Palm Court nightclub while waiting at Bourda Market, filing a police complaint and calling for hate-crime legislation covering sexual orientation and gender identity, which the Ministry of Social Protection condemned while affirming acceptance. Polling shows shifting norms: the 2013 CADRES survey found 24% "hate" homosexuals, 38% "tolerant" and 25% "accepting" with 53% supporting criminalization, while the October 2022 SASOD-commissioned poll of 1,070 respondents found hatred down to 12% from 25% in 2013 and 72.4% accepting and tolerating LGBTQ persons up from 34.5%, concluding "LGBT acceptance was increasing in Guyana." No article-stated transgender-specific facilities, screening, custody or care protections are described beyond general violence and assembly facts.

Article 149 of Guyana's revised Constitution guarantees equality and non-discrimination, and in July 2019 the Government recognized responsibility to remove legal gaps to prevent discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity with active stakeholder dialogue toward filling them, affirmed every individual regardless of sexual orientation/gender identity has the right to live free from violence, abuse and discrimination while condemning a recent attack on a leading LGBTQ activist, and reported Society Against Sexual Orientation Discrimination cooperation with the Guyana Police Force hierarchy to retrain/train officers to respond professionally to LGBTQ complaints and service access alongside cabinet approval of a sexual and reproductive health policy inclusive of sexual orientation.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): this country is one of only five in the region still criminalising consensual same-sex conduct — criminal-law provisions on gross indecency, attempted buggery and buggery with life imprisonment, rarely enforced but fuelling stigma. Five of six parties in the 2025 election, including the ruling party, backed decriminalisation. The cross-dressing law was struck down in 2018 by a regional court ruling; no legal gender recognition; a 2022 poll found 72% acceptance, 13 points less hostility than in 2013.

AP (Feb 2023): 'Hong Kong transgender men win appeal over status change' — the Court of Final Appeal rules full sex-reassignment surgery should not be a prerequisite for changing the gender marker on official identity cards, a far-reaching win in the Henry Tse case.

PinkNews (1 Feb 2019): the HK High Court ruled against trans men Henry Tse, Q and R. Judge Thomas Au's 59-page judgment made full confirmation surgery the 'only objectively ascertainable criterion' and rejected self-ID as leading to 'uncertainty and arbitrariness'. The men had already changed legal gender in Britain; counsel called the requirement 'out of proportion'. Legal gender recognition still requires full sex-reassignment surgery. In Sept 2025 LegCo voted the government's registered-partnerships bill down 71-14.

HKFP opinion by Nury Vittachi (7 Dec 2016), 'HSBC's rainbow lions: Can we have our homophobia back please?': documents the 2016 backlash to HSBC's rainbow-lion installations, a viral local campaign insisting homophobia is homegrown or foreign-imported, framed satirically. Corporate LGBT visibility provokes organised pushback in Hong Kong.

HK Court of Appeal, Leung TC William Roy v Secretary for Justice (CACV317/2005, Sept 2006): judicial review of Crimes Ordinance provisions setting the age of consent for male-male sex at 21 vs 16 for heterosexual acts — the applicant (21, in same-sex relationships since 16) argued the disparity unjustifiably discriminated; the judgment examines whether facially neutral laws can breach equality. Landmark precedent on equal age of consent in Hong Kong.

Cross-dressing per se is not illegal in Hong Kong. Hong Kong law allows change of legal documents such as the ID card and passport, but does not allow birth certificate changes; historically this required full sex reassignment surgery including removal of reproductive organs. Since April 2024, a revised policy allows individuals who have undergone specific gender-affirming surgeries (mastectomy for trans men; penectomy and orchiectomy for trans women) to apply for an ID gender marker change, provided they provide medical proof, live as their identified gender for at least two years, and undergo continuous hormone therapy. A 2019 CUHK survey found 59% agreed and 9% disagreed that transgender people should be able to freely express their gender. Same-sex partners gained spousal visa rights through the Court of Final Appeal ruling of 4 July 2018 (QT case), which mandated immigration authorities to grant spousal visas to same-sex partners married or in civil unions abroad; this became effective on 19 September 2018 when the Director of Immigration announced favorable consideration of such applications. In 2013, trans woman Eliana Rubashkyn was discriminated against and sexually abused by Hong Kong airport customs officers, endured an invasive body search for more than nine hours, and became a stateless person requiring UN and NGO assistance. On 23 July 2025, the High Court ruled in K v Secretary for Environment and Ecology that government regulation prohibiting trans people from using public toilets matching their lived gender identity was unconstitutional under the Basic Law's right to equality. A 2025 report concluded LGBTQ people face exclusion in various domains including personal security. The 2025 ruling on public toilets provides a new legal basis for facility access, though implementation details are not described in the source. Since 2021, step-child adoption has been affirmed for same-sex couples in the Court of First Instance case AA v BB (S v KG), which granted a lesbian couple joint custody, shared care, and guardianship rights over their two children following separation, establishing a judicial mechanism for couples to obtain equal parental rights. Under Cap. 13 Guardianship of Minors Ordinance, the Court of First Instance has full control over appointing or removing guardians. In July 2025, the government introduced the Registration of Same-sex Partnerships Bill granting limited medical decision rights including hospital visits, shared medical information, organ donation, and dealing with remains — but the bill was vetoed by the legislature in September 2025 (71 against, 14 for), leaving same-sex partners without recognized medical decision-making rights. A 2025 report concluded LGBTQ people face exclusion in domains including health. Trans youth seeking gender-affirming care face the requirement of continuous hormone therapy and specific surgical treatments to change ID gender markers, with no comprehensive gender recognition framework existing. A 2025 report concluded LGBTQ people face exclusion including in domains of personal security and violence. Trans people report being susceptible to verbal, physical and sexual abuse in public toilets. Trans people face a high rate of rejection, victimization, and discrimination, with social marginalization leading to negative mental health effects — trans Hongkongers disproportionately experience moderate-to-severe depressive and anxiety symptoms. No hate crime legislation is mentioned; as of 2026 there are no laws against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The Broadcasting Authority ruled in 2007 that the RTHK programme 'Gay Lovers' was 'unfair, partial and biased towards homosexuality' (later overturned by court in 2008). In May 2019, a Cathay Pacific advertisement featuring a same-sex couple was banned by Airport Authority Hong Kong and MTR Corporation, only reversed after widespread public criticism. Political opposition comes from social conservatives, often with evangelical Christian ties; around 80% of 10,775 written submissions on the proposed Registration of Same-sex Partnerships Bill were in opposition. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognized in Hong Kong. The Registration of Same-sex Partnerships Bill was vetoed by the legislature on 19 September 2025 (71 against, 14 for). The Court of Final Appeal in September 2023 directed the government to establish an alternative recognition framework within two years but also ruled no constitutionally guaranteed right to marry exists. Same-sex couples gained spousal visa rights (CFA 2018), joint tax filing (effective 19 September 2018), limited domestic violence protection (2009), and equal public housing rights (Court of Final Appeal, 26 November 2024). Many Hong Kong residents who are British Nationals (Overseas) can register civil partnerships at British consulates in 22 countries. A 2025 report concluded LGBTQ people face exclusion in domains of education. Attitudes toward trans acceptance are directly correlated with educational level. During the Legislative Council debate over unequal age of consent, conservative lawmakers argued legal inequality (21 for gay men vs 16 for heterosexuals) was necessary 'to protect youth and preserve tradition.' Younger people (18-40: 86% support fair treatment in 2022 poll) and non-religious people were more likely to support anti-discrimination protections and same-sex marriage. Trans youth seeking gender marker changes on ID cards must meet criteria including continuous hormone therapy and specific surgical treatment.
Major wire (Feb 2023): apex court bars surgery prerequisite for ID-card marker changes in a landmark trans case.
Rights news (Feb 2019): high court rejected three trans men's bid for marker change without surgery; judge called surgery the only objective criterion.
Independent local daily (Dec 2016): a bank's rainbow installations and the homophobic backlash — climate around corporate visibility.
Court-of-appeal archive (2006): equal-consent litigation examining discriminatory offences — a foundational precedent.

LAWG Education Fund report 'Left in the Dark': Honduras and El Salvador among the world's highest rates of violence against women/LGBTI persons; LGBTI persons — trans women especially — face major obstacles to justice; impunity driven by under-reporting, lack of police/prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and intentional case mishandling (quote: institutions 'fail to effectively investigate and prosecute'). Explains why anti-trans violence goes unpunished.

It records an Aug 2004 church protest at state recognition of three gay groups, 2009-10 items on an LGBT activist murdered amid violence and impunity, extreme violence against the gay community and post-coup abuses, and 2005 coverage of marriage and adoption bans.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Honduras: significant human-rights issues include violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, corruption, and lack of accountability for gender-based violence.

Washington Blade (25 Sep 2017): trans activist and Asociacion Cozumel Trans co-founder (PINU party) ran for Congress in Francisco Morazan at the 26 Nov 2017 election — potentially the first openly trans officeholder; context: Kendra Stefani Jordany's 2017 primary win, Claudia Spellman's 2012 LIBRE run, Victoria Gomez seeking asylum in Spain after threats/attacks in Tegucigalpa. Evidence of both trans visibility and the security costs behind it.

Corresponsales Clave (trans activist Kendra Jordany, 6 Sep 2017), drawing on the torture-prevention centre CPTRT: trans women in Honduras' national penitentiaries are held in the MEN'S system. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the 'La Isla' module (located beside the mentally-ill unit); trans women are forced to cut their hair and barred from presenting as women ('la policia... dicen que ellas son hombres'); conjugal visits are denied. At Penitenciaria de Marcala authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after CPTRT intervention was she isolated from the men and her feminine belongings returned. Documents birth-sex placement with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad-hoc protective isolation, and no placement-by-gender-identity policy.

texts.cleaned_text: Human Rights Watch (7 Oct 2020), Honduras section: 'Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which can lead to physical and sexual abuse.' A Honduran judge told HRW of a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards; the judge said she had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate: 'There's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.'

Under the Constitution, citizens may establish and associate with political parties and interest groups, but initial efforts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met with government opposition or extended delays. The first organizations arose anyway, often in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic, held no legal standing, and were essentially ignored by the Government apart from police harassment. In 2004 the Government extended formal recognition to three LGBTQ rights interest groups despite organized protests from the Catholic Church, Pentecostals and conservative legislators. About 400 people marched in a pride parade in July 2017 in San Pedro Sula. Penal Code Article 321-A (Decree No. 23-2013) punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on listed grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity with three to five years' imprisonment and fines of L.50,000 to L.300,000.

Same-sex unions are not legally recognized. The 2005 constitutional amendment expressly bans same-sex marriage and de facto unions, refuses to recognize same-sex marriages or unions performed legally in other countries (Article 112), and prohibits same-sex couples from adopting (Article 116). Same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. A name change for LGBTI persons is approved, described by the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association as an 'aberration in God's eyes'; no procedure details are given.

The Government offers medical care to all citizens and has been increasingly working with non-governmental organizations to raise awareness on HIV/AIDS, but the socially conservative influence of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestants has made it difficult to implement any comprehensive public program. Female prostitutes and men who have sex with men are identified as the highest-risk groups. The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs gives police permission to raid city streets, entrap sex workers under 'sanitation control' and arrest anyone who 'goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals', a provision LGBTQ organizations say police use to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space. No youth-specific care or medication provisions appear.

In 2013 the National Congress adopted amendments to the Penal Code via Decree No. 23-2013. Article 27 makes hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity an aggravating circumstance in criminal responsibility. Article 321 punishes with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies the exercise of individual and collective rights or refuses a professional service on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity. The new Penal Code took effect in March 2017; LGBTQ rights groups met with Congress to dispel doubts about wording and ensure Articles 321 and 321-A remained, and the anti-discrimination articles were kept.

LGBTQ rights organizations have documented numerous instances of police using the 2001 modesty provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women. International human rights organizations state that the military Government has targeted LGBTQ people for harassment, abuse and murder, and early LGBTQ organizations faced police harassment. Political hostility is visible in the fact that the two major parties have mostly ignored LGBTQ rights, only a handful of dissident members of the Democratic Unification Party expressed interest in working with the LGBT community, and three candidates who backed same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections all failed to win National Congress seats. President Juan Orlando Hernández said on 12 October 2018 that personally as a Christian he is against same-sex marriage, and the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association urged President Xiomara Castro to stop 'immoral laws'.

Penal Code amendments adopted in 2013 through Decree No. 23-2013 added gender identity to Article 27 on aggravating circumstances for crimes committed due to hatred or contempt. Article 321 punishes blocking, restricting or denying rights or professional services based on gender identity with three to five years imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages. Article 321-A punishes public incitement to discrimination, hatred, contempt, persecution, violence or attacks based on gender identity with three to five years imprisonment and a fine of fifty thousand to three hundred thousand lempiras. The new Penal Code that came into effect in March 2017 retained Articles 321 and 321-A after consultation with LGBTQ rights groups. The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs permits arrest of anyone who goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals and is documented as used by police as a pretext for harassing and detaining transgender women. Documented transgender-specific violence outcomes include sixty nine transgender persons among one hundred seventy four violent LGBTQ deaths registered from 2009 to 2014, the shooting dead of transgender activist Cynthia Nicole on 2 January and of trans activist Thalia Rodriguez on 10 January 2022 in Tegucigalpa, and the grant of asylum in Spain in June 2013 to a transsexual woman after a police officer tried to assassinate her. A transgender woman ran as a candidate for the Innovation and Unity Party in the 2017 elections, receiving 11,112 votes and placing 136th for a 128-seat National Congress and was unsuccessful. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1899 with consent required at fifteen years of age, the same as for heterosexual sex. The Constitution was amended in 2005 to expressly ban marriage and de facto unions between persons of the same sex and to refuse recognition of same-sex marriages or unions legally performed in other countries under Article 112. Article 116 prohibits adoption by same-sex couples. Penal Code amendments in 2013 through Decree No. 23-2013 added sexual orientation to Article 27 on aggravating circumstances, to Article 321 punishable by three to five years imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages, and to Article 321-A punishable by three to five years imprisonment and a fine of fifty thousand to three hundred thousand lempiras. Following the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 on access to marriage, Honduran activists filed suit with the Supreme Court in May 2018 to legalise same-sex marriage while a second case was dismissed in November 2018 for technical errors. A bill for same-sex marriage was presented to the National Congress in May 2022 by Libertad y Refundacion deputy Manuel Rodriguez and remained under discussion since 24 May 2022. The article documents no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically. The only general social-conditions statement is that "there is a social environment of historical discrimination against LGBTQ persons motivated by prejudice and machismo." For enforcement, LGBTQ rights organizations have documented numerous instances in which police have used the 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs as a pretext for harassing and detaining transgender women. Reported violence includes one hundred seventy four violent deaths of LGBTQ persons from 2009 to 2014 primarily in Cortes and Francisco Morazan, two hundred sixty four LGBTQ people murdered between 2009 and 2017, and statements by international human rights organizations that the military Government targeted LGBTQ people for harassment, abuse and murder. Specific transgender cases reported are the shooting dead of transgender activist Cynthia Nicole on 2 January, the murder of trans activist Thalia Rodriguez on 10 January 2022 in Tegucigalpa, and the June 2013 grant of asylum in Spain to a transsexual woman after an assassination attempt by a police officer. Protection machinery history notes that initial efforts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met government opposition or extended delays with no legal standing except for police harassment, that formal recognition was extended to three LGBTQ groups in 2004 despite protests from the Catholic Church, Pentecostals and conservative legislators, and that about four hundred people marched in a pride parade in July 2017 in San Pedro Sula.

On 4 May 2005 Honduras by Decree 36 amended Constitution Articles 112 and 116 to provide that only a man and a woman who have that status naturally may contract marriage, prohibiting marriage and de facto union between persons of the same sex.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex conduct legal since 1977; life partnerships since 2014 while the 2013 constitutional referendum banned same-sex marriage; full same-sex adoption rights since 2022 (final court ruling); open military service; hate-crime legislation; Pride events incl. Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac, Pula and the Balkans Trans Inter March; legal gender recognition framework. Wikipedia country coverage: In March 2014 Croatia granted asylum for the first time to a person persecuted on the basis of sexual orientation — a young man from Uganda who fled under the Uganda Anti-homosexuality Act. The text otherwise says nothing about visa rules, passport gender markers, or entry procedures for transgender travellers. Wikipedia country coverage: Croatia has three LGBT centres: the first in Zagreb, a second opened in Split on 24 May 2014, and a third in Rijeka on 16 October 2014 (LGBTIQ+ Druga Rijeka). Zagreb has the biggest gay scene, with clubs, bars and Queer Zagreb programming, while gay-friendly venues and beaches are noted in Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. On health facilities, the blood transfusion institute's rules effectively bar gay and bisexual men from donating blood indefinitely — a 2007 bylaw places MSM under categories of permanent rejection, and as of 2021 this is framed as 'behaviors or activities that expose them to risk of contracting blood-borne infectious diseases'. Wikipedia country coverage: Article 68 of the Life Partnership Act grants life partners the same health insurance and healthcare rights as married heterosexual couples and prohibits adverse treatment of life partnerships in those areas. Reproductive care is unequal: the Medically Supported Fertilization Law limits IVF to married heterosexual couples and single infertile women, effectively excluding same-sex couples (a 2012 law allowed single women but not lesbian couples). Foster care access for same-sex couples only came via courts — the Constitutional Court ruled on 7 February 2020 that excluding them was unconstitutional and discriminatory, and Mladen Kožić and Ivo Šegota became Croatia's first same-sex foster parents in September 2020 after a three-year legal battle; as of January 2024 no national law yet regulates same-sex adoption, protections coming only from court rulings. Youth-specific: children's placement decisions and partner-guardianship (permanent parental rights for a non-biological life partner, first case July 2015) directly shape minors' family lives, and the Center for Social Welfare initially rejected the Kožić/Šegota application twice. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2009 the European Committee on Social Rights found discriminatory statements in a mandatory Croatian school biology textbook, ruling they violated the European Social Charter; on 1 March 2013 the Minister for Science, Education and Sports announced an action to strip homophobic content from elementary and high school books, especially religious education texts. Age of consent was equalised at 14 in 1998 and raised to 15 under the Penal Code of 1 January 2013. Youth/family education support exists: Zagreb Pride's 2016 guide "We Have a Family!" for LGBT parents, and the 2018 picture book "My Rainbow Family" for preschool-age children with same-sex parents (first 500 copies free, French Embassy funding; crowdfunded reprint raised over $7,000). A Eurobarometer-style survey found 64% of Croatians agreed school lessons should include information about sexual orientation diversity and 63% about gender identity; a 2016 study on children in LGBT families found psychosocial adaptation and experiences of stigmatisation. In 2023 the opposition Možemo! party proposed easier legal gender change and IVF inclusivity, but none of those bills had passed as of January 2024.

Intrepid Travel country guide: Croatia 'widely accepts' LGBTQIA+ travellers (legal since 1977, partnership/protection laws) — but PDA may draw unwelcome responses in lesser-populated cities and gay venues are 'virtually non-existent outside Zagreb', now improving with new venues in Split, Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. Visitor-facing nightlife/PDA guidance.

European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Croatia (2024, reporting period 2023): transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including SOGI grounds.

Documents organised community infrastructure on the coast.

CroL (Oct 2014, Croatian): presentation of LGBTIQ+ centre 'Druga Rijeka' in Rijeka, founded to develop the community in Primorsko-goranska county and network with national and international organisations. It is backed publicly by mayor Vojko Obersnel and cultural institutions. Goals include visibility, anti-discrimination work and quality-of-life advocacy. Second major community centre documented.
