A travel guide reports the country widely accepts LGBTQIA+ travellers — but public displays of affection may draw unwelcome responses in less populated cities and gay venues are virtually non-existent outside the capital, now improving with new venues in coastal and interior towns.

A legal experts' country report on non-discrimination (2024, reporting period 2023) covers transposition and implementation of the region's equality directives, including sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds.

A local news report documents a city getting an LGBT centre (the second in the country, first on the coast) before the city's Pride; organisers demanded equal treatment of same-sex families (marriage, joint adoption) and said institutions create 'second-class citizens'; the mayor attended the press conference.

A local news report covers the presentation of an LGBTIQ+ centre in a second major city — founded to develop the community in the surrounding county and network with national and international organisations, backed publicly by the mayor and cultural institutions; goals include visibility, anti-discrimination work and quality-of-life advocacy.

Washington Blade (25 Nov 2019): Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, Haiti's national LGBTQ advocacy organization, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince; poisoning reports were unconfirmed by the Blade. ILGALAC issued a mourning statement. The piece cites the US State Department's 2018 report that attitudes in Haiti 'remained hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince' — a direct climate warning for visibly trans visitors.

HRW World Report 2018 (Haiti chapter): LGBT persons in Haiti continued to face high levels of discrimination. A June 2017 Senate bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs, a good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. In August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy with up to 3 years' prison and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. Both bills awaited a Chamber of Deputies vote as of November 2017.

Haiti's legal framework: same-sex conduct has been legal since 1791, with no legal recognition of gender identity and no anti-discrimination protections. A June 2017 Senate bill would penalise same-sex marriage with up to three years' imprisonment. Transgender people face documented harassment in post-earthquake camps. No prison-placement practice is documented for trans detainees: no rule assigning housing by birth sex versus identity, no separate units for them, and no solitary or segregation practice.

Constitutional guarantees of a right to health care, housing, education, food and social security apply to all citizens, but LGBTQ people often conceal their orientation or gender identity for fear of discrimination, which can impede access. After the 2010 earthquake, gay and bisexual men reported adopting a more masculine demeanor to avoid harassment and reduce chances of being denied emergency housing, healthcare, and food-for-work programs. HIV infection rates in Haiti rose to 4-6% as of 2008, 13% in certain rural neighborhoods, and organizations like Grasadis (founded 1997) work to prevent HIV/AIDS spread among the LGBTQ minority. The Certificat de Bonne Vie et Mœurs, required by many employers and schools, lists homosexuality as a crime that can justify denial of the certificate, directly affecting youth and students. In June 2017 the Haitian Senate launched a bill to regulate who receives this certification. The 1987 Constitution guarantees all citizens a right to education, though LGBTQ youth face pervasive social hostility.

A news report (25 Nov 2019): the president of the national LGBTQ advocacy organisation was found dead at his home in the capital; poisoning reports were unconfirmed. The report cites an official human-rights assessment that attitudes 'remained hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in the capital' — a direct climate warning for visibly trans visitors.

A world human-rights report (2018): LGBT persons continued to face high levels of discrimination; a 2017 senate bill would allow denial of a good-conduct certificate employers and universities require on grounds of homosexuality, and later in 2017 the senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy with up to three years' imprisonment and a large fine — both awaited a vote in the other chamber as of November 2017, status unverified.

texts.cleaned_text: France24 (June 2026) covers LGBTQ rights in Hungary after the election: 'we are very hopeful that changes will be made'.

AP (June 2026) reports that Hungary held its first Budapest Pride in the post-Orbán era. Tens of thousands of people marched in the 31st Budapest Pride, the first since Viktor Orbán was voted out, against the backdrop of the anti-LGBT laws adopted during his rule.

The Dissident analysis (April 2026) by Alejandra Caraballo: what Hungary's election (Tisza's 138 seats, ending Orbán's rule) actually means for LGBTQ people - a return to democratic baseline, not liberation. Details the 'constitutional architecture of erasure': the May 2020 total ban on legal gender recognition (redefining 'nem' as immutable biological sex), forcing trans Hungarians to carry mismatched documents.
Wikipedia's Hungary country overview states that legal gender change has been de facto impossible since 2018 and explicitly illegal since 2020, and that same-sex activity has been legal since 1961.

BBC News (April 2026): the European Court of Justice ruled Orbán-era anti-LGBTQ laws — including the under-18 gender-change ban argued under child-protection law — breached EU rules on several levels, significantly finding a breach of Article 2 of the EU Treaty (an unprecedented finding against founding values). The ruling came nine days after Hungarians voted in the election that ended Fidesz rule.

niHaplus (17 April 2026): after Fidesz lost power in the 12 April 2026 election ending 16 years of Orbán rule, Budapest Pride spokesperson Johanna Majercsik named restoration of the right to assembly as 'the most urgent issue' and said anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds majority; the Tisza party's silence on LGBTQ+ rights under Péter Magyar raises questions about the pace of change.

Hungarian Helsinki Committee / Háttér Society national report (2025) on LGBTIQ detainees in Hungary, part of the EU-funded 'Strengthening the rights of LGBTIQ detainees in the EU' project - the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in Hungarian detention amid the current legal and political climate.

HRW World Report 2025 (Hungary): LGBT people continue to face discrimination and demonization; a 2020 law bans legal gender change for transgender and intersex people, and in September 2024 the CJEU Advocate General called on Hungarian authorities to correct a transgender refugee's gender marker in national registries.

ECJ judgment C-247/23 Deldits (13 March 2025), on reference from the Budapest High Court in an immigration case: Article 16 GDPR requires the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data where it has changed and no longer complies with the accuracy principle of Art 5(1)(d) — the operative authority for updating gender markers on official records.

BuzzFeed News (April 2020, Patrick Strudwick): while ruling by emergency decree during COVID, Orbán's government pushed a bill barring passports and ID cards from reflecting a person's acquired gender — even for those already legally recognized. This is the decree-level rollback that made legal gender recognition explicitly illegal in 2020.

Wikipedia's Hungary country coverage records that in January 2018 the European Court of Justice ruled that asylum seekers may not be subjected by authorities to psychological tests in order to determine their sexual orientation. The May 2020 National Assembly resolution rejecting the Istanbul Convention attacked the treaty's measures as promoting "destructive gender ideologies" and "illegal migration." In October 2020 PM Orbán said "gays are to leave our children alone," and in 2017 he welcomed the World Congress of Families, a group designated a hate group by the Southern Poverty Law Center, at the National Parliament. After a 2021 children's book by the Labrisz Lesbian Association, Fidesz launched a smear campaign confusing homosexuality with pedophilia, and the government-linked media giant Mediaworks published an article calling Labrisz pedophiles without proof. Labrisz won at first instance but the Curia ruled in November 2022 that the article did not violate its right to good reputation, and the case was appealed to the Constitutional Court. In 2014 Jobbik displayed a sign reading "The Parliament Does Not Want Any Deviants" at Budapest Pride and verbally abused attendees. In April 2026 the ECJ found that the 2021 child protection law discriminated against and scapegoated LGBTI residents. Unregistered cohabitation has been recognised since 1996 for any couple, including same-sex couples, giving specified rights with inheritance only by testament and a widow's pension after 10 years. Registered partnerships for same-sex couples have been available since 1 July 2009, carrying the same rights as spouses except adoption, assisted reproduction and taking a surname, while same-sex marriage was banned by the 1 January 2012 constitution. Same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly, stepchild adoption is limited to married different-sex couples, and IVF and donor insemination are unavailable to lesbians in a registered partnership. A December 2020 constitutional amendment further banned adoption by same-sex couples and restricted single-parent adoption. In September 2026 PM Péter Magyar announced intent to repeal the ban on adoption by same-sex couples.

Harvard Crimson (Sept 2022): Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; on a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody, and his mother alleges police beat him — a documented death-in-custody case involving a trans traveler.

The Diplomat (14 August 2026, Robin Vochelet): vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law — President Prabowo Subianto's October 2025 presidential decree listing nonmilitary threats framed LGBTQ+ people within national defense policy. Article ties the violence and the official framing together as one escalation.

ABC News (15 August 2026): attacks on trans women 'did not suddenly appear' — analysis ties the surge to officials' latest verbal attacks and to the October 2025 presidential defense decree treating LGBT people as national-defense 'risks'. Academic commentator: the regulation shifts rhetoric 'into the official doctrine of national defence policy... risks that must be monitored and controlled'.
Reuters (Feb 2025): Aceh province publicly caned two men for a same-sex relationship.

exact_spans: the current-law baseline for this record
texts.cleaned_text: Outright International country page (updated 12 March 2026): Indonesia's new penal code took effect 2 January 2026 (signed December 2022) and penalises all consensual extra-marital sex between adults (reported as up to 2 years' imprisonment). Since same-sex marriage is not permitted, this effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, with prosecution reported as selective.
Human Dignity Trust country profile: two provinces of Indonesia (Aceh and South Sumatra) criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; national-level provisions target morality.

Amnesty International (June 2025): police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor on Sunday 22 June 2025, arresting 75 people (74 men, 1 woman) after public reports of a 'gay party'. Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena called it 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' and said the gathering violated no law — evidence of venue-based raids targeting LGBT gatherings near Jakarta.

HRW (7 July 2026) 'Indonesia: Surge in Abuse Against LGBT Students': HRW has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in Indonesia since 2016, following officials' condemnations of a student group at Universitas Indonesia; Arus Pelangi, Indonesia's LGBT umbrella organization, documented 94 cases. Officials in early July called on parents to monitor children in 'this lifestyle'.

HRW report (10 August 2016) 'These Political Games Ruin Our Lives': the Indonesian Psychiatric Association proclaimed same-sex orientation and transgender identities 'mental illnesses' and recommended psychological 'rehabilitation', while the Jokowi government remained mostly silent — the origin point of Indonesia's institutionalized anti-LGBT posture.

Indonesia censors expression deemed to promote homosexuality: the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction criminalizes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations (up to 7 years prison), and in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned TV/radio programs making LGBTQ behavior appear 'normal.' The government has banned websites and apps containing 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words (including Grindr), shut down the Instagram account of the comic Alpantuni, and in 2025 a new bill was being discussed to explicitly prohibit online content presenting 'lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behavior.' In October 2025, President Prabowo Subianto declared the spread of LGBTQ culture a 'non-military national threat' in a presidential decree, placing it alongside separatism and terrorism.

Transgender Indonesians can change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they may marry someone of the opposite legal gender. Since June 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers (Kartu Tanda Penduduk) across multiple provinces including Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung, and Papua, because many were undocumented, especially where families disapproved, leaving them without access to work or social services. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognized, with no third gender or X option, and transgender Indonesians have their gender at birth printed unless they have already obtained court recognition.

Since 2018, the Jakarta Social Agency has declared transgender women (waria) 'socially dysfunctional,' regularly conducted raids against them, and taken detained trans individuals to city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres where they are incarcerated alongside homeless people and released only after signing a promise not to repeat their 'offence'; officials stated this is meant as a deterrent against being transgender. Conversion therapy is widely practiced and openly advertised in rehabilitation centres, including corrective rape from family members against lesbian women. LGBTQ groups are working on setting up safe houses and evacuation plans, and the Yayasan Srikandi Sejati organization provides HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic; Yogyakarta has the only madrasa for transgender people in the world.

As of 2019, no specific law exists to protect Indonesian citizens from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. Theoretically, protection against discriminatory employment practices on any ground is guaranteed in the Constitution and Human Rights Law (No. 39/1999), and the Attorney General's Office rescinded a public job offer declaring LGBTQ persons need not apply after advice from the National Commission on Human Rights. A police brigadier (TT) was fired for being gay after colleagues outed him; his lawsuit was rejected by the Semarang State Administrative Court in May 2019 on procedural grounds. The police have issued a circular since 2015 to process hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and Regulation of the Head of National Police Number 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation.

texts.cleaned_text: Isle of Man Prison (Jurby), the island's only functioning prison (GBP 41.7m facility at the former RAF Jurby, fully operational 14 August 2008), operated by the Isle of Man Prison Service. Separate units exist for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders and vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit. No birth-sex-vs-identity placement rule, no trans-specific unit, and no trans-specific solitary or segregation practice are documented.

The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender persons to change their legal gender and to have their new gender recognised. The Equality Act 2017, granted royal assent on 18 July 2017 with much of the law in force from 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and ground of non-discrimination. A ban covering sexual orientation and gender identity conversion therapy was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the extensive sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and came into effect in 2024. In 2024 the Isle of Man became the first British territory and the first part of the British Isles to ban conversion therapy. In July 2022 community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. Private and consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with age of consent set at 21, lowered to eighteen by the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3). Until 2021 Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men if under sixteen or committed elsewhere than in private, defined in Section 10 as more than two persons present or in a public-access place, and in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral. The Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021 passed with royal assent in July 2021 and took effect 1 July 2022 by proclamation, pardoning historical gay sex offences committed prior to 1992 explicitly based on the UK Alan Turing law of 2017. Chief Minister Howard Quayle issued an unqualified apology to gay men convicted under previous laws, and in August 2022 on the 30th anniversary of decriminalisation the police commissioner formally apologised for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992. Same-sex couples were granted civil partnerships by the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2) effective 6 April 2011, and same-sex marriage effective 22 July 2016 after royal assent 19 July 2016. By the Civil Partnership Act 2011 same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011, lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates from IVF and surrogacy and no laws acknowledge surrogacy. Under the Employment Act 2006 (c.21) effective 1 September 2006 dismissal on grounds of sexual orientation was made unlawful, and the Equality Act 2017 lists sexual orientation, defined to include attraction to same, opposite, either sex and lack of attraction to either sex, as a protected characteristic.

The parliament's official report (26 April 2016): upper chamber proceedings - third reading of the 2016 marriage bill (same-sex marriage) and consideration of the 2016 equality bill - the primary legislative record of the island's marriage-equality debate.

Broadcast reporting (July 2016): same-sex marriage took effect on the island after assent of the marriage and civil partnership act; the first civil-partnership-to-marriage conversion was completed days after entry into force; civil partnerships legal since 2011.

Broadcast reporting (November 2005): the lower chamber adopted an employment bill amendment protecting gay and lesbian employees from dismissal on sexual-orientation grounds - the island's employment non-discrimination milestone; the 2006 employment act made such dismissal unlawful from 1 September 2006.

A broadcast item (June 2015): the head of government publicly backed same-sex marriage and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition - the political commitment that preceded the marriage act.

A prison profile: the island's only functioning prison, fully operational 14 August 2008, operated by the local prison service, with separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders and vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit; no trans-specific placement rule or practice documented.

A legal compilation: the 2009 gender recognition act allows transgender persons to change their legal gender and have it recognised; the 2017 equality act, assented 18 July 2017 and largely in force 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic; a conversion-therapy ban covering sexual orientation and gender identity passed in 2020 took effect in 2024.

HRW (26 Mar 2026): the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill amends the 2019 law to limit legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups (hijra, kinner) and intersex individuals, removing recognition for those self-identifying as trans men, trans women or non-binary. Rights activists (e.g. Akkai Padmashali) call it criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. Parliament passed it in March 2026.

BBC: India's parliament passed the controversial amendment redefining how transgender people are legally recognised, dropping self-identification amid opposition and LGBTQ-community protests; government frames it as widening welfare access and anti-trafficking protection, critics say it excludes many trans/non-binary/gender-fluid people. India has an estimated ~2 million transgender people.

Times of India (Kolkata): a transwoman alleges an RPF constable groped her at the station under the pretext of 'checking gender', an instance of identity-document and harassment friction travellers face with railway police.
The Probe (18 Jun 2024): transgender persons arrested by the RPF in Assam recount degrading treatment in custody. Victim interviews document police abuse against trans people during detention.

New Indian Express (16 Nov 2024): openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by CISF personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. The discrimination incident at an Indian airport checkpoint drew outrage.

Frontline (6 Sep 2024): replacing the IPC with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence. Trans people fear a rise in assaults as the new criminal code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

GOV.UK policy note (Dec 2025): India bars discrimination on grounds including sex interpreted to cover gender identity; same-sex acts decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018; no same-sex marriage or civil partnership (courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units); limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

Madras High Court judgment (S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, W.P.No.7284 of 2021, 7 June 2021, Justice N. Anand Venkatesh): landmark case brought by a same-sex couple harassed by police - the court's sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation, banning conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.

Constitutional protection covers expression: the Supreme Court has ruled that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls under Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by "sex," and the Allahabad High Court extended this in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. The University Grants Commission prohibits bullying and ragging aimed at students based on sexual orientation or gender identity in higher education. Conservative groups such as the Vishva Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal have labelled same-sex marriage a "Western attack on Indian culture" and have occasionally targeted Pride events.

Facilities for trans people are largely state-level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards that coordinate housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pension schemes, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Federally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors face coercive surgery: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male via non-consensual operations, prompting the Madras High Court in April 2019 to order Tamil Nadu to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants. Acceptance is notably higher among urban youth and students at top-tier universities such as the IITs, which host support groups like Indradhanu (IIT Delhi) and Saathi (IIT Bombay). Colleges such as the American College in Madurai teach specialised curricula on genderqueer and intersex human rights using works by transgender activists A. Revathi and Kalki Subramaniam. Bans on conversion therapy (Madras High Court 2021, National Medical Commission 2022) coexist with clandestine networks still operating nationwide.

Demographic studies report a high prevalence of verbal abuse and physical violence against sexual minorities, and the 2011 census recorded roughly 480,000 people identifying as transgender. Organisations like GayBombay, Good as You (Bangalore) and Sappho for Equality (Kolkata) operate alongside Pride events held annually in dozens of cities since the first parade in Kolkata in 1999. Political visibility includes Shabnam Mausi (first transgender elected official, 1998), transgender mayors and judges, and Menaka Guruswamy, who in March 2026 became India's first openly LGBTQ+ member of the national Parliament.

texts.cleaned_text: Human Rights Watch (21 Nov 2005): two more men executed for homosexual conduct in Iran — recorded state execution practice for same-sex conduct.

Under Article 20, Clause 14, a person who has had sex reassignment surgery may legally change name and gender on birth certification by court order, and corrected identity documents have reportedly been issued efficiently and transparently. Supporters of reassignment also invoke Article 215 of the civil code, covering acts serving a 'rational benefit', though approval by a doctor is required. New military identity cards have listed the exemption subsection applying to gay men and transgender individuals, who are classified as having mental disorders, a disclosure 6Rang warned identifies them and puts them at risk of violence and discrimination. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legally recognized, and no legislation addresses discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Because the government does not allow any political party or organization to endorse LGBTQ rights, that role has fallen to exiled groups such as the Green Party of Iran, the Worker Communist Party of Iran, the Worker's Way, the Glorious Frontiers Party, and the Constitutionalist Party of Iran. Mullah Taha, an Iranian Shia gay cleric, was forced to flee Iran in 2016 after conducting same-sex marriages, and gay Iranian couples report being afraid to be seen together in public while traditional families strongly influence who and when their children marry. The law sets the death penalty as legal for those above 18, and for murder, at the age of 15, and the 2017 US State Department report noted concerns about LGBTI minors. Documented cases involving young people include the January 2008 arrest of Hamzeh Chavi (18) and Loghman Hamzehpour (19) in Sardasht on sodomy and mohārebe charges, the reported 2006 hanging of two youths in north-eastern Iran for 'sex crimes', the 2022 case of two gay men in Maragheh whose death sentences for 'sodomy by force', a charge stemming from an accusation by a 16-year-old boy, were later commuted to life in prison, and the May 2021 murder of 20-year-old Ali Monfared allegedly by relatives. The 2017 report described an April 13, 2017 IRGC raid on a private party in Isfahan Province in which agents reportedly fired weapons and used electric Tasers; the Canadian nonprofit Iranian Railroad for Queer Refugees reported that those arrested were taken to Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan, where they were led to the prison yard and told they would be executed. In February 2008, police in Isfahan raided a party and arrested 30 men who were held indefinitely without a lawyer on suspicion of homosexual activity. Since the mid-2000s the government has provided transgender persons grants of up to 45 million rials (about $1,240) and loans up to 55 million rials (about $1,500) for gender reassignment surgery, and the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labor, and Social Welfare required health insurers to cover such surgery; HIV/AIDS medication is given free of charge to all Iranian citizens and several clinics offer free testing and counselling. Many LGBTQ Iranians seek UNHCR refugee status to be resettled in Australia, Canada, or the United States, and some middle-class Iranians have received education in Western nations. Outcomes have been mixed: the UNHCR rejected a plea in 2001 from an Iranian man who had entered the country illegally and was later convicted of killing his boyfriend; Japan rejected an Iranian gay man's asylum claim in 2005, and Sweden rejected a similar appeal that same year; LGBTQ activist Zahra Seddiqi Hamedani was reported to be living in Cologne, Germany in December 2023. The Netherlands stopped deporting gay men back to Iran temporarily in 2006: in March 2006 Dutch Immigration Minister Rita Verdonk stated there was 'no question of executions or death sentences based solely on the fact that a defendant is gay,' but after internal and external pressure she reversed course in October 2006 and announced Iranian LGBTs would not be deported. The United Kingdom drew criticism for continued deportations, with news reports documenting gay Iranians who committed suicide when faced with deportation, though campaign-backed cases such as Kiana Firouz and Mehdi Kazemi ended in asylum grants. The 2017 report also noted that security forces raided houses and monitored internet sites for information on LGBTI persons, and 6Rang documented forced 'anal' or 'sodomy' tests and degrading treatment of persons charged with homosexual conduct. On education, the government approved a booklet explaining condoms and distributed it to high school students and ran comprehensive HIV/AIDS education by the late 1990s, but no educational campaign for LGBTQ people has been allowed to exist; Kaveh Khoshnood noted that without acknowledging homosexuality's existence, no programs for LGBTQ people can be developed. Youth-facing cultural resources include the 2015 graphic novel Yousef and Farhad, published in English and Persian by OutRight Action International, and Maryam Keshavarz's 2011 film Circumstances about changing Iranian youth mores on sex and dating.

Transgender identity is legally recognized only through sex reassignment surgery, with Article 20 Clause 14 allowing a person who has surgery to legally change name and gender on birth certification upon court order. Legal-religious authorization traces to a 1964 fatwa by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini approving surgery while in exile, a 1983 fatwa allowing operations as a cure for diagnosed transsexuals, and a 1985 reaffirmation, with practice legalized since the mid-1980s under medical approval and partially financially supported by the state. Petitioners invoke Article 215 of the civil code on rational benefit and require medical approval supporting dissonance between assigned gender and true gender, while a 1976 Iranian Medical Association ruling deemed such surgeries unethical except for intersex individuals. Religious authority remains split, with Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei legally recognizing reassignment while Grand Ayatollah Yousef Madani Tabrizi called it unlawful and not permissible, and several Marja stress reassignment is not permissible for cross-dressers or those engaging in same-sex behavior. Some homosexual individuals have been pressured to undergo sex reassignment surgery to avoid legal and social persecution for being gay, with medical-legal endorsement framing reassignment as a means to conform to heteronormative standards and avoid same-sex acts termed hamjinsbaz. Security forces harassed, arrested and detained individuals suspected of being gay or transgender, in some cases raiding houses and monitoring internet sites for information on LGBTI persons, with those accused of sodomy often facing summary trials. No legislation exists to address discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Since the 1979 Revolution the legal code based on Islamic law forbids any sexual activity outside heterosexual marriage, with consensual same-sex activity criminalized and carrying maximum punishment of death, alongside imprisonment, corporal punishment and fines. Article 233 defines sodomy as penetration of genital organ up to foreskin into anus of a male, Article 234 imposes death on the receptive partner and on the insertive partner if force or coercion, married status, or non-Muslim with Muslim receptive partner applies and otherwise 100 lashes, Article 235 punishes intercrural sex with 100 lashes, Article 237 punishes other physically intimate acts between men with 31 to 74 lashes, Articles 238-239 punish tribadism with 100 lashes with death on fourth conviction under Article 136, and Article 114 allows reduction to flogging, imprisonment or reprimand or pardon request if offender repents. The law does not distinguish between consensual and nonconsensual same-sex intercourse, with NGOs reporting victim and perpetrator both held criminally liable in assault cases, and does not prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation. Enforcement has been stricter against gay men than lesbians, with records of at least 107 executions with charges related to homosexuality between 1979 and 1990, death sentences after a video confession in Tehran in March 2005, alleged public hangings in Gorgan in November 2005, hanging of two youths in July 2006, public execution in Kermanshah in November 2006, arrest of 87 including 80 suspected gay men at an Isfahan birthday party in May 2007, raid and arrest of 30 men in Isfahan in February 2008, and arrest of 30 men in Isfahan Province in April 2017 charged with sodomy, drinking alcohol and using drugs. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legally recognized, traditional families exercise strong influence over marriage and dating, few LGBTQ Iranians come out for fear of rejection, and gay couples report fear of being seen together and stereotyping as sex-obsessed child molesters, rapists and disease-ridden. Homosexuals, bisexuals and lesbians are banned from donating blood, and no educational campaign for LGBTQ people on HIV/AIDS has been allowed despite general HIV clinics, free testing, counseling and medication programs. Trans men and trans women are treated differently from each other in Iranian society regarding visibility and acceptance. The documented transgender-specific tolerance statement is: "Trans men are more visible socially and are able to find acceptance in society more easily than trans women, who are often misgendered and put in the same category as gay men." Hujjat al-Islam Kariminia asserts that society is largely unaware of the clear distinction between homosexuality and transsexuality, comparing the gap between the two to the Great Wall of China. For sexuality as distinct from transgender status, few LGBTQ Iranians come out to family due to fear of rejection, traditional families prohibit dating and exercise strong influence over marriage, and gay couples report fear of being seen together amid widespread stereotyping. Documented anti-LGBT violence includes the May 2021 murder of 20-year-old Ali Monfared allegedly by his half-brother and cousins days after the military mailed him an exemption document because of his sexual orientation. LGBTQ Iranians have fled Iran in recent years hoping to gain asylum in Europe, while no domestic protection machinery prohibits sexual-orientation or gender-identity discrimination.

Iranian transgender persons subjected to human rights abuse based on gender identity flee Iran to Türkiye to seek UNHCR asylum, and since 2008-10-08 receive basic necessities, financial aid and private sponsorship for resettlement to Canada through IRQR with Marjan Foundation despite prolonged resettlement waiting periods.

The 27 April 2024 parliamentary vote criminalises "biological sex changes based on personal desires and inclination" with up to three years in prison for both the transgender person and the doctor, excluding court-ordered procedures on intersex people, effectively closing off legal sex-change documentation. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are illegal: the Iraqi Personal Status Law 1959 Article 3 and the Iraqi Kurdistan Personal Status Law 1992 Article 1 define marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and Article 7 requires couples seeking to marry to produce medical documents proving they are not infected with AIDS. The Personal Status Law was amended in 1981 to allow a wife to divorce her husband where he is guilty of a homosexual relationship, treated as infidelity. The 2024 law on homosexual relations carries penalties of up to 15 years in prison with fines and deportation, making removal a stated consequence of criminalised status. Asylum and relocation are handled largely by NGOs: Iraqi LGBT (established September 2005) works on relocating LGBTQ people to safer countries, providing legal help for asylum seekers and maintaining "safe houses" in Iraq, while the International Railroad for Queer Refugees (founded 2008) provides financial and resettlement assistance to LGBTQ asylum seekers fleeing prosecution for sexual orientation or gender identity. OWFI led over 40 local organisations to change Iraq's Anti-Shelter Policy, which had allowed only government-run shelters to exist. Rasan implemented larger projects from 2016 as partners of COC Nederland in the "Pride Program" (locally "Crossing Iraqi Rainbow"). In early 2012 a wave of killings targeted "emo" teenagers accused of homosexuality on the basis of their clothing, the "Emo Killings", carried out by Shi'a death squads of the Mahdi Army; flyers appeared in Baghdad naming people and threatening them unless they cut their hair and gave up nonconformist clothing. Saddam Hussein ordered all Iraqis with AIDS relocated to a special prison facility after the disease reached Iraq in 1986. Iraqueer (formed March 2015) runs education work including published guides on security and health safety, YouTube videos and workshops on gender and sexuality, advocacy and safety in crisis.

Wikipedia country coverage: Iceland's 1996 Penal Code amendments made it illegal to publicly attack a person or group with mockery, defamation, abuse or threats because of their sexual orientation, and a 2014 amendment added gender identity to anti-discrimination grounds. Public expression is visibly supported: Reykjavík Pride drew about 100,000 people in 2015 (roughly 30% of the population), and in 2016 President Guðni Th. Jóhannesson became the first president to attend a gay pride parade. The country has a visible gay scene of bars and cafés in Reykjavík, though elsewhere the sparse population means there is almost no gay scene (Akureyri has no gay bars). Wikipedia country coverage: Stepchild adoption (a person adopting their partner's biological child) has been permitted since 2000, and on 27 June 2006 same-sex couples gained equal access to joint adoption of children alongside public IVF insemination treatment. Registered partnerships from 1996 already granted same-sex couples many of the same rights, responsibilities and benefits as marriage, including the ability to adopt stepchildren. A 2000 Gallup poll found 53% of Icelanders supported lesbian and gay adoption rights, with 35% against. Wikipedia country coverage: Section 178 of the Penal Code criminalized same-sex relations between 1869 and 1940, and public antipathy towards LGBT people remained high until the 1980s: some of the earliest Icelanders to come out publicly, Hörður Torfason and Anna Kristjánsdottir, initially faced public discrimination and ridicule. State hostility has since reversed — the 1996 anti-discrimination amendments, the 2010 unanimous (49–0) same-sex marriage vote, and the 2023 conversion therapy ban (53–0, 3 abstentions) mark the shift. One lingering restriction was the blood donation ban on men who have sex with men, challenged by a lawsuit in 2014, relaxed to a 4-month deferral in September 2021, and lifted entirely from September 2026. Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2008 it has been illegal to discriminate against people on the basis of their sexual orientation in education. Since 2016 the town of Hafnarfjörður has included information about same-sex relationships in its eighth-grade (ages 14–15) sex education lessons, and the Queer Student Association of Iceland runs social activities and field trips for University of Iceland students. On gender, the 2019 self-determination law (effective 1 January 2020, implemented January 2021) lets minors change their legal gender with parental consent, adds an 'X' third-gender option, and bans medical interventions on intersex children against their will except for health-related reasons. The age of consent was set at 14 in 1992 and raised to 15 in 2007, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Times of Israel: 'Most Israelis favor same-sex marriage, but half of MKs mum on issue' - a Channel 10 survey found majority public support for same-sex marriage while half of lawmakers declined to state a position, including a culture minister who has marched in the Pride parade.

Law-journal article documenting that Israel’s response to transgender prisoners’ vulnerability has been to isolate/segragate them, keeping trans inmates apart from the rest of the prison population rather than placing them in facilities matching their gender identity. Establishes that a trans prisoner faces isolation-based custody as the default management practice.

October 2019 precedent-setting case: an Israeli court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one, after ACRI petitioned. The prisoner was initially placed in a separate wing of the women’s prison, and ACRI prepared a further petition to have her housed with the general population — showing case-by-case placement review by the courts, and that trans women have at times been held in men’s prisons in Israel.

Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression has expanded but repeatedly drawn violence: Israel's first LGBT pride march (Alizada) was held 17 September 1977, Tel Aviv's first Pride parade in 1993, and Eilat Pride began in 2001. Jerusalem Pride was initially banned by municipal order until a court overturned it; the 2005 march was attacked by Haredi man Yishai Schlissel (3 stabbed, 10-year sentence), and after his 2015 release he stabbed six marchers, killing teenage girl Shira Banki. The 2018 Aguda-organized LGBTQ strike drew over 100,000 to a Tel Aviv rally, and an estimated 250,000 marched in Tel Aviv Pride in June 2022. The 2025 Tel Aviv Pride (13 June) was cancelled by the municipality after Israeli strikes on Iranian targets, while in 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality raised the Pride flag for the first time along the route from Sacher Park to the Knesset. Wikipedia country coverage: In December 2004 the Tel Aviv District Court ruled the government acted illegally in trying to deport the Colombian partner of a gay Israeli soldier, extending a 1999 Supreme Court rule barring deportation of foreign nationals married to Israeli citizens to common-law and same-sex couples. In March 2008 the Interior Ministry granted a rare residency permit to a gay Palestinian from Jenin to live with his partner of 8 years in Tel Aviv, citing danger to his life in the West Bank. In December 2016 Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit instructed the Interior Ministry to give same-sex couples the same citizenship rights as opposite-sex couples; previously same-sex spouses of Israeli citizens waited up to seven years for citizenship and typically received only permanent residency. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2008 the City of Tel Aviv opened the Municipal LGBT Community Center, the first of its kind in the country. On 1 August 2009 an armed attacker killed two people and injured 15 at a lesbian and gay centre in Tel Aviv, condemned by PM Netanyahu and President Peres. Community infrastructure also includes the Jerusalem Open House, which staged the 21 June 2007 Jerusalem parade after police allocated thousands of personnel to secure the area, and a central Jerusalem square to be renamed "Tolerance Square" in memory of Shira Banki. In 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality hung Pride flags with the Hebrew inscription "equality in life" along the parade route. Wikipedia country coverage: On 14 February 2022 Health Minister Nitzan Horowitz issued an executive directive banning licensed medical professionals (psychologists, social workers, Ministry of Health-licensed therapists) from conducting conversion therapy, though it does not bind rabbis, clergy or alternative practitioners and has not been codified into law by the Knesset. Reproductive care was restricted: a July 2018 surrogacy law excluded single men and same-sex couples, but the High Court of Justice ruled on 27 February 2020 and the Supreme Court unanimously on 11 July 2021 that the ban violated equality and the right to parenthood, effective 12 January 2022. Trans healthcare was historically denied — Attorney General Haim Cohn blocked Rina Natan's sex reassignment surgery in 1954, and legal recognition of sex reassignment only came in 1986; in July 2025 the High Court blocked a fast-track attempt to undo a gender change, holding the 2021 certificate "remains valid." Youth-specific: the governing coalition defeated a bill to ban conversion therapy on 24 February 2016, and the same day defeated a bill to train health professionals on gender and sexual orientation issues. Wikipedia country coverage: Under the British Mandate, official questionnaires documented "unnatural" sexual expression including sodomy between school boys, and Britain pushed criminalization into Palestinian schools and society, a policy carried into the Israeli state. In 1943 the Acre district court tried Mustafa Naif, aged 16, alongside Mustafa Zaharan for sodomy; Naif recanted to protect his friend, was convicted of perjury instead, and faced a sodomy charge carrying up to 10 years' imprisonment. Youth are also direct targets of violence: Shira Banki, a teenage girl, was stabbed to death at the 2015 Jerusalem Pride parade. On family formation, between 2008 and 2017 only 3 of 550 same-sex couples seeking to adopt succeeded (versus over a thousand heterosexual couples), until the government reversed course in August 2017 under Supreme Court pressure; the Knesset also voted in July 2018 to keep single men and same-sex couples out of surrogacy.

Treatment for gender dysphoria in Israel can be paid for using public health insurance if a patient receives approval by the Committee for Sex Reassignment operating out of Sheba Medical Center in Tel HaShomer, composed of an endocrinologist, a urologist, and a plastic surgeon and organized by the Health Ministry, and all sex reassignment surgery operations in Israel are performed by Dr. Haim Kaplan at Sheba under this committee's approval. Many transgender Israelis have had trouble getting approval due to stringent opinions on gender dysphoria, and thus many pay out of pocket for hormone replacement therapy and/or go overseas for sex reassignment surgery. Since 2015 the Health Ministry has allowed transgender people to change legal gender without undergoing sex reassignment surgery or a sex change operation, while a June 2013 Knesset bill to eliminate gender markers on National Identity Cards did not pass. In 2024 the Knesset passed a law allowing transgender individuals to remove their deadname from ID cards, where Israeli law previously required individuals to record all previous names regardless of gender identity. The IDF does not consider gender dysphoria a disqualifying condition for service and considers certain transition-specific medical treatment (hormone replacement therapy and sex reassignment surgery) and counseling medically necessary for those diagnosed with transsexualism and thus pays for said treatments. The IDF determines gender-specific army regulations (length of service, which gender to be housed with, whether to wear a male or female uniform, etc.) on a case-by-case basis for transgender soldiers, but because law makes it difficult to begin transition until age 18 and does not normally allow surgery before age 21, only Shachar Erez has undergone surgery while serving as the first openly transgender officer. Many draftees diagnosed with gender dysphoria can receive exemption from military service at their own request, and officially IDF policy does not prohibit intersex persons from service. Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private were not enforced after a 1953 Attorney General directive by Haim Cohn and a 1963 Supreme Court ruling, and were formally repealed by the Knesset in 1988 by omission from the criminal code, with the age of consent at 16 years for both homosexual and heterosexual acts. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation was prohibited in employment in 1992 with some exemptions for religious organizations, broadened in 1997 to the Libel and Slander Law prohibiting defamation motivated by sexual orientation, with every violent crime motivated by sexual orientation considered a hate crime doubling punishment, and the 2000 Prohibition of Discrimination in Products, Services and Entry into Places of Entertainment and Public Places Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation by providers of products, public services or public places. In April 2020 the Beersheba Magistrate's Court ruled a local print shop must compensate an LGBTQ rights group after refusing to print posters, holding that when beliefs conflict with necessity of providing service to all in public space, the last value holds superior. Same-sex marriage cannot legally be performed in Israel due to absence of civil non-religious marriage, but since 2006 Israeli law recognizes civil same-sex marriages performed elsewhere for registration with the same legal rights, and Israel became the first country in Asia to recognize unregistered cohabitation between same-sex couples, with Tel Aviv recognizing unmarried couples including gays and lesbians as family units for municipal service discounts. Openly gay, lesbian and bisexual soldiers serve without hindrance in all branches after the IDF formally opened the draft to all regardless of sexual orientation in 1993 and ceased linking orientation to security clearances in 1998, with discrimination in recruitment, placement and promotion and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation prohibited and same-sex couples including widows and widowers recognized. In October 2014 the Ministry of Health stated conversion therapy creates false impressions of scientific recognition with no scientific evidence of success and may cause harm and created a complaints committee, while a February 2016 Knesset bill to ban conversion therapy for minors failed 37-45, the Israel Medical Association in January 2019 banned members from performing it, and in July 2020 MPs passed a bill to begin outlawing it requiring two more approvals. Since 1 June 2017 gay and bisexual men were allowed to donate blood following a one-year deferral, with a January 2018 Health Ministry pilot allowing donation regardless of last sex, and from October 2021 gay and bisexual men can donate regardless of when they last had sex.

Court-based legal gender recognition with dead-name removal from IDs (2025) and publicly funded transition healthcare exist; the main international airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition.

No statute or prison-service regulation on trans-prisoner placement is documented; whether case-by-case judicial relief would extend to a detained foreign visitor is not established.
ANSA (appeal confirmed): convictions upheld on appeal for the assault of transgender tourists in Italy — court outcome affirming accountability for violence against trans visitors.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Italy: the Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second year; a cardinal called homosexual acts 'a mortal sin'; homophobic and transphobic violence continued including organised dating-app entrapment schemes targeting gay men; in March the Civil Court of Asti recognised for the first time physical and psychological harm from homophobic mistreatment.

Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report (July 2025) on LGBTIQ detainees in Italy: overview of homolesbobitransphobia and discrimination, pathways to gender affirmation, same-sex relationships, and the legal/policy framework for LGBTIQ people in Italian detention.

HRW World Report 2025, Italy chapter: political rhetoric hostile to LGBT people contributes to a hostile environment, addressed in the report's Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section; the chapter also records constraints on the rule of law and on civil society.
tgcom24 (5 Jul 2024): Milan traffic officer sentenced to 10 months for beating a transgender woman with a baton ('trans bloccata a manganellate') — police-violence conviction against a trans person.
Progetto Gionata reports that transphobia is the most atroce and diffuse discrimination facing transgender people in Italy.
Outright International country overview: Italy at-a-glance — same-sex relations legal nationwide for men and women; legal matrix baseline.
Intrepid Travel presents Italy as an LGBTQIA+ destination for its travellers; the page carries no safety finding specific to Italy.
Frontiers in Psychiatry (2026): thematic analysis of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons — systemic gaps and institutional challenges for incarcerated trans people.

Italy's position on gender identity and sexual orientation rests on court rulings and sectoral statutes rather than a single comprehensive law. Cross-dressing is legal, although the fascist penal code of the 1920s–1940s banned it and police targeted trans people; in 2006 a police officer was reportedly dismissed for cross-dressing in public while off duty. A bill banning homophobic and transphobic advertising in streets and on vehicles passed the Chamber of Deputies 271–16 on 28 October 2021 and the Senate 190–34 on 4 November, was signed by President Mattarella and took effect 10 November 2021; the government forced a single up-or-down vote on the whole bill, so MPs who opposed that provision had to vote for it. A broader anti-discrimination and hate-crime bill passed the Chamber 265–193 on 4 November 2020 but died in the Senate on 27 October 2021 by a 131–154 secret ballot. Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment has been illegal nationwide since July 2003 under Legislative Decree no. 216 of 2003, which implements EU Directive 2000/78/EC; the exemptions for police, armed forces and rescue services were removed by Law no. 101 of 2008. No other nationwide law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and no Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination, so transgender people may face discrimination in goods and services, housing, education and health care; ILGA-Europe's 2021 report notes the absence of nationwide protection for goods and services. A Rome court ruled on 15 January 2023 that firing a trans professor amounted to sex discrimination. Regional statutes cover Tuscany (2004), Liguria (2009), Marche (2010), Sicily (2015), Piedmont (2016), Umbria (2017), Emilia-Romagna (2019), Campania (2020) and Apulia (2024). Legal gender change has been possible since 1982, when Italy became the sixth country worldwide to allow it; since 21 May 2015 neither sterilisation nor sex reassignment surgery has been required. On 23 July 2024 the Constitutional Court, in judgment no. 143, first recognised non-binary individuals as rights-holders under Articles 2, 3 and 32 but declined to add a non-binary registry marker, holding that only Parliament can alter the male/female binary, and struck down the requirement of judicial authorisation for gender-affirming surgery after a legal sex change. Courts in Trento (15 February 2023) permitted legal gender change for transgender minors with parental consent and psychological consultation, and Trapani (6 July 2023) allowed a name and gender change with no surgery or hormones. On 14 April 2025 the Supreme Court of Cassation ordered Italian identity cards to use the gender-neutral term "genitori" rather than "mother" and "father" for children with same-sex parents, finding the previous wording discriminatory. Citing the Constitutional Court's 2010 ruling that recognised same-sex couples as a "legitimate social formation," the Court of Cassation ordered a questura to grant a residence permit to an Algerian citizen married to a same-sex Spanish spouse. Italy recognises persecution based on sexual orientation or gender identity as grounds for asylum under the 1951 Geneva Convention and EU Qualification Directive 2011/95/EU, and Decree-Law No. 130/2020, in force 22 October 2020, simplified asylum procedures and reinforced protection for vulnerable groups including those persecuted on those grounds. Same-sex marriages performed abroad are registered as civil unions rather than marriages (Court of Cassation, May 2018). Gay and bisexual men have been allowed to donate blood since 2001. Since February 2019 puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones have been provided free of charge under the National Health Service, and since 2020 hormone therapy has been fully covered. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, and Italy has had an equal age of consent for homosexual and heterosexual acts since before the 20th century. In 2018 the Italian National Bioethics Committee and the Italian Medicines Agency backed puberty blockers for adolescents with gender dysphoria case by case with safeguards; access still requires medical evaluation, parental consent and exhaustion of other interventions, a position supported by the Italian Society of Endocrinology, the Italian Academy of Pediatrics and six other paediatric and adolescent medical societies. In May 2026 AGESCI, Italy's largest Catholic scout association, decided that sexual orientation and gender identity can no longer exclude adults from leadership and educational roles, after three years of internal debate. Pew found in 2013 that 86% of Italians aged 18–29 accepted homosexuality, against 67% of those over 50.

Amicus brief in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica before the Inter-American Commission (filed Feb 2024): argues Jamaica's continued criminalisation of LGBTQ persons and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable — sections document housing insecurity, educational and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans under the discrimination regime.

UNDP 'Being LGBT in Jamaica' National Survey (March 2023): national survey of LGBT Jamaicans with dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care; quantifies lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.

US DOJ/EOIR Jamaica country packet (2013): Offences Against the Person Act makes 'buggery' punishable by up to 10 years' hard labour; LGBT victims are reluctant to report because police leak incident details, fail to investigate LGBT violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks (documented via the CVC and local organisations).

IACHR Report on the Situation of Human Rights in Jamaica (10 Aug 2012): finds 'the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject in Jamaica to be deplorable'; covers citizen security, police killings including the May 2010 operation, and justice administration, with civil-society input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays (J-FLAG).

HRW letter (30 Nov 2004) citing its report 'Hated to Death: Homophobia, Violence, and Jamaica's HIV/AIDS Epidemic': documents police harassment of gay men and HIV/AIDS outreach workers, community and family violence carried out with impunity, and official indifference; five Jamaican human-rights organisations backed the report's 16 Nov 2004 Kingston launch.

Amnesty International urgent appeal (4 Jun 2006): reports vigilante violence and police ill-treatment or torture of LGBT people in Jamaica — gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once orientation known; lesbians raped and driven into asylum abroad; concern that prominent musicians promote homophobia.

Jamaica Gleaner reporting (5 Feb 2019) on UWI lecturer Carla Moore's 2018 study (Apr-Nov 2018, funded by the Inter-American Institute of Human Rights, the IBA and the UN Latin American Institute for the Prevention of Crime): Jamaicans perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated' in Jamaica's penal institutions and rehabilitation opportunities for them are 'basically non-existent'. Inmates' movement inside facilities is severely curtailed and access to resources often limited because of entrenched homophobia/transphobia - other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners. The study estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities and reported that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'. Evidence that LGB/trans prisoners are socially ostracised and isolated rather than integrated, with no specialised housing policy documented.

US State Dept country report: 'Prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity'; correctional facilities were significantly overcrowded (Tower Street maximum-security cells at three times capacity), with harsh, life-threatening conditions, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. The report also records that Jamaica barred legal gender registration ('Individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender'), that the buggery law (up to 10 years' hard labour) criminalised consensual same-sex conduct, and that no anti-discrimination law protected SOGI. Official-state confirmation that trans prisoners face identity-targeted violence in Jamaican prisons with no gender-recognition framework for accommodation decisions.

In 2012 Maurice Tomlinson sued Jamaican TV stations TVJ, PBCJ and CVM for refusing to air a 30-second advertisement, "Love and Respect," promoting recognition of LGBT people's humanity; the Constitutional Court ruled against him in November 2013, and the Court of Appeal heard the appeal in February 2016 with judgment reserved. The UN Human Rights Committee's 2011 review regretted virulent lyrics by musicians and entertainers that incite violence against homosexuals and urged Jamaica to investigate and sanction those responsible. Dancehall artists including Buju Banton, Beenie Man, Bounty Killer, Elephant Man, Sizzla and Shabba Ranks have written or performed songs advocating attacks on gay and lesbian people, and a 2005 agreement between dancehall labels and groups such as OutRage! and the Stop Murder Music Coalition sought to end anti-gay lyrics in live performance.

In January 2018 Jamaica barred entry to Steven Anderson, a Holocaust-denying anti-gay pastor from Arizona, after an outcry from activists; he said he was told at the airport he would not be allowed into the country.

LGBT Jamaicans have fled abroad for safety. Maurice Tomlinson moved to Toronto in 2011 after death threats, Gareth Henry sought asylum in Canada in 2008, and Simone Edwards was granted asylum in the Netherlands in 2008. Tomlinson's July 2019 IACHR petition asks that Jamaica allow naturalization of same-sex spouses of Jamaican citizens on the same terms as heterosexual spouses. In January 2019 the Director of Tourism, Donovan White, said gay tourists are welcome and that Jamaicans harboured no open hostility toward gay visitors.

In September 2019 Montego Bay Mayor Omar Davis and Councilor Charles Sinclair blocked the local cultural center's use by the local LGBT group to protect the building's "sacredness," and other venues then cancelled reservations over fear of backlash, forcing cancellation of the October 2019 Pride events; police said they could not provide protection to LGBT Jamaicans given the whipped-up hysteria. J-FLAG reported in 2012 harassment of gay and lesbian patients by hospital and prison staff and numerous reports of violence against gay inmates by wardens and other inmates, with few seeking recourse through the prison system. Quality of Citizenship Jamaica, founded in 2013, worked to create safe spaces for LGBT women, youth and transgender people before ending operations in 2018.

In 2011 Parliament passed the Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (Constitutional Amendment) Act, explicitly banning same-sex marriage and any other kind of union from being recognized in Jamaica. In 2019 both Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Peter Phillips announced opposition to legalizing same-sex marriage, and in July 2019 Maurice Tomlinson petitioned the IACHR to rule that Section 18(2) of the Constitution contravenes the American Convention on Human Rights, seeking repeal and recognition of his Canadian marriage. Although lesbian civil ceremonies have taken place, including the 2012 celebration in Jamaica of Jamaican-born Nicole Y. Dennis-Benn and Emma Benn, legally married in New York, Jamaica recognizes no legal basis for partnerships between women.

J-FLAG data showed that young people aged 18 to 29 bore the brunt of violence based on sexual orientation, including 68 reports of sexually motivated harassment or abuse in 2012 with 53 assault cases and at least two killings. In July 2013 a mob in St. James stabbed to death Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old, and the case remained unsolved with no arrests as of 2022. University campuses have been sites of anti-LGBT violence. Students at UWI's Mona campus rioted in April 2006 while police protected a man chased across campus, and in November 2012 two campus security guards beat a reportedly gay student seeking refuge from a mob, after which the University of Technology established a working group on intolerance and bullying. Dr. J. Carolyn Gomes resigned as head of Jamaicans for Justice in 2013 after nationwide pushback on sexual-education leaflets for adolescents that mentioned anal sex.

Polls record deep hostility. 96% opposed legalizing homosexual relations in 2001; 70% said in 2008 that homosexuals are not entitled to the same basic rights; 85.2% opposed legalizing homosexuality among consenting adults in a 2010 survey; 88% disapproved of homosexuality in a 2016 J-Flag poll; and 2023 polling indicates at least 60% oppose acceptance of homosexuality. Time magazine labelled Jamaica "the most homophobic place on Earth" in 2006, and in 2013 the majority of LGBTQ people in the country said they faced homophobic violence in public. J-FLAG, founded December 1998, operates underground and anonymously as Jamaica's first LGBT human rights organization, and co-founder Brian Williamson was stabbed to death in June 2004 with a crowd outside his home celebrating and chanting slurs. In 2012 about a third of the population, over 900,000 Jamaicans, believed the government was not doing enough to protect LGBT people from violence and discrimination.

The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books; the defining case is a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party, whose killing police failed to investigate — now before an international human-rights commission.

A 2018 academic study of the nation's prisons (about 300 of 1,800 prisoners at a major correctional centre belonging to sexual or gender minorities) reports that prisoners perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated', that rehabilitation opportunities are 'basically non-existent', that homophobia/transphobia is entrenched (other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners), and that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'.

A major foreign government's 2023 report confirms 'prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity', in facilities so overcrowded that a maximum-security centre's cells held three times capacity; a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay; the report records that the nation barred legal gender registration.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and community members report that violence against trans people is common but rarely reported; major tourist resort areas are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare.

CAIRO 52 Jordan country profile: new legislation curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access; security forces coerced queer community spaces into closing, pushing transgender and queer people to leave; intersex people can change legal gender markers but transgender people cannot, and gender-affirming healthcare is penalised for providers under medical-liability law.

OutRight International Jordan profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised — Jordan abolished the colonial-era ban in 1951; no clear legal pathway for trans people to change gender markers (allowed 'in some cases'); gender-affirming surgery permitted for intersex people but criminalised for transgender people under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law (25) of 2018.

HRW World Report 2024 Jordan chapter (11 Jan 2024): authorities limited civic space in 2023 and enacted a new cybercrime law undermining free speech and privacy online. Peaceful dissidents and journalists were arrested and harassed under vague, abusive laws, with intrusive digital surveillance, conditions that shape online expression for visitors and residents alike.

CAIRO 52 analysis of Case No. 2092/2014 (Jordan): Jordanian legislation criminalises sex reassignment with penalties up to 10 years' imprisonment (except intersex cases); the plaintiff (born 1977) sought name and gender change from male to female in official records after undergoing hormone therapy and surgery in Australia, since such procedures are unavailable domestically.

HRW (6 Jun 2024): in Jordan, Egypt and Kuwait, authorities harass LGBT people via public-morality and debauchery laws even though same-sex relations are not explicitly criminalised in all three states. Alternative legal avenues substitute for formal criminalisation in these countries.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity' on LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa: despite state-sponsored repression and stigma, LGBT people are speaking out, building alliances and regional movements. Its annex lists laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across the region, including Jordan.

HRW (4 Dec 2023): Jordanian authorities systematically targeted LGBT rights activists in a coordinated crackdown on free expression and assembly around gender and sexuality. Officials smeared activists online by sexual orientation, social-media users posted their photos with messages inciting violence, and two LGBT organisation directors cited official intimidation.

The Jordanian government tolerates a few cafés in Amman that are widely considered gay-friendly. Books@Cafe, opened in 1997, remains a popular bookstore and cafe for patrons supportive of creativity, diversity and tolerance. Homosexuality has not been criminal in Jordan since the 1951 penal code, which legalised private, adult, non-commercial, consensual same-sex acts with an age of consent of 18 regardless of gender or orientation. That revision left an absence of legal protection, and vague morality laws give security forces and private individuals license to target LGBTQ people with impunity. The 2023 Human Rights Watch report found Jordan's cybercrime and morality laws used to persecute LGBTQ people. In August 2023 authorities promulgated a new cybercrime law that could target digital content on gender and sexuality and activists advocating LGBTQ rights, and security forces intimidated activists with threats of violence, arrest and prosecution, forcing several to shut down organisations, stop activities or flee. The Press and Publication Law, amended in 1998 and 2004, replaced a ban on depicting sexual perversion with a requirement that the press respect the values of the Arab and Islamic nation. The 2018 Medical Responsibility Law vaguely outlawed changing of sex while legalising correction of sex, potentially criminalising doctors performing gender-affirming surgery. Honor killings as a legal justification for murder were made illegal under the 2013 revised Penal Code. A 2019 Arab Barometer survey found 93% of Jordanians said society should not accept homosexuality. Jordanian model Khalid Abdel-Hadi described his youth: "Growing up, it was hard for me to find topics, subjects and publications that I could relate to! In my country, most magazines rejected me and my ideas due to my young age at the time, and I felt like an outcast in my own society!" My.Kali, the first LGBTQ publication in the MENA region, launched in 2007 and has been online since 2008.

A country profile by a regional documentation group: new legislation curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access; security forces coerced queer community spaces into closing, pushing transgender and queer people to leave; intersex people can change legal gender markers but transgender people cannot, and gender-affirming healthcare is penalised for providers under medical-liability law.

A profile by an international rights organisation (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised — this nation abolished the historic-era ban in 1951; no clear legal pathway for trans people to change gender markers (allowed 'in some cases'); gender-affirming surgery permitted for intersex people but criminalised for transgender people under Article 8 of the medical health-liability law (25) of 2018.

A national rights report chapter (11 Jan 2024): authorities limited civic space in 2023 and enacted a new cybercrime law undermining free speech and privacy online; peaceful dissidents and journalists arrested and harassed under vague, abusive laws, with intrusive digital surveillance — the environment shaping online expression for visitors and locals alike.

A regional documentation group's analysis of a 2014 court case: national legislation criminalises sex reassignment with penalties up to 10 years' imprisonment (except intersex cases); the plaintiff sought name and gender change from male to female in official records after undergoing hormone therapy and surgery abroad, since such procedures are unavailable domestically.

An international rights report (6 Jun 2024): in this nation and neighbouring states, same-sex relations are not explicitly criminalised in some cases, yet authorities “legally” harass LGBT people via public-morality and debauchery laws — alternative legal avenues substitute for formal criminalisation, so decriminalisation on paper does not equal safety.

A 2018 report on regional activism: despite repression and stigma, LGBT people across the region are speaking out, building alliances and regional movements; it includes an annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across the region, with this nation among them.

An international rights report (4 Dec 2023): national authorities systematically targeted LGBT rights activists in a coordinated crackdown on free expression and assembly around gender and sexuality; officials smeared activists online by sexual orientation and social-media users posted their photos with messages inciting violence — two LGBT organisation directors cited official intimidation.

Asahi Shimbun (9 Sep 2023): Gifu's Kasamatsu Prison — a women's prison — holds an inmate who is listed as female on her family register but identifies as a man (diagnosed with gender identity disorder). The Gifu Prefecture Bar Association demanded the prison allow him male clothes and a male hairstyle; after years with no policy change, the bar association issued a formal 'warning' to the prison in Sep 2023. The case shows Japan places convicted trans inmates in facilities matching their registered (family-register) sex rather than their gender identity, while treatment conditions inside remain contested at the prefecture level.
