texts.cleaned_text: HRW (11 Jun 2025): Tomoya Asanuma, a prominent transgender activist, was arrested in March 2024, held for more than 100 days in pre-trial detention and charged with assault; he was detained among men at a pre-trial detention centre, initially denied hormone treatment (until a doctor recommended it), mocked for his transgender identity in interrogations, and only allowed to shower away from other detained men after requests. HRW frames this as part of Japan's 'hostage justice' detention abuse and the legal limbo trans people face. It documents that a trans man's custodial placement followed his male legal sex, with accommodations (hormones, segregated showers) granted only grudgingly.

Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Japan only briefly, first in 1872 (early Meiji era) and repealed by the Penal Code of 1880, in force from 1882, in line with the Napoleonic Penal Code; the source elsewhere dates the criminalised period to 1873–1881. Since then Japan has had no laws against homosexuality, so sexual activity between consenting adults in private is legal regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The age of consent has been set at 16 years since June 2023, applying equally to same-sex and opposite-sex relations. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex marriages performed abroad are not legally recognised in Japan, and bi-national same-sex couples cannot obtain a visa for the foreign partner based on their relationship. However, the Ministry of Justice applies a general rule of granting the discretionary "designated activities" visa to same-sex married spouses. Since March 2009, Japanese nationals have been allowed to marry same-sex partners abroad, with the Justice Ministry instructing local authorities to issue the required single-status certificates. On gender markers, foreign nationals change their registered gender with their country of nationality and then report the change to the Immigration Services Agency for their residence card — a conflict-of-laws situation the source says can lead to bureaucratic breakdown, illustrated by the 2018 case of US national Elin McCready, whose gender change was refused recognition by Tokyo ward offices.

A 2023 law in this area is symbolic: there is no national anti-discrimination law, legal gender change requires a court process, the top court struck down the sterilisation requirement in 2023, and the same year ruled workplace bathroom restrictions on a transgender woman illegal.

A major national press outlet (September 2023) reports that a women's prison held an inmate listed as female on her family register who is diagnosed with gender identity disorder and identifies as a man, and that a bar association demanded male clothing and a male hairstyle for him before issuing a formal 'warning' to the prison over the lack of policy change.

An international human-rights organisation (June 2025) documents a transgender activist's arrest in March 2024, more than 100 days in pre-trial detention among men, the initial denial of hormone treatment until a doctor recommended it, mockery of his transgender identity during interrogations, and showering away from other detained men only after requests; the organisation frames this within its broader criticism of the nation's general pre-trial detention system.

A dated 2009 shadow report documents invisibility, marginalisation, silent prejudice and stigmatisation plus discrimination across education, employment, housing and health care with little governmental attention at the time.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review covering Jan–Dec 2023 (Kazakhstan): documents access-to-services bias (an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied employment-site registration after listing its focus), bias-motivated violence (an LGBTQI activist almost run over with no investigation), and a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022.

OSCE/ODIHR Hate Crime Reporting 2024 summary for Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to ODIHR since the 2018 report, has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, and would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures — an institutional-gap finding on documentation of bias violence.

HRW (10 Jul 2024): in June 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Information said it was reviewing a 'We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!' petition (Union of Parents) that met the threshold for government consideration; HRW warns the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide — a live, dated legislative threat.

ECOM (2024): ECOM has monitored and documented rights violations against LGBT people since 2017. Its analysis identifies health-right barriers in Kazakhstan alongside informal behavioural practices that policy analysis misses.

HRW (24 Sep 2019): Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments — privacy rights upheld over a 'moral foundations' defence; the women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for safety, illustrating both the privacy remedy and the social risk.

Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults has been legal since late 1997 (de jure 1998), when Article 104 of the Penal Code criminalising 'buggery' was repealed and a common age of consent of 16 was introduced; lesbianism was never a criminal offence. However, on 30 December 2025 President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a law banning 'information containing propaganda of pedophilia and/or non-traditional sexual orientation' in public spaces and media, with violations punishable by a 10-day arrest and a fine. The Mäjilis had approved a harsher version on 12 November 2025, and Kazakhstan now sits alongside Russia, Hungary and Georgia in prohibiting 'LGBTQ propaganda' by law. Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2003 transgender people in Kazakhstan may change legal gender on identity documents, but only after a diagnosis of 'gender identity disorder' involving medical tests and a 30-day psychiatric evaluation by a medical commission. Applicants must pay around ₸100,000 tenge, and although since 2023 commissions can in principle be assembled in every region, in practice the only functioning one is in Almaty because of requirements for separate specialist rooms. A positive decision yields a certificate valid for six months to start medical transition, and since 2011 document changes require gender-affirming surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation; people under 21 cannot change gender on documents at all. Wikipedia country coverage: As of 2020 same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children in Kazakhstan, and in February 2024 President Tokayev signed a law prohibiting adoption of orphans by same-sex couples. Deputy Minister of Education Natalya Jumadildaeva stated that a parent's sexual orientation would play a 'key role' in approval, assessed through a 'special psychological test'. Critics, including independent media, noted the law was modelled on Russian legislation. Wikipedia country coverage: Kazakhstan does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. No laws exist protecting LGBTQ people from discrimination in employment, education, housing, health care, public accommodations or credit, and 89% of people opposed same-sex marriage in a 2015-16 Pew survey.

A regional rights-monitoring annual review covering Jan–Dec 2023: documents access-to-services bias (an education group denied employment-site registration after listing its focus), bias-motivated violence (an activist almost run over with no investigation), and a wave of transgender people arriving from a neighbouring nation since 2022.

An international monitoring body's hate-crime reporting summary for this country: it has not reported hate-crime data since the 2018 report, has no nominated point of contact for hate crimes, and would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures — an institutional-gap finding on documentation of bias violence.

A human-rights organisation (10 Jul 2024): in June 2024 a ministry said it was reviewing a petition against open and hidden LGBT propaganda that met the threshold for government consideration; the organisation warns the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide — a live, dated legislative threat.

A regional report-library page (2024): a regional monitoring programme has documented rights violations against LGBT people; the analysis identifies health-right barriers across the region and individual countries, plus informal behavioural practices missed by policy analysis — abstract level, with country data in the linked report body.

A human-rights organisation (24 Sep 2019): the top court ordered compensation from a social-media user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments — privacy rights upheld over a 'moral foundations' defence; the women fled for eight months fearing for their safety, illustrating both the privacy remedy and the social risk.

UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, Kenya (Feb 2025): same-sex consensual sex between men illegal with prison penalty; no laws on gender identity (no legal change pathway); intersex people legally recognised as third gender; LGBTI civil-society groups may operate but only in restrictive civic space.

CNN 'A Equals' interactive on trans and intersex Kenyans: 26 interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi describe routine police harassment — detention on pretexts like 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion ('look for 5,000 shillings...'), and using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to navigate society safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

KHRC 'Lives on the Line' (Sep 2025): the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering Oct 2023–Sep 2024; explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling (Petition 16/2019) that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence; built with 14+ community organisations.

KHRC press release: Eldoret High Court handed transgender Kenyans a historic victory on 12 Aug 2025, directing the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act after finding prisons fail dignity and privacy protections — from a petition by a trans Kenyan subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered 'gender determination' during incarceration.

GATE.ngo on Nairobi Milimani High Court decision delivered 20 May 2026 (Justice Bahati Mwamuye, Petition 27 of Jan 2020): follows evidence that 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans were refused by civil registration offices, some spending nearly four years' wages on failed document corrections; Kenya has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.
Reuters (Dec 2024): a Kenyan man was sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist.

OutRight International Kenya profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): a decade of court-driven progress — 2018 Mombasa Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional (compensation awarded 2024); 2023 Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination.

The Star (23 Sep 2025) on the KHRC 'Lives on the Line' report: purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision; quotes the finding that despite Constitution Article 28's dignity guarantee, the data 'paints a blunt picture' — active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence.

US State Department Human Rights Report for Kenya (2010 reporting year): LGBT advocacy organisations such as the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya (GALCK) were permitted to register and operate; societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread, causing loss of employment and education; in Feb 2010 Mtwapa religious leaders demanded closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute.

The article states there are no statutory provisions relating to transgender rights and no legal means to change gender in Kenya. The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights reported in April 2012 that transgender people suffer stigma and discrimination and are unable to access gender re-assignment therapy, citing a witness who had undergone all processes but was declined surgery by Kenyatta National Hospital without reasons and whose appeal to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentist's Board was unsuccessful. The same report states police face difficulties deciding whether to detain transgender individuals in male or female cells when arrested, and that transgender people fear using sex-designated bathrooms in entertainment areas for fear of being accused or mistaken as using bathrooms for sexual crimes. It further records that when opposite-sex partners demanding sexual relationships discover they are not female or male, they scream and attract members of the public to the hotel room causing public nuisance, stigma and embarrassment to the transgender person. The article states transgender people face stigma, discrimination and violence in Kenya, with discrimination in particular prevalent as is sexual violence, in areas including government recognition of a third sex, access to justice, employment and other spheres of public life. In August 2025 the High Court found violations of a specific transgender person's rights "including freedom from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, equality and non-discrimination, dignity, freedom and security of the person, and privacy were unconstitutional" and ordered parliament to implement "the enactment of the Transgender Protection Rights Act, or, in the alternative, the amendments of the Intersex Persons Bill 2024". On 20 May 2026 the High Court ruled Kenyans must be allowed to change gender markers on identification documents in response to a lawsuit filed in 2020 by transgender activist Audrey Mbugua and two others seeking to amend birth certificates. Section 162 of the Penal Code makes carnal knowledge against the order of nature a felony liable to 14 years' imprisonment, rising to 21 years where committed without consent or where consent was obtained by force, threats or intimidation, fear of bodily harm, or false representations as to the nature of the act, while Section 163 punishes attempt with 7 years and Section 165 punishes acts of gross indecency between males with 5 years. On 24 May 2019 the High Court refused to declare Sections 162 and 165 unconstitutional in Eric Gitari v Attorney General & another Petition no. 150 of 2016, with a Court of Appeal hearing scheduled for May 2026 and decision pending. On 22 March 2018 the Court of Appeal in Mombasa ruled forced anal examinations on persons accused of same-sex relations unconstitutional, reversing a 2016 High Court decision, after police in February 2015 arrested two men in Kwale County and subjected them to forced anal exams, HIV and hepatitis B tests at Mombasa's Madaraka Hospital, with a later anal examination halted by the Kangundo magistrate court for two men taken from Kakuyuni to Kangundo Level 4 hospital. Article 45(2) of the Constitution effective 27 August 2010 authorises only opposite-sex marriage, the state recognises no same-sex relationships, and the Children Act 2001 makes homosexuals and unmarried couples ineligible to adopt. There are no explicit protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, though Article 27(4)-(5) non-discrimination provisions are argued to allow claims on sexual orientation grounds and the government in a May 2012 UN submission agreed with that interpretation. The Kenya Human Rights Commission in 2011 and the National Gay and Lesbian Human Rights Commission in 2020-2021 reported routine police harassment, detention in remand beyond the constitutional period without charges, presentation on trumped-up charges, extortion and blackmail for bribes, demands for bribes and sexual favours from MSM sex workers, and rape by state security officers. The Family Protection Bill file DLS/NA/BILLS/2/18/2023 introduced in 2023 by MP George Peter Opondo Kaluma would allow "aggravated homosexuality" to be punished with death, criminalize all promotion of LGBTQ+ activity, restrict privacy, assembly and public demonstration, prohibit pride parades, provide for monitoring of private and public spaces, remove LGBTQ+ topics from school curricula, and overturn a 2023 Supreme Court decision affirming the right to form associations, remaining stalled before the Committee on Social Protection for close to two years. These provisions concern same-sex sexual activity and are listed separately from transgender-specific issues, and in 2010-2012 ICCPR and Universal Periodic Review responses the government said it would not decriminalize same-sex unions as taboo and culturally unacceptable while stating it did not support discrimination in access to services including HIV/AIDS prevention under the 2006 Act.

Government policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity (Feb 2025): same-sex consensual sex between men illegal with prison penalty; no laws on gender identity (no legal change pathway); intersex people legally recognised as third gender; LGBTI civil-society groups may operate but only in restrictive civic space.

International news feature on trans and intersex people: 26 interviewees describe routine police harassment — detention on pretexts like 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion (demands for cash), and using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to navigate society safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

Report (Sep 2025): the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in the country, covering Oct 2023–Sep 2024; explicitly challenges a 2019 High Court ruling that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence; built with 14+ community organisations.

Press release: a High Court handed transgender people a historic victory on 12 Aug 2025, directing the government to enact a transgender protection rights act after finding prisons fail dignity and privacy protections — from a petition by a trans person subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered 'gender determination' during incarceration.

Report on a High Court decision delivered 20 May 2026: follows evidence that 94% of trans and gender-diverse people were refused by civil registration offices, some spending nearly four years' wages on failed document corrections; the country has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.

Human Rights Watch World Report 2025, Kyrgyzstan chapter: no content on transgender prisoners or prison housing. Its only prison references concern journalists and opposition activists sentenced to prison terms, covering media repressions and freedom of expression rather than the placement or conditions of trans detainees.

Wikipedia country coverage: Reports of discrimination and violence against LGBTQ people in Kyrgyzstan are frequent, and after the government launched legal reforms including an "anti-gay propaganda law" in 2014 there was a near 300% increase in attacks against LGBTQ people. Police officials were reported in 2018 to be blackmailing LGBTQ people on social media and dating sites, demanding between 5,000 and 30,000 soms (roughly 70 to 500 US dollars). In March 2019, after a march of about 400 people in Bishkek dubbed Kyrgyzstan's "first gay pride march," MP Jyldyz Musabekova publicly called for participants to be beaten, though other deputies condemned her remarks. LGBTQ people fear social ostracism from friends and family, especially in rural areas, and Bishkek's only gay bar, London, closed in 2017.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1998, with an age of consent of 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, but the constitution has explicitly banned same-sex marriage since 2016 and no same-sex unions are recognised. A 2014 bill criminalising expression creating a "positive attitude toward non-traditional sexual relations" via media or networks passed first reading 79–7 in October but expired without a final vote. On 14 August 2023 the president signed amendments to the child protection law (Article 2-1) expanding information deemed harmful to children to include content that "promotes non-traditional sexual relations"; the law does not define key terms or mention sexual orientation explicitly. No non-discrimination statute protecting LGBTQ people is described.

Youth are a specific target: the August 2023 child protection law restricts children's access to information that "promotes non-traditional sexual relations," and the 2014 anti-propaganda-style bill was framed around media accessible to minors, echoing Russia's 2013 law on "propaganda...to minors." On transition care, Clause 47 of the Law on the Protection of the Health of Citizens was amended from 2024 to bar trans people from accessing transition-related care before age 25, where previously the process could start at 18, directly affecting trans youth and young adults. A draft law proposed on 30 January 2026 and passed first reading on 4 June 2026 would prohibit transgender individuals from changing gender markers and accessing gender-affirming care and surgeries, affecting minors as well. The age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

A regional rights-monitoring annual review 2025: anti-LGBT legislative pushes accompanied by a media campaign of homophobic and transphobic statements from legislators; since 2021 trans people cannot obtain legal recognition under civil-status amendments; monitoring data shows high stigma and discrimination, particularly from law enforcement.

A trans-rights index (2024): this country (2021) is among the units that removed the right to legal gender recognition; for this country and several neighbours the 'bare minimum' of not banning recognition is all they score — the regional floor on trans legal status.

texts.cleaned_text: UN in Cambodia page for the UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity visit report: identifies good practices and remaining challenges and formulates recommendations to strengthen protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; an unofficial Khmer translation was prepared for national stakeholders.

OutRight International Cambodia profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex sexual activity (French protectorate 1867, independence 1953); at UPR 2019 accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage and at UPR 2024 accepted all 12 LGBTIQ recommendations incl. seven on marriage equality; legislation contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions.

Phnom Penh Post on a Cambodian Centre for Human Rights (CCHR) report: an overwhelming majority of transgender women on Cambodia's city streets face 'shocking' harassment and abuse (135+ cases documented), including a disturbing Siem Reap police practice of targeting transgender sex workers and forcing them to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water.

Rainbow Community Kampuchea (RoCK) page on Cambodia's 4th-cycle UPR: Cambodia officially accepted all 12 SOGIESC/LGBT+ recommendations in 2024 - marriage equality progress, legal gender recognition for self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures; includes the civil-society joint submission (Dec 2023) and summary factsheets.

UNDP/USAID 'Being LGBT in Asia: Cambodia Country Report' (2014): participatory review of the legal and social environment for LGBT persons and civil society, based on the Cambodia National LGBT Community Dialogue (Phnom Penh, Jan 2013), participant conversations, an NGO/CBO survey and a desk review of published literature.
Frommer's travel guide lists a section titled 'Tips for Gay and Lesbian Travelers' for Cambodia, offering practical travel advice for LGBT visitors.

PinkNews (20 Jul 2019) on Rainbow Community Kampuchea (RoCK) study: 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 suffered emotional abuse by a family member; 35% of under-35 participants considered suicide because of family rejection — including a 27-year-old trans man forced by his mother into rehab to 'fix his gender'.

Khmer Times (19 Feb 2025) reports Cambodian Human Rights Committee president Keo Remy saying, at the handover of an ambulance to Correctional Centre 2 at Prey Sar prison in Phnom Penh, that Cambodia observes transgender prisoners' rights: transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from Correctional Centre 1, the men's facility, to Correctional Centre 2, the women's facility. The statement was made in praise of the centre, not as a published regulation, and no statute or formal policy text is cited. The article also reports that prison overcrowding has worsened because of gang-crackdown arrests.

Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have a visible LGBT scene with bars and clubs catering to the community, and Pride parades have run annually since 2003 (first Siem Reap Pride in 2018). In February 2011 Cambodian tourism businesses launched a global 'Adore Cambodia!' campaign to signal welcome to LGBT tourists, which the Ministry of Tourism endorsed ('We have no policy to discriminate... We really support them'); a 2010 report described a concentration of poor and working-class LGBT people in Beoung Kak 2, dubbed 'Cambodia's first gay town'. Access to services is uneven: Cambodian law does not allow gender marker changes or gender-affirming surgeries, and trans sex workers in Siem Reap reported being forced to bathe in dirty river water, sometimes naked, and to leave the area, while cisgender sex workers were not documented as receiving the same treatment. State posture is officially non-hostile: the Ministry of Information sent a 2015 letter to media outlets asking them to stop mocking the LGBT community, citing the Constitution's protection of LGBT honour and rights, and in 2015 a Council of Ministers spokesman claimed existing law already protected LGBT people, a claim the Cambodian Center for Human Rights disputed. Hostility persists at official and societal level: Prime Minister Hun Sen publicly disowned and disinherited his adopted daughter in 2007 because she is a lesbian, and a 2016 CCHR report found about 38% of surveyed transgender women had been arrested, with over 90% saying it was because they were transgender. The 2017 US State Department report listed violence against LGBTI persons among Cambodia's most significant human rights issues, noting LGBTI people were frequently harassed and bullied over their appearance and their work in entertainment and commercial sex sectors, with more than 100 incidents of violence or abuse reported by a local LGBTI organization; the same report noted increased government restrictions on speech, assembly and press freedom, while finding no official discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, citizenship, education or health care. In June 2017 the Khmer Government announced new life-skills courses covering sexual health, gender-based violence, gender identity and combating discrimination against the LGBT population, which became part of the curriculum in all Cambodian schools in 2018; before that rollout, LGBT activists working with the Ministry of Education trained more than 3,000 teachers in 20 schools across nine Cambodian provinces. Many LGBT Cambodians report bullying at school, and in January 2019 Cambodia received UN recommendations from Iceland, Mexico, Sweden and Uruguay to establish educational programmes and campaigns raising awareness of LGBT people and discrimination. The age of consent is 15 regardless of gender identity or sexual orientation, and in 2019 the director of the Cambodia Human Rights Committee reported rising HIV infections within the LGBT community, especially among people under 30.

The country has never criminalised same-sex activity or gender expression; the government accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations at its 2024 periodic human-rights review, including legal gender recognition, and hosted an independent international expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2023.
A human-rights organisation documents 'shocking' harassment and abuse of transgender women in urban centres, including a reported police practice of targeting trans women (extortion and abuse).

texts.cleaned_text: 76crimes (21 Nov 2016): Kiribati was cited as one of two countries, with Sri Lanka, still maintaining anti-homosexuality laws at the time, in a report on the UN General Assembly's 84–77 rejection of the amendment to defund the SOGI Independent Expert mandate.

Sections 153–155 of the Penal Code make male homosexuality and related acts felonies. Anal intercourse carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, attempts or assault with intent carry up to 7 years, and acts of gross indecency between males carry up to 5 years. The provisions are not enforced and no prosecutions against LGBTQ people have been reported under them. Female homosexuality is legal, though lesbians may face violence and discrimination. In November 2016 Kiribati voted at the UN General Assembly to keep the Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the amendment to block it failed 84–77. Kiribati and Sri Lanka were the only countries criminalising homosexuality that voted this way. Employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been prohibited since 2015 under Article 107(2)(b) of the Employment and Industrial Relations Code 2015. The Marriage Act (Cap 54) does not expressly forbid recognition of same-sex marriages but assumes that the partners are of the opposite sex; its restrictions on marriage cover relatives, parties below age 16, and bigamy. Article 15(3) of the Constitution protects race, place of origin, political opinions, colour and creed, and does not expressly address sexual orientation or gender identity.

The site's Saint Kitts and Nevis tag archive is led by 'Courts are the key to expanding LGBTQ rights in the Caribbean' and 'Lawsuits target 5 Caribbean nations' anti-gay laws', covering regional court challenges to anti-sodomy laws. The ruling took immediate effect, decriminalizing consensual same-sex intercourse between adult males in private in Saint Kitts and Nevis. Wikipedia country coverage: On 23 March 2005 the island of Nevis barred a cruise ship carrying 110 American passengers, mostly LGBTQ, from docking; a police boat halted the Source Events/Windjammer Barefoot Cruises vessel and the ship was ordered to sail on. The exclusion was announced publicly as a cultural decision, with port officials stating Nevis did not want homosexuality 'to be a part of our culture.' Wikipedia country coverage: State hostility is documented in official statements: in 2011 the Government of Saint Kitts and Nevis said it had 'no mandate from the people' to abolish criminalization of homosexuality among consenting adults, and in 2005 port authority Acting General Manager Oral Brandy told reporters that Nevis does not want homosexuality 'to be a part of our culture.' The penal code still does not address discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex unions are not recognized in any form.

Its most prominent trans state-placement case is military: Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, a transgender conscript, was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty. The article records that consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel is criminalised under Military Criminal Act article 92-6 (up to two years' imprisonment; a gay soldier was sentenced to six months in 2017) and that transgender people are excluded from military service. No birth-sex versus identity placement rule, special unit, or solitary or segregation practice for transgender prisoners is described. Wikipedia country coverage: South Korean national law does not recognize same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court's en banc panel ruled that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognized provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children. Wikipedia country coverage: Violence and hostility at LGBTQ events is documented: in Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organizers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. The military ran what Amnesty International called a 2017 "gay witch hunt," criminally charging 32 personnel, including a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex, and Article 92-6 of the Military Criminal Act penalizes consensual same-sex acts with up to two years. Wider abuse includes a 2014 finding that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people recommended conversion therapy (65.4% reporting harm, 94% psychological trauma), and a 2018 study showing 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender, June Green, told NBC News he feels "threatened to just walk on the street" absent a nondiscrimination bill.

Kuwait, based on interviews with 34 activists; six interviewees from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or activism.

Same-sex sexual activity between men is illegal under Kuwait's penal code with penalties of up to seven years in prison, and public morality laws are strictly enforced, leading to regular prosecutions of LGBTQ people. In 2017 Instagram star King Luxy was arrested in Kuwait for allegedly looking too feminine and spent two weeks in custody before release. A 2022 Constitutional Court ruling overturned the criminalisation of 'imitation of the opposite sex', though discrimination by officials persists. Foreigners found to be infected with HIV/AIDS are deported, whereas Kuwaiti citizens who are infected are entitled to outpatient medical care organised by a specialised infectious disease hospital. HIV incidence has remained under 0.1 percent through to the latest 2021 figures, with males aged 25-49 making up 47 percent of those with HIV, and in 1992 the National Assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV; no youth-specific or minor-specific care access provisions are documented. No known association or charity exists in Kuwait to campaign for LGBTQ rights or to organise educational and social events for the LGBTQ community. In 2007 a group of Kuwaitis applied to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs to form such an association and never received a formal reply, and in July 2019 they announced they would reapply after a Ministry of Commerce crackdown on LGBTQ symbols such as rainbows in shops. In August 2023 Kuwait banned the film 'Barbie', claiming it promoted homosexuality; no youth- or education-specific findings about minors are documented.

Human Dignity Trust history: Laos (with Cambodia) achieved independence from France in the 1950s and modelled its penal code on the French system — it has never formally criminalised same-sex conduct, distinguishing it from neighbours that retained colonial sodomy offences.

GlobalGayz first-person account (2000, Richard Ammon): during a week in Vientiane the writer met a small circle of lesbians and gay men whose lives centred on a few restaurants and friendship networks — the country's LGBT scene is small, discreet and social rather than public or institutional.

Al Jazeera in-depth (Oct 2018): government crackdown on social media — influential Facebook users ('net idols') face retribution for posts, and 'Proud to be us Laos', the country's only LGBT advocacy group, is quoted; indicates online LGBT expression operates under tightening state attention.
The EU marked the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia in Vientiane, giving LGBT rights visible diplomatic backing in Laos.

Laos has no law prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation, and the Constitution does not expressly address sexual orientation or gender identity. At the 35th session of the Universal Periodic Review on 21 January 2020, Malta's ambassador recommended Laos improve LGBTI rights and involve LGBTI representatives in decision-making, and Iceland's ambassador recommended comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and gender identity. The Law on Electronic Data Protection (No. 25/NA, 12 May 2017) lists sexual behaviour among prohibited data. In March 2025, National Assembly member Maifong Maixai proposed changing Article 36 of the 2025 revised Constitution to expand room for non-discrimination protections for gender-diverse people.

The government has blocked access to LGBTQ-themed webpages, and discussion of LGBTQ issues in the media is described as rare apart from transsexuals visible as entertainment. It generally tolerates or ignores LGBTQ people unless they campaign for LGBTQ rights or are judged to be too publicly immodest or indecent. A 2014 decree prohibited criticism of all government policies. In the 1990s gay foreigners reported a taboo that made interacting with Laotians difficult except discreetly at night. In 2013 the United States Department of State reported that societal discrimination based on sexual orientation and against persons with HIV/AIDS was prevalent.

Health-sector partners involved in LGBTQ events include the Center for HIV/AIDS/STI (CHAS) at the Lao Ministry of Health, the Lao Positive Health Association, and the Vientiane Youth Center for Health and Development, which was among the organizations that organized the first public LGBT Pride in Laos in June 2012 (100 participants, held on the U.S. embassy sports field in Vientiane). LGBTQ activist Anan Bouapha reported seeing some gay students expressing their identity among their peers and teachers, alongside transgender people wearing traditional costumes to temples and ceremonies. The age of consent is 15 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no further detail is given on school policy, bullying, or education-specific protections for LGBTQ youth, or on healthcare access for trans people and trans youth.

texts.cleaned_text: Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Oct 2024): Rep. Johnson N. Williams is seeking lawmakers' support for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill filed that summer; related proposals would imprison children as young as 10 years old for gay sex.

UNDP/OHCHR 'SOGIR in Africa: Liberia Country Report' (April 2020): a participatory review of the legal, social and human-rights environment for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity in Liberia.

NPR (9 Apr 2012, 'Liberian LGBT Rights Under Spotlight'): anti-gay sentiment growing since the US announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas; new legislation proposed longer jail time for homosexuality and a group distributed fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

The Guardian (19 Mar 2012, Monrovia): Nobel Peace Prize president Ellen Johnson Sirleaf defended laws criminalising homosexuality in a joint interview; her remarks drew international comment on Liberia's stance (Blair declined to comment).

Trans-related care: gender-affirming hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery are not available in Liberia, so trans people have no domestic clinical facility for transition-related care. Wikipedia country coverage states that some private spaces exist where LGBTQ people can be their authentic selves, often sponsored by advocacy organizations such as Stop AIDS in Liberia (SAIL) or the Transgender Network of Liberia (TNOL), or created by private individuals, since LGBTQ Liberians often have to hide their identities in public. Enforcement of the sodomy law is uncommon, but its existence deters LGBTQ crime victims from reporting to police, and some LGBTQ people have been arrested on the basis of their sexuality or gender identity after attackers used their LGBTQ status as an excuse. A 2013 UN-AIDS survey put HIV/AIDS prevalence among Liberian men who have sex with men at 19.8%. Stop AIDS in Liberia (SAIL), the first NGO founded by LGBTQ Liberians for LGBTQ people, was set up to educate MSM about HIV/AIDS, test them, and counsel those testing positive, later expanding services to all LGBTQ people since 2012. Same-sex marriage is not recognized in Liberia. In 2012 then-Senator Jewel Howard Taylor introduced a bill that would have made same-sex marriage a first-degree felony carrying up to ten years; it passed the Senate but not the House, so it never became law, and President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf had threatened to veto either 2012 anti-LGBTQ bill. By contrast, Section 2.4(b)(iii) of Liberia's Decent Work Act (2015) entitles all who seek to work in Liberia to do so regardless of sex, gender identity or sexual orientation.

Erasing 76 Crimes (4 Apr 2017): Caribbean LGBTI activists, United and Strong of St Lucia and ECADE, protested a PinkNews item of 28 Mar 2017 that framed regional sexuality under the banner 'Nothing about us without us'. The item documents regional civil-society pushback against outsider framing of Caribbean LGBT issues.
AP News: St Lucia court ruling that criminalising gay sex is unconstitutional, the Eastern Caribbean litigation striking down the colonial-era law.

United and Strong St Lucia (21 May 2015): human-rights sensitisation training for law enforcement held in Castries on 19 May 2015, bringing together officers from the RSLPF, Air and Sea Ports, Customs and Bordelais Correctional Facility with CariFLAGS, the Canadian HIV-AIDS Legal Network and Maurice Tomlinson; it builds on 2014 sensitisation work.

Same-sex sexual activity became legal on 29 July 2025 when the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court struck down colonial-era buggery and gross indecency offences as unconstitutional. Under the Criminal Code No. 9 of 2004, effective 1 January 2005, as amended following the ruling, Section 132 punishes gross indecency, defined as non-intercourse genital acts for sexual arousal or gratification, with 10 years on indictment or 5 years summarily but exempts private consensual adult acts, and Section 133 punishes buggery, defined as anal intercourse, with life imprisonment if by force without consent, 10 years otherwise and 5 years for attempt or assault with intent, but exempts private consensual acts where both persons are 16 or older. Before being struck down the buggery and gross indecency laws were stated as not enforced, with 2017 statements that no-one was imprisoned for being gay and that gay cruises, couples and visitors stayed safely. Article 131 of the Labour Code enacted in 2006 bans unfair dismissal based on sexual orientation, and the Domestic Violence Act passed 8 March 2022 extends all its protections to LGBTQ people, while Saint Lucia was the only UN member in the Americas to formally oppose the UN declaration on sexual orientation and gender identity. For enforcement and protection machinery, a 2014 human rights sensitisation training educated the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force on general and LGBT-specific content, followed in May 2015 by further training for Air and Sea Ports, Customs and Corrections officers and civil society interfacing with law enforcement. Documented violence includes the 2011 violent attack and robbery of three American gay men in a vacation villa by assailants using anti-gay slurs, and the February 2019 stabbing murder of 27-year-old Guyanese Michael Pooran alleged to be due to perceived sexual orientation, which prompted calls to denounce violence and discrimination and re-examine the buggery laws. In March 2019 the United Kingdom Upper Tribunal decided gay men are at risk of persecution in Saint Lucia and can claim asylum, and March 2019 also saw the suicide of 17-year-old allegedly openly gay Gervais Emmanuel attributed to homophobic bullying and pressure.

On 8 March 2022 Saint Lucia's Parliament passed the Domestic Violence Act 2022 expanding protection to same-sex relationships via gender-neutral definitions of spouse, cohabitant, visiting relationship, domestic relationship, applicant and respondent, defining domestic violence to include economic and sexual abuse, harassment, cyber-stalking, coercion, threats and intimidation, and requiring under Clause 5 that public officers and service providers not discriminate on grounds including sex, gender, sexual orientation and gender identity, giving transgender victims/survivors equal access to remedies including court protection orders.

Human-rights organisation (31 Jul 2025): the high court decriminalised same-sex conduct — struck down the criminal provision as unconstitutional (regional strategic litigation); visitor-facing criminal exposure for consensual same-sex conduct ended.

Reuters feature on small European states, including Liechtenstein, catching up on LGBT equality; the page was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401).

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Liechtenstein' (March 2012): with a population of ~35,000 there is no organised gay scene - friendship networks are the scene; 'few organized enemies... no religious extremists, no right-wing skinheads, no political rogues demanding homophobic laws'; gay people live comfortably with little interference.

360° magazine (Jan 2016, in French): Prince Hans-Adam II called rainbow families 'irresponsible' in his New Year interview, said children have 'a right to a normal family', and suggested Liechtenstein could 'ignore' an adverse European Court of Human Rights ruling; local LGBT organisation Flay said it was 'choqué'; the Freie Liste called the remarks contrary to the Constitution and the ECHR.

Landtag motion (Sept 2022, in German): 'Motion zur Öffnung der Ehe für alle' - MPs' motion to open civil marriage regardless of gender and sexual orientation, removing all remaining legal differences; notes registered partnerships are seen as a 'second-class marriage' and that the Prince had said in 2021 he had nothing against marriage equality except adoption.

On 22 February 2005 the Department of Equal Opportunities (Stabsstelle für Chancengleichheit) was assigned to include discrimination on sexual orientation in its area of responsibility. The Act on Media (Mediengesetz), enacted in October 2005, declares media content illegal if it incites or supports discrimination based on sexual orientation among other grounds. Since 1 April 2016 harassment and incitement to hatred on the basis of sexual orientation has been banned in Liechtenstein. Section 283(1) of the Penal Code punishes public incitement to hatred or discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation with imprisonment of up to two years. Section 283(6) of the Penal Code prohibits discrimination in public facilities on the basis of, among other categories, sexual orientation.

Country overview (updated March 2026): mixed situation — same-sex relations legal and sexual-orientation discrimination banned, but gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics not covered by any anti-discrimination law; no legal gender marker change; intersex interventions not prohibited; marriage and joint adoption available since January 2025; official religion is Roman Catholicism and the archbishop publicly opposed marriage equality; first Pride in 2022.
