texts.cleaned_text: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Sections 365/365A of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women); prosecutions limited but harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services are frequent; no comprehensive anti-discrimination protections; authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence - widely condemned as torture. Legal gender recognition is possible (via a certification process).

exact_spans: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Sri Lanka's criminalisation of same-sex activity.

texts.cleaned_text: ICJ opinion piece (Aug 2023) by Mathuri Thamilmaran: 'Protecting transgender persons: Going beyond rule by circular' - the Sri Lanka Police are the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals; recent months saw both the Police and the Human Rights Commission acknowledging this; argues administrative circulars are insufficient without legal reform.

UK Home Office CPIN Sri Lanka: Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (v6.0, Sept 2024): assessment of risk from state and non-state actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information.

US State Department country report for Sri Lanka (custom URL): official human-rights assessment including the SOGI section - criminalisation under the penal code and police harassment of LGBT persons.

Joint UPR stakeholder report (EQUAL GROUND, Northwestern CIHR, GIHR) for Sri Lanka's 3rd cycle: 'Human Rights Violations Against LGBTIQ Individuals in Sri Lanka' - documents criminalisation and violations by the coalition of NGOs for UPR.

Canada IRB Response to Information Request LKA103948.E (Jan 2012): 'Treatment of sexual minorities in Sri Lanka' - Article 365 criminalises 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' (up to 10 years, men only); Article 365A 'gross indecency' (both sexes, amended 1995 to cover women); rarely enforced with no convictions, but criminalisation 'paves the way for police and anti-gay groups to brand all lesbian, bisexual, transgendered persons as perverts and criminals'.

Sri Lanka's Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing today: Media Spokesperson/Commissioner Gamini Dissanayake (Oct 2024) said current prison facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, and separate accommodation is only planned for prisons built in the future. Placement is decided case-by-case: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card (issued since the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular) are accommodated per their preferred gender 'where possible', while those without it go through a doctor's assessment of whether they 'can be considered a transgender' before placement, weighing inmate preference. Officials explicitly worry about people accused of sex offences 'identifying as transgender' to enter female housing with born-male offenders, a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. Outcome: placement by birth sex is the practical default in the current male/female ward system, with a medicalised, discretionary exception process and no statutory placement rule.

The Morning (original Daily Morning reporting, 4 Oct 2024) of the same Prisons Department statement: Commissioner Dissanayake said 'we always try to accommodate transgender prisoners who have the official identity card', and absent the ID a doctor assesses whether the inmate can be considered transgender, after which 'the preference of the particular inmate' feeds the accommodation decision. The piece also reports the Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners (CPRP) asking that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space (including possible space within prison hospitals), citing that 'developed countries have recognised transgender rights'. Confirms the absence of a codified placement policy and the official preference-assessment route as of Oct 2024.

Wikipedia country coverage: Gender-affirming surgery is relatively inaccessible in Sri Lanka because many hospitals lack the highly specialised surgical units and staff required; a physician interviewed for Human Rights Watch's 2016 'All Five Fingers are Not the Same' report said Sri Lankan doctors were often unfamiliar with surgical treatments for transgender patients. The National Blood Transfusion Service also bars men who have anal sex with men from donating blood, classifying male same-sex intercourse as 'risky behaviour' alongside drug use and having multiple partners. Wikipedia country coverage: Patients report meeting ignorance, curiosity and even ridicule from medical staff when seeking gender-confirming care, and some avoid public hospitals and clinics as a result, raising treatment costs; obtaining hormone therapy is described as similarly fraught. Legal gender recognition since 2016 requires bureaucratic certification that may be onerous to achieve, though no surgical intervention is legally required. Advocacy groups report police routinely ignore complaints from LGBTQ victims, especially involving sexual violence or blackmail, citing Article 365 as justification, and human rights organisations have documented police using the threat of arrest to assault, harass and extort LGBTQIA individuals. No youth-specific care-access findings appear in the source text. Wikipedia country coverage: Sri Lankan family law does not recognise same-sex marriages, same-sex civil unions, or provide equal rights to same-sex live-in couples; the marriage law dates from colonial times and is based on European law. The Catholic Church in Sri Lanka does not recognise same-sex marriages, with Cardinal Malcolm Ranjith stating that same-sex marriages 'are not a human right'. A 2023 report found 69% of the population opposed legalising same-sex unions, with 60% strongly opposed. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2016 the Ministry of Health issued a circular to health services and education institutions about issuing gender recognition certificates to transgender people, following a March 2015 complaint facilitated by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka. In August 2021 a video of a homophobic counsellor caused controversy; the College of Psychiatrists clarified that modern medicine does not consider homosexuality an illness and called for decriminalisation, noting that unlike psychiatrists, counsellors are not regulated and do not require degrees. In March 2022 SJB MP Rohini Kumari Wijerathna tabled a bill to ban conversion therapy, which she said the government failed to support as of July 2024; despite professional college ethics, doctors are reportedly still regularly sought by families to administer 'treatment' to LGBTQ members. Sections 365 and 365A carry aggravated penalties of 10–20 years' rigorous imprisonment where an offence is committed by a person over 18 against a person under 16. Wikipedia country coverage: Sri Lankan society is described as generally tolerant of homosexuality, with politicians from both major parties and across the spectrum expressing support for LGBTQ rights, and the influential Asgiriya Buddhist chapter backing rights extension and constitutional amendment. In March 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa tweeted that he was determined to secure everybody's right to live with dignity regardless of sexuality and gender, which the Financial Times called the first such public acknowledgement by a South Asian head of state. A 2021 Social Scientists Association poll found 72.5% believed LGBT people should not be punished for their sexual identity, 65% said an LGBT person can do a job as well as anyone else, and 51.4% would support rights legislation; a 2018 Equality Fund survey found 12% of respondents were LGBTQI. Community organisations include Companions on a Journey (1994, Sri Lanka's first LGBTQ support group), the Women's Support Group (1999) and Equal Ground, though Article 365 remains cited to justify police harassment and moral policing of LGBTQ people in public and private settings.

Sections 365/365A of the 1883 penal code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women); an international rights body lists the nation as criminalising the gender expression of trans people via vagrancy and 'cheating by personation' provisions.

An international jurists' commission identifies the national police as 'the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals' — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, with formal prosecutions limited.

As of October 2024 the prison department has no dedicated transgender housing — a department spokesperson said current facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, with separate accommodation only planned for prisons built in the future; placement defaults to birth sex, with an ID-gated 'where possible' preference route and a doctor's-assessment path for detainees without the recognition card.

A June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular exists but is not law; officials cite the fear of people accused of sex offences 'identifying as transgender' to enter female housing as a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement; a prisoners'-rights committee calls for future prisons to give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space.

Joint stakeholder UPR report (Oct 2024) by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho on LGBTQ+ rights in Lesotho: documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and community-level SOGIESC discrimination; same-sex conduct is not criminalised but no protections exist.

ICJ UPR submission (Nov 2024) on Lesotho: highlights LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination among three key concerns (alongside inclusive education for children with disabilities and revocation of NGO lawyers' practising certificates).

SALC + People's Matrix Association + WLSA briefing (Oct 2020): 'Legal Gender Recognition in Lesotho' - analysis of law and policy against international best practice; Matrix is the only known LGBTI organisation in Lesotho; researched by Prof Alex Müller with community consultations.

US State Department 2016 Human Rights Report for Lesotho: documents the LDF mutiny arrests, torture of detainees, the killing of Lt-Gen Mahao, and the LGBT section noting no criminalisation but societal stigma.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Lesotho' (2017): constitutional analysis - section 4(1) 'sex' and 'other status' should include gender identity per the UN Human Rights Committee; no law allows gender-marker changes; a trans person using a non-matching passport could be charged; the Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omits gender and sexual orientation.

Lesotho Labour Act 2024 (full text, ILO NATLEX): the new labour law - unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, forced and child labour prohibitions - the current statutory framework for workplace rights.

The Labour Act 2024 bans employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and defines workplace gender-based violence and harassment as violence and harassment including sexual harassment directed at workers, trainees, probationers, applicants, managers, supervisors, customers, clients, suppliers or contractors because of sex, gender or gender identity or affecting persons of a particular sex, gender or gender identity disproportionately. The National Identity Cards Act 9 of 2011 governs national identity cards and Section 8(1) provides that the Director shall take reasonable practicable steps to ensure personal information entered into the Register is complete, accurate and updated where necessary. The article states this provision could be interpreted as allowing transgender people to change their legal gender on identity documents and provides no further procedure, eligibility criteria, penalties, or granted-change outcomes. The article states no transgender-specific provisions on screening, sex-segregated facilities, custody, detention, or gender-affirming care. Historically the article documents boukonchana or inkotshane boy-wives who typically dressed as women and notes that by 1941 public cross-dressing was commonplace, while the 1914 colonial attempt to stop such practices failed and recent discussion has faced suppression and widespread denial. In 2012 male same-sex sexual activity was legalized in Lesotho after previously being illegal as an unenforced common law offence, while female same-sex sexual activity has never been outlawed. Under the Marriage Act No. 10 of 1974 and customary law marriage is permitted only for opposite-sex couples and same-sex marriages or civil unions are not recognised. The Labour Act 2024 bans discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment and Section 127(4) of the Children’s Protection and Welfare Act 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination based on sexual orientation in selection of a diversion programme, process or option with equal access for all children. Since 2013 the Credit Reporting Regulations provide that credit information relating to sexual orientation may not be contained in credit bureau records except to the extent self-evident from marital status and family member list. Under the Child Welfare and Protection Act of 2011 only married opposite-sex couples may adopt jointly and single men and same-sex couples are not permitted to adopt. The 2016 United States Department of State report section included in the article stated that the law at that time prohibited consensual sexual relations between men but authorities did not enforce it and was silent on consensual sex between women, and noted Deputy Prime Minister Mothetjoa Metsing’s June statement after the UN General Assembly High-Level Meeting on HIV/AIDS that the government would look into decriminalizing same-sex relationships to stop HIV spread. Reports of discrimination, family rejection, violence and harassment against LGBTQ people are described as not uncommon, with LGBTQ Basotho facing discrimination in employment, health care, housing, education and other areas and many living secret lives and hiding sexual orientation. Lesotho is described as having the second highest HIV prevalence in the world with reportedly 25 percent of Basotho infected, with LGBTQ activists reaching out to HIV-positive people and offering prevention strategies. The Matrix Support Group, an LGBTQ NGO established in 2009 and fully registered in 2010 to build an environment where LGBTQ people can freely express human rights and contribute to development, organized the first gay pride march on 18 May 2013 in central Maseru with supportive authorities providing an escort, and pride marches have been held annually since attracting a few hundred people. The included 2016 United States Department of State report stated LGBTI persons faced societal discrimination and official insensitivity, same-sex relationships were taboo and not openly discussed, no assaults were reported but incidents often went unreported for fear of stigma, and Matrix operated freely in all 10 districts with a good working relationship with the Lesotho Mounted Police Service including police intervention in December 2015 to enable a lesbian forced from home by brothers to return and supportive police escort for the 21 May march of approximately 200 people from Lakeside to Central Park in Maseru. The same report noted Matrix public outreach through film screenings, radio programs, public gatherings, social media and an electronic billboard in central Maseru supporting LGBTI rights. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically. The only tolerance statement given is LGBTQ-general, namely that attitudes towards members of the LGBTQ community are slowly evolving and becoming more tolerant and accepting, in line with worldwide trends.

Established in 2009, Lesotho's Matrix Support Group is an LGBTI organisation including transgender and intersex people that works for an environment where LGBTI individuals can freely express their human rights and contribute socially, politically and economically regardless of gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation and sex, principally through engagement with partner organisations on gender-based violence.

A joint stakeholder report (Oct 2024) by three rights organisations on LGBTQ+ rights in this country: documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and community-level SOGIESC discrimination; same-sex conduct is not criminalised but no protections exist.

A legal-rights organisation's submission (Nov 2024) to a periodic review: highlights LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination among three key concerns (alongside inclusive education for children with disabilities and revocation of NGO lawyers' practising certificates).

A joint briefing (Oct 2020) on legal gender recognition in this country: analysis of law and policy against international best practice; one local group is the only known LGBTI organisation in the country; researched by an academic with community consultations.

A government 2016 human-rights report: documents military mutiny arrests, torture of detainees, the killing of a senior military officer, and the LGBT section noting no criminalisation but societal stigma.

A rights organisation's paper on transgender rights in this country (2017): constitutional analysis — a constitutional clause on 'sex' and 'other status' should include gender identity per an international human-rights body; no law allows gender-marker changes; a trans person using a non-matching passport could be charged; the labour code's non-discrimination clause omits gender and sexual orientation.

The 2024 labour act (full text, via an international labour-law database): unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, forced and child labour prohibitions — the current statutory framework for workplace rights.

LGL (Lithuanian Gay League) news (Sept 2025): the Constitutional Court refused to address Lithuania's 18-year trans rights gap - a significant setback; the Civil Code grants unmarried adults the right to medically change gender but implementing legislation has never been adopted, leaving trans people in legal limbo.

LGL news (Aug 2025): could courts finally end 17 years of legal limbo for transgender rights? - the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court suspended a civil case on amending civil-status gender documents and referred the question of the laws' compliance with the Constitution to the Constitutional Court.

LRT (Sept 2025): Lithuania's Constitutional Court declined to examine a lower court's request to review the absence of legal provisions allowing trans people to change gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents.
LRT (May 2025): trans people in Lithuania detail workplace harassment - open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse; systemic labour-market discrimination per experts.

LGL news (April 2024): the Seimas Ombudsperson found that police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly - inadequate police response to hostile provocateurs at an LGL assembly; recommended measures to guarantee effective assembly rights.

Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson, 'The Situation of Transgender People in Lithuania - Summary of the National Review 2024': the second national review, after 2019, covering legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and public attitudes. It records the absence of a legal framework and of a strategic approach to trans rights.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Lithuania: systemic lack of targeted LGBTI hate-crime victim support; LGBTI asylum seekers from Cameroon granted protection after a four-year wait, with dire camp conditions and a psychologist convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts; prosecution of former MP Gražulis for anti-LGBTI ridicule complicated by his MEP immunity.

PinkNews (Sept 2013): Lithuania's parliament to consider five anti-gay and anti-trans bills - a ban on gender reassignment ('gender is determined genetically from the very moment of conception'), a same-sex adoption ban, fines up to €1,800 for organisers of events 'denigrating constitutional moral values', and legalisation of anti-gay speech.

PinkNews (July 2009): Lithuania's parliament passed a 'Section 28-style' law banning information on homosexuality in schools and media accessible to minors ('Law on the Protection of Minors'), overriding President Adamkus's veto 87-6; Amnesty called it 'a huge step backwards'.

Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults has been legal in Lithuania since 1993, two years after the end of Soviet occupation; it had been criminal during the interwar period and under Soviet rule. The age of consent was equalised at 14 in 2003 to meet EU accession criteria, then raised to 16 on 2 July 2010 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, a rule that applies equally to gay and straight youth. Public instigation of violence against LGBT people is explicitly banned under Section 170(3) of the Criminal Code; a 2010 preliminary investigation found 160 of roughly 180 hate-speech instances, mostly online, concerned the LGBT community, with perpetrators usually fined and computers occasionally confiscated. Two attempts to criminalise 'public propagation of homosexual relations' with fines of 2,000–10,000 litas were made, in 2011 unanimously rejected by Parliament and in 2013 also rejected. Lithuania's most prominent expression restrictions targeted minors: a 16 June 2009 amendment to the Law on the Protection of Minors banned the 'propaganda of homosexual, bisexual or polygamous relations' for under-18s; the presidential veto was overturned by Parliament, but on 22 December 2009 the anti-LGBT clauses were replaced with a broader ban on information promoting conceptions of marriage or family other than those in the Constitution. That provision was used to restrict a Vilnius Pride 2013 advertisement to night-time broadcast with an adult-content logo over a T-shirt reading 'For the diversity of families', and in 2014 the children's book 'Gintarinė širdis' was age-labelled and then banned by the Ministry of Culture because two stories involved same-sex relationships; the ECHR Grand Chamber ruled in January 2023 that this violated Article 10. On 18 December 2024 the Constitutional Court struck down the anti-LGBT provisions as violating Article 25, freedom of speech. Article 39.1 of the Public Information Act, amended 30 September 2010, briefly barred messages that 'depict or promote a sexual orientation'; this was described as a translation error and removed on 16 June 2011, with sexual orientation added as a protected ground. Pride events have been repeatedly obstructed: Vilnius City Council refused permission in 2007 citing security; Baltic Pride 2010 was halted by a court shortly before it began, overturned one day prior, then held amid heavy policing and violence with 12 protesters arrested; the 2013 march required litigation through all judicial instances to be allowed on Gedimino Avenue, about 500 participants and 28 arrests including MP Petras Gražulis. Participation has since grown, to around 10,000 at the 2019 Vilnius Pride and around 5,000 in 2023. In 2014 all major TV stations refused a pro-tolerance LGBT video clip over fears of breaching the Minors law. In January 2019 the Lithuanian Constitutional Court ruled that foreign same-sex spouses must be granted residence permits, following the 2018 European Court of Justice ruling in Coman and Others. No visa, entry or residence provisions specific to LGBT visitors are set out. Marriage is limited to opposite-sex couples by Article 38 of the 1992 Constitution and Article 3.12 of the Civil Code, and Article 3.229 had restricted partnerships to heterosexual couples. On 17 April 2025 the Constitutional Court ruled that the absence of legal regulation of partnership institutions, including for same-sex couples, contradicts the Constitution, and granted same-sex couples the right to register partnerships through the courts until the Seimas adopts a comprehensive registered-partnership law. A partnership bill had been preliminarily approved 46–17 in May 2017 but remained pending as of 2019, and in May 2021 more than 10,000 people protested against partnership legislation in Vilnius. Adoption remains closed to same-sex couples because marriage is required; although single applicants are theoretically eligible, adoption by single gay people is in practice not legally possible, and President Gitanas Nauseda stated in September 2021 he would do his best to block adoption demands from Kaunas Pride organisers. Only 24 same-sex households were declared in the 2011 census.

The top court refused to address the country's trans rights gap — a significant setback; the civil code grants unmarried adults the right to medically change gender, but implementing legislation has never been adopted, leaving trans people in legal limbo.

A regional district court suspended a civil case on amending civil-status gender documents and referred the laws' compliance with the constitution to the top court — asking whether courts could finally end 17 years of legal limbo.

The top court declined to examine a lower court's request to review the absence of legal provisions allowing trans people to change gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents.
Trans people in the country detail workplace harassment — open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse; systemic labour-market discrimination per experts.

The parliament's ombudsperson found police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly — inadequate police response to hostile provocateurs; recommended measures to guarantee effective assembly rights.

The equal-opportunities ombudsperson's summary of the 2024 national review on the situation of transgender people covers public attitudes, the legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and negative public attitudes; it notes the lack of a legal framework and strategic approach.

An annual review chapter reports a systemic lack of targeted hate-crime victim support; LGBTI asylum seekers granted protection after a four-year wait, with dire camp conditions and a psychologist convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts; prosecution of a former MP for anti-LGBTI ridicule was complicated by his elected-official immunity.

A report on parliament considering five anti-gay and anti-trans bills — including a ban on gender reassignment, a same-sex adoption ban, fines for organisers of events 'denigrating constitutional moral values', and legalisation of anti-gay speech.

A report that parliament passed a law banning information on homosexuality in schools and media accessible to minors, overriding a presidential veto; a rights organisation called it a huge step backwards.
Official Luxembourg government portal (Guichet.lu) page on applying to change one's gender status and first name(s) in the civil register - the administrative procedure for legal gender recognition.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): marriage and adoption; self-determination-based gender markers (no nonbinary markers); discrimination banned on sexual orientation and gender identity but not gender expression or sex characteristics; no measures on conversion practices or intersex interventions; in July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan, criticised by organisations for missing depathologisation and other key elements.

Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale UPR submission (April 2023) for Luxembourg: describes the organisation's services and Luxembourg's equality laws (employment, goods and services, education, health), the CET equality body and the national LGBTI action plan.

Asher Fergusson's LGBTQ+ Travel Safety Index, updated June 2023, ranks countries on laws affecting LGBTQ+ traveller safety and includes a companion Global Transgender Rights Index. Luxembourg appears in both indexes.

Le Quotidien (June 2019, in French): 'Agressions LGBTphobes: un durcissement des sanctions attendu' - Luxembourg law lacks LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances; victims under-report; the justice minister signalled the law would evolve after ECRI's 2017 intervention.

Le Quotidien (May 2017, in French): Justice Minister Félix Braz presented a bill allowing trans and intersex people to change civil-status gender by declaration - replacing the long, costly judicial procedure; welcomed by associations.
In July 2018 the Chamber of Deputies approved a simplified procedure for trans people in Luxembourg to change their civil status (Le Quotidien, July 2018).

L'essentiel (26 August 2015), reporting Justice Minister Félix Braz's parliamentary answer to LSAP MP Cécile Hemmen, documents that Luxembourg prisons place inmates who disclose or openly show LGBT/trans identity so they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans-detainee situations handled case by case (the administration gathers all available information on the prisoner); such cases are described as 'exceptional'. Requests by LGBT detainees to be placed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and the minister warned against solutions that would stigmatise or isolate these detainees. A 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname, and penitentiary staff honour a detainee's chosen 'Monsieur'/'Madame' form of address. The Justice Ministry kept no statistics on LGBT prisoners (disclosure cannot be compelled without illegal privacy interference), and the planned Uerschterhaff prison (Sanem) was designed with multiple sections so detainees could be separated by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, among these, sexual orientation. Outcome: placement follows disclosed identity/need on a case-by-case basis with no codified birth-sex rule and no documented special custody unit or solitary/administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners in Luxembourg.

Luxembourg law prohibits direct and indirect discrimination based on "change of sex" within the definition of sex in employment, education, social security, healthcare, and the provision of goods and services. Hate-crime legislation refers to "change of sex" and recognises it as an aggravating factor. Transgender people are allowed to change legal gender on the basis of self-determination by application to the Ministry of Justice with no surgery, sterilization, divorce or other medical treatment required. Minors even under the age of 5 may apply for a sex change with consent of legal guardians. In the past Luxembourg legally required surgery, sterilization and divorce before a change of gender on identification documents. The reform was approved by the Council of Government on 12 May 2017, submitted to Parliament on 31 May, approved 57-3 on 25 July 2018, cleared by Council of State consent to skip the second vote on 27 July 2018, promulgated by the Grand Duke on 10 August, published in the official journal on 12 September, and took effect on 16 September 2018. The LGBT Action Plan 2018-2023 pledges to combat violence, harassment and discrimination, guarantee equal treatment in healthcare and employment, and assure equality of transgender and intersex individuals. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1794 when the country was a French possession, and Article 372 of the Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. An 18-year limit imposed for same-sex sexual activity in 1971 was repealed in 1992. Partnerships granting many benefits of marriage have been recognised since 1 November 2004 under the French PACS-based partenariat/Partnerschaft model, and same-sex marriage and full adoption rights passed by 56 votes to 4 in June 2014 and took effect on 1 January 2015. Direct and indirect discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited in employment, education, social security, healthcare and provision of goods and services under the Law of 28 November 2006 on equal treatment, and sexual orientation is recognised as an aggravating factor under hate-crime legislation. Luxembourgish nationals are allowed to serve in the Armed Forces regardless of sexual orientation. Since January 2021, donors who have had sexual relations with men who have sex with men are allowed to donate plasma regardless of gender, and are allowed to donate blood after 12 months without sexual contact with MSM. The LGBT Action Plan 2018-2023 pledges inclusive educational opportunities for LGBT students, combating violence, harassment and discrimination, and equal treatment in healthcare and employment.

LSM feature (27 Jun 2025): civil unions for same-sex couples in force since 1 July 2024; transgender and nonbinary Latvians still lack targeted legal change — a trans immigrant describes how legal transition would invalidate his marriage and residency status, and coalition MPs say trans rights 'have not emerged as a major issue yet'; Latvia was the first EU country to elect an openly gay head of state (2023).

ECtHR press release, Hanovs v. Latvia (18 July 2024): the Court unanimously found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 after a 2020 homophobic attack - no criminal charges were brought despite the aggressor admitting anti-gay slurs; the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter with a lenient fine, fostering impunity for hate-motivated offences.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Latvia: an administrative court overturned denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI seeker; the Prosecutor General reopened criminal proceedings in the Khanov hate-crime case after the ECtHR ruling; two people attacked in Daugavpils, with the Prosecutor General ordering the investigation reopened after police closed it; former MEP Mamikins' homophobic posts investigated (he fled to Russia).

Strasbourg Observers analysis (Nov 2024) of Hanovs v. Latvia: further clarification of states' positive obligations in homophobic-attack cases - states must thoroughly investigate and punish hate crimes, sending a message of zero tolerance; notes the troubling pattern of Eastern European states failing to protect LGBTI+ persons and to investigate effectively.

ILGA-Europe Latvia page: includes the July 2024 ECtHR judgment in Hanovs v. Latvia - the Court found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 after Latvian authorities declined to prosecute a homophobic assault on a gay couple in Riga as a hate-motivated offence.

PinkNews (May 2007): Archbishop of Riga Cardinal Janis Pujats called homosexuality 'total corruption in the sexual arena' and 'an unnatural form of prostitution', demanded a referendum on same-sex marriage and crowds of 40,000-50,000 to counter Pride, calling Pride a 'foreign-inspired action'.
Xinhua (June 2018): around 8,000 people marched in Baltic Pride 2018 in Riga - the annual event rotated among Baltic capitals; organised by Mozaika under the motto 'See Diversity! See Freedom!'.

Latvia decriminalised male homosexuality in 1992; female homosexuality was never criminalised. In 1999 the age of consent was equalised at 16 regardless of gender and sexual orientation. The 2006 constitutional amendment defining marriage as a union between a man and a woman frames the family structure in which Latvian children are raised. Latvian law allows any person over 25 to adopt, but persons not married to each other may not adopt the same child, so in unmarried couples only one partner may adopt. Registered partnerships, codified in November 2023 and effective 1 July 2024, carry rights similar to marriage except for adoption and inheritance. In April 2023 the Saeima amended the Law on the Protection of the Children's Rights to ban adoption of Latvian children by foreign same-sex couples. A 2020 court ruling favouring parental leave rights for same-sex couples led to a Justice Ministry draft civil union law in 2022, and lesbian couples can access IVF and assisted insemination treatment. The Ombudsman's 2018 call for a partnership law cited that about half of Latvian children are born out of wedlock and should enjoy legal protections. Only in Riga is there a small gay scene; elsewhere the sparse population means there is none, and the bars, clubs, stores and libraries established since democratisation are concentrated in the capital. In September 2006 the Saeima passed Labour Code amendments prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in the workplace; President Vaira Vīķe-Freiberga refused to sign the bill until that protection was added. The source text describes no discrimination protections on the basis of gender identity. In 2023 ILGA-Europe ranked Latvia 24th out of 27 European Union countries for LGBT rights protection. Surgical gender affirmation and legal identity change are possible in Latvia, with a medical certificate required by authorities, and Latvian law does not define 'sex change'. In 2004 authorities denied a legal identity change to a transgender person after a partial sex change, but the Supreme Court ruled in 2008 that the change should have been granted. A 2009 legislative proposal that would have required sterilisation to change legal gender was rejected by the Saeima. No education-specific findings appear in the source text.

A feature reports civil unions for same-sex couples in force since 1 July 2024; transgender and non-binary residents still lack targeted legal change — a trans immigrant says legal transition would invalidate his marriage and residency status, and coalition MPs say trans rights have not emerged as a major issue; the country was the first in the region to elect an openly gay national leader (2023).

A human-rights-court press release (18 July 2024) reports the Court unanimously found violations of three articles after a homophobic attack — no criminal charges were brought despite the aggressor admitting anti-gay slurs; the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter with a lenient fine, fostering impunity for hate-motivated offences.

An annual review chapter reports an administrative court overturned denial of asylum to an LGBTI seeker; the top prosecutor reopened criminal proceedings in the hate-crime case after the court ruling; two people were attacked in a regional city, with the top prosecutor ordering the investigation reopened after police closed it; a former MEP's homophobic posts were investigated.

An analysis of the ruling clarifies the positive obligations of nations in homophobic-attack cases — thorough investigation and punishment of hate crimes, sending a message of zero tolerance; it notes the troubling pattern of regional nations failing to protect LGBTI+ persons and to investigate effectively.

An organisation's country page records the human-rights-court judgment — violations of three articles after authorities declined to prosecute a homophobic assault on a gay couple as a hate-motivated offence.

A 2007 report quotes a senior cleric calling homosexuality 'total corruption in the sexual arena' and 'an unnatural form of prostitution', demanding a referendum on same-sex marriage and counter-Pride crowds of tens of thousands, calling Pride a 'foreign-inspired action'.
A 2018 report: several thousand people marched in a regional Pride in the capital — the annual event rotating among regional capitals, organised by a local association.

Macau Daily Times (Feb 2015): Rainbow of Macau met Identification Bureau officials to discuss changing gender on Macau ID documents - one individual ('Avery', speaking behind a screen) sought the change; the first organised push for gender recognition in Macau.

Macau Daily Times (May 2016): Rainbow of Macau criticised the government for excluding same-sex relationships from domestic-violence legislation because same-sex partners were not considered 'family members'.

Jason Chao / Rainbow of Macau statement (May 2016): the government knowingly enacted a discriminatory domestic-violence law despite the UN Committee against Torture's 2015 concluding observations requiring protection without discrimination; warns the law signals that sexual-orientation discrimination is justifiable.

Same-sex activity has been decriminalised in Macau since 1996, and the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offences identically. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. A March 2013 bill by Legislative Assembly member José Pereira Coutinho to grant same-sex civil unions the same rights as heterosexual couples was rejected 17 votes to 1 with 4 abstentions and expressly excluded the right to adopt. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples remain ineligible for some legal rights available to opposite-sex couples. Sexual orientation is absent from the non-exhaustive list of prohibited discrimination grounds in Basic Law Article 25; sectoral protections exist in employment (Law No. 7/2008, Article 6/2, fines up to MOP$50,000 per affected worker), personal data (Law No. 8/2005) and the ombudsman (Law No. 4/2012). A 2011 public consultation on domestic violence included "same-sex cohabitants in an intimate relationship" in scope, but the government's 2012 concluding report removed the reference citing "a lack of social consensus", and in 2016 it insisted on the exclusion. In October 2015 Rainbow of Macau complained to the UN Committee against Torture, which urged Macau to protect all domestic-violence victims "without discrimination". The UN Human Rights Committee noted in 2017 that Macau still does not allow transgender people to change gender markers on birth records and identity documents, reportedly for the same reason. The 2015 gender-marker-change study never produced a law. Between 2004 and 28 February 2026 the Identification Services Bureau received eight written requests to change gender on identity documents, all rejected; in April 2026 the Legal Affairs Bureau said there are "no plans" to revise the framework pending "prudent study" of core values, civil law and family relations. The general age of consent for homosexual and heterosexual sex is 14, and under Penal Code Article 166 anal coitus with someone under 14 carries 3 to 10 years' imprisonment, while with a 14-to-16-year-old taking advantage of inexperience it carries up to 4 years. Public expression around LGBT people in Macau is constrained by stigmatising coverage: on 9 June 2015 the newspaper Exmoo ran a front-page story about a high school student alleged to have molested a 9-year-old, titling the perpetrator a "gay demon" (基魔), prompting Rainbow of Macau spokesperson Jason Chao to note that the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offenders identically. In February 2015 a transgender student, Avery (pseudonym), told Macau media about abuse and bullying experienced while studying at a local school. Activism dates from the creation of the Macau LGBT Rights Concern Group in late 2012 and the registration of Rainbow of Macau in April 2013, though gay culture in Macau remains mostly invisible. On 16 August 2018 the deputy director of the Education and Youth Affairs Bureau (DSEJ), Leong Vai Kei, said students with "indications of homosexuality" would be referred to doctors or psychologists for medical examination; she later apologised, claiming misquotation and mistranslation from Cantonese. The lesbian-themed film I'm here, directed by Tracy Choi, won the Macau Indies 2012 Jury's Award at the Macau International Film and Video Festival, depicting problems homosexuals face living in a small town like Macau.

Plataforma Media (8 Sep 2023): transgender residents cannot change sex on Macau ID cards — no data-change policy exists — causing border-crossing confusion (a trans man holding a Hong Kong card marked male is still registered female in Macau); activists press the long-promised legislative reform.

Plataforma Media (7 Apr 2026): the Justice Services Direction (DSAJ) says gender-identity legal recognition still needs 'prudent study' of core societal values, civil and family law, and states there are 'no plans to revise the framework' — Macau remains the only area in China without ID gender-marker change or sex-reassignment provisions (both possible in mainland China and Hong Kong), despite a 31 March 2026 appeal by four trans residents.
Local English daily (Feb 2015): first organised push for gender recognition; claimant shielded behind a screen at the identity bureau.
Local English daily (May 2016): association criticised the domestic-violence law for excluding same-sex partners as non-family.
Public statement (May 2016): the exclusion was knowingly enacted despite a 2015 UN treaty-body direction; warns it legitimises discrimination.

Cairo 52 report 'A Web of Violence: The Systemic Erasure of Transgender People in Morocco' (Jan 2026, by Hamzawya and Nora Noralla): based on interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans - documents an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility; Morocco once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreigners but now enforces a de facto prohibition for its own citizens; Article 489 weaponised to arrest trans people based on gender expression; no legal gender recognition pathway.

Cairo 52 country review of Morocco: no specific provisions on transition, but de facto criminalisation under Article 498 (moral charges, gender-expression discrepancies, involuntary outing); no gender-affirming healthcare framework, leading some to self-medicate; a 2021 recognition process exists for intersex people only; the Grand Mufti opposes transition.
Hindustan Times (Nov 2024): an Instagram model alleges Moroccan police forced her to show her genitals over trans suspicions - reported police abuse of a trans woman based on appearance.

El País (Jan 2019): Moroccan police subjected a Marrakesh cross-dresser to online humiliation - after a minor traffic accident, Chafiq was handcuffed and filmed by bystanders and police officers, who also photographed his ID documents and posted them online; he sought asylum in Europe. Homosexuality is punishable in Morocco.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Article 489 criminalises 'indecent acts' between persons of the same sex (6 months to 3 years) with wide police discretion and arbitrary arrests; 170 people charged with same-sex relations in 2018; HRW documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment of presumed gay and bisexual men; no legal gender recognition; public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence and harassment; authorities block LGBTIQ organisations.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - includes Morocco's Article 489 criminalisation and the annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA.
ILGA's State-Sponsored Homophobia survey (May 2008, Daniel Ottosson) lists Morocco among the countries whose laws prohibit same-sex activity between consenting adults.
Washington Blade (Sept 2014) reports that the UN Human Rights Council adopted the SOGI resolution, establishing an international human-rights scrutiny framework that applies to Morocco.

Morocco has no law against discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no political party has enacted LGBTQ rights legislation. In 2017 former Minister of Justice and Liberties Mustafa Ramid called homosexuals 'trash' in an interview; local human rights associations petitioned Prime Minister Othmani to investigate what they termed his 'discriminatory and unconstitutional statements towards sexual minorities'. Police disproportionately target perceived LGBTQ people, and the names of arrested individuals are publicised before trial. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples.

In December 2007 a court in Ksar el-Kebir convicted six men under Article 489 after an online video of a private party, reported in the press as a 'gay marriage', circulated. Their lawyers said no evidence of prohibited conduct was presented, and the men were sentenced on 17 December 2007 to varying terms. Dozens of people then marched through the streets of Ksar el-Kebir calling for their punishment.

The government has banned books on homosexuality and requires schools to teach a curriculum that 'emphasises ... the danger and depravity of "unnatural acts"'. In 2016 two girls in Marrakesh were arrested after a cousin photographed them kissing and their mother complained to police; the case was postponed to December 2016, when both were acquitted, provoking the #freethegirls outcry.

No current trans-specific healthcare access, identity-document procedure, or shelter provision for trans visitors is recorded. The medical reference is historical: 1950s publicity around the French entertainer Coccinelle helped establish Casablanca as a place where certain doctors were willing to perform sex change operations 'albeit in clandestine circumstances', indicating unregulated care rather than any documented public facility. During the April 2020 outing campaign some landlords ejected tenants who were targeted, pointing to housing insecurity as a documented risk rather than any supportive facility.

In that campaign sociologist Khalid Mouna noted that transgender influencer Sofia Talouni sought to 'isolate young Moroccan homosexuals by breaking up their family unit', and journalist Hicham Tahir reported receiving 'a hundred testimonies' from victims or witnesses; one person allegedly committed suicide. A trans woman was violently beaten in Tangier in November 2022, with three minors and an adult arrested over the assault. In the 2018-19 Arab Barometer survey, 21% of Moroccan respondents said homosexuality is acceptable.

Report by a monitoring organisation (January 2026): based on interviews with trans and non-binary people — documents an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility; the country once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreigners but now enforces a de facto prohibition for its own citizens; one article is weaponised to arrest trans people based on gender expression; no legal gender recognition pathway.

Country review by the same organisation: no specific provisions on transition, but de facto criminalisation under morality provisions (moral charges, gender-expression discrepancies, involuntary outing); no gender-affirming healthcare framework, leading some to self-medicate; a 2021 recognition process exists for intersex people only; the country's top religious official opposes transition.
Media report (November 2024): a social-media model alleges police forced her to show her genitals over trans suspicions — reported police abuse of a trans woman based on appearance.

Media report (January 2019): police subjected a cross-dresser to online humiliation — after a minor traffic accident, the person was handcuffed and filmed by bystanders and police officers, who also photographed his ID documents and posted them online; he sought asylum abroad. Same-sex conduct is punishable here.

Human-rights organisation report (April 2018) on LGBT activism in the region: includes the country's criminalisation provision — an article used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression — and an annex of similar laws across the region.
