French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Queer In The World Monaco guide (updated 3 December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections with room for improvement; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

Wikipedia country coverage: Hate-speech protection rests on Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression, which bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016 (technological crime law), punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2–5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months–3 years. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for 5 days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added 'sexual orientation' to Civil Code articles 238-1 (6 months–1 year for violent acts not causing total incapacity), 239 (10 years for attacking a partner or co-resident) and 421 (5 years' probation for unprovoked attacks on a person or group). Monaco does not recognize same-sex marriage, and ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking (45th of 49 European countries) notes that transgender people cannot alter their legal gender. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a cohabitation agreement (contrat de vie commune), introduced in Parliament on 16 April 2018, unanimously approved by the National Council on 4 December 2019 and in force six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco; it is signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax, not like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and parents/children. Same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. The LGBT community supports some gay-friendly establishments inside Monaco, but there are no official gay bars, clubs or events in the country, unlike nearby French cities Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Monaco is not an EU member, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, though it has strong cultural and economic ties with France. Monaco has no armed forces, only a National Guard; France handles defence and allows openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve. The age of consent is 15 for both same-sex and opposite-sex relationships. The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's article 44 would have required a school programme every year of primary and secondary cycles to sensitise against racism and all article 1 discriminations (including sexual orientation), but the Council of Government did not approve the bill and its 18 December 2012 replacement dropped the sexual-orientation provisions. Same-sex couples' inability to adopt children directly affects family formation for youth, and most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral.

Country overview (last updated March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility is limited.

Travel guide page: no Pride is held anywhere in the destination (visitors are sent to a neighbouring country for one); pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.
Official human-rights report (2023): no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

News report (March 2025): decriminalisation going back centuries, yet the nation ranks near the bottom of regional LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly ten people openly out; a regional watchdog rapporteur called it a sad balance sheet.
Guide (updated December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), Moldova: a trans woman was denied bank service over a document/appearance mismatch and the Equality Council confirmed discrimination, recommending preventive measures; hate speech remained serious with no meaningful state response (echoed in the European Commission country report); election-period political hate speech rose.

Amnesty International Moldova 2025: discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace and freedom of expression and assembly was arbitrarily restricted (impunity for past violations); in Russian-occupied Transnistria new legislation prohibits promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations".

GENDERDOC-M report (2023) citing the Equality Council study "Prejudices and Marginalization in Moldova 2022" (published January 2023): acceptance of LGBT+ people is extremely low. 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% would not accept them as work colleagues (social-distance 5.7), and marginalisation of LGBT+ people increased in 2022.

Attitude (2 February 2026) revisits Moldova Pride 2024: participants of all ages and backgrounds joined the festivities, in a country described as "slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity". Public Pride proceeds openly.

ECOM legislative analysis on SOGI and HIV in Moldova (Tallinn, 2024): identifies legal barriers affecting LGBT people and people living with HIV, covering access to justice, hate-crime provisions and discrimination provisions, based on a survey of local partners and benchmarked against international standards.

PinkNews (19 May 2018): police deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters trying to disrupt the annual Moldova Pride solidarity march in Chisinau (19 May) as marchers carried foam hearts; activists feared a repeat of earlier violent scenes.

PinkNews (1 March 2013): the Balti Court of Appeals ruled on 28 February that the northern city’s "gay propaganda" ban was unconstitutional and violated human rights — local church-led bans struck down after protests against the EU-backed anti-discrimination law.

Ziarul de Gardă (15 June 2024) documents the four-year detention of Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man registered female at birth in 1972 whose documents were changed to male in 2007. He served his sentence in Moldova's penitentiary system, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit ('izolator disciplinar'), supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12, the unit for detainees requiring protection, was refused. He describes forced strip body searches, 'go to the gynaecologist' calls over the intercom, staff opening his bathroom door, and being called 'Natașa' at roll-call, and says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration (ANP) replied that he was detained alone 'at his own written request' with no rights violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. Brumarețchi says he will sue in Moldovan courts and the ECtHR, and ZdG has notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M. The case amounts to de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system, prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option.

Observatorul de Nord (7 April 2025) corroborates the same case: Igor Brumarețchi from Dubna village (Soroca district) spent three years locked alone in a cell at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by prison staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The piece states the authorities admit homophobia still persists in state institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment; the full investigation appeared on anticoruptie.md. Confirms the solitary-style isolation placement practice for a trans detainee in Moldovan prison No. 6 as of 2025.

Transgender people in Moldova are allowed to change their legal name and gender on official documents but require a psychiatric diagnosis confirming their "transgenderism" to do so. Law No. 2 (2023) includes gender identity among grounds protected from "any kind of discrimination," a transgender-specific protection distinct from the law's parallel protection for sexual orientation. Moldova's rise from last among 49 European countries in ILGA-Europe's 2012 LGBT legislation ranking to 23rd place by 2023 is attributed to continued expansion of anti-discrimination laws with regard to sexual orientation and gender identity. On 30 April 2013 the Parliament of Gagauzia approved a bill forbidding "propaganda" of homosexuality, bisexuality and transness such as same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples with no administrative sanctions or fines but with provisions banning registration of LGBT-related organizations and banning LGBT-related clubs and entertainment establishments, which were invalidated by court decision on 20 June 2013 for violating freedom of speech and human rights. In June 2011 Moldova voted against the UN Human Rights Council resolution condemning discrimination and violence against individuals based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The May 2017 march coinciding with the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia was cancelled by police shortly after it started due to safety concerns after fundamentalist Orthodox groups began attacking participants. Consenting adult same-sex sexual activity in private has been legal since 1995, with new laws in September 2002 equalising the age of consent. The Constitution explicitly defines marriage as between a man and a woman, with no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions and consequently little to no legal protection for same-sex couples. Parliament adopted a law banning discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment on 25 May 2012, signed by President Nicolae Timofti on 28 May 2012, effective 1 January 2013. The media law effective 1 January 2019 provides in Article 11 of the Codul serviciilor media audiovizuale al Republicii Moldova that audiovisual programs are prohibited from propagating incitement, promotion or justification of hatred founded on intolerance or discrimination based on sex, race, nationality, religion, disability or sexual orientation. Law No. 2 (2023) separately includes sexual orientation among grounds protected from "any kind of discrimination," distinct from gender identity. Parliament passed on 23 May 2013 a bill banning propaganda of prostitution, paedophilia and "any other relations than those related to marriage and family in accordance with the Constitution and the Family Code" with fines, signed 5 July 2013 and effective 12 July 2013, which did not explicitly prohibit "propaganda" of homosexuality but could have been interpreted as such, with the interpretable content removed by a bill passed 11 October 2013. Since 2012 several cities and districts enacted bans on "propaganda" of homosexuality with no administrative sanctions or fines, including Balti enacted 23 February 2012 and struck down 28 February 2013, Drochia enacted 27 March 2012, Cahul enacted 29 March 2012, and Ceadir-Lunga enacted 10 April 2012. The article states discrimination and violence against members of the LGBT community are commonplace, society remains very conservative, and politicians often make derogatory remarks about the LGBT community. The first pride parade was held in 2002, after which pride parades encountered stiff opposition from authorities and religious leaders and were often cancelled or banned due to safety concerns. On 11 May 2008 police and authorities stood by as crowds surrounded, intimidated and attacked Moldova Pride participants after Mayor Dorin Chirtoaca banned the parade the evening before, and in 2012 the ECHR ruled Moldovan authorities violated human rights by cancelling the 2008 event. The May 2017 march was cancelled by police shortly after it started due to safety concerns after fundamentalist Orthodox groups attacked participants, with President Igor Dodon supporting the attacks stating: "I have never promised to be the president of the gays, they should have elected their own president." The May 2018 17th Moldova Pride succeeded after police protected participants from radicals using tear gas to repel them. In May 2019 human rights lawyer Doina Ioana Straisteanu representing GENDER-DOC suffered an arson attack on her car in central Chisinau and police refused to investigate because it did not consider the damage "significant." The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically, only LGBT-general, gay and lesbian, or homosexuality-specific observations, including a Ministry of Health official letter that homosexuality is not considered a disease and medical services are accessible regardless of sexual orientation.

On 17 June 2011 the UN Human Rights Council adopted by 23 votes to 19 its first resolution on sexual orientation and gender identity expressing grave concern at acts of violence and discrimination committed against individuals because of sexual orientation and gender identity including transgender people and establishing a formal UN process to document abuses by commissioning a global report on discrimination including discriminatory laws and acts of violence and calling for a panel discussion on discriminatory laws, practices and acts of violence against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people.

An annual human-rights review (covering 2023): a trans woman was denied bank service over a document/appearance mismatch and the national equality body confirmed discrimination, recommending preventive measures; hate speech remained serious with no meaningful official response (echoed in a regional commission's report on the country); election-period political hate speech rose.

An international human-rights organisation's 2025 annual report: discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace and freedom of expression and assembly was arbitrarily restricted (impunity for past violations); in a breakaway separatist region occupied by a neighbouring power, new legislation prohibits promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations".

A national LGBT organisation's report (2023) citing a national equality-body study (published January 2023): acceptance of LGBT+ people is extremely low — 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% not as work colleagues (social-distance 5.7), and marginalisation of LGBT+ people increased in 2022.

A media feature (2 February 2026) revisiting the national Pride of 2024: participants of all ages and backgrounds joined the festivities — a country "slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity"; public Pride proceeds openly.

A legislative analysis on SOGI and HIV (2024): identifies legal barriers affecting LGBT people and people living with HIV — access to justice, hate-crime and discrimination provisions — based on a survey of local partners, benchmarked against international standards.

A news report (19 May 2018): police deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters trying to disrupt the annual Pride solidarity march in the capital (19 May) as marchers carried foam hearts; activists feared a repeat of earlier violent scenes.

A news report (1 March 2013): an appeals court ruled on 28 February that a northern city's "gay propaganda" ban was unconstitutional and violated human rights — local church-led bans struck down after protests against a regional-bloc-backed anti-discrimination law.

A national investigative outlet (15 June 2024) documents the four-year detention of a transgender man (registered female at birth in 1972, documents changed to male in 2007), who served his sentence in the national penitentiary system, mostly at a penitentiary in a provincial town. He says he was held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells — including for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit — supposedly for his own safety, while his request for the unit for detainees requiring protection was refused. He describes staff humiliation: forced strip body searches, demeaning calls over the intercom, opening his bathroom door, and name-calling at roll-call, and says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The national penitentiary administration replied that he was detained alone "at his own written request" and without any rights being violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed; he says he will sue in the national courts and an international human-rights court, and the outlet has notified the ombudsman and a local LGBT organisation. Outcome: de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system with prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option.

A second report (7 April 2025) corroborates the same case: a transgender man spent three years locked alone in a cell at a penitentiary, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by prison staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The piece states the authorities admit homophobia still persists in public institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment. Confirms the solitary-style isolation placement practice for a trans detainee as of 2025.

France 24 'Focus' report (Aug 2024): 'LGBT people in Madagascar forced to hide their sexuality' — although homosexuality is not illegal, it is widely considered socially unacceptable; many hide to keep jobs and live in peace, developing their own networks and coded language.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Madagascar: documents the post-coup regime, unlawful killings, and 'societal discrimination and violence against women, persons with disabilities, and the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community'.

BBC News Pidgin overview of decriminalisation in Africa (July 2020): Madagascar entry — same-sex activity legal only from age 21 under the Penal Code (under-21 same-sex acts remain offences); no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions; regional context as ~22 of 53 African states had moved to decriminalise.

Queer In The World Madagascar guide (updated 3 December 2023): same-sex activity legal for over-21s but LGBT people face discrimination and lack civic rights such as marriage and adoption; the legal framework is limited in progress compared with other countries.

Erasing 76 Crimes (17 July 2025): in Madagascar’s fourth UPR (January 2025, 235 recommendations) the government rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent; six Malagasy organisations (Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers’ Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage, Madagascar LGBT+) protested that "Refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence."

Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Madagascar resources: Penal Code Article 331 sets a different age of consent for same-sex acts (indecent-assault band of five to ten years’ imprisonment); documents general societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ people plus state-protection capacity, case law and supporting organisations.

Public expression is constrained: in early July 2021 the Malagasy government cancelled an LGBTQ party held at a bar in Antananarivo on the grounds of "incitement to debauchery". The U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report recorded general societal discrimination, with public attitudes ranging from tacit acceptance to violent rejection, particularly of transgender sex workers, who were frequent targets of verbal abuse, stone throwing and even murder. Supporters of a same-sex couple were subjected to insults and death threats on social media, and religious leaders publicly accused them of "promising homosexuality".

Marriage is closed to same-sex couples. Article 2 of Law No. 2007-022 on Marriage and Matrimonial Regimes prohibits marriage between two persons of the same sex whether before the Civil Registrar or under traditional ceremonies. Article 39 of the same law names "gender identity" as a cause for absolute nullity of marriage, a direct legal exposure for trans people. Law No. 2014-038 on the Protection of Personal Data, Article 18, bars processing of sensitive data including data on health or sexual life, and Law No. 2017-045 on Credit Information Bureaus, Article 2, likewise protects sexual orientation as sensitive data.

Family custody and adoption are restricted to heterosexual married couples. Article 33 of Law No. 2005-014 on Adoption states that "Full adoption is only permitted to heterosexual spouses." Most civic liberties, including the rights to marry and adopt children, are not afforded to LGBTQ individuals. In a 2020 case, a 33-year-old woman was arrested for the statutory rape of a 19-year-old woman after the younger woman's mother filed a complaint, with the mother allegedly acting to cover up an incest and rape accusation against the father.

Access to care and health protection is addressed mainly through HIV policy. Act No. 2005-040 on the Fight against HIV/AIDS requires information, education and communication programs adapted to the sexual orientation of target groups, and Article 26 mandates special provisions to protect vulnerable groups, expressly including young people, sex workers, men who have sex with men and mobile populations, against HIV transmission. Minors under 21 are the class protected by the Penal Code's two-to-five-year penalty for "indecent or against nature" acts, and in the 2020 case a 19-year-old woman was the subject of such a charge. Care access is further complicated by religious leaders offering the young woman conversion therapy, and by the 2011 finding that transgender sex workers faced violent rejection.

News report (Aug 2024): although same-sex conduct is not illegal, it is widely considered socially unacceptable; many hide their lives to keep jobs and live in peace, developing their own networks and coded language.
Government human-rights report (2011): documents societal discrimination and violence against women, persons with disabilities, and the LGBT community.

Broadcaster overview (July 2020): same-sex activity is legal only for adults of 21 and older; same-sex acts involving younger partners remain offences; no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions; many nations in the region had moved to decriminalise.

Travel guide (December 2023): same-sex activity is legal for adults over 21 but LGBT people face discrimination and lack civic rights such as marriage and adoption; the legal framework lags other nations.

News report (17 July 2025): in a fourth international review (January 2025) the government rejected recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent; six local organisations protested.

Refugee-law resource: the criminal code sets a different age of consent for same-sex acts, with an indecent-assault band of five to ten years' imprisonment; documents general societal discrimination against LGBT people, government protection capacity, case law and supporting organisations.

HRMI Maldives Summary Report 2024 (second expert survey): human-rights experts most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people — alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers — as at risk of empowerment-rights violations; political participation scores relatively better at 6.4/10 while other civil and political rights score considerably lower.

Erasing 76 Crimes (1 September 2015): police on Dhaandhoo arrested two men (aged 56 and 27) on 29 August for homosexual activity in their private home; the 2014 Penal Code extended criminalisation beyond Muslims to everyone, with death-penalty provisions theoretically in reach; Rainbow Warriors warned tourists could face similar threats.

UN OHCHR compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/2, March 2015) for the Maldives’ second-cycle UPR: records ICCPR/CEDAW/CRC reservations and concerns including sharia-based treatment of children born outside marriage; the Human Rights Committee recommended anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and action against stigmatisation of homosexuals.

Maldives national UPR report (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/1, April 2015): the government’s own submission — of 126 first-cycle recommendations it fully accepted 89, partially accepted 11, took note of 6 and rejected 20 with reasons; reports full implementation of 58 and partial implementation of 32 over four years.

The article states there is no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. It states the Maldives rejected 60 Universal Periodic Review recommendations that included matters said to contradict the Islamic faith and the Constitution, such as those relating to lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and non-traditional forms of the family. It states the United Nations Population Fund reported that those perceived as homosexual or transgender in the Maldives were the target of hate crimes and other human rights violations and recommended law reform to ensure protection of LGBTQ individuals. It states these recommendations were noted by the Maldives but not accepted. The article states no transgender-specific criminal provision, document, screening, facility, custody, or care rule, with all codified offenses and penalties described concerning same-sex sexual activity and same-sex marriage. The article states section 131 of the Penal Code defines criminal sexual contact as sexual contact without reason permitted under Islamic law, with section 411(2) explicitly naming same-sex intercourse as an offense defined under section 411(f). It states section 410(a)(8), in force since 16 July 2015, criminalizes same-sex marriage where two persons of the same sex enter into marriage. It states that since the amended Penal Code came into effect in 2015 laws tightened, with maximum penalties of up to one year for unlawful marriage under s410(a)(8), up to eight years for criminal conduct under s411(a)(2) and 411(d) with allowance for supplementary 100 lashes under Sharia, and up to four years for unlawful sexual conduct under s412. It states homosexual acts cannot be punished with death under Maldivian law, noting capital punishment suspended since 1953 and that under sections 92(k) and 1205 death is only available for egregious purposeful killing while the Quran specifies no punishment for homosexuality, with plans to restart executions later abandoned. It states homosexuality is rarely prosecuted and notes 2015 arrest of two local men in their private home on an island on homosexuality charges following a public complaint. It states LGBTQ tourists are generally considered welcome at most private tourist islands, resorts and hotels, which are usually isolated from civilian population centers and therefore not subject to Islamic law as evidenced by alcohol sale, while guides advise caution on public displays of affection outside tourist areas. It states there is no legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and that the Maldives signed the 2008 opposing document to decriminalization, rejected 2011 and September 2014 United Nations resolutions on sexual orientation and gender identity, and noted but did not accept 2015 recommendations to decriminalize consenting adult same-sex relations. The article states homosexuality is rarely prosecuted but remains a social taboo. It states those in the LGBTQ community are subject to discrimination, hate crimes and other human rights violations and that anti-LGBTQ discrimination is pervasive though LGBTQ couples visiting resorts rarely experience the reality of Islamic-based law. It cites Rainbow Warriors stating the local Maldives LGBTQ movement is mostly limited to the virtual world operating on the internet due to the intensity of homophobia in the country. It cites the 2020 United States Country Reports finding there were no reports of officials complicit in abuses against LGBTI persons although societal stigma likely discouraged reporting, and that local citizens expressing support for LGBTI rights on social media were targeted for online harassment as apostates or irreligious. It documents the 2013 neck stabbing of gay blogger Hilath Rasheed in Male and the 2014 grant of asylum in New Zealand to gay Maldivian Abraham Naim as at risk of serious harm from state agents, with a Presidents Office spokesman commenting those seeking asylum for sexual orientation discrimination would face prosecution upon return. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically, with all tolerance and hostility descriptions referring to LGBTQ persons generally, homosexuality, or homophobia rather than transgender persons as a distinct group.

Human-rights measurement organisation summary report 2024 (second expert survey): human-rights experts most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people — alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers — as at risk of empowerment-rights violations; political-participation scores were relatively better while other civil and political rights scored considerably lower.

Human-rights journalism outlet (1 September 2015): police arrested two men on 29 August for homosexual activity in their private home; the 2014 penal code extended criminalisation beyond followers of the national religion to everyone, with death-penalty provisions theoretically in reach; a local LGBT-rights organisation warned tourists could face similar threats.

UN human-rights office compilation (March 2015) for this country's second-cycle universal periodic review: records reservations and concerns under international human-rights covenants, including religious-law-based treatment of children born outside marriage; an international human-rights body recommended anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and action against stigmatisation of homosexuals.

This country's national universal periodic review report (April 2015), the government's own submission: of more than 100 first-cycle recommendations it fully accepted the large majority, partially accepted some, took note of a few and rejected others with reasons; it reports full implementation of many and partial implementation of others over four years.

HRW dispatch (31 March 2025) "Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges": calls on Mexico’s states to guarantee administrative legal gender recognition — many states now have LGR procedures, but without recognition, document requests expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation; implementation gaps persist state to state.

HRW report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024), Tabasco: barriers to legal name/gender recognition leave trans people exposed — document mismatch amplifies daily discrimination, set against murders including a trans woman found in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

The Guardian (18 July 2024): Mexico City’s Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" criminalising transfemicide — a watershed named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists say the law is critical for feeling safe.

AP (Jan 2024): 'Wave of transgender killings in Mexico spurs protests' — at least three transgender people killed in early 2024, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca shot in Mexico City, drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

IACHR press release (2024): urges federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanding investigation of all LGBTI violations with gender-identity-respecting methods; warns impunity may reach alarming levels.

Agencia Presentes (Jun 2024): 'Violence against trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders increased in the last year' in Mexico — data report on rising attacks against trans people and killings of defenders.

LSE USAPP analysis by Caroline Beer (22 November 2024): Mexico’s progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly — rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice; the authors explicitly caution their earlier work must not be read as evidence LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence including murder and torture.

Global Affairs Canada advises exercising a high degree of caution across Mexico due to high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with avoid non-essential travel advisories for areas including Baja California Sur and the northwestern mainland coast.

Intrepid Travel LGBTQIA+ Mexico guide: same-sex marriage legalised in 2009 with Mexico City the pioneer and Zona Rosa its gay hub (annual Pride, LGBT-friendly hotels/bars/tours); Cancún is a mainstream hotspot; notes Oaxaca’s indigenous muxé third-gender tradition and advises caution outside tourist hubs.

CNN en Español (19 July 2024): Mexico City’s Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro" law criminalising transfeminicide; Transgender Europe monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023 — second only to Brazil’s 100.

Mail & Guardian (13 January 2007): Coahuila became the third Latin American jurisdiction to approve gay civil unions (20–13 vote) after Mexico City and Buenos Aires, barring adoption and custody for those couples; PRI deputy Julieta Lopez called it "a sensible response" to discrimination, PAN called it an attack on the family.

Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ people in prison' article, Mexico section, records one Mexico-specific policy: in July 2007, through the efforts of the National Human Rights Commission (CDHDF), the Mexico City prison system began allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, with visitors not required to be married to the inmate, applying to all Mexico City prisons. The article contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement (birth-sex vs identity placement), special units, or solitary/segregation practice for Mexico.

Mexico's Wikipedia coverage describes no current statutory criminalisation of homosexuality, citing only historical executions in 1658 and the 1901 Dance of the Forty-One; street prostitution is recorded as illegal in jurisdictions including Mexico City. Same-sex marriage took effect in Mexico City on 4 March 2010, and Coahuila approved civil unions in January 2007. Pride parades have run annually in Mexico City since 1979 (over 1,000 people in 1979, 350,000 at the XXXI edition) and in Guadalajara since 1996, alongside events in over a dozen other cities. The coverage describes a norm of "sexual silence" in which gay men and lesbians conceal their orientation and lead double lives. Police are recorded as corrupt and prone to extortion, and transvestites as subject to police abuse. Government operatives have targeted Zona Rosa nightclubs since 2007 on drug, prostitution and safety grounds, which LGBT groups denounced as homophobic, and some Zona Rosa sites of cohabitation lack safety measures such as emergency exits. Mexican youth are reported committed to psychiatric clinics after coming out to their families, with some 16% rejected by family and a greater percentage physically attacked by relatives. A UAM study found 27% of LGBTQ respondents suffering mental disorders and risk of alcoholism, some 40% with thoughts of suicide and 25% having attempted it. The National Center for the Prevention and Control of HIV/AIDS is listed as an official resource, and Pride events include consciousness-raising about AIDS and HIV, highlighting youth-specific vulnerability in accessing safe care.

On 13 March 2004 amendments to the Mexico City Civil Code allowing transgender people to change gender and name on their birth certificates took effect. In September 2008 the Mexico City Legislative Assembly passed a law making it easier for transgender people to change their gender on birth certificates, and on 13 November 2014 it approved a gender identity law making the process much quicker and simpler. Similar gender identity laws were approved by the Michoacán Congress on 13 July 2017, in Nayarit on 20 July 2017, in Coahuila on 13 November 2018 allowing easier access to birth certificates reflecting new legal gender, in Hidalgo on 25 April 2019, while San Luis Potosí began authorizing legal gender changes on 17 May 2019. On 17 October 2017 the Supreme Court held in a ruling described as the first of its kind that a transgender person could change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, to whose American Convention on Human Rights Mexico is a signatory, ruled that recognition of gender identity on official documents is a protected human right. In July 2003 Amaranta Gómez became the first transgender woman to run for a seat in Congress, and on 17 May 2019 the President declared 17 May the National Day of Fighting Against Homophobia, Lesbophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia with actions including labor inclusion regardless of gender identity, joint work with teachers to eradicate discrimination, and a protocol of action against hate crimes. In 1871 adoption of the Napoleonic Code following intellectual influence of the French Revolution and the 1862-67 French occupation meant sexual conduct in private between adults regardless of gender ceased to be a criminal matter, decriminalizing same-sex sexual acts. On 2 September 1999 Mexico City passed an ordinance banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, the first of its kind, followed by a federal anti-discrimination law passed 29 April 2003 creating a national council to enforce it, a 2001 amendment of Article 1 of the Federal Constitution prohibiting discrimination under the vague term preferences, and insertion of the precise term sexual orientation into Article 1 in June 2011. On 21 December 2009 the Mexico City Legislative Assembly passed a bill legalizing same-sex marriage, adoption by same-sex couples, loan applications, inheritance and insurance sharing, signed eight days later and effective 4 March 2010, upheld 9-2 by the Supreme Court on 5 August 2010 with the adoption law upheld four days later. On 3 June 2015 the Supreme Court released a jurisprudential thesis changing the legal definition of marriage to encompass same-sex couples and deeming man-and-woman-only laws unconstitutional, requiring validation of same-sex unions through amparo injunction, with a similar nationwide jurisprudence for same-sex adoption finalized 23 September 2016. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling though only twenty allowed adoption, while civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacán, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz. On 21 March 2014 Mexico declared 17 May the National Day Against Homophobia by presidential decree, and the rule that five amparo rulings with the same outcome override a statute has often not been followed, with almost 20 injunctions before 2015 legalization in Chihuahua and fines in Tamaulipas for failure to legalize. Acceptance of transgender identities has been documented among various indigenous peoples of Mexico, most notably the Isthmus Zapotecs and Yucatán Mayas. The Isthmus Zapotecs recognize a traditional third gender known as muxe, an intermediate between male and female, assigned male at birth but typically acting and behaving like women and doing both women's and men's work. The article documents that "Having a muxe in the family is perceived as good luck and a blessing." It further documents that "Although they are perceived to be different from the general heterosexual male population, they are neither devalued nor discriminated against in their communities." It notes that Isthmus Zapotecs have been dominated by Roman Catholic ideology for more than four centuries despite this tolerance. It also notes that mestizos, especially mestizo police, occasionally harass and even persecute muxe boys, but Zapotec parents, especially mothers and other women, are quick to defend them and their rights to "be themselves" because "God made them that way."
As of March 12, 2026, legal gender recognition is possible in Mexico, with 22 of 32 states permitting individuals to update official documents without invasive medical or psychological evaluations.

On 10 June 2011 Mexico amended Constitution Article 1 to prohibit any discrimination motivated by gender, sexual preferences, or any other ground attacking human dignity with the object of nullifying or impairing rights and freedoms.

A March 2025 human-rights dispatch: calls on the country's state/province to guarantee administrative legal gender recognition — many now have such procedures, but without recognition, document requests expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation; implementation gaps persist.

A March 2024 human-rights report: barriers to legal name/gender recognition leave trans people exposed — document mismatch amplifies daily discrimination, set against murders including a trans woman found in a river in August 2023.

A July 2024 news report: the capital's legislature approved a law criminalising transfemicide — a watershed named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists say the law is critical for feeling safe.

A January 2024 news report: a wave of transgender killings spurs protests — at least three transgender people killed in early 2024, including an activist shot in the capital, drawing outrage and street protests.

A 2024 regional body press release: urges national and state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanding investigation of all violations with gender-identity-respecting methods; warns impunity may reach alarming levels.

A 2024 analysis: progressive legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly — rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice; the authors caution that earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people are safe from violence including murder.

A foreign government travel-advice page: exercise a high degree of caution nationwide due to high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with regional avoid-non-essential-travel advisories in some coastal areas.

A 2024 report: the capital's legislature approved the transfemicide law; regional monitoring records hundreds of transfemicides from 2008 to 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023 — second only to a neighbouring country's figure.

An encyclopedic survey of LGBTQ people in prison, country section: records only one country-specific policy — a July 2007 policy in the capital, adopted through the human-rights commission, allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation — and no data on trans-prisoner housing placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice.
The Marshall Islands decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2005 and has no criminalisation regime in force.

The 2015 US State Department Human Rights Report on the Marshall Islands listed prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence as significant problems, and recorded no reports of torture, arbitrary killings, disappearances or LGBT-specific abuses.

The Pacific Sexual & Gender Diversity Network profiles Anfernee Nenol Kaminaga, 25, a pansexual genderqueer Marshallese person who co-created and led Brighten the Rainbow, regarded as the first openly LGBTIQ initiative in the Marshall Islands. Kaminaga is also a UNESCO Youth Ambassador and a youth representative at the first UN Youth Climate Action Summit.

Until 2019, there were no legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity in employment or the provision of goods and services. The Gender Equality Act 2019 prohibits direct or indirect discrimination in all areas, in particular in the political, legal, economic, employment, social and domestic spheres, on account of gender identity. The Act requires the Government to adopt measures to eliminate stereotypes, prejudice, and harmful practices on the basis of gender identity. The Act establishes a program to sensitive judicial and law enforcement officers and other public officials. In 2016 the country received recommendations from Germany and Israel to prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity. In 2011 it signed the joint UN statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on gender identity, condemning violence and discrimination. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 2005, with an equal age of consent at 16 regardless of sex and sexual orientation. Until 2019, there were no legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment or the provision of goods and services. The Gender Equality Act 2019 prohibits direct or indirect discrimination in all areas, in particular in the political, legal, economic, employment, social and domestic spheres, on account of sexual orientation. The Act requires the Government to adopt measures to eliminate stereotypes, prejudice, and harmful practices on the basis of sexual orientation and establishes a program to sensitive judicial and law enforcement officers and other public officials. The Code of Judicial Conduct 2008 provides that a judge shall not manifest bias, prejudice or harassment based on sexual orientation and shall require lawyers to refrain from such bias, prejudice or harassment. Same-sex marriages and civil unions are not recognized and same-sex couples lack legal recognition, with households headed by same-sex couples ineligible for the same protections as opposite-sex married couples; the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1988 does not expressly prohibit same-sex marriage but section 428(1) assumes opposite-sex parties with minimum ages 18 for the male and 16 for the female, with marriages performed by a registrar, ordained minister, or High Court or District Court judge and registered by the atoll registrar, and it is unknown if constitutional or statutory non-discrimination on sexual orientation, marital status and family status guarantees a right to marry as the Supreme Court has yet to rule. In 2011 the country signed the joint UN statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation condemning violence and discrimination, and in 2016 received recommendations from Germany and Israel to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

On 22 March 2011 the Marshall Islands joined the Human Rights Council joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity, which expressed concern at killings, rape, torture and criminal sanctions on those grounds and called on states to end violence, criminal sanctions and related violations against individuals because of sexual orientation or gender identity.
A global criminalisation-history source: lists this nation among the countries that decriminalised same-sex conduct in the 2000s, i.e. no current criminalisation regime here.

An archived official human-rights report (2015): significant problems were prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence; no reports of torture, arbitrary killings or disappearances, and no LGBT-specific abuses reported.

A regional diversity network page: profiles a resident community organiser who created and led an openly LGBTIQ initiative — reported as the first of its kind in the country — and represented youth at an international summit.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), North Macedonia: hate speech remained serious with countless reports and no meaningful state response (European Commission country report concurs); in September the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years for assaulting an LGBTI activist with SOGI aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code; ECRI called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries.

Global Voices (30 March 2024): TransFormA’s March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje marked Transgender Day of Visibility with the words "we march bravely". The report also notes a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.

ILGA-Europe/ERA LGBTI Enlargement Review 2024 (covering 2023), North Macedonia chapter with the National Network against Homophobia and Transphobia: top priority is Legal Gender Recognition — the government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the LGR chapter a day before Parliamentary Committee review.
US State Department 2019 Human Rights Report for North Macedonia: its SOGI section documents anti-discrimination law, societal violence and discrimination against LGBT persons.

Washington Blade (13 October 2023): Serbian and North Macedonian LGBTI groups quantify how anti-LGBTQ discrimination harms the economies of Serbia and North Macedonia, casting discrimination as a measurable drag on growth and jobs.

Balkan Insight (February 2012): ILGA-Europe’s Rainbow Europe Index ranked Macedonia worst in the Balkans at −2 on the 17-to−7 scale — the only Balkan country in the "red zone" of gross human-rights violations and discrimination.

Balkan Insight (July 2014): the government submitted a constitutional motion defining marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman — ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption — as an early act of the re-elected Gruevski government, needing two-thirds of MPs with the conservative DPA expected to supply the extra votes.

Constitution and law prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation in access to government services such as health care, and the government enforced such laws according to the 2019 US Country Report. Homosexuality was criminalized until 1996, when decriminalization became a Council of Europe accession condition. Same-sex relationships remain unrecognized, with family law defining marriage as "a union between a man and a woman." A 2015 constitutional amendment that would have barred legal recognition of same-sex relations absent a two-thirds majority passed committee 72-4 and was approved in Parliament on 20 January 2015. The 2019 Criminal Code amendments explicitly listed sexual orientation and gender identity under the hate speech provisions. In January 2019 the ECHR ruled that requiring sex reassignment surgery before changing a gender marker violated human rights and awarded €9,000 in damages, but NGOs report the government still fails to recognize gender identity changes in identification documents. EGAL is described as the oldest organization working on gay and lesbian health issues, and the LGBTI Support Center in Skopje, a subsidiary of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, offers free legal aid. The 2019 US Country Report found the LGBTQ community is "still prejudiced and harassed by the society, media and the authorities," with hate speech on social media following the first Pride Parade in June 2019, and deemed the Skopje public prosecutor ineffective in processing hate speech cases. Strumica Mayor Kostadin Kostadinov nullified all memoranda with LGBTQ organizations in June 2023 and vowed to veto future ones. A 2025 Pride Parade drew lower attendance after organizers declared it a protest, and foreign embassies pulled funding. Polling by the Center for Civil and Human Rights in 2002 found over 80% of respondents viewed homosexuality as "a psychiatric disorder that endangered families" and about 65% considered it a crime warranting jail. North Macedonia ranked 10th worst European country for LGBTQ tourists in 2019. The same 2019 US Country Report details fellow students verbally and physically attacking a gay high school student, breaking his nose; the student reported the incident to the principal but chose not to report it to police. The report cites CSO Coalition Margini documenting 70 cases of violence against LGBTI individuals in 2019, including five discrimination cases and one verbal assault by a police officer, and notes most such violence goes unreported to police or institutions. The report states that "there are many reports about public humiliations, worker firings and even casting homosexual teenagers onto the streets due to revelation of their sexual orientations." The Law on Primary Education adopted in July 2019 introduced anti-discrimination language covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

In January 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that North Macedonia's requirement that transgender people undergo sex reassignment surgery before their gender marker on identification documents can be changed is a violation of human rights. The judgment held that deficiencies in laws concerning modifying gender on official identification documents infringed the private life of transgender Macedonians. On 17 January the Court found a violation of privacy rights and the right to appeal of a transgender person in relation to the gender change procedure and required the government to pay 9000 euros in damages to the applicant. Despite the ruling, non-governmental organizations complained the government failed to recognize gender identity changes in identification documents. In March 2019 Parliament adopted a new anti-discrimination law including gender identity with 52 votes in favour and three abstentions, and the Law on Prevention of and Protection against Discrimination came into effect on 22 May after President Stevo Pendarovski signed it. On 14 May 2020 the Constitutional Court struck down that law on procedural grounds and a similar bill was passed by Parliament on 27 October 2020. The Law on Primary Education adopted in July introduced antidiscrimination language related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and amendments to the Criminal Code specifically list sexual orientation and gender identity in the section regulating hate speech. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity have been legal since 1996 after homosexuality was outlawed until 1996 when sex between people of the same sex was decriminalized as a condition for Council of Europe membership. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples and there is no legal recognition of same-sex couples because family law defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman. In September 2013 a proposed constitutional amendment to define marriage as a union between a man and a woman failed to meet the required two-thirds majority in the Assembly. In late June 2014 the re-elected main party resubmitted the bill and in January 2015 Parliament voted in favour to constitutionally define marriage solely between a man and a woman plus an amendment requiring a two-thirds majority to regulate marriage, family and civil unions, a threshold previously reserved for sovereignty and territorial questions. The parliamentary committee on constitutional issues approved the amendments on 9 January and Parliament approved them on 20 January by 72 votes to 4, but the final session commenced on 26 January never concluded because the ruling coalition did not obtain the required two-thirds majority and remained in recess until the end of 2015 so the amendment failed. From 2008 to 2010 lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender individuals were protected from discrimination in employment but in early 2010 Parliament removed sexual orientation from protected grounds when revising the law, before adopting a new law in March 2019 with 52 votes in favour and three abstentions that includes sexual orientation and came into effect on 22 May after presidential signature, was struck down on 14 May 2020 on procedural grounds, and was replaced by a similar bill passed on 27 October 2020. In 2024 ILGA-Europe ranked North Macedonia 31st out of 48 European countries in terms of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender rights legislation. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically and all tolerance findings address homosexuality or lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex people generally. The country is described as mainly socially conservative towards homosexuality with reports of public humiliations, worker firings and homosexual teenagers being cast onto the streets after revelation of sexual orientations. A 2002 Center for Civil and Human Rights survey found more than 80 percent saw homosexuality as a psychiatric disorder that endangered families and about 65 percent answered that being gay is a crime that warranted a jail term, with women generally more liberal than men and rural inhabitants. The Coalition Margini documented 70 cases of violence against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex individuals, five cases of discrimination and one case of verbal assault by a police officer during 2019, noting most violence is not reported to police or other institutions and the Skopje public prosecutor remained ineffective in processing pending hate speech cases. On 29 June 2019 during the first Skopje Pride reported at about 1000 participants and at approximately 2000 participants in the 2019 country account including the defense minister, the labor and social issues minister, members of parliament and foreign diplomats under police protection, approximately 20 persons chased seven activists down the street, pulled them from a taxi, beat activist Bekim Asani and threatened to kill him and the others, after which police arrested the assailants and opened a criminal investigation while the parade triggered hate speech on social media. In 2019 North Macedonia was ranked the tenth worst European country for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender tourists and in June 2023 the Strumica mayor announced nullification of all memorandums signed with lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender organizations and that future memorandums will be vetoed.
In January 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled in favour of a Macedonian transgender man seeking to change his gender on his birth certificate.

On 14 May 2020 the Constitutional Court repealed the Law on Prevention and Protection against Discrimination, thereby removing legal protection against discrimination including on sexual orientation and gender identity.

Regional monitor annual review 2024 (covering 2023): hate speech remained serious with countless reports and no meaningful government response (the regional commission’s country report concurs); in September the local criminal court sentenced a man to two years for assaulting an LGBTI activist with bias aggravating grounds of the criminal code; the regional rights body called for a ban on nonconsensual surgeries on minors.

News report (30 March 2024): a local trans group’s March for Visibility in the capital marked the international Transgender Day of Visibility — “we march bravely” — while noting a trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.

Regional monitor review 2024 (covering 2023): the top priority is legal gender recognition — the government withdrew the draft civil-registry law containing its recognition chapter a day before committee review.

A foreign affairs department’s 2019 human-rights report for this nation: official assessment including the sexual-orientation and gender-identity section — anti-discrimination law, societal violence and discrimination against LGBT persons.

News report (13 October 2023): economic analysis with local LGBTI groups quantifying how anti-LGBTQ discrimination harms the economies of this nation and a neighbouring one — discrimination cast as a measurable drag on growth and jobs, without country-specific figures in the piece.

News report (February 2012): an international rights index ranked this nation worst in its regional bloc on the graded scale — the only national record in the bloc in the worst tier of human-rights violations and discrimination.

News report (July 2014): the government submitted a constitutional motion defining marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman — ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption — needing two-thirds of legislative votes with conservative support expected.

texts.cleaned_text: There are no anti-discrimination laws protecting the LGBTQ community from harassment and abuse on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. Before December 2024, Article 225 penalizing “public indecency” was frequently used to target LGBTQ individuals and those with nonconforming gender expressions. Laws prohibiting “attacks on morality” are described as used to target LGBTQ persons and as actively enforced. The immediate result of the December 2024 penal code is described as a significant increase in arbitrary arrests and detentions as well as physical abuse directed at individuals based solely on appearance or gender expression. The 2011 human rights findings recorded no publicly visible lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender organizations in the country, with free association impeded by a law prohibiting association “for an immoral purpose.” Homosexuality has been illegal in Mali since December 2024. The Transitional National Council passed a new penal code criminalizing homosexuality on 31 October 2024, and the code went into effect on 13 December 2024. The new code also prohibits “promotion” of homosexuality, a term left undefined, thereby broadening the scope of prosecution. Before this law, same-sex sexual conduct was not explicitly illegal, but Article 225 penalizing “public indecency” was frequently used to target LGBTQ individuals. Mali’s new constitution adopted by referendum in June 2023 limits marriage to a union of one man and one woman, outlawing same-sex marriage since 2023. Article 522 of the Code des Personnes et de la Famille, passed by the National Assembly on 2 December 2011 and signed by the president, forbids same-sex couples from adopting children. The military junta ruling since 2021 justified the criminalization as defending “traditional and moral values,” and Justice Minister Mamadou Kassogue had previously described homosexuality as “unnatural” and pledged to criminalize it. Societal discrimination against the LGBTQ community is described as widespread. No publicly visible lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender organizations were recorded in the 2011 findings, and a law prohibiting association “for an immoral purpose” was cited in 2005 to refuse recognition to a gay rights association in Bamako. The sexuality-specific attitude survey cited found 98 percent of Malian adults in 2007 believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society. The tolerance statement from health provider director Dr. Dembelé Bintou Keita states that Malian society is not tolerant to MSM and that “All cultural beliefs towards MSM are negative”.

On 31 October 2024 Mali's Transitional National Council adopted a new Penal Code promulgated in December 2024 and published in Official Journal Special No.21 of 2024 defining homosexuality as sexual relations between persons of the same sex and punishing it with 2 to 5 years' imprisonment and a fine of 200,000 to 500,000 CFA francs, with no recognition of affirmed gender, exposing transgender visitors to prosecution based on sex assigned at birth and to arrest for perceived same-sex conduct.
An international human-rights organisation (Nov 2024): calls this country's new penal code disastrous for LGBT people, criminalising same-sex conduct with harsh penalties.

Direct evidence of how LGBTI arrivals are treated at the nation's borders.

texts.cleaned_text: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Malta, scoring national compliance by category on the map's red-to-green scale: asylum, civil-society space, intersex bodily integrity, legal gender recognition, hate crime and hate speech, and equality body.

Equaldex data for Malta: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. 84% rate it a 'good place' for gay people; but Maltese rank #1 of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

Legal status: same-sex conduct legal since 29 January 1973; civil unions since 2014 and same-sex marriage since 2017; gender change without surgery; full adoption since 2014; open military service; discrimination protections cover sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics. Malta became the first EU country to ban conversion therapy, with the Affirmation of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression Act passing its final reading unanimously on 6 December 2016 after a bill targeting minors was first tabled by Civil Liberties Minister Helena Dalli in December 2015; the Malta Chamber of Psychologists and related professional associations backed it. Youth-specific legal protections include a December 2016 amendment letting minors aged 16 and over change their legal gender without a court application or parental approval, and the 2015 Gender Identity, Gender Expression and Sex Characteristics Act's worldwide-first ban on sterilising or invasive surgery on intersex infants. In education, MGRM's February 2008 petition to Parliament demanded an anti-homophobic bullying strategy for the island's schools, while in 2015 Education Minister Evarist Bartolo refused to distribute MGRM-donated reading material teaching diverse families including same-sex parenting, and in June 2021 Malta opposed at an EU conference any law prohibiting the teaching and distribution of LGBT information to children. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender.

Academic chapter (Routledge Companion to Gender and Crime, 2025, Mary Grace Vella): Malta records one of the lowest SOGIE physical/sexual victimisation rates in the EU27, yet LGBTIQ+ people still report a higher share of harassment and online hatred, and reporting of violence to the Malta Police Force remains significantly low despite institutional reforms.

University of Malta dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024): four interviews with current and former transgender inmates at the Correctional Service Agency, covering a 25-year cohort, found gaps in healthcare, legislation and knowledge, alongside problems after release, and found Correctional Service Agency practice out of sync with national gender-identity legislation.

texts.cleaned_text: ICJ (30 July 2025): ICJ and partners filed observations in M.S. v. Malta at the ECtHR — an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in Malta in April 2023 received a return decision and removal order to Bangladesh in May 2024; submissions raise ECHR Articles 3/5/13 (non-refoulement, detention conditions, individualised assessment before detention).

MaltaToday (15 April 2014): parliament approved the constitutional amendment naming gender identity — Malta the first European state to do so — and introduced civil unions in the same sitting; Transgender Europe was among the first NGOs to applaud gender identity as a protected ground in the highest legal text.

Malta Today (29 May 2018): the Maltese civil court (Judge Silvio Meli) awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each (€4,000 for breach of rights plus €1,000 for damage to personal dignity) after the prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers (often forgoing washing) and suffered insults and 'continuous sexual abuse and violence'. The court found the authorities had 'knowingly and repeatedly' placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were said to be hostile, so they stayed in the male section. The director of prisons was ordered to pay; the Aditus Foundation human-rights NGO represented the seven women.

University of Malta master's dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024) interviewing four current and former transgender/gender-diverse inmates of Malta's Correctional Service Agency (CSA), a cohort spanning the last 25 years. It records that after Malta's 2013 gender-law reform CSA practice allowed TGD inmates to transfer to the female section, whereas earlier practice had segregated them in a separate dormitory (staff described the rationale as 'the risks of pregnancies'); participants now receive individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers (masculine birth names), gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare gaps, and conclude that CSA practice, policies and procedures lag Malta's progressive national gender-identity law. It also cites the 2018 newspaper report (Agius, Malta Today) of seven TGD inmates winning a court award after rights breaches including strip searches, showering-privacy issues and being treated as males.

A regional rights map country page for the nation with the compliance breakdown across asylum, civil-society space, intersex bodily integrity, legal gender recognition, hate crime/hate speech and equality-body categories, scored per category on the map's red-to-green scale.

Data pages for the nation: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation and gender identity, discrimination illegal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. 84% rate it a 'good place' for gay people; but residents rank top of 30 regional units for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

Legal-status source: same-sex conduct legal since 29 January 1973; civil unions since 2014 and same-sex marriage since 2017; gender change without surgery; full adoption since 2014; open military service; discrimination protections cover sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics.

Academic chapter (2025): the nation records one of the lowest sexual-orientation and gender-identity physical/sexual victimisation rates in the region, yet LGBTIQ+ people still report a higher share of harassment and online hatred, and reporting of violence to the police force remains significantly low despite institutional reforms.

A university dissertation (2024): interviews with current and former transgender inmates (a 25-year cohort) found healthcare, legislative and knowledge gaps plus post-release problems, with institutional practice out of sync with national gender-identity legislation — institutional lag beneath the strong statute book.

News report (29 May 2018): the civil court awarded seven transgender inmates of a prison €5,000 each (€4,000 for breach of rights plus €1,000 for damage to personal dignity) after the prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers (often forgoing washing) and suffered insults and 'continuous sexual abuse and violence'. The court found the authorities had 'knowingly and repeatedly' placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were said to be hostile, so they stayed in the male section. The director of prisons was ordered to pay; a human-rights NGO represented the seven women.
