It also cites the 2018 newspaper report of seven transgender and gender-diverse inmates winning a court award after rights breaches including strip searches, showering-privacy issues and being treated as males.

Outright International overview (updated March 2026): Section 377 used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence; after the 1 Feb 2021 coup risks intensified — torture/sexual violence in detention, Oct 2022 Organization Registration Law (prison terms for NGO non-compliance), compulsory military service announced Feb 2024, seven LGBTQ-themed books banned 2025. Verdict: avoid entirely.

DVB (Jan 2024): post-coup authorities commit attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people; the NUG recorded 17 LGBT killed and 2 critically injured since 1 Feb 2021; 'Rainbow Amid the Storm' found 50% of LGBT respondents have no confidence in the legal system and 68%+ fear repercussions from abusers.

Human Rights Myanmar submission (June 2024) to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions: killing of LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled Myanmar - 5 to 12 individuals dead since the coup; Section 377 enforcement intensified as an aggravating factor; militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life.

RFA (10 Jan 2025): junta banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as 'obscene' with prosecutions announced for publishers; colonial-era law carries up to 10 years for gay sex; LGBTQ+ people hit hard since the Feb 2021 coup.

ASEAN SOGIE Caucus (March 2025, from Queers of Burma Alternative research Jan 2025): the 2024 Conscription Law drives queer people into fear and displacement; Section 377 carries life imprisonment or up to 10 years, and 1945 Police Act s.35(c) (face covering, up to 3 months) is used specifically against transgender people.

Guardian (2 Feb 2016): Colors Rainbow's work in Yangon — trans woman Nat Nat We describes arrest, stripping, a beating and 14 days' detention for walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work; documents routine police violence against trans women.

Washington Blade (2 Nov 2018): Aung Myo Htut (aka Addy Chen), an outspoken HIV-positive LGBTI advocate and Yangon restaurant owner, was charged under Penal Code 377 over an alleged offence against an employee. Section 377 remained in active use, and the community demanded fair media coverage.

HuffPost (17 Oct 2015): colonial-era criminalisation; 2013 Mandalay arrests of trans women forced to strip and parade naked while photographed (police called it a 'public service'); nat kadaws (spirit mediums) are culturally visible transgender women — visibility coexisting with criminalisation.

Wikipedia country coverage: Myanmar does not allow transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth, so the state does not recognise their gender identity. Transgender people are consequently subject to police harassment, sexual assault, mistreatment and extortion, and are frequently targeted using the 'shadow law' in section 35(c) of the Police Act (1945), which lets police detain anyone they consider behaving suspiciously after sunset. The source text describes no legal gender recognition procedure or documentary process for trans people in Myanmar. LGBTQ access to care is shaped by criminalisation and stigma: Section 377 of the Penal Code (up to 10 years' imprisonment for same-sex acts) was called out by Aung San Suu Kyi in 2013 as hampering the country's efforts to combat HIV, and gay men are stigmatised, especially if living with HIV/AIDS. The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights includes LGBTQ individuals as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery, but it is a planning document rather than an enforceable law. On the youth side, the 2019 Child Rights Law contains a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation, but it applies only to children and lacks enforcement mechanisms. Myanmar has no enforceable legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Existing measures are symbolic or non-binding: the 2019 Child Rights Law's non-discrimination clause covers sexual orientation but only for children and has no enforcement mechanisms; the 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines discourage discriminatory media portrayals but carry no legal penalties; and the 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights is a planning document, not law. Following the June 2019 death by suicide of young gay librarian Kyaw Zin Win after workplace harassment, the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission called for enactment of anti-discrimination provisions, and the same year's events prompted a national conversation on LGBT issues. Myanmar does not recognise same-sex marriages or civil unions. In 2014 a Burmese same-sex couple drew widespread media attention by holding an unofficial wedding ceremony after 10 years together, triggering a backlash from social conservatives who questioned why anti-homosexuality laws were not enforced against them. Same-sex couples can cohabit freely in Yangon and Mandalay and celebrate ceremonial marriages without legal persecution, but these carry no legal standing. Youth-specific findings centre on the June 2019 death by suicide of Kyaw Zin Win, a young gay man working as a librarian at Myanmar Imperial University in Yangon, after continuous harassment and bullying from colleagues; more than 600 people attended his funeral and a rainbow flag was wrapped around his coffin. The university opened an investigation and suspended three staff members, and the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission launched a separate investigation and called for anti-discrimination provisions. Legally, the 2019 Child Rights Law includes a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation, but it applies only to children and lacks enforcement mechanisms; meanwhile same-sex conduct remains criminalised under Section 377 with up to 10 years' imprisonment regardless of consent or privacy.

Myanmar does not recognise gender identity and does not allow transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth. Transgender people are subject to police harassment and sexual assault, including rape, mistreatment, or extortion by police. Police often target transgender people using section 35(c) of the Police Act, described as the 'shadow law' or 'darkness law,' which allows detention of anyone considered behaving suspiciously after sunset. Transgender people may face discrimination, family rejection or violence for their identity. Trans women are frequently denied equal access to many professions, limiting opportunities and leading to overrepresentation in certain jobs including spirit mediums and sex work, with only three 'respectable' career options described as beautician, fashion designer, or nat kadaw ('spirit wife' or spirit medium). As a nat kadaw, transgender Burmese people can be afforded respect and veneration otherwise denied to them by Burmese society, and 'Occult' is described as a local term for the transgender community in Myanmar. Same-sex sexual activity is illegal under section 377 of Myanmar's Penal Code 1861, enacted in 1886, which subjects same-sex sexual acts regardless of whether consensual or done in private to up to 10 years in prison. Section 377 prohibits carnal intercourse with any man, woman, or animal and provides imprisonment varying between life and a term of not less than 2 years but which may extend to 10 years and a fine of not less than four hundred rupees but which may extend to one thousand rupees. Heterosexual anal intercourse and oral sex are also illegal, as section 377 prohibits sodomy whether heterosexual or homosexual. The law has not been strictly enforced, but in November 2018 gay activist Aung Myo Htut, also known as 'Addy Chen,' was arrested under the sodomy law. LGBTQ people are also targeted under section 35(c) of the Police Act, which allows police to detain anyone considered behaving suspiciously after sunset, and other provisions cited as usable against LGBTQ people include sections 269 and 270 on negligently spreading a sexually transmitted disease, section 290 on 'public nuisance' with fines up to two hundred rupees, sections 292, 293, and 294 on 'obscene' material, songs or public acts, section 372 on buying or selling a prostitute under eighteen, section 469 on marriage ceremony absent legal marriage, and section 5(j) of the Emergency Provisions Act on anything affecting morality negatively. Myanmar does not recognise same-sex marriages or civil unions, and a 2014 unofficial wedding by a same-sex couple together for 10 years triggered backlash from social conservatives querying why anti-homosexuality laws were not enforced. Myanmar has no enforceable legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, with limited measures described as symbolic or non-enforceable, including the 2019 Child Rights Law non-discrimination clause applying only to children without enforcement mechanisms, the 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines encouraging non-discriminatory portrayals without legal penalties, and the 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights including LGBTQ individuals as a vulnerable group only as a planning document. Burma's social mores about human sexuality have been described as being 'extremely conservative.' In local Buddhist tradition, those born LGBTQ are perceived as facing punishment for sins committed in a past life, and historically official homophobia, limited public awareness, and lack of community role models rendered LGBTQ people invisible in Burmese society. A 2020 poll found 74% agreed being LGBTQ should be legal (23% disagreed) and 81% agreed that 'LGBT people deserve equality and equal treatment just like anyone else in Myanmar' (12% disagreed). LGBTQ activists have noted 'a growing climate of societal acceptance and tolerance toward LGBTQ people, in line with worldwide trends.' Specifically for transgender people, 'As a nat kadaw, transgender Burmese people can be afforded respect and veneration otherwise denied to them by Burmese society.' Mya Thet Mu, described as a gay woman from Myanmar, is documented as stating that 'lesbians are often seen as less acceptable than gay men and transgender people.'

Human-rights organisation overview (updated March 2026): a penal-code provision is used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence; after the 1 February 2021 coup risks intensified — torture and sexual violence in detention, an October 2022 organisation registration law carrying prison terms for non-compliance, compulsory military service announced in February 2024, and LGBTQ-themed books banned in 2025. Verdict: avoid entirely.

Media report (January 2024): post-coup authorities commit attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people; opposition figures recorded LGBT people killed and critically injured since 1 February 2021; a survey of LGBT respondents found most have no confidence in the legal system and most fear repercussions from abusers.

Civil-society submission to an international human-rights process (June 2024): killings of LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled areas — a small number dead since the coup; intensified enforcement of a penal-code provision as an aggravating factor; militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life.

Media report (10 January 2025): the junta banned LGBTQ-themed books as 'obscene' with prosecutions announced for publishers; a historic-era legal provision carries up to 10 years for same-sex conduct; LGBTQ+ people hit hard since the February 2021 coup.

Civil-society research (March 2025, based on local research from January 2025): the 2024 conscription law drives queer people into fear and displacement; the penal-code provision carries life imprisonment or a long term, and a historic-era police-act clause on face covering is used specifically against transgender people.

Media report (2 February 2016): a local trans-support organisation — a trans woman describes arrest, stripping, a beating and two weeks' detention for walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work; documents routine police violence against trans women.

Media report (2 November 2018): an outspoken LGBTI advocate with HIV, a restaurant owner, was charged under the penal-code provision over an alleged offence against an employee — the provision in active use, with the community demanding fair media coverage.

Media report (17 October 2015): historic-era criminalisation; arrests of trans women forced to strip and parade naked while photographed (police called it a 'public service'); local spirit mediums are culturally visible transgender women — visibility coexisting with criminalisation.

Human Dignity Trust records that Montenegro decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1977, placing it alongside Croatia and Slovenia as a European cohort of that year.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2013): Montenegro's first Pride marched through Podgorica — roughly 150 marchers guarded by some 2,000 police, rock-throwing opponents stopped by tear gas; Queer Montenegro's Danijel Kalezic: 'From this day we are no longer invisible.' Shows both state protection and organised hostility.

PinkNews (2 Aug 2019): MPs blocked the same-sex partnership law on 31 July 2019 despite government backing — ERA's Western Balkans office: LGBT people 'forced to live as second-class citizens' (no hospital visitation or shared-benefit rights); a 2018 ERA study found 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins were closeted.

CDM (Dec 2018): the Government adopted the Draft Law on Same-Sex Partnership granting couples near marriage-equivalent rights via registrar ceremony — explicitly excluding parenting, foster care and adoption; shows the reform trajectory before the 2019 parliamentary block.

Transgender people may change legal gender only after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and sterilisation, obtaining a medical diagnosis, and divorcing if married. Discrimination based on gender identity is prohibited in employment, provision of goods and services, education, and health services. This prohibition was established by the Law on Prohibition of Discrimination passed on 27 July 2010, which lists gender identity as a prohibited ground. Hate speech based on gender identity was prohibited by 2013 amendments to the Criminal Code, which came into force on 3 June 2014. The same amendments provide penalty enhancements where a crime is committed based on the victim's LGBT status, which includes gender identity as a protected ground. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is legal, decriminalised in 1977 with an equalised age of consent of 14. The Constitution bans same-sex marriage, same-sex couples cannot marry, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same protections as opposite-sex married couples. Since 15 July 2021 same-sex couples may register a Life Partnership granting almost the same rights as opposite-sex marriage except adoption, approved by Parliament on 1 July 2020 in a 42-5 vote, signed on 3 July 2020 and published on 7 July 2020. Discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned in employment, provision of goods and services, education and health services under the Law on Prohibition of Discrimination passed on 27 July 2010. Hate speech based on sexual orientation was prohibited by 2013 Criminal Code amendments effective 3 June 2014, with penalty enhancements for crimes committed based on the victim's LGBT status. Gays, lesbians and bisexuals are not banned from military service.

Montenegro had not by November 2025 adopted the Draft Law on Legal Recognition of Gender Identity based on self-determination after missing its 2024 adoption deadline under the EU accession programme despite completed legislative steps and consultations, leaving no fair transparent self-determination-based legal gender recognition framework free from abusive requirements in place.

texts.cleaned_text: CNMI Public Law 22-32 (signed Jan 2023): amends the Commonwealth Code to provide criteria for enhanced sentencing of defendants for hate-motivated crimes - the hate-crimes statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

MAP Equality Profile, Northern Mariana Islands, data as of 27 Sep 2026: Sexual Orientation Policy Score 3.5/22 (Low), Gender Identity Policy Score -2/25 (Negative), overall 1.5/47 (Low). Marriage recognition 1/1 since 2015. No comprehensive state nondiscrimination coverage beyond federal EEOC recourse.
Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges. Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised. Protections at the commonwealth level remain limited.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2015. The first same-sex marriage on Saipan was officiated 27 July 2015, as reported by Marianas Variety. Adoption has been available since 2015. Legal gender change is permitted provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process. Discrimination protections extend to government employees only, beyond federal law.
Saipan Tribune: the CNMI's first Gay Pride event was held at the GIG Discotheque in Garapan with about 60 people attending. Organiser Sharmaine Casquero called it a success.

A public law of the commonwealth (signed January 2023) amends the commonwealth code to provide criteria for enhanced sentencing of defendants for hate-motivated crimes - the hate-crimes provision covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

An advocacy equality profile, data as of late September 2026: records marriage recognition since 2015 and no comprehensive nondiscrimination coverage beyond government employment; policy-coverage scores are an advocacy index rather than a legal measure (values not reproduced here).

A legal compilation: same-sex marriage has been recognised since 2015 under the governing state's top court's marriage ruling; consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised; protections at the commonwealth level remain limited.

A legal compilation: same-sex marriage recognised since 2015; the first same-sex marriage on the main island was officiated 27 July 2015; adoption available since 2015; legal gender change is permitted provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process.
A local newspaper: the commonwealth's first Gay Pride event was held at a venue on the main island with about 60 people attending; the organiser called it a success.

Outright International (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct legal since the 2015 penal code; no legal gender recognition procedure exists; societal attitudes broadly neutral but LGBTIQ people face family ostracisation and employment/education barriers; the 2024 opposition pledge by PODEMOS raised community expectations then disappointed. The 2024 penal code removed the employment non-discrimination protection that had existed.

GlobalGayz archive (2006-2011): dated milestones — first newspaper article arguing gay rights (Agencia de Informacao, 7 July 2006), Maputo men petitioning parliament, the LGBT group still unregistered as of March 2011, refugee deaths en route to South Africa; documents early organising under the colonial-era law.
Erasing 76 Crimes (March 2016) from Afrobarometer: Mozambique among Africa's more tolerant — 56% would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour (vs Uganda/Burkina Faso/Niger at 5%).

Global Voices (28 Nov 2017): after a decade of blocked applications (since 2008), the Constitutional Council — supreme court equivalent — ruled Lambda Mozambique's status did not violate the constitution, unblocking registration of the country's only LGBT organisation.

Guardian (30 June 2015): Mozambique's new penal code erased the colonial 'vices against nature' provision; Lambda (not yet officially registered at the time) pivoted to anti-discrimination lobbying; Lambda's Carina Capitine: the LGBT community is not targeted by violence as in some African countries but does face discrimination.

The HRW World Report 2024 Mozambique chapter, published 11 Jan 2024, records general police detentions and election-related arrests. It gives no transgender-specific content and no information on where trans prisoners are housed.

Mozambique's penal code (Law 24/2019, in force 2020) bans hate crimes and hate speech. Article 191 prohibits incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group based on gender identity and also covers defamation, insults and threats against transgender people. Article 160 treats a victim's sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating factor in homicide. The Advertising Code (2016) bars advertisements containing discrimination or harassment on sexual orientation grounds.

Lambda Mozambique was blocked from registering as an NGO from 2008 onward, prompting a UN appeal in 2010. In October 2017 the Constitutional Council struck down the 'moral order' clause (Article 1 of Law No. 8/91) used to refuse registration as unconstitutional.

No legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity exist in education, health, housing or employment. Employment protections in place from 2007 were repealed by Labor Law No. 13/2023, effective February 2024. Hate crimes and violence against LGBTQ people are rare, though discrimination occurs.

Mozambique does not recognise same-sex relationships, and same-sex couples cannot marry or adopt. Protests for same-sex marriage and common-law marriage have run since 2006. A 2017 survey found support for same-sex marriage at 47% in Maputo, 38% in Beira and 42% in Nampula, and a 2017 ILGA poll found 61% of Mozambicans agreed gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as straight people. The 2017 survey found most respondents would not accept a child who came out, with 28% of Beira respondents stating they would assault their child if he or she was gay; 85% opposed violence against LGBTQ people and would help if they were being physically assaulted, and about one-third of respondents personally knew an openly LGBTQ person. A 2013 survey found moderate support for parenting rights, and 55% of respondents in the 2017 ILGA poll believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity decriminalised under the new criminal code effective June 2015; courts ruled LGBTIQ organisations can register (2017); employment discrimination based on sexual orientation illegal since 2007 (a 2007 law) but trans and intersex people not explicitly protected; no legal gender recognition procedure, making trans people particularly vulnerable; societal attitudes broadly neutral but family ostracisation and employment/education challenges occur; during 2024 campaigning an opposition leader pledged to tackle what he called the issue of sexual and ethnic minorities.

A UN development programme report (Dec 2024) marking ten years of a regional human-rights commission resolution on advancing LGBT+ rights - framework document assessing country obligations, protective environments, access to justice and civic space across the region's states.

An LGBTQ+ news archive's country collection (2006-2011): the first newspaper article arguing for gay rights (2006), the first national gay-rights seminar, the national LGBT organisation's registration struggles, constitutional-amendment efforts, and refugee risks.

Decriminalisation-campaign news site (March 2016): a regional public-opinion survey of the most and least homophobic countries in the region - this country among the most tolerant (56% would welcome a homosexual neighbour), behind two regional peers at 74% and 69%.

A global citizen-media outlet (Nov 2017): after 10 years of legal battles, the constitutional council ruled the LGBT organisation's status did not violate the constitution - since 2008 the justice ministry had ignored its registration applications; a step toward legal recognition for the country's only LGBT organisation.

A foreign broadsheet (June 2015): this country's new penal code scrapped the historic 'vices against nature' provision; a spokesperson for the country's only LGBT organisation said the community is not targeted by violent acts as in some countries in the region, though discrimination is real.

Cairo 52 country review: transgender people are effectively criminalised through 'debauchery' provisions. Penal Code Art. 264 carries 1 month to 2 years' jail and 5,000-150,000 ouguiya fines for public indecency and debauchery offences applied to gender nonconformity. US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report (Mauritania): consensual same-sex conduct criminalised but penalties not enforced; reports of violence and threats against LGBT people; civil society objected to scant indictments and officials sometimes acted with impunity.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Jan 2026, from Outright): the Penal Code keeps a maximum sentence of death by stoning for men; the government confirmed a de facto death-penalty moratorium in 2021; arrests and detentions under the provisions continue in recent years; low visibility drives stigma; since 2008 the country has served as refuge for Senegulese LGBTIQ people.

Liberals Mauritania (organisation website, ©2026) campaigns openly from within Mauritania on freethinker and LGBT-adjacent causes. Titles include 'When the Law Deprives Rights and Freedoms' and 'The First Trans Woman to Speak Out in Mauritania's Media', evidence of a minimal but real public advocacy space.

There is no legal recognition of transgender people in Mauritania. There are no legal protections against discrimination or hate crimes for LGBTQ+ people, and the law criminalizes raping women but not corrective rape against LGBTQ+ people. There is no law against conversion therapy with no reports of it occurring, and intersex medical interventions on children are not banned with no reported cases in 2023. In January 2020, ten men were arrested and detained after a video allegedly showing a gay wedding was posted to social media and later revealed to be a birthday party, with the local police commissioner stating the basis was imitating women. According to the police report in that incident, eight of the men confessed to being homosexual and were subsequently persecuted, while one woman present received a one-year suspended sentence for inciting debauchery. Most LGBTQ+ people find it safer to conceal sexual orientation or gender identity or intersex variation amid reported harassment and arbitrary arrest and detention by police, road safety authorities, community members, and family. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity are illegal in Mauritania under law based on Sharia. Article 308 of the 1983 Criminal Code provides that any adult Muslim man who commits an impudent or unnatural act with an individual of his sex will face death by public stoning (Rajm), with unclear application to non-Muslim men. Women who have sex with women face three months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 5,000 to 60,000 Mauritanian Ouguiya. There have been no known cases of executions caused by homosexuality charges, with no death penalty imposed since 1986 and a government-confirmed unofficial moratorium on the death penalty for sexual activity between men in 2021. In January 2020, ten men were arrested and detained after a video allegedly showing a gay wedding was posted to social media and later revealed to be a birthday party. In 2025, two men were arrested after a video of them kissing was widely shared on Facebook. Mauritanian society is largely conservative, with a widely held belief that HIV and homosexuality are brought into the country by Senegalese and Gambian refugees. A survey conducted from 2021 to 2023 found that 77 percent of respondents would either dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbor. LGBTQ+ people often experience discrimination when seeking housing, employment, education, and healthcare, and most find it safer to conceal sexual orientation or gender identity or intersex variation. LGBTQI+ persons were sometimes harassed and arbitrarily arrested and detained by the National Police, the General Group for Road Safety, community members, and family, although local non-governmental organizations report a decrease in harassment from public authorities. Groups for LGBTQ+ rights are not officially allowed and often meet discreetly, with NouakchottSolidarity founded in 2015 as the first association to promote LGBTQ+ rights. No transgender-specific societal tolerance statement is documented; the only tolerance statement is general: "There is little social tolerance for LGBTQ+ people."

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montserrat' (Sept 2012): a 104 km2 island reshaped by Hurricane Hugo (1989) and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption, which wastelanded the south and displaced over half the population north. Gay life barely exists locally: 'gays are everywhere but hardly here,' and the social scene is decimated.

Associated Press report (Jan 2001, via GLAPN): Britain scrapped the anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, saying they violated signed international human rights agreements — the legal basis on which Montserrat's prohibitions were eventually swept away; local politicians and religious leaders opposed, framed as a cultural rift with London.

Wikipedia: Montserrat's gay scene is very limited, with no gay bars, nightclubs or other venues on the island, though several hotels welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies. Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code ban discrimination based on sexual orientation, defining 'discriminatory' as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. As a British Overseas Territory, Montserrat must also comply with international human rights instruments, including adherence to the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, stating that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family. The age of consent is higher for homosexual activity (18) than for heterosexual activity (16). Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been legal since 2001, decriminalised retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000. A cultural account (September 2012): a small island reshaped by a 1989 hurricane and a 1995 volcanic eruption that wastelanded the south and displaced over half the population north; gay life barely exists locally.

texts.cleaned_text: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): trans women in France are held in prisons matching the gender marker on their identity documents (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code) — most end up in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them ('we don't want any women here'), placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework applies to the department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of the CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog (25 May 2021): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across ALL French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons plus on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse sites). Covers placement, isolation, safety and staff-training recommendations. Binds the department's prisons as French establishments.

Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Martinique resource page: same-sex acts decriminalised in 1815; Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department; 2013 marriage-equality law applies; discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation prohibited in goods/services since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code arts. 225-1/225-2) and in employment since Labour Code art. L1132-1 (2008); gender-identity discrimination prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with 'sexual identity' replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. Also lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts.

exact_spans: Its active, dated operation evidences local community infrastructure on the island.
texts.cleaned_text: JM Concept 972 is a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network that provides information, meetings and services to the island's LGBT community and runs private parties and garden parties, with 2025 events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September, supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters.

French law governs Martinique, and the following national provisions apply in the department. Homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comments were made illegal by a National Assembly amendment approved 31 December 2004, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; the same law amended the 1881 Law on the Freedom of the Press to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. Christian Vanneste, an MP in Chirac's UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though the conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Since 1 January 2017 transgender people can change their legal gender without surgery or a medical diagnosis, but must still go before a court to change the gender marker, while a first name change can be done at the registry office. The bill was signed 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly, with the Constitutional Council ruling it constitutional on 17 November 2016 and dropping the original self-certification provision; before that, legal gender change had been banned for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France. A report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims, up from about 1,380 in 2018. Penalties increase where physical assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison. Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published 1 February 2022. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the MSM blood donation deferral was removed on 16 March 2022. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems with gender-affirming healthcare, including extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, with treatment covered by Sécurité Sociale under ALD 31. In March 2024 centre-right Republican senators commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory to report on youth gender care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government with no update since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access. Earlier state hostility includes the 1960 Mirguet amendment treating homosexuality as a 'national scourge' alongside alcoholism and the Vichy age-of-consent law of 6 August 1942 setting 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign against anti-LGBTQ bullying, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day, and in March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms. LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.

A feature (January 2018): trans women in the governing state are held in prisons matching the gender marker on their identity documents (the criminal procedure code's placement article) - most end up in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them.

An opinion of the governing state's detention watchdog (25 May 2021): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all of that state's places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons.

A rights resource directory page for the island: same-sex acts decriminalised in 1815; the constitution applies the governing state's law to the department; the 2013 marriage-equality law applies; discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation prohibited in goods and services since 2001 and in employment since 2008.

An island LGBT network provides information, meetings and services to the island's LGBT community and runs private parties and garden parties, with 2025 events listed, supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters.

A legal compilation: the governing state's law governs the island, and homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comments were made illegal by an amendment approved 31 December 2004, carrying a maximum penalty of a fine and/or imprisonment.

Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: the Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct — advances noted for lesbian, gay and bisexual people with 'less evident' progress for trans or intersex people. No same-sex marriage or civil unions recognised; Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against sexual-orientation discrimination; intersex newborns may be registered 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act but nonconsensual intersex procedures are not banned; legal gender recognition not possible and LGBTI organisations cannot register. Pride held since 2005 with counter-protesters; during the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and others used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech.

AfricLaw (23 August 2024, Lakshita Kanhiya): analyses the historic participation of Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan — the first transgender woman in Miss Universe Mauritius 2024 — against the country's legal obstacles: the Civil Status Act of 1981 and Central Population Database as the framework denying recognition, plus pervasive stigmatisation, with activism by the Young Queer Alliance and Association VISA-G. Concludes legal recognition and protection for trans Mauritians remain inadequate despite the visibility milestone.

US State Department 2016 Country Report — Mauritius: Section 250 almost never reached same-sex couples in court, since sodomy references arose overwhelmingly in heterosexual divorce cases as an aggravating factor. The report documents societal discrimination, with LGBTI victims of family verbal abuse or violence reporting to local NGOs including Collectif Arc-en-Ciel and Young Queer Alliance, and harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing.

Young Queer Alliance policy brief (July 2021): 'Administrative recognition of Trans People in Mauritius' - argues for legal gender recognition; notes the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders (2019) and calls on Mauritius to join countries recognising gender identity in law.

Wikipedia's Mauritius coverage reports that Collectif Arc-En-Ciel, founded in 2005, organised the country's first Pride and has done so for fifteen years, drawing more than 1,200 participants in 2016, when the march moved from Rose-Hill to Port Louis. In 2018 the Pride march was annulled after hundreds of death threats believed to come from religious extremists, and a counter-protest was organised by Javed Meetoo, an Islamic extremist under state surveillance; a strong police force had been deployed earlier in 2018 to protect marchers, and an LGBTQ sit-in at the Caudan Waterfront followed with the Prime Minister's support. AfriGay reports that gay life is fairly quiet, existing mainly online, in private and at occasional parties, though resorts are welcoming and non-discriminatory and no problems with LGBTQ couples sharing hotel rooms have been recorded. LGBTQ people may face discrimination notably in public hospitals; according to the government, hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals, but gender-affirming care is available only in limited form. In 2014 the Ministry of Health amended blood donation policy to allow men who have sex with men to donate, although anecdotally LGBTQI persons have still been prevented from donating on occasion. Section 250 of the Criminal Code of 1838 provided for penal servitude of up to 5 years for sodomy, the law under which a same-sex couple was arrested in 2015 on suspicion of practising sodomy; prosecutions under the law were rare, and on 4 October 2023 the Supreme Court struck it down as unconstitutional, ruling that it must be read to exclude consensual acts. In 2017 the government said it would not repeal Section 250, saying it would address the issue after further consideration, and former Attorney General Rama Valayden's decriminalisation bill failed to pass. Conservative attitudes remain commonplace and LGBTQ people still face discrimination; in 2018 religious extremists issued hundreds of death threats that cancelled Pride and organised a counter-protest, with Cardinal Maurice Piat and other religious leaders condemning the anti-LGBTQ protest and calling for tolerance. State actors have also shown support: police protected Pride marchers, Prime Minister Pravind Jugnauth backed an LGBTQ sit-in, and the Opposition stated that sexual orientation should not be an obstacle to equal rights. LGBTQ people may face bullying in schools, while acceptance is growing particularly among the younger generation, with polls indicating Mauritius is one of Africa's most LGBTQ-friendly countries. In October 2019 a group of young people filed a constitutional challenge to Section 250, supported by the Young Queer Alliance and the Love Honor Cherish Foundation, alongside activist Abdool Ridwan Firaas Ah Seek, 29, backed by Collectif Arc-En-Ciel. The Young Queer Alliance was founded on 1 September 2014 for young LGBTQ Mauritians, engaging in support, advocacy and anti-discrimination campaigns; a 2016 poll found 49% of Mauritians would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): the supreme court repealed the historic sodomy-law provision in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct - advances for LGB people, less evident for trans/intersex people. No same-sex marriage; a 2008 equal-opportunities act and a 2019 workers'-rights act protect against sexual-orientation discrimination; intersex children can be registered as 'undetermined' (a 2021 civil-status act) but nonconsensual procedures are not banned; Pride since 2005 with counter-protests; some anti-LGBTIQ hate speech during the 2024 elections.

Regional legal-aid organisation article (Aug 2024): the historic participation of a trans woman as the first contestant of her gender in the 2024 national beauty pageant marked a milestone; the article discusses the broader legal and social challenges for trans people in this country (a 1981 civil-status act, the national population registry, stigmatisation, lack of legal recognition).
A foreign government's 2016 human-rights report on this country: official assessment - the sodomy-law provision rarely enforced; societal discrimination exists; no legal gender recognition.

Youth LGBT organisation policy brief (July 2021) on administrative recognition of trans people in this country - argues for legal gender recognition; notes the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders (2019) and calls on this country to join states recognising gender identity in law.

A foreign government's mission to the UN (March 2011): post on LGBT rights in the UN context - diplomatic advocacy for SOGI rights at the UN Human Rights Council, relevant to this country's international human-rights environment.

texts.cleaned_text: Human Rights Watch dispatch, 11 July 2024: Malawi's Constitutional Court on 28 June 2024 rejected the challenge to Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156. A three-member panel dismissed the application brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. The sections carry up to 14 years' imprisonment. Faith-based groups filed briefs and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage. The court left any reform to parliament. HRW called it a 'dark day' and warned of heightened arbitrary-arrest and violence risks.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Malawi: documents the July 2011 protest killings (20 dead), harsh prisons, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons'.

Human Rights Watch (26 October 2018), releasing the 61-page report 'Let Posterity Judge' based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre plus lawyers, activists and officials: police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people, sometimes assaulting them, and medical staff denied services on gender-expression grounds (a trans man beaten then refused treatment; nurses mocked people presenting for HIV tests). Men face up to 14 years and women five years under sections 153/156; the 2012 justice-minister moratorium on arrests was reaffirmed in December 2015 but suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 after religious leaders' litigation, leaving its legality contested. People whose gender expression differs from expectations are 'most likely to be targeted'.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 December 2015): two men arrested in Malawi on 7 December on homosexuality charges suffered house ransacking and assault by neighbours, threats of being burned alive, attempted extortion and humiliation by community police — forced stripping, forced medical and HIV/STD examinations, and photos distributed on social media. CEDEP's Gift Trapence contrasts the arrests with government Global Fund money for LGBTI HIV services. Documents the arrest-and-abuse pattern under the penal code.

Erasing 76 Crimes (27 April 2018): police arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, in Mzuzu for suspected homosexuality and charged him under section 156 ('indecent practices between males') rather than section 153 — apparently to circumvent the six-year moratorium on anti-gay arrests while both laws faced a constitutional challenge. Police spokespersons confirmed the custody. Evidence of law-enforcement attempts to elude the moratorium.

Wikipedia country coverage: Malawi's Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, in force from 17 April 2015, bans all same-sex marriages and unions and states that gender is assigned at birth; it does not allow a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery to marry someone of that person's prior gender. The source describes no process for legal gender recognition, and notes there are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Since 2019, limited protection exists only against hate speech, via the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019 (sections 22(1-d) and 30(2-d)), which bar broadcast content likely to incite hatred on account of gender identity or sexual preference. Wikipedia country coverage: In September 2009 Mary Shawa, secretary for nutrition, HIV and AIDS in the president's office, argued Malawi must give gay people access to HIV and AIDS services, saying a human rights approach was needed for risk groups such as men who have sex with men. The June 2021 Lilongwe pride petition to city officials demanded better access to healthcare for LGBTQ people. An October 2018 Human Rights Watch report found LGBTQ community members vulnerable to arbitrary arrest, physical violence and discrimination. Wikipedia country coverage: State hostility is documented at the highest levels: in April 2010 President Bingu wa Mutharika called same-sex marriage "evil and bad before the eyes of God," and in July 2011 he threatened activists Undule Mwakasungula and Gift Trapence, saying he would "hunt you in your homes... smoke you out," forcing them into hiding amid treason threats. The 2011 U.S. State Department report found senior officials created a discriminatory environment, citing tourism minister Daniel Liwimbi calling same-sex activity "very un-Malawian." In January 2016 People's Party spokesperson Ken Msonda posted on Facebook that gays "are worse than dogs" and should be killed; the Malawi Law Society filed charges, but the director of public prosecution took over and discontinued the case on 21 January. In February 2014 the Muslim Association of Malawi called for the death penalty for gay people, and on 4 January 2017 thousands across 28 districts protested against legalizing homosexuality in marches led by the Episcopal Conference of Malawi and the Evangelical Association of Malawi. Media hostility includes the 2010 arrest and 60-day sentence of Peter Sawali for posting "Gay rights are human rights" posters in Blantyre, and international outlets' failure to report trans woman Tiwonge Chimbalanga's gender identity during her trial. Wikipedia country coverage: Malawi does not recognize same-sex unions: the 2015 Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law explicitly bans them, and at the 2011 Universal Periodic Review the government rejected every recommendation to decriminalize same-sex relations, stating it "had no plans to legalize homosexuality" and that it "should not be unduly singled out and unnecessarily pressured." Recommendations came from Sweden, Mexico, France, Canada, Germany, Australia, the UK, Italy, Austria, Ireland, Luxembourg, the United States ("Decriminalize homosexual activity"), Spain, Switzerland and Norway. The UN Human Rights Committee's June 2012 provisional concluding observations urged Malawi to amend the Penal Code and protect same-sex couples from violence, and Malawi failed to file its ICCPR report for over 17 years. Donor pressure has been contested domestically: the Malawi Council of Churches urged international organizations to "refrain from using aid as a means of forcing the country to legalise sinful acts like homosexuality," and Justice Minister George Chaponda blamed civil society leaders for withdrawn foreign aid. Wikipedia country coverage: Malawi is described as "a highly conservative country" where, in the government's own 2012 UN report, "the vast majority of society has not accepted homosexuality and homosexuality is not practiced in the open." Community visibility is emerging but fragile: the country's first pride parade was held in Lilongwe on 26 June 2021, organised by the Nyasa Rainbow Alliance with 50+ attendees delivering a petition for marriage equality and healthcare. Public hostility is documented — bail was denied to Chimbalanga and Monjeza in 2009 because "the public out there is angry with them," and the magistrate said he sentenced them to protect society — while a January 2016 interview in which gay man Eric Sambisa said "Kill us or give us our rights" led to his brief police detention and time in hiding. The 2018 Human Rights Watch report found arbitrary arrest, physical violence and discrimination against LGBTQ community members.

The Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law in force from 17 April 2015 provides that gender is assigned at birth and does not allow a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery to marry a person of that person's prior gender. Since 2019 limited protection against hate speech based on gender identity exists under the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019, which defines hate messages to include speech degrading or inciting violence based on gender identity and prohibits broadcast content likely to incite hatred on account of sexual preference or other status. In late December 2009 trans woman Tiwonge Chimbalanga and Steven Monjeza were arrested in Blantyre after holding a traditional engagement ceremony and were found guilty on 18 May 2010 of unnatural offenses and indecent practices between males under Penal Code sections 153 and 156 and sentenced to 14 years imprisonment with hard labour. Both were pardoned on 29 May 2010 by President Bingu wa Mutharika. On 23 December 2021 a Magistrate's Court in Mangochi convicted trans woman Jana Gonani under section 153(c) for unnatural offences and sentenced her to eight years imprisonment. On 28 June 2024 the High Court sitting as a constitutional court upheld the constitutionality of sections 153, 154 and 156, confirming the validity of such convictions in the consolidated constitutional referral involving Gonani's petition. Penal Code section 153 punishes carnal knowledge against the order of nature or permitting such carnal knowledge with up to 14 years imprisonment with or without corporal punishment. Section 154 punishes attempts to commit those offences with up to seven years imprisonment with or without corporal punishment. Male gross indecency in public or private is punishable as a felony with up to five years imprisonment with or without corporal punishment, and female gross indecency in public or private is punishable with up to five years imprisonment. Same-sex unions are not recognized, and the Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law in force from 17 April 2015 bans all same-sex marriages and unions. A moratorium suspending arrests and prosecutions under sections 153-156 was announced on 5 November 2012 by Attorney General Ralph Kasambara and reaffirmed in July 2014 and on 18 December 2015 by Justice Minister Samuel Tembenu, including after charges were dropped against Cuthbert Kulemela and Kelvin Gonani arrested 7 December 2015 for alleged sodomy. The High Court in Mzuzu granted an injunction on 9 February 2016 ordering police to resume arrests and on 19 February 2016 annulled the moratorium on grounds the executive lacked constitutional authority to suspend parliamentary laws. On 28 June 2024 the Constitutional Court upheld sections 153, 154 and 156 as constitutional, holding they criminalise consensual same-sex conduct among other acts but do not discriminate against homosexual persons because they prohibit all people from certain conduct, and rejecting claims of discriminatory application.

exact_spans: Documents current enforcement-and-exposure risks against queer spaces, including for foreign visitors.
Documents state-sanctioned targeting of trans people in the federal territories.
Documents current enforcement-and-exposure risks against queer spaces, including for foreign visitors.
Documents official targeting of trans people in the country units.

texts.cleaned_text: Human Dignity Trust country profile — Malaysia: federal Penal Code section 377 criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 20 years plus whipping). Sharia enactments across the states prohibit 'cross-dressing' or 'males posing as females', including the Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019 covering 'sodomy' and 'sexual intercourse against the order of nature'. The profile places Malaysia among jurisdictions that criminalise, and lists active litigation alongside cases from Mauritius and Namibia.

Human Rights Watch report (10 August 2022) 'I Don't Want to Change Myself', based on interviews with 73 LGBT people in Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 across seven states plus journalists and lawyers: every state and the federal territories (Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya) maintain Sharia codes criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity ('a man posing as a woman'), while the federal penal code punishes oral/anal sex with up to 20 years plus mandatory whipping. Government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events/media content were censored. The 2021 Nur Sajat case shows enforcement reach — 122 religious officers were mobilised to hunt her over 'insulting Islam' before she fled to Thailand and gained UNHCR protection.

Human Rights Watch (25 June 2019): a transgender woman was killed in Klang, a Kuala Lumpur suburb — the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months — with the piece documenting violence against trans people alongside police mistreatment and impunity ('The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself').
Reuters (August 2023): LGBT people in Malaysia face growing fears as Islamist opposition forecloses reform.

exact_spans: Documents current enforcement-and-exposure risks against queer spaces, including for foreign visitors.
texts.cleaned_text: The Diplomat (10 December 2025): on 28 November police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B — the largest such raid since 2022 — with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked, suspending 17 civil servants identified among them. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground under 377B, yet release was delayed; over 130 remained held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.
Human Rights Law Centre case summary: the Malaysian High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional.
United Nations Development Programme and the Asia Pacific Transgender Network have published a joint publication on Malaysia.

exact_spans: Documents state-sanctioned targeting of trans people in the federal territories.
texts.cleaned_text: International Commission of Jurists (July 2020): Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Mohamad Al-Bakri announced he had given the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) 'full licence to carry out its enforcement actions' against transgender persons; the ICJ condemned the order, demanded its revocation and called for non-discrimination guarantees.

Malaysia4U legal guide (updated July 2026): sections 377A/377B criminalise 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' for any person regardless of gender or consent — maximum 20 years plus whipping — and apply to tourists; state Syariah offences (liwat, musahaqah, cross-dressing) apply only to Muslims (max 3 years, RM5,000 fine, 6 strokes). The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Syariah provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds without decriminalising anything under the Penal Code; enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted. No same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law; sodomy first criminalised in 1871.

Human Rights Watch (24 September 2014) 'I'm Scared to Be a Woman': since the 1980s every one of Malaysia's 13 states has passed Sharia enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people — all 13 bar Muslim men from 'dressing as women' and three also bar 'women posing as men' — enforced by state Islamic religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing. Documents the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of Victoria by religious officials, repeated arrests (one woman over 20 times), routine rejection of gender-marker changes by the Registration Department (a 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery), and prison terms of four months to three years with male-ward sexual violence. Follows the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014 that triggered the Negeri Sembilan constitutional challenge (Court of Appeal decision then expected 7 November 2014).

Wikipedia country coverage: Identity documents are a live battleground: in August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department (NRD) to update a trans man's identity card with his gender identity and chosen name, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity as a male — but this judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented gender-marker change is historical: in 1975 NRD recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim (formerly Mohd Fauzi bin Abdul Karim) as female, and the Johor Deputy Mufti allowed her to marry under sharia law. The 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holds that sex is determined at birth and remains so even after sex reassignment surgery, though it was never gazetted and so is not legally binding. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2001 then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad stated Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay, and warned gay foreign ministers not to bring their partners while visiting. This is the only entry/deportation policy stated in the source; there is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors. Artist pressure has also affected entry: in July 2023 The 1975 was forced to cut short its Good Vibes Festival set after Matty Healy criticised the country's anti-LGBTQ laws and kissed a bandmate, with Healy saying he had not researched the country before booking. Wikipedia country coverage: Custodial and 'rehabilitation' facilities are explicitly prescribed: shariah courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to 6 months (Federal Territories s.56, Kedah s.52, Selangor s.54, Sarawak s.53), and may order cross-dressing or other offenders into counselling/rehabilitation in a religious institution — up to 6 months in Kelantan (s.19-20) and Pahang (s.66), extended to up to 1 year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment. Public-facing venues are also targeted: a Kuala Lumpur gay bar was raided by police and religious enforcement in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants was raided in 2022, and 11 shopping malls were raided in May 2023 over Swatch Pride watches. In November 2024 Kelantan approved amendments to its entertainment law banning activities that promote LGBTQ behaviour. Wikipedia country coverage: Human Rights Watch reports that transgender people face 'discriminatory denial of health care and employment' alongside arbitrary arrest, physical and sexual assault, and imprisonment. Conversion therapy is 'practiced regularly' and openly promoted by politicians and religious leaders, and the 1982 fatwa bars Muslims from sex reassignment surgery unless intersex. The National Blood Centre of Malaysia prohibits homosexuals and bisexuals from donating blood, in a policy that appears gender neutral. No youth-specific health-care or medication-carrying finding appears in the source. Wikipedia country coverage: The source states plainly that 'there are no Malaysian laws that protect the LGBTQ community against discrimination and hate crimes.' By contrast, hate speech rules do cover orientation: the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Content Code 2022, s.6.1(ii), defines hate speech as material that denigrates or devalues a person on grounds including sexual orientation, enforced via s.211 of the Communications and Multimedia Act. Media exclusion is statutory-adjacent: in 1994 the government banned anyone homosexual, bisexual or transsexual from state-controlled media, and Section 377D of the Penal Code (gross indecency, undefined, up to 2 years) remains a discretionary tool. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples have no route to recognition: the source states LGBTQ rights are not pursued by any political party, and at Cambridge Union in June 2019 Mahathir said Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage, calling it 'a regressive way of thinking'. The 1982 fatwa additionally ruled that marriages involving transgender people are invalid, though not gazetted. The single exception is the 1975 sharia marriage of transgender woman Sari Kartina to Abdul Razak Othman in Johor Bahru. Adoption is orientation-neutral: under the Adoption Act 1952 and Registration of Adoption Act 1952 there is no restriction on a single person adopting regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Human-rights legal organisation's country profile: the national penal code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 20 years plus whipping), alongside religious-law enactments across the country units prohibiting cross-dressing or males posing as females, including a 2019 religious-criminal-code enactment covering sodomy and sexual intercourse against the order of nature; situates this country among jurisdictions that criminalise, with active litigation listed alongside comparable cases elsewhere.

Human-rights organisation report (August 2022) based on interviews with 73 LGBT people across the country: every state/province maintains religious codes criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, and the national penal code punishes oral and anal sex with up to 20 years plus mandatory whipping; government-funded rehabilitation retreats had drawn hundreds of attendees by mid-2021, and LGBT events and media content were censored; one case shows enforcement reach — many religious officers were mobilised to hunt a trans woman over an 'insulting religion' charge before she fled abroad and gained international protection.

Human-rights organisation report (June 2019): a transgender woman was killed — the third such killing of a trans woman in this country in fewer than two months — with the piece documenting violence against trans people alongside police mistreatment and impunity.

Source note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying newswire report (August 2023) covers growing LGBTQ fears in this country as religious-conservative groups shatter reform hopes.

texts.cleaned_text: International legal body (July 2020): a religious-affairs minister announced that a national religious department had been given full licence to carry out its enforcement actions against transgender persons; the legal body condemned the order, demanded its revocation and called for non-discrimination guarantees.

Practical travel guide (updated July 2026): national same-sex-conduct provisions criminalise carnal intercourse against the order of nature for any person regardless of gender or consent — maximum 20 years plus whipping — and apply to tourists; religious-code offences apply only to Muslims (maximum 3 years, a fine, and strokes); the national court struck down some state/province religious provisions on division-of-powers grounds without decriminalising anything under the penal code; enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; no same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law; sodomy first criminalised in 1871.

Human-rights organisation report (September 2014): since the 1980s every state/province has passed religious enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people — all bar Muslim men from dressing as women and some also bar women posing as men — enforced by religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing; documents a strip-search and sexual assault of a trans woman by religious officials, repeated arrests (one woman over twenty times), routine rejection of gender-marker changes, and prison terms of months to years with male-ward sexual violence; follows the mass arrest of trans women at a wedding that triggered a constitutional challenge.

BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018): trans women in France are incarcerated per their identity-document gender (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code), typically in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them, placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework binds this department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL (25 May 2021): 'persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty — based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse). Extends to local jails as French establishments.

LINFO.re (French-language report): the French National Assembly voted the simplification of legal gender change (civil-status change for trans people). French law applies to the department, bringing the simplified procedure here.

Erasing 76 Crimes (23 May 2023, Moïse Manoël-Florisse): Bruno Agar, a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte, and his Malagasy partner (pseudonym Abdallah) married at Sada Town Hall after a 'long and complicated' path — showing the gap between formal French rights and lived reality on this predominantly Muslim island. Same-sex marriage is legal here — a rarity in Africa and the Islamic world — since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975.

Avocat Gay-Friendly directory (French): no LGBT-friendly lawyer is yet referenced in Mayotte — the town list (Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada and others) returns 'we do not yet have a lawyer referenced in your region' — while Paris-based Maître Isabelle Zribi (lawyer at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law) is listed as available. Evidence of thin local legal-access infrastructure for anyone needing counsel on the island.

French law bans discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' since July 2012, with article 225-1 of the Penal Code amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement, while transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery performed in-country was legalised in 1979 after previously only accessible abroad. Legal gender change without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or proof of medical interventions was approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly on 24 May 2016, modified on 12 July 2016 to drop self-certification, re-approved on 12 October after rejecting Senate amendments requiring medical treatment, ruled constitutional on 17 November, signed 18 November 2016 and effective 1 January 2017, but still requires going before a court for the gender marker while first-name change can be done at the registry office. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and hate-crime provisions cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination, with a 16 May 2020 report recording a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019 with around 1,870 victims identified by police compared to around 1,380 in 2018. Healthcare provision was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to suffer lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location, with a recommendation for informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine has characterized increased demand as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'primarily social problem' advising extreme caution without changing actual practice. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report critical of youth gender-affirming care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the Macron government with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first national youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by Senate vote 7 December 2020, National Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 and publication 1 February 2022 with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or 30,000 euros fine, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names on student cards and exam forms. Same-sex sexual activity in private was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 with no mention of same-sex relations, retained in the Penal Code of 1810 and followed in nations and French colonies adopting the Code, while a discriminatory age of consent under Vichy article 334 moved to article 331 on 8 February 1945 set 21 years for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974, and repealed 4 August 1982 under President François Mitterrand to equalise at 15. A 1960 Mirguet amendment inserting article 330 alinea 2 doubled the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity to repress pimping and other national scourges, was repealed in 1980 as part of an act redefining sexual offenses, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980 with Senate vote still pending. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been banned since 1985 in employment, housing and public and private provision of services and goods, and the law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal with maximum penalty of 45,000 euros fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité, and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 for injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples with most marriage protections, and same-sex marriage was approved by the National Assembly 12 February 2013 by 329-229, by the Senate 12 April with amendments accepted 23 April, ruled constitutional 17 May 2013, signed 18 May 2013 and published next day, with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier and joint adoption legal since May 2013. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people are allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by Senate 7 December 2020, Assembly 25 January 2022 and publication 1 February 2022, and the 20 June 1983 ban on men who have sex with men donating blood recalled 12 January 2009 was replaced by one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016, four-month abstinence from 2 April 2020, and removal of deferral 16 March 2022 for all regardless of orientation. Same-sex marriage is legal in all overseas departments and territories under French law, with 11 of 27 overseas deputies voting for and 11 against, 1 abstaining and 3 absent.

A feature (January 2018): trans women in the governing state are incarcerated per their identity-document gender (the criminal procedure code's placement article), typically in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them, placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy.

An opinion of the governing state's detention watchdog (25 May 2021): 'persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all of that state's places of deprivation of liberty - based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons plus on-site interviews at four mainland establishments.

A report in the governing state's language: the national assembly voted the simplification of legal gender change (civil-status change for trans people); national law applies to the department, bringing the simplified procedure here.

A rights news feature (May 2023): a teacher at the island's university centre and his partner from a neighbouring island country married at a local town hall after a 'long and complicated' path - showing the gap between formal legal rights and lived experience on a predominantly Muslim island.

A directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers: no LGBT-friendly lawyer is referenced on the island - the town list returns 'we do not yet have a lawyer referenced in your region' - while a mainland-based lawyer admitted to the governing state's highest courts is listed as available.

A legal compilation: national law bans discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' since July 2012, with the penal code amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and the labour code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on that account.

UNDP report (Dec 2024) 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' - regional framework document; Namibia's courts have decriminalised same-sex conduct (2024) and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, though implementation remains contested.

Mambaonline (28 May 2018): Out-Right Namibia opened Namibia's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre, Outreach Health, on 17 May (IDAHOT) at 30 Lister St, Windhoek West — HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, mental and sexual/reproductive health services, with plans for legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. ORN director Friedel Dausab: 'It is a first.' The article notes the colonial-era sodomy law is on the books but not believed used since independence in 1990, and recalls 2016 UN Human Rights Committee recommendations urging SOGI non-discrimination legislation.
