texts.cleaned_text: Daily Maverick (26 June 2014): a Namibian version of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters was launched with identical branding (T-shirts, berets) but an explicitly anti-gay stance, unlike the South African original.

Namibia's Broadcasting Code for Broadcasting Licensees 2018 (General Notice No. 602) bars licensees from broadcasting material that advocates hatred based on gender or sexual orientation, sanctions violence or unlawful conduct on those grounds, and prohibits material likely to incite hatred or severe ridicule against persons because of sexual orientation where that constitutes incitement to harm (Sections 5, 7(2), 7(3)). Public displays of affection between two men can still be treated as "immoral" behaviour punishable under the Combating of Immoral Practices Act of 1980. Open expression has grown: OutRight Namibia organised Namibia's first pride parades, the Windhoek march of December 2013 drew about 100 people, around 200 marched in June 2017, and hundreds marched in Windhoek and Swakopmund in December 2018, none facing government impediment. The first Namibian Lesbian Festival was held in Windhoek in November 2017 with more than sixty young lesbians from eight regions for a week of public performances of poetry, stories, music, drama and dance, repeated in November 2018. Sodomy and "unnatural sexual offences" appeared in the Immigration Act; on 21 June 2024 the High Court of Windhoek declared those references unconstitutional and invalid, and the government appealed in July 2024. Residence rights at the border have been contested: in 2001 a Namibian woman's German wife Elisabeth Frank won a Supreme Court permanent residence permit without the court endorsing same-sex relationships, and in January 2018 Daniel Digashu won a court petition to enter Namibia while his case was reviewed. On 16 May 2023 the Supreme Court ruled that same-sex marriages performed abroad must be recognised, giving non-Namibian spouses the same residence rights as opposite-sex spouses; an act passed in December 2024 explicitly forbids recognition of such marriages. Blood donor screening is relationship-based rather than orientation-based: no more than one sexual partner in the past six months regardless of sexual orientation or gender, with people suspected of an STI such as HIV or syphilis barred. On 17 May 2018 OutRight Namibia launched the Outreach Health drop-in centre in Windhoek, described as Namibia's first LGBTQ health centre. Health professionals are bound by the Ethical Guidelines for Health Professionals (2010, Health Professions Councils of Namibia), whose Sections 2.1.5, 2.6 and 3.2.2 require that personal beliefs not prejudice patient care and bar discrimination including on sexual orientation, while the Ministry of Health and Social Services' Patient Charter makes "Impartiality" a core value requiring equal treatment irrespective of sex, gender and sexuality. The 2009 Ministry regulations on scope of practice for clinical and educational psychologists still treat "sexual and gender identity" as disorders. The Namibian Gays and Lesbian Movement organises educational programs to raise awareness among LGBTQ Namibians, and MPower Community Trust provides sexual health awareness for gay and bisexual men. The SWAPO Party Youth League is listed among parties opposing LGBTQ rights; the government told the UN it had no intention of repealing the sodomy law, and in late 2024 parliament passed a law forbidding recognition of same-sex marriages performed abroad.

Current enforcement evidence for the record.

texts.cleaned_text: Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: in March 2025 Niger explicitly outlawed same-sex acts for the first time — Article 25 of the junta's Charter of Refoundation bans 'LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior' during the five-year transition following the July 2023 coup. No specific penalties are set yet, but a 2023 draft penal code proposes up to five years for same-sex conduct, 20 years for conducting/officiating/witnessing a same-sex marriage and five years for participating in or financing 'homosexual' organisations. Earlier in 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency Article 276 (up to three years) and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them; the code fixes age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts versus 13 for different-sex acts.

BBC News (December 2022): Niger's lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by MP Nana Djibou Harouna of the southern Maradi region, weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges because no legislation criminalised same-sex relationships.

The Guardian (1 July 2026): at least 40 people have been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men, including high-ranking military officials, imprisoned across Niger following the introduction of a new penal code earlier in 2026. Campaigners describe a 'witch-hunt' in a 'toxic' climate, and sources fear an HIV/AIDS resurgence as access to PrEP drugs collapses.
Agence Nigérienne de Presse (1 Jun 2026) reports that Niger criminalises LGBTQIA+ practice in the country under the criminalisation provisions adopted in the 2026 penal code revision.

Oxford Human Rights Hub (Jul 2026): Niger's Feb 2026 penal code revision criminalises 'indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts' (art. 390; 5-10 years + fines), same-sex marriage (art. 391; 10-20 years), and LGBTQIA+ associations (art. 392); art. 390 also criminalises anyone who 'artificially changes sex at birth'. The law is decried as violating intersex and LGBTQIA+ human rights.

El Espectador (29 Jul 2026): Niger's new penal code criminalises same-sex relations, and its broad, confused drafting also reads asexuality as included among sanctionable conduct; part of a wave of African states hardening anti-LGBTQIA+ laws.

Niger's February 2026 penal code punishes creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organizations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, with 10 to 20 years in prison and fines up to 500 million CFA francs (about €762,244 / US$882,829). Two gay rights organizations reportedly operated in secret in Niger, partly because they were not formally registered. After the 2026 law, organizations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working, and a representative warned that people no longer have access to condoms, HIV testing or PrEP. The U.S. State Department's 2013 Human Rights Report found no reports of violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity and no documented cases of discrimination, though it noted that stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported; the same report recorded two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for 'public indecency' and fined. That report also found no documented cases of discrimination in education based on sexual orientation, while cautioning that stigma suppressed reporting. Asylum seekers who staged Niger's first LGBTQ public demonstration in Niamey in 2022, from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire, faced societal discrimination including shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers. After the 2026 penal code, local media reported dozens of people arrested across the country, some imprisoned, including military officials. Niger has no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Article 95 of Law 2022-59 on the Protection of Personal Data prohibits collecting or processing data revealing sexual orientation, punishable by three months to five years imprisonment and fines of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs; the law was published by the Ministry of Communication and New Information Technologies in June 2025. The only other protection, in Law 2015-36 on Illicit Trafficking of Migrants (Art. 4), was repealed in 2023 by decree of President Abdourahamane Tiani, with prior convictions and their effects expunged. In Maradi in 2022 two young women were prosecuted over lesbianism, acquitted because no legislation then existed, but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos on social media allegedly portraying a lesbian act. In Niamey in 2025, two young women reported by a third person were prosecuted for 'public indecency' and acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, sparking widespread debate; the judge was allegedly sanctioned for being too lenient. Under the pre-2025 rules the age of consent was unequal, at 13 for heterosexual acts versus 21 for homosexual acts. LGBTQIA people in Niger face stigmatization among the broader population. Since March 2025, Article 25 of the military junta's 'Charte de la Refondation' has criminalized all LGBTQIA+ acts or practices, and the February 2026 penal code adds 5 to 10 years' imprisonment and fines up to 100 million CFA francs for same-sex relations, public announcement of a same-sex relationship, and changing or attempting to change one's birth sex, with mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences unavailable. Justice Minister Alio Daouda said 'all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be' are 'not in line with our social and cultural values', and President Mohamed Bazoum's 2023 proposals focused public discourse on 'social contagion'. After the 2026 law, LGBTQ people went into hiding; historically many led socially acceptable public lives while keeping relationships private, and Niger's authorities refused to recognise the 2022 protesters' refugee status.

An organisation's country overview (updated 12 March 2026): in March 2025 the country explicitly outlawed same-sex acts for the first time — a provision of the governing military authority's founding charter bans 'LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior' during the five-year transition following the 2023 coup. No specific penalties are set yet, but a 2023 draft penal code proposes up to five years for same-sex conduct, 20 years for conducting/officiating/witnessing a same-sex marriage and five years for participating in or financing 'homosexual' organisations. Earlier in 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under a public-indecency provision (up to three years) and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them; the code fixes age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts versus 13 for different-sex acts.

records.name: Nigeria
exact_spans: documents the only trans-imprisonment case

texts.cleaned_text: BBC (Aug 2024): the beaten body of Abujan trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation.

The Dial (Feb 2025): six months after Abuja Area Mama's killing, no suspects had been charged despite the announced investigation; Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.

Sahara Reporters (Aug 2026), reporting the latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria: LGBT+ travellers warned of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

TimesLIVE (Mar 2025): a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; the SSMPA is described by those affected as a 'weaponised' law creating a climate of hostility.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Aug 2024), marking 10 years of the SSMPA: the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, effectively sanctioning abuse; LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects and attacks have increased since the law passed.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Apr 2024): 'kito' gangs entrap LGBTQ+ Nigerians via Grindr and other apps — victims lured to meetings then beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing; community counters with exposure forums (one admin's alert page drawing 43,000 followers) and sting operations.

UK Home Office CPIN on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026): same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment; Sharia law in all 12 northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.
Reuters (Sept 2022): transgender Nigerians report fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

HRW report (Oct 2016) 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe': the SSMPA reaches far beyond marriage — it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any 'public show of same sex amorous relationship', and gay organisations, with punishments of 10-14 years' prison; the report documents police torture and arbitrary arrests under it.

Wikipedia biography of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman: she pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine. She served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing (BBC Pidgin) openly asked 'which prison they will keep the crossdresser in', reflecting discretionary placement; the article does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section. Outcome/ruling: an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Wikipedia country coverage: men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held in jail for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by end-2011, and mass arrests occurred at hotels (Asaba, Delta State, June 2018, 100+ party-goers; Egbeda, Lagos, August 2018, 57 young men; Warri, Delta State, August 2023, the 'Warri 67'). LGBTQ-friendly venues face closure risk: the House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after its members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008 and some were threatened, beaten and stoned. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes because of arrest and 'kito' extortion risk, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work. The 2015 survey by Bisi Alimi's organisation found only 30% of Nigerians agree LGBTQ persons should receive education, healthcare and housing, while the Constitution (Section 17(3)(d)) nominally guarantees adequate medical and health care to all citizens. NGOs Global Rights and The Independent Project provided LGBT groups with HIV/AIDS awareness training (US State Department 2011 report). The Federal Ministry of Education has a national policy on safety, security and violence-free schools in all Nigerian schools that prohibits discrimination explicitly including on 'sexual orientation', though there is no enacted legislation protecting against discrimination generally, and no political party endorses LGBTQ rights. Youth are heavily targeted by enforcement: in October 2023, 76 people were arrested at a party in Gombe state. Religious institutions play a crucial role in education, and mainstream interpretations of Islam and Christianity drive stigmatization of LGBTQ students.

An August 2024 news report: the beaten body of a transgender social-media personality was found on a highway hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and ordered an investigation — a documented trans-specific killing with official misgendering of the victim.

A February 2025 report: six months after the killing, no suspects had been charged despite the announced investigation; the country has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people and the 2014 prohibition law reinforced historic-era criminalisation — impunity documented.

An August 2026 report of a foreign government's travel advisory office: LGBT+ travellers warned of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under religious law in 12 state/province.

A March 2025 report: police abuse of people perceived as gay under a law described by those affected as 'weaponised', including a man struck in the mouth with a police weapon and freed only after paying almost half of the bribe demanded for 'looking gay'.

An August 2024 report marking a decade of the prohibition law: the law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, effectively sanctioning abuse; people report lost job prospects and attacks have increased since the law passed.

A 1992 law, Article 204 of the Criminal Code, was added by social Christians to a bill originally meant to protect women from rape and made it an offence punishable by up to three years' prison to "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner". President Violeta Chamorro signed it in July 1992 and the Supreme Court rejected an unconstitutionality appeal in March 1994; the language was dropped when a new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008, so same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since. Media reporting is largely suppressed, much of the media having been restricted since the 2018 protests, which limits coverage of LGBT issues.

In June 2014 the Nicaraguan Congress approved a revised Family Code limiting marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples; it took effect on 8 April 2015, and several organizations filed an action of unconstitutionality against it. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples, and Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on voluntary agreement between a man and a woman. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 holds that parties to the American Convention on Human Rights must grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family-registration figures including marriage; no Nicaraguan implementation is recorded.

Sexual-orientation discrimination is barred in several settings. Article 315 of the Penal Code, covering offences against labour rights, punishes discrimination based on "sexual option" by up to one year in prison in employment. Article 3(l) of Law N° 820 prohibits discrimination on sexual orientation grounds in the HIV and AIDS context, Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 bars it in access to health services on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, and Article 36(5) of the Penal Code makes sexual-orientation discrimination an aggravating circumstance when committing any criminal offence.

Violence against the LGBTQ community is generally culturally accepted and legally unenforced, and attacks go largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and poor legal outcomes. A 2012 Center for Justice and International Law survey counted 53 aggressions between 1999 and 2011, among them 15 murders of 10 gay men, 4 transgender people and 1 lesbian, with the true figure expected to be higher. NGO Programa Feminista La Corriente reported 67 assaults, 1 hate crime or murder and 2 suicides in 2021; 39 assaults, 3 hate crimes and 1 suicide in 2022; 35 assaults, 2 hate crimes, 1 murder, 1 suicide, 2 sexual assaults and 1 extortion in 2023; and 13 assaults, 5 hate crimes and 1 missing person in the first two quarters of 2024. Trans women are the most targeted group, and state police are among the aggressors, tied with family members in 2022.

Public opinion is largely opposed. A Pew survey of 9 November to 13 December 2013 found 77% opposed to same-sex marriage, 16% in favour and 7% unsure, while the 2017 AmericasBarometer showed 24.5% support. Visibility is uneven: gay men are generally more visible in public than lesbians, who often socialise privately, and an annual Gay Pride celebration has been held in Managua around 28 June since the country's first public pride festival in 1991.

Article 1 of Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 prohibits discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression, alongside sexual orientation, in access to health services. No transgender-specific hate-crime aggravator is stated; the Penal Code Article 36(5) aggravating circumstance described is framed as motivation by discrimination based on sexual orientation. A 2012 Center for Justice and International Law survey documented 53 aggressions against LGBT people between 1999 and 2011, including 15 murders comprising 10 gay men, 4 transgender people and 1 lesbian, with actual homicides and attacks expected to be higher as many victims choose not to denounce attacks to police. Programa Feminista La Corriente reported for 2021 67 assaults, 1 hate crime/murder, and 2 suicides with the majority of aggressions happening to trans women, occurring mainly in the street or in houses by family members or strangers, with acquaintances and state police each committing 10 documented aggressions. For 2022 it reported 39 assaults, 3 hate crimes, and 1 suicide with trans women continuing as the most targeted group followed by gay men, with street and home as most common places and state police tying family members in number of assaults. For 2023 it reported 35 assaults, 2 hate crimes, 1 murder, 1 suicide, 2 sexual assaults, and 1 extortion with demographic statistics described as consistent with previous years, while partial 2024 data for two quarters as of April 2025 showed 13 assaults, 5 hate crimes, and 1 person missing. The article states violence against the LGBTQ community is generally culturally accepted and legally unenforced, with instances largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and dismal legal results and media reporting largely suppressed since the 2018 protests. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity have been legal since March 2008 under a new Penal Code effective 1 March 2008 that omitted repealed Article 204; the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender and all sexual offenses are gender-neutral under Criminal Code articles 168, 170, 172 and 175. Former Article 204, signed into law in July 1992, imposed up to three years in prison for anyone who induces, promotes, propagandizes, or practices sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner and also covered unmarried sex acts; a November 1992 constitutional challenge by the Campaign for Sexuality without Prejudices was rejected by the Supreme Court in March 1994. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal benefits and protections as opposite-sex married couples; in June 2014 Congress approved a revised family code limiting marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples effective 8 April 2015 with unconstitutionality actions filed, and Constitution Article 72 states marriage and stable unions rest on voluntary agreement between a man and a woman. Article 315 of the Penal Code on offenses against labor rights punishes discrimination based on sexual option with up to one year in prison, and Article 3(l) of Law No. 820 on promotion, protection and defense of human rights regarding HIV and AIDS prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation. Article 36(5) of the Penal Code establishes an aggravating circumstance when a criminal offense is motivated by discrimination based on sexual orientation. On enforcement, the 2012 survey counted 10 gay men and 1 lesbian among 15 murders, La Corriente identified gay men as the second most targeted group in 2022, and the article states anti-LGBTQ violence is generally culturally accepted, legally unenforced, and largely unreported for fear of retaliation and poor legal outcomes.

Nicaragua's Ministry of Health adopted Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 repealing Resolution 249-2009 to require non-discrimination in public and private health units on the basis of gender identity and expression.

On 22 March 2011 Nicaragua joined the UN Human Rights Council joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity calling on states to end violence, criminal sanctions and related human rights violations committed against individuals because of sexual orientation or gender identity.

The Niue Assembly passed the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act in May, in force in June, removing 'buggery', 'attempted buggery' and 'indecent assault on males' (Human Dignity Trust, Niue section). Those offences sat at ss.43-44 of the Criminal Law Code and carried up to 10 years. The law was inherited from New Zealand through the 1901 annexation, retained on self-governance in 1974, and survived New Zealand's own 1986 decriminalisation, which changed New Zealand law only.

UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific - documents the fakafifine of Niue among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that are 'important parts of the cultural treasure of the region'.

Under the Niue Act 1966 (Part 21, Marriage of Minors), the age of majority is 21 for men and 19 for women. The age of consent was equalised in May 2011, per ILGA State-Sponsored Homophobia (May 2011). The sex-asymmetric age of majority remains on the books.

Niue's Criminal Law Code previously criminalised male homosexual conduct: consensual male sodomy carried up to 10 years' imprisonment and indecency between males up to 5 years under sections 43 and 44. Both sections were repealed by the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act 2024, enacted 5 June 2024, decriminalising male homosexual activity. LGBT people in Niue face legal challenges not experienced by non-LGBTQ residents. Same-sex unions are not recognised in Niue, even though they are recognised in New Zealand. Section 6 of the Family Relationships Act 2022 expressly prohibits same-sex marriages. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.

Government.nl (laws in force 1 July 2025): a private-member's bill (Timmermans/Bikker) puts discriminatory motive into law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data.

NL Times (Jul 2026): more than 70 people reported discrimination during the start of WorldPride Amsterdam via the RITA platform — mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants — with RITA warning the reports are 'only a fraction of the total'.

NL Times (Jun 2026): Mayor Halsema told the council Amsterdam will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during World Pride (police/enforcer/organiser agreements to act fast); recent Prides drew 25-45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports (vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation, serious assault), typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.

OSCE/ODIHR hate-crime frameworks page for the Netherlands: Dutch legislation contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime', while police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents (data collection by the police Centre of Expertise Discrimination, ECAD-P).

The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM), criminal-law working group, announced (site date 22 Feb 2024) that it had advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection on the placement of transgender detainees: no law or regulation currently governs their placement, which NJCM calls worrying and undesirable. The note highlights the group's vulnerable position (international research documents human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence), the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and the relevance of CPT standards, pointing to the full letter (PDF) to Minister Weerwind (21 Feb 2024).

NJCM letter to Minister Weerwind (Leiden, 21 Feb 2024) documenting Dutch placement practice for transgender detainees: there is no law, regulation or official policy governing their placement — the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees — and DJI (Prison Service) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the BRP (municipal records) together with case-by-case factors (gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, physical/mental health), while DIZ said it was (unpublished) drafting guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. The letter cites documented cases: a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing at arrival then moved to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling (21 Mar 2016, 15/4323/GB) on a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation in the men's prison; and sentencing rulings by the Limburg court (17 Oct 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624, trans woman facing placement in a men's prison) and The Hague appeals court (29 Jun 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108, trans man in a women's prison) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asks the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity.

Wikipedia country coverage of the Netherlands: gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019, after the House passed the bill 127-23 in 2018 and the Senate 64-11 on 12 March 2019, following earlier cases in which the Dutch Institute for Human Rights treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender'. Since February 2023 sexual orientation and disability are formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution. Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. Legal gender recognition has been administrative since a December 2013 law took effect in 2014, removing the earlier requirement of surgery and sterilization imposed by the 1984-85 laws. Care: Dutch insurance fully covers PrEP and related care for gay and bisexual men from 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices, projected to save €33 million in HIV treatment costs; assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple or a lesbian couple; the 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organizations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16; in July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate; conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and the practice was ultimately banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026. Youth and education: a 2018 Statistics Netherlands survey found 11.4% of LGBTQ youth faced online bullying and harassment, more than double the rate for heterosexual young people, and a 2020 Movisie estimate put homeless LGBTQ youth at 900-2,000, three times the rate for heterosexual youth, with rejection at home a stated cause. The government-financed religious-school 'single fact construction' loophole that let schools fire staff, as in a 2005 case of a teacher in a same-sex relationship, was closed by bills passed in 2014 (House 141-9) and 2015 (Senate 72-3), effective 1 July 2015, so LGBTQ students and teachers cannot be fired over sexual orientation. The age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1971, ending the 1911 Article 248bis rule that set 21 for same-sex activity. Acceptance among adolescents is falling: the Utrecht University/Trimbos HBSC study found positive attitudes toward homosexuality among secondary-school boys dropped from 40% to 22% and among girls from 78% to 51% between 2021 and 2025.

texts.cleaned_text: The Equal Treatment Act 1994 was extended in 2019 to explicitly ban discrimination based on gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, after approval by the House 127-23 on 3 July 2018 and the Senate 64-11 on 12 March 2019. The right of transgender people to change legal gender was established by parliament votes in 1984 and 1985 but required gender-affirming surgery and forced sterilization in force between 1985 and 2014, replaced by a law taking effect in 2014 allowing change of gender on birth certificates and other official documents without sterilization or surgery following overwhelming parliamentary approval in December 2013. The state issued a formal apology in December 2020 and implemented a €5,000 compensation scheme that same month for the estimated 2,000 victims sterilised under the prior law, with the cabinet apologizing in November 2020 and announcing in November 2021 that individuals subjected to surgery and sterilization under the 1985 law would be eligible for compensation after a February 2020 class-action lawsuit. Since 1993 a birth certificate may state "sex cannot be determined" when a newborn's sex is unclear, and courts have extended X markers: the District Court of Limburg granted "sex cannot be determined" on 28 May 2018, Leonne Zeegers received a Dutch passport with an "X" in October 2018 and Nanoah Struik in July 2019 with no general legislation so X designation remains court-decided, while a July 2021 district court allowed a gender X birth certificate for a self-identified non-binary individual and a December 2021 ruling dropped psychologist certification for X in passports. Transgender people are allowed to serve openly in the military, top surgery is available to patients older than 16, and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport 2016 guidelines endorsed by eight Dutch medical and patient organizations recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents of at least Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, with a July 2026 Dutch Health Board review continuing to recommend gender-affirming medical care for trans youth citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and low regret rate. A bill banning conversion therapy defined as attempting to change sexual orientation or gender identity passed the House in September 2025, the Senate on 16 June 2026 and was ratified on 8 September 2026, while offering organizations are ineligible for subsidies and such therapies have been blocked from healthcare insurance coverage since June 2012. In July 2020 it was announced that the Netherlands was considering abolishing gender markers on official identity documents from 2025, and in December 2019 the House unanimously adopted a motion calling on the government to investigate the extent of intersex medical interventions. Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been legal since 1811 when the Napoleonic Code repealed sodomy laws, with no new sodomy laws after independence in 1813 except Nazi-imposed Paragraph 175 during World War II which was repealed after the war and Christian-party Article 248bis in 1911 raising the age of consent for same-sex activity to 21 versus 16 for heterosexuals. Article 248bis was repealed and the age of consent equalised at 16 regardless of gender and sexual orientation in 1971, homosexuality was declassified as a mental illness in 1973 paving the way for gay people to serve in the military, and a ban on discrimination based on sexual orientation in the military was enacted. The Equal Treatment Act 1994 bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, a "single fact" loophole allowing religious schools to dismiss teachers for same-sex conduct was removed by a bill approved 141-9 in the House on 27 May 2014 and 72-3 in the Senate on 10 March 2015 taking full effect 1 July 2015, and protections against discrimination on basis of sexual orientation were formally added to Article 1 of the Constitution in February 2023 after Senate approval 56-15 on 17 January 2023. Registered partnerships for same-sex couples began 1 January 1998, the Netherlands became the first country to legalize same-sex marriage with the law effective 1 April 2001 after House passage 109-33, marriages can be performed in European Netherlands and Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba with marriages performed elsewhere in the Kingdom required to be recognized under Article 40 of the Charter, and since 2014 all marriage officiants are prohibited from refusing services to same-sex couples. Same-sex joint and stepchild adoption was legalized alongside marriage in 2001 with overseas adoption allowed from 2009, lesbian couples have access to IVF and parentage rights with assisted insemination covered by health insurance, altruistic surrogacy is legal while commercial surrogacy is illegal, and at least two IVF clinics began offering surrogacy services to same-sex couples in 2019. Men who have sex with men were subject to a lifetime blood-donation ban until 2015, replaced by a 12-month deferral announced 28 October 2015 after a 6 March 2015 Sanquin/Maastricht University report, shortened to 4 months in February 2019, and since September 2021 gay men in monogamous relationships may donate without waiting while those in non-monogamous relationships retain a 4-month wait, with full PrEP coverage introduced 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices. The legislative history for banning conversion practices targeting sexual orientation includes May 2019 House motions to investigate extent and to legislate a ban, a May 2019 ministerial statement seeing no need to ban, and final passage of the ban bill in September 2025 in the House, 16 June 2026 in the Senate and ratification 8 September 2026. A 2016 report from the Netherlands Institute for Social Research found most Dutch people have a positive attitude towards homosexuality, with only 7% viewing homosexuality and bisexuality negatively and 10% viewing transgender people negatively. The 2023 Eurobarometer found that 91% of Dutch people agreed that "transgender people should have the same rights as anyone else". The same 2023 Eurobarometer found that 84% of people thought that "transgender persons should be able to change their civil documents to match their gender identity". Reporting violence and vulnerability figures only for gays and lesbians at 3.8% victims of violence compared to 2.4% of heterosexuals and for LGBTQ youth generally.

The Netherlands adopted initiative Law 34.650 on 3 July 2018 in the Tweede Kamer and 12 March 2019 in the Eerste Kamer amending the Algemene wet gelijke behandeling to explicitly prohibit unjustified distinction on grounds of sex to include sex characteristics, gender identity and gender expression, thereby providing express equal-treatment protection for transgender and intersex persons, published 25 September 2019 and entered into force 31 October 2019.

The country ranks #13 on a regional rights map for 2026.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Norway: reported hate crimes rose 18% in 2023, with the largest increases in crimes motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity/expression and antisemitism; Zaniar Matapour sentenced to 30 years (the strictest penalty) for the 2022 Oslo Pride mass shooting; a drag bingo event sparked online threats; a knife attack on two people investigated as a hate crime.
Reuters report (2020): Norway outlawed hate speech against trans people through an amendment to the Penal Code.

NRK (May 2024, Norwegian): record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023, but the clearance rate fell from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped; many victims report little trust in police, and a dedicated hate-crime group encourages reporting.

UiO C-REX research blog (Sept 2024): transphobic hostility in Norway manifests mainly among political extremists and religious fundamentalists — the Nordic Resistance Movement's 2017 Kristiansand march advocated 'crushing the gay lobby', and research interviews with far-right activists frame gender diversity as 'degeneracy'.

UiO C-REX (June 2025), HATECYCLE study of 3,000+ survey responses from LGBTQI people: only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police — barriers include mistrust, procedural obstacles and fear of personal costs, and many who did report described dismissive treatment.

OSCE/ODIHR frameworks page for Norway: hate crimes are defined as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability; any offence so motivated is recorded under the framework.

Nordisk Post (Apr 2025): Norway's Police Security Service (PST) reports a 'significant decline' in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, but warns hate speech and intimidation risks remain, especially during Pride — most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than act.

Life in Norway resource page (updated Nov 2020): Norwegians generally hold liberal attitudes toward LGBT people; Norway was among the first countries with anti-discrimination laws; directory of national resources (FRI, Skeiv Ungdom, Transgender Association, Oslo Pride).

Same-sex sexual activity between men has been legal since 1972; same-sex acts between women were never penalized. In April 2022 the government formally apologized to victims of the ban on sex between men. Conversion therapy was banned effective 1 January 2024, approved by Parliament 85-15 on 12 December 2023. Hate speech based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1981 under Paragraph 135a of the Penal Code; in November 2020 the Storting amended the law to also protect bisexual and transgender people. A 2019 Norwegian Institute of Social Research report found 15% of LGBT respondents reported personal threats, mostly online, against 4% of the general population. Access to gender-affirming healthcare in Norway still requires a psychiatric diagnosis and referral to the National Treatment Centre for Gender Incongruence (NTCGI) at Oslo University Hospital; only a quarter of referred patients are allowed access, with those disqualified having no alternative options. Non-binary people were still without treatment as of a 2023 report, despite a 2020 guideline calling for equal access. Minors aged 6-16 may change legal sex with parental consent under the 2016 self-determination law, and 2020 guidelines recommend puberty blockers between Tanner stage 2 and age 16 following interdisciplinary assessment. In 1981 Norway became the first country to enact a law preventing discrimination against LGBT people by amending Paragraph 349a of the Penal Code, prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation in goods/services and public gatherings. Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been banned since 1998. Since 2013 a law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity and expression (Section 5 of the Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination on the grounds of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression), and Norway is one of the few countries explicitly protecting intersex people from discrimination. In 2021 anti-transgender groups such as Kvinneaktivistene and a Norwegian branch of Women's Declaration International formed. In 2023, 2611 feminists including Norway's minister of equality called for a reckoning with transphobia. Some tabloid newspapers have been criticized for publishing transphobic content, with journalism expert Jon Martin Larsen criticizing Klassekampen for contributing to 'incitement and hatred against transgender people.' Bufdir found 11% expressed hostile attitudes towards transgender people in 2017, versus 7.8% towards gay people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 January 2009, granting lesbian and gay couples the same rights as heterosexuals including religious weddings, adoption, and assisted pregnancies. A registered partnership law had been in effect since 1993, and unregistered same-sex cohabitation has been recognized since 1991 for limited rights such as next-of-kin medical decisions. In 2024 Norway was ranked the best country for same-sex couples to legally marry. Homosexual boys reported a six times higher occurrence of bullying in schools than heterosexual boys (2013 University of Bergen survey). Queer Youth (Skeiv Ungdom) is among LGBT associations offering helplines and counselling to LGBT youth.

Since 2013 Norway has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression, covering actual, assumed, former or future identity or expression, and in November 2020 the Storting amended hate-speech law to protect transgender and bisexual people, building on protection for gay and lesbian people since 1981. Since 1 July 2016 legal change of sex is based on self-determination without psychiatric or psychological evaluation, diagnosis or medical intervention for people aged at least 16, with parental consent required for minors aged 6-16, introduced 18 March 2016, approved 79-13 on 6 June, promulgated 17 June, with 190 applications in the first month. Transgender persons may serve openly in the Armed Forces. Access to gender-affirming healthcare still requires a psychiatric diagnosis and referral to the National Treatment Centre for Gender Incongruence at Oslo University Hospital, with only a quarter of referred patients granted access and no alternative if disqualified, and treatment was not offered to nonbinary patients prior to 2020. In 2020 the Directorate for Health recommended puberty blockers between Tanner stage 2 and age 16 following interdisciplinary assessment as reversible with no reliable evidence of adverse long-term effects, while in 2023 the independent non-governmental Healthcare Investigation Board issued a non-binding finding of insufficient evidence for puberty blockers and cross-sex hormone treatments in young people recommending a cautious approach which the Directorate has not implemented. In February 2023 provider Esben Esther Pirelli Benestad was stripped of medical licence over provision diverging from NTCGI guidelines, with licence conditionally restored in part in April 2023 on appeal. A 2023 report found many patients reported negative experiences including not being taken seriously, non-binary people still without treatment despite the 2020 guideline calling for equal access, and lack of competence on gender and sexuality diversity among practitioners. Conversion therapy prohibition came into effect on 1 January 2024 after parliamentary approval by 85-15 on 12 December 2023. Same-sex sexual activity between men has been legal since 1972, same-sex acts between women were not penalized, the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, and the government made formal apologies to victims of the ban in April 2022 on the 50th anniversary. In 1981 Norway amended Penal Code Paragraph 349a to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation in provision of goods or services and access to public gatherings and Paragraph 135a to prohibit hate speech on account of sexual orientation, with employment discrimination banned since 1998. The gender-neutral marriage law granting same rights including adoption and assisted pregnancies was approved 84-41 on 11 June 2008, passed 23-17 in the Lagtinget, granted royal assent and took effect 1 January 2009, replacing the registered partnership law in effect since 1993 and building on unregistered cohabitation recognized since 1991 for limited rights including medical next-of-kin status and wrongful-death compensation. Married and committed same-sex couples are permitted to adopt, with stepchild adoption allowed since 2002 and full adoption since 2009, lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, and a married or stably co-habiting female partner of a woman pregnant through insemination has all parenthood rights and duties from the moment of conception. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people can serve openly in the Armed Forces with full rights and anti-discrimination protections since 1979. The conversion therapy ban approved 85-15 on 12 December 2023 took effect 1 January 2024 after discussion since December 2019, and the Norwegian Psychiatric Association stated in 2000 that homosexuality is no disorder or illness and orientation-change treatment is ethical malpractice. The prior MSM blood-donation ban was replaced with a 12-month deferral implemented 1 June 2017 after June 2016 announcement, with a planned 2024 policy to end discrimination indefinitely postponed, while HIV-prevention drug PrEP has been offered free of charge since the October 2016 announcement. The Directorate for Children, Youth and Family Affairs found the proportion with hostile attitudes steadily decreasing, documenting that "In 2017, 7.8 percent expressed hostile attitudes towards gay people while 11 percent expressed hostile attitudes towards transgender people." A 2013 University of Bergen survey found nine of ten LGBT respondents reported no workplace discrimination or harassment, only a small minority reported physical assault, suicide had significantly decreased since the 1990s, though homosexual boys reported six times higher school bullying than heterosexual boys. The Oslo Police District recorded 238 bias-motivated crimes in Oslo in 2018 of which 20 percent related to LGBT status, and 2019 research found 15 percent of LGBT respondents had been the target of personal threats mostly online compared to four percent among the general population. Since 2021 anti-transgender groups including Kvinneaktivistene and a Norwegian branch of Women's Declaration International formed amid rising transphobia promoted in the name of radical feminism, prompting a 2020 open letter by 2476 feminists for inclusive feminism and a 2023 call by 2611 feminists including the minister of equality for a reckoning with transphobia. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre stated "we know that queer people are the targets of hate, threats and violence. The incitement of hate is especially virulent against trans people. We will not accept this in Norway." In July 2020 the government announced priority for LGBT refugees alongside vulnerable women and children for transfer for permanent resettlement.
In 2013 Norway prohibited discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression.

Approved 6 June 2016 and effective 1 July 2016, Norway's legal-gender-change law gives persons resident in Norway who experience belonging to the other gender than registered in the National Population Register the right to change legal gender by application to the tax office with no surgery, hormone or diagnosis requirement, with self-application from age 16, joint application with holders of parental responsibility for ages 6-16, restriction of under-6 changes to congenital uncertain somatic sex development documented by health personnel, and provides that changed legal gender governs application of other laws except for establishment of parenthood.

In Oslo in 2018, 238 incidents were recorded as hate crime, up 20% from 2017 and up 66% from 2015, with lesbian, gay, bisexual and trans persons comprising 20% of cases as the second-most targeted group after ethnicity at 57%.

In Norway in the year to March 2019, 23% of LGBT people versus 10% of the general population experienced hateful comments, 15% versus 4% experienced threats, mostly repeated, and 16% versus 3% experienced eliminationist statements such as 'you shouldn't have been born' or 'you don't have the right to live,' with the disparity widening further when comments targeting gender identity and gender expression are included, occurring mostly online on Facebook, Instagram and comment sections and disproportionately among young, politically/online-active people and people with two or more minority characteristics, with observing such comments toward one's group alone producing feeling unsafe, while Norwegian criminal code protection against discriminatory/hateful comments in public covered ethnic origin, religion, sexual orientation and functional ability and treated online audiences of 20-30 people as public.

Since 2020 in Norway gender incongruence is not a mental disorder but confers entitlement to municipal and specialist healthcare under least-invasive-first, informed-consent and multidisciplinary assessment principles without psychiatric/psychological assessment as a precondition for gender-affirming care, with adult care requiring persistent incongruence, clarified somatic-psychiatric contraindications, information on irreversible effects and side-effects, fertility preservation and individualized follow-up before hormone therapy initiated mainly in specialist care after GP referral with GP/local hospital follow-up and before breast surgery at regional centres and genital surgery at the national treatment service for binary and non-binary patients with speech therapy reimbursed via Helfo on physician prescription and hair removal covered by health trusts, and with under-18 care centred on municipal supportive counselling and family care with no drug treatment for prepubertal children while puberty-delaying GnRH analogues after puberty onset and estrogen/androgen hormones may be provided only through the national treatment service after paediatric multidisciplinary assessment of maturity, development, psychosocial situation and coexisting conditions.

Official health-rights page (Gender Recognition Act): legal gender is determined by the individual's own perception of gender identity — self-declaration decided at a government office — from age 16 alone, 6-16 with parents, under-6 only for documented congenital conditions; a 2017 regulation covers citizens resident abroad

Annual-review chapter (covering 2024): reported hate crimes rose 18% in 2023, with the largest increases in crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity; the perpetrator of the 2022 Pride mass shooting was sentenced to 30 years (the strictest penalty); a drag event sparked online threats; a knife attack on two people was investigated as a hate crime.
Note: not retrievable at research time (access denied); the underlying news report (2020) covers the parent nation outlawing hate speech against trans people (amendment to the penal code).

News outlet (May 2024, local language): record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023, but the case-clearance rate fell from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped; many victims report little trust in police, and a dedicated hate-crime group encourages reporting

Research blog (Sept 2024): transphobic hostility manifests mainly among political extremists and religious fundamentalists — a 2017 far-right march advocated crushing the local gay movement, and research interviews with far-right activists frame gender diversity as 'degeneracy'

Research blog (June 2025), survey study of 3,000+ responses from LGBTQI people: only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police — barriers include mistrust, procedural obstacles and fear of personal costs, and many who did report described dismissive treatment

International security-organisation frameworks page: hate crimes are defined as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability; any offence so motivated is recorded under the framework

News outlet (Apr 2025): the police security service reports a 'significant decline' in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, but warns hate speech and intimidation risks remain, especially during Pride — most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than act
Resource page (updated Nov 2020): residents generally hold liberal attitudes toward LGBT people; the parent nation was among the first with anti-discrimination laws; directory of national resources

HRW (Feb 2024): calls on Nepal's government to urgently create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure so transgender and third-gender people can obtain official documents — illustrating that despite progressive rulings, no straightforward document-change process exists (photo shows a Kathmandu trans woman holding her 2023 citizenship certificate listing female gender).

Human Rights Watch (31 July 2024): reports the Supreme Court's decision that trans law student Rukshana Kapali be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification; the order applies to Kapali alone, while others must still petition the court and the typical medical and surgical requirements for marker changes persisted for others.

JURIST (Aug 2024): Nepal's Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed 50+ lawsuits since 2021; changing markers to 'female'/'male' has usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations including intrusive post-operative genital exams.

The Diplomat (Feb 2024): Nepal's 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while male/female marker changes lagged — the country's progressive reputation outruns policy.

Kathmandu Post feature (Nov 2024) on trans life in Janakpur: trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment.

APTN (Asia Pacific Transgender Network) publication (Oct 2021, in Nepali): 'Gender Identity Draft Bill 2078: Civil Society Proposal' - by Rukshana Kapali and Allan Bhandari with advocate Subin Mulmi, produced through the Amplifying Trans Advocacy Fellowship; a civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition in Nepal.

The Record (Sept 25, 2020) by Queer Youth Group and Queer Rights Collective: argues that despite the Constitution awarding the right to self-determine name and gender markers (2007 case), 'an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law' is still needed to address inequalities faced by the trans and broader PoMSOGIESC community.

SIT Study Abroad ISP (Spring 2015) by Sophia Greene: 'Gender and Sexuality in Nepal: The Experiences of Sexual and Gender Minorities in a Rapidly Changing Social Climate' - despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in virtually every arena of life amid the clash of patriarchal tradition and modernisation.

Los Angeles Times (2 May 2008): reports that the Nepali Congress Party and the party of the former Maoist rebels — whose leaders had in the past described gays and lesbians as social 'pollutants' — wrote support for gay rights into their platforms. A historical 2008 party-platform change, not evidence of every later policy, and a gay-rights rather than trans-specific commitment.

Same-sex acts have been legal in Nepal since the Supreme Court's December 2007 ruling in Sunil Babu Pant v. Nepal Government, which held homosexuality is not 'unnatural'. The Criminal Codes Act 2017, which replaced the 1963 Muluki Ain, still lists 'unnatural sex' and must be read in light of that ruling. The Muluki Ain criminalized 'unnatural sexual intercourse' with up to one year's imprisonment, and many Nepalese LGBTQI+ people were arrested under it. The age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Judicial recognition of foreign same-sex marriages exists: Suman Pant's Supreme Court case set a precedent for same-sex spousal visas. On 28 June 2023 Justice Til Prasad Shrestha issued an interim order directing the government to 'temporarily register' marriages of non-traditional couples and sexual minorities, and the full bench has yet to deliver a final verdict. In April 2024 the National ID and Civil Registration Department instructed local authorities to enter same-sex marriages into a separate register. Temporary registration grants no equal rights: same-sex couples cannot inherit property, receive tax subsidies, make spousal medical decisions or adopt children, and certificates label them 'groom and bride'. The first marriage of a trans woman and a cisgender man took place in November 2023, and as of June 2025 Blue Diamond Society counted at least 17 documented queer marriages. Implementation is inconsistent: the Kathmandu District Court rejected a registration in July 2023, and compliance by local governments is unknown.

The first gender-affirming surgery in Nepal was performed in June 2025 at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, which has since established a Gender Affirming Clinic. Hormone replacement therapy and sex reassignment surgery remain hard to reach: a six-month hormone supply costs 4,500 rupees, providers are few, and many trans Nepalis take hormones without medical supervision because of stigma. Some travel to India and Thailand for surgery. Conversion therapy is practiced, including treatment in rehabilitation centres and traditional exorcism by family members. Lesbian couples are denied IVF, and research and healthcare addressing LGBT Nepalis' needs are severely lacking. A drop-in centre with free HIV testing operates in Kathmandu through the Blue Diamond Society, which has more than 50 branches; Mitini Nepal, Parichaya Samaj and Sahaayam Nepal also provide resources. UNDP has recommended that transgender and intersex students be given access to safe toilets and bathroom facilities.

The Education Board has implemented information about sexual and gender diversity in the curriculum for grades 7–9 (ages 13–15), making Nepal the second Asian country after Mongolia to do so, and universities offer courses on LGBT issues. Many LGBT children nonetheless face discrimination and leave school because of threats, bullying and neglect by fellow students and teachers, and transgender Nepalis face severe gender-based violence and interrupted education, especially in rural areas. Queer Youth Group has filed writ petitions at the Supreme Court demanding legal recognition of gender identity and has advocated for the citizenship bill. During the 2011 census, some enumerators demanded that a child be stripped when parents listed them as 'third gender'.

On 30 October 2024 the Aamul Paribartan Nagarik Party held a protest rally opposing homosexuality and LGBTQ rights, with Mitini Nepal's executive director noting that anti-LGBTQ sentiments are gaining momentum in Nepal and South Asia. In April 2026 newly elected Prime Minister Balen Shah faced LGBTQ community criticism over a YouTube rap video containing derogatory and homophobic hate speech; after demands for an apology, his supporters markedly increased derogatory comments, hate speech and death threats against the community. The Communist Party of Nepal-Maoist made homophobic statements during the Civil War, describing homosexuality as 'a production of capitalism' and LGBT people as 'social pollutants'. The article also notes that since 2008, with the end of the insurgency, the Maoist Party has supported LGBT rights, so the wartime statements are historical rather than a present-day stance. Media representation of LGBT people has historically been negative or comic relief, with caricatures of transgender people, gay people and lesbians, though positive depictions include Highway (2012) and Soongava (2012). Some observers accused media and activists of pinkwashing and spreading disinformation about same-sex marriage and LGBT rights, and Nepali media has been criticized for forcefully using 'third gender' to describe trans men and trans women. Pride events held annually include Nepal Pride Parade (since 2019), Queer Womxn Pride and Trans Pride Parade (since 2020).

An international observer's report (February 2024) calls on the government to create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure so transgender and third-gender people can obtain official documents, illustrating that despite progressive rulings no straightforward document-change process exists.

An international human-rights report (31 July 2024) records the supreme court's decision that a trans law student must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification; the order applies to her alone, while others must still petition the court and the typical medical and surgical requirements for marker changes persisted for others.

A news report (August 2024) records that the supreme court ruled a trans woman must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed many lawsuits; previously, changing markers usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations.

A news analysis (February 2024) argues that the 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but officials limited changes to people identifying as third-gender while male/female marker changes lagged — the country's progressive reputation outruns its policy.

A news feature (November 2024) records ground-level conditions for visibly trans people in provincial cities: discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions, and frequent physical and sexual harassment.
A community publication (October 2021) records a civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition.

A contributor analysis (September 2020) argues that despite the constitutional right to self-determine name and gender markers, an extensive overhaul of the law is still needed to address inequalities.
A study-abroad paper (2015) records that despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in nearly every arena of life.

A news report (2 May 2008) records that a political party and the party of the former rebels, whose leaders had previously described gays and lesbians as social 'pollutants', wrote support for gay rights into their platforms — a historical 2008 party-platform change, not evidence of every later policy, and a gay-rights rather than trans-specific commitment.

Human Truth Foundation 'LGBT Rights Across the World' (Vexen Crabtree, 2025): the Vexen LGBT Equality Index ranks Nauru 101st at -0.10, far below top-ranked Germany/Spain at 4.88 and below most Pacific neighbours.
The Guardian, 29 May 2016, headline: 'Nauru decriminalises homosexuality and suicide'. The 1899 Queensland-derived criminal code provisions were repealed, including the attempted-suicide provisions.

Kaleidoscope Trust Nauru country page: Nauru decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016 but same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal; intersex and transgender people have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and no employment-discrimination protection for LBTI people; Nauru supported the 2011 UN HRC Joint Statement, and its last CEDAW state report (2016) contained no LBTI-specific information.

texts.cleaned_text: Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in Nauru article: the Nauru Regional Processing Centre (RPC) Rules 2014, made under the Asylum Seekers (Regional Processing Centre) Act 2012, ban discrimination against any person based on sex or gender, sexual preference or gender identity within the RPC immigration-detention facility. This covers immigration detention, not Nauru's criminal-justice prison system, and concerns non-discrimination rather than placement by birth sex vs identity, special units, or solitary-confinement practice. No documented data was found on where transgender prisoners are housed in Nauru's corrections system, nor any trans-prisoner case or ruling.

A foreign mission (March 2011): publishes the full text of a joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity, delivered on behalf of 84 countries — this country is among the signatories, with several other countries
A human-rights foundation's world survey of LGBT rights (2025): a comparative index ranks this country near the bottom of the table, far below top-ranked countries and below most regional peers

A major news outlet (29 May 2016), headline-level (the article body did not survive retrieval — navigation shell only): 'The country decriminalises homosexuality and suicide' — the 1899 foreign-derived criminal-code provisions were repealed, replaced by provisions including attempted-suicide ones

A human-rights trust country page: the country decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016 but same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal; intersex and transgender people have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and no employment-discrimination protection for these people; the country supported the 2011 joint statement, and its last report to a United Nations treaty body (2016) contained no relevant information

RNZ (17 Apr 2024), Official Information Act data: 229 gender-identity-motivated hate incidents reported to police in 2023 vs 161 in 2022 — a 42% rise — with police saying the figure likely understates true anti-trans hate, and a spike in the month anti-trans activist Posie Parker visited (March 2023).

RNZ (27 Feb 2025), Counting Ourselves survey: almost one in five trans and non-binary New Zealanders were threatened with physical violence because of their gender identity in the past four years, and 8% experienced deliberate physical violence — the first clear population picture of violence against these communities.

New Zealand Law Commission Issues Paper 53 'Ia Tangata' (June 2024): a review of the protections in the Human Rights Act 1993 for transgender people, non-binary people and people with innate variations of sex characteristics - official law-reform consultation document.

The Spinoff opinion (2 Jul 2024) by Jennifer Shields: after a spate of rainbow event cancellations and a 2023 Posie Parker protest, calls for more security for rainbow communities — noting statutory wins (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act 2021 easing ID correction; Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2022) alongside a worsening street climate.

Spartacus Gay Travel Index 2026 (Feb 2026): annual index scoring each country's legal situation and living conditions for queer people across 18 categories, from marriage to death penalty; color-coded dark green (most liberal) to red (most dangerous), with negative points for death-penalty laws and Sharia application. Generic index methodology with no New Zealand-specific score or finding stated.

glbtq encyclopedia entry on New Zealand (Andrew Matzner, 2004): long history of liberal reform (women's suffrage 1893); Gay Liberation Front emerged April 1972; decriminalisation followed years of activism; Georgina Beyer reportedly the first transsexual in the world to achieve national office; 13th country with equal marriage (2013).

PrideNZ.com: archive of over 1,000 audio recordings of interviews and events from Aotearoa NZ's LGBTQIA+ communities, a rainbow timeline, over 18,000 GayNZ.com articles (2001-2017), and Homosexual Law Reform 40th-anniversary resources including Hansard transcripts of the parliamentary debates.

New Zealand: citing Dalzell, Pang & Broemdal 2024 (Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry, 'Gender affirmation and mental health in prison'), the article reports that trans people in New Zealand prisons are more likely to have prior experience of abuse and show a higher rate of incarceration, and that the NZ government has declared support for gender-affirming healthcare and gender-affirming clothing for incarcerated persons. No placement rule (birth-sex vs identity housing), special unit, or solitary/segregation practice for New Zealand is described.

texts.cleaned_text: Cairo 52 + White Tent joint stakeholder submission (6 Aug 2025) to Oman's 4th-cycle UN UPR: documents systemic legal and institutional discrimination against transgender people, states recent legislative developments have deepened criminalisation of gender expression, says Oman bans legal gender recognition and explicitly bans gender-affirming healthcare, and reports Oman ignores earlier UPR recommendations on gender identity, expression and health access; recommends ending criminalisation, adopting anti-discrimination law and permitting legal recognition.

Statute-level extraction from Oman's Penal Law (Royal Decree 7/2018): Art 265 public indecency (10 days-3 months + OMR 100-300 fine), Art 266 impersonating/entering women-only venues disguised (1 month-1 year), Arts 267-268 producing or sharing content 'violating public morals' offline and online (up to 1 year / 10 days-1 month), plus Cyber Crime Law 2011 Arts 17/31 used against LGBT expression (1 month-3 years + OMR 100-3000); gender non-conformity punished through Art 266(d).

LegalClarity overview (published 3 Jun 2026): Oman criminalises all same-sex conduct with up to 3 years' prison under the 2018 Penal Code, prosecution often triggered by digital evidence discovered during unrelated investigations without a family complaint (Art 49 dual-criminality exception); Art 60 requires deportation for foreign nationals convicted of a felony (permanent) and allows it for misdemeanours (3-15 years); state ISP Omantel enables surveillance; outing carries social AND criminal risk; assembly/advocacy restricted via the Civil Associations Law.

Visitor-facing incident (27 Feb 2023): a genderqueer/non-binary Indian model-activist arriving at Muscat International Airport on a 10-day tourist visa says friends cleared immigration but she was held for a separate examination, made to remove her shirt and touched inappropriately by officers — direct first-hand evidence of border treatment of visibly gender-nonconforming visitors.

HRW open letter (13 Jul 2020) to Oman's authorities on arrests/convictions under the 2018 Penal Code's 'imitating the opposite sex' provision: Royal Oman Police announced arrests of 'men in women's clothing' after Snapchat photos from a private Salalah party circulated, and an Asian expat in abaya/niqab at an Al Buraimi women-only park hour — shows active enforcement of the cross-dressing offence against gender non-conformity.

HRW regional report (16 Apr 2018) with MENA laws annex covering Oman: documents that Oman's 2018 penal code (effective that year) added a retrograde provision punishing any man who 'appears to dress in women's clothing', alongside regional comparison (Kuwait's 2007 imitation law), and records Oman's existing criminalisation of same-sex conduct and barriers to LGBT organising.

texts.cleaned_text: Shafiqa Ahmadi, 'Islam and Homosexuality: Religious Dogma, Colonial Rule, and the Quest for Belonging' (Journal of Civil Rights and Economic Development, 2012), distinguishes homosexual acts from homosexual persons and notes that some Islamic countries criminalise acts, even by death, without criminalising identity.

Roya News (19 Sep 2018), on the Public Prosecution's announcement: a Salalah preliminary court sentenced two men to four years in jail and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing photos of themselves in women's clothes on social media, and two further men to three years with the same fine for featuring in the video; the sentences fall under the July 2018 Omani Penal Code provision (Article 22), under which 'any male that appears in female clothing or demeanor' may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed up to one year, with additional 'publishing immoral acts on social media' charges. The article notes these follow January 2018 arrests by the Royal Oman Police of a group of men for dressing as women after social-media photos circulated. It documents court-ordered imprisonment of gender-nonconforming people in Oman, but contains no information on where inside the prison system those convicted were housed.

texts.cleaned_text: In 2018, four men who cross-dressed as women in Salalah were arrested. They were imprisoned following the arrest. They were also punished with fines at maximum amounts. The enforcement action was taken under laws against "indecent" dress and behaviour. No separate transgender-specific penal code section number is stated in the article for this enforcement. Homosexuality in the Sultanate of Oman is illegal under §§ 33 and 223 of the penal code. The punishment is a prison sentence of up to three years. The law applies to both men and women. Suspects of homosexual or lesbian intercourse shall be prosecuted without a prior complaint if the act results in a public scandal. In September 2013, all Gulf Cooperative Countries agreed to discuss a proposal to devise a test for homosexuality intended to single out gay foreigners and prevent them from entering any of the countries. The suggested reason for backtracking was concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar and fears of controversy if football fans were screened, with officials insisting it was a mere proposal. LGBTQ people in Oman face significant social and legal challenges not experienced by non-LGBTQ residents. Advocacy for LGBTQ rights in Oman is a criminal act, as in other Gulf countries. Activists use social media with an alias to protect their identities, with very rare exceptions.
