texts.cleaned_text: Two rights organisations' joint submission (6 Aug 2025) to a UN human-rights review: systemic legal and institutional discrimination against transgender people; recent legislative developments have deepened criminalisation of gender expression; legal gender recognition is banned and gender-affirming healthcare explicitly banned; earlier review recommendations on gender identity, expression and health access reportedly ignored; the submission calls for ending criminalisation, adopting an anti-discrimination law and permitting legal recognition.

A rights organisation's statute-level extraction from the 2018 penal code: public indecency (10 days-3 months plus an OMR 100-300 fine), impersonating or entering women-only venues disguised (1 month-1 year), producing or sharing content 'violating public morals' offline and online (up to 1 year / 10 days-1 month), plus 2011 cyber-crime provisions used against LGBT expression (1 month-3 years plus OMR 100-3,000); gender non-conformity punished through the impersonation provision.

A legal-information platform (3 Jun 2026): all same-sex conduct criminalised with up to 3 years under the 2018 penal code; prosecution often triggered by digital evidence discovered during unrelated investigations and without a family complaint; deportation is required for foreign nationals convicted of a felony (permanent) and allowed for lesser offences (3-15 years); the national telecom operator enables surveillance; outing carries social and criminal risk; assembly and advocacy restricted through the associations law.

A visitor-facing incident (27 Feb 2023): a foreign genderqueer/non-binary visitor arriving at the capital's international airport on a 10-day tourist visa says friends cleared immigration but she was held for a separate examination, made to remove her shirt and touched inappropriately by officers — direct first-hand evidence of border treatment of visibly gender-nonconforming visitors.

An international human-rights organisation's open letter (13 Jul 2020): arrests and convictions under the 2018 provision 'imitating the opposite sex'; the national police force announced arrests of 'men in women's clothing' after photos from a private party circulated on social media; enforcement also documented against a foreign expatriate in full-body covering at a women-only park hour — showing active enforcement of the cross-dressing offence against gender non-conformity.

An international human-rights organisation's regional report (16 Apr 2018): the 2018 penal code added a provision punishing any man who 'appears to dress in women's clothing', alongside a regional comparison with another country's imitation law, and records existing criminalisation of same-sex conduct and barriers to LGBT organising.

texts.cleaned_text: A law-journal article (2012) distinguishing homosexual acts from homosexual persons: in some countries guided by religious law, acts are criminalised (even capitally) while identity alone is not.

A local news outlet (19 Sep 2018), on the public prosecution's announcement: a preliminary court sentenced two men to four years in jail and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing photos of themselves in women's clothes on social media, and two further men to three years with the same fine for featuring in the video; the sentences fall under a July 2018 penal-code provision under which 'any male that appears in female clothing or demeanor' may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed up to one year, with additional 'publishing immoral acts on social media' charges. The article notes these follow January 2018 arrests by the national police force of a group of men for dressing as women after social-media photos circulated. It documents court-ordered imprisonment of gender-nonconforming people but contains no information on where inside the prison system those convicted were housed.

AP (Nov 2024): 'Shooting kills 3 transgender women in Pakistan's largest city' — gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near Karachi, the second deadly attack on the community there in a week.

BBC (21 Sep 2025): police found bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead by unidentified assailants on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi — latest in a continuing pattern of lethal violence; article notes estimates of ~500,000 transgender citizens facing social exclusion and abuse.

Justice Project Pakistan policy brief: despite notable legal advances (Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018), protections have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment in practice — the central challenge is implementation failure, not absence of law; brief makes custody/police safeguards recommendations.

UK Home Office country-policy note on SOGI, Pakistan, November 2025 (current-status authority): trans/intersex people protected under the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 though the Federal Shariat Court declared provisions 'un-Islamic' in 2023 leaving ongoing legal disputes; consensual same-sex acts criminalised under PPC s.377 (2 years to life, definition unclear, male-to-male sex), only men criminalised per Human Dignity Trust (Dec 2024); LGBT+ people unlikely to face state persecution.

Amnesty International (19 May 2023): reacting to the Federal Shariat Court's reserved verdict striking down sections of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 — calls the ruling 'a blow to the rights of the already beleaguered group' of transgender and gender-diverse people; Amnesty had warned the government on 17 May 2023 not to adopt amendments violating human-rights standards.

The News, Pakistan (21 Oct 2025): analysis of the gap between law and reality — the 2018 Act affirmed self-perceived gender identity and the 2020 Rules introduced the neutral 'X' marker for administrative recognition, but trans Pakistanis still face bullet-riddled bodies on highways, street harassment, rejection by landlords, dismissal at hospitals and suspicion/ridicule at police stations.

Erasing 76crimes (3 Feb 2026, citing the Guardian): a wave of violence has left Pakistani transgender people afraid to go out — describes the Karachi night-time shooting at activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana (three bullets fired through the door, narrowly escaped); also reports Senator Mushtaq Ahmad proposing a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control trans people's official gender identity — an active retrograde legislative push.

Dawn analysis of the Federal Shariat Court verdict of 19 May 2023, delivered across 12 shairat petitions: the court ruled that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Transgender Persons Act 2018, covering gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity and inheritance for transgender people, do not conform with the petitioners' reading of Islamic principles, and speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women.

The Diplomat (Jul 2025): Pakistan's 2018 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was hailed as a legislative turning point — granting right to self-identify and protection from discrimination in education, employment and healthcare — yet the piece documents citizens 'legally recognized, socially forsaken', i.e. statutory rights not matching lived status.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Pakistan: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised under Section 377; societal violence and discrimination; transgender persons (khwaja sira) have some legal recognition but face harassment and violence.

Wikipedia country coverage: Pakistani media censors LGBTQ-related news stories. The government blocked the website Queerpk.com in late 2013, and the Pakistani edition of the International New York Times (Express Tribune) left a blank space where a photo accompanying a same-sex marriage story should have appeared. Penal Code provisions reinforce this: Article 292 bans sale, distribution, exhibition, ownership or importation of 'obscene' books, pamphlets or images, Article 294 prohibits 'obscene' public acts, songs, music or poems, Article 153 penalises inducing students to political activity that disturbs public order with up to two years' imprisonment, and Article 141 designates an assembly of five or more persons an 'unlawful assembly' if its common object is to commit any offence. Open expression carries personal risk: LGBTQ Pakistanis are generally reluctant to be open about their sexuality for fear of forced marriage, honour killings, humiliation, blackmail or violence, and a person living openly as LGBTQ is likely to face treatment from non-state actors such as Islamist and terrorist groups. A 2016 article by a young Pakistani man in the UK-based Gay Star News had his surname omitted for his security.

Healthcare access is a documented failure point for trans people. In 2016, 23-year-old transgender activist Alisha was shot seven times and left to bleed to death at Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar while staff argued over whether to take her to the men's or women's ward; men there discriminated against and taunted her friends and asked whether her blood was 'HIV-positive'. Some transgender women use hormones and silicone under terrible medical conditions without proper equipment or supervision, since expensive sex change surgery is rarely available in Pakistan due to lack of education and social taboos. In 2010 the Supreme Court ordered provision of free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people, and the 2018 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act prohibits discrimination in healthcare, education, employment, housing and access to goods and services, though the source notes locals often deny trans people basic education and healthcare. The HIV epidemic began in Pakistan in 1987; government estimates (2004) put nearly 3,000 people living with HIV while critics suggest 70,000 to 80,000 and UNAIDS reports possibly up to 210,000, and a 2009 survey found male and transgender sex workers at high risk, with prostitutes lacking access to condoms and little public health education provided.

Same-sex partnership has no legal recognition. The Constitution does not mention sexual orientation or gender identity, Part II 37 pledges to protect marriage and the family and oppose obscenity, and Part IX 227 requires all laws to be compatible with Islam as defined by a government-appointed Islamic council. Article 496 of the Penal Code punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. Same-sex couples can live together only in secret; the source notes the LGBTQ community can socialise, organise, date and, in rare cases, live together as couples, if done mostly in secret, and in 2005 a tribal council in the Khyber region ordered a man who married a fellow tribesman to leave the area or face death. For trans people, a small clerical body in Lahore (Tanzeem Ittehad-i-Ummat) declared transgender marriages legal under Islamic law in June 2016, while in May 2023 the Federal Shariat Court struck down sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the 2018 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act on self-perceived gender, with provisions remaining in force pending appeals.
A newswire report (Nov 2024): gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near the largest city — the second deadly attack on the community there in a week.

A public broadcaster (Sep 2025): police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead on a roadside highway in the largest city — the latest in a continuing pattern of lethal violence; estimates put the number of transgender citizens facing social exclusion and abuse at hundreds of thousands.

A local legal-aid organisation's policy brief: despite notable legal advances (the 2018 Act), protections have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment in practice — the central challenge is implementation failure, not absence of law; the brief makes custody and police-safeguard recommendations.

A foreign home ministry's official country guidance on sexual orientation and gender identity (Nov 2025): trans people are protected under the 2018 Act though the national religious court declared provisions 'un-Islamic' in 2023; consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under an older statute (two years to life, definition unclear, male-to-male acts), with only men affected per a rights organisation; people are unlikely to face persecution by the authorities.

An international human-rights organisation (May 2023): the national religious court's reserved verdict striking down sections of the 2018 Act is 'a blow to the rights of an already beleaguered group'; the organisation had warned the government on 17 May 2023 not to adopt amendments violating human-rights standards.

A national daily (Oct 2025): analysis of the gap between law and reality — the 2018 Act affirmed self-perceived gender identity and the 2020 rules introduced a neutral 'X' marker for administrative recognition, but trans people still face violence, street harassment, landlord rejection, hospital dismissal, and suspicion or ridicule at police stations.

A decriminalisation news outlet (Feb 2026): a wave of violence has left trans people afraid to go out — a night-time shooting at two activists (three bullets fired through a door, narrow escape); a senior legislator proposes a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control official gender identity — an active retrograde legislative push.

An opinion analysis (May 2023) of the national religious court's verdict on the 2018 Act: the court ruled that sections on identity, self-perceived gender identity, and inheritance do not conform with the petitioners' reading of religious principles, and speculated the Act could facilitate rape or sexual assault of women by men 'disguised' as transgender women — framing echoing anti-trans moral panics from abroad.

A foreign-affairs magazine (Jul 2025): the 2018 Act was hailed as a legislative turning point — granting the right to self-identify and protection from discrimination in education, employment, and healthcare — yet citizens are 'legally recognised, socially forsaken': statutory rights not matching lived status.

A foreign government's 2021 human-rights report: same-sex conduct criminalised under an older statute; societal violence and discrimination; transgender persons have some legal recognition but face harassment and violence.

Equaldex data for Panama: homosexuality legal, marriage banned, gender change legal but requires surgery, no nonbinary recognition, no hate-crime protections, no employment/housing discrimination protections, blood donation banned (indefinite deferral), conversion therapy not banned. Only 12% approve of same-sex marriage (AmericasBarometer 2023, ranked #18 of 22).

Washington Blade (16 Feb 2018): Supreme Court Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega withdrew his October 2017 draft ruling against marriage rights — the draft had held the family code's same-sex marriage bars not unconstitutional while suggesting the Assembly consider civil unions; the Panama government signalled it would comply with the landmark 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision.

texts.cleaned_text: BBC features (14 Aug 2018): in Panama's Guna Yala indigenous territory a flourishing 'third gender' community (Omeggid) is accepted as completely normal, with powerful matriarchal figures elevating women's status.

Outright International's current Panama overview: the National Assembly blocked an anti-discrimination amendment in 2024, no acts are recognised as hate crimes, intersex infant surgery is unregulated, the 2025 UPR produced calls for SOGI protections and gender-recognition reform, and reforms remain stalled.

Washington Blade (22 Oct 2017): La Estrella reported Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega's draft ruling finding the family-code sections barring same-sex marriage 'not unconstitutional' while leaving the National Assembly to legislate civil unions ('equality must be constitutionally guaranteed via the law'); the two marriage lawsuits (a UK-marriage recognition suit and a direct family-code challenge) were combined after summer 2017 oral arguments, with amicus briefs from regional marriage-equality advocates and public support from the First Lady, while Catholic and evangelical groups spearheaded opposition.

Wikipedia country coverage: The Panamanian state has repeatedly acted against LGBT legal equality: the Code of Private International Law approved 8 May 2014 (Article 40) states that same-sex marriages are strictly prohibited and foreign same-sex marriages will not be recognized; the Supreme Court ruled on 27 March 2023 (after a seven-year delay) that there is no positive right to same-sex marriage under the constitution; and a constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman was approved by the National Assembly on 29 October 2019 but withdrawn before the referendum after public protests. No laws protect LGBT people from discrimination, and Article 39 of the Constitution, which bars associations contrary to moral or legal order, has been used to refuse registration of gay organizations (as with the first gay group, AHMNP, founded 1996, which only gained legal recognition in 2005 after a three-year battle). Religious and political hostility is documented: the Roman Catholic Church defeated a 2004 civil-union proposal, condemned the 2018 Inter-American Court advisory opinion, and one deputy labelled that opinion "a danger to the human race"; a 2015 bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced. Gay and bisexual men are barred from donating blood, and a 2017 public survey found 78% of Panamanians opposed to same-sex marriage.

International LGBT-rights organisation current overview: amendment of the general anti-discrimination law to include sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds was blocked by the national assembly in 2024 (claiming implicit coverage); no acts are formally recognised as hate crimes; intersex infant surgeries are not prohibited; at the 2025 UN universal periodic review multiple states urged explicit anti-discrimination protections, gender-recognition reform and stronger violence safeguards — legal reforms remain stalled and this country lags much of the region.

Same-sex activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001. The 2010 Constitution bans discrimination on sexual orientation, with protections in place since 2010. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015 and adoption since 2015. None of the roughly 50 residents is known to be in a same-sex relationship. Military service falls under UK responsibility.

The 2010 Pitcairn Constitution Order bans discrimination on sexual orientation. Marriage is defined as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 also recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn. Adoption is open to married, unmarried and single people.

Full Wikipedia republication: same-sex sexual activity legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001; anti-discrimination constitutional protection from the 2010 Constitution Order; same-sex marriage legal 14 May 2015 — ordinance unanimously approved by the Island Council 1 Apr 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair 5 May, published 13 May 2015; adoption legal since 2015; page also indexes the territory within UK LGBT-rights timelines.

A legal compilation: same-sex activity has been legal since 2001; the 2010 constitution bans discrimination on sexual orientation; same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015 and adoption since 2015; none of the roughly 50 residents is known to be in a same-sex relationship.

A legal summary: the 2010 constitution order bans discrimination on sexual orientation; marriage is defined as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015; the 2015 ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed abroad.

An encyclopedic republication: same-sex sexual activity legal since 2001; anti-discrimination constitutional protection from the 2010 constitution order; same-sex marriage legal 14 May 2015 - ordinance unanimously approved by the island council 1 April 2015, signed 5 May, published 13 May.

Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): Congress's committee approved unanimously (for plenary) the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457 (presented by Jorge Montoya and Honor y Democracia party) that threatens trans people's rights by restricting their use of public bathrooms; the article also records community demands — HIV medication supply, scrapping outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.

IDEHPUCP (PUCP human-rights institute) analysis: the bathroom-restriction article openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks — the institute cites IACtHR Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights; also quotes congressman Lizarzaburu's dehumanising comparisons.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024): report finds hate crimes rose in Peru with trans women most affected; co-author Gianna Camacho (trans human-rights defender/journalist) stresses recorded numbers are only a sub-registry; cites the 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work.

BBC News Mundo (19 Dec 2025): three police officers sentenced to 17 years in prison for torture and sexual abuse of Azul Rojas Marín, trans woman and LGBTI activist — Peru's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per the article, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history (case reached the Court via the CIDH).

Infobae Peru (15 Dec 2025): officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León sentenced to 17 years for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas, nearly 20 years after the attack. The judgment was issued after years of litigation.

HRW (19 May 2025): the April-2025 'Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents' mandates public-restroom entry be restricted by 'biological sex', barring trans people — including trans youth — from facilities matching their identity; vague child-protection articles (art.4 media/advertising ban, art.5) enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content; obscenity-minimum sentence raised 3→4 years; HRW says child protection is a pretext for repression and trans scapegoating.

HRW dispatch (27 Jun 2024): Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as 'a step toward dignity' for trans patients in healthcare settings.

Outright International current Peru overview: public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional; April 2025's 'sexual integrity' law restricts restrooms by biological sex; April 2025 NGO foreign-funding law lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order/security' grounds, risking weaponisation against queer organising; Pride marches held annually since 2002 (oldest recorded 1984).

Peru Support Group (Apr 2025): Congress approved bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR (Muñante/Montoya), banning bathroom use contrary to birth sex and inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Willax TV's Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes ('go use the men's room'). Congressional pressure continues against therapeutic abortion at INMP.

The Perchy Bird: Peru's Congress voted to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions. Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carried the repeal, arguing the President lacked authority to issue the anti-discrimination decree, after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a 1M-signature removal petition. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Peru since the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalized sodomy with penalties akin to rape. Age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation per a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, applicable to trans and cis youth. Discrimination and hate crimes on sexual orientation and gender identity were criminalized by governmental decree Nº 1323, in effect 7 January 2017, under Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip the provisions but Kuczynski's veto stood. Law 32331 (enacted 13 May 2025) prohibits trans people from using public restrooms, a state-imposed restriction on trans people's daily movements that could intensify hostile interactions in transit spaces. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity; in 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a 21 October 2016 ruling published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' for health-insurance classification purposes. The 2016 national education curriculum includes information on sexual orientation, sex and gender issues, describing sexual orientation as the result of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and 'not a voluntary choice'. Opinion polls show age-based variation: 18–24-year-olds (66%) were markedly more favourable toward homosexuals than the population overall (49%), and younger people showed higher approval of same-sex marriage (8.3% approval among Peruvians in 2010, higher among younger respondents). Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with specific relevance to trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

A news outlet (Feb 2025): a national-legislature committee in this country approved unanimously a bill threatening trans people's rights by restricting their use of public bathrooms; the article also records community demands — HIV medication supply, scrapping outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and quotas in public office.

A university human-rights institute analysis: the bathroom-restriction provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks — the institute cites a regional human-rights court advisory opinion that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee full rights.

A foreign broadcaster's world service (Dec 2025): three police officers sentenced to 17 years for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman — this country's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per the article, the first torture-by-discrimination case of a regional human-rights court in the region's history.
A news outlet (Dec 2025): the officers sentenced to 17 years for the rape and torture of a trans woman — the sentence landing nearly 20 years after the attack.

An international human-rights organisation (Jun 2024): the health system walked back anti-trans guidance — authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as 'a step toward dignity'.

An international LGBTIQ organisation's country overview: public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a court in the capital ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional; an April-2025 law restricts restrooms by 'biological sex'; an April-2025 law lets authorities revoke registrations on public-order grounds, risking weaponisation against queer organising; Pride marches held annually.

A foreign solidarity-group briefing (Apr 2025): a week of setbacks — the national legislature approved bills banning bathroom use contrary to birth sex and inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'; a media personality publicly harassed the first openly lesbian member of the national legislature; pressure continues against abortion rights.

texts.cleaned_text: Outright/IGLHRC Philippines legal overview (fetched page): lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility updated 2023 to bar SOGI-based discrimination of clients; openly gay/bisexual people allowed in armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017 (uniform policy follows legal gender on birth certificate); Clerical Error Law RA 9048 (2001) blocks administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people (judicial order required) and the 2008 Supreme Court ruling in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan bars legal-gender change even after gender-affirming surgery.

Bulatlat (26 Jun 2025): two killings in days — 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist/activist shot by an unidentified gunman inside a General Santos clinic the same day; Bahaghari says the cases are an urgent reminder to pass the SOGIESC Equality Bill, which has been stuck in Congress for 25 years — no national SOGI anti-discrimination law exists.
Manila Bulletin report (May 2025): a foreigner was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas.

Interaksyon (10 Apr 2024): drag artist Taylor Sheesh (Taylor Swift impersonator) was physically struck on stage by a man from the crowd at Bayambang, Pangasinan's Kalutan Concert on 6 April 2024 — she called the attack traumatic and urged passage of the SOGIE Equality Bill; the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

Rolling Stone Philippines explainer (7 Feb 2025): 25 years of legislative inaction on the SOGIE Equality Bill; patchwork protections that do exist — SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur, Iloilo) and 32 cities/municipalities; Magna Carta for Public Social Workers (SOGIE harassment: P20k-40k fine and/or up to 1 year); Magna Carta of Women and Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic/homophobic/misogynistic slurs and ridicule (fines P1k-10k, up to 30 days, sensitivity seminar).

Rappler: trans Filipinos' legal gender recognition bill would let applicants — including minors with consent — choose markers beyond male/female (X/nonbinary), addressing the lack of a recognition process that drafter Chase Go says drives social exclusion, privacy invasion and violence; the Commission on Human Rights has called the year's trans killings a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide'; allies plan to endorse the bill to the 20th Congress (28 July).

WanderSafe LGBTQ+ travel guide (2026 data as of 18 Jun 2026): Manila 'Generally Safe' — LGBTQ+ 69, but Trans travellers only 62 ('Exercise Caution'), HIV+ 81; same-sex relations never criminalised, deep gender-diversity traditions (bakla/tomboy), vibrant Pride/nightlife scene and high media visibility, but SOGIE Bill (filed since 2000) stuck, no marriage equality, Catholic Church resistance; accessibility caveat: 80% of Metro Manila's 46 train stations lack step-free entrances, only 5 of 46 LRT-1 stations have elevators.

HRW report, 'Just Let Us Be' (21 Jun 2017): documents bullying and discrimination against LGBT students across Philippine schools, with law short on remedies at the time. Provides basis-level evidence of the school-setting climate for gender-diverse youth, and includes a Tagalog summary and recommendations.

Investigative feature on Manila City Jail: transgender women and gay men are held in the ordinary MALE dormitories (mandatory head-shaving on arrival for the male dorm), where they assume housekeeping/entertainer roles and informal same-sex “weddings” with male inmates are widely used by gangs as a survival/protection strategy against abuse. Documents that trans women in Philippine jails are housed by birth sex in male facilities with no gender-matched placement, and that safety comes from inmate hierarchies rather than policy.

Official practice documented: BJMP-Davao Community Relations chief Jail Senior Inspector Ellen Rose Saragena said LGBT detainees at Davao City Jail are relocated in batches to the City Jail Annex “to prevent abuse”, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens; three LGBT groupings live in the annex since its establishment. Shows the official Philippine response is administrative segregation of LGBT detainees into a separate annex for “safety”.

Gender diverse people in the Philippines have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from some private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. Marawi City's December 2004 ordinance bans men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. After the 2017 Marawi siege, individuals perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps. Counseling services and therapy sessions are used to help people escape dangerous and hostile environments, and since the 2000s organizations formed around sexual health (particularly HIV), psychosocial support and spiritual needs; LGBTQ Filipinos have a higher rate of suicidal ideation or attempts. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and in June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, rolling out first to government-owned hospitals. The DSWD and Department of Education allowed students in late 2016 to wear uniforms matching their gender identity, the July 2017 Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy reviews curricula for gender stereotypes and sets June as Pride Month, and the 2013 Anti-Bullying Law's rules list sexual orientation and gender identity as prohibited bullying grounds. Hate crimes and forced conversion therapy have been committed by family members against Iglesia ni Cristo LGBTQ teenagers, backed by the church's central establishment.

Under the Clerical Error Law of 2001 (RA 9048), transgender persons cannot change sex on birth certificates, as "no correction must involve the change of nationality, age, status or sex of the petitioner" without a judicial order, with the only affirmed exception being a Supreme Court decision allowing a marker change due to intersex status. No national law criminalizes cross-gender behavior, but cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequences, including documented refusals of entry and service to gender-diverse people. Marawi City in December 2004 banned men from appearing in public wearing female attire, makeup, earrings "or other ornaments to express their inclinations for femininity," and banned skintight blue jeans, tube tops and other skimpy attire, while women only must not "induce impure thoughts or lustful desires," described by the mayor as part of an Islamic "cleaning and cleansing" drive. Kabacan municipality in Cotabato in November 2019 prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims under penalty of imprisonment. Murders of transgender and gender-nonconforming persons have been reported from at least 2012, including killings by pro-ISIS groups in Marawi, and after the five-month siege of Marawi some residents blamed the city's LGBTQ community for the militias' wrath while individuals perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps. In late 2016 the Department of Social Welfare and Development with the Department of Education allowed students to use uniforms matching their gender identities, and in July 2017 the Department of Education's Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy required review of public school curriculum for all gender stereotypes including LGBTQ-based and mandated observance of June as Pride Month. Protection machinery includes nine provinces prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity — Aklan (2025), Albay (2022), Agusan del Norte (2014), Bataan (2021), Batangas (2015), Cavite (2014-18, gender identity added 2018), Dinagat Islands (2016), Ilocos Sur (2017), Iloilo (2016) — plus an anti-bullying law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, Executive Order No. 51 of 22 December 2023 establishing the Special Committee on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer, Intersex, and Asexual Affairs, and the 2016 election of Geraldine Roman as the first openly transgender woman to Congress. Non-commercial, private, consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal with no recorded evidence of enforced penalties, and the age of consent is equally 16 regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity. Public sexual conduct or affection may be punished under Article 200 of the Revised Penal Code on Grave Scandal, providing penalties of arresto mayor and public censure upon any person who shall offend against decency or good customs by highly scandalous conduct not falling within any other article. Same-sex unions are not legally recognized as marriage or civil unions, with the Family Code recognizing only marriages between "a man and a woman" while the Constitution is silent, though 19th Congress proposals House Bill 1015, the Civil Partnership Act, and Senate Bill 449, the Civil Unions Act, following 2022 refiling of two civil union bills, seek recognition, benefits and protection. Same-sex couples may not file for joint adoption because unions are unrecognized, but no explicit law bars LGBTQ+ individuals from adopting and eligibility requirements do not consider sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTQ adopters may still be deemed unfit for lacking "good moral character" because the Civil Code, Family Code, and Child and Youth Welfare Code require parents to provide moral formation, leaving the term open to state interpretation. In 2025 the Supreme Court ruled concealment of one's homosexuality from a spouse constituted fraud as a valid basis for annulment of marriage. The national SOGIE Equality Bill/Anti-Discrimination Bill seeking equal treatment regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity passed the House 198-0 on 20 September 2017 after 17-18 years but died in the Senate in June 2019 after opposition and failure to tackle, was reintroduced in July 2019, rejected by the government in November 2022 as unacceptable, while Quezon City in June 2023 launched the Right to Care Card via special power of attorney allowing LGBTQ couples to make medical decisions despite hospitals recognizing only legal spouses and next of kin.

On June 26, 2020 in Manila police arrested at least 20 participants in an LGBT Pride protest where there were no allegations of violence and participants wore masks and followed social-distancing protocols, subsequently charging them under the 2019 Law on Reporting of Communicable Diseases and the 1985 Public Assembly Act.

There is a 'near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level': no national legal gender recognition law (identity documents cannot be corrected and retain the birth gender), an anti-discrimination equality bill stalled for 25 years, and no marriage equality; a national human-rights commission investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

Documented violence: the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a foreign national arrested for raping a trans woman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance.

An investigative-journalism investigation (December 2022) records transgender women at the capital's main city jail housed by birth sex in the ordinary male dormitories — with mandatory head-shaving on arrival and safety coming from inmate hierarchies — and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates widely used as a survival and protection strategy against abuse.

A local press report (March 2023) records the official practice of transferring LGBT detainees in batches to a city jail annex 'to prevent abuse', alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens.

Erasing 76crimes (16 Oct 2014): Palau decriminalised homosexuality — per Human Dignity Trust, Palau's Attorney General confirmed the new Penal Code (signed by the President in April 2014) dropped the sodomy offence formerly at s.2803 Ch.28 'Sex Crimes' Title 17 (up to 10 years' imprisonment); at its 2011 UPR Palau had accepted recommendations to repeal criminalisation and combat LGBT discrimination; the move dropped the global anti-sodomy country count to 79.

Scoop/OHCHR Pacific piece (c. 2011): Palau appears among more than 70 Pacific and global jurisdictions with laws criminalising same-sex relations still on the books, and Palau and Nauru accepted recommendations to decriminalise homosexual acts during their Human Rights Council UPR appearances, documenting Palau's stated commitment to repeal.

LGBTQ people in Palau do not possess the same legal protections as non-LGBTQ residents. There are no anti-discrimination laws concerning sexual orientation and gender identity. In 2011 Palau signed the joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity at the United Nations, condemning violence and discrimination against LGBTQ people. No legal gender recognition, identity document, screening, facility, custody, or gender-affirming care provisions specific to transgender people are provided. No transgender-specific penalties, enforcement measures, or protection-machinery outcomes are provided. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 23 July 2014, when the current Penal Code took effect. In April 2014 President Tommy Remengesau Jr. signed the new Penal Code containing no provisions outlawing consensual sex between people of the same sex, following the government's October 2011 Universal Periodic Review promise to fully decriminalise homosexuality. Previously male same-sex sexual activity was illegal and punishable by up to ten years in prison, while female same-sex activity was legal. The Constitution defines marriage as between a man and a woman, with the same-sex marriage ban added in 2008 among 22 amendments passed in the 4 November 2008 referendum. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. There are no anti-discrimination laws concerning sexual orientation. In July 2019 President Remengesau Jr. said he supports striking down the constitutional ban as discriminatory and believes in full equality, with no repeal outcome stated.

On 22 March 2011 Palau joined the Human Rights Council joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity, which called on states to end acts of violence, criminal sanctions and related human rights violations committed against individuals because of sexual orientation or gender identity.

HRW commentary (27 Jan 2009): PNG violence-accountability climate — a mob stripped, beat with hot iron rods and burned a woman accused of sorcery within yards of a police station; provincial commanders recorded 50+ sorcery-related killings in two highlands provinces in 2008 with perpetrators rarely brought to justice; sorcery accusations (linked to HIV deaths) used to hide murders and mitigate sentences; police routinely take no action.

ABC News (8 Oct 2014): Hanuabada village on Port Moresby's outskirts is a safe haven for PNG's gay and transgender community — residents live openly, transgender people wear women's clothes in the street without retaliation, while in Port Moresby gay/trans people are commonly raped or beaten, sometimes by police (documentary maker Vlad Sokhin, who found the village while travelling).

The Guardian (13 Jan 2017) on HRW's annual world-report assessment of PNG: the government of Peter O'Neill has failed to protect women and children and to respond to corruption and police violence — 'police abuse, including of children, continues to be reported with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse'.

Guardian Nigeria (reprint): describes Hanuabada ('big village', built over the sea) as a pocket of tolerance where the gay community is accepted — set against PNG where sex between men is illegal and stigma/violence widespread (a 24-year-old gay man recounts being pelted with stones and bottles); campaigners say attitudes shift with exposure to the LGBT community.

As of 2024, there is no legal recognition of transgender or gender-diverse identities. No transgender-specific criminal provision, penalty, document, screening, facilities, custody, or care rule is stated. The stated criminal penalties concern male same-sex sexual acts and sodomy, not transgender identity as such. The words lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender tend to carry heavy stigma. Transgender Papua New Guineans use the Tok Pisin word palopa, reportedly derived from the name of American singer Jennifer Lopez, to refer to a cultural and traditional third gender. The Sambia recognise a traditional third gender kwolu-aatmwol, literally male thing transforming into female thing. A 2011 study found police were one of the main sources of violence against men who have sex with men and trans people. Male same-sex sexual activity is prohibited by Section 210 of the Penal Code. Anal sex or oral sex, whether heterosexual or homosexual, is punishable as sodomy with up to fourteen years imprisonment. Other same-sex sexual acts are punishable with up to three years imprisonment. There are no legal restrictions against lesbian sex. The law is rarely enforced, with no prosecutions directed at LGBTQ persons in 2012, but arrests occurred in 2015 and 2022. In 2015 a man charged with indecent acts between males pled guilty and received a suspended sentence with community service and mandatory counseling, and in 2022 two men were arrested after having sex. In 2011 decriminalising homosexuality was stated as not a priority, and in 2023 it was confirmed there was no intent to repeal laws criminalising male homosexuality while claiming existing laws protecting against violence and abuse were sufficient. LGBTQ persons reported discrimination in daily life and struggle to find jobs. LGBTQ people experienced rape and violence throughout the country, including Port Moresby, leading many to flee to Hanuabada. In Port Moresby gay men were sexually abused by police, raped and beaten, with abuse commonly continuing even if reported due to imbalance of power and victims often framed as perpetrators. A 2011 study found police were one of the main sources of violence against men who have sex with men and trans people. Hanuabada has been described as a gay village and sanctuary for local LGBTQ people. Public views towards homosexuality are mixed and homophobia is widespread, with homosexuality more accepted in coastal areas than in the Highlands. No documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically is stated, so the coastal-acceptance statement concerning LGBTQ people generally cannot be quoted as transgender-specific.

International human-rights organisation (Jan 2009): report on a country where violence against women is rampant - documents widespread gender-based violence in this country, the context of impunity that also affects sexual and gender minorities.

A foreign public broadcaster (Oct 2014): a coastal village on the outskirts of this country's largest city (notably the home of roughly half of the national team) is a safe haven for gay and trans people in a country where homosexuality is illegal.

texts.cleaned_text: HRW news release (18 Mar 2007): the then government proposed fast-track legislation 'punishing anyone who promotes homosexuality' in schools - dismissal, fines or prison for teachers/students, banning LGBT organisations and safer-sex HIV education, with deputy minister Orzechowski announcing teachers who reveal homosexuality would be fired; HRW wrote to PM Kaczynski.

Wikipedia country coverage: homosexuality was decriminalised in independent Poland in 1932 but criminalised under partition — Congress Poland 1818, Austria 1852, Prussia 1871, Russia 1845, penalised by forced resettlement to Siberia — and recriminalised from 1939 under the German occupation. Polish men in same-sex relationships were punished under Article 175, especially in annexed areas, and the General Government's criminal police could deport them or impose the death penalty; camp prisoners under Paragraph 175 were classified 'political prisoners' with red triangles. Two earlier sodomy sentences were carried out: Wojciech Skwarski of Poznań, burned at the stake in 1561 on a sentence that also counted theft and murder, and Agnieszka Kuśnierczanka in 1642, publicly beaten and exiled; the 1925 Suwałki case sentenced Stefan Góralski and Marjan Kuleszyński to three months under paragraph 516 of the 1903 Russian Penal Code. Post-war, the 1948 law set the age of consent at 15 for all sexual acts and otherwise left the liberal interwar law intact; Operation Hyacinth of 15 November 1985 registered around 11,000 suspected gay men in a national database, and 'pink files' were still held by the Institute of National Remembrance as of 2005 despite activists' requests to destroy them. A 1 January 2004 law barred workplace discrimination on sexual orientation; on 8 July 2024 the Tusk government added a registered-partnership bill (no joint adoption) to the Sejm agenda after its October 2024 presentation by Equality Minister Katarzyna Kotula. Open discussion of homosexuality stayed taboo outside literary circles: the Second Republic magazine Wiadomości Literackie and figures such as Tadeusz Boy-Żeleński and Irena Krzywicka broke taboos on contraception and homosexuality, founding the Liga Reformy Obyczajów in 1935, and 1933 produced three novels with openly lesbian themes including The Well of Loneliness with Krzywicka's preface. Communist authorities censored information about the Kinsey Report, while a 1985 Polityka article 'Jesteśmy inni' triggered a national discussion and Selerowicz's conspiratorial 1983–84 meetings produced the samizdat bulletin Etap; press came-outs followed with actor Marek Barbasiewicz in Kobieta i Życie (September 1992) and Izabela Filipiak in Viva (1998). Media has also carried hostility: the right-wing Gazeta Polska distributed 'LGBT-free zone' stickers, later reworded 'LGBT Ideology-Free Zone' after a court ordered distribution halted; President Andrzej Duda stated in the 2020 election that 'LGBT is not people, it's an ideology, which is more harmful than Communism'; Lech Kaczyński opposed official Pride in 2004–05. Cultural visibility includes the 1987 Polish premiere of Larry Kramer's The Normal Heart in Poznań with a 4 May 1989 TVP broadcast, Karolina Breguła's 2023 'Let Them See Us' billboard campaign, frequently vandalised, and Lambda's Queer Museum in Warsaw, opened 6 December 2024 as the first of its kind in Central and Eastern Europe. Café Fiolka at Puławska 257 in Warsaw, the first official gay club, opened 7 October 1990 and closed in 1992 after repeated vandalism; earlier police targeted cruising spots, with Warsaw's 6th Sanitary-Moral Brigade, joined by the female 1st Brigade in 1925, hunting cruising areas in 1927 and arresting mostly working-class men identifying as 'ciota'. Health and support infrastructure developed around the AIDS crisis: the Ministry of Health established a Plenipotentiary for AIDS and a ten-person expert team in 1985, a year before Poland's first recorded AIDS case; Lambda was registered by the Warsaw Voivodeship Court on 23 February 1990 to spread tolerance and prevent HIV; and the Kochaj, nie zabijaj campaign began in spring 1990. Organisations include Campaign Against Homophobia (2001), the Polish Feminist Lesbian Archive OLA-Archiwum (registered 1998, publishing Furia Pierwsza), the Trans-Fuzja foundation co-founded by MP Anna Grodzka, and Razem for Polish LGBT immigrants in New York (1995). Medical services are documented from the first sex reassignment surgery in 1963 at Szpital Kolejowy in Międzylesie, infrequent for some twenty years, and the first recorded transgender meeting on 10 December 1985 at Warsaw's Department of Sexology. Homophobia is described as a common public attitude driven by Catholic Church influence and widespread social conservatism, with the Church later 'a factor in making homosexuality something scandalous in many social circles' and influencing the 1988 blocking of the Warsaw Gay Movement's legal registration. After 2015, several municipalities and four voivodeships declared 'LGBT-free zones', partly in response to mayor Rafał Trzaskowski's pro-LGBT declaration; in August 2019 LGBT community members said they felt unsafe amid a rise in violence including attacks on the first Białystok Equality March and a foiled bombing attempt at a Lublin march; at a Kalisz rally on 11 November 2021 the organizer called 'LGBT, pederasts and Zionists' enemies of Poland. ILGA-Europe's 2020 report ranked Poland worst among EU countries, and on 7 August 2020 47 people were arrested in the Rainbow Night mass arrest, some peacefully protesting activist Margot's arrest, drawing criticism from the Polish Ombudsman; 50 ambassadors and representatives wrote an open letter on 27 September 2020 affirming that 'Human Rights are not an ideology'. Visibility milestones run from the first Equality Parade in Warsaw in 2001 (over 300 attendees), through banned 2004–05 Prides — the 11 June 2005 march drew about 2,500 in civil disobedience with several brief arrests and a 600–1,000-person 2004 Freedom Veche — to the 2011 election of Poland's first out LGBT MPs, Robert Biedroń and Anna Grodzka; questioned villagers in the 1925 Suwałki case reported no 'abnormality' and accepted the two men in their community.

Transgender people are allowed to change their legal gender following certain requirements which include undergoing hormone replacement therapy and receiving a medical diagnosis, with legal gender changes performed since the 1960s. Only after the legal gender has been changed does a transgender individual gain the right to undergo sex reassignment surgery because any surgery resulting in infertility is prohibited by Penal Code art. 156 §1 with few exceptions such as uterine cancer or myoma, making castration on request illegal. In July 2015 the Sejm approved a transgender recognition bill allowing change without physical interventions on statements from mental health experts of gender dysphoria by 252 to 158, approved by the Senate in August, vetoed by President Andrzej Duda in October, with Parliament failing to override the veto. Until March 2025 a transgender individual had to file a lawsuit against their parents, but on 4 March 2025 the Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court resolved the process should be a non-trial vital-records rectification on request alone with the spouse as the only possible other participant and immediate effect upon positive review. Openly transgender people are officially barred from military service on medical grounds, with a diagnosis of gender dysphoria resulting in automatic assignment as permanently and completely unfit for service in both conflict and peace. No current hate-crime protections exist, with a bill pending as of 2019 for penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by gender, gender identity, age, disability or sexual orientation, legislation agreed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk in November 2024 to add sexual orientation, gender, age and disability to hate speech laws, vetoed on 17 April 2025 by President Duda. The 2019 EU LGBTI Survey II found 1 in 5 trans and intersex people in Poland were physically or sexually attacked in the past five years. Consensual male and female same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized by the 1932 Penal Code with an equal age of consent of 15, reaffirmed in 1948, while homosexual prostitution remained illegal until legalized in 1969 and homosexuality was removed from the list of diseases in 1991. Article 18 of the Constitution places marriage as a union of a man and a woman under protection, and the Supreme Court, Constitutional Tribunal and Supreme Administrative Court have ruled it limits marriage to opposite-sex couples requiring a constitutional amendment, with no legal recognition of same-sex couples except limited rights of shared tenancy, refusal to testify as the closest person under Penal Code Article 115(11), and residency under EU law. On 20 March 2026 the Supreme Administrative Court ruled registries must recognise and transcribe marriage certificates of same-sex couples married in another EU member state, first implemented in Warsaw on 14 May 2026, but on 28 July 2026 the Constitutional Tribunal ruled transcription incompatible with the Constitution, while on 29 May 2026 the Sejm passed the Act on the Status of the Closest Person granting limited notarized cohabitation rights pending Senate and presidential approval opposed by President Karol Nawrocki. Anti-discrimination provisions were added to the Labour Code in 2003 banning employment discrimination based on sexual orientation, the Constitution guarantees equality without enumerated sexual orientation after a 1995 proposal was rejected, the equal-treatment law in force from 1 January 2011 prohibits sexual orientation discrimination in employment only, and in 2019 the Constitutional Tribunal found unconstitutional the Petty Offence Code provision punishing denial of goods and services without just cause after the Supreme Court in 2018 had found a Łódź printer acted illegally refusing banners for an LGBT group. Gay and bisexual men are allowed to donate blood after the 2005 Ministry of Health replaced risk groups with risk behaviours, and gays and bisexuals are allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces since the 1990s with discrimination officially forbidden though an unwritten don't ask, don't tell persists. Same-sex couples are unable to legally adopt and lesbian couples do not have access to IVF, with a July 2020 presidential proposal for a constitutional ban on adoption by same-sex relationships and a March 2021 government announcement to ban adoption by same-sex couples including vetting single applicants for same-sex cohabitation, although in October 2018 the Supreme Administrative Court allowed a lesbian couple to register their 4-year-old boy. In February 2019 MPs submitted a draft bill to ban using, promoting or advertising gay conversion therapy, while in August 2020 the Episcopal Conference recommended counseling centres to help regain natural sexual orientation and dismissed scientific consensus on ineffectiveness and harm as political correctness. On 20 July 2019 the first Equality March in Białystok with about 800 marchers was confronted by more than 4,000 counter-protesters throwing stones, bricks, firecrackers, flash bombs, rotten eggs and bottles filled with urine, requiring heavy riot police intervention to prevent mass casualties.

In February 2025 Poland's Supreme Court ruled that a non-binary casino dealer in Wroclaw dismissed in 2021 for refusing female appearance rules requiring make-up, skirts and high heels had suffered gender-based discrimination, the first explicit recognition under Polish law that non-binary persons can face gender discrimination; Penal Code amendments adopted by parliament in March 2025 and approved by the government in November 2024 to extend hate-crime and hate-speech protection to sexual orientation, gender, age and disability were referred to the Constitutional Tribunal by President Andrzej Duda in April 2025 and ruled unconstitutional on 30 September 2025, so the extended protections including gender never entered into force.

Poland's existing hate-crime law punishes bias-motivated violence, threats, insults and promotion of hateful ideologies only for national, ethnic, racial, political or religious affiliation and not for sexual orientation, sex/gender or gender identity, and after parliament passed the 6 March 2025 amendment adding sexual orientation and sex/gender with up to three years' imprisonment for insulting or inciting hatred, President Andrzej Duda on 17 April 2025 declined to sign it and referred it for preventive constitutional review on free-expression grounds, leaving it not in force.

On 6 February 2024 the Warsaw Voivodeship Administrative Court annulled the March 2019 Mordy commune resolution against "LGBT ideology", removing the last explicit anti-LGBT resolution from legal circulation in Poland, after administrative courts including the Supreme Administrative Court in June 2022 held such resolutions exceeded council powers, grossly breached the Polish Constitution, and violated dignity, honour, reputation and private life of LGBT+ residents through exclusion and stigmatisation, while 11 similar discriminatory acts remained in force including 10 Ordo Iuris Family Rights Charters promoting Catholic family and education models in Tatrzanski, Lancucki and Debicki counties, Gromadka, Odrzywol, Skierniewice and Jedlnia-Letnisko communes and Radzyn Podlaski, Debica, Rypin and Wielun cities, with most other councils having repealed under EU partnership conditionality barring EU support to authorities contributing to segregation or exclusion.
