Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, 'Ley para la protección de la salud y el bienestar de los menores de edad en Puerto Rico' (primary legal text, LexJuris). Article 4 — the operative prohibition — is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments altering the sex biology of a minor 'bajo el pretexto de una transición de género o como parte de un tratamiento de disforia de género'. The Article 3 definition of banned 'chemical and surgical mutilation' is drafted broader than the prohibition: it expressly includes 'el uso de bloqueadores de pubertad y hormonas sexuales (incluyendo bloqueadores androgénicos, estrógenos, progesterona o testosterona) utilizados con el propósito de tratar la disforia de género' — the USE itself of puberty blockers and sex hormones for gender-dysphoria treatment — and defines 'niño o menor de edad' as any person under 21. Article 6 then penalises 'toda persona que viole las disposiciones de esta Ley' with a fixed 15-year term, plus permanent licence loss for professionals and a $50,000 per-violation fine for juridical persons. Legal analysis of this drafting notes a structural tension: the definition speaks of patient 'use' while the operative clause restricts only providers, and the penalty catch-all says 'any person'. Under standard criminal doctrines (definitions create no offence by themselves; a protected class cannot be prosecuted as the perpetrator of its own victimisation; the principle of legality bars analogy; and travel with lawfully prescribed personal medication), a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own prescribed hormones — or of their parents for enabling it — would almost certainly fail, and the statute is a textbook void-for-vagueness candidate. But the textual ambiguity is precisely what legal advocates flag as its chilling effect: it leaves interpretive room for hostile officials to question, detain or investigate trans youth and their families on the ground, with the answer coming only after the fact. For a travelling under-21 trans person the practical reading is: carrying and using prescribed HRT in Puerto Rico sits inside the law's literal definition of banned practice, enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. The ACLU of Puerto Rico had urged a veto before signature, stating the bill 'criminalizes doctors and parents' and creates 'two distinct categories of children' divided by sex-assigned-at-birth identity, and the island's College of Physicians and Surgeons, Psychology Association, College of Social Work Professionals, Bar Association and LGBTQ+ Federation all registered opposition.

Washington Blade (26 Apr 2019): Gov. Rossello announced SB1253 ('clarify religious freedom principles') and SB1254 (conversion-therapy ban with pastoral exemption); LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pair would open discrimination doors, criticizing the religious-freedom carve-out as license to refuse service on orientation/gender-identity grounds.

Washington Blade (25 Jun 2014): four same-sex couples joined the federal marriage lawsuit in PR (filed March; Ada Conde Vidal case), with Lambda Legal and PR Para Todas intervening - one couple married in Canada 2007, another in New York 2012; former National Guard member among plaintiffs. Road to marriage equality in PR ran through federal court.

Washington Blade (18 Mar 2019): the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the PR House blocked a floor vote on SB1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors; Sen. Zoe Laboy (co-sponsor) dissented publicly. Conversion-therapy ban died in the House despite Senate passage and governor support.

Washington Blade (13 Jun 2019): Gov. Rossello asked lawmakers to withdraw SB1253/SB1254 amid sustained opposition; his April announcement had included a pastoral-capacity exemption for clergy in the conversion-therapy ban. Record of LGBT advocates defeating the religious-freedom bill pairing.

Erin in the Morning (2025): PR enacted a trans youth care ban pushed through non-public hearings; law is deliberately vague so doctors and affirming parents facilitating HRT or top surgery risk prosecution; mandates Education/Health department campaigns on 'risks' of trans-affirming care; Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments allowing puberty blockers and continuation of existing HRT, but the enacted text is the most extreme care restriction in US jurisdictions per the report. For a trans visitor the ban closes off all gender-affirming care on the island for anyone under 21, and the deliberately vague facilitation language reaches the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager.

Executive Order 14168 (signed 20 January 2025) directs US federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognize only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order violates the Prison Rape Elimination Act's requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided on an individual safety assessment. Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico as a US territory. No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit, or ruling was located.

Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002, but after the U.S. Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down all state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for it, and threatened doctors who violate the ban with up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine, and permanent loss of their licenses; the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court. An anti-discrimination bill (House Bill 1725) passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, public transportation and public facilities, business transactions and housing, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities remain uncovered. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 bill was withdrawn by Rosselló on 13 June 2019 after House approval amid protests. Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the U.S. federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island. In 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488 (signed 29 May 2013) extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

The ACLU of Puerto Rico called on Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, 'which criminalizes doctors and parents and aims to prohibit gender-affirming medical treatments for individuals under the age of 21'. Policy Counsel Lolimar Escudero Rodríguez stated the bill 'creates two distinct categories of children: one that allows parents to access and authorize treatments if the child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth, and another that prohibits parents the same right if their child's identity is different'. The release records that the bill was authored by Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz and Senator Joanne Rodríguez Veve, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés that the ACLU warned 'do not remedy the violation of fundamental constitutional, civil, and human rights', and was re-approved and returned to the Governor on 28 June. It states the bill's 'text is clearly and exclusively aimed at minors whose identity does not correspond to the sex assigned to them at birth' and that it disregards the specialist consultation process that precedes parents authorising puberty blockers or hormonal treatments, 'and instead, criminalizes them'. Executive Director Annette Martínez Orabona: the measure 'directly discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth, whose very lives may be at risk'. The release lists local opposition from the Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico.

The ACLU of Puerto Rico opposed Senate Bill 350 'because of its direct impact on access to gender-affirming care for trans people, particularly trans youth and trans children, as well as on the rights of families and minors. The measure bans gender-affirming medical treatments for people under 21 years of age.'

AP reported that Puerto Rico's governor signed a bill prohibiting hormone therapy or gender-affirming surgeries for transgender youth, a move that 'has drawn sharp criticism from activists in the largely conservative U.S. territory'. The law applies to those younger than 21 and calls for 15 years in prison for violators, a $50,000 penalty, and revocation of the licences and permits of medical staff.
Amnesty International's Puerto Rico reporting records that 'In July, the government signed Law 63-2025, prohibiting gender-affirming health care for people under the age of 21.'

JURIST reported that Puerto Rico's LGBTQ+ Federation denounced the Law for the Protection of the Health and Wellbeing of Minors in Puerto Rico, which 'prohibits the use of puberty blockers, hormone treatment, and gender-affirming surgeries for anybody under the age of 21' and 'imposes a sentence of up to 15 years and a $50,000 fine on offenders'.

The 2025 minors' wellbeing law (primary legal text). Article 4 - the operative prohibition - is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments that alter sex biology under the pretext of gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment; article 3 defines the banned practice more broadly, naming puberty blockers and sex hormones for gender dysphoria, with the protected class at anyone under 21.

A rights news outlet (April 2019): the governor announced a bill to 'clarify religious freedom principles' and a conversion-therapy ban with a pastoral exemption; an LGBT council president and allies said the pair would open discrimination doors; in June 2019 the governor asked lawmakers to withdraw both measures amid sustained opposition.

A rights news outlet (June 2014): four same-sex couples joined the federal marriage lawsuit (filed March; a named federal case), with a legal-aid organisation and a local campaign group intervening - one couple married abroad in 2007, another on the mainland in 2012; a former territorial guard member among plaintiffs.

A rights news outlet (March 2019): the pro-statehood caucus in the lower chamber blocked a floor vote on a bill that would have banned conversion therapy for minors; a co-sponsor senator dissented publicly; the ban died in the chamber despite senate passage and governor support.

A newsletter (2025): the territory enacted a youth care ban pushed through non-public hearings; the law is deliberately vague so doctors and affirming parents facilitating hormone treatment or surgery risk prosecution; it mandates education and health department campaigns on 'risks' of trans-affirming care; the health secretary's proposed amendments would have allowed puberty blockers and continuation of existing hormone treatment.
A rights organisation's territory reporting records that in July the government signed the 2025 law prohibiting gender-affirming health care for people under the age of 21.

A legal news outlet: the territory's LGBT federation denounced the minors' wellbeing law, which prohibits puberty blockers, hormone treatment and gender-affirming surgeries for anybody under the age of 21, and announced plans to challenge it in court.

A wire report: the governor signed a bill prohibiting hormone therapy or gender-affirming surgeries for transgender youth, a move criticised by activists; the law applies to those younger than 21; opposition was registered by several professional associations and the LGBT federation.

Outright International country page (updated 12 Mar 2026): DPRK Criminal Code (1950, rev. 2009) appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts, but Art. 193 bans import/keeping/distribution of 'decadent culture' incl. sexual recordings and Art. 262 bans collective 'obscene activities'; 2014 KCNA denied homosexuality's existence; an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017; no documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people; no registration route for LGBTI orgs.

Legal Clarity overview: sex-marker change on birth certificate/citizen card technically possible under 'unavoidable circumstances' - application to People's Security Agency plus state forensic medical evaluation, in practice requiring surgical intervention; no law explicitly bans gender-affirming care but the under-resourced health system makes hormones/surgery effectively inaccessible.

BBC Korean feature (10 Oct 2024), 'Does homosexuality exist in North Korea too?': 10 years after the UN COI report, new laws (Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act etc.) tighten control; profiles Jang Young-jin, a novelist who defected in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed, as the first publicly known gay defector; documents how a collective-over-individual regime forces DPRK sexual minorities into silent self-suppression and frames LGBT life as human-rights abuse.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for North Korea: official assessment - the totalitarian regime's pervasive abuses; the report notes no specific law criminalising same-sex conduct but the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life.

US State Department 2020 Human Rights Report for North Korea: official assessment - no reliable information on LGBT persons; the regime's repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality.
CNN, Apr 2017: 'I could not even dream: Life as a gay North Korean' records a defector's account of homosexuality's place in North Korean society and of the punishment it carries.

KCNA commentary (22 Apr 2014): state news agency rejects the UN Commission of Inquiry's DPRK human rights report as a political fabrication and personally attacks commissioner Michael Kirby as 'a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality' to discredit it - official-record evidence of the regime's hostility toward homosexuality even while denying its existence.

A 2023 South Korean Ministry of Unification report (the 584-page 'North Korean Human Rights Report') cites defector testimony alleging that at least one male detainee in a detention camp was secretly executed for homosexuality in 2014. A 2011 Korea Times report, sourced to Free North Korea Radio, claimed North Korea executed a lesbian couple, a North Korean woman and a Japanese woman, for being influenced by capitalism and 'bringing corruption of public morals'. The United States Department of State states that no provisions exist in North Korean law to prohibit discrimination on sexual orientation or identity and that the concepts do not appear. The Constitution, last revised 2024, does not explicitly address discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. As of 2026 no North Korean law recognizes same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships: Article 8 of the Family Law of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea states that 'Marriage may be done only between one man and one woman'. Per the same department's 2020 report, same-sex couples could not legally adopt children in North Korea.

An international advocacy organisation's country page (updated 12 Mar 2026): the criminal code (1950, revised 2009) appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts, but one article bans the import, keeping or distribution of 'decadent culture' including sexual recordings and another bans collective 'obscene activities'; the official news agency denied homosexuality's existence in 2014; an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017; no documented violence against LGBTIQ people by the government or by other actors is recorded, and no registration route exists for LGBTI organisations.

A legal-information overview: sex-marker changes on birth certificates or citizen cards are technically possible under 'unavoidable circumstances' — application to a security agency plus a government forensic medical evaluation, in practice requiring surgical intervention; no law explicitly bans gender-affirming care, but the under-resourced health system makes hormones and surgery effectively inaccessible.

A broadcaster's feature in the local language (10 Oct 2024): in the decade after an international human-rights inquiry's report, new laws including a cultural protection act tightened control; it profiles a novelist who defected in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed, described as the first publicly known gay defector, and documents how the regime forces sexual minorities into silent self-suppression and frames LGBT life as a human-rights abuse.
A national government human-rights report (2022): official assessment — the regime's pervasive abuses leave no space for LGBT life even though no specific law criminalises same-sex conduct.
A national government human-rights report (2020): official assessment — no reliable information on LGBT persons exists, and the regime's repression of all civil society is the dominant reality.

A news report (Apr 2017): a defector's first-person account of the place of homosexuality in the country's society and of its punishment, and of a life in which the person could not even dream openly.

The official news agency's commentary (22 Apr 2014): the agency rejects an international human-rights inquiry's report on the country as a political fabrication and personally attacks one of the inquiry's commissioners with a slur about a decades-long record of homosexuality — official-record evidence of regime hostility toward homosexuality even while its existence is denied.

ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map 2026: Portugal drops one place to 12th at 67%; no affirmative legislation since the 2024 conversion-practices ban, while a new draft bill threatens legal gender recognition based on self-determination and the ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children. No score 67% below Malta/Iceland/Belgium but above most of Europe.
Público (March 2026, in Portuguese): the Portuguese Parliament (AR) approved PSD, Chega and CDS bills reversing the gender-identity law - first vote to roll back self-ID legal gender recognition.

Observador (Mar 2026): parliament debates rolling back the gender-identity regime; psychologists' order and trans groups call it 'retrocesso'; socialists invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta (trans woman killed by youths in Porto) against the rollback, drawing protests from Chega's Hugo Soares. Documents the political fight around the three roll-back bills.

Joint statement: IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal warn three bills debated 19 March, voted 20 March 2026 would seriously attack trans/intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition; if adopted Portugal would lose at least 4 Rainbow Map places, dropping below Sweden, Netherlands, Ireland and France - regression from a European reference point.

Forbidden Colours (20 Mar 2026): Parliament passed the roll-back proposals 124 to 79 (backed by Chega, governing PSD and CDS-PP), sending them to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees; the proposals directly target Portugal's 2018 self-identification law. Called a dangerous turning point for fundamental rights.

KET Brussels (26 Mar 2026): in first reading Parliament backed reintroducing a mandatory medical opinion for any legal gender and name change, undoing the 2018 reform that allowed self-declaration from age 16; human rights groups say it is dismantling the self-determination law.

TVI/IOL: committee-stage analysis (CIG) of the bills warns they worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people and defends schools' existing discrimination-prevention duties; Bloco de Esquerda bill assessed as compatible with school human-rights obligations. Legislative-process detail on the roll-back package.

The Portugal Brief (16 Aug 2026): Justice Ministry data show legal sex/name changes climbing back toward the two-years-prior high-water mark, most in Lisbon (per Expresso) - even as Parliament advances bills to reimpose the medical requirement the 2018 self-determination law scrapped. Uptick before the expected tightening.

European Parliament written question E-001183/2026 (2026), 'Health and safety of transgender people in Portugal'. An MEP questions the Commission on the repeal process for the 2018 gender self-determination law and its health-and-safety impact on trans people.

OSCE hate-crime legislation portal, Portugal: Penal Code makes sexual orientation and gender identity/explicit grounds for aggravated offences - Art. 132/144/145 aggravation when crime determined by hatred on those grounds (aggravated assault up to 4 years), plus 1-8 year penalties for organising discrimination on those grounds or genocide-denial-style apology. Legal framework reference.

Equaldex data for Portugal: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, gender-affirming care legal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. High public support for same-sex parenting (ranked #1 of 30 EU regions).

Provedoria da Justica (Ombudsman): requests constitutional review of Penal Code Article 176-C, which establishes the crime of acts contrary to sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression - the institutional watchdog questioning the hate-speech provision itself.

Portugal's Parliament formally adopted 17 May as the National Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia in 2015, committing to national and international obligations to combat such discrimination. Three draft bills given preliminary approval on 20 March 2026 by a 151-79 vote would ban the inclusion of 'gender ideology' in school curricula, and hundreds protested outside the Assembly against them. Annual pride parades in Lisbon and Porto attract thousands of participants and spectators, and Lisbon hosts Queer Lisboa, one of Europe's largest LGBT film festivals. In 1999 the European Court of Human Rights fined Portugal after a domestic court made homophobic statements in ruling against a gay father's custody of his daughter; the ECHR ruled in the father's favour and ordered custody returned to him. Same-sex couples were barred from adopting and informally forbidden from fostering children until adoption rights took effect on 1 March 2016, after a presidential veto was overridden by Parliament.

This country drops one place on a regional rights map; no affirmative legislation since the 2024 conversion-practices ban, while a new draft bill threatens legal gender recognition based on self-determination and the ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children.
In March 2026: the national parliament approved bills reversing the gender-identity law — the first vote to roll back self-ID legal gender recognition.

Mar 2026: parliament debated rolling back the gender-identity regime; psychologists' and trans groups said it was a regression; a 2006 murder of a trans woman by youths was invoked against the rollback. Documents the political fight around the three roll-back bills.

Joint statement of regional organisations: three bills debated and voted in March 2026 would seriously attack trans and intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition; if adopted the country would lose some places on the regional rights map — a regression from a reference point.

Mar 2026: parliament passed the roll-back proposals 124 to 79 (backed by the government and the far right), sending them to a rights committee; the proposals directly target its 2018 self-identification law.

Mar 2026: in first reading parliament backed reintroducing a mandatory medical opinion for any legal gender and name change, undoing the 2018 reform that allowed self-declaration from age 16; human rights groups say it is dismantling the self-determination law.

Committee-stage analysis of the bills warns they worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people and defends schools' existing discrimination-prevention duties; one bill was assessed as compatible with school human-rights obligations.

In 2026: justice ministry data show legal sex and name changes climbing back toward the prior high-water mark — even as parliament advances bills to reimpose the medical requirement the 2018 self-determination law scrapped; an uptick before the expected tightening.

A 2026 written question on the health and safety of transgender people in this country, on the repeal process for the 2018 gender self-determination law and its health-and-safety impact on trans people.

Official hate-crime legislation portal: the penal code makes sexual orientation and gender identity explicit grounds for aggravated offences — aggravation when a crime is determined by hatred on those grounds (aggravated assault up to 4 years), plus 1-8 year penalties for organising discrimination on those grounds or genocide-denial-style apology.

Regional data: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, gender-affirming care legal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation and gender identity, discrimination illegal, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. High public support for same-sex parenting.

The national ombudsman requests a constitutional review of a penal code provision establishing the crime of acts contrary to sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression — the institutional watchdog questioning the hate-speech provision itself.

AP (Sep 2025): 'For Paraguay's transgender women, survival often means leaving home' — discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of hometowns into migration and sex work.

Amnesty International Paraguay page (2025-26): trans people face obstacles to legal identity-document recognition - two trans migrants were denied identity documents; Asuncion's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March; plus 37 registered feminicides in 2025 and April's bill to merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family.

ecoi / US State Dept reporting: judiciary had yet to issue final rulings on 10 lawsuits filed by trans people for legal name recognition - plaintiffs Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepulveda (suits since 2016) awaited a UN Human Rights Committee decision on their ICCPR Optional Protocol communications. Documented pace of recognition litigation.

PinkNews (20 Oct 2017): political climate report - ruling-party figure Horacio Cartes said he would 'shoot himself in the testicles' if his son married another man (later apologised to those offended); frames the report's account of a push to burn books not promoting 'traditional gender ideology'. Elite-level anti-LGBT rhetoric.

Tico Times (10 Jan 2018): the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' advisory opinion holds that OAS signatories must allow same-sex marriage. Paraguay is an OAS party and therefore bound by the ruling, while Bolivian, Paraguayan and Peruvian law recognise neither same-sex marriage nor unions, leaving local law lagging behind the opinion. About 300 Costa Ricans celebrated the opinion at the court.

ABC Color (30 May 2017): adoption analysis - Law 1136/97 does not explicitly bar same-sex couples or singles from adopting (prohibitions cover only infectious disease, mental disorders or child-abuse records), a legal gap allowing same-sex adoption as couples or as single men/women, amid a society that still closes doors. Adoption-law reality check.

Ultima Hora: post-IACtHR ruling analysis says people in Paraguay must overcome difficulties adapting the country's laws to extend the right to marriage to everyone - the domestic-law gap the inter-American opinion leaves for Paraguay to close.

During the Stroessner dictatorship (1954-1989) LGBT people faced heavy persecution. In the 1959 Caso 108, police arrested and tortured 108 gay men in Asunción and made their names public, and the government publicly encouraged hatred and violence against LGBT people. Violence and discrimination against LGBT community members remain frequent in Paraguay today and are often ignored by the police. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Paraguay since 1990, though the age of consent is 16 for homosexuals and 14 for heterosexuals. There is no broad anti-discrimination law, and a November 2015 bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced since introduction. Limited protections exist in specific contexts: Law 5162/2014 requires that collective dormitory placement for adolescents take into account age, sexual orientation and degree of psychic development; Decree 6973 under Law 577/2016 protects women from violence without discrimination based on sexual orientation; Law 6149/2018 bars discrimination against stateless persons based on sexual orientation and gender identity; Law 6534/2020 treats sexual orientation data as sensitive personal data; Article 28 of the Ministry of Public Defense internal rules prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation against employees. In October 2017 the Government of Paraguay implemented a ban on discussion of LGBT issues within public schools, and the Minister of Education said it might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Transgender people are not allowed to legally change their name and gender on official documents, though in December 2016 two transgender women filed a lawsuit to change their names citing constitutional free expression and identity provisions. In October 2016 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare approved Resolution 695 requiring that all transgender people may use their social name on medical records, medical history and forms, and that health service officials must treat transgender patients using their identified social name. Law 7018 on Mental Health (enacted 15 November 2022) states that a mental health diagnosis cannot be made on the exclusive basis of sexual choice or identity.

Transgender people are not allowed to legally change their name and gender on official documents. A 1993 Civil Court case seeking registration of Ramon Fidel, who had undergone gender reassignment surgery, as a woman did not result in a decision because Fidel died in a traffic accident before it was decided. In December 2016 two transgender women, Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepulveda, filed a lawsuit to change their names invoking Article 25 of the Constitution on free expression and free construction of identity and Article 42 of the Civil Code allowing change of first name. In October 2016 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare approved Resolution 695 providing that all transgender people may use their social name on medical records, medical history and forms and requiring officials in Integrated Networks of Health Services (RIISS) to assist and treat transgender patients using the social name with which they identify. Specific non-discrimination provisions expressly covering gender identity include Article 9 of Law 6149/2018 on Protection and Facilities for Naturalization of Stateless Persons, while a November 2015 bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced. Law 7018 on Mental Health enacted November 15, 2022 provides in Article 3 that in no case can a diagnosis be made in mental health on the exclusive basis of sexual choice or identity. In October 2017 the Government implemented a ban on discussion of LGBT issues within public schools, with the Minister of Education stating consideration of burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1990, with age of consent set at 16 for homosexuals and 14 for heterosexuals. Since 1992 the Constitution limits marriage, de facto unions and the family to one man and one woman under Articles 49, 50, 51 and 52, and Article 140 of the Civil Code expressly prohibits marriage between persons of the same sex. An 8 January 2018 advisory opinion of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights stated that states party to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family registration systems including marriage, and a lawsuit relying on that opinion to recognize same-sex marriage remains pending. Under the Adoption Law Ley 1136 de 1997 in force since 1997, single persons of any sex may adopt regardless of marital status, with equal preference given to opposite-sex marriages and de facto unions and single women. There is no broad anti-discrimination law, but limited protections based on sexual orientation exist including Article 274 of Law 5162/2014 Criminal Enforcement Code requiring consideration of sexual orientation with age and psychic development when housing adolescents in collective dormitories, Decree 6973 regulating Law 577/2016 protecting women in situations of violence without discrimination based on sexual orientation, and Article 28 of the Internal Rules of the Ministry of Public Defense prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination against employees. There is no official prohibition preventing entry of gays, lesbians and bisexuals into the Armed Forces and National Police, after the Chamber of Deputies in June 2010 rejected by 42 votes against and 4 in favor a bill that would have prohibited entry of homosexuals into the Public Force. During the dictatorship of Alfredo Stroessner from 1954 to 1989 LGBT people faced heavy persecution including the 1 September 1959 Case 108 in which 108 gay men blamed for a fire in Asuncion were arrested, tortured and publicly named. The article describes Paraguay as one of South America's most conservative countries where reports of violence and discrimination against members of the LGBT community generally are frequent and often ignored by police. It attributes influence to the Catholic Church, which retains strong influence and presence and has strongly opposed measures to improve LGBT lives, alongside a recent rise in religious fundamentalism causing concern among LGBT advocacy groups. It states general population attitudes toward same-sex marriage and LGBT rights remain low compared to other South American countries, especially Argentina and Brazil, citing 15% support for same-sex marriage with 81% opposed in a Pew survey conducted 26 November 2013 to 8 January 2014 and 26% support in the 2017 AmericasBarometer. It notes LGBT groups have organised pride parades in Asuncion since 2004. These violence, church-influence, attitude and polling statements refer to LGBT people or same-sex marriage generally and are not stated as transgender-specific findings. The only transgender-specific tolerance statement documented is the Minister of Education's statement in connection with the October 2017 ban on discussion of LGBT issues in public schools that "it might even consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people."
In October 2016 Paraguay's Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare Resolution 695 established that trans persons may use their social name in clinics.

Paraguay's Law No. 7018 on Mental Health of 15 November 2022 establishes in Article 3 that mental-health care is governed by non-discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity and that in no case may a mental-health diagnosis be made solely on the basis of sexual choice, sexual orientation, or gender identity.

A news report (Sep 2025): for this nation's transgender women, survival often means leaving home — discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of hometowns into migration and sex work.

An international rights organisation's country page (2025-26): trans people face obstacles to legal identity-document recognition — two trans migrants were denied identity documents; an event honouring a trans rights defender who died in March was banned; plus dozens of registered feminicides in 2025 and an April bill to merge the women's ministry into a family ministry.

A reporting service used for asylum decisions: the judiciary had yet to issue final rulings on ten lawsuits filed by trans people for legal name recognition — the plaintiffs (suits since 2016) awaited a decision from an international human-rights committee on their communications.

A news report (20 Oct 2017): a ruling-party figure made reported crude anti-gay remarks about his son marrying another man (he later apologised); the report frames a push to burn books that do not promote 'traditional gender ideology'.

A regional news report (10 Jan 2018): a regional rights court advisory opinion holds that signatory states must allow same-sex marriage; notes that this nation and two neighbouring states recognise neither same-sex marriage nor unions — the ruling binds this nation as a party though local law lagged.

A national news report (30 May 2017): adoption analysis — the adoption statute does not explicitly bar same-sex couples or single people from adopting, a legal gap allowing same-sex adoption amid a society that still resists.
A national news analysis: after the regional rights court ruling, people in this nation must overcome difficulties adapting the laws to extend the right to marriage to everyone.

texts.cleaned_text: CAIRO 51: Gaza's British Mandate Criminal Code Ordinance No. 74 of 1936 remains in force, silent on trans identities but catching trans people under public-morality provisions, while the West Bank operates under a different penal code. The page advances a pinkwashing critique: the occupation marginalises queer and trans Palestinians alongside everyone else, documenting de facto oppression.

West Bank criminal law derives from the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960. Jordan's 1951 revision dropped consensual private-sex offences and the 1960 code carried that forward. Social and family persecution makes the practical reality harsher than the formal law.

Wikipedia LGBT rights in Palestine: patchwork decriminalisation (British Mandate code in Jordan until 1951; Jordanian Penal Code no prohibition of same-sex acts applied to the West Bank; Israel stopped using the code in 1977); PA has not legislated; no explicit prohibition on trans identity; periodic transphobic threats/attacks; PA a non-signatory to key treaties.

exact_spans: Regional movement context for Palestinian LGBT life.
texts.cleaned_text: HRW 'Audacity of Adversity' (16 Apr 2018): LGBT people across MENA finding ways to speak out - stories, cross-border alliances, national/regional movements combating homophobia and transphobia; accompanies AFE video series of activist messages of support.

Times of Israel: rights groups slammed Palestinian police for banning LGBTQ activity - after the police action against al-Qaws, the foundation received a wave of hate messages which activists said 'pose a serious threat' to the gay community.

HRW (11 Jun 2018), Women's Centre for Legal Aid: interviewed 12 Palestinian women identifying as lesbian/bisexual/queer - widespread discrimination and abuse in public and family settings; Gaza's 1936 Criminal Code s.152(2) punishes consensual same-sex 'carnal knowledge' by up to 10 years (vague 'unnatural offences' concepts violate privacy/non-discrimination per HRW); 1960 West Bank code analysed similarly.

Times of Israel: Israel to allow LGBT Palestinians granted temporary asylum to work - some 90 LGBT Palestinians have received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence in the territories.

Palestinian law is a patchwork of Ottoman, British, Jordanian, Egyptian and Israeli legacies, and the Palestinian Authority has legislated neither for nor against homosexuality. Applicability of the British Mandate Criminal Code (1936), which criminalised sodomy with up to 14 years' imprisonment and 'act against the law of nature' with up to 10 years, is disputed: the Human Dignity Trust and Human Rights Watch hold it in force in Gaza, Amnesty does not report same-sex acts as illegal, and editor-in-chief Anis F. Kassim argues it could be read as permitting homosexuality. The 2003 draft Palestinian penal code criminalised adult consensual same-sex conduct, carrying up to five years for male-male sodomy, and it is unknown whether it was implemented. Equaldex reports no broad legal protections from discrimination for LGBTIQ+ people in Palestine, no legal gender recognition provisions are set out, Palestinian queer organisations operate from within Israel, and statelessness is cited as a structural condition of LGBTQ Palestinians.

HIV prevention and care are described as inadequate: HIV-positive queer individuals often do not receive continuous antiretroviral therapy because medication is limited and social stigma is high, and comprehensive epidemiological surveillance is lacking. Only 98 HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered in Palestine between 1988 and 2017 (79 AIDS, 19 HIV-positive), with the true number likely far higher because taboos hinder data collection. In Gaza since October 2023, collapse of the healthcare system plus Israeli blockades has made access to life-saving HIV medication especially difficult. In Israel, LGBTQ Palestinian asylum seekers are routinely excluded from basic healthcare programs and shelter access available to other asylum seekers, and some have faced house arrest or deportation; only in June 2022 did Israel begin issuing work permits to gay Palestinian refugees granted asylum and those fleeing domestic violence.

Section 152(1)(c) of the British Mandate Criminal Code is the only youth-linked legal provision cited, under which sodomy with a child under sixteen carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, alongside Section 152(2)(b) criminalizing 'carnal knowledge' against the law of nature with up to 10 years. Islamist actors contest LGBTQ content in education and youth spaces: the Palestinian Mujahideen Movement and the Rightly-Guided Caliphs Assembly criticized UNRWA for promoting what they see as un-Islamic values including LGBTQ issues, and the Islamic Movement in Israel opposed Israel's conversion therapy ban, with activist Maisan Hamdan noting that the movement's sole stated aim is Palestine's liberation without LGBTQ inclusion. Public acceptance is ranked Palestine 130 on the Global Acceptance Index with very little change 2010–2020, and civil society groups protecting women and children are 'vulnerable to attack' in Gaza.

Gay Palestinians are often arrested and tortured. According to Shaul Ganon of the Israeli-based gay rights group Aguda, the PA's usual excuse for persecuting gays is to label them collaborators. Ganon states knowledge of two cases in the last three years where people were tried explicitly for being homosexuals. Ganon states that since the intifada, when police increasingly began enforcing Islamic law, it is impossible to be an open gay in the PA. Part of the problem is that gay Palestinians are blackmailed into working as informants by Israeli security services.

A country page of an advocacy organisation: the two parts of the nation run under different penal codes — the code inherited from the historic administration, dated 1936, is still in force in one part and is silent on trans identities, but trans people can be caught by public-morality provisions; a critique warns that the occupation marginalises queer and trans people alongside everyone else; de facto oppression is documented.

A legal-information page: the criminal law in one part derives from a 1960 penal code that carried forward a 1951 revision which dropped consensual-private-sex offences; practical reality is harsher than formal law because of social and family persecution.

A community encyclopedia entry: decriminalisation is a patchwork — the historic-era code applied in one region until 1951, a later code without any same-sex prohibition applied in the other part, and the neighbouring nation stopped using that code in 1977; the national authority has not legislated, there is no explicit prohibition on trans identity, periodic transphobic threats and attacks are reported, and the national authority has not signed key treaties.

texts.cleaned_text: A report of a monitoring organisation (16 Apr 2018): LGBT people across the wider region are finding ways to speak out — personal stories, cross-border alliances, and national and regional movements combatting homophobia and transphobia;

A news report: rights groups condemned the police for banning LGBTQ activity — after police action against a queer organisation, the organisation received a wave of hate messages that activists called a serious threat to the gay community.

A report of a monitoring organisation (11 Jun 2018) prepared with a local legal-aid centre: women identifying as lesbian, bisexual or queer were interviewed and reported widespread discrimination and abuse in public and family settings; a historic-era code provision punishing consensual same-sex acts by up to 10 years, and the 1960 code used in the other part, were analysed as violating privacy and non-discrimination.

A news report: the neighbouring nation will allow LGBT people granted temporary asylum to work — nearly a hundred LGBT people have received temporary permits to seek refuge there after fleeing violence in the nation.

BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018): in France, detention follows the gender marked on an ID, and Article D248 requires separate men's and women's establishments, so trans women holding male markers are held with men. The article treats this as a legal grey area. France's framework governs French Polynesia as an overseas collectivity subject to French law.

CGLPL opinion (25 May 2021) on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: since France's Law 2016-1547 civil-status gender change no longer requires medical transition/surgery, yet no norms were added on how to house detainees accordingly - serious violations persist across French detention. French-framework treatment applicable in French Polynesia's prisons.

Grokipedia entry on trans rights in Tahiti: gender-diverse care is limited by local expertise, and some trans people (raerae) face family rejection and move to mainland France for specialised services. The mahu is a traditional Polynesian social role in which mahu embody both male and female qualities and hold cultural standing.

OutTraveler (4 Jul 2025): 'French Polynesia doesn't need Pride flags' describes openness as ingrained in the culture, with mahu and rae-rae visible in daily life across the 118 islands. A visiting gay couple reports first checking whether the destination is safe, and describes mainstream LGBTQ+ inclusivity and acceptance without Pride displays.

RNZ Pacific: French Polynesia LGBTQIA reflection - churches round table with University of French Polynesia; Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua's government tabled a social-security Bill to fully reimburse hormonal treatment (progesterone/testosterone) like mainland France, but after heated Territorial Assembly debate the Bill failed to gain sufficient support. Concrete care-access reform failed.

Out Adventures presents Tahiti and Bora Bora across the 118 islands as a relaxed, gay-welcoming South Pacific culture. The assessment is travel-oriented and reports no trans-specific finding for French Polynesia.

French national law, drawn from Wikipedia country coverage, with no stated bearing on French Polynesia: sodomy provisions were repealed by the Penal Code of 1791 and the Penal Code of 1810 retained that silence; an indecent-exposure clause (article 330, 2nd alinea) inserted in 1960 by the Mirguet amendment doubled penalties where the act was homosexual and was repealed in 1980, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under it, with the Senate yet to vote. A Vichy law of 6 August 1942 set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 in 1982; LGBTQ people in Alsace and Lorraine were interned in Nazi camps after 1940. The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, punishable by up to €45,000 and/or 12 months' imprisonment, criticised by Reporters Without Borders and defended by the Chirac government; Christian Vanneste was convicted under it in January 2006 and that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Sexual orientation became a protected ground in employment and services in 1985, 'sexual identity' was added in July 2012, and on 18 November 2016 'gender identity' replaced it in article 225-1 of the Penal Code, with the Labour Code covering sexual orientation and gender identity in recruitment and training. Assaults motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract heavier penalties, and in 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. The conversion-therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022; Le Refuge estimated 3-4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy. The Académie Nationale de Médecine described the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem'; a March 2024 report commissioned from The Little Mermaid Observatory called gender-affirming care a 'health scandal' and youth transness a 'social contagion', and a bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 without National Assembly action since 23 July 2024. Late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommend puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) date from 1999; same-sex marriage passed the National Assembly 329-229 on 12 February 2013 and was signed on 18 May 2013, with joint adoption rare thereafter and assisted reproduction extended to lesbian couples from September 2021. Schools observe 17 May under the 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign, enrolment forms use 'parent 1' and 'parent 2', and since March 2019 higher education institutions should use trans students' preferred names. Mayotte reports frequent family rejection and discrimination, and in 2014 only about 20% of overseas residents viewed homosexuality as a sexuality like any other, against 77% in metropolitan France.

A feature (January 2018): in the governing state, detention follows the gender marked on an ID, and the criminal procedure code requires separate men's and women's establishments, so trans women holding male markers are held with men; the article treats this as a legal grey area; that state's framework applies in the territory.

The governing state's detention watchdog's opinion (25 May 2021) on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: since that state's 2016 civil-status law gender change no longer requires medical transition, yet no norms were added on how to house detainees accordingly - serious violations persist; the territory's prisons fall under the national detention framework.

An online entry on trans rights in the territory: gender-diverse care is limited by local expertise, and some trans people face family rejection and move to the mainland for specialised services; the mahu is a traditional social role in which mahu embody both male and female qualities with recognised standing.

A travel publication (July 2025): describes the territory's openness as ingrained in the culture, with mahu and rae-rae visible in daily life across the 118 islands; a visiting gay couple reports first checking whether the destination is safe, and describes mainstream inclusivity without pride flags or organised protest.

A public broadcaster: territory LGBTQIA reflection - churches round table with the territory's university; the vice-president's government tabled a social-security bill to fully reimburse hormonal treatment like the mainland, but after debate in the territorial assembly it did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed.
A tour operator presents the territory across its 118 islands as a relaxed, gay-welcoming island culture; the assessment is travel-oriented and reports no trans-specific finding for the territory.

Social-climate evidence, no legal change.

texts.cleaned_text: HRW (24 Oct 2022): security forces arrested and abused LGBT people - six cases of severe repeated beatings and five sexual harassment cases in police custody 2019-2022, arrests in public places based solely on gender expression and unlawful searches; mistreatment as recent as September 2022 as Qatar prepared to host the 2022 World Cup under global scrutiny.

exact_spans: Baseline legal-persecution picture.
texts.cleaned_text: Wikipedia LGBTQ rights in Qatar: same-sex acts illegal (up to 3 years for Muslims and non-Muslims; Sharia allows a capital sentence never imposed); documented beatings/torture and forced 'conversion therapy' by police; cultural norms view homosexuality and cross-dressing harshly.

exact_spans: Social-climate evidence, no legal change.
texts.cleaned_text: PinkNews (20 Jul 2018): taboo around homosexuality - Doha News' 2016 piece by a gay Qatari ('jarring', 'irreparable damage to mental health') drew extreme reactions; Swansea University lecturer on World Cup conduct; pre-tournament climate report.

Qatar's Penal Code Article 296 (Law 11/2004) punishes sodomy with one to three years' imprisonment. It replaced Article 201 of the 1971 code, which had carried up to five years, and before that Article 171 of the 1956 code and the Indian Penal Code imposed through Order in Council in 1938. Sexual acts between males and between females are illegal and punishable by up to three years in prison for Muslims and non-Muslims alike; for Muslims duly convicted in sharia courts a capital sentence remains a theoretical possibility, though never imposed. Trans people may be detained for up to six months without trial or charge on suspicion of "impersonating the opposite gender" or of violating "public morality" and "community protection" provisions. The government does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and cohabitation is itself illegal. Because same-gender couples cannot marry, the local death penalty for same-gender sex is argued to apply only to Muslims through extramarital-sex provisions.

Detentions and prosecutions have targeted visitors and residents. On 4 February 2024 a dual British-Mexican citizen was arrested after police ran a fake Grindr profile; he was held 44 days, interrogated about other gay men, forced to sign documents in Arabic without a translator and denied a lawyer. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention raised concerns about his treatment, and the detainees in that case were denied access to antiretroviral medicines needed to live with HIV, a denial the Working Group also flagged. In 2016 the Polish Instagram star King Luxy spent two months in custody on suspicion of being homosexual. In 1998 an American visitor was sentenced to six months in prison and 90 lashes for homosexual activity. In May 2023 Gilbert Ignatius, a Qatar Airways employee, was detained by Qatar's Criminal Investigation Department over his appearance, with tinted moisturizer, designer clothing and a bag cited as evidence of prostitution; an officer told him "You have no rights. This is Qatar," and struck him when he asked to contact the Indonesian embassy. He was later deported, fired and banned from Qatar without official explanation. Ignatius reported that post-World Cup secret police crackdowns especially target people who appear to be from the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand. In the 1990s the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration told Philippine workers that gay workers were prohibited in Qatar after mass arrests and deportations.

Abuse by police and other authorities against LGBTQ people has included beatings, torture and forced "conversion therapy". An October 2022 Human Rights Watch report alleged systemic police brutality based on eyewitness accounts from 2019 to 2022. A May 2022 account by Naser Mohamed, the first Qatari to publicly come out as gay, described LGBTQ people being held and physically abused, then promised safety from further torture if they agreed to become informants against others. Trans detainees are required to undergo forced physical detransition, including surgical removal of breast tissue, while held, and must attend conversion "therapy" on release, according to BBC-sourced information that Qatari authorities "categorically rejected". The government does not allow people in Qatar to campaign for LGBTQ rights, and in 2022 police arrested protesters who criticised Qatari law.

In 2013 Kuwait proposed banning gay foreigners from entering any Gulf Cooperation Council country and the GCC agreed to discuss it, then backtracked, possibly over concerns about the effect on Qatar's 2022 World Cup hosting. In May 2022 the Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said LGBTQ visitors would be welcomed to the World Cup but must respect the nation's culture, and in 2013 bid chief Hassan Al-Thawadi said all were welcome provided they refrained from public displays of affection. In May 2022 some hotels on FIFA's official recommended accommodation list refused to serve same-sex couples outright, while others accepted them only if they hid their relationship in public; FIFA said it would remind hotels of non-discrimination requirements. The Australian men's national team publicly called in October 2022 for Qatar to recognise same-sex marriage.

Qatar voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity at the Human Rights Council in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025. In 2018 nine articles on gay and transgender rights were censored from the Doha edition of The New York Times International Edition, prompting the Government Communications Office to pledge an investigation. A 2016 Doha News opinion piece by a gay Qatari man writing as "Majid Al-Qatari" drew extremely strong reactions for allowing the topic to be discussed. In June 2019 state-linked AJ+ marked LGBTQ Pride Month, prompting criticism of the paradox with domestic censorship, and in 2022 Transport for London banned Qatari advertising after Qatar moved to block rainbow armbands, with Qatar subsequently reviewing its London investments. Nasser Al Khater said in December 2021 that public display of affection "is frowned upon", and Major General al-Ansari warned that rainbow flags could be confiscated to "protect" fans.

An international human-rights organisation (Oct 2022): security forces arrested and abused LGB people — six cases of severe repeated beatings and five sexual-harassment cases in police custody between 2019 and 2022, with arrests in public places based solely on gender expression and unlawful searches; mistreatment as recent as September 2022 as the country prepared to host the 2022 global sporting event.

An encyclopedia article on LGBTIQ rights in this country: same-sex acts illegal (up to 3 years); a religious-law capital sentence exists but has never been imposed; documented beatings, torture and forced 'conversion therapy' by police; cultural norms view homosexuality and cross-dressing harshly.

An LGBTIQ news outlet (2018): taboo around homosexuality in this country — an essay by a gay citizen drew extreme reactions; commentators on expected conduct during the upcoming global sporting event; no legal change.

texts.cleaned_text: Yagg (19 May 2016, French): the National Assembly adopted amendment 282 — tabled by about forty Socialist deputies — inserting a Civil Code section to facilitate legal gender change for trans people, though the government's three sub-amendments could limit its scope.

In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness by decree, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale. Discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" was banned in 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" in 2016 including amendment of article 225-1 of the Penal Code on 18 November 2016 and protection in the Labour Code, and since 2017 transgender people have been allowed to change legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis. The legal gender-change regime took effect 1 January 2017 after Senate approval 6 November 2015, Assembly approvals 24 May 2016 and 12 July 2016 and 12 October 2016, Constitutional Council ruling of constitutionality 17 November 2016, signature 18 November 2016 and publication the next day, requiring application before a court without psychiatrist certificates or proof of reassignment surgery while first-name change can be done at the registry office. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and a 16 May 2020 report recorded police identification of around 1,870 victims of transphobic and homophobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Gender-affirming surgery within France was legalised in 1979, and a 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine has characterized increased treatment-seeking as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and "primarily social problem" advising extreme caution without changing actual practice, while a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report led to a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under 18 opposed by the Macron government and unlikely to pass the Assembly with no update since 23 July 2024, and in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by a bill passed by the Senate 7 December 2020, concurred by the Assembly 25 January 2022 and published 1 February 2022 with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or 30,000 euro fine, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education announced institutions should use transgender people's preferred names including on student cards and exam forms. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 with no mention of same-sex relations in private, retained in the Penal Code of 1810 and followed in French colonies adopting the Code, while a discriminatory age of consent of 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual introduced 6 August 1942 and lowered to 18 in 1974 was repealed 4 August 1982 to equalise at 15, and a 1960 provision doubling penalty for homosexual indecent exposure under article 330 alinea 2 was repealed in 1980. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples affording most marriage protections, and France became the thirteenth country to legalise same-sex marriage through a bill approved by the Assembly 12 February 2013 by 329-229 and Senate 12 April 2013, ruled constitutional 17 May 2013, signed 18 May 2013 with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, with joint adoption legal since May 2013. National legislation prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and goods/services was enacted in 1985 and incorporated in the Labour Code, and the law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic comments illegal punishable by up to 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred/violence or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation or disability, while physical assault or murder motivated by sexual orientation carries increased penalties. The December 2004 law created the High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality, the Ministry of Education announced anti-discrimination including homophobia as a 2008-2009 priority and launched the January 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign with reporting services, helpline and LGBTQ guidance plus observance of 17 May, and lesbian, gay and bisexual individuals are allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces. A ban on men who have sex with men donating blood dating to 20 June 1983 was recalled 12 January 2009, replaced by one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016, reduced to four months from 2 April 2020, then removed 16 March 2022 applying the same policy regardless of sexual orientation, and in March 2024 the Assembly unanimously passed a bill for compensation to gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980 pending Senate vote.

exact_spans: Note: the original report was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401);

texts.cleaned_text: Reuters (Oct 2024) reported the CJEU ruling that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights in the Mirzarafie-Ahi case, which concerns recognition of a UK gender recognition certificate in Romania.

ACCEPT Romania (31 Mar 2026): the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity, and the ruling became definitive after the Bucharest Tribunal rejected appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates — building on the CJEU's 2024 ruling that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition. Announced on Trans Day of Visibility; ACCEPT urges others who changed documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering Jan–Dec 2025): anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the 2025 presidential campaign — candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February and PM Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes; the National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint; a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): the CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials; the IPSOS PRIDE 2023 survey found 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition; March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew 13 religious groups' protests and a 50+ organisation counter-response.

Outright International Romania overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide; GO 137/2000 covers sex and sexual orientation but institutional follow-through is limited; no marriage or civil unions (the 2018 constitution-ban referendum failed on low turnout; the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017); legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations can register.

Council of Europe thematic review (Jan 2023): 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania' - national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering legal/policy frameworks, applicable ECtHR case-law and international standards.

ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report (2025), with ACCEPT Romania authoring the Romania chapter (p.29): of nine country submissions, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people — the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period is cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.
AP (Jun 2025): 'Bucharest gay pride march turns 20 as LGBTQ+ Romanians face growing hostility' — tens of thousands march on the 20th anniversary amid rising right-wing hostility.

FRA-commissioned legal study (Feb 2008) by Romanița Elena Iordache and Iustina Ionescu: maps how Romanian law implemented the EU Employment Directive 2000/78/EC and free-movement rules for LGBT partners — national anti-discrimination concepts, CNCD enforcement powers and NGO complaints; a dated baseline for Romania's protection architecture.

Since 1996 it has been possible for someone who has gone through sex reassignment surgery to legally change their sex in official documents. The governing law is vague and incomplete, resulting in inconsistency in judicial practice, with authorities in some cases denying recognition unless a sex-reassignment intervention had occurred. Changing civil status requires a court decision based in practice on a certificate issued by the Institutul Național de Medicină Legală following an intrusive and arbitrary procedure developed ad hoc to fill a legal vacuum. The difficult procedure often makes it impossible to obtain documents reflecting gender identity, leading to difficulties in health care, transportation passes and banking services. In June 2020 parliament passed an education-law amendment placing a blanket ban on gender identity studies without public debate, which Romania's Constitutional Court struck down in December 2020. In April 2022 the Senate passed bills banning "gay propaganda" in schools and banning discussion of homosexuality and gender identity in public spaces, approved by the Human Rights Commission pending Chamber of Deputies approval, but the anti-LGBTQ parts were removed in the final version. Stated anti-discrimination, hate-crime aggravation and incitement provisions are framed on the basis of sexual orientation, not expressly as transgender-specific protections. There are no laws explicitly against gay citizens aside from denial of same-sex marriage rights, with an equal age of consent since 2002 at 15 years, raised to 16 in 2020 for both heterosexual and homosexual sex. Article 200 criminalizing same-sex relations was eliminated by Emergency Ordinance no. 89/2001 adopted in January 2001 and effective in January 2002 after presidential signature, with the last person imprisoned for being gay released in 1998. Marriage is limited to a union between a man and a woman under Civil Code Article 259 and implementing legislation, with same-sex marriage and civil partnership bills rejected in 2013-2015 and constitutional ban attempts withdrawn. The European Court of Justice ruled in Coman and Others in June 2018 that same-sex spouses married in an EU country have residence rights, Romania's highest courts ruled in 2018 for same residency and legal rights, and the European Court of Human Rights ruled on 23 May 2023 that failure to allow marriage or partnership breaches Article 8, while the Prime Minister said in November 2023 Romania will not legalise either. A 2000 law bans sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, goods and services, housing, education, health care, audiovisual programming, justice, public services and social security, enforced by the National Council for Combating Discrimination, including a fine against TAROM for refusing same-sex partners couples discounts in 2005. The Penal Code was amended in 2006 to add incitement to discrimination, discriminatory homophobic bias as an aggravating circumstance allowing higher sentences, and incitement to hatred and harassment on sexual-orientation grounds, though application is described as difficult to assess or not yet applied. Men who have had sex with men remain banned from blood donation under a rule found illegal sexual-orientation discrimination in September 2007, with a January 2008 Health Ministry removal law not yet implemented. In 2021 the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 8 and 11 for failure to effectively investigate the 20 February 2013 homophobic disruption of an LGBTQ film screening, finding discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds. "Attitudes in Romania are generally conservative, with regard to the rights of gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender citizens." A 2019 poll of approximately 3,200 people found 53% of LGBTI people were "(Almost) never open" about being LGBTI, with 23% rarely open, 18% fairly open and 7% very open. An ACCEPT 2010 survey reported 68.2% had suffered discrimination or exclusion because of sexual orientation or identity, with over 50% insulted, 30% threatened with physical violence, 25% deliberately excluded or avoided and 25% suffering sexual harassment, occurring most on streets at 49.5% followed by gay venues at 27.9%. A 2013 Fundamental Rights Agency survey framed in terms of homophobic behavior and sexual minorities ranked Romania third after Croatia and Bulgaria, with 21% reporting attack or threat of violence in the past five years in settings including streets and schools. Open homosexuality remains uncommon outside major urban centers with rural gay and lesbian Romanians typically remaining closeted, while visible LGBTQ communities and annual pride parades exist in Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca, Iasi and Timisoara, with the 18th Bucharest Pride drawing a record 25,000 participants. Most attitude surveys cited concern gay, lesbian, homosexuality or LGBTQ rights generally, without a separate transgender-specific tolerance figure beyond the conservative-attitudes statement.

In Romania during January-December 2025 legal gender recognition had no fair, transparent self-determination-based framework free from abusive requirements with a non-binary option, with the 7 June 2025 Bucharest Pride march of approximately 31,000 people during the first full Pride Month demanding simplified legal gender recognition procedures, civil union legislation, and protection against hate speech and prejudice-based crimes; hate crime and hate speech protections lacked express coverage of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics; during the 2025 presidential campaign Prime Minister Marcel Ciolacu opposed amendments to identity documents to accommodate legal gender recognition as creating confusion and eroding traditional norms, and in October 2025 political figures claimed children could choose their gender without parental consent following the European Commission LGBTI Equality Strategy 2026-2030 recommendations; in October 2025 three training-of-trainers sessions were held for police officers, prosecutors and social workers to recognise, investigate and respond to hate crimes targeting LGBTI people; on 5 June 2025 B1 TV's News Pass framed Pride as a provocation with derogatory portrayals of LGBTI visibility, resulting in an August 2025 public warning from the National Audiovisual Council for breach of the Audiovisual Code prohibition on generalised defamatory statements against groups defined by sexual orientation; July 2025 Oradea Pride proceeded despite a third-year municipal ban attempt under heavy police supervision with nine organisers and participants fined and a subsequent application to the European Court of Human Rights, while Pride events in Cluj-Napoca, Brasov, Timisoara and Iasi took place without incidents.

Emergency Ordinance No. 89/2001 adopted 21 June 2001 and in force 26 June 2001 repealed Penal Code Article 200 thereby decriminalizing consensual adult same-sex sexual relations and redefined Articles 197, 198, 201 and 202 in gender-neutral terms applying equally to sexual acts with persons of different sex or same sex, with pending investigations/trials and custodial sentences under former Article 200(2)-(4) to be maintained only if the facts were also punishable under other Penal Code or special-law provisions with reclassification by the execution court.
