exact_spans: Background/history only, not current visitor risk.

texts.cleaned_text: Outright International Rwanda overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, but the Human Rights First Rwanda Association's 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents law-enforcement abuses against transgender people — harassment at identity checks and arbitrary arrests on 'vagrancy'/'public order' grounds; LGBTIQ organisations cannot register openly, a public Pride event was held in 2021, and NGO Law No. 058/2024 (adopted June 2024) raises freedom-of-association concerns.

Vice (20 Nov 2020): reports violent detentions of transgender people in Rwanda. On Christmas Day 2018, Bella, a singer booked to perform at a hotel in Kigali, was stopped by police officers on the street after her show; her name was changed due to concerns for her safety.

KT Press (25 Sep 2016): asked at Rwanda Cultural Day in San Francisco about LGBT life in Rwanda, President Kagame replied 'it hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem'; the piece cites Article 26 of the constitution, which recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman.

Queerstory Files blog (8 Oct 2012): historical overview of the Great Lakes region. Anthropologists reported that same-sex relations among young Tutsi and Hutu men existed pre-colonisation but were private and secret. The piece situates Rwanda alongside Uganda and Burundi (independence 1962) and post-1994 genocide memory.

Wikipedia country coverage: Homosexuality is a taboo topic in Rwanda with no significant public discussion, and LGBTQ people face stigmatization among the broader population. In September 2019 gospel singer Albert Nabonibo came out as gay on a Christian YouTube channel, causing shock in a country where such a public assertion is described as unheard of, with horrible reactions from family and friends, though the Minister of State for East African Community Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, publicly backed him. The Horizons Community Association of Rwanda has conducted public advocacy for LGBTQ rights since 2005, but its members have often been harassed by the government. The Anglican Church of Rwanda condemned non-biblical behaviors of Western churches in 2007 and refused to support ordination of LGBTQ clergy. In September 2016 President Paul Kagame said homosexuality hasn't been our problem and we don't intend to make it our problem. Rwandan law forbids changing legal gender, so no legal gender recognition path exists for transgender people. The Constitution (adopted May 2003), Article 26, states only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman is recognized, so same-sex marriages, civil unions and similar unions are not recognized. Same-sex sexual activity is legal, with an age of consent of 18 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. In 2024 the Government issued immigration and asylum protections covering LGBTQ people, and in April 2022 a transgender claimant was granted refugee status. The Asylum and humanitarian protection decision making Standard Operating Procedures (2024) require that interviews be conducted so the individual can present the grounds of their application comprehensively, with trained interviewers taking account of gender and any circumstance including sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. The Manual on Refugee Appeal Tribunal Standard Operating Procedures (2014) similarly requires hearings to take account of the appellant's sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. Standard Operating Procedures on identifying and safeguarding vulnerable persons under the Migration and Economic Development Partnership (2024) define Vulnerable Persons to include individuals whose gender identity and/or sexual orientation place them at higher risk, expressly naming lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons. LGBTQ Rwandans have reported being harassed, blackmailed, and even arrested by police under various laws dealing with public order and morality, and LGBTI rights groups reported occasional harassment by neighbors and police (U.S. State Department 2016 report). The Patients Rights and Responsibilities Policy (2018) issued by the Ministry of Health states that all Rwandans, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, age, religion, cultural belief, or disability are equally entitled to receive health services to promote and maintain good health, applying across public, private and NGO sectors. No youth-specific or minor-specific care access findings appear in the source text. There are no anti-discrimination laws afforded to LGBTQ citizens, and the Constitution's non-discrimination provisions (Articles 15 and 16) do not ban discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity; Article 16 lists ethnic origin, sex, religion, disability and other grounds but not SOGI. Limited protections exist: the Human Resource Management Policy (2015) of the Office of the Auditor General of State Finances lists sexual orientation as a prohibited ground for harassment; the Code of Conduct of the Public Private Partnership Guidelines (2018) bans discrimination against bidders on grounds of sexual orientation; and Law 058/2021 on Protection of Personal Data and Privacy protects a person's sexual life as sensitive personal data. The age of consent in Rwanda is 18, regardless of sexual orientation or gender. Historically, in the old Kingdom of Rwanda male homosexual relations were common among young Hutus and Tutsis: boys training as warriors and Tutsi boys training at court formed emotional and often sexual relationships, sometimes lasting into adulthood, and were sometimes made sexually available to guests; societal acceptance disappeared after the arrival of European colonialists and Christianity. No contemporary youth-, minor- or education-specific findings (school policy, bullying, medication carriage by minors) appear in the source text.

An international rights group overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, but a 2025 local human-rights group's submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents law-enforcement abuses against transgender people — harassment at identity checks and arbitrary arrests on 'vagrancy'/'public order' grounds; LGBTIQ organisations cannot register openly, a public Pride event was held in 2021, and a 2024 NGO law (adopted June 2024) raises freedom-of-association concerns.

A news report (20 Nov 2020) documents violent detentions of transgender people in the country: a trans woman singer was stopped by police in the capital as she left a hotel and shown her service card; her name was changed for safety in reporting.

A news report (25 Sep 2016): the president said LGBT life 'hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem'; the report cites a constitutional article recognising only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman.

texts.cleaned_text: LegalClarity (4 Jun 2026): Saudi Arabia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity with no codified penal code — judges apply an uncodified sharia interpretation; penalties range from flogging and lengthy imprisonment to death in the most severe cases; visitor-facing explainer of the laws, how enforcement works and rules for visitors.

Outright International Saudi Arabia overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): criminal penalties are based on Shari'a; same-sex relations illegal for men and women; no legal gender recognition; LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country.

Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute Saudi Arabia profile (MENA Trans Archives): deviating from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence in Saudi Arabia, with provisions applied through enforcement against gender-nonconforming people.

Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Saudi Arabia' (fetched 2026): same-sex conduct illegal with penalties including capital punishment, indeterminate prison terms, flogging and fines; no gender-identity recognition, no discrimination protections, no same-sex relationship recognition; law uncodified on a Wahhabist interpretation of sharia (Quran/Sunnah), with documented enforcement cases and living conditions. Wikipedia country coverage: In May 2023 the Saudi Tourism Authority's FAQ page was updated to state that all visitors, including LGBTQ visitors, are welcome, though homosexuality remains illegal and enforcement is described as not universal. Entry and exit visa paperwork does not ask about sexual orientation, but does ask nationality, sex, religion and marital status; tourist visas were introduced in 2019 alongside a Public Decency Law fining public displays of affection and immodest clothing. In September 2013 Gulf states discussed a proposal to test and ban gay foreigners, which officials later downplayed as a mere proposal. Foreigners face deportation as a penalty for homosexuality, and work-visa applicants must pass an HIV test on arrival and before permit renewal, with infected foreigners deported. Wikipedia country coverage: Bars and nightclubs are illegal, and public movie theaters—permitted only since 2018—have LGBTQ themes edited out of films, with customs maintaining a banned list of films and TV shows. The government has designated several hospitals to treat people with AIDS/HIV, but other hospitals often refuse care or treat patients without compassion, and condoms were until recently rarely available outside certain hospitals or medical supply stores. In June 2022 officials in Riyadh seized rainbow-colored products in a crackdown framed as curbing promotion of homosexuality. Observers reported that MDLBeast Soundstorm, an annual multi-day music festival in Riyadh, included public display of LGBTQI+ culture, while appearing to support homosexuality can result in prosecution for individuals and clubs alike. Wikipedia country coverage: Public education is required to teach Islamic values strongly condemning homosexuality, and Ministry of Education textbooks stated that homosexuality is "one of the most disgusting sins and greatest crimes" with capital punishment as the penalty for public homosexual intercourse—though in 2020 the Ministry was found to have removed the death-penalty condemnation from textbooks. In 2012 the government asked the CPVPV to help expel students judged to be gay or lesbian based on their mannerisms and fashion taste. The June 2022 rainbow-goods seizure explicitly targeted "the young generation," confiscating children's hair accessories, backpacks, pencil cases and rainbow-striped crayon packs. HIV prevention education for men who have sex with men is minimal, though a 2024 Saudi AIDS National Program report makes some mention of them; private schools, mainly serving expatriates, have discretion over curriculum on homosexuality.

[4] BBC News: 'Meeno'. Mohammad Amin, a Pakistani transgender woman, died in Saudi custody after a roundup with 34 others in Azizia prison, Riyadh. Pakistani activists say she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes, aggravating a chronic heart condition, while Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack; family and trans-rights activists dispute the official account.

Gulf News (25 Oct 2021): five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media — cross-dressing/gender-nonconformity enforced as a criminal matter.

Human Dignity Trust country profile: Sudan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with sentences including a maximum of life imprisonment and, historically, the death penalty for a third offence.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Sudan: its LGBT section notes criminalisation under Article 148, with flogging and death penalty provisions. The report also documents extrajudicial killings, torture and abuses of the Bashir regime.

Berkouwer, Sultan and Yehia (2014) worked with activists of Bedayaa, the LGBTQI organisation for the Nile Valley, on 'Homosexuality in Sudan and Egypt: Stories of the Struggle for Survival'. The work records daily struggles, discrimination and violence against LGBTQI people rooted in societal gender and sexual norms.

Rainbow Sudan, a Sudanese community magazine, documents an organised local community presence through sections on LGBTI rights in Sudan, including history and analysis, and profiles of Sudanese LGBTI organisations.

76crimes (15 Jul 2020): Sudan's Sovereign Council removed the death penalty for homosexuality — maximum now life imprisonment for a third offence — abolished the 100 lashes for same-sex intimacy, and set up to five years' imprisonment for a first offence in the criminal-code amendment.

The only criminal offence described is sodomy under Article 148 of the Criminal Act of 1991, defined as anal sex whether same-sex or opposite-sex, with no transgender-specific criminal provision described. The penalties described for that sexuality-conduct offence after 9 July 2020 are up to five years for a first offence, up to seven years for a second offence, and life imprisonment for a third offence. For transgender-relevant protection, official discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity occurred. In 2011 there were no known lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender (LGBT) organizations. No transgender-specific facts on documents, screening, facilities, custody, or care are stated. Same-sex sexual activity is illegal for both men and women under sodomy law. Sodomy is defined as anal sex whether same-sex or opposite-sex and is prohibited by Article 148 of the Criminal Act of 1991, as amended in 2009. On 9 July 2020 the Transitional Sovereignty Council abolished the death penalty for anal sex and eliminated 100 lashes. The retained penalties are up to five years imprisonment for a first offence, up to seven years for a second offence after adding two years, and life imprisonment for a third offence, changed from death or life imprisonment. There were no documented cases of executions for sodomy prior to repeal of capital punishment, and in 2011 there were no reports of antisodomy laws being applied. Sudanese LGBTQ activists described the 2020 reform as a 'great first step' but said it was not enough, with the end goal decriminalisation of gay sexual activity altogether. Official discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity occurred, and societal discrimination against LGBT persons was widespread. Vigilantes targeted suspected gay men and lesbians for violent abuse and targeted LGBT people for violent abuse, with public demonstrations against homosexuality, and few people were prepared to speak openly about LGBT issues. In the 2019 Arab Barometer Survey, 17% of Sudanese said homosexuality is acceptable. No tolerance figure specific to transgender people is given, only combined LGBT or homosexuality-specific findings. No known lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender organizations existed in 2011. Freedom Sudan founded in December 2006 showed no internet presence since 2013, Rainbow Sudan founded 9 February 2012 ceased internet presence after January 2015 after providing sexual education, psychological and emotional support, and protection, and Bedayaa founded in 2010 continues to serve the LGBT+ community in the Nile valley region of Sudan and Egypt. Sudan called for a No Action Motion on 4 February 2011 that passed 9-7 to prevent voting on consultative status for the LGBTQ group at the UN Economic and Social Council, and has voted against every supportive resolution of LGBTQ rights at the United Nations.

Human Dignity Trust country profile: Senegal criminalises same-sex sexual activity under Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, with a maximum of five years' imprisonment.

76crimes (16 Jul 2024) reports that anti-LGBT forces in Senegal are pushing for 15-year prison sentences for gay sex, up from the current maximum of five years. The debate has run since 2020, and abuses against LGBT+ people are commonplace in the West African nation.

BBC News reports that a political activist and a preacher were jailed in Senegal for criticising opposition leader Ousmane Sonko and fined 100,000 CFA francs ($165, £130) each. They had been angered that Mr Sonko allowed a visiting French politician to express his support for same-sex marriage, and were arrested after posting a video attacking him for giving the politician a platform. Homosexual acts are banned in Senegal and are punishable by up to five years in prison.

The US State Department's 2012 Human Rights Report for Senegal documents preelectoral violence, torture, and violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons among the major human-rights problems.

76crimes (24 Sep 2018) reports that four LGBT people, two women and two men, were detained in Dakar for 'acts against the order of nature'. The detentions came amid a wave of politically motivated arrests ahead of the 2019 elections, triggered after videos circulated.

Metro (Nov 2023) reports that a man's body was dug up and burned in the street in Senegal after it was revealed he was gay. Four men have been arrested in connection with the incident, though images from the scene show a crowd of hundreds gathering around the fire. The 31-year-old man, named locally as Cheikh Fall, had been buried in Léona Niassene cemetery.

The quoted text of Article 319 addresses only an improper or unnatural act with a person of the same sex with 1 to 5 years imprisonment and 100,000 to 1,500,000 francs fine, with no reference to transgender status, gender identity or gender expression. The law adopted 12 March 2026, signed 30 March 2026 and published 31 March 2026 adds an explicit ban on the promotion, financing and support of homosexuality, bisexuality and transsexuality alongside 5 to 10 years imprisonment, 100,000 to 10,000,000 CFA francs fines and a penalty for abusive relationships conducted in bad faith. Transgender persons as part of LGBT are described as often facing criminal prosecution, arrest, widespread discrimination, social intolerance and acts of violence, with local groups maintaining an exceedingly low profile due to laws against homosexuality and stigma and media rarely reporting hatred or violence. In October 2009 and October 2013 recommendations to amend or repeal legislation punishing on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, establish a moratorium on Article 319, ensure non-discrimination, protection and integration, and criminalize orientation-based violence were made and refused on the ground that being homosexual is not a crime though same-sex acts are. On 6 February 2009 it was stated that the president had authorized a homosexual to have his name changed to a woman's name to emphasize feminine side with no shock, indicating past allowance of name change reflecting feminine presentation. Around mid-2009 bodies of deceased goor-gigen, defined as man-woman, were dug up from cemeteries including the May 2009 Thies case where a corpse reputed homosexual was twice disinterred, left near the grave then dumped outside the family home after reburial, without identification of victims as transgender. Article 319 punishes an improper or unnatural act with a person of the same sex by 1 to 5 years imprisonment and 100,000 to 1,500,000 francs fine, with the maximum always applied if committed with a person below 21 years. The bill presented 25 February 2026, adopted 12 March 2026, signed 30 March 2026 and published 31 March 2026 raises punishment for unnatural acts to 5 to 10 years imprisonment and 100,000 to 10,000,000 CFA francs fines. Enforcement included arrest of nine men 19 December 2008 in a Dakar flat, conviction 6 January 2009 to 5 years for indecent conduct and unnatural acts plus 3 years for membership of a criminal group, with repeated torture in police custody and segregated holding due to inmate threats, followed by overturning of convictions in April 2009 with immediate release. Further enforcement included September 2018 arrest of two men and two women in Dakar after neighbourhood circulation of videos, February 2026 arrest of 22 gay men within two weeks for acts against nature including 20 February detention at the Senegal-Gambian border while attempting to leave, and August arrest of 99 men with 28 released and 71 facing up to 20 years after doubling of the maximum. Police practice included arrest based only on second-hand reports and poor treatment in detention due to sexual orientation, with January detention of two women after circulation of a kissing video released on bail without formal charge and October Dakar sentences of four years plus 200,000 CFA francs fine for acts against nature plus arms and battery and three years for the other man. There are no laws broadly protecting LGBTQ people against discrimination, with only limited prohibitions on revealing or stigmatizing depiction of sexual orientation. Physical violence documented includes December 2012 beating of a gay male couple near Dakar by a parent after being caught having sex, May 2009 twice-disinterred corpse in Thies, and 28 October 2023 exhumation and burning of Cheikh Fall's body in Kaolack with four suspected masterminds apprehended 30 October 2023.

In February 2026 Senegal's government adopted a draft bill to harden repression of same-sex 'acts against nature,' already punishable by 1 to 5 years imprisonment, by raising fines from 1.5 million to 10 million CFA francs and targeting organizations promoting LGBT philosophy via film, television or writing, amid 17 arrests for 'acts against nature' in early February 2026.

Senegal Penal Code Article 319(3) punishes an improper or unnatural act with a person of the same sex with one to five years imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 1,500,000 francs, Senegal provides no legal gender recognition procedure, and in the 2009 and 2013 Universal Periodic Reviews Senegal rejected recommendations to decriminalize same-sex conduct and to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, maintaining criminal liability and enforcement risk.
International legal-aid trust country profile: this country criminalises same-sex sexual activity (a provision of the 1965 penal code, up to 5 years' imprisonment).

Anti-criminalisation news platform (July 2024): anti-LGBT forces in this country seek longer prison time - after the head of government alleged homosexuality is 'tolerated', a legislator proposed a bill mirroring a failed 2022 initiative raising sentences to 10-15 years for 'offences of bisexuality [including homosexuality], transsexuality, necrophilia and zoophilia' plus fines of up to millions in local currency; abuses against LGBT+ people are commonplace.

Foreign public broadcaster (June 2024): two men jailed in this country for 'spreading false news' after accusing the head of government of tolerating homosexuality - an activist and a prominent religious leader received three months and fines; the head of government had said homosexuality was 'not accepted, but tolerated' after a foreign politician expressed support for same-sex marriage at a student forum in the capital.

A foreign government's 2012 human-rights report on this country: documents preelectoral violence, torture, and 'violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons' among major human-rights problems.

Anti-criminalisation news platform (Sept 2018): a wave of politically motivated anti-gay arrests as the 2019 election approached - two women and two men detained in the capital for 'acts against the order of nature'; a local LGBT organisation warned that 'the hunt for sexual minorities begins' as the government defended itself against 'pro-homosexual' accusations; a regional LGBT body called for accountability.

Local daily (Nov 2023): a man's body was exhumed and set on fire in the street after locals found out he was gay - a case that shocked this country, where homosexuality is punishable with prison time.

Outright International Singapore overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations legal for men and women; legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations cannot register — registration remains the structural gap despite decriminalisation.

Straits Times (15 Nov 2023): the Singapore Prison Service reported 10 transgender inmates currently behind bars and no recorded cases of assault against transgender inmates — a rare official datum on trans prisoners in the system.

Reuters feature (June 2023): Singapore's LGBT community feels safer as the end of the 377A ban brings change.

South China Morning Post (3 Jul 2025): a clause of the radio broadcast code grouping homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as forbidden 'lifestyles' sparked calls for review — a former radio DJ and actor argued the grouping 'has no place in a post-377A Singapore'. Media-regulation residue after decriminalisation.

F&M Global Barometers Singapore country profile: interactive scores across unified/gay/transgender rights indices and an LGBTQI+ perception index, 2011–2024, covering de jure protections and lived experience.

Intrepid Travel 'Is Singapore LGBTQIA+ friendly': describes a thriving LGBTQIA+ social scene — gay-friendly bars (e.g. Backstage Bar in Chinatown), pop-ups and exhibitions — alongside practical guidance on solo travel and room sharing for its own trips. Visitor-facing operator guidance.

Singapore's media regulator limits the "promotion or glamorisation of the homosexual lifestyle" on television and radio, imposing higher age ratings (NC16, M18, R21) on shows or films depicting same-sex sexual activity. In 2019 rapper Joshua Su (The G3sha) withdrew from a TEDx radio talk after being asked not to make "sensitive" comments about his sexuality. Public-order provisions still reach expression: gay men were charged with soliciting in 11 cases between 1990 and 1994 (fines of $200–$500), and Section 294 of the Penal Code covers obscene acts in public places (maximum three months' imprisonment, a fine, or both). Pride expression continues regardless: Pink Dot SG has been held annually since 2009, with record crowds of approximately 28,000 in recent years.

Yale-NUS College and Tembusu College of the National University of Singapore provide gender-neutral toilets for their students. During Wikimania 2023 at the Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre (16–19 August 2023), a female toilet was temporarily converted to a gender-neutral one, drawing public backlash: the Facebook group "We Are Against Pinkdot in Singapore" threatened a boycott of Suntec and users sought petitions against it. Pink Dot SG and non-profit group Oogachaga responded that gender-neutral toilets complement gendered toilets rather than replace them. Government representatives also noted in 2014 that gay bars and clubs operate in Singapore.

In January 2006 the Ministry of Community Development, Youth and Sports granted S$100,000 (US$61,500) to Liberty League, an "ex-gay" conversion-therapy organisation; activists pressured the group into returning the grant and it has been defunct since 2014. In May 2020 Health Minister Gan Kim Yong wrote that the Ministry of Health expects doctors to practise evidence-based best practice and to respect patients' preferences and circumstances including sexual orientation, with complaints to the Singapore Medical Council as the recourse, though no such complaint had been received from self-declared LGBTQ patients in the prior three years. A May 2019 National University of Singapore study estimated 210,000 men who have sex with men in Singapore, more than double the previous estimate of 90,000, who "could be at risk of a concentrated epidemic of HIV." Same-sex couples cannot access the healthcare benefits available to heterosexual couples because their relationships are unrecognised. On youth acceptance, a 2021 TODAY Youth Survey found 80% willing to work with LGBTQ people (6% disagreed), 75% willing to form close friendships (10% disagreed) and 58% willing to accept LGBTQ family members (18% disagreed).

Singapore does not recognise same-sex relationships in any form, whether marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and does not recognise adoption of children by same-sex couples generally. On 29 November 2022 Parliament passed both the repeal of Section 377A and a constitutional amendment protecting Parliament's right, rather than the judiciary's, to define marriage, leaving open a future simple-majority legalisation of same-sex marriage or civil unions. Combined with the Women's Charter precedent that a marriage not between a woman and a man is void, only heterosexual marriages are recognised. One exception: in December 2018 a gay Singaporean man won a landmark appeal to adopt his son fathered through surrogacy in the United States, after which Social and Family Development Minister Desmond Lee said in January 2019 the government does not support "the formation of family units with children of homosexual parents through institutions and processes such as adoption" and would seek to strengthen adoption laws, a statement not yet made into law. Without recognition, same-sex couples cannot access healthcare benefits, inheritance rights or social security benefits.

texts.cleaned_text: As of 25 Apr 2026, same-sex sexual activity is legal in the territory, discrimination protections have been in force since 2009, and same-sex marriage has been legal on Ascension Island since 2017 (Alchetron).

Consensual same-sex relations became lawful in 2001. The age of consent is equalised at 16 territory-wide. The territory is an Overseas Country or Territory of the EU, with EU Charter applicability (GayLawNet, accessed 23 Jun 2013, citing ILGA State-sponsored Homophobia).

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha - discrimination banned territory-wide since 2009; same-sex marriage legal since 2017 (Ascension 1 Jan, Tristan da Cunha 4 Aug, Saint Helena 20 Dec); adoption since 2017; detailed vote records of the Ascension Island Council (5-0).
Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights on Ascension Island. The marriage ordinance was approved 31 May 2016 (5-0), signed and gazetted 20 June, and commenced 1 January 2017.

No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care, or violence provisions are documented. The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of the importance of equality, and works towards elimination of unlawful discrimination. The Commission may conduct inquiries and investigations on persons suspected of having committed an unlawful act, including unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or "gender reassignment". Under the Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015, "gender reassignment" means "an intended, current or past process (or part of such a process) for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent or not culturally associated with their assigned sex at birth". No extension of the Constitution Order 2009 sexual-orientation discrimination ban to gender reassignment, and no transgender-specific marriage, adoption, or penalty provisions, are documented. Homosexuality is legal in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, defining "discriminatory" as "affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status." The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes "understanding of the importance of equality" and works towards elimination of unlawful discrimination, with power to conduct inquiries and investigations into suspected unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Under the Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015, sexual orientation means "a person's sexual orientation towards— (a) persons of the same sex; (b) persons of the opposite sex; or (c) persons of either sex". Same-sex marriage has been legal on Ascension Island since 1 January 2017 under the Marriage (Ascension) Ordinance, 2016, on Tristan da Cunha since 4 August 2017 under the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance, 2017, and on Saint Helena since 20 December 2017 under the Marriage Ordinance 2017, with the first same-sex marriage in Saint Helena occurring on 31 December 2018. Under the Saint Helena Welfare of Children Ordinance 2010 for Saint Helena and Tristan da Cunha and the Ascension Island Child Welfare Ordinance 2011 for Ascension Island, single and married people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, while a 2006 UK Government report recorded no adoptions in Saint Helena or Ascension Island for many years.

Tristan da Cunha legalized same-sex marriage through the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance 2017 effective 4 August 2017, defining marriage as the union of two persons regardless of sex and extending eligibility, formalities, rights and recognition to same-sex couples on equal terms with opposite-sex couples.

Wikipedia country coverage: The climate is defined by decriminalization since the 1880s and repeated official rejection of reform: the Law Reform Commission proposed legalizing gay and lesbian sexual activity in December 2008, but the move was strongly opposed, and the government told the United Nations in 2011 it had no intention of decriminalising homosexuality. Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare publicly opposed same-sex marriage in a 2017 speech to a local church group, and in June 2018 Governor General Frank Kabui acknowledged that being gay or lesbian 'is said to be biological and is beyond individual control' while still condemning any legal change, citing both the criminal code and the Bible. Enforcement is nonetheless absent: the U.S. Department of State reported no arrests or prosecutions directed at LGBTQ people in 2010, 2011, 2012 or 2013, and the source notes the law is not enforced. Constitutional reform has narrowed visibility of the issue — a 2009 draft constitution listed 'sexual orientation' as a prohibited ground of discrimination, but the 2011, 2013 and 2014 drafts dropped it, with reform still ongoing as of 2019.

texts.cleaned_text: Foreign Policy (9 Mar 2020, Anna-Catherine Brigida): prosecution of the death of Camila Díaz Córdova, a transgender Salvadoran woman, as a hate crime — activists called it an advance toward El Salvador's first hate-crime homicide conviction while documenting continuing discrimination and abuse of LGBTQ citizens.

texts.cleaned_text: Dilemas journal article (Arévalo et al., Fundação Oswaldo Cruz, 2024): 'Denied deaths' builds a profile of crimes, victims and perpetrators of homicides against LGBTI+ people in El Salvador across 2000-2020.

HRW report 'Every Day I Live in Fear' (7 Oct 2020): El Salvador (with Guatemala and Honduras) fails to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, driving asylum claims to the US; documents obstacles to obtaining protection.

HRW report (Jan 2021) 'I'm Lucky to Still Be Alive': violence and discrimination against LGBT people in El Salvador - full report with recommendations to the president, attorney general, congress and ministries.

HRW (31 Jul 2020): San Salvador judge found three police officers guilty of the January 2019 killing of transgender woman Camila Díaz Córdova and sentenced each to 20 years; the 28 July 2020 judgment is the first homicide conviction in El Salvador for killing a transgender person, hailed by HRW as pivotal for transgender Salvadorans' rights.

Washington Blade (9 Sep 2015): National Assembly approved legal-code reforms so killings motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender draw 30-60 years under Article 129 — the enhanced hate-crime penalty framework on the books since.

GatoEncerrado (Oscar Hernandez, 26 Feb 2024): since the state of exception began (Mar 2022), trans women arbitrarily captured in mass raids are held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. Jennifer, arrested 14 Apr 2022 in San Salvador, was held first at the 'El Penalito' police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair ('para que sepan lo que son'), singled her out with another trans woman (Rosa) for outdoor punishment drills (handcuffed, forced squatting in the sun), and denied her HIV clinic access; a judge freed her after ~4 months finding the arrest unsupported, while Rosa remains imprisoned. Organisations (Socorro Juridico Humanista, Cristosal) link the abuse to the absence of a Gender Identity Law. Documents birth-sex placement in the general prison system with trans-targeted abuse and no special custody provision.

El Salvador's Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court ordered in 2022 that the Name Law be reformed to allow individuals to change their names to match their gender identity, holding the existing laws unconstitutional because they discriminated on the basis of gender; the case originated in a 2016 lawsuit by a transgender activist. As of 2023 the Legislative Assembly had taken no action to guarantee changes of name and gender in legal documents, so transgender Salvadorans still cannot update official papers. Same-sex marriage is not recognized: the Family Code's Article 11 defines marriage as a heterosexual union, individuals may adopt but same-sex couples cannot adopt as a couple, and the Law on Family Violence does not apply to same-sex couples. Prison conditions are explicitly hostile: homosexual inmates are strictly forbidden from dressing or behaving in an effeminate manner, and men are targeted by police officers, soldiers, and prison guards for effeminate behavior or dress through unwarranted searches, theft of property, sexual assault, and other physical violence. In the 1999 investigation of Doris and Maricela, the two transvestites were forced to wear men's clothing for their hearing. Hospital specialists frequently dismiss trans patients' problems as a side effect of being transgender, and patients are sometimes made to wait longer or denied care, though this can be done discreetly. Transgender health care access is severely restricted: there is a lack of protocols and programs for hormone therapy and sex reassignment surgery, and one study found that many trans women did not seek medical help after suffering side effects from surgeries, having learned not to trust the system. For LGBT people in general, even when individuals reach out for psychological care they feel insecure and report prejudice, and such care often arrives in the form of conversion therapies, frequently deployed by parents attempting to change a child's sexual orientation; LGBT community members experience suicide ideation and attempts at higher rates than the general population. In April 2009 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Assistance published guidelines banning discrimination against LGBT and HIV-positive people in health services, a 2009 national HIV/AIDS health plan included a prohibition on sexual orientation-based discrimination in health care, and since 2005 a national HIV/AIDS policy has developed with the first National HIV testing day established in 2007. Gay and bisexual men are allowed to donate blood, though policy prohibits those who 'engage in risky behaviours' from donating. Same-sex marriage is not legal, and since 2006 there have been proposals to amend the Constitution to restrict recognition even of same-sex couples married legally abroad. Two legal challenges to the ban were dismissed by the courts on technical and procedural grounds (20 December 2016 and 17 January 2019), although the Constitutional Court declared a proposed marriage ban unlawful in January 2018 and admitted a lawsuit for recognition of same-sex marriage for a hearing in August 2019, following a January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion holding same-sex marriage to be a human right. A 2010 poll showed only 10% support for legalizing same-sex marriage, and the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 19% support. Sexuality is absent from school curriculum, in line with societal expectations, which leads many LGBT students to remain invisible in school to avoid discrimination; LGBT students, particularly those whose gender expression does not match that assigned at birth, drop out of school at high rates, and some LGBT students have been expelled outright for their sexuality and identity. No known universities or graduate programs offer Sexuality Studies programs; academic publications exist, most from the University of El Salvador, often from psychological or legal science perspectives, but with varying levels of support within them. Where LGBT children do come out, families may subject them to conversion therapy or family prayers to convert them to heterosexuality, and when these methods fail, families sometimes expel the child from the home and sever all connections. Young Salvadoran homosexuals now encourage older homosexuals to come out, and globalization is slowly changing the young LGBT community, though it still faces heavy unacceptance. A 2013 study showed that 62% of Salvadorans do not accept homosexuality and 85% believe it acceptable to attack a transgender individual on the basis of their identity, and El Salvador is described as one of the most socially-homophobic countries in Latin America. Over 50% identify as actively practicing Catholics, many of the rest attend evangelical churches, and church leaders have organized opposition to LGBT rights legislation; an embedded machismo culture holds that being Salvadoran means being virile, heterosexuals are described as afraid of defending or befriending gay people for fear of stigma and of being accused of being gay themselves, and being 'gay friendly' is seen as against nature, anti-religious, and anti-masculine. About 500 hate crimes against LGBTQ people were reported between 1998 and 2015 (with many unreported), police have shown blatant refusal to cooperate in LGBT death investigations, and gang violence includes targeting of LGBT people through physical and sexual assault, forced recruitment, and 'taxing' for safety; on 28 July 2020 a San Salvador judge convicted three police officers of killing transgender woman Camila Díaz Córdova, sentencing them to 20 years each. Entre Amigos organized El Salvador's first Gay Pride Parade in June 1997 to commemorate the massacre of trans women in the 1980s and it continues today, San Salvador authorized permanent rainbow paintings at several crossroads in July 2017, a 2015 hate crime law added sexual orientation and gender identity provisions to the Criminal Code (three to six years imprisonment), and a 2018 Institutional Policy for the Care of the LGBT Population allows LGBT people to file legal complaints against discrimination.

San Marino decriminalised homosexuality in 1864. Article 274 of the Criminal Code, which had punished 'habitual' homosexual acts causing public scandal with 3 months to 1 year imprisonment, was repealed in September 2004 and was never reported as applied. In 2008 the Grand and General Council amended the Penal Code to outlaw discrimination and hate speech based on sexual orientation, effective 3 May 2008, with penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation.

Civil unions, in force 5 December 2018 and fully operational from 11 February 2019, grant same-sex and opposite-sex couples rights with respect to residency and citizenship as well as pensions, healthcare, succession and stepchild adoption. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and Sammarinese same-sex couples are still banned from marrying. No other custody-specific provisions are recorded. In December 2017 the Grand and General Council approved a budget-law amendment allowing foreign same-sex couples to marry in San Marino to encourage tourism, but as of 2024 the implementing legislation does not appear to have been drafted. Gay and bisexual men are allowed to donate blood.

Discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned under 2019 constitutional amendments, and the Penal Code provides penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation was added to Article 4 of the Declaration of Citizens' Rights after a 2 June 2019 referendum passed with 71.46% in favour; the March 2019 council vote fell short at 35 for, 8 against, 1 abstention, needing 39. There are occasionally reports of violence and hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. In November 2019 San Marino accepted UPR recommendations to outlaw gender identity discrimination.

The age of consent is 14 for both opposite-sex and same-sex sexual acts, and it is an offence to incite a minor under 18 to sexual corruption. San Marino's sex education programme, together with emotional education programmes, expressly provides for knowledge of LGBTQ rights, and the 'Curriculum of education to citizenship' also covers LGBTQ matters. Until recently LGBTQ people in San Marino went unnoticed, with very few public debates in media, society or politics, and in the early 2000s the government rejected LGBTQ groups' request to recognise 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia. In 2022 Paolo Rondelli's election as Captain Regent made San Marino the first country in modern history with an openly homosexual head of state.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Somalia's criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity: up to life imprisonment under the 1964 penal code, and the death penalty under Sharia in some regions.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Somalia: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 3 years); al-Shabaab enforces strict Sharia with death as possible punishment; pervasive violence and statelessness.

US State Dept 2022 Country Report, Somalia: criminalizes 'carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex', 3 months' to 3 years' imprisonment, no official reports of enforcement available; under local interpretations of sharia, homosexuality is punishable by death; no known state-conducted executions of that sort reported. Impunity generally remained the norm.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Somalia (archived): documents the conflict, al-Shabaab abuses, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and the death penalty under Islamic law in areas under insurgent control.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Feb 2016) on Benjamin Christman's 'Report on the Treatment of Gay Persons in Somalia' (published 2 Feb 2016): evidence that gay persons should not be returned to Somalia due to persecution risk, supporting refugee-status claims and forming a non-refoulement basis for LGBT asylum seekers.

Al Jazeera (Jul 2013) 'Gay Somali refugees face death threats': refugees in Kenya face threats and racist discrimination; Al-Shabaab publicised intent to 'enforce harsh punishments' against homosexuality, and senior figures claimed a 'death chamber' for gay and lesbians if returned, while UN officials nevertheless pushed return. The account records persecution driving displacement.

Under Article 409 of the Somali Penal Code (1973), sexual intercourse with a person of the same sex is punishable by three months to three years' imprisonment, and an 'act of lust' other than intercourse by two months to two years. Article 410 permits an additional security measure, usually police surveillance, to prevent re-offending. The Marriage Law of 1974 defines marriage as 'a contract between a man and a woman having equal rights and duties with the object of creating a family,' which excludes same-sex unions from legal recognition. In al-Shabaab-controlled areas and Jubaland, capital punishment is imposed for consensual same-sex sexual activity, with punishment at a judge's discretion. ILGA reported killings by al-Shabaab or other non-state armed groups of alleged homosexual activity: two male teenagers aged 15 and 18 together with a man aged 20 in 2017, a young man in 2018, and two men executed by Al-Shabaab in 2024. In government-controlled areas, civil law specifies prison sentences of up to three years, and LGBTQ people are regularly prosecuted. The law does not prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, as reported by the U.S. Department of State in 2022. Pervasive social stigma attaches to same-sex relationships, and sexual orientation is a taboo topic with no public discussion in any region of the country, per U.S. Department of State reports from 2010 and 2022; severe societal stigma prevents LGBTQI+ individuals from making their sexual orientation or gender identity known publicly as of 2022. Stigmatisation and criminalisation occur where 99% of the population follows Islam amid decades of civil war and unstable government. Human rights and LGBTQ activists and those accused of homosexuality have been forced to flee the country for fear of execution or assassination. Family planning services and fact-based information on human sexuality are hard to access, and Islamic social mores often make it difficult to publicly discuss HIV transmission. Since 1999, much AIDS/HIV education and care has come from international organizations such as the United Nations. Somalia has one of the lowest HIV infection rates on the continent, with adult prevalence estimated at 0.5% in 2007. As of 2004, one group reportedly existed for LGBTQ people in Somalia, and by 2022 there were few, very discreet, and mostly online-based LGBTQI+ organizations holding events.

Serbia decriminalised same-sex activity in stages: the 1860 Kaznitelni zakon (Penalty Act) of the Principality punished intercourse 'against the order of nature' between males with 6 months to 4 years' imprisonment and did not mention lesbian sexuality; the 1929 Yugoslav Criminal Code banned 'lewdness against the order of nature' between heterosexuals and homosexuals alike; the SFRY narrowed the offence in 1959 to homosexual anal intercourse with the maximum cut from 2 to 1 year. Same-sex intercourse was legalised in Vojvodina in 1977 but male homosexuality was re-criminalised when Vojvodina was reincorporated into Serbia's legal system in 1990. Male homosexual intercourse was officially decriminalised in 1994 by amending article 110 (act against order of nature), though a new subsection 4 then banned male same-sex acts for males aged 14 to 18 with up to one year's prison; an equal age of consent of 14 regardless of sexual orientation or gender took effect on 1 January 2006 under the current Criminal Code. Public expression of LGBT identity has repeatedly been suppressed: the first Belgrade Gay Pride in 2001 ended in extreme violence, and Pride events in Belgrade (2004, 2009) and Novi Sad (2007) were cancelled because police could not guarantee safety against violent opponents. The 2010 Belgrade Pride went ahead with about a thousand participants but was met by the Belgrade anti-gay riot, attended by 6,000 anti-gay protesters and extreme nationalist group members; Amnesty International noted in May 2014 that public authorities had repeatedly banned pride parades on the basis of violent threats from homophobic groups and had failed to protect LGBTQ individuals and organisations from verbal, social media and physical attacks. Belgrade Pride successfully took place in September 2014 and has been held annually since, except in 2020 when it moved online for COVID-19, with local mayors and some ministers attending. EuroPride in September 2022 was initially banned by authorities on security grounds and opposed by President Vučić, but proceeded on 17 September along a shortened route under heavy police protection, with organisers reporting almost 10,000 attendees; Novi Sad held its first gay pride rally on 17 May 2019. Serbia had no legal protections specifically aimed at LGBTQ rights until 2002, when the Broadcasting Act barred broadcasters from spreading information encouraging discrimination, hate and violence based on sexual orientation and the Information Act of 2003 added comparable media duties; the Radiodiffusion Agency never effectively acted against offenders. In 2005 the Labor Act banned sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, the Act on Higher Education guaranteed equal rights regardless of sexual orientation in higher education institutions, and on 5 July 2011 Parliament approved a youth act prohibiting discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation and regulating local-government measures for young people. On 26 March 2009 Parliament approved the unified Anti-Discrimination Act, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and transgender status in all areas, with 2021 amendments adding sex characteristics, making Serbia one of the first Western Balkan countries to do so. A Penal Code hate crime provision covering sexual orientation and gender identity was adopted on 24 December 2012, with the first conviction in 2018; enforcement remains weak, and Amnesty International noted in 2014 that authorities had failed to protect LGBTQ individuals and organisations from discrimination including verbal and social media threats and physical attacks. Sex change surgeries have been partially covered by Serbia's statewide basic medical insurance since a Health Insurance Act change approved on 28 July 2011 (effective 2012), with government-financed insurance covering up to 65% of surgery costs and the patient paying the remainder; hormone replacement therapy is not financed by health insurance. Belgrade was described by The New York Times in 2012 as a hub for sex reassignment surgery because prices were far lower than in neighbouring and Western countries. Access remains poor in the eyes of those affected: a reported 90% of LGBT individuals in Serbia say medical institutions are not adequately responding to their needs, and Jovanka Todorović of Gayten-LGBT said about 80% of Serbian transgender people are not willing to undergo surgery. The Ministry of Health barred people with a 'history of homosexual relations during the last five years' from donating reproductive cells for artificial insemination or IVF in early 2019, removing the provision on 23 April 2021; official medical textbooks circulated classifying homosexuality under 'sexual deviations and disorders' until the Serbian Medical Society confirmed in a 2008 letter to Labris that same-sex orientation is not a disease, homosexuality having been removed from the official disease list in 1997 with ICD-10. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Map ranked Serbia 29th of 49 European countries with a 34% score, down from 27th in 2024. Same-sex couples have never been recognised by law, and the Serbian Constitution adopted in November 2006 effectively bans same-sex marriage through Article 62, which defines marriage as entered into based on the free consent of a man and a woman; civil unions and domestic partnerships are neither explicitly mentioned nor prohibited. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couples cannot legally adopt. Plans to legalise domestic partnerships by amending the Civil Code were announced in June 2019, covering joint property and alimony but not inheritance, adoption or surrogacy; in July 2019 a Novi Sad lesbian couple, Jelena Dubović and Sunčica Kopunović, were turned away when they tried to register a civil partnership and sued, with legal experts doubting they would win. Minister Gordana Čomić announced in November 2020 that a same-sex partnership law would reach parliament in the first half of 2021, and a draft went to public consultation in February 2021, but President Vučić said in May 2021 he would not sign it as unconstitutional, the bill stalled without a vote, and he reaffirmed in August 2023 he would sign no such law in his term. In September 2024 the Green-Left Front submitted a new Draft Law on Civil Partnership covering maintenance, inheritance and health and social insurance, still unscheduled for a vote as of 2026; the 2023 ECHR Grand Chamber ruling in Fedotova and Others v. Russia holds that Council of Europe states including Serbia have a positive obligation to provide some form of legal recognition for same-sex couples. Public opinion is split: 2021 Civil Rights Defenders data shows 26% support for same-sex marriage but 80% believing LGBTI+ persons should have at least some of the rights in a same-sex union law, second-highest in the Western Balkans after Montenegro, with 2018 data cited by the U.S. State Department showing 70% opposing an LGBT person inheriting a deceased partner's property. Attitudes toward LGBT young people and parenting remain hostile: 2018 data cited in the U.S. State Department human rights report found 48% of parents would seek medical treatment for their LGBT child and 90% opposed child adoption by an LGBT person, while a 2022 World Values Survey found 65% of Serbians disagreed that homosexual couples are as good parents as other couples. Support is markedly higher among younger (18 to 29) and university-educated respondents in Belgrade and Vojvodina, and 2021 Civil Rights Defenders data records a general improvement in attitudes toward LGBTI+ issues over the preceding five years, though 57% still believe homosexuality is a disease.

The US State Department's 2015 Human Rights Report for Suriname records discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex (LGBTI) persons and other minorities. The same report also documents the Bouterse trial, police brutality and corruption.

Submission to the UN Human Rights Committee (115th session) from LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata: despite constitutional protection LGBTI persons still face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatization. It records that in March 2015 Penal Code Articles 175, 175a and 176 were revised to cover discrimination and hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation.

Human Rights Committee review of Suriname, July 2024: the State asserted its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, backed by monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission, while experts pressed on implementing the Inter-American Court's judgment on transgender identity. The Committee welcomed abolition of the death penalty in the Penal Code (2015) and Military Code (2021).

UN UPR pre-session summary of March 2016 from the Suriname LGBT Platform: since the 2011 UPR the State revised the penal code to equalise the age of consent for same- and opposite-sex conduct and to add sexual-orientation discrimination provisions. The platform also reports it has been excluded from state consultative processes despite repeated requests.

Gender identity was protected for the first time under the Employment Equal Treatment Act 2022, which bans workplace discrimination based on gender identity among other grounds. In January 2017 the Eerste Kantongerecht granted a transgender woman the right to have her gender formally changed with the Central Bureau of Civil Affairs and ordered the registry to officially change her registration to reflect her amended status. The Association of Pentecostal Churches in Suriname and the Suriname Islamic Association, which had protested against and opposed the right to recognize a gender change, indicated they would "accept the verdict". In February 2017 the Central Bureau of Civil Affairs formally appealed the court ruling. In January 2022 the Suriname Court of Appeal ruled in favor and ordered the gender change on the birth certificate of the transgender woman who had undergone sex reassignment surgery in 2009. Male and female same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1869 with an equal age of consent of 16 regardless of sexual orientation after Article 302 of the 1910 Penal Code, which set 18 for same-sex acts, was amended in 2015. In March 2015 articles 175, 175a and 176 of the Penal Code were updated to include sexual orientation as a ground for hate speech non-discrimination complaints, with violation punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine. Articles 176c and 500a forbid discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment and the provision of goods and services. Same-sex marriages, civil unions or domestic partnerships are not recognised by law, and in February 2023 the Constitutional Court ruled the ban does not violate the constitution or obligations under the Interamerican Convention on Human Rights while finding the Civil Code outdated and needing modernization following public debate. On 13 February 2025 Judge Shanti Bikhari ruled the laws used to disallow same-sex marriage conflict with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the Interamerican Convention on Human Rights, ordered the state to change the relevant laws and required the Bureau of Civil Affairs to register the marriages, though this may still be overruled. Suriname is legally bound to the January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruling holding same-sex marriage is a human right protected by the American Convention on Human Rights.

On 31 January 2023 the Constitutional Court held the Civil Code to be very outdated, not keeping pace with contemporary developments and urgently requiring amendment, and in the referenced transgender Yvanna precedent the Hof van Justitie had ordered the State/CBB to amend her identity in the public population registers after a gender change completed abroad because outdated legislation could not justify violating her human rights.

On 11 January 2017 the Kantongerecht in the Eerste Kanton granted a post-operative trans woman who underwent male-to-female surgery on 22 April 2009 and had obtained a forename change on 12 January 2011 an order changing her legal sex registration from male to female, holding that the contradiction between socio-psychological gender role and birth-certificate registration violated the right to respect for private life under Article 17 Constitution, Article 17 ICCPR and Article 11 ACHR, and, finding Suriname law provides no statutory procedure for transsexual gender-marker change, broadly interpreted Articles 17 and 64-67a Civil Code under Articles 106 and 137 Constitution to order the civil registrar to add a marginal note recording her as belonging to the female sex.

On 21 January 2022 Suriname's Hof van Justitie granted official recognition of gender change to Yvanna Paris Simpson, establishing a court-based precedent allowing transgender persons to seek amendment of sex and name on birth certificates and official registers, with execution via the Ministry of Interior Affairs still sought and comprehensive self-determination legislation to allow change without lengthy, degrading treatment still lacking.

A regional rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal for men and women nationwide; legal gender recognition NOT possible; LGBTI organisations CAN register; a constitution clause of 'any other status' is read by the authorities as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity despite no explicit statutory protection.

A civil-society report (July 2024): the constitution covers SOGI only implicitly through 'any other status', and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since 1869; the report urges a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

A national government's annual human-rights reporting (2015) for this country: documents a former leader's trial, police brutality, corruption, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex (LGBTI) persons and other minorities'.

A submission to a UN human-rights body from local groups and partners: despite constitutional protection, LGBTI persons still face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation; in March 2015 a penal code was revised to cover discrimination and hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation.

A UN human-rights committee review of this country (July 2024): the authorities asserted their laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, backed by a national inclusive labour-market commission, while experts pressed on implementing a regional human-rights court's judgment on transgender identity; the review welcomed the abolition of the death penalty in the penal code (2015) and military code (2021).

A UN pre-review summary (March 2016) from the local platform: since a 2011 review the country revised its penal code to equalise the age of consent for same- and opposite-sex conduct and to add sexual-orientation discrimination provisions; the platform also reports exclusion from official consultative processes despite repeated requests.

On 12 October 2022 a 19-year-old attacker whose primary target was then-prime minister Eduard Heger, with the LGBT bar Teplaren as 'plan B', arrived about 18:35 and at 19:11 fired eight shots at Teplaren, killing two and injuring one.

Feature of 7 February 2023: Slovakia's trans community remains precarious after the 12 October 2022 terrorist attack on the Bratislava LGBT bar, which rights groups say 'marked a new era' for trans people in the country. Existing transition rules already required surgical sterilisation before changing documents, and the aftermath brought even greater fears about the future.

Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Dunja Mijatović's letter (April 2023) to the Slovak National Council: six months after the Tepláreň attack, no discernible progress; human rights of LGBTI people appear more, not less, at risk; concerned about regressive legislative proposals including the LGR ban bill.

Same-sex sexual activity was legalised in Czechoslovakia in 1962, and the age of consent was equalised at 15 in 1990 after previously standing at 18 for same-sex activity. The Criminal Code amendment of May 2013 added sexual orientation as a hate-crime ground carrying harsher penalties and outlawed hate speech on that basis. The Anti-Discrimination Act, adopted in 2004 to meet EU requirements and broadened in 2008, outlaws discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity across employment, education, housing, social care and the provision of goods and services; Article 2 lists sexual orientation among protected grounds. The Act applies to the military, where LGBT people serve openly, though a 2005 Pravda report described a 'very homophobic environment' in the armed forces. Bills to criminalise trans lives were tabled by ĽSNS on 12 February 2021 and by the Republic Movement on 23 September 2021, and again on 13 January 2023; they sought to ban legal gender change and, in the 2023 version, to outlaw medical transition with a prison sentence of at least four years. All failed, mostly on abstentions. A bill of 24 February 2023 restricting legal gender change to people whose sex was 'wrongly assigned at birth', provable only by a karyotype test, passed first reading with 87 votes. Slovakia's first gay Pride, held in Bratislava on 22 May 2010, drew about a thousand attendees confronted by right-wing groups who threw stones at speakers, dispersed tear gas and infiltrated the march, forcing cancellation of the city-centre route; 29 people were arrested. On 3 July 2024 the serving Minister of Culture, Martina Šimkovičová, made a public homophobic and racist statement claiming Europe is dying because of 'an excessive number of LGBT people'. Transgender people in Slovakia have difficulty accessing healthcare. Following the revocation of the Ministry of Health's standards of care on 18 May 2022 under pressure from the Conference of Slovak Bishops and MPs, no valid standards existed, and as of 18 November 2022 healthcare providers were refusing transgender care, forcing trans people to seek treatment abroad. Standards were republished on 3 March 2023, but their implementation in care access and civil registries 'remains to be seen', and the guideline allowing document change without surgery was revoked on 21 November 2023 on grounds of 'government coalition stability'. In practice surgical sterilisation has usually been required for legal gender change, and registry offices refuse to process gender changes pending new standards. Gay and bisexual people are barred from donating blood if they had unprotected sex within one year, and any existing marriage is invalidated on change of legal gender. Slovakia recognises no civil unions or same-sex marriage. Bills introduced in 1997, 2000, 2012, 2018, 2021 and 2022 were all rejected (2012: 94 against to 14 for; 2018: 31 of 150 in support; 2021: 7 for, 67 against). Since 1964 the law recognises only a 'close person' (sibling or spouse) with limited rights, mainly inheritance. In June 2014 a constitutional amendment (Article 41) defining marriage as 'a unique union between a man and a woman' passed 102–18, potentially rendering future recognition laws unconstitutional. As of 2025 only married couples may adopt, barring same-sex couples, single people and unmarried partners. Under the ECJ's Coman ruling of 5 June 2018, same-sex couples resident in Slovakia who married in an EU state where one partner is an EU citizen enjoy full residency rights, and the Interior Ministry announced immediate compliance. The Alliance for the Family's 2014 petition demanded a ban on same-sex adoption, the prohibition of sex education in schools and a referendum question barring schools from requiring children to take sexual-behaviour education. The third question was ruled unconstitutional, and the referendum of 7 February 2015 on the rest was invalid at 21.07% turnout after opponents urged a boycott. In the 2017 Iniciatíva Inakosť survey nearly 40% of LGBT respondents had faced active discrimination (15.2% in the last year); many reported low self-esteem, anxiety, depression, alcohol abuse and suicidal feelings from homophobic persecution, and fewer than half were willing to hold a partner's hand in public. The same year's survey found family disclosure reactions mixed, with 54% of mothers, 42% of fathers and 49.5% of grandparents accepting, while 28.5% of fathers and 29% of grandparents were indifferent. The shooting outside Tepláren, a well-known Bratislava gay bar, on 12 October 2022 killed two people plus the perpetrator and wounded a third. Slovakia is described as having some of the worst LGBTQ rights in the EU and less supportive public opinion than the Czech Republic; support is volatile, from 66% acceptance in a 2007 Pew survey to 29–57% backing civil unions in 2019, falling to 40% after the 2022 attack, while the 2015 Eurobarometer put Slovakia fourth-lowest in the EU on same-sex marriage at 24% and PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index ranked Slovakia 47th against Czechia 18th. The gay scene is small, consisting of a few bars and clubs in Bratislava.

An encyclopedia article on the October 2022 shooting in the capital: a radicalised teenager fired shots at an LGBT bar, killing two and injuring one; the bar was the secondary target of an attacker whose primary target was the head of government; the article documents the planning, the LGBT-venue target and the aftermath.

A regional investigative-journalism feature (Feb 2023): in the shadow of the attack, the situation of trans people in this country remains precarious — existing transition rules already required surgical sterilisation before changing documents, and the aftermath brought greater fear about the future; rights groups say the attack 'marked a new era'.
thin: no usable finding

texts.cleaned_text: Country overview updated 12 Mar 2026: Slovenia is regarded as among the most progressive countries in Central and Eastern Europe on LGBTIQ rights - same-sex relations legal nationwide, legal gender recognition possible, LGBTI organisations registerable - with comprehensive antidiscrimination laws enacted since 2016 explicitly covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

exact_spans: No substantive finding recorded.

texts.cleaned_text: Ministry of the Interior notice of 29 October 2022: the local-jurisdiction step in legal gender-change procedures was abolished on the recommendation of the Advocate of the Principle of Equality, so transgender persons are no longer exposed to involuntary disclosure of transgender identity in their local environment.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): Legebitra documented 17 cases of bias-motivated speech and TransAkcija documented 25 cases of direct bias-motivated incidents in 2023. After Pride, LGBTIQ+ organisations held a press conference about attacks and rising hate while the Prime Minister took three days to react and the Interior Minister made no statements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): the Health Ministry officially confirmed to the Interdisciplinary Council for Gender Recognition that medical treatment is not required for legal gender recognition and formally asked the Interior Ministry to amend the relevant Civil Registry Act sub-article. The review also notes the death at 73 of a founder of Slovenia's grassroots LGBTI movement.

US State Department 2023 report on Slovenia: no laws criminalise consensual same-sex conduct and there were no reports of state-condoned violence, but authorities recorded violence incidents without tracking case numbers and local NGOs called violence against LGBTQI+ persons prevalent and under-reported. In June 2023 a woman wearing a rainbow flag was assaulted near the Ljubljana Pride route, marchers had eggs thrown at them and rainbow flags were burned on video.

ENACT national report of January 2025 (EU CERV-2023 project): civil society provides LGBTI hate-crime victims counselling, advocacy and safe spaces, but LGBTI persons using generic victim-support services face heteronormative hurdles. The report documents institutional shortcomings in the anti-LGBTI hate-crime framework.

UPI report of 25 July 2006: Slovenia passed a law legalising same-sex marriage but restricted the ceremony to the two partners plus a local community registration official - no friends or relatives. Gay and lesbian organisations welcomed the move as a concrete step while criticising the law as 'insufficient'.

Inquirer/AFP (Dec 2015): Pope Francis urged Slovenian politicians to 'support the family' four days before the referendum on the gay-marriage law adopted by parliament in March - the referendum (later lost) followed a conservative challenge.

Expression rights are exercised publicly but contested. The annual Pride Parade in Ljubljana on 17 June 2023 drew roughly 3,500 participants under the slogan 'Več skupnosti, en boj' and was attended by President Nataša Pirc Musar. During and after the march attendees faced threats, violence, insults, flag burnings and property destruction. Police received a report of an unidentified suspect who physically assaulted two people, causing minor injuries, and were investigating attacks, theft and public-order disturbances. A Pride Parade Association representative said there had not been such hostility for years. Condemnations came from the Human Rights Ombudsman, the National Assembly president, the president and, on 20 June, the prime minister, while opposition leader Janez Janša and two ministers stayed silent. Youth-specific findings are limited to the political and educational sphere. Anti-discrimination rules in place since 2003 bar sexual-orientation discrimination in education, and the anti-discrimination bill approved 21 April 2016 and promulgated 9 May 2016 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. The 2016 law and the earlier rules are described as vague, open to interpretation and very rarely enforced. Youth wings are also a source of hostility: members of the youth wing of the Slovenian Democratic Party used biblical arguments at the June 2023 Pride Parade, and social media posts associated with them carried anti-LGBTIQ+ sentiment.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): this country is among the most progressive in its region on LGBTIQ rights — same-sex relations legal nationwide, legal gender recognition possible, LGBTI organisations able to register — with comprehensive anti-discrimination laws enacted since 2016 covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2024 (covering 2023), chapter on this country: a national LGBT advocacy organisation documented 17 cases of bias-motivated speech and a trans advocacy organisation documented 25 cases of direct bias-motivated incidents in 2023; after the pride march, LGBTIQ+ organisations held a press conference about attacks and rising hate, the head of government took three days to react, and the interior minister made no statements.
