exact_spans: Note: not retrievable at research time (access denied); the underlying repository entry (April 2024) covers the parliament approving new acts on legal gender and medical procedures performed on genitalia.

texts.cleaned_text: A Library of Congress entry dated April 2024 records Sweden's parliament approving new acts on legal gender and on medical procedures performed on genitalia.

TGEU report of 16 July 2025: Sweden's new Legal Gender Recognition Act came into force on 1 July 2025, simplifying the procedure but falling short of a full self-determination model, with medical barriers remaining.
SVT reported in October 2025 that the swimming-pool chain Medley stopped trans customers from choosing their changing rooms, an everyday facility-access restriction affecting trans visitors.

Brå (National Council for Crime Prevention) report 2024:13: supplements Swedish hate-crime statistics with a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences where police identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives - the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025): a bill would extend protection of victims of conversion practices when carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure. In November the Church of Sweden decided new priests must be willing to marry same-sex couples, passing 141 votes at the 2025 Church Council.

Open-access article in Sexuality Research and Social Policy (4 February 2016, vol 13, pp 119-129): traces LGBT policy development in Sweden's military from 1944 to 2014 - the historical record behind current service conditions.

2019 edition of the Spartacus Gay Travel Index reported by Newsweek: Canada, Portugal and Sweden tied as the most LGBT-friendly travel destinations - third-party evidence on Sweden's standing as a visitor destination.

TT/The Local, 28 January 2017: Sweden's main national board decided transgender people will no longer be classified as 'mentally ill', the depathologisation step for trans residents' diagnostic status.

Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity was legalized in Sweden in 1944 (age of consent 18); an equal age of consent of 15 was set in 1972. Homosexuality was declassified as an illness in October 1979; the coverage dates declassification of transgender status inconsistently, to 2017 in one place and 2009 in another. A 1987 law banning sex in gay saunas and prostitution, passed to combat HIV, was repealed in 2004. Until 2013, legal gender change required sterilization and sex reassignment surgery; these requirements were ruled unconstitutional in January 2013 and removed by the Riksdag in July 2013, with roughly 600–700 people later compensated 225,000 SEK each (law passed March 2018) for forced sterilization. Sweden's hate speech law covers sexual orientation (added by Riksdag vote in 2002, effective 1 January 2003) and 'transgender identity and expression' (effective 1 January 2019); transgender identity and expression were added to hate crime legislation on 1 July 2018, with sexual orientation added in 2010. The law has been criticised as 'selectively applied': authorities refused to prosecute a Halmstad imam who called homosexuality a 'virus' in 2015, and Pentecostal preacher Åke Green was convicted then acquitted through to the Supreme Court, which held European Convention religious-speech protections barred punishment. Anti-gender actors also target expression through knowledge production, labelling gender studies and intersectional feminist scholarship 'ideological or unscientific'. The source contains no visa or entry rules for LGBTQ travellers; the nearest material is that a 1978 state inquiry into the living conditions of gays and lesbians suggested granting refugee status to persecuted LGBTQ people, and that RFSL counselling centres in Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö assist people with contact to authorities and 'legal assistance with, for example, asylum and wills'. A 2021 study found migrant LGBTQ people have worse sexual health, avoid healthcare more, are more exposed to sexual violence and are more dissatisfied with their sexual life than other groups. Sweden has seen a rise in domestic anti-gender campaigns tied to a transnational movement opposing gender equality and transgender rights, mobilising around the pejorative concept of 'gender ideology'. Actors include the far-right Sweden Democrats and Christian Democrats, who oppose trans-rights legal reforms while framing opposition as protecting women's rights and Swedish values, and 'gender-critical' radical feminist groups — notably the Swedish Women's Lobby (SWL, founded 1997, umbrella for 57 associations representing over 130,000 women and girls), which in 2025 launched the Women's Platform for Action International (WoPAI) promoting 'sex-based rights'. Scholars document 'insidious de-democratization' and report growing political violence and intimidation against trans advocates, feminist scholars and racialized activists, including online harassment, threats and public vilification. Separately, misinformation that Sweden had banned gender-affirming care for minors spread on social media and was cited by US Republican politicians to justify outright bans. In March 2021 the Karolinska Institute stopped providing puberty blockers or gender-affirming hormone therapy to children and teens under 16, and to 16–18-year-olds outside approved clinical trials; on 22 February 2022 the National Board of Health and Welfare said puberty blockers should be used only in 'exceptional cases' backed by 'uncertain science' (guidance, not a ban). In 2021 the Board cut gender-affirming clinics from seven to three (those three yet to be chosen). In April 2024 the Riksdag approved new laws (234 for, 94 against) effective 1 July 2025 lowering the minimum age for legal gender change without a gender-dysphoria diagnosis from 18 to 16, requiring a doctor/psychologist statement plus National Board approval, and guardian approval for 16–17-year-olds; genital surgery is limited to 18+ and gonad removal to 23+ absent exceptional reason. Nationwide Board data released in 2026 showed trans children prescribed puberty blockers had slightly increased since the 2022 guidance. Anti-gender efforts also target gender studies and feminist scholarship in education, and Sweden's age of consent has been equal at 15 since 1972.

Academic article (2016): traces LGBT policy development in the parent nation's military from 1944 to 2014 - the historical record behind current service conditions.

News outlet (28 January 2017): the parent nation's main national board decided transgender people will no longer be classified as 'mentally ill', the depathologisation step for trans residents' diagnostic status.
As of 12 March 2026, same-sex relations are illegal for men and women throughout Eswatini. Legal gender recognition is not possible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register.
Freedom in the World 2024: Eswatini rated Not Free with an overall score of 17/100 (Political Rights 1/40, Civil Liberties 16/60) - an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space.

BTI 2024 country report: the government denies LGBTQ+ groups the ability to register as organisations, within a wider pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment under an oppressive environment ('Mswati must fall' having become a common protest slogan).

US State Department 2021 report on Eswatini: some traditional, religious and government officials criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In June, LGBTQI+ persons conducted a virtual Pride celebration without incident.
Swazi Media Commentary of December 2018: a church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened - religious-space inclusion documented alongside 'no let-up on discrimination in the kingdom'.

MambaOnline, July 2018: the first eSwatini Pride was declared a 'perfect success' - the inaugural Pride in the kingdom, marking public LGBT visibility in a state where same-sex conduct remains illegal.
MambaOnline, July 2019: Eswatini's registrar of companies refused to register an LGBTI group - the documented administrative blocking of organisational recognition in the kingdom.

Wikipedia country coverage: Rock of Hope states that with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and most choose to remain in the closet or move to South Africa. In April 2022 the High Court, while upholding refusal to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities, accepted that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. Officials refused to register ESGM in June 2019 on the grounds of morality. Same-sex couples are prohibited from adopting children, while prospective heterosexual adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced. There is no legal recognition of same-sex relationships. In June 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini said people of the same sex cannot even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not even ready to consider it; in 2014 Press Secretary Percy Simelane said the government was closely monitoring the situation with a view to take a legal position. A 2019 survey found 59% of LGBTQ Swazis had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities, with 30% denied healthcare services. In February 2012 public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign urging gay people to test for HIV, and Deputy Director of Health Simon Zwane said the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples, a move LGBTQ groups welcomed. Section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion. The National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (2021) state that the right to equality includes freedom from discrimination because of one's sex or sexual orientation, define gender-based violence to include violence directed at a person based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity, and name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. The National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 lists sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles. The 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation. A 2013 survey found 43% of lesbian and transgender respondents had attempted suicide in the past year and 78% regularly used intoxicating substances to feel normal. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. Limited protections exist in policy: the 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as free from discrimination including sexual orientation. In 2012 former Foreign Affairs Minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a UN working group call for an LGBTQ protection law, saying so few gays lived in Eswatini that drafting one was not worth the effort; in May 2017 the UN Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): common law criminalises consensual same-sex intimacy; no legal gender recognition and limited gender-affirming healthcare; intersex people lack safeguards; in April 2022 the high court rejected an LGBT organisation's bid for registration, but in June 2023 the supreme court declared the registrar's decision void; the commerce ministry still refuses registration, claiming the organisation's name and objectives 'seek to offend against customary principles'.

Freedom-watchdog annual assessment (2024): this country is rated 'not free' (17/100) - an absolute monarchy; political dissent harshly punished; discrimination against women and LGBT+ people among the human-rights problems.

Governance-index country report (2024) by a political foundation: the last absolute monarchy in its world region - the king and queen mother hold veto powers over all branches of government; governance and human-rights context.
A foreign government's 2021 human-rights report on this country: official assessment - sodomy laws (common law) remain; significant societal stigma; no legal protections for LGBT persons.

Media commentary site (Dec 2018): a church welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened in a residential area outside the capital; an activist at an LGBT advocacy organisation welcomed it while noting religious hate speech; a regional gender-rights report described a meeting where 20+ pastors called LGBTI behaviour 'demonic' and refused to let gay people 'flaunt' themselves.

Independent news site (July 2018): history made as the country's first Pride was declared a 'perfect' success - more than 2,000 people attended in the capital, with a police-escorted march around the main stadium; the organiser, an LGBT activist, was 'beyond thrilled'.

The same independent news site (July 2019): the country's registrar of companies refused to register the leading sexual- and gender-minorities organisation, calling its objectives a 'negative mindset' - other groups had to include 'acceptable' health/HIV aims to register; that organisation's first objective is to advance LGBT rights.

Cornell Law gender-justice page: under the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) Section 5, protected characteristics now include sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status, giving an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences. The Constitution separately guarantees freedom from torture (Art 16) and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex (Art 27).

PinkNews, 18 May 2016: Seychelles repealed colonial-era Penal Code Section 151, which had allowed up to 14 years' imprisonment for male same-sex sex - framed as the popular holiday destination 'opening its arms to LGBT people'.
The 2016 decriminalisation of same-sex acts is recorded as a significant legal change for the islands, and legal and social conditions for visitors continue to vary from the statutory position.

Erasing 76 Crimes, 27 September 2024: a newly revised law calls for increased prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward victims' sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability - per the Human Dignity Trust, after South Africa Seychelles is only the second African country to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation. Before 2016 the penal code punished male same-sex intimacy with up to 14 years.

Seychelles does not recognise same-sex marriage or same-sex civil unions. In June 2015, two men, one British national and one Seychellois national, were married at the British High Commission in Seychelles by Lindsay Skoll, the High Commissioner, through a foreign mission rather than under Seychellois law.

Legal-information institute's gender-justice page on this country: under the penal code amendment act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) section 5, protected characteristics now include sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status, giving an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences; the constitution separately guarantees freedom from torture (Article 16) and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex (Article 27).

Travel guide: notes the 2016 decriminalisation of same-sex acts as a significant victory for the country, while advising both local residents and tourists to stay vigilant and informed about the current legal and social landscape — practical visitor guidance for the destination.

texts.cleaned_text: Country overview updated 12 March 2026: Syria's legal landscape remains highly restrictive - Penal Code Articles 520 ('acts against nature') and 517 (public indecency) criminalise same-sex conduct for both men and women; legal gender recognition impossible; LGBTI organisations cannot register.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021): documents LGBT activism across the Middle East and North Africa including Syria, with tallies that ISIS claimed at least 16 killings in Syria for alleged sodomy as of June 2016 (23 in Iraq, 3 in Libya). Activists worked to draw attention to the killings including at the UN Security Council.

Syria Direct feature of 11 October 2020 (Will Christou, Alicia Medina): LGBT Syrians describe life at home and abroad - in Damascus homosexuality and 'public decency' offences are illegal, and a 36-year-old (Amira al-Tabbaa) describes living 'only in whispers' when meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes.

Newsweek, 2015: two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever meeting on LGBT rights at the UN Security Council - a closed session co-sponsored by the US and Chile - about the constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.

PinkNews, 23 June 2010: Syrian authorities raided several private gay parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men in the latest swoop - most charged with 'homosexual acts', others with dealing or buying drugs, per gaymiddleeast.com.

Expression is criminalised and chilled: Article 520 of the 1949 penal code prohibits "carnal relations against the order of nature" with up to three years' imprisonment, and a 2010 police crackdown arrested over 25 men on charges including homosexual acts, encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. Public cultural expression has been squeezed since the civil war: the region's only gay tour (Damascus and Aleppo, run by Bertho) stopped operating, and the underground LGBTQ hubs of Damascus have been eradicated. Hammams in Aleppo and Damascus were the main venues of the pre-2011 tour, described by its organiser as "a paradise for gay people" where "we never had any problems," but the civil war ended that activity. Digital expression persists anonymously: the "One of you" movement began on Facebook in March 2020, later moving to Twitter, with university students painting LGBTQ flag colours on their fingers and photographing themselves by a faculty building under #oneofyou, most using fake accounts for fear of being identified; reactions ranged from defence to threats of blood before it faded amid COVID-19. Earlier literary expression includes Nizar Qabbani's 1971 poem "The Evil Poem," describing a relationship between two women.

Health care access is shaped by official stigma and under-provision: in 2005 the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments publicly called HIV/AIDS "divine punishment" for fornication and homosexuality, while the Health Ministry claimed only 369 people were infected and offered free medicines, a figure NGOs estimated at least five times too low, and the UN chastised the government for ineffective prevention. The state runs voluntary HIV testing clinics, distributes pamphlets, tolerates the work of some NGOs, and offers a limited HIV/AIDS educational program for youth in secondary schooling; comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people does not exist. Prevalence is low, under 2 per 100,000 in the general population and under 1% among most-at-risk populations in 2018, with 1,013 reported cases through Q3 2019 since the first reported infections in 1987. Physical safety is also a care barrier: beatings and torture of LGBTQ people occur frequently, including attacks by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State, which reported executing at least 30 people for "sodomy" in its areas, an issue reported to the UN Security Council in August 2015 in the Council's first-ever discussion of LGBTQ concerns.

There is no anti-discrimination protection; the state criminalises same-sex conduct instead. Violence comes from non-state armed actors as well, and political actors endorse harsher treatment: Free Syrian Army member Nasradeen Ahme said he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals, while secular leader Miral Bioredda said Syrian society would say "no way" to gays claiming rights. In the diaspora, Syrian LGBTQ+ refugees face discrimination and exclusion in host countries based on race, language, skin colour and religious background.

Youth are both a target and an organising force. Abdulrahman Akkad, a Syrian young man in Germany, came out publicly on Facebook in July 2017 while under family pressure to marry against his will, and his case was raised in the German Parliament's 2020 human rights session. The 2017 film Mr. Gay Syria follows two gay Syrian refugees rebuilding their lives.

A monitoring organisation's report of April 2025: working through an on-the-ground reporter network, the organisation investigated and found inaccurate a report claiming LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted and targeted in a city, debunking it to avoid stirring incitement against the community.

Wikipedia country coverage: There are no laws formally restricting LGBTQ+ people's freedom of expression, association, or peaceful assembly, but discrimination and marginalization effectively limit these rights in practice. Chadian activists say social and familial pressure has been used to coerce LGBTQ+ people into changing their sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression. LGBTQ+ people continue to hide their identity to protect their safety, per the U.S. State Department's 2023 report. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal gender recognition in Chad, so transgender people have no pathway to amend official documents. The 2017 penal code (in force 1 August 2017) criminalizes same-sex sexual activity under Article 354, with imprisonment of three months to two years and fines of 50,000 to 500,000 CFA francs (about 89 to 885 USD). Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Chad, so same-sex couples cannot adopt children together. Single people may adopt, but this requires a social services investigation that includes an inquiry into the applicant's moral standing, which can be used as grounds to deny adoption — a route that can be weaponized against LGBTQ+ applicants. Wikipedia country coverage: Men who have sex with men (MSM) are unlikely to be able to donate blood, not because of a formal ban but due to discrimination and hostility when accessing healthcare. Because homosexuality is criminalized, authorities refuse to investigate or prosecute crimes committed against LGBTQ+ people, and local civil society members say dozens of LGBTQ+ people are imprisoned under the pretext of other charges. LGBTQ+ Chadians also have difficulty obtaining housing, employment, and government services. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in Chad. The one exception is Article 350(i) of the Penal Code, which imposes ten to twenty years' imprisonment when rape is committed because of the victim's sexual orientation. Despite constitutional universal suffrage, LGBTQ+ people are often denied voter registration by local authorities. Wikipedia country coverage: Former Prime Minister Delwa Kassiré Coumakoye defended the 2017 criminalization law on religious grounds, saying homosexuality is condemned by all religions. The National Assembly passed the penal code on 12 December 2016 by 111 votes to 1 with 4 abstentions, and after the 2013 arrest of two gay men in Abéché for celebrating their wedding, religious groups, women's groups, and youth associations petitioned the government to punish the men. LGBTQ+ people are societally viewed as threats to family, procreation, and marriage, homosexuality is perceived as a Western invention, and in a 2024 survey only 15 percent of Chadians felt their local area would be a good place for gay and lesbian people to live. Wikipedia country coverage: There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Chad. In 2013, two gay men were arrested in Abéché for celebrating their wedding — before the penal code formally outlawed homosexuality — the bar was ordered closed for two years, and both men were fined and initially given two-year prison sentences, with community outcry following their suspended sentences on appeal. Wikipedia country coverage: Article 360 of the Penal Code, Chapter III on sexual offenses against minors, punishes anyone who, without violence, maintains a sexual relationship or practices sexual touching on a person of the same sex under eighteen years of age with one to three years' imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 500,000 francs (about 177 to 885 USD). Youth associations were among the groups that petitioned the government after the 2013 Abéché wedding arrests, and Chadian activists report social and familial pressure used to coerce people into changing their sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression.

texts.cleaned_text: There is no legal way to change one's gender on government documents in Togo. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity and no law protects persons from discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. There is no law explicitly against cross-dressing, yet a transgender person was arrested in March 2018 for supposed cross-dressing. In 2023 TikTok influencer Bobo Períta, known for cross-dressing, was arrested for violating public decency, convicted on 1 June that year and sentenced to a civil prison in Lomé. In November 2019 police followed a transgender person home and refused to let her go until she had sex with them, with sexual assault prevented only by the presence of the victim's mother. These transgender-specific facts are distinct from sexuality-law provisions criminalizing same-sex intimacy, which do not on their face criminalize transgender status. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is illegal in Togo, first made illegal in 1884 under the German Togoland protectorate and continued under the Penal Code of 13 August 1980. The 1980 Code imposed one to three years imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 500,000 CFA francs. The 2015 Penal Code retained one to three years imprisonment but under Article 393 defined the offense as an indecent or unnatural act committed with a person of the same sex and increased the fine to one to three million CFA francs. LGBTQ advocacy is criminalized under Article 392 for spoken words, writing or images perceived as violating public decency, and LGBTQ organizations may register as health organizations but not as LGBTQ advocacy organizations. Enforcement includes arbitrary arrests and disproportionate use of neutral loitering and immorality laws against LGBTQ people, including the January 2021 arrest and imprisonment of a gay man and his partner until Afrique Arc-En-Ciel paid for their release. In custody and care, prison chaplains have refused communion to LGBTQ prisoners who have not repented for homosexuality, LGBTQ prisoners are denied HIV/AIDS treatment and condoms, and providers at HIV and STD treatment centers often discriminate against LGBTQ patients causing avoidance of care. Limited protection machinery includes Article 5 of the Press and Communications Code Law 2020-001 prohibiting dissemination of defamatory comments including homophobic defamation, and Decree No. 2023-116/PR Articles 17, 27 and 39 requiring passenger screening by the Passenger Information Unit to be non-discriminatory and not based on sexual life or sexual orientation and protecting sexual orientation in data processing. For LGBTQ people generally, intimidation, death threats and physical assault are reported, with mistreatment by civilians or state authorities tending to go unpunished and victims deterred from reporting by stigma and possible legal consequences from criminalization of homosexuality and LGBTQ advocacy. In 2020 there were 33 reported instances of human rights violations towards LGBTQ people, described as most likely a small fraction of overall cases. Religion plays a significant role in stigmatization of LGBTQ people generally, with Catholic bishops blaming misfortunes and disasters on homosexuality and religious programs used to perform conversion therapy. LGBTQ people generally experience discrimination in employment, housing, education and healthcare, including refusal of housing, family rejection, denial of healthcare, and additional discrimination against people with HIV such as expulsion by family or viewing illness as moral punishment.

LegalClarity (June 2026): marriage equality since January 2025 and anti-discrimination law since 2015, yet no mechanism to change the sex marker on birth certificate, national ID or passport (title prefixes locked to sex at birth; Name Act 1962 partial workaround) — precise current documentation-status read.

texts.cleaned_text: Fulcrum/ISEAS (June 2025): analyses the government's push to position Thailand as an LGBTQ+ tourism hub (Bangkok Pride 4 June backdrop) alongside marriage equality — weighs opportunities and challenges of a state strategy whose motives range from genuine commitment to economic opportunism

GlobalGayz archive (2007-10): index of Thai LGBT news of the era — the National Human Rights Commission's role, constitutional-charter gay-rights campaigns, Phuket acceptance/rejection accounts, and the 'Please call me Miss' debate on trans legal title — historical baseline showing how long recognition questions have been live.

NBC News/AP (29 Jan 2017): the Thai Department of Corrections says LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993; at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men. Trans woman Theerayut Charoenpakdee, stopped by police and expecting to be 'thrown in prison with all the men because I still have the title of Mr.,' was instead held in the separated wing. The government was also discussing what could be the world's first exclusively-LGBTQ prison facility (the Min Buri pilot), while accepting that transgender women elsewhere usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary. Of roughly 300,000 Thai prisoners, more than 6,000 were registered as sexual minorities.

Coconuts Bangkok (30 Aug 2016): trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested in June 2015 while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility; prison officials told her that under Thai law 'she remains a man' and no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, and during intake she was harassed and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections then announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility to prevent abuse of trans inmates, after Pattaya men's prison had already begun separating trans prisoners from cis men following reports of abuse. DOC figures: ~4,448 of ~300,000 prisoners identified as LGBT, 34 of them transgender. Activists welcomed the pilot but feared it 'could encourage exclusion' and insisted placement 'should be an option, not an obligation.'

The Gender Equality Act B.E. 2558 passed 13 March 2015 and in force 9 September 2015 bans discrimination based on gender identity and was the first law in Thailand to contain language mentioning LGBTQ people, punishable by up to six months in prison and a fine of up to 20,000 baht with an exception for education, religion and the public interest, with implementation described as spotty and inadequate in a 2021 Human Rights Watch report and low awareness in a 2019 UNDP report finding only 44% of LGBTQ respondents knew about the law. Gender-affirming surgeries have been performed since 1975 with Thailand among the most popular destinations globally, and puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones are available to minors, but there is no legal gender change mechanism as the Persons' Name Act debated in 2007 created an avenue to change names but not legal gender with approval discretionary to individual administrators. Post-operation male-to-female transgender government employees are not granted the right to wear female uniforms and are still expected to perform military service, and specific inequality includes a hospital refusal to allow a transgender woman who had undergone sex reassignment surgery to stay in a woman's ward, while a July 2019 proposal would allow those who underwent surgery to change legal gender on official documents plus name changes, marriage rights and conscription. All citizens age 21 and over assigned male at birth must undergo conscription via volunteering or lottery, with transgender women exempt on the basis of having gender identity disorder only if they can prove gender through medical examination described as stressful and humiliating, where those with hormone replacement therapy or breast augmentation have a high chance of exemption and those without must submit to extensive psychological evaluation. Blood donation rules allow transgender women who have not had sex with a male partner to donate while men who have sex with men remain banned, and prison policy places inmates in cells based on stated gender and sexual orientation as verified by a prison doctor meaning only medically transitioned trans women or kathoeys are placed with other women while non-transitioned kathoeys can request placement with other kathoeys. The Department of Corrections reported 4,448 LGBTQ prisoners in 2016 including 1,804 katoey and 34 male-to-female transgender people, with plans for a central prison for only LGBTQ inmates delayed over concerns about placement away from hometowns and relatives, and homosexual male prisoners like all male prisoners have heads shaved while female inmates are not allowed make-up but gay male inmates are. Transgender people face substantial employment barriers including full-time work, executive positions or promotions with daily discrimination and humiliation cutting short careers, and in education most schools require gendered uniforms according to sex assigned at birth causing discomfort, mental trauma and dropout, with a 2019 UNDP survey finding 32% of trans women faced workplace discrimination and among trans women 61% verbal abuse, 22% sexual assault, 11% physical abuse and 8% police harassment. Private, adult, consensual and non-commercial sodomy was decriminalized in 1956, the age of consent was set at fifteen regardless of gender or sexual orientation through the Penal Code Amendment Act of 1997, homosexuality was no longer regarded as a mental illness or disorder by the Ministry of Health in 2002, and in 2007 the definition of sexual assault and rape victim was expanded to include both women and men with marital rape prohibited. Same-sex marriage began performance and recognition on 23 January 2025 after the bill passed the House on 27 March 2024 and the Senate on 18 June 2024, was endorsed and published in the Royal Gazette on 24 September 2024 effective 120 days later, making Thailand the first Asian UN member state and 38th country with a comprehensive same-sex marriage law, amending the Civil and Commercial Code to replace men and women and husband and wife with individuals and spouses. Adoption by married same-sex couples became legal on 23 January 2025 under the Marriage Equality Act while single people and unmarried couples regardless of orientation or sex cannot adopt except single women for a special-needs child, and the law does not replace mother and father with gender-neutral parent raising activist concern over parental rights, with in vitro fertilisation access expected but requiring law change and surrogacy law amendment pending. Commercial surrogacy for foreigners travelling to Thailand was banned by Parliament in 2015 with only married couples as Thai residents allowed commercial surrogacy contracts, and Bangkok's Dusit district issued legally non-binding partnership certificates to same-sex couples from 14 February 2023 as the first jurisdiction. The same Gender Equality Act B.E. 2558 bans discrimination based on sexual orientation with the same penalties and exceptions, while the Thai Armed Forces lifted the ban on LGBT serving in 2005 after prior exemption as mental disorder, and the Thai Red Cross Society reaffirmed in May 2009 and October 2021 the ban on men who have sex with men donating blood citing higher HIV risk and a requirement that the rate fall below 1 in 100,000. Violence data includes the 2009 Chiang Mai pride parade violently protested leading to cancellation commemorated as Saturday the 21st with 21 February observed as the day against violence against LGBTQ, and a 2019 UNDP survey showing 53% verbal harassment, 16% sexually assaulted, 42% pretended straight, 49% contemplated suicide and 17% attempted, with corrective rape and murders categorized as crimes of passion noted due to absence of a hate crimes concept. The article states that "those whose gender expression or behavior falls out of social norms are less likely to be tolerated or accepted." The article states that "Transgender people are quite common in Thai popular entertainment, television shows and nightclub performances; however, transgender people lack various legal rights compared to the rest of the population, and may face discrimination from society." Employment exclusion is documented by the statement that "the doors of government agencies and large corporations are still closed to transgender women." Additional conditions include 2015 International Labour Organization research finding daily discrimination and humiliation cutting short transgender careers and discouraging job seeking, and a 2014 Matthayom 1 textbook describing transgender people as suffering from gender confusion khon long phet with officials reported to investigate after criticism that kham phet was more suitable. School uniform requirements according to sex assigned at birth cause discomfort, mental trauma and dropout pushing many toward sex work or high-risk behaviour, while broader surveys show 47.5% experienced family discrimination and difficulty accessing mental health and health care with discrimination.

The 2 July-6 August 2020 draft to amend Books 1, 5 and 6 of the Civil and Commercial Code would allow same-sex as well as different-sex couples to lawfully engage at age 17 as 'engager'/'engaged person' and marry at age 18 (earlier with court permission for reasonable cause), replacing 'man/woman' with 'person' and 'husband/wife' with 'spouse' to extend identical spousal rights and duties on cohabitation, maintenance, property, debts, contracts, divorce, compensation, guardianship, adoption and spousal inheritance to same-sex spouses.

By 8 September 2013 Thailand's Tourism Authority had launched the 'Go Thai Be Free' campaign to market Thailand as a pink/LGBT destination while same-sex marriage and civil union remained impossible, transgender men and women remained legally identified as their sex at birth with no gender-title change, and the Civil Partnership Bill after five reviews and public hearings in all four regions including a House Committee on Justice and Human Rights forum two months earlier remained off the House agenda after securing 20 MP signatures but only about 4,000 of the required 10,000 public signatures, leaving same-sex and transgender partners without spouse/partner inheritance, medical-care decision, and government spousal-benefit protections, so trans visitors receive tourist-oriented economic welcome and anonymity but not legal recognition or resident-equivalent rights.

The nation has no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, and no document of the nation can identify a trans woman as female; the 2015 gender-equality act is weakly enforced and there is no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime — the 2025 murder of a trans woman in a resort city highlighted the gap.

Same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025; the border authority runs a dedicated initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender; gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The prison authority told press (2017) that LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993 and that at one remand prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men; a trans activist detained in June 2015 while protesting the junta was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility, told that under the nation's law 'she remains a man'.

The prison authority announced a pilot using a prison in the capital as an LGBT facility, reported in 2016-17 as a possible world-first exclusively-LGBTQ prison; authority counts at the time recorded roughly 4,448 LGBT-identified prisoners among about 300,000 (34 transgender), with a 2017 figure of more than 6,000 registered as sexual minorities.

No current official placement rule or national special-unit or solitary-practice rule for trans prisoners is documented; whether a detained foreign visitor would be routed like the documented resident cases is not established.

Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression of support for LGBTQ people is effectively suppressed, and public attitude toward LGBTQ people has been described as "entirely negative," with a state of "hypervisibility" in which homophobic and transphobic remarks from politicians form part of everyday politics. The Supreme Mufti, Saidmukarram Abdulkodirzoda, has called same-sex relations a "disaster," condemned countries legalising same-sex marriage, and spoken against human-rights activists and anti-discrimination laws. LGBTQ groups operate anonymously, one focused solely on trans issues and one on general LGBTQ issues, and activists have no access to the Ministry of Health or other state authorities, making state-level advocacy impossible. Gender-affirming medical services are not available in Tajikistan, so trans individuals must go abroad to medically transition, and most doctors have no expertise in the treatments trans people need. Legal gender change is blocked in practice: Tajik law allows reassignment on some documents, but medical institutions issue no official documents for the purpose. A diagnosis of transsexualism is required, surgeries are required for transgender women but not men, and evaluation is by commissions of three psychiatrists on an unregulated case-by-case basis in which activists say bribes are often necessary. Only three to six people have successfully changed legal gender. A trans-focused NGO has drafted a hormone-replacement-therapy protocol used to educate endocrinologists. LGBTQ patients report disrespectful treatment by medical staff, and some Tajik psychologists and doctors offer pseudoscientific "cure methods" that treat homosexuality as an addiction like alcoholism or drug addiction. Same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to married heterosexual couples, and no relationship-recognition framework exists. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since May 1998, consensual sex between women was never criminalised, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The country's first anti-discrimination law, adopted in July 2022, dropped sexual orientation and gender identity as protected grounds, leaving only "sex." No findings on LGBTQ minors, education-sector policies or school environments.

texts.cleaned_text: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): the April 2022 Criminal Code retained the 'sodomy' provisions and increased both the severity and scope of punishments. Torture and inhumane treatment remain present throughout the country, with relatives reporting LGBTI people subjected to them.

US State Dept 2021 Human Rights Report, Turkmenistan: lists among significant human-rights issues laws criminalizing consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults, alongside officials in security services committing abuses and engaging in corruption with impunity.

EHPV mid-term UPR stakeholder submission (2020): LGBT persons and people living with HIV in Turkmenistan 'have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights'; identifies article 135 of the Criminal Code criminalising consensual same-sex acts between adult men as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination, and notes increasing flight abroad.

ECOM legislative analysis, 'Legislative analysis related to LGBT rights and HIV in Turkmenistan' (Tallinn, 2019, 11pp, with Turkmen.news): sets out the statutory provisions and barriers facing LGBT people and PLHIV, compiled for use by NGOs, community activists and government in planning advocacy.

Columbia Law School (May 1, 2007): the Sexuality and Gender Law Clinic secured US asylum (DHS) for an anonymous Turkmen woman persecuted because she is a lesbian and for her political opinions — believed to be the first-ever asylum granted to a lesbian from Turkmenistan; documents persecution grounds cited by people fleeing the country.

Goldberg Kohn (Sept 2019): attorneys secured asylum for a lesbian couple from Turkmenistan who feared persecution including imprisonment and torture; homosexuality is punishable by up to 2 years; suspects face interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals; women are vulnerable to sexual violence and 'honor killings'.

Per Wikipedia country coverage: male homosexuality is illegal under Criminal Code Chapter 3, Article 135 section (1), punishable by up to 2 years in prison, with additional terms of 2 to 5 years in a labor camp possible; Article 19 allows increased penalties for repeat convictions, and a 2019 amendment raised the prior 1997 maximum of 2 years. Enforcement was rare before Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow became president in 2006, and reported consequences now include state-sponsored violence and torture during criminal investigation, plus vigilante attacks, especially in prison. Investigations into offences under Article 135 are grossly humiliating and may involve torture by state and non-state actors, and repeat convictions can lead to compulsory psychiatric admission with involuntary conversion therapy; homosexuality is institutionally perceived as a form of mental disorder within these facilities. In October 2019 a gay doctor was tortured by the state apparatus over a long span before temporarily disappearing. In May 2020 multiple well-known figures from the modelling industry were arrested on charges of homosexuality. Transsexual people are an unacknowledged category in Turkmen law, as are homosexual women, for whom no penal provisions exist. The government has justified its discriminatory frameworks in UN dialogue by arguing that any deviations pose a potential threat to the fabric of Turkmen traditions and society, and it has rejected anti-discrimination legislation despite requests made via three Universal Periodic Reviews, though in February 2021 it told the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights it intended to 'study the option of introducing anti-discrimination legislation'. LGBTQ people in Turkmenistan face active discrimination and stigmatization compared to non-LGBTQ residents, and the country is one of only two post-Soviet states where male homosexual activity remains criminalized, alongside Uzbekistan. Media is entirely state-owned and no civil society exists, which the source identifies as the reason data on these issues is scarce. No youth- or minor-specific care access findings appear in the source.

texts.cleaned_text: Same-sex sexual acts have been legal in Timor-Leste since 1975. The UN Human Rights Council joint statement on sexual orientation and gender identity was adopted in 2011. Timor-Leste voted in favour of the 2013 UN resolution on vulnerability and disability.

New Naratif (June 2018): Timor-Leste's first-ever Pride parade in 2017 drew international attention and a televised endorsement from the Prime Minister. The report also records day-to-day rejection, including messages sent to the organiser's family.
VOA (July 2018): East Timor held its second annual LGBT pride parade in Dili on July 20.

Star Observer (July 2019): an estimated 3,000 people joined the 'Marsa Diversidade' Pride March in Dili on July 12, six times the turnout of the 2017 first parade. President Francisco Guterres publicly backed the event, stating 'I am a President for all people'.

Law No. 13/2022 Article 3-2(o), second amendment to Health System Law, requires health policy to ensure access to family planning, reproductive, school, visual, oral and mental health and early diagnosis without discrimination based on gender identity and sexual orientation. Law No. 6/2023 Article 6(n) provides all children and young people equal rights and prohibits discrimination based on sex, gender, sexual orientation, among others, and Ministerial Decree No. 11/MSSI/V/2024 requires all children and youth regardless of gender, nationality, sexual orientation, religion or disability to have adequate access to protection services and protection from violence including sexual and gender-based violence, abuse and exploitation. That 2024 child-protection SOP defines non-binary gender identity as any gender identity or expression not fitting binary man/woman or girl/woman, defines LGBTI children to include transgender children with different gender identities from birth assignment, states that "transgender children may be at greater risk of prejudice, stigma, violence or difficulties accessing humanitarian services," and requires case managers to respond to needs based on gender identity and sexual orientation and to treat survivors fairly regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity. Ministerial Decree No. 10/MSSI/V/2024 on management of gender-based violence expressly extends protection to lesbian, bisexual, transgender and intersex people, defines LGBTQI to include transgender people, prohibits social workers from discriminating based on gender and sexual orientation, and requires prioritizing victim safety without judgment, understanding LGBTQI terminology, reflecting on preconceptions, not taking gender identity or sexual orientation into account, using non-critical language, and not revealing gender identity and sexual orientation without authorization. CODIVA noted that transgender members of the community were particularly vulnerable to harassment and discrimination, transgender students were more likely to experience bullying and drop out at secondary level, and a 2017 survey of 57 young lesbian and bisexual women and transgender men found 86% had experienced both physical and psychological violence including domestic violence, forced marriages and attempts by family to change sexual orientation or gender identity. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity have been legal since 1975, with age of consent at 14 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. There is no legal recognition of same-sex unions: Civil Code Law No. 10/2011 Article 1467 defines marriage as a contract between two people of different sex, and Article 1517 declares marriage contracted by two people of the same sex legally non-existent, while Law on Domestic Violence No. 07/2010 treats people who live or have lived in conditions analogous to spouses as family even without cohabitation and broadly encompasses intimate relationships regardless of gender. There is no specific broad anti-discrimination law based on sexual orientation, and a clause against discrimination based on sexual orientation in the original draft Constitution was voted out by 52 of 88 MPs before the Constitution took effect in 2002. Specific laws ban sexual-orientation discrimination: Penal Execution Regime Decree-Law No. 14/2014 Article 3(3) requires impartial execution without discrimination based on sexual orientation; Land Law No. 13/2017 Article 2(i) includes sexual orientation in vulnerable groups; Law No. 3/2017 on trafficking Article 3 requires victim protection without discrimination based on sexual orientation; and since 2009 bias based on sexual orientation is an aggravating circumstance for crimes. National Police statutes ban sexual-orientation discrimination: Decree-Law No. 44/2020 Article 13(1) requires respectful treatment without discrimination based on sexual orientation, Decree-Law No. 69/2022 Articles 15(6)(f) and 18(b) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, and Decree-Law No. 35/2024 Articles 16(f) and 17(b) require missions and action without hindrance or discrimination by reason of sexual orientation. There are no explicit legal prohibitions against LGBTQ people serving in the Defence Force under Decree-Law No. 17/2006, Decree-Law No. 33/2020, Decree-Law No. 3/2021 and Decree-Law No. 5/2022, but there are no inclusive anti-discrimination measures, and the constitution and law are described as silent on same-sex relations with physical abuse in public or by public authorities uncommon but LGBTI persons often verbally abused and discriminated against in some public services including medical centers and with no specific employment protection based on sexual orientation. CODIVA noted that "transgender members of the community were particularly vulnerable to harassment and discrimination." The national child-protection SOP states that "transgender children may be at greater risk of prejudice, stigma, violence or difficulties accessing humanitarian services." While physical abuse in public or by public authorities was described as uncommon, LGBTI persons were often verbally abused and discriminated against in some public services, including medical centers. "Transgender students were more likely to experience bullying and drop out of school at the secondary level," with access to education limited for some LGBTI persons removed from the family home or fearing abuse at school. A November study for Rede Feto with lesbian and bisexual women and transgender men in Dili and Bobonaro documented corrective rape, physical and psychological abuse, ostracism, discrimination and marginalization by family members. A 2017 survey of 57 young lesbian and bisexual women and transgender men found 86% had experienced both physical and psychological violence, including domestic violence, forced marriages and attempts by family members to change sexual orientation or gender identity.

In 2017 in Timor-Leste same-sex sexual conduct was not criminalized but the law provided no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and transgender persons remained particularly vulnerable to societal discrimination, stigma and violence limiting access to employment, education and healthcare with no government action to prevent discrimination or violence.

texts.cleaned_text: Trinidad and Tobago Newsday (July 2024): 'Long way yet for recognition, safe spaces' - TT Transgender Coalition director Rae Alibey says the trans community is the most marginalised and not even recognised in T&T; gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation; gender-identity markers on institutional forms are absent; national discussions and attitudinal research needed.

Newsday (Nov 2024): police warning over cyber criminals - Grindr hook-ups ending in cars, cash and phones stolen; criminals create fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings followed by armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault; two separate incidents reported in one week.

Newsday editorial (June 2024): 'Grind hate to a halt' - a spate of Grindr-related attacks (almost half a dozen in recent months); Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne points to gaps in the law: 'We don't have a specific hate crime category in legislation'; the editorial argues the gap must be closed.

CNC3 (23 Aug 2024): the PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected adding sexual-orientation protections to the national constitution (decision announced at a special convention); CAISO's Dr Angelique Nixon said the community has 'been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection'. Documents LGBTQ-rights exclusion from the 2024 constitutional-review process.

GlobalGayz (Aug 2012) travel and culture profile states that homosexuality is illegal but that the laws are mostly ignored in practice, and describes the tourist-facing social scene and island context. The profile predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling, so its statement of the law does not reflect current law.

PinkNews (21 Nov 2017): first-person appeal by activist Jason Jones during his High Court challenge to T&T's same-sex criminalisation, stating he faces up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner. Marks the constitutional challenge that put the criminal law in play.

Erasing 76 Crimes (23 Jun 2016): PM Keith Rowley told Parliament (17 Jun 2016) the state must protect all citizens 'regardless of whom they sleep with', while refusing to repeal the same-sex criminal laws; cites Newsday. Documents the reform-refusal gap in official rhetoric as of 2016.

Trinidad Express (Camille Hunte, 28 Nov 2018) reports on the official 'Justice through a Gender Lens' Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers (launched Nov 2018 by the CCJ, CAJO, UN Women, JURIST Project, TTAWJ and the Judicial Institute of TT). The Protocol states that 'in Trinidad and Tobago, there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities'. It directs judicial officers sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to make recommendations to prison authorities so that provisions are in place for the inmate's physical safety, and instructs courts to refer to intersex and transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and to permit court access irrespective of dress. Housing placement for trans prisoners is therefore discretionary and unsafe, resting only on sentencing recommendations, with no facility of its own.

Wikipedia country coverage: Under Section 8 of the Immigration Act, homosexual men and women who are not citizens are prohibited from entering Trinidad and Tobago, though this law is not known to have been enforced. In 2016 the Caribbean Court of Justice ruled that neither Trinidad nor Belize violated Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson's freedom of movement, but clarified that neither state can ban homosexuals from CARICOM countries from entering due to treaty obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas, notwithstanding their laws that ban the entry of gays. Trinidad and Tobago does not recognize same-sex marriage or civil unions, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights and benefits as opposite-sex couples. In July 2018 Justice Frank Seepersad approved a property dispute resolution between two gay partners, noting unequal treatment under current law and warning that without agreement the court would have had to rely on innovative applications of trust law to determine property division after dissolution of a same-sex union. Same-sex couples are unable to legally adopt in Trinidad and Tobago. The Silver Lining Foundation is an LGBTQ group that seeks to end bullying against LGBTQ youth. A 2009 University of the West Indies study for the Ministry of Social Development found that four of every five Trinbagonians believed in denying someone rights or equality based on sexual orientation, prompting the founding of CAISO to encourage public discussion and legislative protections.

The courts struck down the historic buggery laws (2018 legal challenge, upheld on appeal); there is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Police have publicly warned of a spate of dating-app ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024); community advocates report trans people are still 'beaten, stoned and chopped,' with most incidents never reported.

The 2018 gender-equality protocol for judicial officers says plainly that 'there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities'; the only mechanism is a judicial officer's sentencing recommendation that prison authorities make provisions for the inmate's physical safety; the Protocol was a justice-sector initiative launched in November 2018 by a coalition of regional and international judicial bodies and national judicial institutions.

texts.cleaned_text: Erasing 76 Crimes (27 Sep 2017): Tunisia pledged to the UN to stop forced anal testing in homosexuality cases, but kept the anti-gay law itself; Kapitalis warns the pledge does not decriminalise anything.

Legal recognition for transgender or gender non-conforming people in Tunisia is described as inconsistent. Cross-dressing is not expressly illegal, although transgender people, along with gay people, are often accused of violating Article 226 of the Penal Code which outlaws "outrages against public decency". On 22 December 1993, the Court of Appeals in Tunis rejected a trans woman's request to change her legal gender (statut civil) from male to female, declaring her gender change a "voluntary and artificial operation" that does not justify a change in legal status. In 2018, a trans man succeeded in changing his legal status in what is described as a revolutionary judgement. No transgender-specific provisions on detention procedures, identity documents beyond civil status change, screening, facilities, custody, care, or protection machinery are stated. Article 230 of the Penal Code of 1913 (largely modified in 1964) punishes private consensual sodomy between adults with imprisonment of up to three years, covering both male and female same-sex sexual activity, rendered in Arabic as "Liwat" (male homosexuality) and "El Mousahaka" (female homosexuality). Authorities occasionally use the anti-sodomy law to detain and question persons about their sexual activities and orientation. Enforcement involves anal examinations as evidence, with refusal treated as evidence of guilt, including a June 2017 case where a 16-year-old was sentenced to four months in jail for homosexuality after refusing examination. On 7 December 2016 two men were arrested in Sousse on suspicion of homosexual activity, subjected to anal probing and forced to sign confessions of sodomy, and on 11 March 2017 while on bail were given eight-month prison sentences. On 3 June two men were arrested on suspicion of same-sex conduct and subjected to attempted anal examination, followed by sentencing for homosexuality reported on 6 July 2020. Recorded enforcement totals were 56 jailed in 2016, 79 in 2017, and 127 in 2018, with at least 22 arrests by April 2019. In September 2017 Minister Mehdi Ben Gharbia agreed to stop forced anal tests, stating exams could no longer be imposed by force, physical or moral, or without consent, yet courts continued ordering anal tests throughout 2018 and 2019. LGBTQ Tunisians face both legal and social discrimination. Reports of family rejection, violence in public spaces, violence within families and suicides are quite common. No shelter, victim-protection, medical care, custody, facility-access, or other protection machinery specific to transgender visitors is described. Documented tolerance figures and official statements in the article address homosexuality or sexual orientation generally, not transgender people specifically, including opposition to same-sex marriage and support for punishing homosexuals and official descriptions of homosexuality as perversion or illness requiring treatment. The article contains no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically to quote.
The Court of First Instance in Tunis held that gender identity disorder is a psychological condition that permits legal change of sex.

texts.cleaned_text: Human Rights Watch (22 May 2008): launches the 123-page report 'We Need a Law for Liberation' from 70+ interviews over three years — documents a continuing history of beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people in Turkey.

SCF (18 Dec 2025): transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and Turkish rights groups (coordinated from Human Rights Association / IHD branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakir, Mersin and Aydin) demanded an independent investigation and changes to 'detention practices affecting transgender prisoners'. Kaos GL-cited accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers say four transgender inmates were collectively sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators only entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; opposition MP Sevda Karaca (EMEP) raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025. The case documents that Turkey holds trans prisoners in gendered facilities by registered sex (a trans man was held in a women's prison) and that trans-prisoner custody conditions were formally contested at the state level in late 2025.

Kaos GL (7 May 2024), covering the Prison Insider Country Profile report on Turkey prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association (CISST) and using ILGA World data: LGBTI+ prisoners in Turkish prisons are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches and to de facto isolation, being placed in solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and sometimes refusing to go to hospital out of fear of other male prisoners during transfers. CISST observations quoted in the article state that there is no policy or staff training to identify and address LGBTI+ prisoners' needs, that Turkish prison administration is built on a binary, heteronormative system, that LGBTI+ prisoners are frequently transferred (disrupting visits and solidarity), and that complaints are ineffective and can lead to further violence. The piece documents that Turkey manages trans and LGBTI+ prisoners through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement.

Turkey has no visa, entry or border rules specific to LGBTQ travelers; the available material concerns people already in the country. LGBT individuals are among the most vulnerable asylum seekers and refugees in Turkey, and their access to rights and services is limited by anti-LGBTQ sentiment among state actors and the general public.

Sex reassignment surgery is available in Turkey's major cities (Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir and Antalya) and the minimum age for the procedure is 18. To change the gender marker on an identity card, the procedure must be conducted at a state hospital. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors needing continued medication must arrange and pay for it privately.

Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no direct discrimination protection regarding gender identity in Turkish law. The EU Commission's 2025 annual report wrote that legal protection of LGBTIQ persons is insufficient and not aligned with the EU acquis, and that authorities were granting official permissions for demonstrations promoting exclusion and discrimination. Bills to introduce such protections have been repeatedly proposed (CHP, February 2015) and constitutional protection agreed in 2013 draft talks, but the drafts were cancelled; KAOS GL has a case pending since 2023 alleging ineffective remedies against discrimination such as Pride bans. The government considered legislation criminalizing public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with one to three years' imprisonment, though it was not included in the 2026 judicial package.

Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as joint parents. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, which made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, but these carry no legal marital status. Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, so individuals who have legally changed their registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender; LGBT marriage for non-trans people remains legally impossible.

Youth opinion is more accepting: a 2020 Pew Research Center survey found acceptance of homosexuality higher among youth (34%) and educated respondents (41%) than the 25% national figure, and Kadir Has University polling showed support for equal rights rising from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020. Student organizing exists: the Lesbian and Gay Inter-University Organization (LEGATO) formed in 1996 with groups at several universities by 2014, yet in May 2019 police broke up a student Pride march at Middle East Technical University, arresting at least 25 students. Minors are a stated focus of the crackdown: Erdoğan's May 2025 "Decade of Family and Population" declaration (starting 2026) attacked the LGBTQ movement as a threat to children, and the September 2026 "My Family is Safe" raids against LGBTQ+ and HIV support organizations were framed as protecting children, with 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses under investigation. In April 2026 the İzmir group Genç LGBTI+ was ordered to dissolve with eleven founders put on trial, and RTÜK's stated goal includes "protecting children, youth and the family structure," backing fines against Amazon Prime Video, Disney+, HBO Max, Netflix and Mubi for LGBTQ+ content. For trans youth, the minimum age for sex reassignment surgery is 18 and the procedure must be performed at a state hospital to change an identity-card gender marker.
