ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Tuvalu: male same-sex conduct is criminalised under colonial-era provisions.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Tuvalu: traditional customs perpetuate religious and social discrimination including against women; no government abuses; the LGBT section notes criminalisation under the Penal Code but no prosecutions.

Tuvalu Ministry of Health Global AIDS Progress Report 2017 (UNAIDS) sets out the national HIV response, which draws on the Pacific Multi-Country Mapping and Behavioural Study on HIV and STI risk vulnerability among key populations, including MSM and transgender Tuvaluans.

US Mission Geneva release, 22 Mar 2011: Tuvalu is among roughly 80 signatory states of the UN joint statement recalling General Assembly resolutions on human rights, sexual orientation and gender identity, documenting Tuvalu's 2011 diplomatic position.
The GlobalGayz Tuvalu archive records Tuvalu's colonial-era sodomy-law status and carries an OHCHR Human Rights Day op-ed urging states to decriminalise consensual same-sex relations.

Wikipedia country coverage: Sections 153, 154 and 155 of the Penal Code make male homosexual intercourse, attempts and gross indecency between males felonies punishable by up to 14, 7 and 5 years' imprisonment respectively, creating a theoretical custody exposure for trans women perceived as male. In practice the source reports the law is not enforced, with the US Department of State noting no prosecutions of consenting adults under these provisions as of 2013. No detention-conditions, strip-search or specific custody-treatment findings for transgender detainees appear in the text. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2011 Tuvalu signed the UN "joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity," condemning violence and discrimination against LGBTQ people. The source does not document any specific hate-crime incidents, statistics or hate-crime legislation for Tuvalu. Wikipedia country coverage: The Labour and Employment Relations Act 2017 bans workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation, covering a broad list of protected grounds including gender, sex, pregnancy, marital status, HIV/AIDS status and disability. Constitutional protection is weaker: the freedom from discrimination in section 27 of the Constitution (as amended in 2023) lists sex among protected attributes but does not refer to sexual orientation. No gender-identity or gender-expression protection is described anywhere in the text. Wikipedia country coverage: Tuvalu does not recognize same-sex marriage or civil unions; the 2023 constitutional amendments banned same-sex marriage, and the Charter of Duties and Responsibilities in section 43(2)(b) defines a family unit as "a marriage as between a man and a woman to the exclusion of all others." The Marriage Act (Cap 29) does not expressly prohibit recognition of same-sex unions but generally assumes the parties are male and female, and same-sex marriages do not appear in its "restrictions on marriage" section. No partner-visa, next-of-kin, or foreign-union recognition provisions are discussed. Wikipedia country coverage: A 2005 study found about 14% of young Tuvaluan men aged 15 to 24 had had sex with a male partner at some point in their lives. The age of consent is 15 for heterosexual vaginal sex and lesbian sex, while the Penal Code's male homosexual provisions carry separate felony penalties (14, 7 and 5 years), an asymmetry that affects young men who have sex with men. 2017 UNAIDS estimates put the population at about 300 MSM and about 40 pinapinaaine nationwide; no education-policy, school-bullying or youth-service findings are given.
A country page on an international legal-rights database: documents this country's legal status — male same-sex conduct criminalised under historic provisions.

A foreign government's 2013 human-rights report on this country: traditional customs perpetuate religious and social discrimination including against women; no government abuses; the LGBT section notes criminalisation under the penal code but no prosecutions.

The health ministry's 2017 global AIDS progress report (UNAIDS): the national HIV response, drawing on a regional multi-country mapping and behavioural study on HIV and STI risk vulnerability among key populations (including MSM and transgender residents).
A foreign mission's post (March 2011) on LGBT rights in the UN context - this country was among the states of its region signing a joint statement of support for decriminalisation and SOGI rights.

LGBT travel-news archive: includes a UN human-rights office opinion piece on decriminalising homosexuality as a first step toward equality (Oct 2011), noting this country among regional states supporting the UN call.

Taiwan Insight (Feb 2026): 'What about trans rights? Taiwan's ongoing struggle for self-ID' - the 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery to change legal gender blocks an estimated 90% of trans people from obtaining matching national ID; every ID-requiring aspect of daily life (clinics, airport security) becomes a potential site of distress and discrimination; the Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013.

Taiwan Insight (Jan 2026): the Taiwanese government continues to flounder on transgender rights in 2025 amidst continued transphobia - no tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction; pending conscription-criteria changes could actively harm trans people; anti-gender movement activity rising, with organisations supporting Trump's anti-trans policies and the Taiwan Solidarity Party calling for a 'two genders' position.

Taipei Times (Aug 2024): the Ministry of Environment will invest NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms nationwide (623 to 1,246 by 2029); of trans and gender-neutral survey respondents reporting discrimination, 17% occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms.

Focus Taiwan (Nov 2025): 'Most Taiwan all-gender restrooms do not meet standards: Rights group' — an LGBTQ+ rights group finds only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage.
The source page addressing Taiwan's transgender rights, covering laws, protections and gaps, was unavailable at research time (HTTP 404, page removed).
New Bloom (Nov 2024): analysis of the wave of anti-gender discourse in Taiwan - rising anti-gender movement activity and its political context.

TaiwanPlus (Aug 2024): a Taipei court denied a transgender woman's request to change the gender marker on her government ID without requiring surgery or a psychological evaluation; the supporting rights group says they will likely appeal.

JURIST dispatch (Nov 2025): the 7th annual Taiwan Transgender March in Taipei drew an estimated 3,000 people despite rain, with international participants; calls for an end to discrimination against trans people as the rights debate continues.

Utopia Asia Taiwan travel and resources page: 'one of Asia's most progressive countries for LGBT rights, and certainly the most liberal of the Chinese diaspora'; notes Taiwan regularised adoption for same-sex parents on May 16, 2023; listings of organisations, bars, spas and venues across 12 cities.

Wikipedia country coverage: Private, consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Historically, a 1740 Qing decree criminalised voluntary homosexual intercourse between adults (punishable by a month in prison and 100 heavy blows), while the Republic of China's provisional criminal code abolished explicit prohibitions on 'consenting ji jian' around 1912 and sodomy was decriminalised when the ROC took over Taiwan after World War II under the 1935 criminal code. During martial law, LGBT people were harassed and detained under general public order laws (Temporary Provisions against the Communist Rebellion), repealed in 1991. Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression is open and expanding: the first Taiwan Pride was held in Taipei on 1 November 2003 with over 1,000 attendees, growing to about 80,000 by 2015, 137,000 in 2018 and 170,000 by 2019, with pride events also held in Kaohsiung (since 2010) and Taichung (20,000 in 2016). LGBTQ representation in literature and film — from Pai Hsien-yung's novel Crystal Boys in the 1970s to Ang Lee's Brokeback Mountain (2005) and Zero Chou's Spider Lilies (2007 Berlin Teddy Award winner) — is described as instrumental in raising public awareness. In 2022 Taiwan withdrew from hosting WorldPride 2025 over the disputed name 'WorldPride Kaohsiung,' which the public and government considered offensive, and the event moved to Washington, D.C. in June 2025. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples can legally adopt, and since May 2023 legislation has granted full adoption rights, replacing the partial (stepchild-only) adoption rights in place since 2019. Until 2023 they could only adopt the biological child of their partner; a January 2022 court order had already allowed a same-sex couple to adopt before the legislature codified full rights. Taiwan law also permits single individuals, including individual LGBT people, to adopt depending on circumstances, while the Artificial Reproduction Act limits IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies to legally married heterosexual couples, specifically excluding same-sex female couples and single women. Wikipedia country coverage: Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender characteristics has been banned in education nationwide since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004 (fine of NT$100,000 for schools discriminating in admission, instruction or assessment). Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 2007–08 amendments to the Employment Service Act and the Act of Gender Equality in Employment, with fines of NT$300,000 to NT$1,500,000. The Long-Term Care Services Act (January 2017) contains an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and Judicial Yuan Interpretation No. 748 (24 May 2017) held that the Constitution's Article 7 grounds of discrimination are 'illustrative, rather than exhaustive,' so sexual orientation is protected by the right to equality. Wikipedia country coverage: Discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in education has been banned since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004, with sexual-bullying prevention and reporting duties added in June 2011. In November 2018 voters passed a referendum question to ban LGBT-inclusive sex education in schools (Question 11) and rejected the pro-inclusion Question 15; Education Minister Yeh Jiunn-rong said LGBT content would be reviewed against the result, and an earlier Ministry of Education curriculum reform (announced March 2010, effective 2011) had already been watered down to 'respecting diverse sexual orientations' after anti-LGBT opposition. Following that referendum, suicide hotlines reported a 40% surge in calls from LGBT individuals, particularly adolescents and young adults. Youth-relevant health measures include the 22 February 2018 Ministry of Health and Welfare letter effectively banning conversion therapy, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.

Amnesty International report (Jan 2024, AFR 01/75/33/2024, 'We Are Facing Extinction'): documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people in Tanzania, with legislation on same-sex relations deferred after protests, in a documented climate of discrimination limiting rights enjoyment — national-level findings.

Interview (Rainer Ebert, 4 Sep 2020) with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists: documents substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence against LGBT people in Tanzania and denial of basic rights, with homophobia and transphobia driving the urgency of rights advocacy; includes definitions of sexual orientation, gender identity and trans woman terms.

Zanzibar Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004 (full text, PDF): enacted by Zanzibar's House of Representatives; defines 'gross indecency' broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse, sets sexual-offence age thresholds (absolute under 12; under-18 and marriage distinctions) and penalties including imprisonment for three years — Zanzibar-specific criminal law applying to the semi-autonomous islands alongside mainland law.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Tanzania: the three most widespread problems were security-force excessive force, gender-based violence including FGM/C, and lack of access to justice; also 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' and societal violence against persons with albinism.

Government respect for freedom of speech and freedom of assembly is described as declining, and UN human rights defenders in Tanzania may not make public statements supporting tolerance for fear of reprisals. The 2018 broadcast content regulations bar inciting hatred on grounds of sexual preference; the online content regulations issued the same year banned such hate speech but were completely repealed by the 2020 online content regulations. The Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics for Media Professionals still bars hate speech, stereotypes and discrimination based on sexual orientation. Activists Maria Sarungi Tsehai, Fatma Karume, Mwanahamisi Singano, Carol Ndosi, Zara Kay, Khalifa Said and Goodluck Haule have openly backed LGBTQ rights against officials such as Magufuli, Paul Makonda, Ally Hapi and Hamisi Kigwangalla, who pushed persecution. In October 2017 the government deported staff of several HIV/AIDS groups on the basis of 'promoting homosexuality', directly disrupting services. In 2018 a 'witch hunt' against gay people was declared in Dar es Salaam, where gay men were forced to undergo anal examinations and torture. Also in 2018 Paul Makonda, the Dar es Salaam Regional Commissioner, announced a 17-strong committee of police, lawyers and doctors to identify and punish homosexuals, scouring the internet for videos of supposedly LGBTQ people; the Foreign Ministry said the crackdown lacked government support and Denmark withheld 65 million kr (about US$9.8 million) in aid. A 2013 Human Rights Watch and Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition report documented torture of LGBT people in police custody, including a 19-year-old gay man arrested after leaving a nightclub in Mbeya who said police raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. The US State Department's 2013 report likewise details police custody abuse and describes Tanzania's human rights record as poor. There are no gay bars in Tanzania, although some places exist where gay men meet, and lesbians are less visible than gay men. Tanzania has a high HIV/AIDS rate with reportedly one million people infected. On the policy side, the 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards commit to services 'regardless of age, parity, marital status, creed, race, color, or sexual preference', counselling 'any woman, man, couple, or young person regardless of age'; the Nursing and Midwifery (practice) Regulations 2010 bar withholding nursing care based on sexual orientation; and the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care require non-discriminatory care. No youth-specific healthcare provision beyond the age-inclusive family planning counselling language is stated. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition anywhere in Tanzania, so no partner can be sponsored, inherited from, or recognized as next of kin through relationship status. Adoption requires a married couple, so a same-sex couple cannot adopt jointly. Same-sex sexual acts between men carry a maximum penalty of life imprisonment under the Penal Code as revised by the Sexual Offences Special Provisions Act 1998 (section 138A 'gross indecency', 1–5 years or fines of TSh 100,000–300,000 for the general offence), and Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934 (as amended 2004) outlaws sex between women with up to five years' imprisonment or a TSh 500,000 fine. Heterosexual oral and anal sex is also illegal.

A legal-news outlet (9 Jun 2024): a human-rights office condemned as 'horrendous' the attack on a transgender activist — abducted by 12 men, found beaten in a forest with her ears cut — calling for 'bold action to combat discrimination against LGBTIQ+ people'; it flagged possible violations of international and constitutional equality guarantees.

Amnesty International (23 Oct 2024) report 'Everybody Here Is Having Two Lives or Names': the devastating impact of criminalisation on digital spaces for LGBTQ people in Uganda — widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence (doxxing, impersonation, hacking, disinformation); the AHA 2023 fostered a climate of impunity forcing people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.

AP (Feb 2026): 'Ugandan police arrest two women for allegedly kissing in public' — two women detained in Arua after neighbours reported them; one of the first known arrests under the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Uganda: the three most important problems included 'violence and discrimination against marginalized groups (women...; children...; persons with disabilities; and the lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender community)' - the era of the Anti-Homosexuality Bill debates.

Wikipedia country coverage: In October 2021 trans woman Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro was issued identification documents identifying her as female, the first Ugandan to have a change of gender legally recognised; the source does not address broader document or legal gender recognition processes beyond this case. In June 2021 a raid on the Happy Family Youth Shelter in Kampala resulted in forty-four arrests, with police claiming an illegal same-sex wedding was being held, and several detainees alleged police performed invasive anal examinations. Under the Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023, people convicted of homosexuality or attempted homosexuality cannot be employed in childcare facilities even after release; minors convicted of homosexuality face three years imprisonment; sexual intercourse with a person younger than 18 is classified as 'aggravated homosexuality' punishable by death; and 'purporting to contract a same-sex marriage' or knowingly attending a purported same-sex marriage ceremony carries imprisonment of ten years. A provision of the 2023 bill that would have criminalised merely identifying as gay or non-binary with ten years in prison was proposed but ultimately excluded. Same-sex marriage has been constitutionally banned since 29 September 2005, when President Museveni signed a constitutional amendment stating 'Marriage between persons of the same sex is prohibited.' Human Rights Watch reported in 2005 that Uganda's abstinence-until-marriage programs discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation, denying young LGBTQ people information that could save their lives and reinforcing stigma; a 2018 article in African Health Sciences stated that Uganda's high HIV rate has roots in stigma against same-sex sexual behaviour and sex work, and the source does not address healthcare access barriers specifically for trans people. LGBTQ people in Uganda face severe discrimination actively incited by conservative political, religious and community leaders, with violent attacks and harassment common and often performed or incited by state officials. In October 2010 the tabloid Rolling Stone published names, addresses, photographs and hangouts of 100 allegedly gay and lesbian Ugandans with a call for their execution, and activist David Kato was murdered in 2011 shortly after winning a lawsuit against the paper. Pride Uganda was cancelled in August 2017 after threats of arrest, and in June 2012 the government banned 38 NGOs accused of promoting homosexuality. A 2013 Pew survey found 96 percent of Ugandans believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society, while a 2017 ILGA poll showed 59 percent agreed gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as straight people.

A human-rights organisation's report (26 May 2025): the 2023 law — death penalty for aggravated same-sex conduct, lengthy prison terms for promoting such conduct — unleashed arrests, shelter raids, evictions and public outings; many LGBT people in hiding, with a small group of mothers speaking publicly for their LGBT children.

A human-rights organisation (4 Apr 2024): the national constitutional court upheld the 2023 law's core provisions — including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties up to 20 years — rejecting public-participation challenges; contrasted with the same court voiding a similar 2013 law on procedure.

Human Rights Watch essay (15 May 2024) 'When Laws Fail to Protect Trans People': Ukraine-trans war-displacement case work — cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and the often-humiliating Military Medical Commission confirmation; a Ukrainian activist notes commission hours (8am-8pm) and gatekeeping ('if a doctor says I'm a woman, the state can shrug').
France24 (June 2022) reports on Ukraine's trans community caught in the crosshairs of war.

ZMINA (28 Jul 2026): trans women in Ukraine now find it harder to obtain a diagnosis — stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers; Trans Forum 2026 (Kyiv, early June 2026) discussed the new draft Civil Code's effect on transition procedure and whether being trans grounds exemption from mobilisation — visitor-relevant documentary friction for trans Ukrainians and those crossing borders.

Gender Stream (Ukrainian NGO): consultations and support — advises and accompanies LGBTQI+ people and families evacuating from frontline regions to western Ukraine/EU, and helps with processing/reissuing documents for transgender people, including those planning to legally cross the border; documents that since martial law, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service.

European Parliament written question E-002018/2022 (Jun 2022): on the situation of transgender people in Ukraine amid the Russian invasion, in the context of Parliament's resolution on war's impact on women.

Amnesty International (16 May 2013) report 'Nothing to Report': Ukraine's government must legislate against discrimination and violent attacks on a sexual-orientation/gender-identity basis amid a pervasive climate of homophobia; lawmakers urged to vote down proposals to criminalise; attacks routinely used as pretext to deny LGBTI people rights to expression and peaceful public events.

Erasing 76 Crimes (30 Aug 2016): among three-country advances, a Ukrainian court ordered changes requested by two trans people to their passports and all other documents WITHOUT requiring sterilisation — a concrete legal-gain data point for document amendment.

Human Rights Watch (26 Jun 2012): LGBT activist Taras Karasiichuk was attacked near his Kyiv apartment — the second violent attack in six weeks after threats forced cancellation of a pride parade; diagnosed concussion and broken jaw, police did not immediately respond despite medical referral; HRW urged investigation into homophobic motive.

Ukraine's first LGBTQ rights group, Our World (Nash Svit), was created in 1998 as a community centre and human rights advocacy organization. In 2008, LGBTQ organizations formed the Union of Gay Organizations of Ukraine coalition, and the Gay Alliance of Ukraine was founded in 2009. The source text does not describe trans-specific facilities or shelters. Clause 211 of the Family Code of Ukraine explicitly bans same-sex couples from adopting children, while single Ukrainian citizens of any sexual orientation are permitted to adopt. Lesbian couples have greater parenting access than gay male couples because IVF and assisted insemination treatments are legal. A revised Civil Code draft submitted to Parliament on 22 January 2026 would automatically annul marriages if one spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment, directly targeting trans people's family recognition. Foreign adopters must be married in a registered different-sex marriage.

Ukraine's path to partner recognition has been long and uneven: a 2015 government action plan promised a civil partnership bill by 2017, but the Ministry of Justice declared in 2018 it could not proceed due to pressure from religious organizations. A civil unions bill was introduced in Parliament in March 2023, and on 14 May 2025 the government's EU accession roadmap (p. 3.11) set a Q3 2025 deadline for a registered partnerships law. On 10 June 2025 the Desnianskyi District Court recognized actual marital relations between two Ukrainian men, the first such ruling in Ukraine, and on 22 January 2026 the Supreme Court in Kyiv rejected a challenge to a lower-court ruling recognizing same-sex couples as de facto family. A January 2023 NDI/KIIS poll found 56% of Ukrainians supported civil partnership registration for same-sex couples. A June 2024 KIIS poll found 28.7% supported civil partnerships without adoption, 35.7% opposed and 25.6% indifferent.

A summer 2015 British Council survey found one in five Ukrainian youth would be uncomfortable having lesbian and gay people as friends. Most Ukrainians grew up with little or no comprehensive, fact-based public education about human sexuality, sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap the source says promotes viewing homosexuals as dangerous and as sources of HIV/AIDS. The Ukrainian Council of Churches opposed the Istanbul Convention partly on grounds it could "distort" younger generations' sexual identity, framing anti-LGBTQ policy as youth protection. One source anecdote describes a 19-year-old confined indoors for over a year by parents after they discovered messages to his boyfriend. At a 14 November 2024 meeting with the Ukrainian Students Association, a student representative asked President Zelenskyy whether he would sign registered partnerships legislation and he replied "Yes!"

Transsexuality is classified as a psychiatric disorder in Ukraine, and sex reassignment surgery is legal only for those over age 25. In 2011 the Civil Code was amended to allow transgender people who had undergone gender-affirming surgery to change their name to reflect gender identity, with seven surgeries and five new documents reported in 2014. Since December 2016 new identity documents are issued before surgery following an August 2016 ruling ordering passport and document changes for two transgender people without surgery, and married people or those with an underage child may also apply for transition. Previously applicants required permission from a Ministry of Healthcare special commission, 30 days in a psychiatric hospital, typically in wards with patients considered "mentally ill," and a diagnosis of transsexuality, requirements now removed. On 12 November 2015 Parliament approved a Labor Code amendment banning gender identity discrimination at work as an EU visa-free requirement, and in December 2022 Parliament unanimously passed a media bill banning hate speech and discrimination based on gender identity. The Criminal Code provides harsher penalties only for racial, national or religious intolerance, not gender identity, and an April 2020 draft to add gender identity and sexual orientation as hate-crime grounds was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of those terms in legislation. On 14 May 2025 the Cabinet approved a rule-of-law roadmap planning registered-partnership status by Q3 2025 and, by Q2 2026, administrative liability for discrimination, gender identity and sexual orientation as criminal aggravating circumstances, criminal liability for public calls for violence, and free secondary legal aid with registration in the Unified register, while a 22 January 2026 draft Civil Code would define family as man-woman cohabitation and automatically annul marriage if a spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment. Male same-sex sexual activity was legalized in 1991, female same-sex activity was never a crime, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, with law as of 2018 only addressing prostitution involving minors or public conduct violating public decency. Article 51 of the 1996 Constitution defines marriage as a voluntary union between a man and a woman, with no legal recognition for same-sex marriage or civil partnerships, confirmed by the Justice Ministry in June 2018 after a 2015 action-plan promise of partnerships by 2017 was declared unimplementable in early 2018. After a July 2022 petition exceeding 28,000 signatures, President Zelenskyy asked the Prime Minister to review same-sex civil partnerships but said marriage could not be introduced during wartime because the Constitution cannot be changed under martial law, later answering "Yes!" on 16 November 2024 when asked if he would sign registered partnerships, with a 14 May 2025 EU roadmap scheduling partnership legislation for Q3 2025. On 10 June 2025 the Desnianskyi District Court recognized "existence of actual marital relations" between two men in a first for Ukraine, and in March 2026 the Supreme Court in Kyiv rejected a challenge to a lower-court ruling recognizing same-sex couples as de facto family. Single citizens may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, but same-sex couples are explicitly banned under Clause 211 of the Family Code, foreign adopters must be in registered different-sex marriage, and lesbian couples have IVF and assisted insemination access. On 12 November 2015 Parliament banned sexual orientation discrimination at work after failures on 5 and 9 November, and in December 2022 unanimously banned sexual-orientation hate speech and discrimination in mass media to align with EU Directive 2018/1808, while hate-crime aggravation still excludes sexual orientation. Homosexuality is not a legal ground for exemption from military service, and on 8 February 2022 the Health Ministry enacted 2016-proposed rules allowing gay and bisexual men to donate blood after previously listing homosexuality as "risky behaviour" barring donation. "Sexual orientations and gender identity remain taboo subjects in Ukraine." "Most Ukrainians affiliated with the Orthodox or Catholic Church tend to view homosexuality and non-traditional gender roles as signs of immorality," compounded by lack of fact-based sexuality education and Soviet-era labeling of non-heterosexual relations as abnormal. The article states the "ex-gay" movement "believes that lesbian, gay, or bisexual sexual orientations, as well as transgender identities, can be 'cured' through therapeutic or religious programs," with the largest group Love Against Homosexuality viewing LGBTQ people as "sexual perverts" needing cure. In 2011 there were frequent reports of harassment and violence against LGBTQ people, many reported needing to lie about sexual orientation or gender identity to avoid discrimination or violent harassment, with a perception that such violence is frequently tolerated by the Government. Ukrainian police "hardly ever detain attackers," creating pressure to remain in the closet especially for public figures, while pride events required heavy protection, e.g., 1,500 participants guarded by 5,500 police and 1,200 National Guard in Kyiv on 12 June 2016 and earlier cancellations in May 2012 and July 2014 over safety guarantees. General LGBTQ acceptance polling rose from 28% in a 2010 European study saying LGBT individuals should live freely however they like to 70.4% in 2024 agreeing LGBTQ people should have same rights, up from 67.3% in 2023 and 63.7% in 2022, with 28.7% approving civil partnerships without adoption, 35.7% opposed and 25.6% indifferent.

Effective from late December 2016, Ukraine no longer requires transgender people seeking legal gender change to petition a board of mental health professionals or spend a month in a psychiatric facility.

texts.cleaned_text: Outright country overview as of 12 Mar 2026: same-sex relations are legal nationwide, legal gender recognition is possible, and LGBTI organisations can register, while protections on intersex bodily autonomy remain incomplete.

Full text of Law No. 19684 (26 Oct 2018), Uruguay's Comprehensive Law for Trans People. It sets out state-guaranteed identity, health and anti-discrimination rights for trans persons and forms the statutory basis of the country's trans-protection regime.

Equaldex status grid for Montevideo, where national law applies: marriage, legal gender change, non-discrimination, the conversion-therapy ban and an equal age of consent are all legal or protected, and hate-crime rules cover SOGI.
Presidencia release: the Executive promulgated the Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons (Ley 19684, Oct 2018), officially confirming that the comprehensive trans-rights statute entered into force.
Freedom House Uruguay 2024 rates the country Free at 96/100, with political rights at 40/40 and civil liberties at 56/60, indicating a strong general rights climate for trans visitors.

TDoR 2025 record: Joana, a 29-year-old trans woman, was shot dead in her Montevideo home on 28 Jul 2025. A suspect was subsequently sentenced to 7 years for the murder. The case documents lethal violence against a trans person with judicial follow-through.

la diaria (May 2024): trans health-service user Andreina Stuart denounced mistreatment and discrimination at San Carlos hospital (Maldonado); criminal complaint pending, hospital director pledged an administrative investigation after the judicial stage; local officials pressed for health-system updates.

Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, sued state bank BROU over discriminatory handling by a Prosegur guard and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; prosecutor Tania Vidal compelled the bank to produce material; Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

PinkNews (28 Dec 2007): Uruguay became the first Latin American country to recognise same-sex civil unions. President Tabare Vazquez signed the law granting couples who had cohabited for five or more years rights equivalent to marriage.

MercoPress (29 Jul 2023), citing Uruguayan authorities and officials: as part of a new prison planned for Montevideo there will be a specific sector for the trans population, which Parliamentary Commissioner for the prison system Juan Miguel Petit called 'good news for a very vulnerable population' and estimated would be ready in less than two years. National Rehabilitation Institute (INR) Director Luis Mendoza told a parliamentary hearing that 'if the trans person enters the system they have the right to decide if they want to go to a men's or women's prison,' and that while trans women are currently placed in female prisons, cohabitation entails 'a whole process' of adaptation; he also noted the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles would for the first time account for the trans population, adding 'the laws are very advanced in Uruguay, but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line.' The article cites official figures of 14,965 people deprived of liberty, including 28 trans women and nine trans men (Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Prison System).

Wikipedia country coverage records the following. Incitement to hatred on the grounds of sexual orientation and sexual identity has been prohibited since 2003, and Penal Code article 149ter provides enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by those characteristics. Gay, lesbian and bisexual people have served openly in the military since May 2009 under a Defence Minister decree. The 2018 Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons stipulates the free development of personality according to chosen gender identity and calls on government to ensure trans people are treated respectfully by authorities. The 2017 Mental Health Law (Law No. 19529) bars any mental-health diagnosis being made on the exclusive basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Since October 2018 no surgery, hormone therapy or diagnosis is required to change legal gender on official documents; name and legal gender changes have been possible for adults since October 2009, and for minors with parental consent since the October 2018 law. A non-binary marker does not exist, only female and male, even though Law 19,684 (article 4c) recognises non-binary people in its definitions. The 2018 law calls on government to ensure transgender people are included in housing programmes and are not denied health services, and in July 2019 the state water company Obras Sanitarias del Estado began offering jobs to transgender people in compliance with it. From 16 December 2020 gay and bisexual men have been able to donate blood under the same conditions as the rest of the population, ending the previous 12-month abstinence requirement. The 2004 anti-discrimination law created an Honorary Commission to Combat Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and other forms of Discrimination to investigate allegations of unlawful discriminatory conduct, covering sexual orientation and sexual identity. The 2018 law passed 62-26 in the Chamber and 17-12 in the Senate, allows minors to change legal gender with parental consent, and mandates that transgender people receive 1 percent of public and private educational scholarships. Youth outcomes are severe: 25 percent of transgender Uruguayans left home before age 18 after family rejection, 87 percent did not finish secondary school, and other studies show about 75 percent expelled from the education system. Same-sex couples have been able to adopt jointly since September 2009, a first in Latin America, and same-sex marriage has been legal since August 2013; the age of consent has been equal at 15 regardless of orientation or gender since 1934. Article 22 of Law No. 19580, in force since January 2018, prohibits unnecessary medical procedures on intersex children and teenagers. A 2014 poll found about 71 percent of Uruguayans supported same-sex marriage, the highest in South America, and in 2016 Americas Quarterly named Uruguay the most LGBT-friendly country in Latin America, calling it a model for social inclusion. Uruguay hosted the region's first international LGBT rights conference in July 2016, with hundreds of diplomats, politicians and activists attending. The Montevideo Pride parade has run annually since the 1990s and drew an estimated 120,000 people in 2018, alongside Punta Pride in Punta del Este each February, and Montevideo has several gay bars, restaurants and pubs. The 2015 Gay Happiness Index ranked Uruguay fifth with a score of 73, on par with Canada and Nordic countries. The Archbishop of Montevideo called same-sex adoption a serious error, and between November 2018 and March 2019 about 69,360 signatures were gathered for a pre-referendum against the trans law, though only about 10 percent of voters turned out on 4 August 2019, short of the 25 percent needed. About two-thirds of transgender Uruguayans report having been victims of physical violence, and their life expectancy is around 45 years against a national average of 77.

Since October 2009, transgender people over age 18 have been allowed to change name and legal gender on official documents to match gender identity, and since October 2018 sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy or any diagnosis are not required. The October 2018 Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons, passed 62-26 in the Chamber and 17-12 in the Senate, allows minors to change legal gender with parental consent and stipulates free development of personality according to chosen gender identity, respectful treatment by authorities, inclusion in housing programmes, access to education, and non-denial of health services. The same law provides monetary reparations to transgender individuals persecuted during the Uruguayan Dictatorship, estimated at around 50 people, mandates 1 percent of public and private educational scholarships for transgender people, and was implemented in part when the state water company began offering jobs for transgender people in July 2019. A pre-referendum to repeal the law held 4 August 2019 failed when only about 10% voted versus 25% of the electoral roll, about 650,000 people, required to trigger a repeal consultation, so the law remains in force. Law 19,684 article 4c recognizes non-binary persons in definitions but no third gender marker beyond female and male is available, which the 2022 Non-binary people survey cites as deterring use of the legal change procedure. Protections include Penal Code article 149ter enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by sexual identity, a 2003 ban on incitement to hatred on sexual identity, a 2004 anti-discrimination law creating an Honorary Commission covering sexual identity discrimination, 2017 Mental Health Law No. 19529 barring diagnosis solely on gender identity, and January 2018 Law No. 19580 article 22 prohibiting unnecessary medical procedures for intersex children and teenagers. The article reports about 1,000 transgender Uruguayans with life expectancy 35 to 45 versus 77 nationally, severe Dictatorship-era torture, sexual violence and unjustified imprisonment, 25% leaving home before 18 after family rejection, 87% not finishing secondary school, about 75% expelled from education, only 23% with formal employment, 67% engaging in prostitution for income, six trans women dying since early 2017, and about two-thirds reporting physical violence. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1934 with an equal age of consent at 15 regardless of sexual orientation and/or gender. Civil unions have been available since 1 January 2008 under law signed 27 December 2007, requiring at least five years together and granting health benefits, inheritance, parenting and pension rights, while same-sex marriage has been allowed since August 2013 after Chamber approval 71-21 on 11 April 2013 and Senate approval 23-8 on 2 April 2013, signed 3 May and effective 5 August. Joint adoption by same-sex couples in a civil union has been allowed since September 2009 after Chamber approval 28 August and Senate approval 9 September by 17 of 23 senators, making Uruguay the first Latin American country to allow it, the 2013 marriage law allows lesbian couples in vitro fertilisation, and a 3 October 2018 family judge ruled barring an unmarried lesbian couple from giving twins both surnames was sexual orientation discrimination. Anti-discrimination protections include a 2003 ban on incitement to hatred on sexual orientation, Penal Code article 149ter enhanced penalties for orientation-motivated crimes, and a 2004 law creating an Honorary Commission to investigate sexual orientation discrimination. Gay, lesbian and bisexual people have been allowed to serve openly in the military since May 2009 under a Defence Minister decree ending orientation discrimination in recruitment. Gay and bisexual men could previously donate blood only after 12 months without sex, but since 16 December 2020 they donate under the same conditions as the rest of the population, and 2017 Mental Health Law No. 19529 bars diagnosis solely on sexual orientation. The article cites the 2015 PlanetRomeo Gay Happiness Index ranking Uruguay fifth with score 73 alongside Canada, Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Iceland, and 2016 Americas Quarterly naming it the most LGBT-friendly country in Latin America. A 2014 poll found about 71% of Uruguayans supported same-sex marriage, the highest in South America and second in the Americas behind Canada, and the article states societal acceptance of homosexuality and same-sex relationships is very high. By contrast for transgender people specifically, the article states: "Nevertheless, transgender people still face discrimination and stigma." The source text also reports beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse against transgender people in ICE custody, and notes that advocates have compared the administration's actions to the early stages of genocide. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): Executive Order 14168 (January 20, 2025) redefined sex for the federal government as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). On the same day Trump rescinded Executive Order 13988, which had sought to protect LGBTQ rights in federal prisons and prevent discrimination. Other measures include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers providing gender-affirming care to transgender youth; the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): The source text states that during the second Trump presidency the US government has taken actions to persecute transgender people, accompanied by anti-transgender rhetoric and misinformation often to dehumanize and scapegoat them. Anti-transgender campaigning was a large part of the 2024 Trump campaign, with spending on anti-transgender advertising exceeding spending on housing, immigration, or the economy; Trump repeatedly made false claims that schools were performing "gender-affirming surgeries on children without their parents' consent," claims conservative groups called "valid" while acknowledging they were untrue. Censorship measures include a January 2025 list of "forbidden terms" including "gender," "transgender" and "LGBT" in health agencies, removal of words from federal websites including the Stonewall National Monument site, and revocation of scientific grants mentioning LGBT topics. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): Executive Order 14190 (January 29, 2025), "Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling," directs law enforcement to investigate schools for promoting "gender ideology" and to criminally prosecute teachers who facilitate a transgender minor's social transition — including using preferred names or pronouns — potentially as sexual exploitation of a minor and/or practicing medicine without a license, with federal funding revoked for violating schools. Executive Order 14187 (January 28, 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the DOJ subpoenaed "over 20" hospitals for full records of patients under 19 including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialized LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; in August 2025 it threatened to pull federal funding from sex education programs mentioning transgender people (11 states and 2 territories complied by November 2025); and in October 2025 proposed HHS rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, with gender-affirming care for children already banned in 27 states. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): In January 2025 a list of "forbidden terms" was distributed within government health-related agencies instructing employees to avoid words including "gender," "transgender," or "LGBT," and such words were widely removed from federal agency websites including the National Park Service Stonewall National Monument site. United States: same-sex marriage is recognized nationwide under Obergefell v. Hodges (26 June 2015), and the Respect for Marriage Act of December 2022 repealed DOMA and required all states to recognize existing same-sex marriages; DOMA had barred federal recognition of same-sex unions until it was ruled unconstitutional in 2013. Recognition still varies: same-sex marriages are not licensed or recognized in American Samoa, status differs across sovereign Native American tribal nations, and adoption remains state-dependent, with some states allowing same-sex couple adoption and others banning all unmarried couples. Berkeley, California became the first jurisdiction to recognize same-sex unions in 1984 through domestic partnership health benefits for city employees, California passed the first state domestic partnership law in 1999, and Vermont was the first state to legalize civil unions. Expression has been both suppressed and asserted: during the reservation era, Christian missionaries and federal agencies forced Native American LGBTQ people into prescribed dress and grooming, such as making males cut their hair and females wear dresses, while both Native and non-Native LGBTQ people lived in hiding because homosexuality was a criminal offense. William Dorsey Swann, born enslaved in Maryland, organized drag balls in Washington, D.C. in the 1880s and 1890s and was arrested repeatedly, including the first documented case of arrests for female impersonation on April 12, 1888. The military's Don't Ask, Don't Tell policy (1990s-2011) explicitly barred soldiers from coming out, and gender expression-related bullying contributed to a wave of teenage and young adult suicides in 2009-2010 that prompted the It Gets Better Project. Gallup found 7.6% of U.S. adults identified as LGBTQ or another non-heterosexual orientation in 2024, rising to 22.3% among Gen Z (born 1997-2012) and 9.8% among Millennials, versus 1.1% of the Silent Generation. Visibility grew through media: Ellen was cancelled in 1998 after its star came out, while Will & Grace premiered that same year and is credited with helping increase public acceptance, and Gay Straight Alliance clubs are linked to greater safety, inclusion, wellbeing and educational attainment for LGBTQ students. The FBI reports bias against sexual orientation has consistently accounted for between one-seventh and one-fifth of single-bias reported hate incidents this century, 37 states still lacked anti-bias statutes for gender-identity crimes as of 2019, and the Transgender Day of Remembrance is held annually for transgender murder victims.

On January 20, 2025 President Donald Trump issued an executive order directing the United States government to remove all federal protections for transgender individuals and remove all recognition of transgender identity, declaring that only male and female genders are recognized and that official documents must reflect biological sex assigned at birth. Previously it was possible for US passport holders to receive either gender marker, or an "X" marker, simply by declaration during a passport application. Trump also banned trans people from military service and halted financing to gender-affirming care for individuals younger than 19, while references to transgender people were scrubbed from government websites and over 350 pages about the LGBTQ community at large were removed entirely. Twenty-two states plus Washington, D.C. outlaw discrimination based on gender identity or expression, and in June 2020 the Supreme Court in Bostock v. Clayton County held gender identity is included under "sex" as a prohibited ground of employment discrimination under the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Hate crimes based on gender identity are punishable by federal law under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, but many states lack such laws and only 23 states cover gender identity in state bias-motivated violence statutes. In 2023 more than 190 of over 470 introduced anti-LGBTQ bills were specifically anti-trans, with most passed bills focused on banning gender-affirming health care, while top contested areas are bathroom access, athletics, and transgender-related healthcare for minors. Beginning with Illinois in 1962, states began to decriminalize same-sex sexual activity, and in 2003 through Lawrence v. Texas all remaining laws against same-sex sexual activity were invalidated, though 12 states have still not formally repealed their sodomy laws. Beginning with Massachusetts in 2004, states began to offer same-sex marriage, and in 2015 through Obergefell v. Hodges all states were required to license and recognize it, with adoption of children by same-sex married couples legal nationwide since that ruling. Twenty-three states plus Washington, D.C., Guam, and Puerto Rico outlaw discrimination based on sexual orientation, while U.S. federal law does not explicitly include protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. In June 2020 the Supreme Court ruled in Bostock v. Clayton County that sexual orientation is included under "sex" as a prohibited ground of employment discrimination in the Civil Rights Act of 1964, effectively meaning no employer can fire an employee on the basis of sexual orientation. Hate crimes based on sexual orientation are punishable by federal law under the Matthew Shepard Act, and 34 states cover sexual orientation in state statutes criminalizing bias-motivated violence or intimidation. Open service by gays, lesbians and bisexuals has been permitted since September 20, 2011 after the Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act of 2010, with military sodomy provisions limited by Lawrence and Article 125 later amended to forcible sodomy in 2013 and repealed in 2017. The article states "Public opinion on transgender issues is divided." It identifies top issues regarding gender identity as bathroom access, athletics, and transgender-related healthcare for minors. A 2025 Gallup poll cited found 69% of Americans supported laws requiring transgender athletes to participate in sports aligned with their assigned sex at birth, including 90% of Republicans, 72% of independents and 41% of Democrats. The same polling found 66% of Americans supported laws requiring assigned sex at birth to be listed on government documents such as drivers licenses and passports, including 89% of Republicans, 66% of independents and 38% of Democrats. Only 40% of Americans believed that gender transition is morally acceptable, including 70% of Democrats, 45% of independents and only 9% of Republicans. The article also notes transgender people faced significant erosions in rights on the state level in Republican-run states over the course of three years before the 2025 federal actions.

This is the current Holy See posture on blessing gay couples.

Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, 'Dignitas Infinita' (2 April 2024): doctrinal declaration stating that 'any sex-change intervention, as a rule, risks threatening the unique dignity the person has received from the moment of conception', while not excluding medical assistance for genital abnormalities evident at birth or developing later, which in that case would not constitute a sex change in its sense; it condemns 'gender theory' as 'extremely dangerous since it cancels differences' and separately denounces the imprisonment, torture and killing of people solely because of their sexual orientation. Like the 2019 instruction, it states the governing institution's position rather than a rule binding visitors.

No documented modern criminal-law persecution of consensual homosexual conduct in Vatican City itself (decriminalisation has nineteenth-century roots); the Holy See's institutional posture against homosexuality and gender theory drives policy, the legal baseline distinguishing the Church's diplomacy from the city-state's own law.

In 2021, Vatican foreign minister Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher delivered a letter to the Italian ambassador to the Holy See expressing concerns over an Italian parliamentary bill meant to legally protect LGBTQ Italians against violence and discrimination. The objection specifically targeted the section prohibiting incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. The letter claimed that prohibition constituted a violation of freedom of speech and of religion. It asked for the draft law's text to be reformulated. Since 1890 the territory of what is now Vatican City has had no criminal laws against non-commercial, private, adult and consensual same-sex sexual activity under a legal code based on the Italian Zanardelli Code of 1889 in force since the founding of the sovereign state in 1929. The age of consent is set at 18 years for all persons regardless of gender, except for sexual relations within marriage recognized as valid by the Catholic Church and Vatican City laws where the legal age is 14. Foreign diplomats must not be part of a same-sex family and must not be divorced to be accredited, with openly gay French nominee Jean-Loup Kuhn-Delforge in a civil pact rejected in 2008 and openly gay practising Catholic single nominee Laurent Stefanini rejected in 2015, leading France to leave the post vacant from March 2015 to May 2016 before nominating another diplomat in May 2016. Vatican City has always expressed disagreement with any civil recognition of same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and granting of adoption rights to same-sex couples, and while Pope Francis in 2023 expressed support for same-sex civil unions outside the Catholic Church he remained firm that the Sacrament of Marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God. The Vatican reserves the right to remove, suspend and dismiss immediately any official and employee who publicly admits to being gay or questions the general policy of the Vatican towards homosexuals. In 2021 Vatican foreign minister Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher delivered a letter to the Italian ambassador expressing concerns over an Italian bill meant to legally protect LGBTQ Italians against violence and discrimination, claiming the prohibition of incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation violated freedom of speech and religion and asking for reformulation. On 13 January 1998 LGBTQ activist Alfredo Ormando set himself on fire on St. Peter's Square under Vatican jurisdiction in protest against deep-rooted refusal expressed by the Catholic religion towards homosexuality and died days later in hospital from severe burns.

exact_spans: The sole prison-axis source is a general reference article on crime in the nation, used as a last resort.
texts.cleaned_text: The nation operates no prison system — only a few cells used for pre-trial detention — and persons sentenced to imprisonment by the nation serve their time in another nation's prisons with costs covered by the nation; there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case.

The 2024 declaration states that 'any sex-change intervention, as a rule, risks threatening the unique dignity the person has received from the moment of conception', while not excluding medical assistance for genital abnormalities evident at birth or developing later, which in that case would not constitute a sex change in its sense; it condemns 'gender theory' as 'extremely dangerous since it cancels differences' and separately denounces the imprisonment, torture and killing of people solely because of their sexual orientation. The sources report no documented mechanism for changing a gender marker on identity documents and no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity; an educational document (2019) opposes 'gender theory' as denying natural difference. The 2024 declaration and the 2019 educational document express institutional doctrine, not rules binding visitors.

A 2023 declaration permits spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage, with a January 2024 clarification reiterating that blessings never extend to the unions themselves.

Nothing in the criminal law addresses being transgender. The sources cited record no trans-specific practice at entry, at screening, or in access to facilities for a trans visitor, and do not establish what document checks or screening visitors face; neither trans-specific danger nor trans-specific safety can be inferred from them.

texts.cleaned_text: Same-sex sexual acts are criminalised under Section 146 (buggery, up to 10 years) and Section 148 (gross indecency, up to 5 years). The laws address neither discrimination nor harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, leaving LGBTQ people without legal protection when they speak out. No associations or organisations dedicated to LGBTQ people exist, and no helpline or help centre for LGBTQ youth operates, so dedicated support and care access is absent. Healthcare, medication, and HIV services are not covered. LGBTQ life is invisible and stigmatised. In September 2011 a same-sex couple's article 'Not Easy Being Gay in St. Vincent and the Grenadines' in the Vinci Kallaloo drew over 3,400 hits in under a day and 50+ comments, several containing violent murderous threats. In September 2018 three cross-dressing young men were physically attacked; Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves condemned the attacks, called such homophobia unacceptable, and called for an open conversation on homosexuality. In April 2019 Leswan Stewart, a 'cross-dressing gay' teenager, was the victim of a transphobic assault and was then charged with fraud for allegedly pretending to be a woman; the prosecutor withdrew the charge in May 2019 without giving a reason. In 2011 three lecturers at the St. Vincent and the Grenadines Community College were targeted by the college's director in an orchestrated scheme accusing them of 'homosexual tendencies', allegedly to fire political opponents. Two men left the country because of the law. Javin Johnson, 22, successfully claimed asylum in the United Kingdom in 2017 after establishing he could not live as a gay man in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Sean Macleish, 53, a Vincentian resident of Chicago, publicly advocated to the Prime Minister for removal of the laws so he could return home with his partner, without effect. In their 2019 affidavits the two petitioners stated that the legislation had exiled them from the country due to its severely draconian and damaging effects. The country does not recognise same-sex unions in any form, whether marriage or partnerships, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the same rights given to married couples. In 2024 Saint Vincent and the Grenadines upheld its ban on same-sex sexual activity in its High Court, affirming it was legal to outlaw homosexual activity. The Prime Minister said any change would be an OECS-wide decision because constitutional and legislative provisions are similar across member states.

Washington Blade (10 Sep 2024): LGBTQ Venezuelans face unprecedented persecution following the disputed July 2024 election, and the persecution is tied to the political crisis; the opposition presidential candidate fled the country on 7 Sep 2024.
The EUAA country-focus on Venezuela, covering the reference period through 2025, includes a dedicated LGBTIQ+ profile of conditions in the country, used in international protection decisions.
An LGBTQ guide covering Venezuela was published by AFS and the Vance Center in Oct 2024.

Sydney Morning Herald (8 Aug 2015): Tamara Adrian, Venezuela's first transgender candidate, ran for the National Assembly -- landmark trans political candidacy under Venezuela's gender-recognition law context.

Cronica Uno poll (2-3 Mar 2023): a majority of Venezuelans agree the LGBTIQ population should have the same rights as other citizens; 82% know the LGBTIQ+ term (13% do not); 36% think gay/lesbian/bisexuality is innate -- dated public-opinion data.
Aporrea reported on 31 Jan 2014 that an equal-marriage bill was to be presented to Venezuela's National Assembly that week, a legislative push for same-sex marriage; no later enactment is recorded.

El Mundo (13 Dec 2015): Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla -- Voluntad Popular deputy and Venezuela's first openly gay parliamentarian -- a prisoner of conscience held in SEBIN custody; he turned 33 in his cell -- state persecution of an openly gay politician.

Venezuela has marked the International Day Against Homophobia since 2000, and the government has recently begun participating in Pride events. In May 2016 the National Assembly unanimously passed a resolution establishing 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia, and the Supreme Court suspended that resolution in August 2016. Tamara Adrián and Rosmit Mantilla were elected Alternate Deputies in the 2015 parliamentary election, the first LGBT members of Venezuela's legislature. Police harassment remains a serious problem: in May 2026 NGOs including the Observatorio Venezolano de Violencias LGBTIQ+, Caleidoscopio Humano and Movimiento SOMOS denounced the detention of around 30 people in a police raid on an LGBTQ+ venue in Barquisimeto, Lara state, where officers allegedly entered without proper warrants, extorted detainees and accused them of 'committing the crime of homosexuality', despite homosexuality being legal. The law sets no general healthcare or transition-care provisions, lesbian couples are allowed to access IVF, and same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children. For legal gender recognition, a 2017 constitutional action before the Supreme Justice Tribunal requires each case to be individually assessed with certified birth certificates and a psychiatric and psychological report from a specialist demonstrating the veracity of the intended sexual identity, and the Tribunal still has not granted the requested name and gender changes. Trans people also remain unable to change identity-card information: although SAIME announced in September 2016 that transgender people may request a new identity card matching their gender identity, there is currently no administrative procedure or mechanism to enact the relevant article. The universal age of consent is 16, with no differential age for same-sex conduct. On 15 December 2016 the Supreme Tribunal of Justice ruled that a baby may be registered in the Civil Registry with both mothers' surnames, basing the decision on Article 75 of the Constitution, and declared that the state must protect all families without distinction, so that children and teenagers born into same-sex families enjoy all the rights and guarantees of children born into opposite-sex families. Same-sex couples are still unable to legally adopt, though a 2023 Equilibrium CenDE poll found 48% of Venezuelans supported adoption by same-sex couples (34% totally, 14% somewhat) versus 39% opposed. A 2013 Pew survey found 57% of 18–29-year-olds believed homosexuality should be accepted by society, compared with 51% of 30–49-year-olds and 45% of those over 50.

texts.cleaned_text: DW (late Sept/Oct 2025): Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events — HRW Asia director Patricia Gossman calls it worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against Vietnam's long regional-tolerance reputation; notes the 2015 lifting of the same-sex-marriage ban left unions still without legal recognition.

Outright country overview (updated Mar 2026): the law granting official transgender recognition promised for 2017 still not implemented — obstacles to gender-affirming care and legal gender-marker change persist; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of Feb 2026. Same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts but confer no rights; LGBTIQ organisations operate openly though under government surveillance; Health Ministry declared (Aug 2022) same-sex attraction and trans identity are not mental disorders; no law against non-consensual intersex medical interventions.

Amnesty International Viet Nam 2025 report: LGBTI people's rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice; sits alongside wider repression — vague Penal Code arts 109/116/117/331 used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, proposed press-law source-disclosure rules; Viet Nam re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council until 2028.

Lighthouse Vietnam study (Oct 2024): 'Exploring the lived experiences of conversion efforts (SOGICE) among LGBTIQ people in one national context' - documents experiences and forms of SOGICE in the Vietnamese context, with comprehensive data needs analysis.

UN Viet Nam feature (30 Nov 2024): transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters ('Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?'), heightened scrutiny, and economic/stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence — especially northern-province and ethnic-minority trans women; framed as case for accessible legal recognition.

Saigoneer (June 2023): Nov 2015 milestone let people who changed gender apply for civil-status change and set out legal gender recognition, but implementing guidance stalled — policy gaps persist, same-sex marriage legal but unrecognised; four trans Vietnamese describe respectful healthcare providers undone by administrative red tape.

IRB Canada Response to Information Request VNM201080.E (30 Jun 2022): Vietnamese law provides no discrimination protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds (Freedom House, 3 Mar 2021). The briefing draws on multiple sources and addresses treatment by society and authorities in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City across education, employment, housing and health care.

Viet Nam News (Nov 2018): National Assembly expected to discuss a draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights, targeting completion by 2020 — the law never materialised; per Outright (Feb 2026) a recognition draft law was still under consideration seven years later.

VietnamNet (16 Jan 2015) reports a proposal by the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute to Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security to house homosexual and transgender prisoners in jails separate from the general prison population, to protect them from sexual harassment. The institute cited US California statistics that 67% of homosexual and transgender prisoners had suffered sexual harassment, and a 2014 survey finding that most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. It stated that under Vietnam's then-current prison infrastructure transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, meaning no housing wing matched to a prisoner's gender identity existed, and asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome has been documented.

Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is legal and has never been criminalized in Vietnamese history, and the Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Historically, the 1812 Gia Long Code (Article 332) banned prostitution and illicit sexual activity including extra-marital sex, which in rare cases allowed homosexuality to be prosecuted under labels such as "extramarital sex" or "rape", though pre-colonial enforcement was so inconsistent that little to no known state action was taken. In 2002 the Ministry of Labour – Invalids and Social Affairs declared homosexuality a "social evil" comparable to prostitution, gambling and drug use and promised legislation to combat homosexuality and arrest same-sex couples; fines on same-sex marriages were abolished by government decree on 24 September 2013 (effective 11 November 2013). Since 3 August 2022 conversion therapy has been outlawed via Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC from the Ministry of Health, which states that homosexuality, bisexuality and being transgender are not illnesses and that LGBTQ+ people may not be forced into "treatment". Wikipedia country coverage: Vietnam's first gay pride parade was held in Hanoi on 5 August 2012, and by 2017 pride events were held in around 34 other cities and provinces, with over 35 similar events held annually in cities including Haiphong, Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City and Cần Thơ. Hanoi Pride ran for a fifth consecutive year from 18–24 September 2017 drawing thousands (versus about a hundred at the first parade), and its sixth edition in November 2018 saw more than 1,000 participants cycling to campaign for transgender rights and same-sex marriage; several events were aired on state channels VTV4, VTV6 and VTV9. Media coverage has shifted: in 2002 publications such as Thế Giới Phụ Nữ and Tiếp thị & Gia đình described homosexuality as a disease and "deviant behavior", while in September 2010 Tuoi Tre Online became the first major state media outlet to agree that "homosexuality is normal". The 2013 sitcom My Best Gay Friends was published on YouTube because Vietnamese broadcasters were reluctant to air it. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2006 the government enacted legislation protecting citizens infected with HIV and people living with AIDS from discrimination, and health care is provided free to all Vietnamese citizens. The 2022 conversion-therapy dispatch (No. 4132/BYT-PC) mandated enhanced public communication and dissemination among medical facilities nationwide so staff and patients better understand LGBTQ+ individuals, and advised that psychological support be provided by people with an understanding of gender identity. Sex reassignment surgery was previously illegal, forcing transgender people to travel to nearby Thailand for the procedure; the 2015 Civil Code amendment (passed 24 November 2015 by 282–84, effective January 2017) allows those who have undergone sex reassignment to register under their preferred sex, but a further implementing bill is still required, so the law is not fully enforced. Under the Law on Citizen Identification effective 1 July 2024, transgender citizens may change their ID card when undergoing gender transition but must present confirmation documents, and legal effect depends on the Gender Affirmation Law being passed first. Wikipedia country coverage: The age of consent is 16 under the Vietnamese Penal Code, regardless of gender or sexual orientation. A 2015 study found around 44% of Vietnamese LGBT students aged 14–22 faced stigma, discrimination and violence because of their identities, and a 2014 USAID report showed 54% of LGBT students said their school was not safe, with many dropping out; of those who experienced violence, one third thought about committing suicide and half of those attempted it. 85% of transgender students said they dropped out because of assault and bullying, while a 2015 UNESCO study found 19% of students perceived bullying against LGBT students as "harmless" and 70% of Hanoi parents said they would not allow their children to talk to gay students, with some believing conversion therapy could "cure" LGBT children. A 2007 poll of 300 junior-high and high-school pupils at Ho Chi Minh City Pedagogical University found 80% answered "no" to "Is homosexuality bad?", and 2023 Pew data shows support for same-sex marriage is highest among 18–34-year-olds at 79% versus 57% for those aged 35 and above.

Why do you look so different to your ID card?'), heightened scrutiny, and economic/stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence — especially for trans women in outlying provinces and ethnic minorities; framed as a case for accessible legal recognition.
