exact_spans: Relevant as the French prison framework Wallis and Futuna inherits (French law applies unless locally overridden).
Relevant as the French prison framework Wallis and Futuna inherits (French law applies unless locally overridden).
texts.cleaned_text: BuzzFeed News (Jan 2018): trans women in France whose legal gender is marked male — largely those without sex-reassignment surgery — are incarcerated in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; example of a trans woman transferred to Lille's men's facility in 2014.

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French detention, based on referrals about ~40 transgender detainees since 2010 and interviews with associations/experts; extends a 30 June 2010 opinion on trans prisoners. This French detention framework applies in Wallis and Futuna as a French collectivity.

Grokipedia compilation on transgender rights in Wallis and Futuna: French civil-law gender-marker recognition available without surgery or diagnosis since the 2016-17 French reforms; gender-identity discrimination protections since 2012 (employment, housing, services); but ~11,000 population, isolation and dominant Catholic/Polynesian norms leave practical healthcare and acceptance barriers, with fakafafine-type roles coexisting alongside stigma/concealment.

Discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' has been banned since 2012, with the term replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016 amending article 225-1 of the Penal Code, and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships, sanctions, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. Effective 1 January 2017 after a Constitutional Council ruling on 17 November 2016, signature on 18 November 2016 and publication the next day, transgender people can legally change gender without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical proof, but must go before a court, while first-name change can be done by registry office after the self-certification provision was dropped. Gender identity disorder was removed as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names including on student cards and exam forms. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access to gender-affirming healthcare and recommended informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine characterized the rise as an epidemic-like and primarily social phenomenon urging extreme caution without changing practice. After a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report critical of youth gender-affirming care, a bill to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the Macron government and stalled since 23 July 2024, while late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 retained in the Penal Code of 1810 for colonies, while the 1960 Mirguet amendment doubling the penalty for homosexual indecent exposure under article 330 alinea 2 was repealed in 1980 and the discriminatory age of consent of 21 then 18 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual relations was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, still pending Senate vote. Sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services has been banned since 1985 with Labour Code protection, and same-sex marriage signed 18 May 2013 after Constitutional Council approval 17 May 2013 with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier following PACS partnerships from 1999 and joint adoption since May 2013 is stated as legal in all overseas departments and territories. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments punishable by up to 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on sexual orientation, with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation, creating the High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality. Police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019 versus around 1,380 in 2018, after President Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as unworthy of France. Conversion therapy was banned by law published 1 February 2022 after Senate passage 7 December 2020 and Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 carrying two years imprisonment and/or 30,000 euro fine, and the MSM blood-donation ban from 20 June 1983 recalled in 2009 moved from one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016 to four months from 2 April 2020 to removal on 16 March 2022 for all regardless of orientation, with lesbian, gay and bisexual individuals allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces.
National press feature: trans women imprisoned by legal-sex assignment under state/province rules reaching this collectivity.
state/province detention watchdog (2021): persistent serious violations against transgender detainees, framework-wide.

Rights overview for this collectivity: metropolitan law applies (marker change without surgery since the 2016-17 reforms; 2012 protections); isolation, tiny population and religious-customary norms create practical barriers; no local specialists; third-gender presence coexists with stigma.

APTN (9 May 2024): a convening in Nadi, Fiji gathered gender-diverse community members from Samoa, Cook Islands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Fiji, Tonga, West Papua and PNG, documenting the Pacific MVPFAFF+ spectrum of identities that Samoa's fa'afafine community is part of: fa'afafine in Samoa and American Samoa, fakaleiti in Tonga, fakafifine in Niue and others.
Samoa's Crimes Act 2013 criminalises same-sex activity, with penalties of up to 5 years, as documented in the Human Dignity Trust country profile.

Samoa Fa'afafine Association (SFA) stakeholder report for Samoa's UPR (39th session, 2021): 'The Protection of the Rights of Fa'afafine/Fa'atama/LGBTIQ/SOGIESC persons in Samoa' - describes the culturally unique third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documents lived experiences and struggles, with the aim of establishing grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature covers Samoa's third gender (fa'afafine) delicately balancing sex and religion.
The APTN socio-economic study covering Samoa is published as a scanned image document, so its contents could not be extracted in text form.

RNZ Pacific (3 May 2013): Samoa's new Crimes Act, in force that week, scrapped the crime of impersonating a woman — Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief; interview also confirms the community was not then agitating to repeal sodomy provisions, i.e. decriminalisation outcome on that front remained unchanged.

Schmidt, 'Redefining Fa'afafine: Western Discourses and the Construction of Transgenderism in Samoa' (Intersections, Aug 2001): fa'afafine = 'in the manner of a woman'; academic analysis argues fa'afafine identities are both viewed through and reshaped by Western sexuality/transgenderism discourses, with Auckland's Samoan diaspora as a contact zone — background for how visitors may encounter the term.

UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific - documents the fa'afafine of Samoa (with American Samoa and Tokelau) among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that are 'important parts of the cultural treasure of the region'.

Samoa has a large transgender or "third gender" community called fa'afafine, with fa'afatama described as people assigned female at birth who embody both gender traits. Fa'afafine are assigned male at birth and explicitly embody both gender traits ranging from extravagantly feminine to conventionally masculine, recognised as a gender identity/gender role since at least the early 20th century. On 1 May 2013, the Crimes Act 2013 (Tulafono o Solitulafono 2013) removed provisions from the now-repealed Crimes Ordinance 1961 which criminalised males "impersonating" females in a public place, which had been used to target transgender women and gender-diverse people. The Ombudsman's first National State of Human Rights Report released in August 2015 referred to fa'afafine as "the third gender that has always existed in Samoa" and noted their hard work in carrying out both men's and women's family roles and responsibilities. Crimes motivated by gender identity are criminalised under Section 7(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act 2016 (Tulafono o Faasalaga 2016). The Samoa Fa'afafine Association (S.F.A.) is described as fostering collaboration between the fa'afafine and LGBTQ communities and aiming to promote a positive attitude toward the Samoan fa'afafine community while balancing Samoan values with Western influences. Sections 67, 68 and 71 of the Crimes Act 2013 (Tulafono o Solitulafono 2013), which took effect on 1 May 2013, criminalize same-sex sexual acts and also prohibit heterosexual anal intercourse and oral sex. Section 67 makes sodomy complete upon penetration with no defence of consent, Section 68 makes attempts to commit sodomy liable to imprisonment up to five (5) years, and Section 71 makes keeping a place of resort for homosexual acts liable to imprisonment up to seven (7) years. "Sodomy" was defined in the 2007 case of Police v Poi as penetration of the male or female victim's anus by the offender's penis, replacing Sections 58D, 58E, 58G and 58J of the repealed Crimes Ordinance 1961 which had criminalised same-sex acts. The article states the law is not enforced, and notes that in June 2010 the Samoa Law Reform Commission recommended repealing all criminal penalties for sodomy and related acts in private between consenting adult males with majority public support, but the Government rejected the recommendation and a reported 2011 decriminalisation proposal. Section 20(2) of the Labour and Employment Relations Act 2013 prohibits direct and indirect discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment policies, procedures or practices, and Section 7(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act 2016 criminalises crimes motivated by sexual orientation. There is no recognition of same-sex relationships, with prime-ministerial statements in 2012, 2013 and 2017 rejecting same-sex marriage on Christian and traditional grounds, and Samoa rejecting first-cycle UPR recommendations by Canada, France and Norway to repeal criminalisation and second-cycle recommendations except Slovenia's on reducing violence, stating decriminalisation was not possible because of cultural sensitivities and Christian beliefs. In 2011 Samoa signed the UN "joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity," and the Mental Health Act 2007 published 2 February 2007 states people are not to be considered mentally ill if they refuse or fail to express a particular sexual orientation and prohibits conversion therapy by mental health professionals. The article states: "Samoan society tends to be very tolerant of being transgender, but not of homosexuality." It states Samoa is fairly progressive in terms of gender identity and expression because of its large fa'afafine community, with fa'afafine described as a recognised part of traditional Samoan customs allowing transgender people in particular trans women to be accepted as they have always been part of Samoan culture. In the UPR process Samoa stated Fa'afafine, gays and lesbians were integral members of society and heirs to family chiefly titles and lands through extended family consensus, but that sexual orientation was a sensitive issue given religious and cultural beliefs of mainstream society requiring education and sensitisation for acceptance. The Samoa Fa'afafine Association sees anti-gay laws as hindering full incorporation of both fa'afafine and gay and lesbian Samoans, stating in 2017 its priority is "the promotion of human rights and the reduction of discrimination and violence based on gender identity" and in 2018 that "marriage is the least of our worries when you don't have a job, it's not a priority." In 2009 the Censorship Board banned screening of Milk about gay activist Harvey Milk while allowing Lesbian Vampire Killers, and in 2019 banned Rocketman about Elton John, actions criticised as "hypocritical," "ignorant" and "selective morality" and protested by the Samoa Fa'afafine Association. In 2026 Samoa held its first LGBTQ Pride Week with LGBTQ residents and allies gathering to celebrate the community.

An advocacy network (9 May 2024): a convening gathered gender-diverse community members from countries across the region — documenting a regional spectrum of third-gender identities as living community infrastructure this country participates in.

Mar 2026): constitutional ban on SO discrimination (art. 24) plus the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination covering gender identity — but implementation inconsistent; PM Kurti's April 2024 pledge to legalise same-sex civil unions stalled, and as of Feb 2026 Parliament still failed to adopt the new Civil Code amid fierce opposition including from the ruling party.
Reuters (May 2024): Muslim-majority Kosovo considering same-sex unions amid fierce opposition.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Kosovo: PM Kurti said during Pride week he would 'do his utmost' to get the Civil Code adopted (2022 parliament had voted against same-sex-couple recognition amendments); a Justice Ministry working group was drafting a bill; CSGD's 2022 annual report found intolerance and hatred, with politicians' hate speech common during Civil Code debates; an artist received death threats over a painting; Kosovo Pride Week held with the motto 'I love you as you are!'.

Prishtina Insight (Jan 2019): ECtHR ruled Macedonia's surgery requirement for gender-marker change violates private-life rights (X v FYROM); Kosovo's Blert Morina — who has his own Constitutional Court case on name/gender change on Kosovo IDs — watched the ruling closely, documenting that Kosovo's legal gender recognition route ran through the courts at that time.
Euronews (March 2022): Kosovo's parliament rejected the new law recognising same-sex civil unions.

Prishtina Insight: third annual Pride Parade in Prishtina, with week-long exhibitions, parties, conferences and discussions by the Center for Equality and Liberty (CEL) — slogan both an appeal for tolerance and an invitation to join the parade; visible, public LGBTI organising in the capital.
IntelliNews: "Kosovo's new Civil Code opens the way for gay marriage", an analysis of the Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language and its implications.

Transgender people are not allowed to legally change their gender in Kosovo even if they have undergone sex reassignment surgery. Kosovo's Anti-Discrimination Law was amended on 26 May 2015 to add gender identity and took effect in July 2015, banning discrimination including in employment, membership of organizations, education, provision of goods and services, social security and access to housing and defining discrimination to include direct and indirect discrimination as well as harassment, victimization and segregation. The new Criminal Code that went into force in April 2019 provides additional penalties for commission of a hate crime motivated by the victim's gender identity. In 2017 Kosovar citizen Blert Morina submitted a court case seeking to change his name and gender on official identification documents after rejection by Kosovo's Civil Registration Agency, with constitutional review requested in July 2018. In December 2019 the Basic Court of Pristina ruled in Morina's favour affirming his right to change both name and sex marker on identification documents, with his lawyer stating that "for the first time the court has decided to recognize the right to gender identity without offering evidence for surgical intervention or any medical change". The Ministry of Justice and the Civil Registration Agency have stated that the judgment will not be considered precedent and other transgender people will have to go through a similar court procedure. Same-sex sexual intercourse has remained legal in independent Kosovo since 2008, following legalization under Ottoman rule in 1858, legalization of male same-sex intercourse in 1994 in the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija when part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the 2004 UNMIK setting of the age of consent at 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation with all sexual offenses made gender-neutral. Article 24 of the 2008 Constitution bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. The 2004 Anti-Discrimination Law bans discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, membership of organizations, education, provision of goods and services, social security and access to housing and explicitly includes direct and indirect discrimination as well as harassment, victimization and segregation. The new Criminal Code in force from April 2019 provides additional penalties for hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. Article 14 of the Law on Family defines marriage as a legally registered community of two persons of different sexes, although in 2014 the President of the Constitutional Court said Kosovo de jure allows same-sex marriage and Article 144(3) requires Constitutional Court approval of amendments to ensure they do not infringe previously guaranteed civil rights, while a 7 July 2020 proposal for same-sex civil partnerships in the new Civil Code was rejected by the Assembly on 16 March 2022 with only 28 of 120 MPs voting in favour and on 25 April 2024 Prime Minister Albin Kurti announced intent to legalize same-sex unions. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people are allowed to serve openly in the military though they may face discrimination by peers, while a 2018 Blood Donation Week guideline bars those who have "intimate relationships with the same sex" from donating blood. LGBTQ people tend to avoid reporting discrimination or abuse to police, with 10 bias-motivated crimes against LGBTQ people reported to authorities in 2019 and a further 13 reported only to LGBTQ organizations. In February 2019 authorities initiated a case against a Ministry of Justice official who called for LGBTQ people to be beheaded and police took him into custody. The article states discrimination and stigmatization against the LGBTQ+ community remains very rampant amongst the general population even though it is outlawed, which refers to LGBTQ+ generally and not to transgender people specifically. The Center for Social Emancipation describes gay life in Kosovo as being "underground" and mostly secretive with one gay bar in Pristina, which refers to gay life specifically. A 2015 National Democratic Institute survey found 81% of LGBTQ+ Kosovars said they had been subject to psychological abuse and 29% reported being victim of physical violence, while a National Democratic Institute study found over 97% not willing to accept their child if they came out as lesbian or gay. Pride events celebrating the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia have been organized since 2007, with the first pride parade in Pristina in May 2016 and annual Pride Week since 2017, including the October 2019 march from Skanderbeg Square down Mother Teresa Boulevard to Zahir Pajaziti Square with the slogan "Whoever your heart beats for" held without incidence but under multiple threats especially in 2017 with anonymous threats warning people not to attend. Government support included a late 2013 Parliament bill to create a coordinating group for the LGBTQ community and a 17 May 2014 march against homophobia by politicians and diplomats welcomed by the European Union office and the government with a large LGBTQ flag covering the front of the government building that night. The article provides no documented direct quoted statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically distinct from the LGBTQ+, gay, and lesbian or gay references above.

Kosovo's Constitution adopted 9 April 2008 and in force 15 June 2008 guarantees equality before the law and prohibits discrimination on grounds including gender and sexual orientation and protects human dignity as inviolable.

In December 2019 the Basic Court of Pristina granted Blert Morina legal change of name and sex marker, establishing that gender identity in Kosovo can be legally recognized without proof of surgical intervention or other medical change.

In Kosovo CSGD provides LGBTQI+ people free confidential legal aid and psychological support in person and online via app.csgd-ks.org, tailored reproductive and sexual health services including support navigating hormonal procedures for transgender people in cooperation with the Ministry and free HIV testing, with free PrEP HIV-prevention treatment available at the QKUK Infectious Disease Clinic since June 12, 2024 following CSGD advocacy.

International LGBT-rights organisation overview (updated March 2026): a constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination plus a 2015 anti-discrimination law covering gender identity — but implementation inconsistent; the head of government's April 2024 pledge to legalise same-sex civil unions stalled, and as of February 2026 parliament had still failed to adopt the new civil code amid fierce opposition, including from the ruling party.

texts.cleaned_text: Amnesty International campaign story (26 Nov 2024), 'Madalitso's story': a Zambian medical professional, 36, had served three years by Nov 2024 for consensual same-sex conduct; his medical expertise lost to a health system short of workers; illustrates the persecution of LGBTI people in Zambia.

US State Dept 2021 Country Report, Zambia: government continued to reject recognition/protection of LGBTQI+ rights; police perpetrated violence and verbal/physical harassment based on gender identity and sexual orientation; LGBTQI+ people at risk of societal violence from prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of law; advocacy groups report police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTQI+ individuals (fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha / $30-$900); discrimination in employment, housing, education and health continued.

HRW report 'Dignity Debased' (12 Jul 2016): documents forced anal examinations in at least eight countries including ZAMBIA — less frequent there than Egypt/Tunisia but prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal exams as court evidence in sodomy cases (incl. a mass trial of ~20 men); recommends worldwide ban; such exams are treated by victims as painful, degrading sexual violence.

US State Dept 2022 Country Report, Zambia: no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons; when police detain LGBTQI+ members they often threaten charges under other laws to extort bribes for release; no credible reports of government agents condoning violence, but President Hichilema's 30 May statement opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage produced a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults; societal violence and employment/housing/education/health discrimination continued.

Freedom of expression on LGBTQ matters is effectively barred: the Zambian government does not permit advocacy of LGBTQ rights, and the U.S. Department of State's 2021 report concluded that 'Freedom of expression or peaceful assembly on LGBTQI+ matters remained nonexistent.' In 1998 Vice President Christon Tembo called for the arrest of people promoting gay rights, and the Registrar of Societies stated he would refuse to register any LGBTQ organisation. In The People v. Paul Kasonkomona (2013), an activist arrested after calling for decriminalization on a TV talk show was cleared: the Magistrate Court and then the High Court ruled he was reasonably exercising his right to freedom of expression, with the High Court rejecting the 'soliciting', 'public place' and 'immoral purposes' charges, though the government contested the decision.

LGBTQ people in Zambia are subjected to human rights violations by police, arbitrary arrest and detention, and violence and abuse in custody; police threaten and extort LGBTQ persons. The U.S. State Department's 2021 report states police perpetrated violence and verbal and physical harassment based on gender identity and sexual orientation, and that LGBTQI+ persons faced 'prolonged detentions'. Those prosecuted for same-sex conduct are subjected to forced anal examinations for evidence-gathering, described by Amnesty International in a 2014 case as 'tantamount to torture and scientifically invalid' and condemned by the WHO and medical authorities.

There are no broad legal protections against discrimination in health care, but limited standards exist: the Health Professions Council of Zambia's 2014 Code of Ethics bars practitioners from discriminating in patient management based on sexuality, and the Ministry of Health's 2022 Zambia Consolidated HIV Guidelines require facilities to serve all adolescents regardless of sexual orientation or sexual behaviour. As of July 2007 no public or private programmes provided HIV-related counselling to homosexual men (adult HIV prevalence about 17 percent), the government National AIDS Control Program does not address same-sex relationships, and the 2021 State Department report notes LGBTQI+ persons faced 'inability to access healthcare services'. Societal discrimination in access to health care is documented (US State Dept 2010; Global Rights/IGLHRC). The National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health Policy (2015) recognises sexual orientation and gender identities as central aspects of being human, and Section 158(3) of the penal code subjects only same-sex conduct between minors to court-determined community service or counselling, with no equivalent provision for opposite-sex minors. No information on trans-specific healthcare or medication appears. Section 158(3) of the penal code, amended in 2005, targets children who commit 'gross indecency' with another child of the same sex, in public or private, or who attempt to procure such acts, making them liable to 'such community service or counseling as the court may determine in the best interests of the child', with no parallel offence for minors of opposite sex. Societal discrimination is reported in access to education for LGBTQ people (US State Dept 2010; Global Rights/IGLHRC). Younger generations are beginning to show slightly more positive, open-minded attitudes toward LGBTQ peers, driven by the internet and the country's fast digitization exposing people to more stories from different facets of life.

Social attitudes are mostly negative, coloured by perceptions that homosexuality is immoral and a form of insanity, reflecting evangelical religious influence and colonial-era attitudes; a 2010 survey found only 2 percent of Zambians find homosexuality morally acceptable, nine points below Uganda's 11 percent. Anti-LGBTQ mobilisation is organised: the NGO Zambia Against People with Abnormal Sexual Acts (ZAPASA) formed in 1999 'to combat homosexuality'. Violence is frequent and communal: threats, stalking, vandalism, hate crimes including murders, with little recourse from police; in May 2014 residents of Marapodi, Lusaka apprehended two suspected lesbians and demanded their arrest, and in January 2015 an openly gay man was attacked by a mob that reportedly included three police officers. Most LGBTQ people in Zambia are closeted due to fear of targeting, with lesbians especially vulnerable in the patriarchal structure. The internet and digitization are credited with reducing prejudice among growing youth, and in 2013 Christine Kaseba, wife of then-President Michael Sata, said silence around men who have sex with men should end and no one should be discriminated against on the basis of sexual orientation.

New Zimbabwe, 9 July 2018: the health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gays, sex workers and transgender/non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty ('nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups'), issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff. For a trans visitor: formal policy guarantees health-service access including transition-relevant care at public facilities, though day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

Mabvurira et al., 'The politics of sexual identities in Zimbabwe: A Social Work perspective?' (Int'l Journal of Humanities and Social Science, July 2012): homosexuals live secluded lives due to prejudice; argues homosexuality is 'as African as the baobab tree and as Zimbabwean as the Great Zimbabwe Ruins', tracing same-sex relations in pre-colonial and post-colonial Zimbabwe; social workers should promote social justice for the gay community.
An article in the Journal of Homosexuality, published by Taylor & Francis, examines homosexuality in Zimbabwe.

GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe) is a voluntary membership organisation established in 1990, with more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres. Services include legal support, explicitly covering arrests for 'sodomy', counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. Legal aid and counselling remain reachable for an LGBTI traveller despite criminalisation.

Gender marker change is not allowed. Section 18(2) of the Births and Deaths Registration Act permits a first-name change only by application to the Registrar General with evidence justifying the need, and the Registrar General's discretion may prevent a change based on gender identity. Activist Jordan Chanetsa is documented as commenting that transgender people face difficulty accessing legal work because official documents do not reflect their gender. In 2014 activist Rikki Nathanson was arrested for using a women's bathroom under a criminal nuisance charge, the charge was thrown out, she sued for damages and won, and in 2015 she established Trans Research, Education, Advocacy & Training (TREAT). Health Ministry training manuals require health professionals to support the unique healthcare needs of transgender and non-gender conforming people alongside sex workers, men who have sex with men, and people who inject and use drugs, stating that criminalization of sex work, drug use and some sexual acts creates disproportionate harms, undermines HIV prevention for the whole nation, and impairs access to healthcare. Sodomy is classified as unlawful sexual conduct under the Criminal Code, defined as anal sexual intercourse or any "indecent act" between consenting adults, with common-law definitions covering "unlawful and intentional sexual relations per anum between two human males" and "unnatural offences." A 2006 revision expanded sodomy to any "act involving contact between two males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as an indecent act," criminalizing same-sex hand-holding, hugging or kissing as "sexual deviancy" among 15 additions to the Criminal Code. Same-sex marriage is banned by the Constitution, which was amended in 2013 to define marriage as between a man and a woman, and in May 2019 Cabinet approved marriage-law amendments to align the ban on same-sex marriage. LGBTQ people have no general legal protections from discrimination, violence and harassment, except explicit protection based on sexual orientation regarding personal information under the Freedom of Information Act (2020) and the Cyber and Data Protection Act (2022). Since 1995 the Government has carried out campaigns against homosexual men and women, with enforcement including infiltration of GALZ, bribery, detention, beating, killing and rape by authorities and reported use of the Central Intelligence Organisation to beat and arrest homosexuals. Section 11 of the Censorship and Entertainments Control Act prohibiting undesirable publications defined as "indecent or obscene or is offensive or harmful to public morals or is likely to be contrary to public health" has been used to harass LGBTQ people and activists. In 1998 former President Canaan Banana was found guilty on eleven charges of sodomy, attempted sodomy and indecent assault after 1996 arrest, sentenced to 10 years imprisonment, defrocked, and served 6 months in an open prison.

In early July 2006 Zimbabwe amended its criminal code to add a 'sexual deviancy' offense that criminalizes holding hands, hugging or kissing between two people of the same sex and expands sodomy beyond sexual activity to any contact between two males that a reasonable person would regard as an indecent act.

The Guardian (26 July 2025) on German Pride parades facing a rise in attacks: Berlin CSD organisers urge vigilance with hundreds of thousands expected; the amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-extremist attacks on Pride events nationally in 2024 and 30 so far in 2025 across ~120 parades (including an attack with boiling water), and runs a €100,000 CSD support fund focused on eastern Germany; Maneo, the Berlin anti-violence documentation project, states big-city parades like Berlin and Cologne were not specifically threatened and that smaller towns are hardest to police; a Berlin-Neukölln queer café owner reports 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.

MANEO, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, recorded 723 LSBTIQ+-hostile incidents in Berlin in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, from 1,014 new reports, a new high. Its 12 May 2026 release lists insults, threats and physical attacks in public transport, parks and streets, with Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten most affected, plus 58 attacks on LSBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events. MANEO says the figures capture only part of reality because of a high dark figure, and that the counselling centre itself was attacked several times in 2025. Neukölln is named among the worst-hit districts.

MANEO reports that at the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day a vehicle drove into a crowd in the Tiergarten area, killing one woman, injuring several people and forcing the event to be cancelled. The project offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line (030-2163336, daily 17:00-19:00).

The Berlin state government's prison-service page states that legislation has created a basis for considering trans, inter* and non-binary people held in custody, that Berlin prison staff are responsible for taking each detainee's individual needs into account within the legal framework, and it details gender-segregated placement, intake procedures and counselling and support offers for detainees in Berlin prisons such as JVA Moabit and JVA für Frauen Berlin.

Hirschfeld's Institute for Sexual Science held studies of the first gender-affirming surgeries among decades of research, destroyed when the institute at In den Zelten was sacked on May 6, 1933 and burned. The article states there were no explicit laws against exhibiting non-gender-conforming behavior, so enforcers criminalized queer women through other provisions with incarceration for so-called anti-social behavior under an extremely vague definition and no reliable numbers. Contemporary Berlin is described as having a rise of queer spaces catering to marginalized groups within the LGBTQ community such as transgender individuals. FLINTA spaces are defined as "Frauen, Lesben, Intergeschlechtliche, Nichtbinäre, Trans und Agender Personen," meaning those who do not fit into a cis male gender identity, motivated by discomfort around cis men and male-domination of many queer spaces. Male-exclusive venues Lab.Oratory and Boiler historically catered exclusively to male patrons with cases of feminine men and gender queer individuals rejected, with entry policy evolving since the 2000s to include more types of non-female gender expressions though instances of exclusion still occur, while a concept of queer masculinities including gay, bi, trans and queer men reshapes selection. Cited studies indicate gay, lesbian, and trans individuals especially may engage in drug use as a means of coping with societal marginalization and discrimination, exacerbated by multiple minority stress including gender identity. Several thousand men were sentenced under Section 175 of the Reich Criminal Code between 1933 and 1945, with about 6,000 actually interned to camps with a presumed high death rate, and upon liberation inmates feared re-incarceration with fears justified. In 1950 East Germany returned to the pre-Nazi version of Section 175 while Section 175a continued to be applied, from the late 1950s homosexual acts among adults were no longer punishable, and in 1968 a new penal code made same-sex sexual acts with minors punishable for both women and men in §151, deleted with effect from July 1, 1989. West Germany retained the Nazi-era versions of Sections 175 and 175a for two decades, convicting 50,000 men from 1945 to 1969, roughly the same amount as during the Nazi era. Reforms in 1969 and 1973 effectively made only sexual acts with males under age 18 punishable, while the age of consent for lesbian and heterosexual acts was 14 years. Section 175 was completely repealed in 1994, four years after unification, for the territory of the old Federal Republic. Those punished under the broader version in effect until 1969, many suffering imprisonment and entry in the national criminal record with life-long employment and housing consequences, were not rehabilitated until 2017. Compensation, only for actually convicted men still alive and eligible, was 3,000 euros and an additional 1,500 euros for each year of detention suffered, described as negligible.

texts.cleaned_text: National framework applying to Bavaria. Adults have been able to change legal gender since 1980. The Self-Determination Act was approved by the cabinet in August 2023 and passed the Bundestag 374-251 on 12 April 2024; it lets adults over 18 change first name and gender by self-determination with three months' notice, in force since 1 November 2024. Same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since 2017, and discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity is banned nationwide in employment and goods and services, with some protections varying by region.

The Self-Determination Act (SBGG), the federal law the Bavarian Bundesrat initiative sought to tighten, passed the Bundestag on 12 April 2024 by 374-251 with 11 abstentions and the Bundesrat on 17 May 2024, was gazetted 21 June 2024, and allowed changes to be registered from 1 August 2024, taking effect 1 November 2024. Adults declare the change themselves before the registry office. Those aged 14-17 need a guardian's consent or the family court's; for under-14s only the guardian can declare. A three-month waiting period applies, with a one-year lockout after a change. The Bundesrat's criticism of 20 October 2023 held that the draft let parents decide under-14 gender-entry changes 'without any counselling, examination and investigation of the child's welfare', the contested point behind the Bavarian-led tightening initiative.

The page states that hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned nationwide in Germany, but that some states have laws banning all forms of discrimination in their constitutions - Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Saarland and Thuringia - and that in those states hate speech based on both sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited. For Saarland this is a jurisdiction-specific enforcement difference: transphobic hate speech is prohibited under the state constitution, unlike in most of Germany, and the federal General Act on Equal Treatment (in force since 18 August 2006) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, health services and the provision of goods and services.

Since 2006 Amazonas state policies include discrimination based on gender identity, and since 2019 transphobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to racism. Since the March 2018 unanimous Supreme Federal Court ruling, transgender people may change legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial authorization or medical report, with registry-office gender changes reported up 59% by 2024. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender; in 2022 Álex Souza de Sá became the first non-binary person recognized, requiring rectification in Rio de Janeiro and six months of insistence plus intervention by the Public Defender's Office to obtain recognition in Manaus where the registry lacked a gender-neutral marker. For facilities, on 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. For care, in November 2023 the State Public Defender's Office opened monitoring of public health services for transgender and travesti people including hormones and surgeries, in August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended the state formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualization services including sexual reassignment surgeries with deadlines for submission to the Ministry of Health, and on 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18. For protection machinery, in 2021 the State Public Defender's Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group focused on human rights violations and training security agents, and in August 2024 the State Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right! for LGBTQ youth expelled from homes stating conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective." Cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state are described as underreported, with 43 cases registered according to Brazilian Public Security Forum data cited in research. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Amazonas since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision following the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision, with a 328% increase between 2020 and 2025, 287 unions registered in 2024 and 98 in the first five months of 2025. Same-sex adoption was first authorized in Amazonas in November 2012 by a state court judge, with nationwide legalization by the Supreme Federal Court in 2015. Since 2006 state policies include discrimination based on sexual orientation, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to racism. Assembly and expression restrictions include State Law 6,469/2023 prohibiting participation of children and adolescents in pride parades with fines up to R$10,000, and the 17 October 2024 law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality, amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaça de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, with prior bullying reported by area residents.

In March 2018 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ruled that transgender people may change their legal name and gender marker on civil records without sex-reassignment surgery, hormonal treatment, or judicial authorization.
On 18 October 2022 Manaus sanctioned a municipal law prohibiting multigender/unisex restrooms.
In August 2024, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended that the state of Amazonas guarantee integral health care to the LGBTQIAPN+ population, including trans people.

In Amazonas as of 1 November 2023 the State Public Defender's health unit opened a collective procedure to audit SUS care for trans people covering access to hormonization, outpatient services, and lack of accreditation for gender-affirming surgeries including sexual reassignment, and in October 2023 the Manaus Municipal Health Secretariat committed to dispense standardized medications to trans people on prescription from the Codajás Outpatient Clinic that handles hormonization and to designate reference UBS primary-care units in each city zone, while the State Health Secretariat was ordered to report on equitable integral care including remedying hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under Federal Council of Medicine Resolution No. 2,265 of 2019.

On 10 October 2023 Amazonas State Law No. 6,463 expressly prohibited use of neutral language, non-binary dialect, or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of schools and public agencies statewide.

In Amazonas as of August 2024, LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents facing family discrimination and expulsion are guaranteed under ECA Article 17 physical, psychological and moral integrity including identity and autonomy and under Constitution/ECA duties of family, society and State to ensure health, food, education and protection from negligence and discrimination with equal treatment of children regardless of sexual orientation, with bullying criminalized under Law 14.811/2024 by fine to 4 years' imprisonment, homophobia criminalized per 2019 STF ruling as imprescriptible and non-bailable, conversion/"gay cure" therapy prohibited as illegal and ineffective, and legal support available through the Defensoria Especializada em Direitos Humanos.

On 28 June 2021 the Amazonas Public Defender's Office created the permanent Working Group on Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship to identify LGBTQIA+ human-rights violations in public security, train public-security agents for service to LGBTQIA+ people, and issue recommendations and extrajudicial measures, while LGBTQIA+ victims in Manaus can obtain assistance via Disk 129 Monday-Friday 8am-2pm through the Specialized Human Rights unit, in a context where Amazonas led North and Central-West states with 4.66 LGBTQIA+ persons murdered per million inhabitants in 2018.

On 23 May 2019 a majority of Brazil's Supreme Federal Tribunal (6 of 11 justices) voted to criminalize transphobia under Brazil's 1989 racism law punishable by up to five years' imprisonment until Congress enacts specific LGBT-discrimination legislation, to take effect after all justices voted on 5 June 2019.

In Amazonas during 2021-2022, crimes involving transsexual persons formed part of only 0.36% of total reported crimes in the capital and interior, police occurrence reports did not identify transfobia or gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality markers, trans victim data were few and badly structured with victims not infrequently inverted to accused through faulty BOs, and unprepared public agents and defective registration mechanisms left trans subjects invisibilized and without protection.

texts.cleaned_text: El Tiempo data investigation (2025): Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader who had campaigned with the 'No Es Hora De Callar' movement and joined its sixth symbolic return march of more than 500 survivors of sexual violence, was killed - the article calls it a trans feminicide - in Bolívar on 22 May, in Carmen de Bolívar; more than 19 days later the circumstances remained unclear, and friend and fellow social leader Yirley Velasco remembers her as having taken up the fight for trans rights in the municipality. The piece exposes the gap between official and NGO figures: the Fiscalía's own data base records 3,322 intentional homicides of people identified as LGBTIQ+ between January 2010 and May 2025, 431 for 2024 versus about 160 reported by the NGO (267 fewer), and 39 homicides in one Fiscalía dependency's 2025 data versus 156 in the policies-and-strategies base; experts cited describe the information system as neither unified nor reliable.

COPFS 'Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26' (30 Jun 2026): 7,115 hate-crime charges in total, up 17% on 2024-25 and the highest since 2003-04. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, up 21% from 86, the highest level since the 2021 Act took effect.

Scottish Government 'Hate crimes recorded by the police in Scotland, 2024-25' (pub. 17 Feb 2026): police recorded 8,538 hate crimes, with the highest rates per 10,000 residents in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh (about 32.25 each); 62% carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator — first annual report under the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021.

Under the Gender Recognition Act 2004, transgender people in Scotland may change their legal gender. In 2018 the Scottish Government announced plans to provide an "X" sex descriptor on identity documents and to lower the minimum age of transition to 16. A Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill to reform the 2004 Act was introduced in March 2022 and passed in December 2022 by 86-39, applying only to Scotland. The Bill was blocked by the UK government under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998, the first use of that power to overturn Scottish legislation, while awaiting royal assent. The Equality Act 2010 covers gender reassignment and outlaws discrimination, harassment and victimisation because a person belongs to, is thought to belong to, or is associated with a protected group. Scotland enacted 2009 legislation providing penalty enhancements where crime is motivated by the victim's gender identity, and hate-crime legislation passed in March 2021 by 82-32, receiving royal assent a month later and taking effect 1 April 2024, explicitly includes gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity was legalised in Scotland by Section 80 of the Criminal Justice (Scotland) Act 1980, in force 1 February 1981, and the age of consent was equalised at 16 in 2001. Section 2A prohibiting promotion of homosexuality was repealed in Scotland by the Ethical Standards in Public Life etc. (Scotland) Act 2000. The Historical Sexual Offences (Pardons and Disregards) (Scotland) Act 2018, passed in June 2018 and effective in October 2019, issued symbolic pardons to men convicted of consensual same-sex activity before decriminalisation and allows an accepted disregard application to prevent inclusion in disclosure checks and treat the offence as not occurred. Civil partnerships for same-sex couples have been available since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004, conferring property, inheritance tax, social security, pension, parental responsibility, maintenance, tenancy, insurance and next-of-kin rights with formal dissolution akin to divorce. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 16 December 2014 under the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Scotland) Act 2014, passed 4 February 2014 by 108-15 with royal assent 12 March 2014, with first ceremonies 31 December 2014 and no obligation on religious organisations or celebrants to perform them. Same-sex couples obtained joint and stepchild adoption rights from 28 September 2009, with the Looked After Children (Scotland) Regulations 2009 allowing consideration as foster parents on the same basis as others. The Equality Act 2010 outlaws discrimination, harassment and victimisation based on sexual orientation, and 2009 legislation provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation, with sexual orientation explicitly included in the 2021 hate-crime law effective 1 April 2024.

A prosecuting-authority report (June 2026) records 7,115 hate-crime charges in 2025-26 — the highest total since 2003-04 — with the transgender-identity aggravation at 104 charges, up 21% from 86 the year before.

A government report (February 2026) records 8,538 hate crimes recorded by police in 2024-25, the first annual report under the 2021 hate-crime statute, with most carrying a race aggravator and about a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator; the highest per-resident rates were in the region's two largest cities.

BBC News (8 September 2025): guidance supporting transgender pupils was withdrawn from the Northern Ireland Education Authority's website after Education Minister Paul Givan requested removal, arguing it conflicted with departmental policy and the law in Northern Ireland; the guidance had recommended that trans pupils be allowed to use changing rooms matching their gender identity, and teachers' representatives warned removal 'ignores the practical realities'.

BBC News (14 December 2025): other executive parties blocked justice minister Naomi Long's plan to add transgender people as a protected characteristic in Northern Ireland's new hate-crime legislation (approval sought early November, response deadline mid-November; bill had executive agreement from December 2024). Long cited PSNI statistics of close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes.

The Gender Recognition Act 2004 applies to Northern Ireland and provides for a person's change of gender to be officially recognised, introduced after the 2002 case of Goodwin v United Kingdom in which the European Court of Human Rights ruled the United Kingdom's failure violated articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights. To change gender, a person must demonstrate gender dysphoria and have lived in the relevant gender for two years before applying for a gender recognition certificate. Before the 2020 introduction of same-sex marriage, a person had to be unmarried before changing legal gender. In May 2021 a Northern Ireland court judgment on a challenge to the UK gender recognition law made a binding ruling that gender dysphoria based on an individual's mental dynamic is no longer legally required, due to the WHO decision in 2019 no longer treating gender identity disorder under DMD-IV as a mental illness or mental disorder. That ruling applies only to Northern Ireland so far and not the rest of the UK, but sets up a legal precedent for the rest of the UK in the future. The Sex Discrimination (Gender Reassignment) Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1999 provides a degree of protection for transgender people who are undergoing gender reassignment in employment and vocational training. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1982 under the Homosexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 1982 which came into force on 8 December 1982, following the 22 October 1981 European Court of Human Rights 15-4 ruling in Dudgeon v United Kingdom that criminalisation of male homosexual acts under the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 violated Article 8. Anti-LGBT criminal provisions were removed throughout Northern Ireland by section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 abolishing buggery and gross indecency, with private gay sex between more than two people legalised but cottaging remaining illegal, and the age of consent equalised at 17 by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2000 effective in 2001 then reduced to 16 by the Sexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 2008. Civil partnerships have been available to same-sex couples since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004, and same-sex marriage took effect on 13 January 2020 under regulations signed 19 December 2019 after UK Parliament legislation receiving royal assent on 24 July 2019 required extension if the Assembly did not reconvene by 21 October 2019, with the first wedding on 11 February 2020 after a 28-day notice period and religious and church same-sex weddings permitted since 1 September 2020. Same-sex couples were granted full adoption rights in 2013 after High Court 2012 and Court of Appeal 2013 rulings that the ban was discriminatory and a breach of human rights and rejection of a further Supreme Court appeal. Section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 requires public authorities to have due regard to promoting equality of opportunity between persons of different sexual orientation through Equality Schemes monitored by the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland. The Employment Equality (Sexual Orientation) Regulations (NI) 2003 effective 2 December 2003 prohibit discrimination and harassment in employment, higher education and vocational training, and the Equality Act (Sexual Orientation) Regulations (NI) 2006 effective 1 January 2007 prohibit discrimination in goods and services, premises, education and public functions. The permanent blood donation ban on men who had sex with men moved to a one-year deferral effective 1 September 2016, to a 3-month deferral effective 1 June 2020, and from August 2021 monogamous gay and bi men may donate without a waiting period while non-monogamous gay and bi men must wait 3 months, and historic convictions became eligible for pardon under the Policing and Crime Act 2017 Alan Turing Law extended by a November 2016 Legislative Consent Motion, though by June 2019 only two men had sought pardons and both failed.

A national broadcaster (8 September 2025): the regional education body's 2019 guidance on supporting transgender pupils is withdrawn from its website after a supreme-court ruling on biological sex; the education minister requested the withdrawal, said the guidance did not reflect departmental policy and was inconsistent with local law, and called it a product of activist campaigning; opposition parties press for reinstatement and disclosure of the legal advice.

A national broadcaster: the justice minister's attempt to add transgender people as a protected group in hate-crime sentencing reform is being stalled, with the main unionist party reported to be blocking the measure.

A newspaper: an exploding pipe bomb was thrown through the window of the home of a 27-year-old trans woman while she watched television; the police force treated it as a hate crime with sectarian framing and she was forced to move out.

An LGBTQ monitoring organisation's hate-crime page: an average of about 290 reported anti-LGB&T incidents and crimes per year (2013–2017), reporting stagnant, and quarterly series running back to 2004/05 including a separate transgender-identity strand.

A national broadcaster: the health minister publicly defends an uplift of more than three-quarters of a million (local currency) for gender-identity health services against unionist criticism, evidencing a divided executive rather than uniform hostility.

Welsh Government LGBTQ+ Action Plan document for young people (posted January 2026): part of the standing devolved inclusion programme whose update page answers the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025.

Welsh Government statutory school guidance "Rights, Respect, Equality" (consultation May 2025): obliges schools to challenge bullying and harassment on sex, gender-reassignment and sexual-orientation grounds, with incident recording/monitoring and a parental escalation route.

The Welsh Government's February 2023 LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales aims to make Wales 'the most LGBTQ+ friendly nation in Europe'. Deputy Minister Hannah Blythyn announced it in the Senedd on 21 June 2022 under the 2021 Welsh Labour–Plaid Cymru agreement. It was built on 61 recommendations from the Independent LGBTQ+ Expert Panel (March 2021) and a 12-week public consultation with 1,328 responses, and it funds a Grassroots Pride Fund. The government pursued a Welsh-specific ban on conversion practices, forming a Working Group on Banning Conversion Practices in December 2022 (gov.wales 'Banning conversion practices in Wales', May 2024). The plan records the UK Government's blocking of the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill in January 2023. Welsh NHS commissioners stated in March 2024 they had no plans to develop a children's gender service, and parents of transgender children called for more help (BBC, March 2024).

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Wales since 1967, the age of consent was equalised in 2001, remaining restrictions were removed in 2003, legal gender recognition has been available since 2004 under the Gender Recognition Act, civil partnerships since 2005, same-sex marriage since 2014, and full adoption rights since 2005, with discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity. Trans adults in Wales were historically referred to London clinics for transgender healthcare until the first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019 (BBC).

texts.cleaned_text: BBC News (19 June 2026): Lady Ross of the Court of Session ruled unlawful Scottish Prison Service guidance that allowed some trans prisoners to be housed according to gender identity, holding that sex segregation in prisons must be based on biological sex, in line with the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 definition-of-a-woman ruling. The Supreme Court had already held that Article 8 confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex, and that UK-wide ruling governs England's prison and custody decisions. The first minister said the government will consider the judgment.

The UK Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling is the predicate for England's EHRC code and BTP strip-search policy, and a judicial review reported by BBC News on 5 February 2026 tests how far it reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide. In argument, government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy 'Orwellian'.

texts.cleaned_text: The Home Office's England-and-Wales statistics (published 9 October 2025) record 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025, with the transgender strand down 11% and the sexual-orientation strand down 2% against the previous year; the bulletin cautions that recorded figures understate prevalence - the Crime Survey estimate is about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year - and that a February 2024 MPS recording-system change means earlier years over-counted.

BBC News reports the UK Supreme Court's unanimous judgment in the For Women Scotland case (handed down 16 April 2025) that 'woman' and 'sex' in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological woman and biological sex, meaning a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections; Lord Hodge said the ruling should not be read as reducing the Act's protection against discrimination for transgender people. The judgment fixes the definitions that govern services, searches and detention allocation in England.

BBC News reports (20 May 2025) that the Equality and Human Rights Commission - the body enforcing the Equality Act 2010 in England and Wales - updated its code of practice after the Supreme Court ruling, advising that services and businesses may ask for a person's birth certificate where there is 'genuine concern' about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport 'when necessary' for safety. This is the operative enforcement guidance a trans visitor to England meets at venues, transport and services day to day.

In 1970 Corbett v Corbett barred transgender people from changing the sex marker on their birth certificate, which also prevented legal marriage to a person of the other gender as it would have been treated as an unrecognised same-sex marriage. In 1996 P v S and Cornwall County Council held that European anti-gender discrimination law applied to trans people, and in 2002 Goodwin v United Kingdom found the UK in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights for maintaining that status quo, leading to the Gender Recognition Act 2004. A December 2002 Lord Chancellor's policy document categorically stated that transsexualism "is not a mental illness." Since 4 April 2005 the Gender Recognition Act 2004 has allowed transgender people to change legal gender and obtain a new birth certificate giving full recognition of acquired sex for all purposes. Applicants must present evidence to a Gender Recognition Panel for a Gender Recognition Certificate, must have transitioned for two years before issuance, and are not required to have undergone sex reassignment surgery though such surgery counts as supporting evidence, with formal approval for medical gender reassignment available on the NHS or privately. Under the Act as originally framed, a married transgender applicant was required to divorce or annul the marriage before issuance of a certificate, and a married couple including a transgender partner could not directly re-register but had to dissolve the marriage, obtain gender recognition, then register for civil partnership with associated paperwork and costs. ILGA-Europe's executive in 2020 expressed concern about a "hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups" as the UK fell to ninth place with 66%, dropping further to 22nd place with 45% by 2025. The 1533 Buggery Act made male anal sex a civil offence punishable by death in England and Wales, later removed as capital by section 61 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 while male homosexual acts remained imprisonable, and lesbian acts were never criminalised as civilian offences. The Sexual Offences Act 1967, receiving royal assent 27 July 1967, provided limited decriminalisation in England and Wales only where the act was consensual, in private limited to two persons, and both were aged 21, a higher threshold than 16 for heterosexual acts and strictly interpreted to exclude hotel rooms or homes with a third person present. Equalisation came through the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2000, in force 8 January 2001, lowering the age of consent to 16 throughout the UK and for the first time creating an age of consent for lesbian acts, followed by the Sexual Offences Act 2003 in force 1 May 2004 which removed privacy conditions and created sex-neutral offences. Section 28, introduced in the 1980s to prohibit "promotion of homosexuality" by schools and local authorities, was repealed in 2003, while discrimination protections in place since 1999 were extended to all areas by the Equality Act 2010 and the ban on open service by LGBT personnel was officially lifted in 2016 after non-enforcement since 2000. The Merchant Shipping (Homosexual Conduct) Act 2017 repealed sections 146(4) and 147(3) of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, and the Policing and Crime Act 2017 in effect 31 January 2017 provided posthumous pardons and a disregard application process for historic convictions, with "disregards" available since 2012 under the Protection of Freedoms Act. Civil partnerships with most rights of marriage were legalised by the Civil Partnership Act 2004 effective 5 December 2005, adoption by same-sex couples in England and Wales took effect 30 December 2005 under the Adoption and Children Act 2002, and same-sex marriage in England and Wales was allowed by the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 in force 13 March 2014 with first marriages 29 March 2014. ILGA-Europe gave the UK the highest score in Europe in 2015 with 86% progress toward "respect of human rights and full equality" for LGBT people, but the score fell to 66% and ninth place by 2020.

News reporting (19 June 2026): a judge ruled that guidance of a prison service allowing some trans prisoners to be housed by gender identity is unlawful — sex segregation in prisons must be based on biological sex, applying the April 2025 definition ruling of the country's highest court. The judgment confirms the biological-sex custody logic that the same ruling imposes on this state/province's prison and custody decisions; the first minister said the government will consider the judgment, and the country's highest court had already held that the human-rights convention confers no automatic right to opposite-biological-sex accommodation.

Same-sex marriage is legal nationwide under the CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), with adoption permitted since 2010 and full rights since 2015. Gender-marker change requires no surgery, hormones or diagnosis under the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option exists nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020, and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022.

Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America: same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment of 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice. Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianopolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure. Smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

Rondonia has no state law prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity, but since 2019 such discrimination is criminalized nationally by a Supreme Federal Court ruling equating it with the crime of racism. On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. In July 2022 Hanier Miranda became the first person in the state to obtain a birth certificate with sex marker X after initial denial at the registry for lack of a regulated third-gender procedure and a year-long lawsuit by the Center for Legal Practices, Research and Extensions at the Catholic Faculty of Porto Velho. On 28 August 2025 an ordinance signed by Appellate Judge Daniel Ribeiro Lagos guarantees transgender people the use of their social name and the use of bathrooms and locker rooms in accordance with gender identity. Between 2017 and 2021 there were 12 murders of transgender people in the state, with Rondonia ranked as the 3rd state with the highest homicide rate in the North Region of Brazil. In 2025 federal and state prosecution and defender bodies recommended training on gender identity for police officers and firefighters and inclusion of LGBTQ population data in official reports. State Law no. 5123 banning gender-neutral language in schools, approved in October 2021 and signed on the 19th by Governor Marcos Rocha, was blocked in November 2021 by preliminary injunction and struck down on 10 February 2023, while a law passed on 10 July 2026 requiring parental authorization for classes on gender identity was struck down on 17 August by the Court of Justice of Rondonia. Homosexuality has been legal in Rondonia and throughout Brazil since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. On 26 April 2013 the General Inspectorate of Justice published Provision 008/2013-CG providing for direct same-sex marriage and conversion of stable union into marriage in civil registration records. Rondonia has no state law prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation, but since 2019 such discrimination is criminalized nationally by a Supreme Federal Court ruling equating it with the crime of racism. In 2025 federal and state prosecution and defender bodies recommended training on sexual orientation for police officers and firefighters and inclusion of LGBTQ population data in official reports. A law passed on 10 July 2026 requiring parental authorization for students to attend classes on sexual orientation, sexual diversity and gender equality, enacted by Assembly President Alex Redano after Governor Marcos Rocha neither vetoed nor signed, was struck down on 17 August by the Court of Justice of Rondonia. Between 2020 and 2021 there were 240 police reports of violence against LGBTQ people recorded in the state. In 2022 Rondonia was named the worst Brazilian state in terms of public policies for the LGBTQ community.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court criminalized transphobia throughout Brazil including Rondônia by applying Law 7.716/1989 Article 20 to anti-LGBTI discrimination and offenses, punishable by 1 to 3 years' imprisonment as a non-bailable and imprescriptible crime.

On 5 May 2025 MPRO, MPF, MPT, DPU and DPE-RO jointly recommended to Rondônia's SESDEC and SEJUS regular training for military police, civil police, firefighters, penitentiary and socioeducational agents on respect for LGBTQIA+ rights and improved service, requiring response in 20 business days and a training plan within 60 days with schedules for 2025 and following years, plus mandatory recording of gender identity, sexual orientation and social name in police occurrence reports and prison records with data protection and privacy to monitor violence including domestic and family aggression against transsexual women and travestis, after a civil inquiry found only partial compliance including no specific firefighter courses and no adequate SEJUS computerized registration and confidentiality system, in a context of 240 police occurrences involving anti-LGBTQIA+ violence in Rondônia in 2020-2021.

On 1 March 2018 in ADI 4275 the Supreme Federal Court held that equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity and expression and authorized change of name and gender on the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization based on self-declared identity.

Rondônia issued its first birth certificate with non-binary sex designation to Hanier Miranda with legal assistance from the Center for Legal Practices, Research and Extensions (NPPEJ) at the Catholic Faculty of Porto Velho.

In November 2021 Justice Edson Fachin suspended Rondônia's state law prohibiting gender-neutral language in schools and on 10 February 2023 the STF plenary confirmed the injunction and declared the ban unconstitutional, so gender-neutral language is permitted and cannot be prohibited or penalized in Rondônia schools.
Rondônia's 10 July 2026 law allowed parents to veto gender topics in schools until the Rondônia Court of Justice struck it down on 17 August.
Rondônia recorded 12 murders of trans people over a five-year period.
