texts.cleaned_text: In 2021, state representative Mara Lima introduced a bill to ban unisex bathrooms statewide, and on November 16, 2021, Curitiba approved a similar ban introduced by councilman Ezequias Barros. On October 4, 2023, the Curitiba City Council approved a motion of protest against a Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship resolution recommending students use school restrooms according to gender identity. In 2023, the Court of Justice of the State of Paraná published a provision guaranteeing inclusion of 'non-binary' in the Civil Registry gender marker, but in November 2023 revoked it, limiting administrative replacement of first name and sex to 'male' and 'female' only. In 2025, the Court of Justice of the State of Paraná authorized a third gender option on documents. On April 26, 2024, Londrina enacted a law banning transgender people from competing in sports according to gender identity, with a R$10,000 fine for non-compliance. On February 26, 2026, the City Council approved a motion to bar transgender athlete Tiffanny Abreu from the Brazilian Women's Volleyball Cup, the Brazilian Volleyball Confederation filed suit in the Supreme Federal Court, and Justice Cármen Lúcia issued a preliminary injunction the same day allowing competition. In March 2026 LGBTQ rights organizations filed suit against the Londrina law in the Supreme Federal Court, and on August 7, 2026 rapporteur Justice Cristiano Zanin voted to strike down the law. On June 13, 2019, the Brazilian Supreme Court ruled that discrimination on the basis of gender identity is a crime akin to racism. In 1830, Emperor Pedro I sanctioned the Imperial Penal Code removing all references to sodomy from Brazilian law. In 2004, the first recognition of same-sex union in Brazil occurred in Curitiba for an English-Brazilian couple cohabiting fourteen years, granted common-law marriage status previously limited to opposite-sex couples. On March 26, 2013, the General Inspector of Justice of Paraná ruled that same-sex marriage and conversion of stable unions to marriage must use normal marriage procedures. On May 14, 2009, the 2nd Court of Childhood, Youth and Adoption granted the first gay-couple adoption right in Paraná to a Curitiba couple, finding a stable and affectionate union able to raise a child in a healthy environment. On October 27, 2010, Cascavel justice authorized irreversible adoption of an eight-year-old child with cerebral palsy by a gay couple together twelve years, granted by Judge Sergio Luiz Kreuz under Superior Court of Justice precedent. On September 16, 2011, Maringá justice authorized adoption of two children by a lesbian couple. On June 13, 2019, the Brazilian Supreme Court ruled that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is a crime akin to racism.

On 26 March 2013 Paraná authorized same-sex civil marriage in all cartórios statewide under the same procedure and documentation as heterosexual marriage and allowed conversion of stable union into marriage without judicial authorization.

In Londrina, Paraná, a municipal law prohibiting transgender athletes from participating in sports competitions was suspended by STF injunction and Minister Cristiano Zanin voted to declare the ban unconstitutional.

On 19 September 2023 Resolution 2/2023 of the Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship provided in article 5 that educational institutions must guarantee use of bathrooms, changing rooms and other gender-segregated spaces according to each student's gender identity and expression while recommending additional individual-use bathrooms in public spaces, but the Ministry clarified it has no binding effect and no school is obliged to adopt it, and on 4 October 2023 the Curitiba City Council approved in symbolic vote a protest motion against the resolution to be converted into an official letter to the federal government.

In 2021 Mara Lima (PSC) presented a Parana state bill prohibiting unisex bathrooms and requiring separate male and female bathrooms, and on 16 Nov 2021 Curitiba approved Ezequias Barros (PMB)'s municipal bill prohibiting unisex bathrooms, limiting access to sex-separated facilities relevant to trans visitors.

On November 10, 2009, the Legislative Assembly of Piauí enacted Ordinary Law No. 5,916, which authorizes transgender and travesti individuals to use their chosen name on official documents. In March 2018, the Brazilian Supreme Federal Court unanimously ruled that transgender people may change their legal gender without undergoing surgery or hormonal therapy, which were previously requirements. A transgender individual seeking to reflect gender identity can now apply at a registry post without a judicial document or any medical report. On July 20, 2021, the Court of Justice of Piauí authorized for the first time a non-binary person to rectify documents to reflect gender identity. Since 2019, discrimination based on gender identity has been prohibited nationwide through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On June 17, 2026, the Teresina City Council approved by 12 in favor, 5 against and one abstention a bill to prohibit transgender women and travestis from using women's public restrooms. On July 30, Mayor Sílvio Mendes signed the bill into law after LGBTQ rights activists protested the approval as unconstitutional. In a 2015 Grupo Gay da Bahia report, Piauí was listed as the second Brazilian state with the highest risk of LGBTQ people being murdered, stated as LGBTQ-wide rather than transgender-specific. Homosexuality is legal in Piauí. On December 14, 2012, the Court of Justice of Piauí began granting same-sex couples marriage licenses through all notaries statewide. Couples do not need a judge's approval to get married under this change. The change was published officially in the Diário de Justiça on December 17, 2012. In 2012, Judge Maria Luiza de Moura de Melo e Freitas of the 1st Children and Youth Court granted adoption rights to a lesbian couple living together in a stable union since 2007. On December 29, 2004, the Governor of Piauí signed Ordinary Law No. 5,431 banning discrimination based on sexual orientation.

Piauí Law No. 5,916 enacted 10 November 2009 and published 12 November 2009 guarantees travestis and transexuais the right to identification by nome social on registrations, forms, prontuários and related documents when using services of all direct and indirect state public administration bodies, defines nome social as the name by which they recognize themselves and are recognized socially, requires the social name to appear first and prominently with civil identification below, directs the Executive within 60 days to designate the body responsible for registration and issuance of social-name identification, and retains use of the civil name where public interest or third-party rights require.
On July 20, 2021, the Piauí judiciary granted civil registration as a non-binary person to a young person, the first recognition of a non-binary gender marker in Piauí.
Teresina enacted a municipal law on bathroom use by trans women, approved June 17, 2026 and sanctioned July 30, 2026.

Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Brazil' states, in its Politics section, that LGBTQ people have a special place in Brazilian prisons, separate from other prisoners; that transsexuals have the right to be called by their social name rather than their birth name and to be forwarded to women's prisons; and that LGBTQ people in prisons may choose male or female clothing. The passage is footnoted to G1's 17 Apr 2014 report 'Governo publica portaria com direitos para presos gays e travestis' (archived 12 Jul 2018), so the cited legal grounding is a 2014 federal portaria granting rights to gay and travesti prisoners. On paper, placement follows gender identity, with separate custody for LGBTQ prisoners, social-name use and clothing choice. The underlying citation is dated 2014, and its current status was not independently re-verified.

Wikipedia overview article (fetched 4 Oct 2026). Its Transgender issues > Brazil section contains no trans-prisoner placement rule, only discussion of social vulnerability, stigma and fragmented identity of travestis and transgender people during rehabilitation. International sections document placement norms elsewhere, including Canada placing by gender identity and Italy's admission discretion. This general overview records no Brazil-specific trans-prisoner housing policy, special unit or segregation-for-placement practice.

G1 (17 Apr 2014): a federal portaria from the Secretaria de Direitos Humanos da Presidência da República sets housing rules for LGBT prisoners across Brazil's prison system, applying in Minas Gerais' state system. Transsexual men and women must be forwarded to female prison units. Gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons must be offered specific conviviality spaces. LGBT inmates may use their social name, which must appear in the admission record, and choose male or female clothing. No sanctions are provided for non-compliance, and the report documents no Minas Gerais-specific implementation, wing, segregation practice or case.

On 15 December 2017 Decree No. 47,306 created the Social Name Card authorizing trans and travesti individuals to use social names for identification purposes. On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration without surgery or professional evaluation, while since 2023 the Minas Gerais Public Defender's Office has held free Pride Month initiatives to assist non-binary people with name and gender marker changes, with Tai Barreto changing documents on 29 May 2025 through a Defender lawsuit though non-binary individuals still face challenges. In 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled discrimination based on gender identity illegal nationwide, supplemented by municipal bans on gender-identity discrimination in Juiz de Fora (Law 9791, 12 May 2000), Alfenas (Law 3,277, 11 September 2001) and São João del-Rei (Law 4,172, 12 December 2007). On facilities, Uberaba's ban on unisex restrooms enacted 7 October 2022 after 12 September 2022 approval was struck down in 2024 after a 2023 Defender lawsuit, and Belo Horizonte's law signed 20 November 2023 authorizing religious institutions to prohibit transgender people from using restrooms corresponding to gender identity was struck down by preliminary injunction in August 2025. In August 2026 the Court of Justice ordered a Contagem shopping mall to pay 2,000 reais compensation to a trans woman denied women's restroom access in a 2019 incident where a guard demanded proof of "sex change," reversing a Contagem court denial for insufficient evidence. On violence and protection, a 1 July 2024 Federal University of Minas Gerais and Public Prosecutor study found 60% of deaths involving trans people and travestis resulted from violence with 74% of victims Black or Pardo, in 2025 Minas Gerais tied Ceará for highest murders of trans people and travestis, and on 15 July 2026 the Court of Justice with the National Council of Justice launched an incident reporting mechanism for LGBTQ violence in Belo Horizonte. Homosexuality has been legal since 1830 when Emperor Dom Pedro I sanctioned the Imperial Penal Code removing sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Minas Gerais since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision in compliance with the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision. On 24 May 2011 the Court of Justice authorized adoption by a lesbian couple in Patos de Minas, and since 2015 same-sex adoption has been legal nationwide through a Supreme Federal Court decision. At state level, on 15 January 2002 Law No. 14,170 prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation and on 3 January 2007 Law No. 16,636 established May 17 as State Day Against Homophobia, while in 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled discrimination based on sexual orientation illegal nationwide. Municipal protection includes Belo Horizonte Law 8176 of 29 January 2001 and Law 8719 of 11 December 2003, Contagem Law 3506 of 10 January 2002, Juiz de Fora Law 9791 of 12 May 2000, Alfenas Law 3,277 of 11 September 2001 and São João del-Rei Law 4,172 of 12 December 2007 prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination, plus Alfenas Law 4,120 of 18 May 2009 on Municipal Day of Struggle against Homophobia. Despite measures, violence is frequent with Minas Gerais ranked second-highest for violence against LGBTQ people in 2017.

On 15 December 2017 Minas Gerais instituted the Carteira de Nome Social for travestis and transexuais for exercise of rights under Decree No. 47,148 of 27 January 2017, defining social name as the designation by which the travesti or transexual person identifies and is socially recognized, providing issuance by the Civil Police via the Identification Institute with model, requirements and specifications by resolution of its Chief and validity for nominal treatment and identification in state public administration, prohibiting alteration of the social name after issuance, requiring prior civil identification in the Minas Gerais Registro Geral, and requiring regulation and start of issuance within 120 days with entry into force on publication.
The Court of Justice of Minas Gerais declared unconstitutional Uberaba's municipal law prohibiting unisex bathrooms almost two years after its enactment, invalidating the ban.
In August 2025 the judiciary suspended Belo Horizonte's law restricting bathroom use by gender in temples and schools, blocking enforcement of its ban on gender-aligned bathroom access.

Major cities including Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianopolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

Since 2006 Amazonas has included gender identity in its state anti-discrimination policies, and since 2019 transphobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. Since March 2018 transgender people may change their legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial order or medical report, with registry gender changes up 59 percent by 2024. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender, and in 2022 Alex Souza de Sa became the first non-binary person in the state to obtain recognition after rectification in Rio de Janeiro and intervention by the Amazonas Public Defenders Office in Manaus where no gender-neutral marker existed. On 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. In November 2023 the State Public Defenders Office opened a process to monitor public health services for transgender and travesti people including provision of hormones and surgeries, and in August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutors Office recommended that Amazonas formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualization services including sexual reassignment surgeries with deadlines for approval and presentation to the Ministry of Health. On 10 June 2025 the governor signed Law 7552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under age 18. In 2021 the State Public Defenders Office created the Sexual Diversity Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group focused on human rights violations and training of security agents. Homosexuality has been legal in Amazonas and throughout Brazil since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Amazonas since 2013 via a National Council of Justice decision following a 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision. In November 2012 a judge of the Amazonas Court of Justice authorized the first same-sex couple adoption in the state, and in 2015 the Supreme Federal Court legalized same-sex adoption nationwide. Since 2006 Amazonas has included sexual orientation in its state anti-discrimination policies, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. In August 2024 the Amazonas State Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right aimed at LGBTQ youth expelled from homes stating that conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective". State Law 6469 of 2023 prohibits participation of children and adolescents in pride parades with fines of up to 10000 reais for non-compliance. On 17 October 2024 the Legislative Assembly enacted a law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality, amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media. Research from the Brazilian Journal of Public Security finds that cases of violence against LGBTQ people in Amazonas are underreported. Data from the Brazilian Public Security Forum shows cases of violence against LGBTQ people have increased with 43 cases registered. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaca de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, and residents reported he had previously been bullied by other young people in the region. The killing is documented as homophobic and the 43 cases are documented as LGBTQ-general, with no disaggregation for transgender victims stated. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

In March 2018 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ruled that transgender people can change their legal name and gender marker on civil records by self-identification without requiring surgery, hormonal treatment, or judicial authorization.
On 18 October 2022, the city of Manaus enacted a municipal law prohibiting multigender/unisex restrooms.

As of 1 November 2023 the Amazonas Public Defender's health unit (Nudesa) had opened a collective preparatory procedure to enforce SUS access for trans people covering hormonization treatment, outpatient services and lack of authorization for transexualizing surgeries including sexual reassignment, and after an October 2023 meeting Manaus municipal health officials committed to dispense standardized medications on Ambulatório Codajás prescriptions for hormonization and to designate reference UBS primary-care units in each city zone while the state health secretariat was required to report on equitable care and hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under CFM Resolution 2.265/2019.

These guarantees apply nationwide and cover visitors in Santa Catarina. In National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014) the Supreme Court recognized a "third gender," affirming freedom from discrimination and right to equality, and Kerala became the first state to follow up with a government transgender policy in 2015 addressing the right to identify as "male", "female" or "TG" (Third Gender) with provisions for equal access to social and economic resources, equal treatment under law, life, liberty and justice, and non-discrimination based on sex. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 bans unfair discrimination against transgender people in educational establishments and services, employment, healthcare, use of goods, accommodation, services, facilities, benefits, privileges or opportunities available to the public, right to movement, right to reside, purchase, rent or occupy property, opportunity to stand for or hold public or private office, and in government or private establishments. In 2016 the State Government proposed free sex reassignment surgeries in government hospitals, Kannur district allocated budget for employment and skill training, and the government later provided reimbursement for gender affirming surgeries plus scholarships for transgender students in classes 7 to 10, but lack of training means many government hospitals cannot offer surgery forcing reliance on costlier private institutions with stigma, lack of care standards and fund-disbursement problems because patients must raise funds before refund. The Government Medical College Hospital in Kottayam opened in 2017 a clinic exclusively attending to the transgender community with a specialized panel, described as the first government clinic of its kind and also open to sex workers after a DLSA proposal following health-concerns campaigning, while a February 2016 Gender Park in Kozhikode opened by President Pranab Mukherjee was dedicated to gender equality and LGBT issues. A 2017 Social Justice Department workshop in Kozhikode with around 30 transgender representatives discussed identity cards, pension for those over 60, skill development training, scholarships and educational loans, and driving lessons for employment as Uber drivers, and Kochi's 2016 first transgender school for 10th and 12th board exams and vocational training for 10 students aged 25-50 ceased functioning as a school after three months and became a hostel for transgender Kochi Metro staff. A recent spate of killings of transgender people with lack of responsible police investigation raised security concerns, alongside a rise in police harassment when transgender people approach stations to file complaints that resulted in a DGP direction to address grievances without delay. The suicide of Anannyah Kumari Alex alleging botched gender affirmation surgery triggered protests and discussion of irregularities and absence of specific protocol in private hospitals, leading the state to appoint an expert committee on transgender health-sector issues and initiate steps for free surgeries in government hospitals, while the suicide of Praveen Nath drew attention to mushrooming transphobic groups rooted in religious fundamentalism. Homosexual intercourse was criminalized under Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code in 1861 as voluntarily having "carnal intercourse against the order of nature." In 2009 the Delhi High Court in Naz Foundation v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi found Section 377 prohibitions on private, adult, consensual, non-commercial same-sex conduct violated fundamental rights, but on 11 December 2013 the Supreme Court overturned that order while noting Parliament should debate the matter, followed by protests, and on 28 January 2014 dismissed review petitions by the Central Government, Naz Foundation and others. On 2 February 2016 the Supreme Court agreed to review criminalisation and on 6 September 2018 unanimously struck down Section 377 as unconstitutional for infringing autonomy, intimacy and identity, legalising same-sex sexual activity in India including Kerala. Same-sex marriages are not recognised or performed in India, though movements for recognition have emerged in Kerala and nationally. In line with Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is prohibited via Article 15 of the Constitution, but this extends only to discrimination by state or government bodies. Gay conversion therapy is widely practised by both licensed psychiatrists/psychologists and quacks despite position statements by multiple psychiatrist/psychologist organisations condemning the practice as unscientific and illegal. For transgender-specific conditions, the article reports "societal discrimination, particularly in employment and housing, and various implementation issues remain major problems" despite Kerala's early policy lead. Transgender activist Vijayarajamallika, head of Kochi's transgender school, stated "the school aims at making transgender people eligible for taking decent jobs and living a dignified life," reflecting employment barriers, while Minister R. Bindu blamed cyber bullying and transphobia in the media for the suicide of Praveen Nath, Kerala's first transgender bodybuilder, describing him as a martyr amid mushrooming transphobic groups rooted in religious fundamentalism. More broadly for LGBT visitors, the article notes historical and contemporary opposition especially due to meninist groups, conservative political groups, religious organizations and social conservatism, with increasing recent opposition including hate-speech allegations against mainstream politicians and all-time-high cyberbullying linked to suicides of at least two LGBTQ persons. In December 2023 the High Court of Kerala described cyber attacks against the LGBT+ community as a 'serious issue' and asked authorities to take necessary action. The October 2023 annual pride march in Malappuram was attacked by a homophobic mob leading to lathicharge by police, while Kerala Queer Pride since July 2010 in Thrissur and annual walks by Queerythm since 2017 focus on sensitisation of police and media to prevent violence and discrimination. Community protection resources noted are Queerala campaigning for sensitisation of healthcare, curriculum and workplace policies, Queerythm running a 24X7 helpline for members in distress, and Sahayathrika for female-born LGBTIQA+ members, amid an easing climate from prior invisibility where few opted to come out for fear family would "take them to a psychiatrist or file a police complaint against friends."

On 15 April 2014 the Supreme Court recognized hijras/transgenders as a third gender who could no longer be forced to identify as male or female and required their treatment as socially and economically backward with OBC reservation in educational admission and employment, Centre and state social welfare schemes, public awareness to erase stigma, construction of special public toilets and provision for special medical needs, legal entitlement to affirmed sex after surgical change without discrimination, and protection from harassment and discrimination including misuse of IPC section 377, with the ruling limited to eunuchs/hijras/transgenders and not to gay, lesbian and bisexual persons.

In November 2015 Kerala adopted India's first transgender policy to improve living conditions, and in March 2016 the social justice department proposed free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals, at least in medical colleges, from the next financial year, addressing the absence of any SRS facility in-state that forced travel to Chennai/Bengaluru for procedures costing Rs 2-5 lakh for male-to-female and Rs 4-8 lakh for female-to-male plus 6 months-2 years counselling, 1+ year hormone therapy and post-surgery observation, with implementation pending health ministry approval and training of multidisciplinary urology, endocrinology, sexology and psychology teams, alongside a transgender-owned and operated G Taxi equality-taxi service for all passengers to provide livelihood and public visibility, in a context where ~25,000 transgender persons were estimated in-state with ~81% wishing to transition and 76% concealing identity for fear of non-acceptance.

By mid-February 2017 the Government Medical College Hospital in Kottayam was to open Kerala's first government clinic exclusively for transgender persons, operating twice a month with specialist doctors and also serving sex workers, with distribution of health cards denoting transgender status after a District Legal Services Authority proposal prompted by transgender persons' reported apprehension about approaching hospitals and reliance on self-medication, while DLSA also proposed separate public toilets for transgender persons to the district collector, and in January 2017 the Government Medical College Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram had completed its first sex reassignment surgery through staged procedures over three years.

Federal law has recognized transgender identity since NALSA v. Union of India in 2014. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 prohibits discrimination based on gender identity. In 2025 Goa formed the Model Transgender Welfare Board under the provisions of that Act to facilitate welfare schemes for transgender people. The 2011 census counted 398 transgender people in Goa, but as of 2024 only 12 transgender people were registered in electoral rolls, with the first registrations occurring in 2022. A 2018 Goa Livelihoods Forum study found 87% of transgender respondents had dropped out of school due to harassment. Same-sex activity was decriminalized at federal level in 2018 by Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India. In 16th century Goa, the Goa Inquisition criminalized same-sex activity with death penalty by burning to ashes and confiscation of property to the Crown, as applied in 1528 to a Muslim man and later to 16-year-old Portuguese army soldier Alberto Homem. Under the 1568 Constitutions of the Archbishopric of Goa, same-sex activity was classified as a serious sin punishable by deposition from office and lifelong penance in a religious institution for a clergyman and excommunication until repentance and required penance for a layman. In 1644 the Tribunal of Goa sought clarification on female same-sex acts and the majority concluded such acts generally did not constitute sodomy but sexual immorality rather than the crime of sodomy. Goa applies the Goa Civil Code defining marriage as between a man and a woman with no legal recognition for same-sex marriages or civil unions, though in 2023 the Supreme Court noted same-sex couples have the right to cohabit and enjoy some protections under law. Following the Supreme Court's 2023 decision not to legalize same-sex marriage, activists in Goa urged legislative steps but no bills have been introduced. There are currently no state-level anti-discrimination laws protecting sexual orientation in Goa.

On May 7, 2025 Goa constituted a 14-member Model Transgender Welfare Board headed by the Chief Secretary under the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 and Rules of 2020 to oversee implementation of welfare schemes and safeguard transgender persons' rights in healthcare, education, employment, and housing.
The 2011 Census recorded 398 transgender persons in Goa out of 487,803 nationally.

Union of India, striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution, and preserving the provision for non-consensual acts. In July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omits Section 377 entirely. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019) is the national statute governing transgender people in Punjab. It was passed by the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on November 26, 2019, received presidential assent on December 5, 2019, and has been in force since January 10, 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA ruling, it grants transgender people the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people; criticism holds that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On January 27, 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality. No statute in Punjab targets trans people, and this is the framework a trans visitor to Amritsar stands under.

texts.cleaned_text: Since 2006 Amazonas state policies prohibit discrimination based on gender identity, and since 2019 transphobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. In 2021 the Amazonas State Public Defender's Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group to address human rights violations and train security agents, and in November 2023 it opened a process to monitor public health services for transgender and travesti people including provision of hormones and surgeries. In March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court unanimously ruled transgender people may change legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial document or medical report, with registry gender changes reported up 59% by 2024. On 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended Amazonas formally enable outpatient and hospital services for the transsexualization process including sexual reassignment surgeries, with deadlines for approval and presentation to the Ministry of Health. On 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under age 18. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender, and in 2022 Alex Souza de Sa became the first non-binary person recognized in the state after rectification in Rio de Janeiro and intervention by the Public Defender's Office to secure recognition in Manaus after six months when the local notary lacked a gender-neutral marker. Homosexuality has been legal in Amazonas and Brazil since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision following the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision, and same-sex adoption was first allowed in Amazonas in November 2012 by an Amazonas Court of Justice judge before nationwide legalization by the Supreme Federal Court in 2015. Since 2006 Amazonas state policies prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. The August 2024 Amazonas Court of Justice booklet Home is a Right! for LGBTQ youth expelled from homes states that conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective." Research from the Brazilian Journal of Public Security states that cases of violence against LGBTQ people in Amazonas are underreported. Data from the Brazilian Public Security Forum indicates cases of violence against LGBTQ people have increased, with 43 cases registered. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaca de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, and residents reported he had previously been bullied by other young people in the region. The Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, the Order of Attorneys of Brazil and federal deputy Erika Hilton expressed regret over the incident. the above violence figures refer to LGBTQ people generally not to transgender people specifically.
In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended that the state of Amazonas guarantee comprehensive health care for the LGBTQIAPN+ population, including trans people.

In Amazonas in October-November 2023, trans access to SUS was under enforcement review for primary care, outpatient services, hormonization, and lack of local authorization for transexualizing surgeries including sexual reassignment, with the municipal health authority committing to dispense standardized hormone medications on Ambulatório Codajás prescriptions and to designate a reference UBS in each city zone and the state health authority required to report on equitable integral care and hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under CFM Resolution No. 2.265/2019.
On 18 October 2022 the municipality of Manaus sanctioned a law prohibiting multigender/unisex bathrooms.

On 10 October 2023 Amazonas Law No. 6,463 prohibited the use of gender-neutral language, non-binary dialect, or any expression deviating from standard Portuguese in the curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of educational institutions and public offices throughout the state of Amazonas.

In Amazonas since August 2024, LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents facing family discrimination and expulsion from home are affirmed as protected by ECA Article 17 guaranteeing physical, psychological and moral integrity including identity, autonomy and beliefs, by Constitutional/ECA duties of family, society and State to ensure health, food, education and protection against negligence and discrimination with equal treatment of all children regardless of sexual orientation, by Law No. 14.811/2024 criminalizing bullying with penalties ranging from fine to 4 years' imprisonment, by the 2019 STF recognition of homophobia as an imprescriptible and unbailable crime, and by the prohibition of conversion/"cura gay" therapies as illegal and ineffective, with legal support available from the Defensoria Especializada em Direitos Humanos.

On 28 June 2021 the Amazonas Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) created the permanent Working Group "Diversidade Sexual, Identidade de Gênero e Cidadania" to defend LGBTQIA+ rights and identify human rights violations in the area of public security. Its mandate includes training public security agents for service to LGBTQIA+ persons and issuing recommendations and other extrajudicial referrals. Victims of LGBTphobia are served by the Specialized Human Rights Defensoria via Disk 129 in Manaus Monday to Friday 8h-14h, in a context where Amazonas led North and Center-West states with an average of 4.66 LGBTQIA+ persons murdered per million inhabitants in 2018.

In Amazonas during 2021-2022 trans persons faced persistent diverse violence intensifying each year while only 0.36% of crimes reported in the capital and interior involved homosexual, lesbian, bisexual and transsexual victims, police occurrence reports did not identify homophobia and transfobia motives or gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality markers, victim data were few and poorly structured with victims at times inverted to accused through faulty reports, and unprepared public agents and defective registration mechanisms produced invisibilization and lack of protection for trans victims.

Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The bill stood at committee stage in February 2025 as national legislation binding Ica.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) states that on 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The analysis concerns the national framework, which governs Ica.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024), covering the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with multiple gunshots or stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias in 2020. The report also recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. The figures cover Peru as a whole rather than Ica.

texts.cleaned_text: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion (dictamen) merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The measure stood at committee stage in February 2025.

texts.cleaned_text: The national administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law. Buenos Aires-based activists told the Washington Blade on April 10, 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, up 62% year-on-year, a ten-year record of one crime every 38 hours. According to Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026, 32% of the crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities, security-force violence multiplied from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), and trans women and travestis concentrated 62.5% of victims (142 cases). Most perpetrators were security personnel and unknown assailants.

Via emergency decrees published in February 2025, DNU 62/2025 modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law (Law 26743) to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for persons under 18, and DNU 61/2025 re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty, inviting the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. The latter decree prohibits those who legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons if detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts call the decrees illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention.

Profiles Paola, an Argentine trans woman transferred to a men's facility in 2014 and met with shouts of 'We don't want any women here', despite a passport listing her as female, because French law does not recognise her Argentine legal gender for placement purposes. Documents inconsistent access to treatment and a 2,000-euro symbolic damages award over detention conditions, with the justice minister pressed to amend D248.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 of the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL), unofficial English translation: official inspectorate opinion on the treatment of transgender persons in ALL places of deprivation of liberty; built on about forty referrals received since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, and five on-site inspections (Fleury-Mérogis men's and women's prisons, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station - eight trans women and one trans man interviewed); finds persistent serious violations of fundamental rights of trans detainees, isolation and overcrowding risks; recommends that the 2016 depathologising law (no more surgery requirement for civil-status change) be translated into prison regulations; explicitly extends to intersex and non-binary people.

France legalised same-sex marriage and full adoption in 2013, and civil solidarity pacts have existed since 1999. Penal Code article 225-1 has covered 'gender identity' since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced 'sexual identity', protected since 2012, and homophobic hate speech has carried penalties up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment since a 31 December 2004 amendment. On legal gender recognition, a bill approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and by the National Assembly on 24 May 2016 was signed into law on 18 November 2016 and took effect on 1 January 2017. It abolished the sex-reassignment-surgery and forced-sterilisation requirements, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires going before a court rather than any medical intervention. Transsexualism is classed under long-term-illness ALD 31, so gender-affirming treatment is funded by the Sécurité Sociale. These are the national rules on documents, protection and care that a trans visitor to Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes encounters; the region's own page carries no trans-specific content.

texts.cleaned_text: Index of Spain's regional LGTBI legislation; states expressly that Ceuta and Melilla have no autonomous LGTBI laws and rely on the national framework and central-government equality policies.

Melilla has no autonomous LGTBI or gender-identity statute, so the national framework governs there. A registry for unmarried same-sex couples was created in the autonomous city of Melilla in 2008, alongside Ceuta in 1998 and all 17 mainland communities, granting unmarried couples benefits regarded as mainly symbolic; this is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute. The national framework applying in Melilla provides same-sex marriage and adoption nationwide since July 2005, bans hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity since 1995 with crime-law penalty enhancements for such motives, and has allowed legal-gender self-determination on documents without surgery or sterilisation since the trans law approved 16 February 2023 (vote 191-60 with 91 abstentions, applying to people over 16). National criminal and equality law and the state police govern in Melilla.

State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the national 'Trans Law' for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of LGBTI rights, applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, including this one. Adults may rectify the registered sex entry without prior surgical reassignment, the right grounded in the free development of personality (art. 10.1 CE). The law defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges discrimination data collection broken down by the causes covered, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances.

The Region of Murcia's own LGTBI-equality statute sits beneath the national framework. Ley 8/2016 of 27 May 2016 (BOE-A-2016-6170) prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics in public and private activity in the region, and within its scope bars any requirement to prove declared gender identity by psychological or medical report. Article 5 creates the Observatorio regional contra la discriminación por orientación sexual e identidad de género, a participation and consultation body in which LGTBI entities are represented. Title IV sets a sanctioning ladder: minor breaches draw a warning or a fine of up to €3,000; serious breaches run €3,001 to €20,000 and cover degrading remarks or incitement to violence against LGBTI persons or their families in the provision of services; very serious breaches run €20,001 to €45,000, with accessory penalties such as exclusion from regional public aid for up to one year. Multiple discrimination raises the infraction grade.

The Spanish Wikipedia article on LGBT rights in Spain records that the first wave of autonomous-region LGTBI and trans-equality laws was approved in the 2010s in eight regions, listing Murcia alongside País Vasco, Andalucía, Galicia, Extremadura, Madrid, Baleares and Aragón. It dates the state framework applying here: same-sex marriage legalised on 2 July 2005, with some 4,500 same-sex couples married in the law's first year; the 2007 gender-identity law; and the Ley 4/2023 trans-equality law approved in February 2023, permitting registered sex change from age 16 without medical reports or hormonal treatment, whose implementation falls to the regional government. The operative regional instrument is Ley 8/2016 de la Región de Murcia.

texts.cleaned_text: Under Türkiye's national framework, which applies in Niğde: homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and those receiving an 'unfit report' may face later discrimination in public life. Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions, and ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th out of 49 countries. A court case to close Lambda Istanbul was overruled by the Constitutional Court. A February 2026 press report of draft legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison was not included in the 12th judicial package, whose passage removed provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible.

Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Zamfara State, set out the state's account of its Sharia adoption at a JNI-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000. He details Zamfara's enabling legislation, the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999, enacted under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution, which established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and enabled the codification of a Sharia Penal Code. The Grand Kadi took over court administration on 29 June 2000, alongside policy moves against prostitution and gambling. The account documents the adoption process that began Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave in Zamfara.

Zamfara's governor appointed a committee in June 1999 mandated to study implementing Sharia, including the full scope of Islamic criminal law. By the end of 2000 eleven other northern states had adopted the application of Sharia. The codification of offences and punishments produced a penal-code architecture that the Sharia courts of the twelve states apply, a framework Zamfara pioneered across the northern bloc.

texts.cleaned_text: Wikipedia's Nigeria LGBT-rights overview records that same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916, and that the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law in January 2014, criminalises all forms of same-sex unions with a maximum federal penalty of 14 years' imprisonment, the death penalty applying only in the twelve northern Shari'a states. Delta-specific entries on the page record that in June 2018 Nigerian police arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, on charges that they were gays and lesbians, and that by July 2018 they were facing homosexuality-related charges in court; in August 2023 police raided a gay wedding in Warri, Delta State, arresting dozens in the case known as the 'Warri 67', of whom 67 were charged to court following a mass arrest at a party or marriage ceremony. The 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment in Delta, and no state-specific protective statute exists.

The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note documents the national criminal framework applying across all states: the 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment, Section 217 of the Criminal Code makes male gross indecency a felony liable to three years' imprisonment, and the death penalty is confined to the twelve northern Shari'a states. Citing the USSD 2023 human rights report, it records that on 27 August 2023 police in Delta State raided a 'white party' organized by the LGBTQI+ community and detained more than 200 individuals, with police alleging the event was a same-sex wedding while some civil society representatives disputed that account. It also quotes a human rights lawyer based in Warri, Delta state, on 'kito' (predatory same-sex assault) victims under-reporting for fear of prosecution. State-level documentation is thin, which does not demonstrate safety.

Daily Post reports that police officers from Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area of Delta State arrested 67 suspects on 27 August 2023 at 9 pm at Teebolus Hotel, Refinery Road, Ekpan, for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding ceremony between Daniel Pius (the groom), 22, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo (the bride), 20. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a male cross-dresser's confession that he was a member of a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival but 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. Edafe said the suspects and exhibits were in custody and efforts continued to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution, and that one suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated. The incident shows the national anti-LGBT framework actively enforced in Delta State (Warri), with incidents frequently framed together with drug allegations.

texts.cleaned_text: Ostien's sourcebook reproduces Niger State's own Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 in full — a law to amend Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein, gazetted in the Niger State of Nigeria Gazette No. 8, Vol. 25 of 9 March 2000 (pp. B29-B36) and coming into force on 4 May 2000. The enactment defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment (with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68), while the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies. Niger, like the other northern bloc states, built a distinct criminal track for Muslim defendants.

Niger: Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (HB.4/2000) was signed into law on 22 February 2000 and came into operation on 4 May 2000, gazetted as Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8 of 9 March 2000. The editor notes that it is not a complete Sharia Penal Code: it amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims, and it is printed in its entirety in Part IV of the same chapter. An outed Muslim visitor in Niger State therefore stands under a harsher parallel legal frame than federal law alone.

Article 25 of the Refoundation Charter, adopted in March 2025, criminalizes all lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual acts or practices, expressly including transgender acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes LGBTQIA+ acts or practices with 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine up to 100 million CFA francs (€152,448.94; US$176,604.56). The punishable practices expressly include changing or attempting to change one's birth sex. Creating, managing, financing, or participating in LGBTQIA+ organizations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison and a fine up to 500 million CFA francs (€762,244.71; US$882,829). Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences cannot be applied to these penalties. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity. After the 2026 code took effect, dozens of people were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, including military officials, and LGBTQ people went into hiding. Same-sex sexual activity was explicitly outlawed in 2025 and penalized in 2026, and before that change the age of consent was 13 for heterosexual acts and 21 for homosexual acts. Article 25 of the March 2025 Refoundation Charter criminalizes same-sex sexual relations and LGBTQIA+ acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes same-sex sexual relations with 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine up to 100 million CFA francs, covering same-sex sexual activity and public announcement of one's romantic relationship with a person of the same sex. Creating, managing, financing, or participating in LGBTQIA+ organizations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison and a fine up to 500 million CFA francs, with no mitigating circumstances or suspended sentences allowed. Since March 2025 under Article 24 marriage is defined as a union between a man and a woman, and since June 2026 getting married to a person of the same sex and officiating, organizing or bearing official witness to same-sex weddings is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison. There are no broad protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation, but Article 95 of Law 2022-59 punishes collecting and processing data revealing sexual life or sexual orientation with three months to five years imprisonment and a fine of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs, while Law 2015-36 which had prohibited discrimination including sexual orientation was repealed in 2023 with convictions expunged. Enforcement included two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for public indecency and fined a small fee, two young women in Maradi in 2022 prosecuted for lesbianism and acquitted for lack of legislation but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act, and two young women reported as lesbians in Niamey in 2025 prosecuted for public indecency but acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere with the judge allegedly sanctioned for leniency. After the 2026 code, dozens were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, LGBTQ people went into hiding, and organizations providing HIV prevention services to MSM stopped working, ending access to condoms, HIV testing and PrEP. Gay men and lesbians experienced societal discrimination with strong pressure to conform to societal norms, leading many to lead socially acceptable lives in public while seeking LGBT relationships privately. No violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity was reported and no documented cases of discrimination in employment, housing, education, health care or statelessness based on sexual orientation were recorded, though stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported. Two gay rights organizations operated in secret partly because they were not formally registered. Asylum seekers from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire who held LGBTQ public demonstrations in Niamey in 2022 were denied refugee recognition hindering relocation and faced shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers. Niger's attitude toward LGBTQ issues is described as usually discreet, even though male prostitution was prevalent in Niamey and effeminate men were known for having always been part of Niger's culture by organizing traditional wedding ceremonies and supporting themselves that way. The 2025 acquittal of two women prosecuted for public indecency caused widespread debate ranging from approval to outrage. The article documents no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; the only official cultural-values statement concerns LGBTQ practices generally: "all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be (...) are not in line with our social and cultural values".
Niger criminalizes LGBTQIA+ practice.

As of 8-9 December 2022 Niger had no specific law criminalising same-sex relationships, while Maradi lawmaker Nana Djibou Harouna presented to the Speaker of Parliament a proposal backed by nearly all MPs to criminalise same-sex relationships with punishment unspecified and no scheduled debate, following weeks earlier a Maradi court acquitting two young women of lesbianism-related charges for lack of clear legislation but sentencing them to two years imprisonment for posting nude social-media videos allegedly showing a lesbian act.

Cross River falls under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 makes same-sex marriage or civil union, and registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or publicly showing same-sex affection, punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment nationwide. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men (14 years) and gross indecency between men (3 years). The twelve northern states under Shari'a law carry up to a death-penalty maximum: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. Cross River is not among them. The source documents the nationwide 'kito' entrapment-and-blackmail scheme targeting gay men and trans women, police profiling and extortion of people perceived as gay, and mass arrests (42 men in Lagos, August 2017; 53 charged in Kaduna, April 2017; 100+ detained after a Delta hotel raid, June 2018; 67 in Warri, August 2023; 76 in Gombe, October 2023). No anti-discrimination protections exist for LGBTQ people.

texts.cleaned_text: Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion using threats and acts of physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. texts.cleaned_text: UK Home Office country policy note on Russia, SOGI (June 2025), names the North Caucasus, including Dagestan, as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities from 2017 to 2024, involving abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings, and assesses trans people and visible advocates specifically.

Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia. It flags frequent terrorist attacks in the republics of Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and Stavropol Krai. Entry to certain areas and regions requires special permission from the Ministry of the Interior. The advisory also warns of violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons, particularly in the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, who works in exile, told the Human Rights House Foundation: 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families.' He said the situation worsens year on year.

In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition that prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, and transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned. In April-May 2023 proposals sought to rule out the possibility of changing a person's gender purely by changing the documents and to ban gender reassignment without surgery, with the Duma Speaker claiming 2,700 such document changes had been made in recent times amid claims men sought changes to avoid conscription for the special operation. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living in a foreign country may adopt only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The 1 July 2003 military medical expertise statute provides that people who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences can only be drafted during war times, while officials stated different sexual orientation should not be considered a deviation and non-standard orientation does not forbid service but should not be revealed to avoid beating. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated teaching children that instead of men and women there are supposedly some other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after 1993 removal of Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, but neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed and July 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage with no legal recognition offered. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, with an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 including 365 fatalities and annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors and was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age group. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, where leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols is a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay bar and club owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025 and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings. Between March and May 2026 city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist with founders convicted for leading an extremist organisation, including Centre T, Coming Out, LGBT Resource Centre, Irida, Kallisto movement, Moscow Community Center for LGBT+ Initiatives, Parni Plus, Russian LGBT Network, and T9 NSK. In Chechnya since February 2017 authorities conducted forced disappearances including secret abductions, imprisonment and torture targeting persons based on perceived sexual orientation with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three dead in extrajudicial killing, followed by a December 2018 purge with around 40 detained and two killed, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report as ignored by authorities and leading to EU economic sanctions in March 2021 on two officials. In 2010 the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating by systemically refusing permits for pride parades, and in August 2012 the Moscow City Court upheld blocking Moscow Pride permits yearly through 2012 citing possibility of public disorder.

On 30 November 2023 Russia's Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT public movement' as extremist and outlawed it, banning LGBT including trans organization, advocacy and symbols nationwide including in Dagestan and exposing trans visitors to administrative and criminal liability for public expression, display, or advocacy.
In 2026 Russia, including Dagestan, scored 2% among the lowest in Europe and maintained explicit bans/legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically impossible.

Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. In 2022 the propaganda law was expanded to apply to anyone regardless of age group and to prohibit distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. In 2024 Russia passed a law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living abroad may adopt only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The 1 July 2003 military medical expertise statute provides people who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences can only be drafted during wartimes, with officials stating non-standard orientation should not be revealed while serving because of risk of beating, while authorities claimed some 2,700 legal gender changes were made recently to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated it is unacceptable to teach children that instead of men and women there are supposedly some other genders and to offer sex-change surgeries, linking transgender rights abroad to willingness to use all means against Ukraine. Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 with removal of Article 121, and the age of consent is 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, but same-sex marriages and civil unions are prohibited and a July 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. The 2013 law criminalising distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement has included arrests of gay club owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag designated as the movement symbol including earrings, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist including Centre T, Coming Out, Russian LGBT Network and others. Documented violence includes an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities rising from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, premeditated group attacks often using dating apps to hunt homosexuals led by groups like Occupy Pedophilia active in 40 regions, and Chechnya purges since February 2017 with over 100 detained and tortured and at least three extrajudicial killings confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report leading to EU sanctions on two officials in March 2021.

In November 2023 the Supreme Court of Russia designated the 'international LGBT public movement' as extremist and banned its activities throughout Russia including Udmurtia, making display of LGBT symbols, advocacy, organizing, participation and support punishable as extremism with fines, administrative detention and criminal imprisonment, exposing trans visitors to detention, prosecution and imprisonment for visible gender-identity expression, association or advocacy.

In the 2026 ranking Russia scored 2%, among the lowest in Europe, and maintains explicit bans or other legal limitations that make legal gender recognition practically impossible with no self-determination procedure.

Official asylum-assessment country guidance (June 2025, updated Aug 2026): same-sex activity not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and legal gender recognition banned (2023); guidance treats trans people, open activists and residents of one conflict-affected region cluster as facing heightened risk even where general state risk is not established.

Human-rights organisation report (June 2025): 101 'extremism' convictions since the 2024-effective designation of the 'international LGBT movement'; 'propaganda' penalties rose to 257 in 2023-24 from 22 in 2021-22; support groups report departures and the closure of queer spaces.

Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and in July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition that prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright. In April-May 2023 preceding proposals sought to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban gender reassignment without surgery. In 2022 the propaganda law was expanded to apply to anyone regardless of age and to prohibit distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. In 2024 Russia passed a law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions. Russian officials linked the transition restrictions in part to draft avoidance, claiming many young men sought sex changes to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation and citing 2,700 such decisions in recent times. On 30 September 2022 President Putin said: "Do we want them to be taught that instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries? This is unacceptable to us." Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults was re-legalised in 1993 with removal of Article 121 from the RSFSR Penal Code, and the age of consent stands at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, and in July 2020 voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage. Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 State Duma proposals to prevent trans women from changing legal gender from male to female without surgery and to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and foreign single-person adoption is permitted only where the country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The article links legal gender change to conscription avoidance, stating that many young men have turned to private clinics to provide a sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation and that Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin claimed 2,700 such decisions in recent times. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated "Do we want them to be taught that instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries? This is unacceptable to us." while invoking transgender rights in justification for action against Ukraine and willingness to use all means at disposal. Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121, which had previously punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under 1934 Article 154-a and up to five years under 1961 Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage in July 2020, no legal recognition is offered despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling finding a human rights violation, and only married heterosexual couples may adopt jointly though single persons regardless of sexual orientation may adopt domestically. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors and was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement includes arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings, at least one death in custody as of April 2025, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine organisations including Centre T, Coming Out, Russian LGBT Network and others with convictions of founders for leading an extremist organisation. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, with estimates of 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, and group-organised hunting via dating apps including Occupy Pedophilia active in 40 regions. In Chechnya, authorities targeted persons based on perceived sexual orientation with forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killing, with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three dead from February 2017 and around 40 detained and two killed from December 2018, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by March 2021 EU sanctions on two officials.

In 2026 Russia, including Mari El, scored 2% at the bottom of Europe with explicit bans/legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically impossible without self-determination or fully depathologised trans healthcare, and without full SOGIESC anti-discrimination coverage or hate-crime/hate-speech protection based on gender identity.
