exact_spans: Named-in-source access/security facts for this record.
Regional testimony underpinning this record's risk framing.

texts.cleaned_text: Global Affairs Canada advises avoid all travel to Russia and lists Ingushetia among the republics with frequent terrorist attacks, alongside Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai. The advisory notes surveillance of foreigners and states that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, their allies and their families have been attacked, harassed and abused. Since January 2024, organisations advocating for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as 'extremist'. The Ministry of Interior requires special permission to enter certain areas.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by Human Rights House Foundation, states: 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families.' He attests that conditions in the region have deteriorated year on year.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): treats the North Caucasus (incl. this republic) as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory Russia finding — trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; documents systematic regional campaigns 2017–2024; 2023 'extremist' designation exposes LGBT+ activity to 2–6 (organising 6–10) years' imprisonment, violence spreading beyond the region.

In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living abroad may adopt only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations and persons, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement has included arrests of gay club owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings, addition of activist Karèn Shainyan to the terrorist and extremist list with a 5-year prison sentence in absentia, and March-May 2026 court outlawing of nine LGBTQ organisations including Centre T with convictions of founders for leading an extremist organisation. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after 1993 re-legalisation removing Article 121, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment and a maximum five years under the 1961 revision, and the age of consent stands at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, marriage is defined as between a man and a woman with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, and in the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia case the European Court of Human Rights ruled failure to offer any legal recognition violated rights, though Russia left the court in 2022. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors and was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people, does not officially record hate crimes against the community, and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation. Adoption is allowed for single persons regardless of sexual orientation but for couples jointly only if a married heterosexual couple, and foreign single adopters are barred if their country recognises same-sex marriage. Authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations and to authorize pride parades, with a 2010 European Court of Human Rights fine for discrimination over pride bans and an August 2012 Moscow City Court ruling upholding a yearly ban through 2012 citing public disorder, while pro-LGBTQ groups have been declared extremist and prohibited. Documented violence includes an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010-2020 with 365 fatalities, tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015 with premeditated group hunts via dating apps, and Chechnya purges involving forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment and torture with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three extrajudicial killings from February 2017 and around 40 detained and two killed in the December 2018-January 2019 purge, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by March 2021 EU sanctions on two Chechen officials.

On 30 November 2023 the Supreme Court of Russia designated the 'international LGBT public movement' as extremist and banned it nationwide including Ingushetia, prohibiting LGBT including trans advocacy, organizing and public display of symbols and exposing violators to extremism-related fines, detention and imprisonment.

In 2026 Russia scored 2% as one of the lowest-ranked countries in Europe and maintains explicit bans or legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically impossible with no self-determination procedure.

texts.cleaned_text: The UK Home Office country policy and information note on SOGI for Russia (June 2025) names Moscow and St Petersburg as the large urban centres where survey data suggests LGBT+ people feel more able to be open and where relocation may be a reasonable option. A 2023 Coming Out and Sphere Foundation survey found 57% of St Petersburg respondents out to most friends, 19% to most relatives and 24% to classmates or colleagues, against Moscow at 50%/15%/19%. The note records two St Petersburg policewomen fired for allegedly flirting on social media, and an August 2024 Citizens' Watch/Sphere Foundation study of enforcement of the 'propaganda' articles whose respondents included 13% living in St Petersburg. Nationally, same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, the LGBT+ movement was designated 'extremist' in November 2023, and at least 139 individuals were affected by enforcement in 2022-2024.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) reports that Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions connected to the 'International LGBT Movement' since its November 2023 designation, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. A further 81 people in 98 cases have been found guilty since January 2024 of article 20.3 administrative offences for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. St Petersburg appears in the article only in a photo caption for the 'X St.Petersburg Pride' rally of 3 August 2019.

Wikipedia's biography of Vitaly Milonov documents the city-level origin of the anti-LGBT law a trans visitor to Saint Petersburg stands under. As a member of the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly (2007-2016), he is recorded as the principal sponsor of the legislation criminalising 'homosexual propaganda directed toward minors', the city ban enacted in 2012 that the New York Times report 'Anti-Gay Law Stirs Fears in Russia' (29 February 2012) covered. The page quotes his statement that he fully intended to catch Madonna committing a possible offence under it when she visited the city. It also records Milonov stating in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics if they promoted homosexuality to minors, and his protests against the city's Side by Side LGBT film festival in November 2013.

exact_spans: Regional testimony underpinning this record's risk framing.

texts.cleaned_text: Human Rights House Foundation interview with David Isteev (North Caucasus SOS): 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families.' He reports year-on-year deterioration as an on-the-ground defender in exile, covering the North Caucasus republics including Karachay-Cherkessia.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): singles out the North Caucasus (incl. this republic) as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory Russia finding — trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; systematic regional campaigns 2017–2024; 2023 'extremist' designation → 2–6 (organising 6–10) years' imprisonment.

Russian law prohibits transgender people from changing their legal gender and bans gender-affirming care. The ban was enacted in July 2023 and prohibits both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents without surgery. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transition and applies to all age groups. A 2024 adoption law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transition, and single-person foreign adoption is permitted only if that country recognises neither same-sex marriage nor gender transition. Military-related discussion in 2023 linked legal gender change to draft avoidance, with proposals aimed at preventing trans women from changing legal status from male to female without surgery and the Duma Speaker claiming about 2,700 such decisions had been made. President Putin stated on 30 September 2022 that teaching children about other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable. Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, following 1993 re-legalisation that removed Article 121 of the RSFSR Penal Code, which had punished consensual sex between men with up to five years imprisonment under the 1961 code and three to five years under Article 154-a added in March 1934. The age of consent has stood at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Russian law provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, and same-sex couples are ineligible for protections available to opposite-sex couples, with neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions allowed and a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage. A 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors, expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added to the unified terrorist and extremist list on 22 March 2024, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement since the ruling has included arrests of gay bar owners, fines or imprisonment for displaying the rainbow flag, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist with convictions of founders for leading an extremist organisation. Documented enforcement and violence linked to sexual orientation includes the reported detention and torture of over 100 men since February 2017 in Chechnya with at least three extrajudicial killings reported 1 April 2017, a further purge reported in January 2019 with around 40 detained and two killed, and an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities.
Russia scored 2% in the 2026 European LGBTI legal and policy ranking and maintains explicit bans/legal limitations that make legal gender recognition practically impossible.

records.name: Chechnya
exact_spans: The core sourced basis for this record's extreme-risk profile.
The freshest official-assessment source for the record's trans-specific claim.

texts.cleaned_text: Human Rights Watch (26 May 2017) documents the Feb 2017 Chechen police purge: men believed gay were rounded up, held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured. Some were forcibly disappeared; others returned to families barely alive from beatings, with captors outing them and urging honour killings. The report establishes that top regional officials knew of the operation despite Kadyrov's denial.

Novaya Gazeta (11 Jan 2019, Russian): learned of renewed persecution of gay men in Chechnya — warnings circulated via VKontakte LGBT-group admins telling those still at large to leave the republic; Kadyrov press secretary Alvi Karimov denied the reports. Follows the paper's April 2017 investigation into torture and killings of gay men for which no criminal case was opened. Establishes the purge reactivated within two years, not a one-off.

The Insider (4 Sep 2024): SK SOS reports Chechen security forces coercing detained gay men into military service — at least seven sent to frontlines in Ukraine, one already killed; methods began before the 21 Sep 2022 mobilisation order. In early Sep 2022 six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned they'd be sent to front. Establishes detention-to-frontline blackmail as an ongoing persecution vector since 2022.

OC Media (Memorial Human Rights Centre investigation): a mass wave of unlawful detentions sweeping Chechnya with detainees forcibly sent to fight in Ukraine — people detained over minor pretexts (missing insurance documents), taken to police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse, forced to sign contracts; families sometimes must recruit two 'volunteers' to free a detained relative. Complements the gay-specific coercion reports: conscription machinery as a generalised coercive tool of the Chechen security apparatus.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns across this republic and the wider North Caucasus 2017–2024 (abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings); assesses that in the North Caucasus trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; notes the 2023 'extremist organisation' designation of the international LGBT+ movement, exposing support or activity to 2–6 years imprisonment and organising to 6–10 years, with violence spreading beyond the region.

As part of the Russian Federation, Russia's LGBT laws formally apply in Chechnya, but de facto there are no protections for LGBT citizens and authorities allegedly encourage families to kill those suspected of homosexuality. Homosexuality was criminalized after the Russian conquest in the late 1800s, decriminalized after the October Revolution, recriminalized under Stalin, and relegalized in Russia in 1993, while in 1999 Chechen president Aslan Maskhadov introduced sharia law under which sharia courts imposed the death penalty for homosexuality and adultery. Current Chechen imposition of Islamic law contradicts Russian federal law and the Chechen constitution's provision that Chechnya is secular and no religion may be made official or mandatory. Russia's June 2013 anti-gay propaganda law bans distribution of "propaganda for nontraditional sexual relationships" among children. Beginning February-March 2017, law enforcement rounded up more than 100 and possibly several hundred men on suspicion of being gay or bisexual, holding them in a secret prison in Argun and multiple detention centers where they were beaten, tortured with electric shocks, and at least three and reportedly up to 20 were beaten to death. A renewed purge beginning December 2018 detained around 40 persons including gay men and women with two killed, and by May 2019 police renewed unlawful detentions, beatings and humiliation of men presumed gay or bisexual. In March 2021 the EU imposed sanctions on two Chechen government officials for government-sponsored violence against LGBTQIA+ individuals.

In Chechnya in late March-early April 2017 security forces under Ramzan Kadyrov rounded up dozens of men suspected of being gay and subjected them to detention, torture, humiliation, enforced disappearance and severe beatings with at least three deaths, while LGBT people faced ongoing risk of persecution by authorities and honour killings by relatives with no safe complaint or judicial recourse because retaliation was practically inevitable.

In late March 2017 authorities in Chechnya detained over 100 men across Grozny and other settlements for actual or suspected non-traditional sexual orientation, including muftiate religious figures and television presenters who had concealed their orientation, with at least three detainees killed and further killings alleged, while those released fled the republic and users abandoned LGBT messenger groups and closed social-media accounts because non-traditional orientation carries lethal honor-based retaliation risk amid close social monitoring.

Country-wide survey of legal gender recognition: 22 of 32 states had legislated an LGR procedure by March 2025, while six states (Aguascalientes, Chiapas, Durango, Querétaro, Tabasco, Tamaulipas) had reformed nothing, leaving trans people's documents permanently mismatched; also documents coercive detention and border scrutiny risks for document-mismatched travellers.

Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Mexico' page sets out the state-level legal picture a Quintana Roo visitor stands under. Same-sex marriage has been permitted in the state since 2012: two marriages were performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011, annulled by the governor in April 2012, and reinstated on 3 May 2012 once the state conceded its Civil Code sets no gender requirement. The state congress legalized adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022. Quintana Roo enacted legal gender recognition in 2020 and banned conversion practices on 15 December 2023, and its penal code punishes crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender as hate crimes. The state ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination, and Cancún is among Mexico's principal gay-tourism destinations.

Local reporting (Tribuna de la Bahía, 15 December 2023) states that the Quintana Roo congress, following Morelos, banned conversion practices. Both legislatures approved initiatives prohibiting and sanctioning 'Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género' (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies. Penalties are two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA (measurement and updating unit) value for those who carry out such practices. The reform dated 15 December 2023 applies across the state, including tourist corridors such as Cancún and the Riviera Maya.

Same-sex marriage in Yucatán was established first by the courts and then by statute. On 1 July 2013 the Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled that two petitioners were able to marry, and on 8 August 2013 the first same-sex couple legally married in the state. The Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015 and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022. Yucatán is listed as enacting a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban on 25 August 2021, in effect alongside the state bans from Mexico City (31 July 2020) and other states. Federally, same-sex acts have been decriminalised since 1871, sexual diversity is documented as tolerated among Yucatán Maya groups, and the Chamber of Deputies passed a conversion-therapy ban in March 2023 by 267-104 after a 69-16 Senate vote in October 2022.

The March 2025 Human Rights Watch state-by-state rundown of legal gender recognition states that in 2024 Yucatán's congress passed a reform to the Civil Registry Law creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, published in the Diario Oficial of 26 April 2024 on yucatan.gob.mx. Yucatán therefore offers an administrative, rather than court-ordered, route for transgender people to update legal gender.

Mexico has no national administrative procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without enactment, and six legislatures had enacted none. Only seven states extend recognition to children. In 2022 the Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where no procedure exists, trans people face identity-document mismatch that drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. Recognition in Mexico depends on the state a person is in.

HRW and the Community Center for Inclusion reported on 6 March 2024 that Tabasco has no legal gender-recognition procedure. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. Context includes the Aug 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and the fact that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022. Trans people in Tabasco live without documents that match their gender.

On 13 March 2004 amendments to the Mexico City Civil Code took effect allowing transgender people to change gender and name on their birth certificates. In September 2008 the Mexico City Legislative Assembly passed a law making it easier for transgender people to change their gender on birth certificates. On 13 November 2014 the Legislative Assembly of Mexico City approved a gender identity law making the process for transgender people to change gender much quicker and simpler. On 13 July 2017 the Michoacan Congress approved a gender identity law and on 20 July 2017 a gender identity law was approved in Nayarit. On 17 October 2018 the Supreme Court held that a transgender person could change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity. On 13 November 2018 Coahuila passed a gender identity bill allowing transgender individuals easier access to birth certificates reflecting their new legal gender. On 25 April 2019 the Hidalgo Congress approved a gender identity law and on 17 May 2019 San Luis Potosi began authorizing legal gender changes for transgender people. Private same-sex sexual conduct between adults ceased to be a criminal matter in 1871 through adoption of the Napoleonic Code. On 2 September 1999 Mexico City passed an ordinance banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, the first of its kind in the country. A federal anti-discrimination law took effect on 11 June 2003 creating a national council to enforce it. Article 1 of the Federal Constitution was amended in 2001 to prohibit discrimination under the term preferences and in June 2011 the more precise term sexual orientation was inserted. Mexico City passed same-sex marriage on 21 December 2009 with effect on 4 March 2010 and the Supreme Court upheld its constitutionality on 5 August 2010 by 9 to 2. On 3 June 2015 the Supreme Court released a jurisprudential thesis deeming laws restricting marriage to a man and a woman unconstitutional and requiring every judge to validate same-sex unions through amparo, with a nationwide adoption jurisprudence finalized on 23 September 2016. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling though only twenty allowed those couples to adopt children. Civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacan, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz. Acceptance of transgender identities has been documented among Isthmus Zapotecs and Yucatan Mayas, with Zapotecs recognizing a traditional third gender known as muxe intermediate between male and female. Muxes are assigned male at birth but typically act and behave like women and do both women and men's work, and having a muxe in the family is perceived as good luck and a blessing. The article states: "Although they are perceived to be different from the general heterosexual male population, they are neither devalued nor discriminated against in their communities." It further states: "Mestizos, especially mestizo police, occasionally harass and even persecute muxe boys, but Zapotec parents, especially mothers and other women, are quick to defend them and their rights to \"be themselves\", because, as they put it, \"God made them that way.\"" It adds: "I have never heard an Isthmus Zapotec suggest that a muxe chose to become a muxe." Visible and well-attended LGBTQ marches and pride parades have occurred in Mexico City since 1979, in Guadalajara since 1996, and in Monterrey since 2001.

In late August 2008 Mexico City's legislature passed 37-17 a law formalizing the procedure for transgender people to legally change names and obtain revised birth certificates reflecting gender identity, replacing a prior process lacking specific rules that could take years in court, pending mayoral signature.

The country's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the state/provinces and extended the right to minors in 2022; the regional human-rights court likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. texts.cleaned_text: Full text of Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13 (the Bangsamoro Administrative Code), begun 29 March 2019, published by the Bangsamoro Official Gazette. The act prescribes the structures and rules of governance of the autonomous region and guarantees religious freedom. Its justice-dispensation clause reads: 'in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws'.

Bangsamoro Parliament (2026-07-14) proposed a Shari'ah Justice Code of 10 books extending Shari'ah jurisdiction beyond the personal-status law confined since PD 1083 (1977) into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and ADR, resting on BOL authority and the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. Marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums with written-opt-in clauses for civil entities, the legal-pluralist marriage regime that applies to a visitor married to a Muslim spouse.

In August 2024 President Marcos Jr. signed a law creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, expanding the Shari'ah court system beyond the Bangsamoro into majority-Christian northern Mindanao, Davao-region provinces, parts of the Visayas, Luzon and Metro Manila; parliament passed it unanimously. Christianity Today reported it in 2024-11 with local Christian-leader reaction. The measure carries Bangsamoro's Shari'ah personal-law regime onto a national footing.

texts.cleaned_text: Wikipedia's article on Kalinga, a landlocked province in the Cordillera Administrative Region formed out of Kalinga-Apayao on 8 May 1995 by Republic Act No. 7878 with Tabuk as capital, records the province as a flashpoint between the Marcos martial-law government (declared September 1972) and its indigenous peoples over the Chico River Dam Project, which would have displaced about 100,000 indigenous people. It states that the 24 April 1980 murder of tribal leader Macli-ing Dulag turned public opinion and made the dam dispute a landmark ancestral-domain case in the country, and records the September 1986 Mount Data Peace Accord that created the Cordillera Autonomous Region, with later plebiscites failing to ratify autonomy.

Wikipedia's article on the Cordillera Administrative Region describes the country's only landlocked region, created on 15 July 1987 and comprising Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Kalinga and Mountain Province centred on Baguio. It identifies the region as the least populated in the country according to the 2020 Census of Population and Housing, with fewer residents than the national capital. It records numerous ethnic groups including a majority-Igorot province, a continuing Cordillera autonomy movement, and the earlier Cordillera People's Liberation Army ceasefire secured by the Aquino government.

There is no legal gender recognition. There are no laws protecting LGBTQ people from discrimination in health, employment, education, and access to goods and services. Openly LGBTQ people cannot serve in the military. There are no laws against psychology or medical practices being used as conversion therapy on LGBTQ people. Law 24-001 on the Protection of Personal Data protects sexual orientation as sensitive data, with Article 17 stating "Any processing of sensitive data is prohibited due to risks of discrimination or infringement of personal freedoms"; the article describes this protection only for sexual orientation and does not state coverage for gender identity. The Central African Republic signed a joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity at the United Nations condemning violence and discrimination against LGBTQ people. Male and female same-sex sexual activity are legal. The penal code criminalizes public expression of love between persons of the same sex with imprisonment for six months to two years or a fine of between 150,000 and 600,000 CFA francs ($300 and $1,200). When one participant is a child, the adult may be sentenced to two to five years imprisonment or a fine of 100,000 to 800,000 CFA francs ($200 and $1,600). In 2012 there were no reports that police arrested or detained persons under these provisions. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples, and same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned under Article 7 which defines marriage as the union between one man and one woman with family and marriage under protection of the State. Alternatives Centrafrique has documented cases of people being arrested due to false accusations of same-sex intercourse. "societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons was entrenched, and many citizens attributed the existence of homosexuality to undue Western influence." Cultural stigma continues to persist, and due to criminalization of public same-sex affection along with cultural stigma the LGBTQ community has to conceal itself. LGBTQ people face discrimination in education, healthcare, and employment. Religious preach conversion, but this is rarely enacted since people keep their LGBTQ identities hidden. While there were no reports of violence against LGBTQ people, it is unclear if this is due to lack of incidents or victims not reporting it. Alternatives Centrafrique states that LGBTQ people have experienced mistreatment and torture by law enforcement. Being diagnosed with HIV is used as a source of stigmatization in the workplace leading to harassment, blackmail, and firings.

Outright International country overview (last updated 12 March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination is described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is limited.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Queer In The World Monaco guide (updated 3 December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections with room for improvement; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

Wikipedia country coverage: Hate-speech protection rests on Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression, which bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016 (technological crime law), punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2–5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months–3 years. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for 5 days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added 'sexual orientation' to Civil Code articles 238-1 (6 months–1 year for violent acts not causing total incapacity), 239 (10 years for attacking a partner or co-resident) and 421 (5 years' probation for unprovoked attacks on a person or group). Monaco does not recognize same-sex marriage, and ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking (45th of 49 European countries) notes that transgender people cannot alter their legal gender. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a cohabitation agreement (contrat de vie commune), introduced in Parliament on 16 April 2018, unanimously approved by the National Council on 4 December 2019 and in force six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco; it is signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax, not like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and parents/children. Same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. The LGBT community supports some gay-friendly establishments inside Monaco, but there are no official gay bars, clubs or events in the country, unlike nearby French cities Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Monaco is not an EU member, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, though it has strong cultural and economic ties with France. Monaco has no armed forces, only a National Guard; France handles defence and allows openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve. BBC Indonesia (26 February 2016) reports that on the night of Wednesday 24 February 2016 Yogyakarta's Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, a religious school where trans women ('waria') study Islam, was closed after the hardline Front Jihad Islam (FJI) threatened to seal it, amid what the BBC describes as rising hate speech against LGBT people 'especially in Yogyakarta'. Banguntapan district head (camat) Jati Bayubroto justified the closure on the grounds the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site; founder Shinta Ratri said about 20 waria attend the weekly weekend classes, which teach ordinary Islamic instruction. The report documents an enforcement-adjacent event in Yogyakarta against a trans institution, and shows the shutdown proceeded on administrative and religious grounds rather than an enacted regional anti-trans regulation.

Rappler Indonesia's 25 February 2016 report details the closure meeting: on 24 February 2016 at about 20:00 WIB a two-hour meeting at the Jagalan ward office in Yogyakarta, attended by ward and residents' officials, the lurah, the local military district commander and, in the earlier 19 February session, the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief (Kapolsek), ended with an agreement to shut the Al-Fatah waria pesantren after the Front Jihad Islam demanded it. A waria witness said an FJI leader delivered 'fiery' anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of 'Allahu Akbar' and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, calling LGBT people 'sama-sama anak bangsa' (fellow children of the nation) and saying the regional government would study the issue. The shutdown concluded on administrative and community grounds without any provincial anti-trans statute being cited.

DW Indonesia (21 June 2021) reports that Yogyakarta's trans women ('transpuan'/'waria'), most working as street performers or wedding make-up artists and attached to the Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, saw earnings fall by about 60 percent during the COVID-19 pandemic and were 'ignored by the government', struggling to pay rent and buy food. The article describes a 12 June 2021 aromatherapy-candle making class at the Al-Fatah pesantren in Yogyakarta, run with local small business Malini.yk to teach new income skills, and says the waria kept performing despite donors refusing even masked performances. The pesantren and the Yogyakarta waria community are operating again years after the 2016 closure, while economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province persists.

Cross-dressing is not, per se, illegal in Indonesia, and transgender people are allowed to change legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they can marry people of the opposite legal gender. Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and the Indonesian Ulama Council ruled transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating if they are "not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously" they must be willing "to accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed." The judicial system takes the contrary position, with Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar as the first trans Indonesian legally recognized as female, and there have been cases where perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community were arrested and prosecuted. Targeted enforcement includes January 2018 North Aceh police arrest of twelve transgender women with forcibly cut hair, compelled men's clothing and closed beauty salons, and Jakarta Social Agency declaration of waria as socially dysfunctional with regular raids and incarceration in city-owned "rehabilitation" centres with homeless people, beggars and buskers until documentation and signed pledge, with officials stating this creates deterrent against being transgender and continued violations will result in jail time. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with Kartu Tanda Penduduk including residents of Papua, but recognizes only "male" and "female" with no third gender/X designator and prints gender at birth unless court recognition obtained, citing undocumentation where families disapprove blocking work or social services. Transgender people who do not hide gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are thus often forced into prostitution and other illegal activities to survive, with discrimination and harassments not uncommon though violence quite rare. In the military, Aprilio Manganang in 2021 became the first service member to legally change gender from female to male, although his case was intersex assigned female at birth and raised as a girl. Private, non-commercial consensual sexual activity between consenting adults of the same sex has been allowed nationally since 1993 at 18 years of age, with no explicit sodomy law unlike Malaysia, and a 2003 national bill to criminalize same-sex activity with cohabitation, adultery and witchcraft failed with no subsequent reintroduction. In December 2022 Parliament passed a Penal Code criminalizing sex outside marriage upon complaint by immediate family, set to take force on 2 January 2026 with up to one year in prison for unmarried partners, while the draft spokesperson stated it will not criminalize private sexual orientation including LGBTQ persons and Coordinating Minister Mahfud MD said it only targets adults who commit "sexual violence" or rape of underage same-sex children and public immoral acts, though same-sex marriage is not legally recognized effectively placing all same-sex sexual activity outside legal recognition. Aceh, allowed special autonomous Sharia law under 2014 Qanun Jinayat, punishes consensual adult same-sex acts by up to 100 lashes or up to 100 months (8 years) imprisonment, with public caning imposed including two young gay men aged 20 and 23 in 2017 and two men aged 20 and 21 sentenced 11 August 2025 for kissing after April arrest when police broke into toilet. Police have repeatedly raided private "gay parties" and gay saunas under national pornography law in the 2010s-2020s, including November 2016 Jakarta raid, May 2017 arrest of 141 men with ten charged and detention of 144 at Atlantis Gym Jakarta, October 2017 arrest of 51 with six charged, February/May/June 2025 South Jakarta hotel/villa raids detaining 56, nine and 75, August 2025 arrest of three for creating LGBTQ Facebook page facing up to 12 years and 6 billion rupiah fines, and 22 May 2026 sentencing of 25 to prison for violating anti-pornography law. Indonesian law does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships or adoption by same-sex couples, limiting adoption to husband-wife married couples, and as of 2019 provides no specific anti-discrimination protection nor hate-crime prohibition based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Limited protection machinery cited is a 2015 police circular to process hate speech related to sexual orientations and gender identity, Regulation of Head of National Police No. 8 of 2009 duty to protect special rights of minority groups including sexual orientation, and theoretical constitutional and Human Rights Law No. 39/1999 guarantee against employment discrimination on any ground. UNSW Human Rights Research Centre reports that transgender women face the highest rates of violence among LGBTIQ Indonesians, with survey data on relative social hostility. The report covers the January 2018 detention of twelve transwomen. Its scope is Indonesia-wide rather than Aceh-specific.

Cross-dressing is not per se illegal in Indonesia, and transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. Transgender people are allowed to change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they can marry a person of the opposite legal gender, exemplified by Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar as the first trans Indonesian legally recognized as female and by Aprilio Manganang in 2021 as the first service member to legally change gender from female to male although his case was intersex assigned female at birth. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers including Kartu Tanda Penduduk for residents of Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua, recognizing only male and female descriptors with no third gender/X option and printing gender at birth unless court recognition was already obtained, on the stated reasoning that many were undocumented where families did not approve. Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are thus often forced into prostitution and other illegal activities to survive. In Aceh transgender people have faced targeted enforcement: in January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing, and closed their beauty salons, and in a January 2018 parlour raid in Aceh police tortured LGBTQ citizens, shaved the heads of transgender women, stripped their shirts and bras, and paraded them in the street forcing them to shout "to become men". In Jakarta the Social Agency declared waria to be socially dysfunctional and regularly conducts raids against transgender women, taking detained individuals to city-owned rehabilitation centres where they are incarcerated with homeless people, beggars and street buskers and only released upon documentation of lack of homelessness and a signed promise not to repeat the offence, with officials stating this is to create a deterrent against being transgender and continued violations will result in jail time. The Indonesian Ulama Council ruled transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating if not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously they must accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed, while the judicial system takes the contrary position recognizing actual genders and authorities have in some cases arrested and prosecuted perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community. Aceh has special autonomous status implementing Islamic Sharia-based criminal law (Qanun Jinayat), with authority granted in 2005 to introduce Sharia law for Muslim residents and the 2014 Qanun Jinayat providing that consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults are punishable by up to 100 lashes or up to 100 months (8 years) imprisonment, set for enforcement by the end of 2015. Enforcement outcomes in Aceh include the 2017 sentencing of two young gay men aged 20 and 23 to public caning, several high-profile cases of men publicly caned after guilty findings for same-sex relations, and the 11 August 2025 sentencing of two men aged 20 and 21 to public caning for kissing after April arrest when police broke into a toilet. Nationally Indonesia has allowed private consensual same-sex activity since 1993 at age 18, has no explicit sodomy law unlike Malaysia, and the Penal Code does not prohibit non-commercial private consensual activity between consenting same-sex adults. In December 2022 Parliament passed a Penal Code criminalizing sex outside marriage upon complaint by immediate family, set to take force on 2 January 2026 with up to one year imprisonment for unmarried partners, with the spokesperson stating the draft will not criminalize private sexual orientation including LGBTQ persons and Coordinating Minister Mahfud MD stating it did not criminalize an LGBTQ person and only targets adults committing sexual violence or rape of underage same-sex children and immoral acts in public, while Article 421(1) punishes obscene acts against a same-sex person in public with maximum 1 year and six months imprisonment or maximum fine category III. Indonesian law does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, households headed by same-sex couples lack the same legal protections as opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couples are ineligible to adopt as only married husband-wife couples can adopt. As of 2019 no specific law protects from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity nor prohibits hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity, though a 2015 police circular states processing of hate speech related to sexual orientations and gender identity and Head of National Police Regulation No. 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect special rights of minority groups including sexual orientation. Police have conducted repeated raids and detentions for gay parties and saunas under pornography-related offences, including the November 2016 Jakarta raid after an Islamic Defenders Front tip-off, May 2017 arrest of 141 men for a gay sex party with ten charged and detention of 144 in the Atlantis Gym raid, October 2017 arrest of 51 in a Central Jakarta sauna with six charged including the owner, and 2025 raids detaining 56 on 1 February, nine on 24 May, and arresting 75 on 22 June near Jakarta. The article states: "While transgender people in Indonesia are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have, in recent years, faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more and more popular in Indonesia." The article states "some public tolerance is given to some transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry, most notably the celebrity talk show host Dorce Gamalama." The article states transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. The article states discrimination and harassments directed at transgender people is not uncommon, though violence is quite rare, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often face employment exclusion forcing reliance on prostitution and other illegal activities. The article reports officials justify rehabilitation detention as creating a deterrent against being transgender and cites the Ulama Council position that those unwilling to cure themselves medically and religiously must accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed, evidencing institutional rejection despite noted cultural presence.

Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat enacted in 2014 and enforced from 23 October 2015 defines liwath in Article 63 as sexual acts between males and musahaqah in Article 64 as sexual acts between females as determined by birth sex and punishes each with up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold, thereby exposing trans visitors in Aceh to caning, imprisonment and fines where presentation, identity documents, or partner sex are policed as same-sex conduct.

Aceh is Indonesia's only province that criminalizes same-sex relations and enforces Islamic law in addition to the national criminal code, and on May 23, 2017 in Banda Aceh an Islamic court applied its 2014 anti-homosexuality provisions for the first time by having two men publicly caned with 82 lashes each for gay sex before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque.

Documented Minnesota DOC placement practice, birth-sex determined: CeCe McDonald, a transgender woman, pleaded guilty to second-degree manslaughter and was sentenced on 4 June 2012 to 41 months; her attorneys acknowledged there was 'no way' she would be sent to a women's prison and 'really no history of transgender people being placed according to their gender identity'. The Minnesota Department of Corrections placed her in an adult male facility, Minnesota Correctional Facility - St. Cloud, after a state gender assessment concluded she would be held in a men's facility; despite a later transfer to a second facility she remained quartered with men throughout her imprisonment (a petition during her imprisonment led DOC to administer the correct hormone regimen). She was held in segregated custody while awaiting trial, and in May 2012 a fellow inmate attacked her with a glass, causing a wound requiring eleven stitches; the attacker pleaded guilty in April 2013 to third-degree assault and received six months' jail time plus probation.

Minnesota has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity since 1993 in employment, housing, public accommodations, insurance, goods and services, contracts, health benefits and hospital visitation rights, and a May 2023 omnibus community justice bill explicitly added "gender identity" separately from sexual orientation and repealed exemptions for nonpublic service organizations, effective immediately. Hate-crime law provides additional penalties for crimes committed based on gender identity since its 1993 expansion to include that category. Changing legal gender on Minnesota birth certificates does not require sex reassignment surgery and requires a physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition or a court order for gender change plus a notarized Birth Certificate Application and fee, with the old certificate kept confidential, while Driver and Vehicle Services updates a driver's license or state ID upon individual request with no documentation required. Since October 2018 driver's licences and state IDs allow M, F, or X upon request with no documentation for intersex, non-binary and ambiguous-sex people, but no X option is available for birth certificates. State Medicaid policy covers transgender-related care and Minnesota law prohibits health insurers from excluding transgender-specific coverage or discriminating against transgender patients, and gender-affirming services were protected by a March 2023 executive order codified in April 2023 by House File 146, the "Trans Refuge Bill," signed by Governor Tim Walz effective immediately. Conversion therapy was banned statewide effective August 1, 2023 after a July 2021 executive order and prior city ordinances, and the "trans panic defense" was abolished in the omnibus justice reforms bill signed May 29, 2024 effective August 1, 2024 after a 34-33 Senate vote. The Minnesota high school transgender athlete policy has been challenged in the courts by attorneys representing 3 school softball players. Bans on same-sex sexual activity dating to 1849 territorial adoption of Wisconsin laws and the 1851 code, increased in 1909 to 20 years imprisonment and expanded in 1921 to include fellatio, were reduced in 1967 to a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in jail and/or $1,000 fine after a 1973 repeal attempt failed 46-69 with 19 abstentions, were invalidated for private adult consensual non-commercial acts in Doe et al. v. Texas, and were formally repealed in May 2023 by the Omnibus Judiciary and Public Safety Bill signed by Governor Tim Walz effective immediately. texts.cleaned_text: The Movement Advancement Project equality-map entry carries the per-state list of bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities matching their gender identity, with the year each was enacted. For Wyoming it documents the facility bans signed in March 2025.

Erin Reed's July 2026 legal-risk assessment lists Wyoming among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults. It draws on five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric for the worst bills, and was republished on 27 August 2026 by a regional LGBTQ outlet. The assessment also records federal policies that keep creating legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide.

Wyoming News Exchange reported that on Monday, March 3, 2025, Gov. Mark Gordon signed two facility measures into law. House Bill 72, the 'Protecting privacy in public spaces act,' covers sex-designated restrooms, showers, sleeping quarters and locker rooms at public facilities. Senate File 62, 'Sex-designated facilities and public schools,' requires public school children from pre-kindergarten up, including charter school students, to use restrooms aligned with sex assigned at birth. SF 62 requires districts to provide a 'reasonable accommodation' to any student who does not wish to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender at that student's birth.

Wyoming state statutes do not address discrimination based on gender identity, but the United States Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v Clayton County protects LGBT employees from workplace discrimination under federal law, and the cities of Jackson, Casper and Laramie have ordinances prohibiting discrimination covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations. Wyoming has no state hate crime law, but the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr Hate Crimes Prevention Act of 2009 expanded the federal definition to include gender identity. Changing the gender marker on a Wyoming birth certificate requires undergoing sex reassignment surgery and obtaining a court order stating sex has been changed, with submission to Vital Statistics Services of a letter requesting the change, a photocopy of current ID, a certified copy of the court order, and a doctor letter confirming surgery was performed. Correction of the gender marker on a driver's license or state ID requires a completed Gender Designation Change Request Form signed by the applicant and a physician, therapist or counselor, psychiatric social worker or other medical or social service provider confirming gender identity. A bill passed in March 2023 explicitly bans transgender athletes from playing on any female sports and athletics teams, which became law without the governor's signature or veto and took effect July 1, 2023. A bill passed by both houses in March 2024 explicitly bans sexual reassignment surgery and gender-affirming care on children, which the governor signed to take effect July 1. House Bill 72 signed in April 2025 requires all public restrooms in the state to be segregated by biological sex and takes effect July 1, 2025. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since Wyoming decriminalized consensual sodomy in February 1977, with common-law liability for anal intercourse abrogated in 1982, and the age of consent for all consensual sexual activity is 17. Same-sex marriage has been recognized since October 21, 2014 after state officials declined to appeal the October 17 federal decision in Guzzo v Mead finding the ban unconstitutional, replacing a statutory ban in place since 1977 and made more explicit in 2003, under which legal relationships of same-sex couples had been recognized only for divorce. A 2013 domestic partnership bill to provide immediate-family rights was approved 7-2 in House committee on January 28 but rejected 24-35 by the full House on January 30. Married same-sex couples are permitted to adopt and lesbian couples can access in vitro fertilization, with state law recognizing the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent after donor insemination irrespective of marital status. State law does not authorize or prohibit gestational surrogacy contracts leaving review case-by-case, and an August 2021 law explicitly legalizing surrogacy contracts uses the terms mother and father instead of parent or parents to exclude single people and same-sex couples. State statutes do not address discrimination based on sexual orientation, with prohibitory bills rejected by the House on January 31, 2011 and by the Senate 15-13 on January 31, 2013, and bill SF 115 approved 24-6 by the Senate and 6-2 in House committee in February 2015 but rejected 26-33 by the House on February 24, 2015. Jackson, Casper and Laramie have ordinances prohibiting discrimination covering sexual orientation in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Cheyenne and Gillette prohibit city employment discrimination on sexual orientation only, and federal Bostock protections apply to sexual orientation in the workplace. Wyoming has no state hate crime law following hot debate after the 1998 murder of Matthew Shepard near Laramie, but the federal 2009 Act covers sexual orientation, and a state obscenity-material law affecting certain LGBT books was enforced in October 2021 when a Gillette librarian was charged by the district attorney and sheriff office.

Wyoming enacted House Bill 72 signed by Governor Mark Gordon on March 3, 2025 after 52-8 House passage on February 7, 2025 and 25-6 Senate passage, effective July 1, 2025, defining male and female by biological sex and requiring public facilities to reserve multi-occupancy restrooms, changing areas and sleeping quarters exclusively for males or exclusively for females and prohibiting entry into facilities not matching biological sex, allowing only reasonable accommodations that do not include opposite-sex multi-occupancy access, and creating a cause of action for a person encountering an opposite-sex person in a sex-designated restroom or changing area where the facility permitted it or failed to prohibit it and for a person required by a correctional or educational facility to share sleeping quarters with the opposite sex.
On March 1, 2023, the Wyoming Legislature approved SF133 banning transgender students from playing sports consistent with their gender identity and advanced the bill to Governor Mark Gordon's desk.

The gay and/or trans panic defence was abolished and repealed by legislation passed 144-1 in the House in March 2021 and 29-0 in the Senate in April 2021, signed May 5, 2021 by Governor Phil Scott and effective July 1. Use of conversion therapy on LGBT minors, which includes transgender minors, was banned by a bill approved unanimously in the Senate March 17, 2016, approved with amendments in the House April 26, accepted by the Senate April 29, signed May 25 by Governor Peter Shumlin and effective July 1, 2016. Vermont permits both preoperative and post-operative transgender individuals to change the gender marker on birth certificates and other state-issued documents upon court order supported by a letter from a licensed medical or mental health practitioner of surgical, hormonal, or other appropriate treatment for gender transition, while effective July 1, 2022 individuals born in Vermont can legally change sex marker to male, female or X based on self-determination without court order, mental health diagnosis, surgery, divorce or medical permission under a bill signed in April 2022, and since July 1, 2019 the Department of Motor Vehicles has offered X on driver's licences and state IDs with no documentation needed. Since July 1, 2018 all single-user public bathrooms must be marked as gender-neutral under a bill signed in May 2018, since 2013 all health insurers underwriting in Vermont are required to cover transgender care including sex reassignment surgery, and in May 2023 a law effective immediately by emergency clause legally protects, defends and shields transgender and non-binary people accessing gender-affirming healthcare across state lines coming into Vermont. In October 2023 the Department of Education unanimously passed a policy to protect and defend transgender and non-binary students within schools and classrooms, while in 2023 Mid Vermont Christian School's girls' basketball team forfeited a match against a team fielding a transgender girl citing fairness and safety and was as a result forbidden from competition by the Vermont Principals' Association. Vermont reduced the penalty for sodomy from capital punishment to life imprisonment in 1861, enacted a 1937 law punishing oral sex participation with 1 to 5 years in state prison applicable to both heterosexual and homosexual activity, repealed that statute in April 1977, with adult private consensual noncommercial sodomy unenforceable under Lawrence v. Texas. Civil unions for same-sex couples were introduced in July 2000 as the first state status identical to marriage following a 1999 Vermont Supreme Court equal marriage benefits ruling, same-sex marriage has been legal since September 1, 2009 as the first state via legislature and governor rather than court decision, and benefits to same-sex partners of state employees have been provided since 1994. Vermont law permits single LGBT individuals and same-sex couples to petition to adopt, provides lesbian couples access to in vitro fertilization with recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent to a child born via donor insemination irrespective of marital status, and in June 1993 the Vermont Supreme Court ruled in favor of a lesbian seeking to adopt her partner's two biological sons. Discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices was banned with protections added in 1992, with the anti-bullying law also prohibiting bullying including cyberbullying and harassment based on sexual orientation in all educational institutions. Hate crime legislation enacted in 1990 including sexual orientation provides additional penalties for a crime committed based on the victim's sexual orientation. Use of conversion therapy on LGBT minors was banned by a bill approved unanimously in the Senate March 17, 2016, approved with amendments in the House April 26, accepted by the Senate April 29, signed May 25 by Governor Peter Shumlin and effective July 1, 2016, and the gay panic defence was abolished and repealed by the 2021 bill passed 144-1 and 29-0 and signed May 5, 2021 effective July 1.

Vermont enacted S.132 (Act 138) signed May 25, 2016 prohibiting conversion therapy on minors and treating its performance on minors as unprofessional conduct under 18 V.S.A. §§ 8351-8353 and related 26 V.S.A. licensing statutes.
Vermont enacted H.628 as Act 88, approved April 6, 2022, amending 18 V.S.A. § 5112 to allow issuance of a new birth certificate to reflect gender identity.

Report of September 13, 2026: on Friday September 11, 2026 a 27-year-old Black trans woman (Sophie Lee) was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died - the second Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks.

Maryland's Trans Health Equity Act passed the Maryland House of Delegates as of May 20, 2024, sponsor Del. Anne Kaiser, D-Montgomery, extending Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming treatment. The measure's path runs through the Maryland Senate.

Federal policy on housing transgender prisoners moved in both directions between 2015 and 2018. A January 2015 ICE memo directed that transgender immigration detainees be housed according to gender identity, and in 2016 the US Department of Justice released guidelines forbidding corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy. In 2018 the Federal Bureau of Prisons revised its Transgender Offender Manual, deleting the sentence that the Transgender Executive Council 'will recommend housing by gender identity when appropriate' and replacing it with placement on 'a case-by-case basis' in which 'biological sex' is 'the initial determination' and gender identity is used only 'in rare cases'. No Delaware- or Maryland-specific placement policy is covered.

Trans women held in men's facilities are subjected to V-coding, the assignment of trans women to aggressive cisgender male cellmates, characterized as 'a central part of a trans woman's sentence'. Trans women who physically resist sexual assault are often criminally charged with assault and placed in solitary confinement, with the charge then used to extend the sentence and deny parole. A 2021 California study found that 69% of surveyed trans women prisoners reported being made to perform unwanted sexual acts, 58.5% reported violent sexual assault, and 88% reported a 'marriage-like relationship'. Maryland has no documented placement rule, special unit, or named case.

Discrimination based on gender identity has been prohibited statewide since the Fairness for All Marylanders Act of 2014 took effect October 1, 2014, after prior coverage only in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Howard County, Hyattsville, and Montgomery County. The hate-crime law provides additional penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, clarified by a 2021 amendment effective October 1, 2021 to list gender identity as a separate category, and the common-law gay or trans panic defense was abolished by HB231 effective October 1, 2021. Maryland declared itself a sanctuary state for protecting and defending transgender individuals by a law passed 33-13 in the Senate and 97-38 in the House, signed by Governor Wes Moore and effective October 1, 2024, following a June 2023 executive order protecting unimpeded access to gender-affirming healthcare and a January 1, 2024 insurance law described as the most transgender healthcare friendly policies within the United States. Medicaid explicitly covers sexual reassignment surgery for eligible residents over 18 under a bill passed March 2023, signed April 2023, and effective January 1, 2024. Birth-certificate gender-marker change has been allowed since October 1, 2015 without surgery or sterilization upon certification from a licensed healthcare provider confirming gender identity, though X remains unavailable on birth certificates as of 2023, while Motor Vehicle Administration IDs and voter registration allow X since October 1, 2019 without legal or medical documentation, and the University of Maryland will add X in 2026. Name-change privacy reform HB39 effective October 1, 2021 repealed the 1971 requirement to publish names in a newspaper before a legal change on a birth certificate. On facilities and sports, a March 2018 federal court ruled transgender students may use restrooms and locker rooms aligning with gender identity striking down Talbot County policy, Montgomery County by 9-0 vote in July 2022 and Baltimore provide gender-neutral bathrooms by ordinance, and a February 2022 county report notes transgender athletes may participate per gender identity without proof, documentation, or medical or legal transition after 2022-2023 bills to restrict teams by biological sex failed. Private consensual same-sex sexual activity was invalidated by courts through Schochet v. State in 1990, Williams v. Glendening in October 1998 for oral sex, and a 1999 settlement for anal sex, with formal legislative repeal of the anal-sex provision effective October 1, 2020 and repeal of the oral-sex ban passed in 2023 and effective October 1, 2023 without Governor Wes Moore's signature. In July 2021 several men were arrested for gay sex but not heterosexual sex under the Unnatural or Perverted Sexual Practices Act still on the books because the 2020 Senate amendment left the oral-sex ban intact after a 2022 repeal attempt died in committee. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited statewide since the Antidiscrimination Act of 2001 effective November 21, 2001, and the hate-crime law adds penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage has been legal since January 1, 2013 under the Civil Marriage Protection Act approved 72-67 in the House on February 17, 2012 and 25-22 in the Senate on February 23, 2012, signed March 1, 2012, and approved by 52.4% of voters November 6, 2012, following a 1973 ban, domestic partnerships since 2008, and recognition of out-of-state marriages since 2010. Conversion therapy by licensed practitioners on minors was banned effective October 1, 2018 after passage in April 2018 and signature in May 2018, with a federal constitutional challenge dismissed in September 2019. Protection machinery includes Montgomery County's unanimous October 2020 LGBTIQ+ bill of rights ordinance, a 15-member Commission on LGBTIQ+ Affairs established by HB130 effective October 2021 and expanded to 21 members in April 2023, and HB1380 effective October 1, 2022 automatically restoring honorable discharges retrospectively to LGBT individuals who lived in Maryland at the time.
In 2014 Maryland signed the Fairness for All Marylanders Act into law establishing statewide nondiscrimination protections based on gender identity in employment, housing, and public accommodations.

texts.cleaned_text: North Dakota Legislative Branch overview of HB 1522 (2023): an act creating new sections of the North Dakota Century Code 'relating to preferred pronouns and providing accommodations to a transgender student,' with a penalty provision and an emergency clause. The page records the 2023 regular-session progression and the final disposition — governor signed, with the last official action filed with the Secretary of State on May 9, 2023.

Movement Advancement Project's identity-document policy tracker states that North Dakota's 2023 law 'bans all gender marker changes on birth certificates with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery', calling it a stricter, more explicit surgical requirement than in many other states, and marks North Dakota a 'negative law' state in its map. The tracker therefore places North Dakota among the states that restrict birth-certificate gender-marker changes.

North Dakota statutes do not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity, though the United States Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15 2020 established that Title VII protects employees from workplace discrimination on the basis of gender identity, with limited city-level protections in Grand Forks for city employees and applicants and in rental housing from 2013 and an April 2021 state law allowing student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students. Birth certificate gender changes were addressed by a May 2023 bill restricting changes to cases with surgery for anatomically correct genitalia, but accompanying regulations were rejected leaving in place a 2008 regulation restricting changes to those who have undergone a sex conversion operation, while the Department of Transportation updates driver license and state ID gender markers upon receipt of a physician or therapist letter stating the applicant completed a permanent gender role transition. Providing gender-affirming care to minors is illegal under a bill passed by a veto-proof majority on April 5 2023. Transgender girls were targeted by 2021 legislation banning participation in girls school sports teams passed 69 to 25 in the House and 27 to 20 in the Senate and vetoed by Governor Doug Burgum on April 21 2021, followed in April 2023 by two bills signed into law banning individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletics in schools and higher education respectively. A May 2023 law signed by the Governor and effective July 1 forbids schools and government entities from requiring or prohibiting preferred pronoun use but requires disclosure and outing of transgender students to parents in state-run schools, after a March 2023 bill requiring parental and administrative approval for preferred pronoun use in state-run schools and classrooms was vetoed. An April 2023 law signed by the Governor and effective July 1 explicitly allows restriction of transgender individuals public bathroom usage in many state-run facilities. State hate crime law does not cover gender identity, though federal law since the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act allows federal prosecution for crimes based on gender identity, and a June 2021 committee regulation bans conversion therapy by social workers, psychologists and counselors. Private adult consensual homosexual relations were legalized in 1973 as part of a Criminal Code revision setting universal age of consent at eighteen, after prior sodomy prohibitions dating to 1862 and expansions in 1885, 1903 and State v. Nelson in 1917 and a forced sterilization law expanded in 1927 to habitual criminals, moral degenerates and sexual perverts and repealed in 1965. Same-sex marriage has been legal since June 26 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges after prior constitutional and statutory restriction to one man and one woman, with proceedings in Ramsay v. Dalrymple suspended in January 2015 and the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians legalizing same-sex marriage on its reservation by 6 to 2 in August 2020. Adoption by individuals is permitted with no express ban on LGBTQ people or same-sex couples, though a 1980s Supreme Court ruling made parental sexual orientation decisive in custody because of societal prejudices before reversal in 2003, while state law expressly allows private adoption agencies to discriminate based on sincerely held religious belief. Lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilization with state law recognizing the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent after donor insemination irrespective of marital status, with gestational surrogacy expressly permitted for intended parents whether same-sex or different-sex and traditional surrogacy prohibited. State statutes do not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, though Title VII protects employees after Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15 2020, with Fargo since 2001 and Jamestown protecting city employees on sexual orientation and Grand Forks from 2013 protecting city employees and applicants and rental housing, while a February 17 2015 Senate bill banning sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations passed 25 to 22 but failed in the House. An April 2021 law allows student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students despite institutional non-discrimination policies upheld in Christian Legal Society v. Martinez in 2010, and a March 2023 bill passed to allow businesses to refuse service on any grounds based on religious objective alone awaited gubernatorial action. State hate crime law does not cover sexual orientation, though federal law since 2009 allows federal prosecution for crimes based on sexual orientation. In July 2020 North Dakota Republican delegates voted for the party 2020 election platform opposing absolutely any civil rights protections for LGBTQ people while accusing transgender people "of preying on women" and LGBTQ people of "recruiting children". Many Republican delegates condemned the platform. Governor Doug Burgum opposed the platform calling it "divisive and divisional" and stating "As I've long said, all North Dakotans deserve to be treated equally and live free of discrimination". A 2022 Public Religion Research Institute poll found 78 percent of residents supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity while 22 percent were opposed. The article states perceptions toward gender and sexuality within Native American tribes both were and still are different than those of people from European descent with traditions of "third gender" people also called "two-spirit" who perform tasks and wear clothes considered gender non-conforming, identified as skuxát among the Arikara and miati and mihdeke among the Hidatsa and Mandan and wįktą, winkta and wíŋkte among the Assiniboine, Dakota and Lakota.
