texts.cleaned_text: Louisville Public Media reports that on March 29, 2023 the Kentucky legislature overrode Gov. Andy Beshear's veto, enacting Senate Bill 150, which bans gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors in Kentucky and restricts which bathrooms those students can use in public schools.

The Kentucky Department of Education released guidance in April 2023 for school districts implementing the state's 2023 anti-LGBTQ rules, advising districts to remove sex education from fifth-grade curriculum and to tread cautiously with the bathroom-ban provisions. School districts carry out the 2023 facility restriction.

On July 14, 2023, U.S. District Judge David Hale lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month, allowing Kentucky's ban on gender-affirming care for minors to take effect and preventing transgender minors from accessing puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Seven transgender children and their parents had sued to block the law, and the ACLU of Kentucky called the ruling a temporary setback.

Kentucky permits post-operative transgender people to amend sex on birth certificates by sending a doctor's letter stating gender-affirming surgery was performed directly to the Department of Vital Statistics in Frankfort, after previously requiring a court order for a Kentucky-born person. Minors cannot receive gender-affirming care as of July 14, 2023 with no phaseout for those already receiving care, and on September 28, 2023 federal appeals judges allowed the ban to remain in effect while legal challenges are pending. Senate Bill 83 banning transgender athletes from female sports teams passed the General Assembly in March 2022, was vetoed by Governor Andy Beshear in April 2022 for constitutionality and vagueness concerns, and the veto was overridden the same month with the law taking effect immediately. House Bill 470's anti-transgender provisions including the ban on gender-affirming care for minors advanced March 2, 2023 and passed March 17, 2023, was vetoed by the Governor, and was overridden March 29, 2023 by simple majority votes while police arrested 19 capitol protesters for criminal trespassing. Workplace discrimination based on gender identity is banned in Kentucky under the March 7, 2018 Sixth Circuit decision in EEOC v. R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes holding Title VII prohibits discrimination against transgender people and that employers may not use the Religious Freedom Restoration Act to justify anti-LGBTQ discrimination, supplemented by executive-order protections for state public employees and 19 city Fairness Ordinances covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations. Kentucky hate-crime statutes cover sexual orientation but expressly do not cover gender identity. Conversion therapy on minors is illegal statewide since Governor Beshear's September 18, 2024 executive order, following prior city bans in Covington in March 2020 by 5-0, Louisville in September 2020 by 24-1, and Lexington in May 2021 by unanimous vote. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the Kentucky Supreme Court invalidated KRS 510.100 in Kentucky v. Wasson in 1992 under the state constitution, a result reinforced by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003, though the unenforceable statute remains on the books after previously punishing same-sex genital-oral, genital-anal and anal-oral conduct as a misdemeanor up to 12 months in jail and $500 fine with solicitation up to 90 days and $250. State public-employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is barred by Governor Steve Beshear's June 2008 executive order reinstating Governor Paul Patton's 2003 protections after removal by Governor Ernie Fletcher in 2006, with Berea Mayor Steve Connelly extending a similar order to town employees in February 2013. Nineteen cities maintain Fairness Ordinances barring sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, including Lexington-Fayette County in 1999, Louisville Metro in 1999, Covington in 2003, Frankfort, Morehead and Vicco in 2013, Danville in 2014, Midway in 2015, Paducah and Maysville in 2018, Bellevue, Dayton, Georgetown, Henderson, Highland Heights and Versailles in 2019, and Cold Spring, Fort Thomas and Newport in 2020. Kentucky hate-crime law covers sexual orientation, enforced in the April 2011 beating of Kevin Pennington at Kingdom Come State Park near Cumberland that led to March 15, 2012 arrests by Kentucky State Police with the FBI of David, Anthony, Mable and Alexis Jenkins, with Mable and Alexis Jenkins pleading guilty after advocacy by the Kentucky Equality Federation. The 2013 Religious Freedom Act requires the state to show clear and convincing evidence to burden sincerely held religious beliefs, was vetoed by Governor Beshear over vagueness and risk of overriding local non-discrimination ordinances, and was enacted by override votes of 79-15 in the House and 32-6 in the Senate. Service-access limits include Senate Bill 17 signed by Governor Matt Bevin in March 2017 allowing religious student organizations use of school facilities and control of internal affairs cited as permitting sexual-orientation discrimination, and an August 2020 district court ruling that Christian photographer Chelsey Walker as a public business cannot be compelled to photograph same-sex weddings because photos are art and speech protected against compulsion and against her religious beliefs.

On June 2, 2008, Kentucky prohibited hiring or firing state employees based on sexual orientation or gender identity, restoring protections first issued in 2003 and removed in 2006 that had allowed dismissal simply for being gay or transgender.

On March 7, 2018, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit covering Kentucky held in EEOC v. R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits firing an employee for being transgender or transitioning because it penalizes failure to conform to birth-assigned sex stereotypes and necessarily takes sex into account, and that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act does not permit a private employer to fire a transgender worker on religious belief that sex is immutable God-given sex, after funeral director Aimee Stephens was fired in 2013 for disclosing her planned transition.

Contrast tier: worst-law states carry up to 5-year prison terms (Idaho) or arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use (Florida).

MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map (data as of 27 Sep 2026) lists New Mexico as 'State has shield law or executive order 2023': the shield/refuge law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care legal here was banned in the home state — directly relevant to visitors travelling from ban states. State law effective July 1, 2003 prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, later expanded by repeal of the 15-or-more-employees exemption effective July 1, 2019 and by 2023 legislation explicitly covering local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under emergency clause, with Albuquerque amending its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024 to align. Since November 1, 2019 transgender people may change legal gender without surgery under legislation repealing the 1984 surgery requirement and providing male, female and X neutral designation on birth certificates, driver's licenses and state IDs, passed 26-13 in the House and 33-14 in the Senate and signed by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham. Applicants need only submit a completed Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form with fees, with parental consent for minors, and a Request for Sex Designation Change form to the Motor Vehicles Division for licenses and IDs, replacing the prior requirement for a perjury statement from an institution or physician of surgical change plus certified name-change order. Since July 1, 2019 businesses and public facilities with single-occupancy restrooms must mark them gender-neutral available to any person regardless of gender identity or sex under legislation passed 54-12 in the House and 23-15 in the Senate and signed by the Governor. In March 2023 HB7 codified protection for gender-affirming care and sexual reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions even for interstate travellers, making New Mexico a sanctuary state for transgender youths, while HB31 repealed the requirement to publish a legal name change in a newspaper that risked privacy, safety and lives of transgender individuals, and in 2026 the health care authority announced use of state funds to maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a federal rule to exclude it. In February 2022 the Legislature passed omnibus crime bill HB68 repealing the common-law gay and trans panic defence, signed March 9, 2022, and there is no state law prohibiting transgender girls' sports participation with eligibility determined by birth certificate original or amended and no further guidance from the New Mexico Activities Association. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since repeal of the anti-sodomy law in 1975, with a 1986 attempt to reinstate it failing. Same-sex couples have had the same marriage rights as different-sex couples since the December 19, 2013 state Supreme Court ruling requiring equal marriage rights, making New Mexico the 17th state to recognize same-sex marriage, with benefits for same-sex partners of state employees since 2003 and statutory codification passed 62-0 in the House and 39-0 in the Senate in March 2019, signed in April by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham effective July 1, 2019. Single persons, same-sex couples and second-parent adoptions are permitted with no prohibition, lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilization and donor insemination regardless of sexual orientation or marital status with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized as legal parent, and no statute or case law prohibits gestational or traditional surrogacy which courts generally recognize. State law effective July 1, 2003 prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, supplemented by a 1985 executive order barring sexual-orientation discrimination in public employment, with enforcement upheld unanimously in Elane Photography v. Willock in 2013 for refusal to photograph a same-sex commitment ceremony. Since 2003 hate-crime law explicitly covers violence based on actual or perceived sexual orientation, and March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students on the basis of sexual orientation effective July 1, 2019. Sexual orientation change efforts on minors are prohibited under SB121 passed 32-6 in the Senate and 44-23 in the House, signed April 7, 2017 by Governor Susana Martinez effective July 6, 2017. The common-law gay panic defence was repealed through omnibus crime bill HB68 passed in February 2022 and signed March 9, 2022 after unanimous Senate-only passages in 2019 and 2021 that died without House action. Historically the Navajo recognized four gender roles including nadleehi defined as a male-bodied person with a feminine nature, who due to perceived balance between sexes were typically chosen for certain societal and communal roles such as spiritual healers. They would traditionally wear female clothes and do female work, and some would have sexual relations with men which was accepted by the tribe, with similar recognized roles including Zuni lhamana and katsotse and equivalents among Mescalero Apache, Tiwa, Tewa and pueblos. As a result of colonization much of this cultural acceptance has disappeared, Navajo nadleehi became the subject of ridicule, and Christian converts among the Hopi were prohibited from attending the traditional snake dance because male cross-dressing could be observed. Will Roscoe is documented as writing about the "tolerance or even respect of transgender people" as fueling Spanish explorers' argument for colonization of native peoples and their lands in the name of Christianity. Today LGBTQ Navajo may find it difficult being accepted by family, with 70% of LGBT Navajo youth reportedly attempting suicide. Statewide polling showed 73% supported anti-discrimination legislation protecting LGBTQ people in 2018 and 64% supported a law covering sexual orientation and gender identity in 2017, while Santa Fe is cited as a gay capital and Albuquerque including its metropolitan area as a gay-friendly city.

texts.cleaned_text: Erin In The Morning's February 2026 'Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map' places Indiana among the harshest anti-trans states in the country, citing the state's 2026 ID policy and bathroom-ban escalation as drivers of adult risk.

Indiana residents lost the option to change their gender marker on driver's licenses or other identification cards when the Bureau of Motor Vehicles' new ban took effect on Feb. 1, 2026, ending the long-standing route of obtaining such a change through a court-ordered gender change or physician statement. The ban culminates an administrative rule change the BMV initiated; LGBTQ advocates who testified warned it will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents. Pending Indiana Senate Bill 182 would create legal definitions for sex and gender, ban amendments to birth certificates, restrict bathrooms in public schools and restrict housing in prisons.

On Jan. 27, 2026, Indiana Senate Republicans approved Senate Bill 182 by a 37-8 party-line vote and sent it to the House; the bill would require public K-12 schools and state universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females based on their reproductive biology at birth, barring transgender students from facilities matching their gender identity. Author Sen. Liz Brown, R-Fort Wayne, said the proposal lets women 'continue to have their private spaces'; opponents including GenderNexus argued that letting anyone 'directly or indirectly injured' sue a school over an alleged violation would encourage harassment-style enforcement.

One case involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation allowed her school to restrict her bathroom access.

Transgender persons could change legal gender on Indiana birth certificates with a court order from 2014 until 2025, when Governor Mike Braun's March 2025 executive order defining sex solely as assigned sex at birth directed the Department of Health to stop updating gender markers, a policy extended by the Bureau of Motor Vehicles in February 2026 to prohibit gender-marker changes on driver's licenses despite pushback and challenged by an ACLU lawsuit. An "X" marker is no longer offered, having only been available from March 2019 to January 2020 upon presentation of an amended birth certificate or physician's statement confirming permanent gender change before rejection after public hearing and a March 2020 Attorney General opinion that only the General Assembly could authorize non-binary designations. As of April 2026 state law imposes no restriction on transgender people using restrooms aligned with gender identity, with Indianapolis and Bloomington ordinances expressly protecting such use, while repeated criminal-ban proposals since 2021 died in committee and an August 2023 Seventh Circuit decision upheld a preliminary injunction barring schools from limiting transgender students' bathroom use pending litigation. A 2026 Senate Bill 182 to define gender as sex assigned at birth, permanently ban birth-certificate changes, bar placement in prisons misaligned with birth sex, and restrict school and university bathrooms and sleeping facilities passed the Senate but received no House hearing. Senate Bill 480 passed March 2023 and signed April 2023 by Governor Eric Holcomb under emergency clause prohibits physicians from providing gender transition procedures to persons under 18 or aiding such care, with a phase-out for existing patients, temporarily enjoined June 16, 2023 but effective February 27, 2024 after stay and upheld November 2024 to ban surgery, puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors. House Bill 1569 signed April 2023 effective July 1, 2023 bans use of state or federal funds for sexual reassignment surgery for offender patients in prisons, exempting approvals before that date. House Bill 1608 signed May 2023 prohibits classroom instruction on human sexuality in kindergarten through third grade and compels schools to notify a parent in writing if a non-emancipated minor requests use of a different name, pronoun or title. Employment protection for state workers based on gender identity and expression rests on 2004 and 2005 executive orders rather than statute, supplemented by county and city ordinances in Marion, Monroe, Tippecanoe, Vanderburgh and numerous cities, an April 2015 RFRA clarification barring denial of services, facilities, goods, employment, housing or public accommodation based on gender identity, and an April 2019 hate-crimes law allowing enhanced sentences for crimes motivated by perceived or actual characteristics including gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized in 1976 effective July 1, 1977 with age of consent 16 after history including death penalty for sodomy and later 2-14 year penalties, and a 1977 House committee rejected 6-4 reinstating consensual sodomy as felony. Same-sex marriages have been recognized and performed since October 2014 when a federal district ruling declaring the ban unconstitutional took effect after the U.S. Supreme Court refused appeal in Baskin v. Bogan on October 6, 2014, ending annual amendment efforts since 2004. On April 4, 2017 the Seventh Circuit ruled 8-3 in Hively v. Ivy Tech that employment discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the prohibition on sex discrimination in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, binding in Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin, though Indiana statutes still omit sexual orientation as a protected category. State-level workplace protection rests on 2004 and 2005 executive orders covering state employees, while Marion, Monroe, Tippecanoe, Vanderburgh counties and many cities prohibit employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and Lake County, Fort Wayne and Whitestown do so on that basis alone. The March 26, 2015 Religious Freedom Restoration Act drew boycott threats and protests alleging targeting of LGBT rights and was clarified April 2, 2015 to provide that it does not authorize providers to refuse services, facilities, goods, employment, housing or public accommodation based on sexual orientation. Indiana tracked bias crimes including sexual-orientation bias since 2003 without sentencing enhancement until the April 3, 2019 hate-crimes law making intent to harm or intimidate based on perceived or actual characteristics an aggravating circumstance allowing harsher sentences for sexual-orientation-motivated crimes, also covered federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act. In May 2023 the governor signed a law barring city and county governments from enacting conversion-therapy bans by ordinance or executive order, effectively keeping the practice legal statewide.

Clayton County workplace discrimination based on gender identity is illegal under Title VII, though the article notes practice may continue because Oklahoma is at-will employment allowing firing without stated reason. State hate-crime law does not cover gender identity, but the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act signed October 2009 provides additional penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity prosecutable in federal court. Texas, although the legislature has not repealed its sodomy laws, which historically punished sodomy with up to one year then up to 10 years from 1890, were revised in 1997 to 2 years and/or $1,000 fine, and were replaced in 1999 with up to 20 years for same-sex sodomy before being invalidated. Kern declared it unconstitutional January 14, 2014 in Bishop v. United States, the Tenth Circuit upheld July 18, 2014, and the U.S. Supreme Court denied appeal October 6, 2014 prompting county clerks to issue licenses. State statutes do not prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, with only Norman covering private employment, housing and public accommodations and Edmond, Oklahoma City and Tulsa covering public employment, but Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15, 2020 made workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation illegal under Title VII, and state hate-crime law excludes sexual orientation while federal law since October 2009 allows federal prosecution with enhanced penalties. Oklahoma retains a no promo homo law forbidding promotion of homosexuality in schools and requiring HIV education to teach that not engaging in homosexual activity prevents HIV spread, passed a diversity-training ban in April 2021 signed by Stitt effective immediately, and saw 2021 Senate Bill 1141 proposed to let public-university students avoid courses addressing gender, sexual or racial diversity unless required for their major.

On August 1, 2023, Oklahoma Governor Kevin Stitt signed an executive order requiring state agencies to define female, woman, girl and mother as a person whose biological reproductive system is designed to produce ova and male, man, boy and father as a person whose biological reproductive system is designed to fertilize the ova of a female based on sex assigned at birth, restricting legal recognition of transgender people for state agency purposes including women's spaces.

texts.cleaned_text: Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, 'Ley para la protección de la salud y el bienestar de los menores de edad en Puerto Rico' (primary legal text, LexJuris). Article 4 — the operative prohibition — is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments altering the sex biology of a minor 'bajo el pretexto de una transición de género o como parte de un tratamiento de disforia de género'. The Article 3 definition of banned 'chemical and surgical mutilation' is drafted broader than the prohibition: it expressly includes 'el uso de bloqueadores de pubertad y hormonas sexuales (incluyendo bloqueadores androgénicos, estrógenos, progesterona o testosterona) utilizados con el propósito de tratar la disforia de género' — the USE itself of puberty blockers and sex hormones for gender-dysphoria treatment — and defines 'niño o menor de edad' as any person under 21. Article 6 then penalises 'toda persona que viole las disposiciones de esta Ley' with a fixed 15-year term, plus permanent licence loss for professionals and a $50,000 per-violation fine for juridical persons. Legal analysis of this drafting notes a structural tension: the definition speaks of patient 'use' while the operative clause restricts only providers, and the penalty catch-all says 'any person'. Under standard criminal doctrines (definitions create no offence by themselves; a protected class cannot be prosecuted as the perpetrator of its own victimisation; the principle of legality bars analogy; and travel with lawfully prescribed personal medication), a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own prescribed hormones — or of their parents for enabling it — would almost certainly fail, and the statute is a textbook void-for-vagueness candidate. But the textual ambiguity is precisely what legal advocates flag as its chilling effect: it leaves interpretive room for hostile officials to question, detain or investigate trans youth and their families on the ground, with the answer coming only after the fact. For a travelling under-21 trans person the practical reading is: carrying and using prescribed HRT in Puerto Rico sits inside the law's literal definition of banned practice, enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. The ACLU of Puerto Rico had urged a veto before signature, stating the bill 'criminalizes doctors and parents' and creates 'two distinct categories of children' divided by sex-assigned-at-birth identity, and the island's College of Physicians and Surgeons, Psychology Association, College of Social Work Professionals, Bar Association and LGBTQ+ Federation all registered opposition.

Road to marriage equality in PR ran through federal court.

For a trans visitor the ban closes off all gender-affirming care on the island for anyone under 21, and the deliberately vague facilitation language reaches the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager.

Executive Order 14168 (signed 20 January 2025) directs US federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognize only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order violates the Prison Rape Elimination Act's requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided on an individual safety assessment. Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico as a US territory. No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit, or ruling was located.

Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002, but after the U.S. Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down all state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for it, and threatened doctors who violate the ban with up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine, and permanent loss of their licenses; the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court. An anti-discrimination bill (House Bill 1725) passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, public transportation and public facilities, business transactions and housing, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities remain uncovered. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 bill was withdrawn by Rosselló on 13 June 2019 after House approval amid protests. Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the U.S. federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island. In 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488 (signed 29 May 2013) extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

The ACLU of Puerto Rico called on Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, 'which criminalizes doctors and parents and aims to prohibit gender-affirming medical treatments for individuals under the age of 21'. Policy Counsel Lolimar Escudero Rodríguez stated the bill 'creates two distinct categories of children: one that allows parents to access and authorize treatments if the child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth, and another that prohibits parents the same right if their child's identity is different'. The release records that the bill was authored by Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz and Senator Joanne Rodríguez Veve, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés that the ACLU warned 'do not remedy the violation of fundamental constitutional, civil, and human rights', and was re-approved and returned to the Governor on 28 June. It states the bill's 'text is clearly and exclusively aimed at minors whose identity does not correspond to the sex assigned to them at birth' and that it disregards the specialist consultation process that precedes parents authorising puberty blockers or hormonal treatments, 'and instead, criminalizes them'. Executive Director Annette Martínez Orabona: the measure 'directly discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth, whose very lives may be at risk'. The release lists local opposition from the Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico.

The ACLU of Puerto Rico opposed Senate Bill 350 'because of its direct impact on access to gender-affirming care for trans people, particularly trans youth and trans children, as well as on the rights of families and minors. The measure bans gender-affirming medical treatments for people under 21 years of age.'

AP reported that Puerto Rico's governor signed a bill prohibiting hormone therapy or gender-affirming surgeries for transgender youth, a move that 'has drawn sharp criticism from activists in the largely conservative U.S. territory'. The law applies to those younger than 21 and calls for 15 years in prison for violators, a $50,000 penalty, and revocation of the licences and permits of medical staff.
Amnesty International's Puerto Rico reporting records that 'In July, the government signed Law 63-2025, prohibiting gender-affirming health care for people under the age of 21.'

JURIST reported that Puerto Rico's LGBTQ+ Federation denounced the Law for the Protection of the Health and Wellbeing of Minors in Puerto Rico, which 'prohibits the use of puberty blockers, hormone treatment, and gender-affirming surgeries for anybody under the age of 21' and 'imposes a sentence of up to 15 years and a $50,000 fine on offenders'.

Since the law passed May 5, 2015, signed July 14, 2015 and effective immediately, transgender people may change the gender marker without sex reassignment surgery simply by request, with an updated birth certificate requiring a completed Application for Amendment to Birth Record and affidavit from a licensed physician and an updated driver's license or state ID requiring a Gender Designation Form completed by a medical or social professional confirming gender identity. An X sex option on driver's licenses and birth certificates was passed in May 2019, signed June 26, 2019 and effective July 1, 2020, with change by request and no medical documentation required. Health care provisions include insurance coverage of sex reassignment surgeries under the 2016 insurance nondiscrimination rule, mandatory coverage effective January 1, 2023, and inclusion of transgender individuals in health insurance planning under a bill passed May 2022 with emergency clause signed a month later effective immediately, replacing male- and female-only planning since 1980. The gay and trans panic defenses were abolished by a bill passed April 2019 through conference committee April 26, signed June 26, 2019 effective immediately, while anti-bullying law covering gender identity and expression including cyberbullying in public elementary and secondary schools and a July 2018 Title IX law effective January 1, 2019 ensure students are not denied programs or extracurricular activities because of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the beginning of 1973 following repeal in April 1972 with sex offences revised in 1986, replacing the 1850 anti-sodomy statute that punished both heterosexual and homosexual consensual adult conduct with up to 20 years' hard labor and a $1,000 fine and was last enforced in the 1958 case Territory v. Bell. The age of consent was lowered to 14 in 1986 regardless of gender or sexual orientation and raised to 16 in 2001. Same-sex couples have been allowed to marry since the Hawaii Marriage Equality Act passed the Senate 20-4 on October 30, 2013, the House 30-19 on November 8, 2013 and final Senate approval 19-4 on November 12, signed November 13 with marriages beginning December 2, 2013, following the May 1993 Hawaii Supreme Court finding of unconstitutional restriction, a 1994 statutory ban, November 1998 Constitutional Amendment 2 passed with 70 percent to allow legislative ban leading to dismissal, and repeal by November 5, 2024 referendum with 55.9 percent. Reciprocal beneficiary relationships for same- and opposite-sex couples were established in 1997, a civil union law vetoed in 2010 was signed February 23, 2011 effective January 1, 2012, and benefits to same-sex partners of state employees have been provided since 1997. Adoption is allowed for same-sex couples, lesbian couples can access IVF and artificial insemination with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized if married, surrogacy is legal with courts ruling for gay male gestational surrogacy, HB1096 passed April 2021 and signed July 2021 recognized unmarried same-sex parentage effective immediately, and Act 298 effective January 1, 2026 implements gender-neutral parentage by voluntary acknowledgment or court adjudication. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited in employment since 1991 and in housing since 2005 and public accommodations since 2006, hate-crime law covers actual and/or perceived sexual orientation defined as heterosexuality, homosexuality or bisexuality including history or identification, and conversion therapy on minors has been banned since July 1, 2018 after House and Senate passage in April 2018 and conference agreement in May 2018 signed by Governor David Ige. The gay panic defense was abolished with the trans panic defense in 2019 effective immediately, and 2023 FDA rules permit gay and bi men to donate blood on condition of being monogamous.

Hawaii's 1998 constitutional provision authorizing the legislature to reserve marriage to opposite-sex couples was replaced by the 2013 Hawaii Marriage Equality Act allowing same-sex marriage and was repealed by voter approval on November 5, 2024 with 55.94% voting yes to delete Article I Section 23's opposite-sex limitation, leaving marriage not restricted to opposite-sex couples under the state constitution while state law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender and gender identity and provides a 2022-established LGBTQ+ Commission on equal treatment.

texts.cleaned_text: Korea Times report (28 April 2024) on the Seoul Metropolitan Council's abolition of the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance twelve years after the Seoul office adopted it: the ordinance model was 'first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province'; abolition was pushed by the ruling People Power Party council after an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to its sexual-orientation clause; six regional education offices - Gyeonggi, Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju - still enforced comparable ordinances at publication; the (Seoul) superintendent began a sit-in protest against the abolition, and the opposition-led National Assembly said it would legislate a national student-rights act regardless of regional decisions. A quoted Gyeonggi-based teacher defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition.

Gyeonggi-do Province enacted South Korea's first student human rights ordinance in 2010, and that ordinance includes non-discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, the provisions most disputed in the 2024-26 repeal wave. Gyeonggi-do and Seoul are the only two jurisdictions whose ordinances include the right not to be discriminated against on the basis of pregnancy. In Gyeonggi-do the Superintendent of Public Instruction conducts an annual survey on student human rights, and the province marks a Student Human Rights Day.

BBC News, 12 January 2010: Italy announced plans for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons at Pozzale, near Florence, converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison into a specially equipped detention centre for about 30 of Italy's roughly 60 transgender prisoners, mostly convicted of drug or prostitution offences. Gay-rights groups welcomed the dedicated space and its psychological support. Before then transgender prisoners had been held in women's prisons, 'where they are often segregated for their own safety', which established the 2010 placement practice in Italy. Repubblica reported in 2013 that the Pozzale project was abandoned.

La Repubblica investigative report 'La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere', 28 August 2013: the prison administration counted 69 transsexual prisoners across ten Italian facilities. Placement tracked legal sex, so female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who 'according to their identity card, count as men'. Trans women were held in men's sections, and those who had already undergone sex-change surgery were 'destined for the women's sections'. In some prisons trans prisoners were put in isolation when cells were lacking, described as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety. Protected sections such as the G8 section at Rebibbia in Rome and the protected section at Poggioreale in Naples imposed limitations, including on partner visits. In the 2011 Terni case the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for the prisoner's hormone therapy 'to guarantee psychophysical integrity'; the ruling was appealed and a July 2012 appellate decision followed. The Pozzale transgender prison project of 2008-2010, which would have drawn trans women from the special wing of Sollicciano in Florence, was shelved.

The state government says it is reviewing the recommendations, and local advocacy groups will press for their implementation.

Victoria legally recognizes gender transition, with birth certificates issued by the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages and driver licences carrying no recorded gender marker while marriage and passports remain Commonwealth matters, and since November 2025 updated regulations removed all fees and costs for applications to change sex on a birth certificate. Past law required a person be unmarried and undergo sexual reassignment surgery to change recorded sex; the unmarried requirement was due to lapse in December 2018 after federal same-sex marriage legalisation in 2017 but was removed early by Parliament in May 2018, while an August 2016 Andrews Government bill to remove both the unmarried and surgery requirements and allow parents to alter a child's gender descriptor with the child's informed consent failed. Gender identity has been a prohibited discrimination ground since 2000 under the Equal Opportunity (Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation) Act 2000 amending the Equal Opportunity Act 1995, retained in the replacement Equal Opportunity Act 2010, with sex characteristics added effective 2021, and the Justice Legislation Amendment (Police and Other Matters) Bill 2022 passed in September 2022 extended protection to on-duty Victoria Police officers on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds. Exemptions in the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 still allow religious organisations such as adoption/fostering agencies and charities that do not receive government funding to discriminate against and reject LGBT employees and clients, though the Equal Opportunity (Religious Exceptions) Amendment Bill 2021 passed December 2021 and effective 15 June 2022 bars religious schools and organisations from discriminating against employees because of sexual orientation, gender identity or marital status and bars government-funded bodies refusing services on those grounds except where conformity with doctrine is an inherent requirement such as hiring a religious studies teacher. Vilification based on gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation was criminalised by the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-vilification and Social Cohesion) Bill passed March/April 2025, assented 8 April 2025 and effective 30 June 2026, with maximum 5 years imprisonment and political, religious and academic exemptions plus a Sam Kerr clause, amid reported funding cuts risking backlog at the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission established in 1975. Conversion practices are prohibited under the Change or Suppression (Conversion) Practices Prohibition Bill passed by the lower house 55-0 in December 2020 and the Legislative Council 27-9 on 5 February 2021 with penalties up to approximately $200,000 AUD or up to 10 years jail effective February 2022 one year after royal assent, preceded by the Health Complaints Act from the Health Complaints Bill 2016 effective 1 February 2017 empowering the Health Complaints Commissioner to issue warnings and temporary or permanent bans following a May 2018 investigation. Victoria is the only state with an LGBTIQA+ Commissioner, with inaugural Gender and Sexuality Commissioner Ro Allen appointed July 2015 to streamline federal and state laws to align passports and birth certificates with affirmed gender and strengthen workplace protections for transgender workers, later renamed Commissioner for LGBTIQ+ Communities, and in August 2024 the Supreme Court of Victoria upheld allowing puberty blockers for transgender children with stress and anxiety. Buggery was a crime in Victoria from 1958 until December 1980 when the Hamer Liberal government repeal passed 72-7 effective March 1981, with the death penalty on the books for sodomy until 1949, an equal age of consent set at 18 then lowered to 16 by the Crimes (Sexual Offences) Act 1991, and a loosely worded soliciting for immoral purposes clause enabling continued police harassment of homosexual men until the late 1980s including entrapment mass arrests at Black Rock Beach reported in 1976. Any remaining legislation banning sex between consenting adults in private was removed by royal assent effective 1 March 2022 and in effect by May 2022. Intentional HIV transmission singled out under Crimes Act Section 19A with up to 25 years imprisonment compared to 20 years maximum for manslaughter was repealed by the Crimes Amendment (Repeal of Section 19A) Act 2015 passed 28 May 2015, assented 2 June 2015 and effective immediately with conduct now dealt with as causing serious injury, while an April 2022 Act repealed all HIV legislation on mandatory public health notifications, blood donations and human tissue services effective 15 February 2023. Victoria was the first state to create an expungement scheme for historical homosexual offences no longer criminal, passed 15 October 2014 and effective 1 September 2015 allowing the individual or representative of a deceased person to apply to the Secretary of the Department of Justice and Regulation, after which the person may lawfully claim not to have been convicted and the conviction does not appear on a police records check avoiding travel and employment restrictions, followed by a formal parliamentary apology on 24 May 2016. texts.cleaned_text: The equality timeline for Tasmania is dated precisely. After the Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994, Tasmania still refused to repeal its anti-gay Criminal Code provisions and, faced with a likely High Court loss in Croome v Tasmania, decriminalised male homosexuality with effect from 14 May 1997, the final Australian jurisdiction to do so. The age of consent in Tasmania is 17, shared only with South Australia. Same-sex couples can enter registered domestic partnerships in Tasmania with an optional official ceremony. Equality of adoption rights for same-sex couples applied in all states and territories from April 2018. As of 2019 Tasmania issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates.

texts.cleaned_text: ABC News reported on 11 April 2019 that Tasmania's House of Assembly passed the Marriage Amendments Bill the previous day, 10 April 2019, after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition; the legislation had already passed the Legislative Council. The reforms make gender on birth certificates optional, remove the requirement that transgender people undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised, and let people aged 16 or older change their registered gender without parental approval. The Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out later repeal.

Cross-dressing was an offence under the Police Offences Act 1935 until repealed in 2001, with Tasmania described as the only Australian state to have criminalised cross-dressing. Convictions for cross-dressing prior to 2001 and homosexual sexual offences prior to 1997 are eligible for expungement under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017 effective 9 April 2018 and for up to $75,000 compensation payments effective 2 August 2026. Legal gender change is governed by 2019 amendments to the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1999 receiving royal assent 8 May 2019 and taking effect 5 September 2019, requiring only a simple declaration with no forced divorce, sex reassignment surgery or other medical requirement. The same laws allow parents to choose whether a child's gender is recorded, allow individuals to remove a gender descriptor entirely, lower the age to change legal gender without parental permission to sixteen, allow parents to change the legal gender of their children, and extend the registration period for parents of intersex children to 120 days after birth. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 (Tas) prohibits discrimination on gender identity and was amended in September 2013 to extend protections to transgender and intersex people and to prohibit offending, humiliating, intimidating, insulting or ridiculing on the basis of actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation and/or gender identity, with state law also updated to incorporate gender expression. A hate crimes bill passed the lower house in September 2025 that explicitly includes gender identity within the 1997 sentencing act, with the upper house yet to vote. Consensual homosexual activity was decriminalised by the Criminal Code Amendment Act 1997 passed 1 May 1997 with royal assent 13 May 1997 and effect the next day, after penalties of up to 21 years described as the harshest in the Western world and following the United Nations Human Rights Committee decision in Toonen on 31 March 1994 and the federal Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 section 4 legalising adult consensual sexual activity in private nationally. The age of consent in Tasmania is 17 years and is equal for all forms of sexual activity. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 (Tas) prohibits discrimination on lawful sexual activity and actual or perceived sexual orientation, amended in September 2013 to prohibit offending, humiliating, intimidating, insulting or ridiculing on that basis, with additional federal protection under the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013. A hate crimes bill passed the lower house in September 2025 explicitly includes sexual orientation within the 1997 sentencing act, with the upper house yet to vote. As of September 2026 conversion therapy practices remain legally permitted within Tasmania. Historic convictions for consensual homosexual activity prior to 1997 are eligible for expungement from 9 April 2018 under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017 and for up to $75,000 compensation effective 2 August 2026, following an official parliamentary apology on 13 April 2017.

In Tasmania since Royal Assent on 21 November 2017, charges and convictions for cross-dressing offences under section 8(1)(d) of the Police Offences Act 1935 as in force before 12 April 2001, including attempts and inciting/instigating/aiding/abetting, are eligible for expungement on application to the Secretary by the charged person or, if deceased or lacking capacity, by specified representatives.

From 8 May 2019 Tasmania permits self-declared gender registration for Tasmanian-registered births with no medical certificate or medical document required, allowing persons aged 16+ to register male, female, indeterminate gender, non-binary or other self-described neither-entirely-male-nor-female gender via statutory gender declaration of identity and lived/seeking-to-live gender subject to Registrar refusal power for non-prescribed terms, allowing parents/guardians to register a gender for under-16s supported by the child's gender declaration where able or statements of consistency with will and preference plus optional counselling evidence where under 18, while birth sex registration remains male-or-female only and unchangeable except to correct initial error but ceases upon gender registration, and expands Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 protections to gender expression, gender identity including being transgender/transsexual and identifying/living as another gender, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics including as a ground for incitement-of-hatred prohibition.

texts.cleaned_text: News reporting (11 April 2019): the lower chamber of the legislature of this state/province passed the marriage amendments bill the previous day (10 April 2019) after the presiding officer of the elected chamber crossed the floor to vote with the opposition, the legislation having already passed the upper chamber. The reforms make gender on birth certificates optional, remove the requirement that transgender people undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised, and let people aged 16 or older change their registered gender without parental approval, with the administration having opposed the amendments and declining to rule out later repeal.

The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) protects the attribute 'gender history', defined as living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex. Complaint eligibility is tied to recognition certificates or a registry change under the Births, Deaths and Marriages framework.

WA Government guidance (first published 6 Aug 2020, last updated 12 Feb 2026): gender history is a protected attribute under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) — a person has gender history if they identify as a member of the opposite sex by living or seeking to live as such; direct discrimination (including treating a person as their former sex) and indirect discrimination are unlawful.

On 16 April 2024, WA Premier Roger Cook and Attorney-General John Quigley announced that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Bill 2024 would be introduced to State Parliament that week. The Bill repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishes the Gender Reassignment Board, which the ministers describe as the only remaining board of its kind in Australia, replacing it with a streamlined administrative process through the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages. Applicants would no longer need medical or surgical reassignment, providing instead a statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling. A 'non-binary' sex descriptor would become available, stricter rules would apply to under-18s through parental consent or Family Court of WA permission, and the Bill contains a statutory review clause after three years. The announcement implements the WA Law Reform Commission's 2018 recommendations and links the reform to a planned new Equal Opportunity Act and a conversion-practices ban in 2025. The 2024 Act removes medical and surgical prerequisites for registering a sex or gender change in Western Australia.

The WA Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet states that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 (WA), passed with commencement still to be proclaimed, amends section 4(1) of the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) by deleting the definition of 'gender reassigned person' and inserting a new definition tied to recognition certificates under the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 or registration of sex or gender under the amended regime. The amendment will not operate retrospectively. Gender history discrimination complaints under the Equal Opportunity Act will need to be made in compliance with the new registration requirements once the Act commences. The Act also repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and the Gender Reassignment Regulations 2001. The 2024 reform feeds back into the scope of WA's 'gender history' attribute for complaints purposes, and substantive commencement is by proclamation.

Justice Connect's WA-specific resource, dated 16 April 2026, states that a discrimination complaint in Western Australia can be made to the WA Commissioner of Equal Opportunity under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA), with a 12-month lodgement window, acknowledgment of receipt within one week, and a free conciliation conference as the next step. A federal route is also available: a complaint to the Australian Human Rights Commission under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) within 24 months, or 12 months for employment matters. Only one route, state or federal, can be chosen. TransFolk of WA and the Freedom Centre provide trans-specific support in WA, the latter for under-26s. The state-level protective attribute in WA is 'gender history' rather than 'gender identity', and state complaints run through the Equal Opportunity Commission.

Western Australian law recognises a transgender person's change of sex, with sterilisation required before 2012 until the High Court in AB v Western Australia (2012) held two transgender men who had undergone mastectomies and hormone treatment did not need sterilisation to obtain a gender recognition certificate. Legislation introduced in August 2018 repealed the requirement to be unmarried for a change of sex on a birth certificate, passing the lower house on 20 November 2018 and the upper house on 12 February 2019, receiving royal assent on 19 February 2019 and commencing on 19 March 2019. The Births, Deaths, Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 passed both chambers in September 2024 to formally abolish and repeal the WA Gender Reassignment Board, receiving assent on 26 September 2024 and taking effect on 30 May 2025. That Act permits male, female, indeterminate/intersex and nonbinary options and allows change of sex on a birth certificate once a year on appropriate clinical treatment signed off by a doctor, nurse or psychologist with no sexual reassignment surgery required, subject to a $195 non-refundable fee and up to 4 weeks waiting. Reported November 2020 policy allows transgender prisoners to be housed according to their own gender identity for strict health and safety reasons so long as they have no sexual offences on their criminal record. In October 2021 a Western Australia Supreme Court order in an Australian legal first removed custody entirely from a family for continuing abuse of their transgender child, following the April 2021 suicide of a 15-year-old transgender teenager in Perth that prompted calls to immediately reform archaic birth-certificate sex or gender legislation. For protection, transgender Western Australians are currently classified as Gender History under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 and Gender Reassignment Act 2000 only if reassigned gender as certified, providing technically less protection than sexual orientation, with announced reforms to add gender identity and sex characteristics, repeal the exemption allowing discrimination by religious schools, and a 2026 Public Order Bill to criminally ban harassment based on gender identity still passed only in the lower house, while no law currently bans conversion therapy. Private same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Law Reform (Decriminalisation of Sodomy) Act 1989 effective 23 March 1990, but the Act set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual male acts versus 16 for heterosexual acts and created offences of promoting or encouraging homosexual behaviour in primary or secondary teaching or public policy. Equal age of consent at 16 and repeal of the promotion offences came via the Acts Amendment (Gay and Lesbian Law Reform) Act 2002. Historical homosexual convictions became expungeable under the Historical Homosexual Convictions Expungement Bill 2017, passed by the Assembly on 22 February 2018 and the Council with amendments on 23 August 2018, approved on 11 September 2018, assented on 18 September 2018 and effective 15 October 2018, requiring a mandatory test of historical homosexual offence considering consent and ages and allowing family members of deceased persons to apply, accompanied by the Premier's formal parliamentary apology to the LGBTIQ community. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2002 to prohibit sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, education, accommodation and provision of goods, services and facilities, supplemented federally by the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013. No law in Western Australia currently bans conversion therapy, with the government stating a bill would only be introduced after the March 2025 state election, leaving WA as the only mainland state to legally allow the practices and, as of September 2026 with Tasmania, the only Australian places without explicit criminal prohibition. A 2026 Public Order Bill to explicitly criminally ban harassment based on sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics passed the lower house but had yet to pass the upper house.

On 6 October 2011 the High Court of Australia held under the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 (WA) that female-to-male persons who had bilateral mastectomies and androgen therapy and lived as men were entitled to recognition certificates as male without hysterectomy, oophorectomy or genital reconstructive surgery, establishing that Western Australia permits legal gender change without sterilisation or genital surgery.

Western Australia assented on 26 September 2024 to the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 (Act No. 031 of 2024) amending births, deaths and marriages registration law on sex or gender changes.
In November 2020 Western Australia improved its prison policies for transgender inmates.

Government guidance (first published 6 August 2020, last updated 12 February 2026): gender history is a protected attribute — a person has it if they identify as a member of the opposite sex by living or seeking to live as such; direct discrimination (including treating a person as their former sex) and indirect discrimination are unlawful.

Government announcement (16 April 2024): the registration amendment bill was to be introduced that week, repealing the older reassignment statute, abolishing the state/province reassignment board — described as the last such board in the country — and favouring a streamlined administrative process; applicants would no longer need medical or surgical reassignment, a non-binary sex descriptor would become available, stricter rules would apply to under-18s, and a statutory review clause would follow after three years.

Equal-opportunity commission factsheet: the recently passed registration amendment, with commencement still to be proclaimed, amends the equal-opportunity statute by deleting the former definition and inserting a new one tied to recognition certificates or registration under the amended regime; it will not operate retrospectively, and 'gender history' complaints will need to comply with the new registration requirements once commencement occurs.

Legal resource (last updated 16 April 2026): a complaint can be made to the state/province equal-opportunity commission under the equal-opportunity statute with a 12-month lodgement window, a one-week acknowledgement and a free conciliation conference; the alternative route is a complaint to the national human-rights commission under the sex-discrimination statute within 24 months (12 months for employment), choosing only one route. It also records the existence of local trans-specific support groups.

texts.cleaned_text: Nunatsiaq News reports (22 March 2022) that Nunavut's Health Department began funding transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents - breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty are named - under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal; local LGBTQ group Positive Space called the move overdue while flagging information gaps for residents outside the capital.

Nunatsiaq News, 13 March 2017: Nunavut MLAs voted unanimously on third and final reading of Bill 31 amending the territory's Human Rights Act, adding 'gender identity' and 'gender expression' alongside sexual orientation as protected grounds. Justice Minister Keith Peterson said the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. The article notes that at the time nine provinces and one territory listed gender identity or expression in their human-rights laws, making Nunavut the first Canadian territory to do so.

As of 2017, all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground of discrimination in their human rights acts, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations. The Supreme Court has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15(1) of the Charter to include transsexuality, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions in Canada including law enforcement authorities. Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause, with controversy over its requirement that schools obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request the use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, but the government shielded them by passing Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm, institutional bias and rights violations toward Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against transphobia and other marginalization, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69 (Bill C-150) was brought into force upon royal assent. Since June 2019 the general age of consent for all sexual activities has been 16, with age 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency and close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15, after former section 159 criminalizing anal intercourse was repealed by Bill C-75 receiving royal assent on June 21, 2019. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the equality clause of the Charter as an analogous ground under section 15, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 it found failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law itself violated section 15. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide on July 20, 2005 with the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to legalize it, following court rulings between 2002 and 2005, while same-sex adoption was legalized in all provinces and territories with Nunavut last in 2011. In 2022 Canada statutorily banned conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and made it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined in the Criminal Code, the third country in the world and first in North America to do so. On June 21, 2018 royal assent was granted to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allowing the RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records of pre-1969 homosexual convictions and section 159 convictions, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from a pardon or record suspension, following the Prime Minister’s formal apology on November 28, 2017. On sexuality-specific tolerance, 2020 Pew Research showed that 85% of Canada’s general population (92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29) favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessing same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing that “same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt children as heterosexual couples do” and 76% agreeing that “same-sex couples are just as likely as other parents to successfully raise children”. Canada was referred to as the most gay-friendly country when ranked first for least dangerous in Asher & Lyric’s LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024. The largest cities feature gay areas including Toronto’s Church and Wellesley, Montreal’s Gay Village, Vancouver’s Davie Village and Ottawa’s Bank Street Gay Village, with Pride celebrated every summer in major cities with federal, provincial and municipal political figures. Distinct from sexuality tolerance, on transgender-specific tolerance the article documents that “87.6% said they would be ‘comfortable’ if a neighbour was a transgender person” in a 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office, compared to 91.8% saying they would be “comfortable” if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual.

Assented 2019-06-21, S.C. 2019, c. 25 repealed Criminal Code section 159 criminalizing anal intercourse and barred conviction for any historical sexual offence unless the act would constitute an offence if committed on the day the charge was laid, eliminating criminal liability in Nunavut for consensual conduct previously captured by the repealed provision.

Charter equality protections apply to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement but not directly against the private sector, are subject to reasonable limits under section 1 under the Oakes Test and to section 33's notwithstanding clause, which has never been used by the federal Parliament. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is prohibited by all provinces and territories as well as the federal government, explicitly listed as a prohibited ground in all human rights acts as of 2017. Section 15(1) Charter equality concepts of sex and physical disability have been interpreted to include transsexuality and HIV/STDs, applying to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, while claims against private businesses proceed under applicable federal or provincial human rights statutes interpreted consistently with Charter values. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories, which therefore includes Yukon, under varying rules, with vital statistics and identity documents such as birth certificates falling under provincial and territorial jurisdiction. Saskatchewan's Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of gender-related preferred name or gender identity and was passed while invoking the Charter section 33 notwithstanding clause. Alberta's 2024 Health Statutes Amendment Act, Education Amendment Act, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act were met with legal challenges in Alberta courts but shielded by Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, which used the notwithstanding clause. Canada in 2022 became the third country and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults, making it a crime under the Criminal Code to subject anyone to it, and in December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for institutional bias and pledged to stand against transphobia through an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee. Since June 2019 the general age of consent for all sexual activities is 16, rising to 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency or an exploitative relationship, with limited close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15, and former Criminal Code section 159 on anal intercourse was repealed by Bill C-75 receiving royal assent June 21, 2019. In Egan v Canada (1995) the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under section 15 Charter equality as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law itself violated section 15, with all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly including sexual orientation as of 2017. Canada became the fourth country and first in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage nationwide on July 20, 2005 through the federal Civil Marriage Act, following 2002-2005 provincial and territorial court rulings and a December 2004 Supreme Court reference, as the first country to do so without a residency requirement. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is prohibited by all provinces, territories and the federal government, and adoption by same-sex couples was legalized in Yukon in 2003 as part of nationwide legalization completed in all jurisdictions by Nunavut in 2011. On June 21, 2018 royal assent to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allows persons convicted of certain homosexual acts before 1969 legality or anal intercourse under repealed section 159 to have the RCMP and federal departments destroy or remove judicial records, with provincial and municipal police and courts notified, available to living and deceased and distinct from pardon or record suspension, following the November 28, 2017 prime ministerial apology. In a 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office, "87.6% said they would be 'comfortable' if a neighbour was a transgender person." In the same poll, 91.8% said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, providing a direct comparison point. The article records that many transgender people in traditional Indigenous roles were in positions of reverence, acting as caretakers of children who had lost families, spiritual healers and warriors in battle, with distinct terms such as Cree napew iskwewisêhot and iskwew ka napewayat, Ktunaxa titqattek, Blackfoot aakii'skassi, Inuit sipiniq, and Ojibwe ikwekaazo and ininiikaazo, among others. It states those traditions declined after colonisation and spread of Christianity with forced assimilation to Europe-centric culture, and that in the early 1990s Indigenous LGBTQ groups proposed "two-spirit" to reclaim a traditional cultural "third gender," now frequently used with 2S included in LGBT2S and LGBTQ2S designations. It records the December 2020 Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apology acknowledging contribution to institutional bias, intolerance, personal suffering, shame, trauma and distrust toward Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities and stating the need to stand together against homophobia, transphobia and other marginalization.

It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.
