It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior.

Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). As of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

USA TODAY (7 Mar 2025): Trump executive order requires all US identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; ACLU sued the State Department for seven plaintiffs; trans/nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad.

Lambda Legal's FAQ sets out passport and identity-document rules for TGNCNBI people under the current federal policy change: which documents to consider, how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the current status of document updates.

HRC (updated 2025): since Jan 2025 executive order, new/renewed US passports show sex assigned at birth regardless of gender identity or name change; the 'X' marker (available since 2022) eliminated; policy challenged in federal courts -- current passport posture for trans US travelers.

Condé Nast Traveler (Feb 2025) reports that the State Department stopped processing X-marker passports and markers not matching sex assigned at birth; existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration; new applications are processed only as M or F per supporting documents.

ILGA monitor items: (Sep 2023) the US Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee; (Jun 2023) a federal civil action cited a 'hostile work environment' in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity; (Feb 2023) a 51-year-old man charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Federal measures reaching US territories through federal agencies in 2025: EO 14168 (binary sex, documents, federal facilities, care funding), EO 14187 (care funding), EO 14201 (sports; State Dept visa ban with SWS25 marking).

The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates should only be altered to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption. The Office of Vital Statistics has interpreted this ruling to cover applications from transgender individuals. The Office will change the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order. The Office may change the gender marker on a birth certificate with medical documentation of the sex change. The first criminal law against sodomy was enacted in 1963 and made male homosexual and heterosexual sodomy illegal, but did not address lesbian sex. In 1979 the Fono revised criminal law so that consensual sodomy was no longer illegal unless it involved public acts, prostitution, minors or people unable to give consent due to mental illness, with the law taking effect in 1980. The age of consent is set at 16 years, regardless of gender and/or sexual orientation. The American Samoa Code does not specify the sex of the parties to a marriage but refers to the age of "the male" and "the female" and prescribes a form in which parties identify as "son" and as "daughter," and a 2003 bill to ban same-sex marriage was voted against by the House Judiciary Committee and then the full Senate. Same-sex marriages are currently not licensed in American Samoa, with the Attorney General in July 2015 reviewing applicability of Obergefell v. Hodges and the Governor stating the ruling does not apply due to preamble, constitution, Christian values and unorganized and unincorporated political status. Under the Respect for Marriage Act passed by the 117th United States Congress and signed by President Joe Biden in 2022, all territories including American Samoa are required to recognize, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples. The article states American Samoa remains the only part of the United States along with select Native American tribal jurisdictions to enforce a ban on same-sex couples marrying, while same-sex couples married legally in other jurisdictions are recognized and must be treated equally under US federal law since 13 December 2022. The article states "American Samoa, like the neighboring country of Samoa, tends to be tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities." It notes a long-standing tradition of raising some boys as girls to play an important domestic role in Samoan communal life, with such individuals known as the fa'afafine. It states nevertheless American Samoan society is highly religious and conservative attitudes regarding gender and sexuality tend to dominate. It states open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. The main LGBTQ organization is the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (S.O.F.I.A.S.) which annually organizes events and festivals and campaigns for the betterment of the fa'afafine community. The first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei with pageant, song, dance and poetry choral competitions, beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community are quite popular, and families generally turn up en masse to support candidates.

On 20 March 2003 the American Samoa Senate rejected Representative Sua Carl Schuster's bill to outlaw same-sex marriage after the House judiciary committee recommended it be killed, with fa'afine witness Tiffany Poutasi testifying that fa'afine are men who express femininity through dress and speech and oppose marriage with other men as against Christian upbringing.

As of July 10, 2015, American Samoa had not authorized same-sex marriage and no same-sex marriage license applications had been filed while Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale reviewed the U.S. Supreme Court marriage-equality ruling for applicability to the territory, which maintained a tradition of embracing faafafine — males raised as females taking on feminine traits — alongside dominant conservative Christian churches.

Academic research guide on regional gender identities (maintained; last updated 2026-07-23): records an established local third-gender society, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride; defines the role as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional culture'; historic suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming.

Travel column (2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about this state/province: the two neighbouring nations share the chiefly family system; tens of thousands of residents; 'culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected'; homosexuality a widely accepted part of the local culture, unlike the hostility recorded in one neighbouring nation; indigenous third-gender locals reportedly court Western gay men; a local artist calls the place a homeland of third-gender culture; hotels skew business-travel.

I don't know', while other parts of the same parent nation moved to apply it. Tens of thousands of residents, conservative religious society; third-gender tradition noted; a prominent figure says many traditional-role advocates don't push marriage out of respect for culture/religion, yet would herself be first to apply; no marriage applications had been made; local-law experts said recognition required voluntary adoption or litigation, warning the review had a chilling effect.

The legislature's upper chamber voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after a committee recommended the bill be killed; the bill sought to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in the parent nation. During committee consideration local third-gender witnesses opposed the bill on cultural and religious grounds

In January 2016 the legislature's upper chamber unanimously confirmed the former top government lawyer as a district-court judge, filling a retiring seat. texts.cleaned_text: Bernews (Feb 2018): Bermuda's Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples - the reversal that made Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.

Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, July 12) as 'incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre', an instance of organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples.

LGBTQ Nation/AP (July 2013): Bermuda's Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination); same-sex marriage not then permitted.

Royal Gazette (14 May 1994): the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two Criminal Code sections. The debate split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.

The article states there is no legal recognition of transgender people in Bermuda. The article states that, by omission, there is thus no protection from discrimination for transgender people. The article states that the ability of persons to express their gender identity is often difficult. As its example, the article states that in 2006 the Government attempted to ban Mark Anderson, also known as the drag queen "Queen of Bermuda" Sybil, from participating in a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities. The article provides no transgender-specific provisions on documents, screening, facilities, custody, care, enforcement, penalties, or protection machinery beyond that omission and example. Homosexuality is legal in Bermuda; lesbian activity has never been illegal, while consensual private sexual conduct was legalised by the Stubbs Bill in 1994 after prior liability of up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex. As of 2022 the age of consent remains unequal at 18 years for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019 versus 16 for other sexual activity, after a prior higher age of 18 for gay male conduct found in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights, and the Criminal Code provision on gross indecency between men was repealed in 2019. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2013, following failed and dropped proposals in 2004-2006 and 2009. Same-sex marriage is not legally available since 2022, having been legalised by the Supreme Court in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche marriage-license case under the Marriage Act 1944 and Human Rights Act, replaced by domestic partnerships by law given royal assent 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, restored by the Supreme Court on 6 June 2018 and Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, then banned again by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on 14 March 2022 with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. Same-sex couples are allowed to adopt equally under the Adoption of Children Act following the February 2015 Supreme Court ruling on marital-status and sexual-orientation discrimination, and binational same-sex partners were granted equal employment and benefits by the Supreme Court in November 2015. The Bermuda Regiment, formed by random lottery-style conscription, does not discriminate on grounds of sexual orientation and officially prohibits discrimination or harassment of LGBT soldiers, though such activities have been reported as tolerated by officers to the extent one conscript described the Regiment as "the most homophobic environment that exists". Gay and bisexual men may donate blood with the Bermuda Hospitals Board if they have not had sex with another man in the past 12 months, with a 12-month deferral likewise for women who have sexual relations with men who have sex with men. In November 2020 reporting, the government spent approximately £150,000 to legally appeal an unconstitutional case of a man charged and threatened with jail under the archaic "obscene behaviour law" for importing DVDs of gay porn into Bermuda.
1994: assembly voted 22-16 to decriminalise sex between adult males, removing two criminal-code sections.
2018: governor's assent to the Domestic Partnership Act replaced same-sex marriage with partnerships — the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.
2007: premier defended allowing an entertainer's gay-family cruise to dock against church objections; documents tourism-related LGBT friction.

PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.
International rights news (Apr 2023): parliament repealed the historic-era offences; effective 1 June 2023; up-to-10-year terms had gone unenforced.
International rights news (Oct 2020): the bill stalled again; penalties stood at seven years; comment notes pre-historic acceptance.
International rights news (Aug 2017): draft crimes code (partner-drafted) to remove sections with 7- and 5-year penalties; local association called them draconian relics.
Partner public radio (Aug 2017): parliament opened submissions on the replacement crimes bill; the LGBTI association filed in support.

texts.cleaned_text: GlobalGayz (updated Jan 2017): profiles the ABC islands (Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao) as 'quiet nests of gay-friendliness' inside the Kingdom of the Netherlands; Curaçao-specific findings: it opened an LGBT 'Pink House' centre in 2010, has full autonomy except defense/foreign affairs/Supreme Court alongside Aruba, and (with Sint Maarten and Aruba) acts as driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships 8 Sept 2016 —

Caribisch Netwerk (22 Apr 2015, Dutch): representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should quickly receive equal rights; Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels (Pueblo Soberano) publicly backed 'equal rights for everyone' despite party colleague Winifred Raveneau's fierce opposition — Raveneau had forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel via a last-minute exceptionally strict permit. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites Curaçao's IGLTA award as 'most gay welcoming in the region'; a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is legal in Curaçao with an equal age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. Same-sex marriage has been legal since the 12 July 2024 ruling of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upholding the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Prior to that ruling, Curaçao was required as part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to recognize as valid same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, with no in-island marriage, civil union or other recognition available. The Criminal Code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including "heterosexual or homosexual orientation," with Article 1:221 defining discrimination as any distinction affecting recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights in political, economic, social, cultural or other social life fields. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year imprisonment. Relevant history includes the April 2015 agreement of all four constituent countries for equal rights throughout the Kingdom, the August 2015 Oliari and Others v. Italy ECHR ruling applicable to Curaçao requiring legal recognition, a 2017 limited-rights proposal to the Estates, and a marriage bill submitted 4 June 2019 and withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support.
Travel-culture report: the group (with two neighbours) described as tolerant and mostly open within the nation.

PinkNews global legality roundup (Jul 2017): lists the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, and states that it has been illegal there for decades. The partially-recognised state, an African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara. The status recorded for July 2017 is criminalised.

A 2009 USCRI report found that Sahrawi government officials running refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges even while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence. Multiple sources (Council for Global Equality, Equaldex, ILGA) describe same-sex sexual activity as illegal in the SADR for both males and females, punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it', and CEAR concludes this leaves no legal protection for LGBTQ people against discrimination or violence. Same-sex activity is also illegal in Morocco, which occupies most of the territory the SADR claims. Most residents of the country are Muslim and same-sex relationships are seen as a foreign phenomenon. The region was under Spanish colonial rule until 1976, and homosexuality was not decriminalized in Spain until 1979, shaping the legal and social inheritance of the territory.

PinkNews (9 Nov 2006): LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to sexual-orientation discrimination and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; at the time the Faroes (population ~47,000, self-governing within Denmark) had neither protection, leaving homophobia legally unaddressed.

PinkNews (7 Sep 2010): Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic PM Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion — signals the prominence of religiously motivated opposition to openly gay public figures in Faroese politics.

Gay Iceland (Jul 2015): when Faroese MP Jenis av Rana demanded Pride be banned (held two days before the national holiday), singer Eivor Palsdottir publicly urged people to ignore him; his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality — documents anti-Pride pressure and organised public pushback.

Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was legalized across the Kingdom of Denmark; the age of consent was then set at 18 for male same-sex relations, and the Faroe Islands did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988. The only criminal penalties touching LGBTQ people in the text are under the anti-discrimination law: anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. That provision took effect on 1 January 2007, making the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to ban discrimination and harassment based on sexual orientation. Wikipedia country coverage: Expression has been a recurring flashpoint: the first gay pride march in 2005 provoked much controversy, and in June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter to the editor, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre. Public petitioning also figures: a petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures, while an internet petition after the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen collected 20,000 signatures and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2006 openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out, and he and his family then received threatening telephone calls; police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, became mentally ill and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn — nowhere else had the group been attacked. The 2007 law criminalises public threats, insults or degrading statements against LGBT people with a fine or up to two years' imprisonment.
Rights news (Nov 2006): ~20,000-signature petition demanded anti-discrimination protection; violence against out gay people recorded as 'not uncommon' with no legal recourse.
Rights news (Sept 2010): a centrist MP refused a state/province banquet for a neighbouring country's gay female head of government, calling the visit a provocation.
Regional LGBT news (July 2015): the same politician demanded a Pride ban; a nationally famous singer urged the public to ignore him.
States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 records the review of Adoption Law at p.1170, which led to adoption rights for same-sex couples.

BBC (10 Dec 2015): States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting both civil-partnership-only and single 'Union Civile' alternatives; implementing legislation separate and not expected before 2017. Charity Liberate: 'historic day'; debate described as 'extremely positive'.

BBC (24 Jun 2015): Guernsey repealed its 50-year Adoption Law's ban on unmarried couples adopting — States agreed same-sex couples may adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners (Jersey had approved the same change two days earlier).

BBC (23 Sep 2011): Guernsey adopted the UK's relaxed blood-donor rules — gay/bisexual men eligible after 12-month deferral, targeted ~7 Nov 2011 to match the UK change, ending the local 1980s HIV-era ban; other donation restrictions unchanged.

Guernsey's only prison, Les Nicolles, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages; it has 11 wings, capacity 139, is operated by the States of Guernsey, and held about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal in Guernsey for both men and women. It was criminalised until decriminalisation prior to 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the UK; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences in its criminal law, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for private-life conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Transgender people have been able to legally change their gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law only allows a new birth certificate to be issued and does not amend or remove records from existing birth certificates, so prior gender markers remain on the original record. Guernsey is also the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil partnership legislation, though UK civil partnerships were recognised for succession purposes from 2 April 2012.

A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 banned discrimination based on gender identity. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had specifically outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States of Guernsey passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously (33-0) explicitly including sexual orientation, rejecting all amendments proposing exemptions for small businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations; it takes effect from 1 October 2023.
2015: official legislative-business record including the adoption-law review that led to same-sex couples' adoption rights.
Dec 2015: states approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting partnership and single 'civil union' alternatives; a campaigner called it a historic day; legislation expected no earlier than 2017.
June 2015: adoption-law change lets same-sex couples adopt; the 50-year-old law had barred all unmarried couples; civil-partnership recognition and equal parental responsibility included.
Sept 2011: following the metropole's relaxation, gay and bisexual men may donate after a 12-month deferral, ending the 1980s-era ban.

The UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's Seventh Report (2007-08) on Overseas Territories sets accountability and good-governance expectations that apply to Gibraltar as an overseas territory; it also records corruption concerns raised in Turks and Caicos.

El País in English (15 Aug 2016): Gibraltar put a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act for same-sex marriage before Parliament after a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarized; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, with popular consultation and main parties suggesting support for the change.

Gibraltar Chronicle (22 Jul 2021): the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Gibraltar - legal since 1993, equal age of consent since 2012, adoption right by Supreme Court ruling 2013, civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since Dec 2016 (passed unanimously), discrimination protections for sexual orientation and 'gender reassignment' since 2007; transgender persons not allowed to change legal gender.

Wikipedia country coverage: Gibraltar's Parliament passed a bill on 19 September 2013, given royal assent on 25 September and in force on 10 October, amending the Crimes Act 2011 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime. In July 2021 the Justice Ministry began investigating a further proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, prompted by what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for 'transgender identity'. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption, after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption for lack of legal recognition of their relationship challenged the law; the government amended the law through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt children without discrimination. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy. The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender was equalised at 16. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set an equal age of consent of 16 that took effect on 23 November 2012. Before that, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009. The Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 enquiry into overseas territories recommended making discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status illegal in all overseas territories.

The Equal Opportunities Act 2006, in force on 1 March 2007, prohibits discrimination in employment and the provision of goods and services on the ground of "gender reassignment". The Act defines "gender reassignment" as "a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex". The 2008 Foreign Affairs Committee enquiry into the overseas territories concluded that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status should be made illegal in all overseas territories. In July 2026, Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for "transgender identity". In July 2026, Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy, stated generally without specifying sexual orientation versus transgender scope in the excerpt. Male same-sex sexual activity defined legally as male sodomy was decriminalized in Gibraltar in 1993 following pressure from the European Court of Human Rights and Government of the United Kingdom, with no equivalent provision for women because Victorian-drafted law only addressed men. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that an age of consent of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, mandating 16 and decriminalising heterosexual anal sex at 16, implemented in statute by the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011 approved in August 2011 and effective 23 November 2012 setting 16 regardless of sexual orientation. Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014 granting most rights of marriage including adoption as mandated by the 2013 ruling, and same-sex marriage was legalised by the Civil Marriage Amendment Act 2016 passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, receiving royal assent on 1 November and taking effect on 15 December 2016 with the first marriage the next day, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar where a deputy registrar opts out. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Constitution, in effect de jure legalising LGBT adoption, followed by civil partnership law amendments and effective 18 April 2024 the Adoption Act 2023 explicitly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority amended IVF policy to allow lesbian couples access to assisted reproductive technology, and in February 2021 surrogacy law allowed non-commercial altruistic surrogacy for individuals and married or civil-partnered couples unable to conceive with automatic recognition for children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. The 2006 Constitution does not mention sexual orientation after 2002 proposals omitted it, but the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 effective 1 March 2007 prohibits discrimination in employment and goods and services on grounds including sexual orientation defined as orientation towards persons of the same sex, opposite sex, or both. Amendments to the Crimes Act 2011 approved 19 September 2013, assented 25 September and effective 10 October 2013 criminalised hatred and harassment on the ground of sexual orientation, while in July 2021 the Justice Ministry was investigating proposals against lurking homophobia including a possible specific offence of denigrating a person as a result of sexual orientation.

French law applicable in Guadeloupe decriminalised same-sex relations in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained this in the 1810 Code, while public morality laws continued to be used against LGBTQ people; in Alsace and Lorraine, annexed in 1940, men were interned in Nazi camps and persecuted under Vichy despite the absence of a sodomy law. Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942 (later 331) set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. The Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity (art. 330, 2nd alinea), repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or €30,000. The law of December 2004, passed 31 December 2004, made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders called it a serious infringement of free speech. It created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, an MP from the ruling UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Pride has been held in Paris since 4 April 1981 (Place Maubert, about 10,000 people), reaching 500,000 participants in 2019, with events in dozens of other cities. Transgender people have changed legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis since 1 January 2017 (law signed 18 November 2016), but must still appear before a court to change the gender marker; a first name change can be done at the registry office. Self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were both dropped from the final bill. Until 2015 France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens, leaving many in legal limbo; the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change, while a 2017 legal bid for 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation. In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness, removing gender identity disorder by decree, though French trans rights organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent, self-determination model. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned the Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender care, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'; a bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access, though this did not change actual practice. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks, and a report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away. In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline for students and staff, and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms; in February 2019 the use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage. Legislation to ban medical transition for under-18s passed the Senate in May 2024, prompting large-scale protests, making trans minors a direct legislative target.

France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, becoming the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as mental illness, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale. Since 1 January 2017 under the law signed 18 November 2016 after the Constitutional Council ruling of 17 November, transgender people may change legal gender marker by court order without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatrist certificate or medical diagnosis, with first-name change available at the registry office. This followed a decades-long legislative ban on legal gender change despite the 1959 change for Coccinelle and 1979 legalisation of gender-affirming surgery inside France, overturned only after the 1992 B. v France case at the European Court of Human Rights. Discrimination on the ground of "sexual identity" was prohibited from July 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" on 18 November 2016 amending Penal Code article 225-1 and Labour Code protections covering recruitment, internships, training, sanction and dismissal. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Gender-affirming healthcare was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to lack self-determination with extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access recommending informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine advises extreme caution and actual practice is unchanged. For youth, the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the first national guidelines in late 2024 recommending puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements, while a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under age 18 following the March 2024 Little Mermaid Observatory report has had no update since 23 July 2024 and is opposed by the Macron government. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the Penal Code of 1810 applied to nations and French colonies, ending ancien régime capital punishments including castration, dismemberment and burning with the last burning on 6 July 1750. A discriminatory age of consent of 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual relations introduced 6 August 1942 as article 334, moved to article 331 in 1945 and lowered to 18 in 1974, was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under President Mitterrand, while the discriminatory 1960 Mirguet amendment to Penal Code article 330 alinea 2 doubling penalty for homosexual indecent exposure was repealed in 1980 with a March 2024 National Assembly unanimous compensation bill for pre-1980 Article 330 victims pending Senate vote. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1985 in employment, housing and public and private provision of goods and services, codified in the Labour Code. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments with a maximum penalty of 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment and amended the Law on Freedom of the Press of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation or disability, while physical assault or murder motivated by victim sexual orientation carries increased penalties, and created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité. Same-sex marriage following civil solidarity pacts in 1999 was legalised in 2013 with the law signed 18 May 2013 after the 17 May Constitutional Council ruling and first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, and is legal in all overseas departments and territories, with French Guiana's two deputies recording one vote in favour and one abstention. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people may serve openly in the Armed Forces, men who have sex with men blood-donation abstinence requirements of one year from 10 July 2016 and four months from 2 April 2020 were fully removed 16 March 2022 to an orientation-neutral policy, and the conversion therapy ban passed the Senate 7 December 2020, the National Assembly 25 January 2022 and was published 1 February 2022.

In August 2015 the Guam Legislature unanimously passed Bill 102-33 which bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity or expression in employment. Discrimination against government employees based on sexuality or identity is also forbidden. Federal law has covered hate crimes based on gender identity since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Hate Crimes Prevention Act. To change legal gender on a birth certificate transgender people must provide the Office of Vital Statistics a sworn statement from a physician that they have undergone sex reassignment surgery after which the Office amends the certificate. The Motor Vehicle Division Supervisor issues an amended drivers license upon receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicants sex has been surgically changed. In May 2018 Senator Fernando Esteves introduced a bill to permit legal gender change with judicial permission and a letter confirming gender identity supported by documentation from a certified psychologist social worker therapist or other licensed professional with no surgery required. On December 13 2018 the Legislature postponed a vote on the bill until medical and law enforcement process issues were addressed and the bill failed on December 17 2018 by a 6 to 7 vote. Private adult consensual and noncommercial homosexual acts have been legal in Guam since reform of the Criminal Code in 1978. The 1933 penal code ordained by the Naval Governor and identical to Californias prohibited sodomy fellatio and cunnilingus whether heterosexual or homosexual with between one and ten years imprisonment. The only reported sodomy case in Guam occurred in the early 1950s in Pennington v Government which resulted in victory for the defendant solely on procedural grounds when the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held the trial court had been without authority to try Pennington without a jury. Bill 102-33 passed unanimously in August 2015 bans employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and discrimination against government employees based on sexuality is also forbidden. Federal law has covered hate crimes based on sexual orientation since 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The article states "The Chamorro people have traditionally accepted homosexuality and transgender people." It further describes Chamorro society as very sexually tolerant but specifies for sexuality that homosexuality was never viewed as taboo but "was taken for granted as part of life". For contemporary conditions the article states Guam is regarded as tolerant and accepting of LGBTQ people with very few reports of societal discrimination or harassment which is a general LGBTQ finding not a transgender specific finding. It reports a visible LGBTQ social scene since the 1990s with a handful of nightclubs and social functions and annual Guam Pride held since 2017 attracting a few hundred people. It notes Guam is a member of the International Gay and Lesbian Travel Association and has begun commercializing itself as a tourist destination for LGBTQ people and these contemporary observations are framed as LGBTQ general findings rather than transgender specific findings.

texts.cleaned_text: Isle of Man Prison (Jurby), the island's only functioning prison (GBP 41.7m facility at the former RAF Jurby, fully operational 14 August 2008), operated by the Isle of Man Prison Service. Separate units exist for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders and vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit.

The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender persons to change their legal gender and to have their new gender recognised. The Equality Act 2017, granted royal assent on 18 July 2017 with much of the law in force from 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and ground of non-discrimination. A ban covering sexual orientation and gender identity conversion therapy was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the extensive sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and came into effect in 2024. In 2024 the Isle of Man became the first British territory and the first part of the British Isles to ban conversion therapy. In July 2022 community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. Private and consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with age of consent set at 21, lowered to eighteen by the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3). Until 2021 Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men if under sixteen or committed elsewhere than in private, defined in Section 10 as more than two persons present or in a public-access place, and in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral. The Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021 passed with royal assent in July 2021 and took effect 1 July 2022 by proclamation, pardoning historical gay sex offences committed prior to 1992 explicitly based on the UK Alan Turing law of 2017. Chief Minister Howard Quayle issued an unqualified apology to gay men convicted under previous laws, and in August 2022 on the 30th anniversary of decriminalisation the police commissioner formally apologised for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992. Same-sex couples were granted civil partnerships by the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2) effective 6 April 2011, and same-sex marriage effective 22 July 2016 after royal assent 19 July 2016. By the Civil Partnership Act 2011 same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011, lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates from IVF and surrogacy and no laws acknowledge surrogacy. Under the Employment Act 2006 (c.21) effective 1 September 2006 dismissal on grounds of sexual orientation was made unlawful, and the Equality Act 2017 lists sexual orientation, defined to include attraction to same, opposite, either sex and lack of attraction to either sex, as a protected characteristic.

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montserrat' (Sept 2012): a 104 km2 island reshaped by Hurricane Hugo (1989) and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption, which wastelanded the south and displaced over half the population north. Gay life barely exists locally: 'gays are everywhere but hardly here,' and the social scene is decimated.

Associated Press report (Jan 2001, via GLAPN): Britain scrapped the anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, saying they violated signed international human rights agreements — the legal basis on which Montserrat's prohibitions were eventually swept away; local politicians and religious leaders opposed, framed as a cultural rift with London.

Wikipedia: Montserrat's gay scene is very limited, with no gay bars, nightclubs or other venues on the island, though several hotels welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies. Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code ban discrimination based on sexual orientation, defining 'discriminatory' as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. As a British Overseas Territory, Montserrat must also comply with international human rights instruments, including adherence to the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, stating that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family. The age of consent is higher for homosexual activity (18) than for heterosexual activity (16). Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been legal since 2001, decriminalised retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000. Lesbian activity was never illegal, while group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences.
2012 report: gay life decimated by the 1989 hurricane and 1995 volcanic disasters that made the south a wasteland; recovery partial.

texts.cleaned_text: JM Concept 972 is a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network that provides information, meetings and services to the island's LGBT community and runs private parties and garden parties, with 2025 events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September, supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters.

French law governs Martinique, and the following national provisions apply in the department. Homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comments were made illegal by a National Assembly amendment approved 31 December 2004, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; the same law amended the 1881 Law on the Freedom of the Press to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. Christian Vanneste, an MP in Chirac's UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though the conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Since 1 January 2017 transgender people can change their legal gender without surgery or a medical diagnosis, but must still go before a court to change the gender marker, while a first name change can be done at the registry office. The bill was signed 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly, with the Constitutional Council ruling it constitutional on 17 November 2016 and dropping the original self-certification provision; before that, legal gender change had been banned for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France. A report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims, up from about 1,380 in 2018. Penalties increase where physical assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison. Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published 1 February 2022. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the MSM blood donation deferral was removed on 16 March 2022. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems with gender-affirming healthcare, including extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, with treatment covered by Sécurité Sociale under ALD 31. In March 2024 centre-right Republican senators commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory to report on youth gender care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government with no update since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access. Earlier state hostility includes the 1960 Mirguet amendment treating homosexuality as a 'national scourge' alongside alcoholism and the Vichy age-of-consent law of 6 August 1942 setting 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign against anti-LGBTQ bullying, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day, and in March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms. LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.

BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018): trans women in France are incarcerated per their identity-document gender (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code), typically in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them, placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework binds this department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL (25 May 2021): 'persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty — based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse). Extends to local jails as French establishments.

LINFO.re (French-language report): the French National Assembly voted the simplification of legal gender change (civil-status change for trans people). French law applies to the department, bringing the simplified procedure here.

Erasing 76 Crimes (23 May 2023, Moïse Manoël-Florisse): Bruno Agar, a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte, and his Malagasy partner (pseudonym Abdallah) married at Sada Town Hall after a 'long and complicated' path — showing the gap between formal French rights and lived reality on this predominantly Muslim island. Same-sex marriage is legal here — a rarity in Africa and the Islamic world — since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975.

Avocat Gay-Friendly directory (French): no LGBT-friendly lawyer is yet referenced in Mayotte — the town list (Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada and others) returns 'we do not yet have a lawyer referenced in your region' — while Paris-based Maître Isabelle Zribi (lawyer at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law) is listed as available. Evidence of thin local legal-access infrastructure for anyone needing counsel on the island.

French law bans discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' since July 2012, with article 225-1 of the Penal Code amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement, while transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery performed in-country was legalised in 1979 after previously only accessible abroad. Legal gender change without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or proof of medical interventions was approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly on 24 May 2016, modified on 12 July 2016 to drop self-certification, re-approved on 12 October after rejecting Senate amendments requiring medical treatment, ruled constitutional on 17 November, signed 18 November 2016 and effective 1 January 2017, but still requires going before a court for the gender marker while first-name change can be done at the registry office. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and hate-crime provisions cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination, with a 16 May 2020 report recording a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019 with around 1,870 victims identified by police compared to around 1,380 in 2018. Healthcare provision was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to suffer lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location, with a recommendation for informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine has characterized increased demand as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'primarily social problem' advising extreme caution without changing actual practice. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report critical of youth gender-affirming care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the Macron government with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first national youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by Senate vote 7 December 2020, National Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 and publication 1 February 2022 with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or 30,000 euros fine, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names on student cards and exam forms. Same-sex sexual activity in private was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 with no mention of same-sex relations, retained in the Penal Code of 1810 and followed in nations and French colonies adopting the Code, while a discriminatory age of consent under Vichy article 334 moved to article 331 on 8 February 1945 set 21 years for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974, and repealed 4 August 1982 under President François Mitterrand to equalise at 15. A 1960 Mirguet amendment inserting article 330 alinea 2 doubled the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity to repress pimping and other national scourges, was repealed in 1980 as part of an act redefining sexual offenses, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980 with Senate vote still pending. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been banned since 1985 in employment, housing and public and private provision of services and goods, and the law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal with maximum penalty of 45,000 euros fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité, and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 for injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples with most marriage protections, and same-sex marriage was approved by the National Assembly 12 February 2013 by 329-229, by the Senate 12 April with amendments accepted 23 April, ruled constitutional 17 May 2013, signed 18 May 2013 and published next day, with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier and joint adoption legal since May 2013. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people are allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by Senate 7 December 2020, Assembly 25 January 2022 and publication 1 February 2022, and the 20 June 1983 ban on men who have sex with men donating blood recalled 12 January 2009 was replaced by one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016, four-month abstinence from 2 April 2020, and removal of deferral 16 March 2022 for all regardless of orientation. Same-sex marriage is legal in all overseas departments and territories under French law, with 11 of 27 overseas deputies voting for and 11 against, 1 abstaining and 3 absent.

Same-sex marriage has been available in this collectivity since France's 2013 marriage-equality law, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on France's first same-sex wedding under that law.

French law extends marriage equality to this collectivity. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.

Yagg (July 2012, French): 'identité sexuelle' (sexual identity) became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code via the sexual-harassment law — enabling prosecution of discrimination and transphobia as discrimination. French law applies to the collectivity, and the same provision was updated to read 'gender identity' in 2016.

Transgender people can change legal gender without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical diagnosis under the law signed 18 November 2016 after a 17 November Constitutional Council ruling, effective 1 January 2017, but must still go before a court, while first-name change can be done at a registry office. France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 as the first country to declassify gender dysphoria, though transgender organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale and in-country gender-affirming surgery legalised since 1979. Discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" has been banned since July 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" in Penal Code article 225-1 on 18 November 2016, and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on that ground. For care, a 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location and recommended informed consent and self-determination, the National Academy of Medicine characterised increased demand as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and "primarily social problem" advising extreme caution without changing practice, and late-2024 pediatric guidelines recommend puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. A Senate bill passed in May 2024 to ban medical transition under age 18 after a March 2024 Little Mermaid Observatory report calling care a health scandal, but it has had no update since 23 July 2024, is opposed by the Macron government and unlikely to pass the Assembly amid large protests, while in 2022 the DILCRAH scientific committee president was revealed as a member of the Observatory which called care "mutilation," leading to one committee resignation. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 and that approach was retained in the Penal Code of 1810 applied in adopting French colonies, ending ancien régime capital punishment involving castration, dismemberment and burning with the last burning on 6 July 1750. A discriminatory age of consent under Vichy article 334, moved to article 331 in 1945, set 21 years for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974, then equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under President Mitterrand. A 1960 Mirguet amendment inserting Penal Code article 330 alinea 2 doubled the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity and was repealed in 1980, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed compensation for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980 with Senate vote still pending. National legislation since 1985 prohibits sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments with a maximum €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité, amended the 29 July 1881 Press Law on injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on sexual orientation, and increases penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage has been legal in all overseas departments and territories including New Caledonia under the law signed 18 May 2013 after a 17 May 2013 constitutional ruling, following registered PACS partnerships since 1999. Police recorded around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018, after President Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as unworthy of France.

Same-sex activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001. The 2010 Constitution bans discrimination on sexual orientation, with protections in place since 2010. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015 and adoption since 2015. None of the roughly 50 residents is known to be in a same-sex relationship. Military service falls under UK responsibility.

The 2010 Pitcairn Constitution Order bans discrimination on sexual orientation. Marriage is defined as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 also recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn. Adoption is open to married, unmarried and single people.

Full Wikipedia republication: same-sex sexual activity legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001; anti-discrimination constitutional protection from the 2010 Constitution Order; same-sex marriage legal 14 May 2015 — ordinance unanimously approved by the Island Council 1 Apr 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair 5 May, published 13 May 2015; adoption legal since 2015; page also indexes the territory within UK LGBT-rights timelines.
Encyclopaedic summary: legal since 2001; 2010 constitution bans SO discrimination; same-sex marriage since May 2015 (no known same-sex couples among ~50 residents); adoption 2015.
Encyclopaedia mirror: marriage defined without reference to sex/orientation/gender identity; the 2015 ordinance recognises foreign civil partnerships; adoption open widely.
Wiki mirror: legal 2001, protections 2010, marriage + adoption 2015; defence is the administering state's responsibility.

BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018): in France, detention follows the gender marked on an ID, and Article D248 requires separate men's and women's establishments, so trans women holding male markers are held with men. The article treats this as a legal grey area. France's framework governs French Polynesia as an overseas collectivity subject to French law.

CGLPL opinion (25 May 2021) on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: since France's Law 2016-1547 civil-status gender change no longer requires medical transition/surgery, yet no norms were added on how to house detainees accordingly - serious violations persist across French detention. French-framework treatment applicable in French Polynesia's prisons.

Grokipedia entry on trans rights in Tahiti: gender-diverse care is limited by local expertise, and some trans people (raerae) face family rejection and move to mainland France for specialised services. The mahu is a traditional Polynesian social role in which mahu embody both male and female qualities and hold cultural standing.

OutTraveler (4 Jul 2025): 'French Polynesia doesn't need Pride flags' describes openness as ingrained in the culture, with mahu and rae-rae visible in daily life across the 118 islands. A visiting gay couple reports first checking whether the destination is safe, and describes mainstream LGBTQ+ inclusivity and acceptance without Pride displays.

RNZ Pacific: French Polynesia LGBTQIA reflection - churches round table with University of French Polynesia; Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua's government tabled a social-security Bill to fully reimburse hormonal treatment (progesterone/testosterone) like mainland France, but after heated Territorial Assembly debate the Bill failed to gain sufficient support. Concrete care-access reform failed.

Out Adventures presents Tahiti and Bora Bora across the 118 islands as a relaxed, gay-welcoming South Pacific culture. The assessment is travel-oriented and reports no trans-specific finding for French Polynesia.

French national law, drawn from Wikipedia country coverage, with no stated bearing on French Polynesia: sodomy provisions were repealed by the Penal Code of 1791 and the Penal Code of 1810 retained that silence; an indecent-exposure clause (article 330, 2nd alinea) inserted in 1960 by the Mirguet amendment doubled penalties where the act was homosexual and was repealed in 1980, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under it, with the Senate yet to vote. A Vichy law of 6 August 1942 set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 in 1982; LGBTQ people in Alsace and Lorraine were interned in Nazi camps after 1940. The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, punishable by up to €45,000 and/or 12 months' imprisonment, criticised by Reporters Without Borders and defended by the Chirac government; Christian Vanneste was convicted under it in January 2006 and that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Sexual orientation became a protected ground in employment and services in 1985, 'sexual identity' was added in July 2012, and on 18 November 2016 'gender identity' replaced it in article 225-1 of the Penal Code, with the Labour Code covering sexual orientation and gender identity in recruitment and training. Assaults motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract heavier penalties, and in 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. The conversion-therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022; Le Refuge estimated 3-4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy. The Académie Nationale de Médecine described the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem'; a March 2024 report commissioned from The Little Mermaid Observatory called gender-affirming care a 'health scandal' and youth transness a 'social contagion', and a bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 without National Assembly action since 23 July 2024. Late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommend puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) date from 1999; same-sex marriage passed the National Assembly 329-229 on 12 February 2013 and was signed on 18 May 2013, with joint adoption rare thereafter and assisted reproduction extended to lesbian couples from September 2021. Schools observe 17 May under the 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign, enrolment forms use 'parent 1' and 'parent 2', and since March 2019 higher education institutions should use trans students' preferred names. Mayotte reports frequent family rejection and discrimination, and in 2014 only about 20% of overseas residents viewed homosexuality as a sexuality like any other, against 77% in metropolitan France.
