As of 25 Apr 2026, same-sex sexual activity is legal in the territory, discrimination protections have been in force since 2009, and same-sex marriage has been legal on Ascension Island since 2017 (Alchetron).

Consensual same-sex relations became lawful in 2001. The age of consent is equalised at 16 territory-wide. The territory is an Overseas Country or Territory of the EU, with EU Charter applicability (GayLawNet, accessed 23 Jun 2013, citing ILGA State-sponsored Homophobia).

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha - discrimination banned territory-wide since 2009; same-sex marriage legal since 2017 (Ascension 1 Jan, Tristan da Cunha 4 Aug, Saint Helena 20 Dec); adoption since 2017; detailed vote records of the Ascension Island Council (5-0).
Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights on Ascension Island. The marriage ordinance was approved 31 May 2016 (5-0), signed and gazetted 20 June, and commenced 1 January 2017.

No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care, or violence provisions are documented. The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of the importance of equality, and works towards elimination of unlawful discrimination. The Commission may conduct inquiries and investigations on persons suspected of having committed an unlawful act, including unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or "gender reassignment". Under the Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015, "gender reassignment" means "an intended, current or past process (or part of such a process) for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent or not culturally associated with their assigned sex at birth". No extension of the Constitution Order 2009 sexual-orientation discrimination ban to gender reassignment, and no transgender-specific marriage, adoption, or penalty provisions, are documented. Homosexuality is legal in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, defining "discriminatory" as "affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status." The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes "understanding of the importance of equality" and works towards elimination of unlawful discrimination, with power to conduct inquiries and investigations into suspected unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Under the Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015, sexual orientation means "a person's sexual orientation towards— (a) persons of the same sex; (b) persons of the opposite sex; or (c) persons of either sex". Same-sex marriage has been legal on Ascension Island since 1 January 2017 under the Marriage (Ascension) Ordinance, 2016, on Tristan da Cunha since 4 August 2017 under the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance, 2017, and on Saint Helena since 20 December 2017 under the Marriage Ordinance 2017, with the first same-sex marriage in Saint Helena occurring on 31 December 2018. Under the Saint Helena Welfare of Children Ordinance 2010 for Saint Helena and Tristan da Cunha and the Ascension Island Child Welfare Ordinance 2011 for Ascension Island, single and married people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, while a 2006 UK Government report recorded no adoptions in Saint Helena or Ascension Island for many years.

Tristan da Cunha legalized same-sex marriage through the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance 2017 effective 4 August 2017, defining marriage as the union of two persons regardless of sex and extending eligibility, formalities, rights and recognition to same-sex couples on equal terms with opposite-sex couples.

texts.cleaned_text: Vatican City operates no prison system: the article states there are only a few cells used for pre-trial detention, and persons sentenced to imprisonment by Vatican City serve their time in Italian prisons, with costs covered by Vatican City. Because no domestic prison system exists, there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case for this jurisdiction.

In 2021, Vatican foreign minister Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher delivered a letter to the Italian ambassador to the Holy See expressing concerns over an Italian parliamentary bill meant to legally protect LGBTQ Italians against violence and discrimination. The objection specifically targeted the section prohibiting incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. The letter claimed that prohibition constituted a violation of freedom of speech and of religion. It asked for the draft law's text to be reformulated. Since 1890 the territory of what is now Vatican City has had no criminal laws against non-commercial, private, adult and consensual same-sex sexual activity under a legal code based on the Italian Zanardelli Code of 1889 in force since the founding of the sovereign state in 1929. The age of consent is set at 18 years for all persons regardless of gender, except for sexual relations within marriage recognized as valid by the Catholic Church and Vatican City laws where the legal age is 14. Foreign diplomats must not be part of a same-sex family and must not be divorced to be accredited, with openly gay French nominee Jean-Loup Kuhn-Delforge in a civil pact rejected in 2008 and openly gay practising Catholic single nominee Laurent Stefanini rejected in 2015, leading France to leave the post vacant from March 2015 to May 2016 before nominating another diplomat in May 2016. Vatican City has always expressed disagreement with any civil recognition of same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and granting of adoption rights to same-sex couples, and while Pope Francis in 2023 expressed support for same-sex civil unions outside the Catholic Church he remained firm that the Sacrament of Marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God. The Vatican reserves the right to remove, suspend and dismiss immediately any official and employee who publicly admits to being gay or questions the general policy of the Vatican towards homosexuals. In 2021 Vatican foreign minister Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher delivered a letter to the Italian ambassador expressing concerns over an Italian bill meant to legally protect LGBTQ Italians against violence and discrimination, claiming the prohibition of incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation violated freedom of speech and religion and asking for reformulation. On 13 January 1998 LGBTQ activist Alfredo Ormando set himself on fire on St. Peter's Square under Vatican jurisdiction in protest against deep-rooted refusal expressed by the Catholic religion towards homosexuality and died days later in hospital from severe burns.

Discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' has been banned since 2012, with the term replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016 amending article 225-1 of the Penal Code, and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships, sanctions, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. Effective 1 January 2017 after a Constitutional Council ruling on 17 November 2016, signature on 18 November 2016 and publication the next day, transgender people can legally change gender without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical proof, but must go before a court, while first-name change can be done by registry office after the self-certification provision was dropped. Gender identity disorder was removed as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names including on student cards and exam forms. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access to gender-affirming healthcare and recommended informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine characterized the rise as an epidemic-like and primarily social phenomenon urging extreme caution without changing practice. After a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report critical of youth gender-affirming care, a bill to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the Macron government and stalled since 23 July 2024, while late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 retained in the Penal Code of 1810 for colonies, while the 1960 Mirguet amendment doubling the penalty for homosexual indecent exposure under article 330 alinea 2 was repealed in 1980 and the discriminatory age of consent of 21 then 18 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual relations was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, still pending Senate vote. Sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services has been banned since 1985 with Labour Code protection, and same-sex marriage signed 18 May 2013 after Constitutional Council approval 17 May 2013 with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier following PACS partnerships from 1999 and joint adoption since May 2013 is stated as legal in all overseas departments and territories. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments punishable by up to 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on sexual orientation, with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation, creating the High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality. Police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019 versus around 1,380 in 2018, after President Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as unworthy of France. Conversion therapy was banned by law published 1 February 2022 after Senate passage 7 December 2020 and Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 carrying two years imprisonment and/or 30,000 euro fine, and the MSM blood-donation ban from 20 June 1983 recalled in 2009 moved from one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016 to four months from 2 April 2020 to removal on 16 March 2022 for all regardless of orientation, with lesbian, gay and bisexual individuals allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces.
